s: Lacking kindness, sympathy, benevolence, gratitude, or similar; cruel, harsh or unjust; ungrateful.
Not kind; contrary to nature or type; unnatural.
Having no race or kindred; childless.
e: Inherited from Middle English unkynde; equivalent to un- + kind.

s: The period of time when a nation or people is at peace, not fighting a war.
Resembling a scoop; shaped like a scoop.
A characteristic of yarn: the proportion of fibre ends that stick out and are not embedded in the yarn body.[http://www.fibre2fashion.com/industry-article/5483/methods-of-testing-yarn-hairiness]
Visually suggestive of a swirl, whorl, or vortex.
That moves in a whirling motion.
A snowy whirlwind in the Antarctic.
An idiot; a fool; an imbecile.
A person who has a chip in their brain which makes them incapable of doing anything without an order.
e: Hiberno-English and Scottish English pronunciation of idiot.

s: To disinfect, purify, or rid of vermin with the fumes of certain chemicals.
To check (a train) for stragglers and remove them before a turnaround.
e: Borrowed from Latin fūmigātus, perfect passive participle of fūmigō (see -ate), from fūmus (“smoke”).

s: The light emitted by a lamp.
e: From Middle English lampe lyght, laumpe-lyth, lombe-lyȝt, equivalent to lamp + light. Compare West Frisian lampeljocht (“lamplight”), Dutch lamplicht (“lamplight”), German Lampenlicht (“lamplight”), Danish lampelys (“lamplight”), Swedish lampljus (“lamplight”), Icelandic lampaljós (“lamplight”).

s: Of, pertaining to or suffering from agoraphobia.
The pastime or sport of skating on rollerblades.
One who devises puzzles for others to solve.
A video game in which the player is presented with (usually abstract) puzzles to solve.
A person who solves puzzles as a hobby.
The act by which somebody is goaded.
The state of being gay (colorful or festive); display or dressiness.
The state of being gay (cheerful); gaiety.
The state of being gay (homosexual); homosexuality; demeanor stereotypically representative of it.
Abandoned by a deity or God.
refusing to believe; skeptical or incredulous
A cover over a lamp to either diffuse the light or to block it in certain directions to avoid glare in the eyes.
To intentionally call attention to the improbable, incongruent, or clichéd nature of an element or situation featured in a work of fiction within the work itself.
To wear an oversize top with skintight thigh-high boots and no leggings.
To adorn with one or more lampshades.
e: From lamp + shade. The verb sense comes from the idea of making something more conspicuous by hanging a lampshade on it.

s: Given to excessive sexual activity and debauchery.
The property of being infallible; the ability to never make a mistake.
Such that it cannot be repaired.
Any convent (religious community) or the buildings thereof.
The residence of a female religious community, a monastery or abbey for nuns.
e: From Middle English nonnery, nonnerie, equivalent to nun + -ery. (brothel) Compare typologically Czech nevěstinec (nevěstka nevěsta).

s: from the nose (usually, blood flow exiting the nostrils that originates from the nasal cavity).
overload (usually attained as a result of having to comprehend new and/or complex concepts or languages that one is not particularly skilled with).
A man who delivers milk to households and sometimes businesses early in the morning.
A black man who prefers dating white women.
Characterized by rugged, sharp, or coarse features.
A saw, with a blade that is put under tension, for cutting metal
Making a show of being morally better than others, especially hypocritically pious.
A hand tool for adjusting nuts and bolts.
Any of certain types of such a tool that have a pin or hook to engage the driven object.
One who, or that which, spans.
A (usually sparse) graph whose shortest path distances approximate those in a dense graph or other metric space.
A hand tool shaped like a small crank handle, for winding the spring of a wheel lock on a musket.
A device in early steam engines for moving the valves for the alternate admission and shutting off of the steam.
A problem, dilemma or obstacle; something unexpected or troublesome (in the phrase spanner in the works)
A stupid or unintelligent person; one prone to making mistakes, especially in language.
To use a spanner; to fix with a spanner

e: From Middle English sternly, sternely, sterneliche, sturnely, sturneliche, from Old English stirnlīċe, styrnlīċe, stiernlīċe (“harshly; severely; sternly”), equivalent to stern + -ly.

s: In a cautious and delicate manner; (very) carefully or cautiously.
Chiefly of dancing or walking: done with small, dainty steps; daintily; also, with excessive delicacy; affectedly, mincingly.
Often of movements: very careful, cautious, or delicate.
Often of a person or the way they move: dainty, delicate; also, excessively delicate; affected, mincing.
e: The second element is -ly; the first element may be Anglo-Norman gençur or Old French gençor, gensor, comparative forms (also attested as positives) of gent (“beautiful, noble, pleasant, courteous”). The Oxford English Dictionary notes, however, that there is a gap of a few centuries between the last appearance of gençor, etc., and the first appearance of gingerly.

s: a substance that is a hallucinogen.
Making arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive and forceful manner.
Characterized by sudden violence or vehemence.
e: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).

s: The sound of metal on metal, or glass on glass.
Stress cracks produced in metal ingots as they cool after being cast.
To make a clinking sound; to make a sound of metal on metal or glass on glass; to strike materials such as metal or glass against one another.
e: From Middle English clinken, from Old English *clincan (compare clynnan, clynian (“to sound; resound”)), from Proto-Germanic *klinganą (“to sound”). Cognates include Middle Dutch klinken and German klingen. Related to Doublet of cling#Etymology 2, clang. May be further related to call. Perhaps of onomatopoeic origin, as metal against metal.
From the Clink prison in Southwark, London, itself presumably named after sound of doors being bolted or chains rattling.

s: The act by which an engine is revved.

A technique for reducing web page loading times by assigning far-future expiration dates to the resources on the page (so that the browser caches them indefinitely) and, if changes are needed, using different filenames for those resources.

A garment, usually consisting of a top and trousers (commonly known as tracksuit bottoms) worn as an outer layer by participants in sporting events such as athletics. The tracksuit is usually designed to be easily removed or replaced, before or after competing. Tracksuits have also been adopted in s
A copy made using a photocopier.
To make a copy using a photocopier.
Having no cord; especially using batteries instead of mains electricity.
The area near a domestic fire or hearth.
A supplementary meeting in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
A person who is habitually drunk.
e: From earlier droncarde, from Middle English *druncard (attested as a surname, Druncard), possibly from Middle Low German drunkert, equivalent to drunk + -ard (“pejorative agent suffix”). Compare German Trunkart. Compare braggart.

s: a hiding place, somewhere one can go to get away from other people
Capable of being stored out of sight when not in use.
A dark brown pigment made from the secretions of the cuttlefish.
A dark, slightly reddish, brown colour.
e: Borrowed from Latin sēpia (“cuttlefish”), from Ancient Greek σηπία. Cognate with Italian seppia, Portuguese siba and Spanish sepia.

s: In marine mammals such as whales (or other secondarily aquatic animals such as sea turtles), a wide, flat limb adapted for swimming.
A wide, flat, paddle-like rubber covering for the foot, used in swimming.
A flat lever in a pinball machine, triggered by the player to strike the ball and keep it in play.
A small flat used to support a larger one.
A type of ball bowled by a leg spin bowler, which spins backwards and skids off the pitch with a low bounce.
A kind of false tooth, usually temporary.
Someone who flips, in the sense of buying a house or other asset and selling it quickly for profit.
Someone who flips in any other sense, for example throwing a coin.
To lift one or both flippers out of the water and slap the surface of the water.
In which the dialogue is translated into another language, and displayed, in text, at the bottom of the screen.
Lacking piety or respect for the sacred; resembling blasphemy.
e: From Latin blasphēmus (“blaspheming”), from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (“uttering ill-omened words”), equivalent to blaspheme + -ous.

s: The motion of something that flops.
A network of sewer pipes that geographically transfers wastewater; a sewer system.
To become not salty, to lose its salinity. (of water)
To begin or resume giving milk, especially after calving; to cause to resume giving milk.
To refresh; to revive; to renew.
To make green (vegetation that has become dry).
To remove or cover unpleasant qualities such as staleness, bad odour or taste (in air, breath, water, etc.).
To touch up (makeup); to give (a body part, especially the face) a quick wash.
To touch up the paint on (something).
To give redness to (the face or cheeks of a person with light skin).
To make less salty; to separate, as water, from saline ingredients.
To relieve, as a rope, by change of place where friction wears it; or to renew, as the material used to prevent chafing.
Showing anger or indignation, especially at something unjust or wrong.
e: Borrowed from Latin indignāns, present participle of indignor (“to consider as unworthy, be angry or displeased at”), from in- (“privative”) + dignor (“to deem worthy”), from dignus (“worthy”).

s: A pad of paper, often bound, in which one jots down notes; a notebook.
The practice in which a nonblack person blackens their face using theatrical makeup in order to portray a caricature of a black person.
A sheep of the Scottish Blackface breed.
An independent, telephonic communication system, set up around and throughout a building, complex, or residence, typically for access control.
The quality of being shy; a fear of social interactions.
Causing more sober thought or concern.
A large stately tomb or a building housing such a tomb or several tombs.
A gloomy, usually large room or building.
e: From Middle English mausoleum, from Latin Mausōlēum, from Ancient Greek Μαυσωλεῖον (“Mausoleum, the grand tomb built around 353–351 BCE at Halicarnassus for Mausolus, a ruler of Caria and satrap of the Achaemenid Empire; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World”), from Μαύσωλος + -εῖον. Mausolus + -eum.

s: A repeated expression, often originating in popular culture.
A signature phrase of a particular person or group.
e: From catch + phrase, from the notion that the phrase will catch in the mind of the user.

s: In a hysterical manner; showing signs of hysteria.
With, or causing, very much laughter.
Having an unvarying pitch or tone.
Tedious, repetitious, or lacking in variety.
One who performs docking, as of tails.
One who engages in the sexual practice of docking (where the tip of one participant's penis is inserted into the foreskin of the other participant).
The action of stealing goods from a shop, store or other place of business.
A theft from a shop during trading hours.
e: shoplift + -ing. The noun sense (from 1690) predates the verb.

s: Towards the back or rear; backwards.
In the rear; a distance behind.
Backward against the mast; said of the sails when pressed by the wind from the "wrong" (forward) side, or of a ship when its sails are set that way.
e: From Middle English abak, from Old English onbæc, equivalent to a- (“towards”) + back. Compare West Frisian tebek (“aback”), Swedish tillbaka (idem.).

s: Pertaining to the universal Church, representing the entire Christian world; interdenominational; sometimes by extension, interreligious.
growing inwards or abnormally towards (a part of the body)
An informal conversation, usually about everyday matters; a chat, a gossip.
A person who removes muck (waste, debris, broken rock, etc.), especially from a mine, construction site, or stable.
A comrade; a friendly, low-ranking soldier in the same situation.
To scrape together (money, etc.) by mean labour or shifts.
That has been stocked to an excessive degree; overfilled.
A member of the genus Prunella of herbaceous plants, the allheals.
Any of various diseases characterised by inflammation of the mouth or throat.
A smooth worsted or silk fabric, generally black, formerly used for making shoes and clergymen's gowns.
e: From post-classical Latin prunella, from brunus + -ella, perhaps because of the plant's brown sepals.
From post-classical Latin prunella, alternation of brunella (“infectious epidemic”), from brunus + -ella.
Probably a variant of prunello, with reference to the colour of the fabric. Compare French prunelle.

s: A nightgown; (usually female) attire designed to be worn to bed.
Affected with scabs; full of scabs.
Injured by the attachment of barnacles to the carapace of a shell.
Working against union policies, working to bust unions; in particular, being a scab (worker who crosses a union picket line).
e: From Middle English scabby, scabbie, equivalent to scab + -y. Doublet of shabby.

s: A round lump of a coagulated fat used in cooking such as butter or margarine.
A small North American duck, the bufflehead, Bucephala albeola.
A sound, usually made with a closed mouth pouting, indicating annoyance, indignation, disapproval, doubt, or sighing.
To utter "humph!" in doubt or disapproval.
e: A natural utterance, first recorded in the mid-16th century.

s: The action of one who skulks.
A supreme commander of the armed forces of a country, especially one who is also a political leader.
Chiefly in the form a smidgen of: a very small amount or quantity; a bit, a trace.
Chiefly in the form a smidgen of a: a very small or insignificant person or thing; also, an instance of such a person or thing.
e: Uncertain; possibly from smitch (“(originally Scotland, chiefly US) very small amount or quantity”) + possibly -in (a variant of -ing). Smitch is possibly.

s: An animal's pushing or exploration with the nose.
That part of the treadboard of a stair that projects over the riser.
Any similar projection, such as the projecting edge of a moulding.
A traditional French Provençal stewed vegetable dish consisting primarily of tomatoes, zucchini and eggplant.
To control someone as though they were a puppet.
e: French ratatouille, from Occitan ratatolha (ratatouille is a dish originally from Nice, and is also found in Provence), French form from diminutive prefix tat- + touiller (“to stir”), from Latin tudiculō (“grind, mix”), from tudes (“hammer”), from Proto-Indo-European *tud-, from *(s)tewd-.

s: A delicate and intricate ornamentation made from platinum, gold or silver (or sometimes other metal) twisted wire.
To decorate something with intricate ornamentation made from gold or silver twisted wire.
e: From French filigrane, from Italian filigrana, from Latin fīlum (“thread”) + grānum (“grain”).

s: The thin, horny, transparent plate covering the upper surface of the end of a toe.
To fasten two pieces of lumber together by applying nails or screws into both boards at an angle.
Behaving as though affected by alcohol including exhilaration, and a dumbed or stupefied manner.
e: From Latin inēbriātus, past participle of inēbriō (“intoxicate”) from in- + ēbrius (“drunk, intoxicated”) from Proto-Italic *ēɣʷrios, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ēgʷʰ-ryo-s from root *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”); whence also ebrious and inebriate.

s: A small box, usually a small cardboard box, in which matches are kept.
Any small, die-cast toy car, usually a collectible.
e: By genericization from the die-cast toy car brand Matchbox owned by Mattel, so-called due to the size of the toys to fix in matchboxes. thumb|matchbox.

s: To leave; to literally or figuratively say “adios” to.
e: Borrowed from Spanish adiós; see there for more. Doublet of adieu.

s: The final result, or outcome of something.
A positive aspect or consequence, often either unexpected or in contrast to other negative aspects.
e: Presumed from up- + shot, referring to the last shot in a match of archery.

s: A name loosely applied to various snakes more or less resembling a viper.
A small venomous serpent of the genus Vipera
A puff adder, of Africa (genus Bitis).
Any of several small nonvenomous snakes resembling adders
Certain venomous snakes resembling other adders
A sea stickleback or adder fish (Spinachia spinachia).
Someone who or something which performs arithmetic addition; a machine for adding numbers.
An electronic device that adds voltages, currents or frequencies.
e: From Middle English addre, form of naddre with rebracketing of /n/ as part of the indefinite article a(n), from Old English nǣdre (“snake”), from Proto-West Germanic *nadrā, from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ, from pre-Germanic *néh₁treh₂, variant of Proto-Indo-European *n̥h₁trih₂, from *(s)neh₁- (“to spin, twist”).

s: A horse used primarily for manual labor: a draft horse (draught horse).
A person or piece of equipment that performs a lot of work, especially one heavily relied upon to perform consistently and regularly.
Any species of Cottus; a sculpin.
A crustacean of the suborder Dendrobranchiata.
A crustacean, sometimes confused with shrimp.
Syn of butterface: a woman with an attractive body but an unattractive face.
A man with an attractive body but an unattractive face.
e: First attested early 1400s as various Middle English forms prayne, prane, praune, and prawne, which present no clear cognates in languages other than English. The forms suggest a hypothetical Old English form *prægn, where *æg would have evolved into Middle English *ay, but it is unclear if the word is of Germanic origin, from another European language, or loaned from a.

s: Grown or planted in a plant pot.
Prepared in advance, as though preserved by potting.
of a biographical or historical account
Expressed in a relatively short, brief form.
e: From pot + -ed. Adjective meaning "prepared in advance" by analogy with potted meat (canned meat), first used in a published work by L. Susan Stebbing in her Pelican classic Thinking to some purpose (1939), where "potted thinking" is defined as "a compressed statement to save us the trouble of thinking".

s: Foodstuffs that taste very sweet, taken as a group; candies, sweetmeats and confections collectively.
The business or occupation of manufacturing confectionery; the skill or work of a confectioner.
A store where confectionery is sold; a confectioner's shop.
A device that circulates fresh air and expels stale or noxious air.
A machine that moves breathable air into and out of the lungs of a patient who is unable to breathe sufficiently.
Some behaviour or happening that relieves a tense atmosphere or situation.
A play or an actor so bad as to empty the theater.
Action of the verb to thrash.
A beating, especially a severe one.
The fragrant wood of Dalbergia nigra, a Brazilian tree in the legume family, which has a sweet smell.
Any of several dozen woods, resembling that of Dalbergia nigra in some respect.
The wood of a South American tree, Aniba rosaeodora, in the laurel family, with fragrant wood from which an essential oil is distilled.
Wood and plant of Pterocarpus spp., for example African rosewood or mukula or Burmese rosewood (Pterocarpus indicus, syn. Pterocarpus santalinus).
e: A compound of rose + wood, originally so named because of the rose-scented aromatic oil derived from it; applied in later senses on account of these woods’ predominantly reddish-brown colour.

s: A machine or container for frying food.
A young chicken suitable for frying; a pullet or cockerel.
A loose-fitting garment worn over regular clothes to protect them.
Loose-fitting pants with supporting cross-straps and a panel of material in the chest (called a bib), often associated with farm work.
A ship designed to break through ice so that it, or other ships coming behind, can navigate on frozen seas.
A game, activity, humorous anecdote, etc., designed to ease tension and encourage interaction among individuals in a situation where they do not know each other well.
A lively song and dance routine at the start of a musical.
e: From ice + breaker, in the figurative sense from the expression to break the ice.

s: An artificial intelligence researcher who believes that intelligence is too complicated (or computationally intractable) to be solved with the sorts of homogeneous system favoured by the "neats".
A flat round pancake-like pastry from Lower Brittany, made with wheat.
A soft thin light fabric with a crinkled surface.
Crepe paper; thin, crinkled tissue paper.
Rubber in sheets, used especially for shoe soles.
A death notice printed on white card with a background of black crepe paper or cloth, placed on the door of a residence or business.
To crease (paper) in such a way to make it look like crepe paper
e: Borrowed from French crêpe, from Latin crispus. Doublet of crisp, crape.

s: Gorged, filled to near the point of bursting, especially with food or drink.
of a subcategory s of c
Isomorphism-closed: Inheriting all the isomorphisms of C. Formally: such that for any isomorphism f in C, if f 's source is in S, then f and f 's target is also in S.
To fill to repletion, or restore something that has been depleted.
e: From Middle English replete and repleten, from Old French replet, from Latin repletus.

s: A standstill resulting from the opposition of two evenly matched forces; a stalemate or impasse.
An inability to continue due to two programs or devices each requiring a response from the other before completing an operation.
To cause or come to a deadlock.
To bring to a state of deadlock.
A loaf of fish, meat, or vegetables baked in a pastry shell.
Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of birds; avian.
One who is addicted to sex.

e: Borrowed from Yiddish צרות, plural of צרה (“trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (“trouble, tragedy, calamity”).

s: To file incorrectly; to file in the wrong place or the wrong way.
The act of washing something again
The rhythm or meter of a line or verse.
The act of analyzing the meter of poetry.
Of text, to put into a rhythmic form or meter.
e: From Late Latin scansiōnem, accusative singular of scansiō (“the act of climbing”), from scandō (“to climb”).

s: Behaviour adopted to demonstrate one's superiority; pretentious or snobbish behaviour; airs and graces.
Flighty, giddy, or silly behaviour; also, noisy merriment.
A young woman regarded as flighty, giddy, or silly.

Affected or pretentious, sometimes with the implication of displaying an air of excessive fanciness or ostentation; pompous, self-important, snobbish; often displaying a feeling of patronizing self-aggrandizing or arrogant class superiority.
Flighty, giddy, silly; also, merry in a noisy manner.
Expressing disapprobation or surprise at acts or words that are pompous or snobbish, or flighty.
e: Probably from hoit (“to behave frivolously and thoughtlessly; to play the fool”) + -y, reduplicated with a change of the initial consonant. The noun is attested earlier than the adjective.

s: To whine or complain, often needlessly and incessantly.
A person who endlessly whines or complains; a person who finds fault with anything.
An instance of kvetching; a complaint or whine.
e: From Yiddish קוועטשן, from Middle High German quetschen (“crush, press”).

s: of a speech or an argument
Lacking matter; empty; devoid of substance.
In the manner of ice; with a cold or chilling effect.
In an uncaring or coolly angry manner.
Marked or covered with large, irregular spots.
e: From an alteration (due to splotch) of Middle English splotty, equivalent to splotch + -y.

s: A speech made when leaving or parting company.
A word or phrase said upon leaving, such as "farewell" or "adieu".
A word or phrase used to end a letter or message.
e: Borrowed from New Latin valedictiō, from valedīcō (“to bid farewell”) + -tiō, from valē (“farewell, so long”) + dīcō (“to say”). valedict + -ion.

s: Of, pertaining to, containing, or characteristic of plums.
Rich, mellow and carefully articulated, especially with an upper-class accent.
e: From plum + -y. In the sense of a voice, because of the supposed similarity to speaking with a plum in one's mouth.

s: Not schooled; not having been to school.
Inexperienced; not having developed skill or knowledge in some area.
A long, narrow, polelike club carried by police and security personnel, for use in self-defense.
A person who spends much time in bars and nightclubs, and generally indulges themselves during the night.
In a thoughtful or reflective manner.
Not amused; thus often offended or put off.
To sow (to disperse or plant seeds).
To impregnate (to cause to become pregnant).
e: Borrowed from Latin inseminātus, the perfect passive participle of insemināre (“to sow”). in- + seminate.

s: To revolve round a central point; to move spirally about an axis, as a tornado.
To revolve and behave unsteadily around a central axis.
Syn of hairball; a ball of fur, especially one coughed up by a cat.
A particularly furry person or animal.
A large, disorganized battle involving many different aircraft (especially fighters) or warships.
Any small passerine bird mostly of the genus Baeolophus, which are found in the woods of the Northern Hemisphere and of Africa.
e: From Middle English titmose, compound of tit#Etymology 3 (“small bird”) and mose, from Old English māse (“titmouse”), from Proto-West Germanic *maisā, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ (compare Dutch mees, German Meise, Old Norse meisingr, French mésange), from *maisaz (“tiny, puny”) (compare Norwegian meis (“skinny weakling”)).

s: Constantly complaining, especially in a childish way due to insignificant matters; fretful, whiny.
Quick to become bad-tempered or cross, especially due to insignificant matters; irritable, pettish, petulant.
Of weather: blustery, windy; also, of wind: cold and strong; bitter, sharp.
Harmful, injurious; also, mischievous; or malicious, spiteful.
Obstinately in the wrong; perverse, stubborn.
Of a thing: evoking a feeling of distaste, horror, etc.
e: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English pievish, peuysche, pevish, pevysh (“capricious, wilful; perverse, wayward”); further etymology Uncertain, possibly from one of the following: The adverb is derived from the adjective.

s: A person who is skilled at, professes, or practices seismology.
In a scornful manner; contemptuously, derisively.
e: Inherited from Middle English scornfully; equivalent to scornful + -ly.

s: The act by which something is blighted.
To approach and speak to boldly or aggressively, as with a demand or request.
To join side to side; to border.
To sail along the coast or side of.
To approach; to come up to.
To speak to first; to address; to greet.
e: From Middle French accoster, acoster, from Old French acoster (“to stand beside”) (whence Medieval Latin accostare), from Old French a- + coste (“side, flank”).

s: Gerund of dawdle: the act of one who dawdles.
A musical instrument consisting of a flat sounding box with numerous strings placed on a horizontal surface, played with a plectrum or fingertips.
Related or similar instruments in other cultures, such as the Chinese guqin or Norwegian harpeleik; especially any chordophone without a neck, and with strings that pass over the body.
To make a sound similar to that made by a zither; to move while making such a sound.
e: Borrowed from German Zither, from Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (“a kind of harp”). Doublet of cithara, cither, guitar.

s: The state of being grandiose (pompous or pretentious).
A pair of knee-breeches made of leather, typical of Bavaria and Austria.
e: Borrowed from German Lederhose. The final -n probably from the German plural; alternatively influenced by Lederhosn. 180px|right.

s: The ability to be, or the characteristic of being, at all places at the same time (usually only attributed to God).
The act of making something quiet.
In an indignant manner; with indignation.

An approach focusing on observable behavior which, generally assuming that behavior is determined by the environment and denying any independent significance for mind, largely ignores any pathophysiological processes which may, or may not, underlie subjective, behavioral phenomena.

The theory that a mental state is identical to the disposition or tendency to behave in accordance with the physical causes; statements about the mind are reducible to statements of physical behavior.
The side of a right triangle opposite the right angle.
e: From Latin hypotenusa, from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνουσα πλευρά (“side subtending [the right angle]”), from ὑποτείνουσα (“stretching, extending, subtending”), active participle of ὑποτείνω (“subtend, stretch under”).

s: Of or relating to the glottis.
A sound made with the glottis
The muscular substance of the heart; the middle of the three layers forming the outer wall of the human heart.
e: From New Latin myocardium, from Ancient Greek μῦς (“muscle”) + καρδίᾱ (“heart”).

s: A whirling or turning on the toes in dancing, primarily in ballet.
The whirling about of a horse.
A wooden mouthpiece assembly or lip rest used in some European double-reed instruments.
To perform a pirouette; to whirl on the toes, like a dancer.
e: Borrowed from French pirouette, see there for more; attested since 1706.

s: Irritable; impatient; short-tempered; often, in a condescending way.
e: From snip + -y. Compare snippig, snippich (“short, brief, blunt”), Dutch snippig (“snippy, shrill”), Low German snippig (“snippy, snappy”), German schnippisch (“snippy, snappy”).

s: An undertaker or funeral director; especially, one who is also the embalmer or cremator.
A room, rooftop, balcony, or terrace, used for its abundant sunlight, especially when used as a medical treatment.
Synonym of tanning salon, a room or business used for its sunlamps or tanning beds.
An earthen structure constructed by certain ants for the purpose of brood incubation.
e: Borrowed from Latin sōlārium (“sundial, place for enjoying sunlight”), from sōl (“sun”) + -ārium (“-arium: indicating related places or devices”).

s: An acrobat who is capable of twisting their body into unusual positions.
One who twists words and phrases.
In mort, bridge, and similar games, the partner of dummy.
A crustless quiche: a molded omelette in which vegetables, cheese, etc., are mixed into the eggs and cooked together.

e: None of the various attested forms appear in the OED, in Victor & Dalzell’s Concise New Partridge Dictionary of Slang and Unconventional English, nor in Webster’s New Universal Unabridged Dictionary. According to the RHD, 'looky' (also 'lookee') is an interjection attested from 1875–80 which is an alternative form of the imperative look ye! Similarly, the linguist Andrew L.

s: In an authoritative manner; with authority.
e: From Middle English auctoritatively, auctoritativeli; compare Medieval Latin auctoritātīve; equivalent to authoritative + -ly.

s: The sound of fabric or fur moving in the air.
The movement that produces such a sound.
A switching; a beating with twigs or a cane.
The mutual exchange of pre-owned clothes, especially at an organised party.
Having a round, spherical or curved shape; circular; orbicular.
Having a round body shape; portly or pudgy; obese.
Full and rich; orotund; sonorous; full-toned.
e: Latin rotundus (“round”), from Latin rota (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreth₂- (“to run, to roll”). Doublet of round.

s: To cause (a sound) to be (repeatedly) bounced against one or more surfaces; to re-echo.
Followed by on (to): to deflect or divert (flames, heat, etc.) on to something.
To heat (something) by deflecting flames on to, or passing flames over, it.
To repeatedly reflect (heat, light, or other radiation).
Of sound: to (repeatedly) bounce against one or more surfaces; to echo or re-echo, to resound.
Chiefly followed by to or with: of a place or thing: to ring or vibrate with many echoing sounds; to re-echo, to resound.
Often followed by from: of heat or light: to be (repeatedly) reflected.
Of a thing: to be heated by having flames, hot gases, etc., deflected or passed over it.
Ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds; re-echoing, resounding, reverberating.
e: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, perfect passive participle of reverberō (“to rebound; to reflect; to repel”) (see -ate), whence Middle French reverberer (French réverbérer) and Middle English reverberen (“to send back”)), from re- and verberō (“to beat; to lash, whip”) (from verber (“rod; lash, whip”) + -ō).

Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate for more. (“ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds”) was popularized by its use in Twelfth Night (written; published 1623) by the English playwright William Shakespeare (1564–1616): see the quotation.

s: In a rueful manner; causing, feeling or expressing regret or sorrow.
Characterized by brawn; muscular, thewy; strong.
Prim and fussy; too precise; overparticular.
e: 1895, either an alteration of precise, prim + sissy, or a prim + fussy; first attested in a work of American writer Joel Chandler Harris.

s: An American feline carnivore (Leopardus pardalis, syn. Felis pardalis) covered with blackish ocellated spots and blotches which are variously arranged.
e: From French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Classical Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).

s: A Mexican dish made by wrapping a filling in a tortilla, then baking in a sauce.
e: From Spanish enchilada, a use of the of enchilar (“to add chili pepper to”).

s: Soft serve; a cone of soft serve
The act of one who tills.
e: From Middle English tillynge, tiliyng, tilyenge, tylynge, from Old English tiliende, tilġende, equivalent to till + -ing.
From Middle English tyllynge, tiling, tilinge, telynge, from Old English tilung, teolung, equivalent to till + -ing.

s: Of a person: attractive or pleasing to look at; beautiful, handsome; also, attractive but not particularly beautiful or handsome.
Of a person, an action, behaviour, etc.: meeting accepted moral or social norms; appropriate, becoming, proper.
Of a thing: beautiful, elegant, well-composed; also, delicate, fine.
Pleasing to the feelings or senses; agreeable, nice, pleasant.
e: The verb is derived from the adjective.
From Middle English comli, cumly, cumeliche (“beautifully, handsomely; gracefully; splendidly; fittingly, properly; well”), from Old English cȳme (see etymology 1) + Middle English -li.

s: A game in which each player acts out a word or phrase, usually based on puns of each syllable and without speaking, for the others to guess.
e: See charade. As a game, originally a clipped form of acting charades or, without talking, dumb charades but now usually understood as a plurale tantum.
From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).

s: The mechanical widening of a narrowed or totally obstructed blood vessel generally caused by atheroma.

e: From Middle English fomy, from Old English fāmiġ, fǣmiġ (“frothy, foamy”), from Proto-West Germanic *faimag, *faimīg, equivalent to foam + -y.

s: A fly ball that is weakly hit just over the infielders.
A filmed or videotaped outtake that has recorded an amusing accident or mistake.
A gaff-rigged fore-and-aft sail set from and aft of the aftmost mast of a square-rigged ship; a spanker.
A radio which interferes with other radios, causing them to bloop (squeal loudly).
The Vietnam-era M79 grenade launcher (due to its distinctive report).
Containing or using more words than necessary; long-winded, wordy.
Producing detailed output for diagnostic purposes.
e: From Latin verbōsus (“prolix, wordy, verbose”). Verbōsus is derived from verbum (“word”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to say, speak”)) + -ōsus. Equivalent to verb + -ose.

s: A sylvan deity or demigod, male companion of Pan or Dionysus, represented as part man and part goat, and characterized by riotous merriment and lasciviousness, sometimes pictured with a perpetual erection.
Any of various butterflies of the nymphalid subfamily Satyrinae, having brown wings marked with eyelike spots; a meadow brown.
e: From French satyre, from Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος.

s: To grant a sublease out of property held under a lease.
A French parfait (parfait glacé), an iced dessert made with egg yolks, sugar, cream, and flavouring (usually fruit), sometimes with the addition of a liqueur.
An American parfait, a layered dessert often consisting of fruit, ice cream, pastries, whipped topping, etc. and served in a glass, often a parfait glass.
A smooth pâté, usually made from liver and flavoured with liqueurs.

Someone skilled in the writing of shorthand or the use of a stenotype machine, especially for the purpose of rapid transcription of speech. One employed in such a role: a professional transcriptionist who employs shorthand.
One who invents or studies systems of shorthand.
An electronic device that produces special effects on the sound produced by an electric guitar etc.
Fictional energy weapon, with multiple settings for degree of intensity, from the television series Star Trek (1966–69).
To shoot with a phaser weapon.
One who studies or practices zoology.

e: Thumb|Pre-sliced American baloney Phonetic spelling of bologna.
Origin unclear. Perhaps from the slang word balonie.

s: Characterized by giving love and affection.
Showing a decline of mental faculties, especially when it occurs in old age.
The sound produced when someone or something bellows
The act by which somebody is bewitched; a curse or enchantment.

e: [[File:024 WanAlbum (2) (7975894513).jpg|thumb|A couple in Malaysia at their nuptials]] From nuptial, borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”) (also plural only), from nūpta, from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *sneubho-, *snewbʰ- (“to marry, wed”).

s: An eccentric, crazy or foolish person.
Someone addicted to crack cocaine (i.e. a drug addict).
e: Mostly likely a back-etymology of pot, to form crack + pot. Originally, from crack + pate. Compare typologically Russian чо́кнутый (чо́каться, onomatopoeic), see crack for the further typology.

s: Form of The ordinal numeral form; last in order of a series of a thousand; next after the nine hundred and ninety-ninth.
The person or thing in the thousandth position.
One of a thousand equal parts of a whole.
A semi-aquatic, herbivorous, African hoofed mammal of the family Hippopotamidae.
e: From Latin and New Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος, from ἵππος (“horse”) (English hippo-) + ποταμός (“river”).. (from native Old English nicor) and river horse.

s: Something or someone that is physically attractive.
Something that is a remarkable example of its type.
e: Either a back-formation from beauty or a clipping thereof.

s: Of or pertaining to the Puritans, or to their doctrines and practice.
Precise in observance of legal or religious requirements; strict; overscrupulous; rigid (often used by way of reproach or contempt).
The act of something being hurtled or thrown.
To open or undo, as what is wrapped or folded.
To flatten (a three-dimensional model) into a two-dimensional plane.
To work against; to oppose (especially to incite a reaction).
The act or process by which a document is proofread.
Causing physical harm or injury; harmful, hurtful.
Causing harm to one's reputation; invidious, defamatory, libelous, slanderous.
e: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.

s: of an alcoholic beverage, especially wine
Disparaging or derisive in an insinuative way.
An underhanded, tricky person given to sharp practice; a sharper; a cheat.
e: Probably from a dialectal variant of Doublet of snithe. See snithe. Alternatively, possibly a metathetic corruption of Middle English snythand (“piercing (the heart), cold, biting”). More at snithe. Compare typologically cutting, Russian ко́лкий (akin to коло́ть).

s: Specifically, a person whose job it is to kill insects and other pests in a building.
To drive back or beat back; to repulse.
To deny the truth of something, especially by presenting arguments that disprove it.
e: Inherited from Middle English rebutten, rebouten, from Old French reboter, rebuter, rebouter, etc., from re- + boter, buter, bouter (“to butt”). Entered English around 1302-1307.

s: an affront to one's dignity or pride
Of or relating to the brain.

Any of a class of non-inflecting words and multiword terms typically employed to connect a following noun or a pronoun, in an adjectival or adverbial sense, with some other word: a particle used with a noun or pronoun (in English always in the objective case) to make a phrase limiting some other wor
A proposition; an exposition; a discourse.
e: From Middle English preposicioun, from Old French preposicion, from Latin praepositio, praepositionem, from praepono (“to place before”), equivalent to pre- + position. Compare French préposition.

s: The act of removing somebody's clothes.
Reducing grief, sorrow, or disappointment; comforting.
The act by which somebody is consoled.
A person who sometimes wears clothes traditionally worn by and associated with the opposite sex; typically a male who cross-dresses occasionally by habit or personal choice.

A person, typically a heterosexual male, who compulsively seeks and derives paraphilic sexual arousal from cross-dressing, especially if the urges and behavior cause the patient distress or social impairment.
An animal that engages in sexual mimicry.
e: Borrowed from Latin trāns + vestītus, form of vestiō (“to clothe, to dress”) (as in English vestment, vest). Literally, a "cross-dresser". From transvestitism, from German Transvestitismus, coined in 1910 by Magnus Hirschfeld (the practice itself is much older).

s: A mountebank, someone who addresses crowds in the street; (especially), an itinerant seller of medicines or drugs.
A malicious trickster; a fake person, especially one who deceives for personal profit.
e: From Middle French charlatan, from ciarlatano (“quack”), a blend of ciarlatore (“chatterer”) + cerretano (“hawker, quack”) (Cerreto di Spoleto being a village in Umbria, known for its quacks).

s: To act as a detective; to try to discover who committed a crime, or, more generally, to solve a mystery.
A wireless telecommunications device that receives text or voice messages.
A computer program running in a text terminal, used to view (but not modify) the contents of a text file moving down the file one line or one screen at a time.
Something (a document, book etc.) that has a specified number of pages.
One who makes up type into pages of a book; one who binds or sorts pages into a book.
To tear up (a plant, etc.) by the roots, or as if by the roots; to extirpate, to root up.
To destroy (something) utterly; to eradicate, exterminate.
To remove (someone or something) from a familiar circumstance, especially suddenly and unwillingly.
Of oneself or someone: to move away from a familiar environment (for example, to live elsewhere).
Of a pig or other animal: to dig up (something in the ground) using the snout; to rummage for (something) in the ground; to grub up, to root, to rout.
e: From up- + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place; to eradicate, exterminate”). Root is derived from root (“underground part of a plant”), from Middle English rote, from Old English rōt, rōte, from Old Norse rót, from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).

s: Scented, having been given a pleasant smell.
Matter that is composed of the antiparticles of those that constitute normal matter.
A form of matter that has a key property, such as charge, opposite to that of ordinary matter.
e: From anti- + matter. Coined by Arthur Schuster to describe matter that resists gravity in a jocular article in Nature titled "Potential Matter.—A Holiday Dream", but not used in a modern sense until the 1940s.

s: The act of one who gloats.
A short flash of light, usually when reflected off a shiny surface.
To glance; to peep forth, as a flower from the bud; to glitter.
To cause to flash or gleam; to reflect.
e: 15th century. Borrowed from Scots glint, from Middle English glenten (“to shine, gleam; flash”), probably from Old Norse *glenta, from Proto-Germanic *glantijaną, causitive of Proto-Germanic *glintaną (“to gleam, shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to shine”).

s: To arrange or score music for performance by an orchestra.
To compose or arrange orchestral music for a dramatic performance.
To arrange or direct diverse elements to achieve a desired effect
The state or quality of being strange, odd or weird.
The product or result of being strange.
One of the quantum numbers of subatomic particles, depending upon the relative number of strange quarks and anti-strange quarks.
A release of emotional tension after an overwhelming vicarious experience, resulting in the purging or purification of the emotions, as through watching a dramatic production (especially a tragedy).
Any release of emotional tension to the same effect, more widely.
A purification or cleansing, especially emotional.

A therapeutic technique to relieve tension by reestablishing the association of an emotion with the memory or idea of the event that first caused it, and then eliminating it by complete expression (called the abreaction).
A purging of the digestive system.
e: From Ancient Greek κάθαρσις (“cleansing, purging”), from καθαίρω (“I cleanse”). Coined in the dramatic-emotional sense by Aristotle.

s: Any of the about 250 species of flowering plant of the genus Nepeta, family Lamiaceae, certain of which are said to have medicinal qualities.
Nepeta cataria and Nepeta grandiflora (and perhaps other species), which are well-known for causing an apparently harmless pheromone-based intoxication among certain cats.
Something that causes excitement or interest.
e: Compound of cat + nep, nip (“catnip”), from Middle English nep, from Old English nepte, from Proto-West Germanic *nepetā, from Latin nepeta (“catnip”). Compare earlier catmint (“catnip”), from Middle English catt mynte, which very likely existed in Old English (as *cattes minte) as well.

s: A robe usually made of terrycloth intended to be worn when one is still damp from bathing or when there is no immediate need to dress fully.
A motion or gesture that darts.
The use of darts (folds stitched on a garment).
A young person who causes trouble or violence, typically as a member of a gang or other group.
A member of the United States Coast Guard.
A type of fish, an anadromous smelt, Thaleichthys pacificus, found in the North Pacific.
e: Probably a variant of the Irish surname Houlihan, 1890s.
Borrowed from ulakan, from Clatsop, with spelling and pronunciation influenced by the preceding.

s: To trace (a line, etc. in drawing) again.
To go back over something, usually in an attempt at rediscovery.
The period when the beam of the cathode-ray tube returns to its initial horizontal position in order to start the next line of the display.
In a surreptitious manner; stealthily, furtively, secretly.
Consisting of two terms, or parts.
Of or relating to the binomial distribution.
A quantity expressed as the sum or difference of two terms.
A scientific name at the rank of species, with two terms: a generic name and a specific name.
e: Formed from Late Latin binōmium + -al. The derivation of binōmium is unclear. It was used by Gerard of Cremona in the 12th century. Suggested sources are the Latin nōmen (“name”), the Ancient Greek νομός (“distribution, pasture”), or the Old French nom (“name”).

s: A catecholamine hormone and neurotransmitter; as a hormone, secreted by the adrenal gland in response to stress (when it stimulates the autonomic nervous system); as a neurotransmitter, synthesized from norepinephrine. It is also used as a medication.
Sexual intercourse by people who are not married to each other, or which is considered illicit in another way.
e: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).

s: A receptacle for ash and butts from cigarettes and cigars.
To live longer than; continue to live after the death of; overlive; survive.
To live through or past (a given time).
To live longer; continue to live.
A woman's private sitting room, dressing room, or bedroom.
e: Borrowed from French boudoir, from bouder (“to sulk”), of origin.

From Middle English hondywerk, handiwerc, from Old English handġeweorc (“work done by hand, creation”), from hand (“hand”) + ġeweorc (“work”). Equivalent to hand + work, though it may now be reinterpreted as handy (“skilful”) + work. Compare Hondwierk, Dutch handwerk, German Handwerk.

s: Like a living being; resembling life; being an accurate representation.
Wild, uncontrolled, especially of animals not domesticated or trained to human contact.
e: From Middle English untamed, untemed, equivalent to un- + tamed and/or untame + -ed. Compare Dutch ongetemd (“untamed”), German ungezähmt (“untamed”), Danish utæmmet (“untamed”), Swedish otämd (“untamed”), Icelandic ótamin (“untamed”).

s: Strong muscles or lean flesh, especially of the arm, leg or thumb.
Head cheese; a terrine made from the head of a pig or calf; originally boar's meat.
Make fat, especially of a boar.
Become fat, especially of a boar.
e: From Middle English brawne, from Old French braon (“slice of meat, fleshy part, buttock”), from Frankish *brādon, *brādan, oblique forms of *brādō (“roasted meat, ham”), from Proto-Germanic *brēdô (“meat, roast”), of uncertain further origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“to burn, heat”).

s: The branch of mathematics that deals with the relationships between the sides and angles of (in particular) right-angled triangles, as represented by the trigonometric functions, and with calculations based on said relationships.
e: From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (“triangle”) + μέτρον (“measure”), equivalent to trigon + -metry.

s: to feel empathy for another person
Not conscionable; unscrupulous and lacking principles or conscience.
Inclined or having a propensity to love, or to sexual enjoyment.
Of or relating to, or produced by, love.
Affected with love; in love; enamored.
e: From Middle English amorous, amerous (14th century), from Old French amoros, amoreus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, from Latin amor (“love”), related to amāre (“to love”). Compare French amoureux (“in love”). Doublet of amoroso, amoureux.

s: The act of one who parades.
An excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures or scandalous and immoral activities, involving sex, alcohol, or drugs without inhibition.
A portable, usually hand-held, funnel-shaped device that is used to amplify a person’s natural voice toward a targeted direction.
Mouthpiece or promoter; one who speaks for or publicizes on behalf of another.
To use a megaphone; to speak through a megaphone.
A cytotoxic neolignan obtained from the laurel Aniba megaphylla.
Not sufferable; very difficult or impossible to endure; intolerable, unbearable.
Preoccupied with something to the exclusion of everything else.
Finalized, written in large letters. (of a document)
To discover again; especially something previously lost or forgotten.
flowers in the family Caryophyllaceae, sometimes called carnations.
The traditional scarlet jacket(s) worn by fox-hunters in the United Kingdom.
Of or pertaining to an acrobat.
A shining with fast intermittent light.
A very short period, notionally the time it takes to blink the eyes.

Any of numerous hemiparasitic evergreen plants of the order Santalales with white berries that grow in the crowns of apple trees, oaks, and other trees, such as the European mistletoe (Viscum album) and American mistletoe or eastern mistletoe (Phoradendron leucarpum).
A sprig of one such plant used as a Christmas decoration, associated with the custom that a man may kiss any woman standing beneath it.
e: From Middle English mistelto, mistilto (“European mistletoe”), from Old English misteltān (“mistletoe”), from mistel (“mistletoe; basil; birdlime”) + tān (“sprig, shoot, twig”), possibly as a Calque of Old Norse mistilteinn; equivalent to mistle + tan (“twig”). This was mistaken for the plural of tā (“toe”).

s: The act of placing a telephone call.
Inclined to drowse; heavy with sleepiness
Causing someone to fall sleep or feel sleepy; lulling; soporific.
e: From drowse + -y, despite the fact that drowsy (1520) is recorded before drowse (1570). Compare Old English drūsian (“to droop, drowse, become languid”).

s: Said to wish a final farewell; goodbye.
A farewell, a goodbye; especially a fond farewell, or a lasting or permanent farewell.
e: From Middle English adieu also adew, adewe, adue, from Old French adieu (“to God”), a shortening of a Dieu vous comant (“I commend you to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Doublet of adios.

s: Of an inappropriately or unusually low weight.
Not too heavy for an intended purpose.
Being less invested in a particular area than market wisdom suggests.
The state or quality of being underweight.
To give insufficient weight to (a consideration); to underestimate the importance of.
To invest in less than conventional wisdom would dictate.
Thin nylon tights worn over the legs, usually tan in color.
A martial art from Korea, known for its elaborate kicking techniques. The sparring aspect is a recognised Olympic sport.
Having been fully removed, including the roots.
Having been removed from a familiar circumstance, especially suddenly and unwillingly.
A small carved or molded figure; a statuette.
To make reparation, compensation, amends or satisfaction for an offence, crime, mistake or deficiency.
To bring at one or at concordance; to reconcile; to suffer appeasement.
To agree or accord; to be in accordance or harmony.
To absolve (someone else) of wrongdoing, especially by standing as an equivalent.
e: From atone (“reconciled”), from Middle English atone, attone, atoon (“agreed”), equivalent to at + one. Compare Latin adūnō (“to unite, make one”) for the similar formation. Regarding the different phonological development of atone and one, see the note in one.

s: Very good, excellent, typically used sarcastically to indicate a state of misery, resentment or great frustration.
A footman, a liveried male servant.
To attend, wait upon, serve obsequiously.
e: Borrowed from Middle French laquais, which is probably (via Old Occitan lacai?) from Spanish lacayo, itself perhaps from Italian lacchè and Greek λακές, from Turkish ulak. Another possibility is through French, from Arabic الْقَائِد. See French laquais.

s: Of or pertaining to an archetype.
In a clear and unambiguous manner.
or spreading at right angles to the axis.

e: From eerie + -ly. Compare Old English earglīċe, earhlīċe (“in a cowardly manner, timidly, fearfully”).

s: A protective system in automobiles in which when a crash occurs, a bag containing nitrogen, formed by the explosive decomposition of sodium azide, quickly inflates in front of the driver or passenger, preventing injury to the head. Side air bags, including the back seat passengers, also prevent inju
A similar inflated bag used in performing stunts, or for lifting objects in firefighting, etc.
A person who talks too much; a windbag or gossip.
The act of one who basks.
Whining; tending to whine or complain.
Having a nasally or high-pitched voice.
Stuck; incapable of proceeding without help, though not having crashed.
The act of burrowing a tunnel.
The quantum mechanical passing of a particle through an energy barrier.
A type of fraud where assets and profits are transferred out of firms for the benefit of those who control them.
A feature of the file system that allows files to preserve certain properties, such as creation date, even after being deleted and recreated.
One blade of a pair of scissors.
To cut using, or as if using, scissors.
To excise or expunge something from a text.
To reproduce (text) as an excerpt, copy.
To move something like a pair of scissors, especially the legs.
To engage in scissoring (tribadism), a sexual act in which two women intertwine their legs and rub their vulvas against each other.
To skate with one foot significantly in front of the other.
e: From Middle English cysour, cysoure, cysowre, altered from sisours (“scissors”), from Old French cisoires, cisours, cisur, from Latin caedere (“to cut”); current spelling influenced by Latin scindere, scissus (“to split”).

s: The use of a word or phrase to replace another one that is more offensive, blunt or vulgar.
A word or phrase that replaces another in this way.
e: Recorded since 1656; from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός, from εὐφημίζω, from εὔφημος (“uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (“well”) + φήμη (“a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φημί (“to speak, say”).

s: An instance or example of such overstatement.
e: From Middle English iperbole, yperbole, from Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (“excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (“above”) + βάλλω (“to throw”). Doublet of hyperbola.

s: Resembling or having the consistency of mush; semiliquid, pasty, or granular.
Overly sappy, corny, or cheesy; sentimental, especially in a romantic way; maudlin.
To lay (something) as in a bed; to lay in surrounding matter; to bed.
To encapsulate within another document or data file.
To define a one-to-one function from one set to another so that certain properties of the domain are preserved when considering the image as a subset of the codomain.
One thing embedded within another, as
An embedded reporter or journalist, such as a war reporter assigned to and travelling with a military unit, or a political reporter assigned to follow and report on the campaign of a candidate.
An element of an advertisement, etc. serving as a subliminal message.
A digital object embedded within another, which is often a document.
A piece of computer hardware embedded within another physical object, which is often a larger IT device.
To place within a fluid (generally a liquid, but also a gas).
out as a result of the wicket-keeper breaking the wicket with the ball while the batsman is out of his crease.
A Y-shaped stick with an elastic sling between the arms used for shooting small projectiles.

A stationary, often triangular object that launches any ball that hits its longest side back at a high force, now usually located above the flipper and between it and the inlane, with one each for both lower flippers.
An implement of a broad fabric worn around and connecting both bicipites brachii to support benching the most heavy weights.
The act of passing cars queuing in the left-hand lane and using the right-hand lane to go around a roundabout, exiting at the desired junction having avoided the queue.
To move or cause to move in a manner resembling a projectile shot from a slingshot.
To use the gravity of a moving planet to add momentum to a spacecraft.
To perform the slingshot manoeuvre (see Noun).

e: Borrowed from (Hindi पैजामा / Urdu پائِجامَہ), from پایجامه, archaic form of پاجامه.

s: A car with a sloping, hinged rear door that opens upwards.
To attach or connect in a secure manner.
To cause to take close effect; to make to tell; to land.
e: From Middle English fastenen, from Old English fæstnian, from Proto-West Germanic *fastinōn (“to secure, fasten”). Equivalent to fast + -en.

s: Something that causes moisture or a condition of wetness; something that makes things moist.
A person or animal who drools.
An extremely stupid person; a moron.
A heavy, ungainly shoe or boot.
A box of confectionery, delivered with a greeting or other prepared message, often used for Valentine's Day dances.
Someone who makes a list or lists.
A charity event in which participants knit.
Form of obsolete or nonstandard form
A baked dish of macaroni, ground beef, cheese and tomato sauce.
Used by a listener to confirm that they have understood something said to them: I got it, I heard you, I understand.
Used by a speaker to confirm that the listener has understood something said to the latter: did you hear me?, get it?, understood?
e: From the spoken equivalents of either of the following: of capire (“to understand”), from Latin capere, the of capiō (“to capture, catch, seize; to comprehend, understand; etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grab, seize; to hold”).

s: A frozen dessert consisting of crushed ice and colored fruit flavoring, usually served in a cone or a cup.
One with a morbid paroxysmal craving for alcohol; an alcoholic.
A persistently drunken person; a drunkard.
The act by which something is garbled or confused.
The process of removing the unwanted substances present in crude drugs after drying.
The sound of walking with heavy footfalls.
The state of being old; age.
e: From Middle English oldnesse, possibly from Old English ealdnes, ealdnyss (“oldness; age”), equivalent to old + -ness.

s: Jokey; inclined to or characterised by quipping.
The act or characteristic of being aggressive or combative.
Agent noun of skulk; one who skulks.
One who stays where they cannot be seen (often in a cowardly way or with the intent of doing harm).
One who moves in a stealthy or furtive way; one who comes or goes while trying to avoid detection.
One who avoids an obligation or responsibility.
e: From Middle English sculkere, from skulk, -er; equivalent to skulk + -er. Compare Norwegian skulkar and Old Swedish skulkare.

s: Anything that provides guidance; a guideline.
A skin-tight garment covering the torso and the legs, sometimes the arms and feet.
An expression of sorrow or mourning.
A navel that protrudes from the abdomen.
A vulva with external labia minora.
A penis, seen as an everted version of a vulva.
A British soldier (stemming from the military uniform of British infantry since the 17th century).
A member of the entertainment staff at Butlin's holiday camps in the United Kingdom, who wear red blazers.
To work as a redcoat (Butlin's entertainer).
The swede, or Swedish turnip; the European plant Brassica napus var. napobrassica
The edible root of this plant
e: Borrowed from Swedish rotabagge, a dialectal word from Västergötland, from rot (“root”) + bagge (“lump, bunch”).

s: Of, relating to, or resembling a word; verbal.
Meek, timid; lacking character or effectiveness.
A person of meek or timid disposition; a person who lacks character or effectiveness.
e: Named after Caspar Milquetoast, a character from the comic strip The Timid Soul, created by American cartoonist Harold Tucker Webster (1885–1952) and first published in 1924; the character was named after the American dish milk toast (“a food consisting of toasted bread in warm milk”), from en:milk> + toast.

s: An iron collar formerly used in Spain to execute people by strangulation.
Something, especially a cord or wire, used for strangulation.
To execute by strangulation, to kill using a garrote.
To suddenly render insensible by semi-strangulation, and then to rob.
Never tiring or lacking energy; without rest; without slowing.
Broken or strained so as to have an upward curve between the ends.
A formerly defined psychological disorder characterized by excessive preoccupation or worry about having a serious illness. No longer a current medical diagnosis; see hypochondriasis for more.
e: From New Latin hypochondria (the morbid condition so called, supposed to have its seat in the upper part of the abdomen), from hypochondrium (see English hypochondrium for more).

s: To render again with different simulated lighting conditions.
A long tunic worn in the Eastern Mediterranean.
A long dress or shirt similar in style to those worn in the Eastern Mediterranean.
e: Via Russian кафта́н, from Ottoman Turkish قفتان, from خَفْتَان, which occurs already in the Shahnameh.

s: A cut of beef taken from the thick end of the short loin; it has a T-shaped bone and a large piece of tenderloin; a porterhouse steak.
A public house where porter was sold; often also served steaks, chops etc.
The time when one takes a short sleep.
gossip; the telling of tales or of confidences
An extremely dangerous location, structure, or device.
A plot device where a villain in a story puts a hero in an elaborate dangerous situation for the purposes of attempting a sadistic murder.
A bold dance performed in groups of eight in which women lift their skirts to display their ankles.
A kind of woollen material for women's skirts.
e: First use appears c. 1750, in the sense of the dance, from French cotillon (“petticoat”), extended to the dance because of the distinctive lift of dress revealing the petticoat, from cotte (“dress”) + -illon. Said to derive from the then-popular song Ma commère, quand je danse, mon cotillion va-t-il bien.

s: To separate something into different categories, or compartments.
A small ornamental piece of lace or linen or paper used to protect a surface from scratches by hard objects such as vases or bowls; or to decorate a plate of food.
A similar circular piece of lace worn as a head-covering by some married Jewish women.
An old variety of woollen material.
e: From Doiley, the name of a 17th-century London draper. The surname is Anglo-Norman, from d'Œuilly, name of several places in Calvados, from Old French oeil (“eye”).

s: The spiracle, on the top of the head, through which cetaceans breathe.
A hole in sea ice where cetaceans and pinnipeds come to breathe.
A top-facing opening to a cavity in the ground very near an ocean's shore, leading to a marine cave from which wave water or bursts of air are expelled.
A vent for the escape of steam or other gas.
An unintended cavity filled with air in a casting product.
A vertical opening in the top of a computer case that lets hot air (primarily from the CPU heat sink) escape quickly.
To fill or be filled with air in an unintended cavity.
A joyful, somewhat muffled laugh, rather like a snorting chuckle.
A similar sounding vocalisation of various birds.
To laugh with a chortle or chortles.
e: Perhaps a chuckle + snort. Coined by Lewis Carroll in his poem Jabberwocky, completed in 1855 but only introduced to the public in his 1871 novel Through the Looking-Glass.

s: A person who recycles, or a machine used to recycle.
The act of stealing from the pocket of a passerby; the crime committed by a pickpocket.
Lacking in conscience or moral principles; unscrupulous.
One who has behaved badly, or illegally.
One not restrained by moral principles; an unscrupulous villain.
One who holds a false religious belief; a misbeliever.
e: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

s: Susceptible to being opposed or resisted.
Capable of being placed opposite something else.
The act of one who romps.
A panel or molding between the floor and the interior wall of a structure.
A similar panel at the base of a piece of furniture or equipment.
A tag with one's name inscribed on it.
Used in speech to indicate the end of a quotation.
To convert (a quoted expression) back to its original form.
e: From un- + quote; possibly an eggcorn of end quote.

s: To release from a previously locked or frozen state.
To release previously suspended financial assets.
To do an excessive amount in one area in an effort to overcome a perceived lack in another area.
To provide with excessive pay or reward for work performed.
To act in a way perceived as insecure about one's masculinity or a supposedly small penis (especially, by buying or using a large object).
In a manner that leaves no possibility of doubt.
A spraying or washing with a hose.
Overindulgence in either food or drink; overeating.
A sickness or condition caused by overindulgence.
To feed (someone) to excess (on, upon or with something).
To make (someone) sick as a result of overconsumption.
To supply (someone) with something to excess; to disgust (someone) through overabundance.
To overeat or feed to excess (on or upon something).
e: From Middle English surfeite, surfet, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit and Old French sorfet, sorfait, past participle of surfaire (“to augment, exaggerate, exceed”), from sur- (“over”) + faire (“to do”). The adjective is derived from the noun.

s: A behavior among male giraffes where they hold combat for social dominance using their necks as weapons.
Making out; kissing profusely, especially on the neck.
A Philadelphia snack food consisting of chopped steak and melted cheese in a bread roll.
To cause to be or become black.
To cook (meat or fish) by coating with pepper, etc., and quickly searing in a hot pan.
The act of one who paws.
Having been the subject of a scandal; disgraced.

A structure, usually at a circus or amusement park, enclosing several interactive attractions such as distorting mirrors, ramps, slides, stairs, rotating barrel slides, etc., that usually do not involve performers.
The section of a passenger ship that provided inexpensive accommodation with no individual cabins.
The effect of the helm on a ship.
Any plant of the genus Nigella of about twelve species of annual flowering plants, the blooms of which are generally blue in colour but also found in shades of pink, white and pale purple.
The seeds of the plant Nigella sativa, used as a culinary spice.
e: Borrowed from Nigella, from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle.

s: A multiservice tactical brevity code for communicating the altitude of friendly aircraft.{{ref|group=n|{{cite-book
Respiration, breathing, seen as a life principle or life force.
Of or pertaining to imperialism or imperialists; favoring imperialism.
Affectionate in a rather mushy or oversentimental fashion.

A quantity of thread, yarn, etc., wound on a reel then removed and loosely knotted into an oblong shape; a skein of cotton is formed by eighty turns of thread around a reel with a fifty-four inch diameter.
A thing resembling a skein (noun) of thread, yarn, etc.
The membrane of a fish ovary.
A group of wildfowl (for example, geese or swans) in flight.
A tangle, a weave, a web.
A series created by a web#Noun.
To weave or wind (thread, yarn, etc.) into a skein (noun).
To intertwine or weave (something) with another thing.
A thin strip of an osier used in basketmaking.
A metallic strengthening band or thimble on the wooden arm of an axle of a wagon.
e: The is derived from Middle English skaine, skayne (“quantity of string, thread, etc., wound on a reel; the string, thread, etc., so wound”), from Old French escaigne (modern French écagne, écaigne (Picardy)); further etymology uncertain, probably from Proto-Celtic, from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to split off”). The is derived from noun.

From Dutch scheen (“strip of metal or wood; (anatomy) shin”), from Middle Dutch schene, from Old Dutch *skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu (“bar; track; (anatomy) shin; spine”), from Proto-Germanic *skinō (“piece; plate; rim; (anatomy) shinbone”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect; to split”). Doublet of shin.

s: One who, or that which, slams.
A tequila cocktail that is slammed onto a surface to induce fizzing.
One who takes part in slam-dance.
One who competes in a poetry slam.
In the game of Pogs, the heavier piece used to strike the stack of counters.
A fraudster who carries out slamming (fraudulent changes to a customer's service).
To change the appearance of a place by altering the decor.
Any large outdoor light used to illuminate a public area, usually urban.
The light produced by these lights.
To oust or destroy the leadership or ruling body of (a government etc.).
Affection for the home and its comforts.
A pedal cycle that only has one wheel.
To travel or move around by unicycle.
A failure that leads to further misfortune.
Either of two aromatic plants, costmary or sweet yarrow.
Affectionate or sentimental in an effusive, tearful, or foolish manner, especially because of drunkenness.
Extravagantly or excessively sentimental; mawkish, self-pitying.
e: From Middle English Maudelen, a dialectal form of Mary Magdalene (typically depicted weeping), from Old French Madelaine (whence Doublet of Madeleine), from Late Latin Magdalena (see Doublet of Magdalena, Magdalene, Maudlin).

s: A former unit of volumic radioactivity: the quantity of radon (ignoring its daughters) per litre of air which ionizes a sustained current of 0.001 esu.
Glutinous rice balls flavoured with coconut and pandan.
e: + (unit) From German Mache, surname of Heinrich Mache.
+ (food) Compare Tagalog matse, masi, mutsi (“moche”). See also buchi, muah chee, 麻糍.

s: The state of having carbon dioxide gas dissolved in a liquid; the act or process of creating that state.
The amount or level of dissolved carbon dioxide remaining in solution.
The replacement of calcium hydroxide with calcium carbonate triggered by a chemical reaction.
The act or process of charging excessively
A folding knife with a blade which opens automatically (under spring pressure) when a button is pressed.
To attack or cut with a switchblade.
To (cause to) make a sudden move or transition.
To surgically remove a part of the body, especially a limb.
e: From Latin amputō (“prune, cut away”). The original sense of pruning (a tree, etc.) became obsolete. The OED considers uses related to anything other than an animal limb to be figurative uses of the modern sense.

s: Any of several fungi of the genus Melanogaster.
The motion of something that is whisked.
The movement of an animal's whiskers.
To recreate an event, especially a historical battle.
The act by which somebody or something is pelted.
To make slippery or smooth (normally to minimize friction) by applying a lubricant.
To cause someone to become drunk, especially to make them more sociable or talkative.
e: Borrowed from Latin lūbricātus, perfect passive participle of lūbricō (“make slippery”) (see -ate for more), from lūbricus (“slippery”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *slewbʰ- (“slip, slide”).

s: The process or action of spilling.
A thin, watery porridge, formerly eaten primarily by the poor and the ill.
A whirr, the sounds of a whirr.
Producing a whirr; giving off a whirring noise.
The transport of slaves, especially by sea.
A motion or gesture that swats; a swat.
The action of making an illegitimate call to the police so as to have a SWAT team dispatched to a location.
Distant from the lives and everyday concerns of ordinary people; esoteric, exclusive, select.
Elevated in style or nature, sublime; of high intellectual or moral value.
episcopal: pertaining to a bishop of any church
Resembling or characteristic of a rat; ratlike.
Crazy, mad; ridiculous; slightly strange, eccentric; also (followed by about, on, or over), attracted to, infatuated with.
Accustomed, adapted or hardened to some environment or circumstance.
Resembling beads; small, round, and gleaming.
Bright and penetrating. (of eyes or a look)
Covered or ornamented with, or as if with, beads.
A three-dimensional display of a scenery, often having a painted background in front of which models are arranged, e.g. in a museum where stuffed animals are presented against a painted landscape.
A ceiling fan whose blades are close to the ceiling.
To conceal; to lurk in ambush.
A little sip; less than a serving of some particular drink.

e: Inherited from Middle English drupi, from drup (“sad”), from Old Norse drúpr (“drooping sadness”); related to Middle English drupen, droupen (“to sag, droop”), also from Old Norse. droop + -y.

s: One who steals from the pocket of a passerby, usually by sleight of hand.
fitted or installed at a later date
Overly, affectedly or unnecessarily cute; too cute to be taken seriously.
A device for making things sharp.
An alcoholic drink taken at the start of the day, or just before a meal.
Having a specified kind of pelt.
A one-piece skintight garment with or without sleeves and without legs (often worn by gymnasts, acrobats, wrestlers, female swimmers, etc.)
An itinerant composer and performer of songs in medieval Europe; a jongleur or travelling minstrel.
e: From Old Occitan trobar (“to find”) via Old French troubadour..

s: A long loose robe worn mainly by women for sleeping in.
A marine crustacean of the subclass Cirripedia that attaches itself to submerged surfaces such as tidal rocks or the bottoms of ships.
In electrical engineering, a change made to a product on the manufacturing floor that was not part of the original product design.
On printed circuit boards, a change such as soldering a wire in order to connect two points, or addition such as an added resistor or capacitor, subassembly or daughterboard.
A deprecated or obsolete file, image or other artifact that remains with a project even though it is no longer needed.
An instrument like a pair of pincers, to fix on the nose of a vicious horse while shoeing so as to make it more tractable.
A good job, or snack easily obtained.
Infl of hafta: Contraction of has to.
A hand gesture used to depict the meaning of a song
A spear carried by early Roman legionaries.
e: Written form of a reduction of has to.

s: A part of poultry when prepared as food
A short item of news, gossip, or information.
An act of bolting or running away.
A sifting, as of flour or meal.
A private arguing of cases for practice by students, as in the Inns of Court.
A soldier trained in special infiltration tactics.
A member of the Sturmabteilung, a Nazi street militia.
(slang) Someone who is bad at aiming.
e: A calque of German Sturmtruppen, from Sturm (“storm”) + Truppen (“troops”), equivalent to storm + trooper. Sense 3 is based on the Stormtroopers from Star Wars.

s: An illegal saloon or tavern, especially one operated during the American Prohibition period in the 1920s.
In modern times, a legal bar in the style of a speakeasy, i.e. one that is hidden away and has a quiet atmosphere.
e: Deverbal from speak#Verb easy#Adverb (= speak quietly [interj.]); for the history, see Wikipedia at speakeasy § Etymology.

s: Plural of taper; thin candles used for lighting other candles.
A dish made of melted cheese, or chocolate etc., or of a boiling liquid into which food can be dipped.
To prepare or serve as a fondue.
That appeals to, or stimulates the appetite.
any food traditionally eaten with a bagel, as an accompaniment, topping or filling; including dairy products and pareve but not meat
e: Calque of French appétissant, French -ant being equivalent to -ing. See also appetite.

s: Any person involved in the production of video material, but especially a person who uses a video camera.
Having a specified kind of staple.
Agent noun of bite: someone or something who bites or tends to bite.
A fish that tends to take bait.
A person who takes up an offer or request.
A stone that barely touches the outside of the house.
One who copies someone else's work, style or techniques, especially in hip-hop.
Something (a data unit, machine etc.) with a width of a specified amount of bits.
e: From Middle English biter, bitere, equivalent to bite + -er. Cognate with West Frisian biter (“biter”), Dutch bijter (“biter”), Low German Bieter (“biter”), German Beißer (“biter”).
Representing an aphetic pronunciation of potato. Compare patater (“potato”), 'mater (“tomato”), and 'naner (“banana”).

s: To make an incorrect interpretation; to misunderstand.
