e: Likely borrowed from French amniotique, from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (“vessel for collecting the blood from sacrifices”). Equivalent to amnion + -otic.

s: A sweater that must be put on by pulling it over the head; a sweater without buttons or a zipper in front.
An exercise performed lying on the back in which the arms are extended behind the head and exertion lifts the weight above the head.
An exercise in which the gymnast pulls up from a hang lifting the legs up and over the bar thus rolling into a support position.
An instance of a vehicle being pulled over.
Being the opposite or logical inverse of a familiar person, place, or situation.
e: Variant of bizarre, equivalent to bizarre + -o; see that entry for more information. In the sense of “logical inverse”, derived via the comic book character Bizarro, an inverted version of Superman from a planet where “good” means “bad” and so on, and further popularized by "The Bizarro Jerry", a 1996 episode of the sitcom Seinfeld.

s: A stag that has failed to grow antlers; a cow that has not developed horns.
Especially in hummel corn: grain that lacks awns (beards or bristles), or has had its awns removed (barley, oats, etc.).
Of an animal: to remove the horns; to poll.
To separate (barley, oats, etc.) from the awns.

In an unapologetic manner; in a manner that withholds or refuses to offer an accompanying apology for having said or done something that causes actual or potential harm, especially when being apologetic would be appropriate.
Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
The human-readable, textual form of an assembly language instruction, not including operands.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (“pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic. Mνημονῐκός is derived from μνήμων (“mindful, remembering”) + -ῐκός; while μνήμων is from μνάομαι (“to be mindful, remember”) (from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think”)) + -μων.

Noun sense 1 (“something used to help in remembering a thing”) is borrowed from Latin mnēmonicum (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), from Ancient Greek μνημονικόν (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), a noun use of the neuter form of μνημονῐκός: see etymology 1.
Probably from skite (“to move lightly and hurriedly; to move suddenly, particularly in an oblique direction (Scotland, Northern England)”) + -ish; compare skitter.

s: The act of sending a ping, as by a submarine or over a computer network.
Any microorganism; especially, a harmful bacterium.
e: Borrowed from French microbe, from Ancient Greek μικρός (“small”) and βίος (“life”). micro- + -obe.

s: A lamp which operates by burning piped illuminating gas (or town gas).
The light produced by the burning gas in such a lamp.
To manipulate someone such that they doubt their own memory, perceptions of reality, or sanity, typically for malevolent#Adjective reasons.
To deceive, trick, or lie to.
e: From gas (“flammable gaseous hydrocarbon or hydrocarbon mixture used as a fuel”) + light.

From the 1938 stage play Gas Light by the English playwright and novelist Patrick Hamilton (1904–1962), and its 1940 and 1944 film adaptations, in which a husband attempts to convince his wife and others that she is insane by manipulating small elements of their environment. For more details, see also Gaslighting § Etymology on Wikipedia.

s: An object given by a person and retained in memory of something or someone; something kept for sentimental or nostalgic reasons.
Specifically, a type of literary album popular in the nineteenth-century, containing scraps of poetry and prose, and engravings.
Appealing or stylish in appearance or manner; classy, flashy.
Of a person: elegant in dressing; of clothes: elegant, fashionable.
Adept or ingenious in behaviour or operation; excellent, nifty.
e: Unknown; the following etymologies have been suggested.

s: Of, relating to, or having clairvoyance.
Able to see things that cannot be perceived by the normal senses.
Relating to a form of parallel processing algorithm given advance information about the problem.
A person able to see things that cannot be perceived by the normal senses
A person able to foresee the future
e: From French clairvoyant, from clair (“clear”) + voyant (“seeing”), present participle of voir (“see”).

s: One who derives pleasure through cruelty or pain to others.
e: From the name of the Marquis de Sade; see sadism.

s: A fan, especially a young female fan of a male singer or rock group, who seeks intimacy (most often physical, sometimes emotional) with a celebrity; usually with a rock 'n' roll artist or band member.
A group photo including the photographer; a group self-portrait.
e: From group + -ie. In the fan sense, from 1967.

s: A bottle, flask or similar vessel having a vacuum between its inner and outer silvered walls; designed to maintain the temperature of its contents
A unit of measure whose identification remains very unclear.
e: Genericization of the trademark Thermos, from Ancient Greek θερμός (“warm”). Possibly related to English Doublet of warm.

s: A deep-bowled spoonlike utensil with a long, usually curved, handle.
A container used in a foundry or steel mill to transport and pour out molten metal.
The float or paddle on a mill wheel.
An instrument for drawing the charge of a cannon.
A ring, with a handle or handles fitted to it, for carrying shot.
To pour or serve something with a ladle.
e: From Middle English ladel, from Old English hlædel, derived from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną (“to load”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”), same source as Lithuanian kloti (“to spread”), equivalent to lade + -le (“agent suffix”).

s: The act of one who smirks.
Mixed in a circular pattern with both original components distinguishable.
The point in the launch of a rocket or an aircraft where it leaves contact with the ground.
The point at which a person or animal leaves the ground, as for example when jumping.
The point of launching into success or action.
The necrosis and rotting of flesh, usually caused by lack of blood supply.
To corrupt; To cause to become degenerate.
e: Borrowed from French gangrène, from Latin gangraena, from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (“gangrene”).

s: A lewd and disreputable person, often female, especially an unattractive person with an air of tawdry promiscuity.
Anything that is particularly foul, unhygienic or unpleasant.
A dance performed to ska, dub, or reggae music.
A style of rhythmic guitar strumming in ska, reggae, and punk.
To play guitar with a skank rhythm.
To be dishonest or unreliable, to defraud or deceive, to steal.
The act of cheating a person.
To cheat or betray, especially a friend.
To steal, or otherwise acquire underhandedly.
e: Unknown. Perhaps from skag (“unattractive woman”), but the origins of skag are unknown. Compare scold (“troublesome woman”), skeevy (“disgusting”). Attested from the 1960s.

Originally Jamaican, attested from the twentieth century, but earliest source is uncertain. The verb sense be dishonest is evidently older. Perhaps originally Onomatopoeic. The dance senses may come from a resemblance to motorcyclists weaving between larger vehicles. Compare skanker.
Slang word used in Northern England. Unknown. Perhaps from etymology 2, above; attested in West Indian and UK black slang from the twentieth century.

s: The vice of eating to excess.
e: From Old French glutonie, from gloton + -ie, from Latin glutio, equivalent to glutton + -y.

s: Of an object: not strong or sturdy, as because of poor construction or upkeep; not safe or secure.
Affected with or suffering from rickets; rachitic.
e: From dialectal ricket (“unstable, rickety”) + -y, and/or ricket (“to move noisily and in a reckless way”) + -y. Alternatively, and perhaps less likely, from rickets + -y.

s: Having an upbeat rhythm, suitable to skip to.
Carpet or a piece of carpet, especially when speaking of installation or removal.
Moving with a slow pace or motion; not swift.
Ineffectual; slow-witted, slow to act, or dull.
Unwary; unready (especially in the phrase take (someone) tardy).
A piece of paper given to students who are late to class.
An instance of a student's being marked as tardy by a teacher on the teacher's attendance sheet.
e: From an earlier tardive, from French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus (“slow”, “sluggish”), of obscure origin.

s: A woman who has never been married, especially one past the typical marrying age according to social traditions.
One who spins (puts a spin on) a political media story so as to give something a favorable or advantageous appearance; a spin doctor, spin merchant or spinmeister.
Someone whose occupation was spinning thread.
A woman of evil life and character; so called from being forced to spin in a house of correction.
A spider; an insect (such as a silkworm) which spins thread.
e: From Middle English spynnestere (“woman who spins fibre”), from c. 1350; equivalent to spin + -ster. The semantic development is from a historical notion of unmarried women spinning thread for a living.

s: The act of fastening a buckle.
A folding into hills and valleys.
The action of giving in (slightly) to pressure or stress by developing a bulge, bending or kinking (with the eventual risk of collapsing).
A young male domestic goat of between one and two years.
e: From the verb to buckle, equivalent to buckle + -ing.
From German Bückling or Swedish böckling. Cognate with Middle High German bockinc and Middle Dutch bocking (itself from bok (“buck”), referencing the foul smell).

s: The smooth transformation of one image into another using digital tweening.
To fall upon; fall all over; overtake.
Case; instance; circumstance; event; incident; accident.
e: From Middle English bifallen, from Old English befeallan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifallan, from Proto-Germanic *bifallaną; equivalent to be- + fall.

s: The act or process by which something is sanded; the application of sandpaper, etc.
A type of dancing where the floor is covered in sand. See Sanding (dance).
The process of testing the surface of gilding, after it has been fired, with fine sand and water.
The process of burying oysters in sand.
The process of applying sand to rails in railway track to aid adhesion.
A coating of sugar crystals on confectionery, especially on jellies.
The act of giving a frown.
The individual in a graduating class who delivers the farewell or valedictory address, often the person who graduates with the highest grades.
The individual in a graduating class who graduates with the highest grades.
e: Formed 1759, from valedictory (“of a speech made when leaving”) + -an.

s: The act or result of making a burrow.
To refuse to own, or to refuse to acknowledge one’s own.
To repudiate any connection to; to renounce.
To detach (a job or process) so that it can continue to run even when the user who launched it ends his/her login session.
The act by which something is flung.
Having one or more nicks; notched.
Affected or covered with scurf or scabs; scurfy, scabby; also, of or relating to a skin disease causing scurf or to scurvy.
Of growths on plants: resembling scurf; scurfy.
Of a person or thing: disgustingly mean; contemptible, despicable, low.
Of the way someone is treated: poor, shabby.

A disease caused by insufficient intake of vitamin C, leading to the formation of livid spots on the skin, spongy gums, loosening of the teeth, and bleeding into the skin and from almost all mucous membranes; an occurrence of this disease.
A cattle disease, perhaps affecting the skin.
Mawkishly good; weakly benevolent or pious.
A well-behaved person with no obvious human failings, with the possible exception of smugness and self-satisfaction.
A long rope with a sliding loop on one end, generally used in ranching to catch cattle and horses.
An image-editing function allowing the user to capture an irregularly-shaped object by drawing an approximate outline.
e: From Spanish lazo, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lace.

s: In a horrible or terrible manner; in a terrifying way.
e: From Middle English grisely, grysly, grissliȝ, griselich, grislich, from Old English grisliċ (“grisly, horrible; dreadful, horrid”), from grīsan (“to shudder with horror; to tremble, to be terrified; to make tremble, to terrify; to agrise, grise”) (unattested but implied in āgrīsan) + -lic.
From grisle (“horror, terror”) + -ly; compare Middle Dutch griselike, Middle Low German grislike.

s: A person who owns, plays or practices with the saxophone.
An older person who accompanies other younger people to ensure the propriety of their behaviour, often an older woman accompanying a young woman.

A protein that assists the non-covalent folding/unfolding and the assembly/disassembly of other macromolecular structures, but does not occur in these structures when the latter are performing their normal biological functions.
An employee sent by a British company to the European Union to work with a client there, to circumvent restrictions imposed after Brexit.
A great amount of amusement, usually accompanied by much laughter.
e: From Latin hilaritās (“cheerfulness”), from hilaris (“cheerful”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (“cheerful”). la:hilarō + -i- + -ty.

s: Having a punch; effective; forceful; spirited; vigorous.
Involving or resembling a punch with the fist.
Behaving or appearing punch-drunk, reacting poorly.
Of groomed snow: unable to support the weight of a skier, especially when the skier’s weight is all on one ski, resulting in a ski punching through the surface of the snow.
The motion of something that twirls.
To lay (someone, or part of their body) down to rest.
To rest (oneself), especially by going to sleep.
Followed by from or (obsolete) of: to cause (oneself) to take a rest from some activity; also, to allow (oneself) to recover from some activity.
To lean or recline, sit down, or lie down to rest; to rest.
Followed by on or upon: of a thing: to lie or be physically positioned on something, especially horizontally; to rest on or be supported by something.
Followed by on or upon: of light, a look, etc.: to fall or rest (and often remain for a while) on something; to alight, to dwell.
Followed by on or upon: to be based on; to depend or rely on.
To cease activity to rest or recover; also, to have a period free from activity or disturbance.
To have faith in; to confide, to trust.
Temporary cessation from activity to rest and recover, especially in the form of sleep; rest; an instance of this; a break, a rest; a sleep.
The state of being peacefully inactive or relaxed, or being free from disturbances or worries; calmness, ease, peace, quietness.
Calmness of the mind or temperament; composure.
Of the face, a muscle, etc.: the state of being relaxed and not in tension.
The state of lying still and unmoving; calmness, tranquillity; an instance of this.
Relief or respite from something exhausting or unpleasant; an instance of this.
Unimportant or insubstantial talk, events, or actions; drivel.
To spit, vent, or eject, as froth.
(literally) To spew saliva as froth; (figuratively) to rage, vent one's anger.
e: From Middle English froth, frooth, froþ, likely a borrowing from Old Norse froða, from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ; Old English āfrēoþan (“to foam, froth”) is from same Germanic root. Verb attested from late 14th century. Compare Swedish fradga.

s: A person who wanders from place to place; a nomad, a wanderer.
A person without settled employment or habitation who usually supports himself or herself by begging or some dishonest means; a tramp, a vagabond.
Any member of the species Vagrans egista of widely distributed Asian butterflies of the family Nymphalidae.
An animal, typically a bird, found outside its species' usual range.
Wandering from place to place, particularly when without any settled employment or habitation.
Of or pertaining to a vagabond or vagrant, or a person fond of wandering.
Moving without a certain direction; roving, wandering; also, erratic, unsettled.
e: From Middle English vagraunt, vagaraunt (“having no proper employment; having a tendency to go astray or wander; wayward”), from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”); see further at etymology 1.

s: In the singular number; in terms of a single thing.
Any computer that has a far greater processing power than others of its generation.
In an energetic manner; with great energy.
Past the middle of life; in the third stage.
Relating to colors associated with autumn.
Subject to frequent changes in direction.
Moving from one object to another; not looking directly and steadily at the person with whom one is speaking.
Having the appearance of being dishonest, criminal or unreliable.
full of, or ready with, shifts or expedients.
To utter words indistinctly or unintelligibly; to utter inarticulate sounds
To talk incoherently; to utter meaningless words.
To talk too much; to chatter; to prattle.
To make a continuous murmuring noise, like shallow water running over stones.
To utter in an indistinct or incoherent way; to repeat words or sounds in a childish way without understanding.
To reveal; to give away (a secret).
Inarticulate speech; constant or confused murmur.
A sound like that of water gently flowing around obstructions.
A plant of the Brassicaceae family, Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus, having an edible root.
The root of this plant used as food. Some varieties are pungent and usually eaten raw in salads, etc., while others have a milder taste and are cooked.
Some other root plant of genus Raphanus or family Brassicaceae.
e: From Middle English radiche, from Old English rǣdiċ, from Proto-West Germanic *rādik, borrowed from Latin rādīcem (“root of a plant; radish”); later influenced by Anglo-Norman radich and Middle French radice, borrowed from Italian radice, from the same Latin source. Doublet of radix.

s: Used to express sudden or exuberant joy, happiness, excitement, approval or delight.
A room near the rear of a premises.
Especially, one that is only accessible to a privileged few and can be used as an inconspicuous meeting place, where secrecy, anonymity and even crooked dealings may occur.
A storeroom in the rear of the premises.
Having a mental age of between seven and twelve years.
Behaving in the manner of a moron; idiotic; stupid.
Any of many herbs, of the genus Ranunculus, having yellow flowers; the crowfoot.
Any flower of the genus Narcissus; a daffodil.
An affectionate or ironic term of address.
e: From butter + cup. Both and are from the flowers' association with butter, from their yellow colour. Compare butterflower for a similar derivation; outside of English, compare Dutch boterbloem, German Butterblume.

s: A dialogue between master and student designed to obtain an intuitive truth.
e: From the title of the 1962 Italian cult documentary film Mondo cane, Italian for "A Dog's World", from mondo (“world”) and cane (“dog”). The film featured bizarre scenes, leading to English use of mondo as an adverb meaning "very, extremely" in mock-Italian phrases like mondo bizarro. Doublet of monde.

s: Having the characteristics of a quilt; specifically, having two layers of cloth sewn together, with a layer of padding between them.
Having characteristics that approximate the above to some degree.
Without the ability to help oneself.
Without the ability to react actively.
Relating to the 200th anniversary of an event or happening.
The 200th anniversary of an event or happening.
The act or process of soaking or boiling cloth in an alkaline liquid in the operation of bleaching.
The liquid used in this process.
The process of breaking up or pulverizing ores.
The process of cutting a felled and delimbed tree into logs.
The act of a quadruped kicking both hind legs upward at once.

An instrument or tool used for picking things up without touching them with the hands or fingers, consisting of two slats or grips hinged at the end or in the middle, and sometimes including a spring to open the grips.

A large scissors-like two-piece center-hinged forged-iron implement with oval-loop handles and with pointed tips turned inward (in the same plane as and perpendicular to the handles) to facilitate lifting and carrying a block of ice. Often called ice tongs.
e: From Middle English tonges, equivalent to tong (“tool for manipulating things in a fire”) + -s.

s: The act by which something is crammed, or stuffed full.
An intensive course of hard study, as for an examination.
Pertaining to antiquaries, or to antiquity.
A collector or student of, or expert in, antiquities or antiques.
A bitless headpiece of rope or straps, placed on the head of animals such as cattle or horses to lead or tie them.
A rope with a noose, for hanging criminals; the gallows rope.
One who halts or limps; a cripple.
e: From Middle English halter, helter, helfter, from Old English hælfter, hælftre (“halter”), from Proto-West Germanic *halftrijā (“harness”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut”), equivalent to half + ter.

s: A companion for someone (especially a child) to play with.
e: From play + mate. Compare earlier playfeer (“playmate”) of similar construction.

s: A device in an internal combustion engine where fuel is atomized (vaporized) and mixed with air before intake and ignition.
A device for enhancing illuminating gas by mixing in carbon-rich fuel.
A water pipe or bong; a device or contrivance for mixing air with burning cannabis or cocaine.
e: Attested from 1862, from carburet + -or. The motor vehicle sense is attested since 1896.

s: A showing of a movie, sporting event, or theatrical performance in the morning or afternoon.
A woman's dress to be worn in the morning or before dinner.
To put on a matinee performance (of).
Seedlike; having the flavour of seeds.
Having a peculiar flavour supposed to be derived from the weeds growing among the vines; said of certain kinds of French brandy.
Shabby, run-down, possibly connected with bad, dishonest or illegal activities, somewhat disreputable.
Suffering the effects of a hangover.
e: From Middle English sedy, equivalent to seed + -y. The senses with negative connotation, first attested by 1725 in slang, originally especially “poor, out of money”, probably arose from the metaphor of a flower that has gone to seed, and is no longer considered beautiful.

s: In a skillful manner; with skill.
A book, used by a student, in which answers and workings may be entered besides questions and exercises.
A book, used by a business, containing a record of work to be done, or work completed.
A collection of spreadsheets stored in the same file.
Undergraduate education; the status or period of being an undergraduate student.
The act of thinking too much about something.
Articles made from glass, especially drinking glasses, jugs and other tableware made of glass.
Having died as a result of suffocation.
A small industrial vehicle with a power-operated fork-like pronged platform that can be raised and lowered for insertion under a load, often on pallets, to be lifted and moved.
To move or stack with, or as if with, such a vehicle.
Any of various venomous American snakes, of genera Crotalus and Sistrurus, having a rattle at the end of its tail.
The act by which something is pecked.
The ancient skill of shaping stone into tools, containers, or artworks.
The game of throwing pebbles at birds.
An undercover agent, spy or intelligence analyst.
A metaphysical manifestation; an artificial distinction or construct.
A player who engages in hole carding by attempting to glimpse the dealer's hole card when the dealer checks under an ace or a 10 to see if a blackjack is present.
To frighten or make nervous (especially by startling).
e: Borrowed from Dutch spook (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch spooc (“spook, ghost”), from Old Dutch *spōk, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *spōk. Cognate with Middle Low German spôk, spûk (“apparition, ghost”), Middle High German gespük (“a haunting”), German Spuk, Danish spøge (“to haunt”), Swedish spöke (“ghost”).

s: Excessively concerned with rules and order, always serious.
A violation of a law, duty or commandment.
An act that goes beyond generally accepted boundaries.
A relative rise in sea level resulting in deposition of marine strata over terrestrial strata.
e: From Middle English transgressioun, from Old French transgression, from Late Latin trānsgressiō, from Latin trānsgressus (perfect active participle of trānsgredior (“to step across”)) + -iō.

s: To make final or firm; to finish or complete.
To prepare (an object) for garbage collection by calling its finalizer.
A derogatory hint or reference to, or (often sexual) insinuation about, a person or thing.
A remark that is suggestive of something sexual without stating it explicitly.
A rhetorical device with an omitted but obvious conclusion, made to increase the force of an argument.
Part of a pleading in cases of libel and slander, pointing out what and who was meant by the libellous matter or description.
To interpret (something libellous or slanderous) in terms of what was implied.
e: From the Latin innuendō (“by nodding”), ablative singular form of innuendum (“a nodding”), gerund of innuō (“to give a nod”).

s: A synthetic fibre known for its exceptional elasticity.
e: Coined as an anagram of the word expands.

s: The shelf above a fireplace which may be also a structural support for the masonry of the chimney.
A maneuver to surmount a ledge, involving pushing down on the ledge to bring up the body.
To surmount a ledge by pushing down on the ledge to bring up the body.
e: Middle English ang A variant of mantle (“cloak, robe”) now distinguished in sense.

s: Capable of being reclined, or moved into a more horizontal position.
Bending away from the perpendicular; recumbent.
The act of one who reclines.
Deeply divided; cut into many segments.
One or more loans or other borrowings that repay and replace previous financings.
Fat that, after roasting a joint, hardens and crispens
The crispy rind of roast pork.
A crispy, fried skin or rind, especially of pork.
The making of small, sharp cracks or reports, frequently repeated.
Food for dogs, made from the refuse of tallow melting.
Three stripes of velvet worn on the sleeves of students at St John's College, Cambridge.
Sounding with small, sharp cracks or reports, frequently repeated.
Able to be masked by a dominant allele or trait.
Not dominant; whose effect is masked by stronger effects.
e: From Latin recēdō ive, or directly from New Latin recessīvus.

s: A device with a canister holding medicine (either in powder or gas form) which is sprayed and inhaled by the patient, often for treating asthma and other respiratory diseases.
A hot tub or whirlpool bath with underwater jets that massage the body.

e: Written form of a reduction of could have.

s: A band passed under the belly of an animal, which holds a saddle or a harness saddle in place.
The part of an animal around which the girth fits.
One's waistline circumference, most often a large one.
A small horizontal brace or girder.
The distance measured around an object; the circumference.
The length of the shortest cycle in a graph.
To bind as if with a girth or band.
e: From Middle English girth, gerth, gyrth, from Old Norse gjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *gerdō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- (“to encircle, enclose; belt”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌰, Icelandic gjörð. Also related to German Gurt, English gird, Albanian ngërthej (“to tie, bind, fasten”).

s: to change the appearance, layout, or furnishings of
Proivided with, or strengthened by, iron; shod with iron.
That has been put in irons; shackled.
That has been pressed or smoothed with a hot iron; pressed.
(Of hair) Treated as with a hair iron; curled with a curling iron, or straightened with a straightening-iron or with electric straighteners.
Of, or relating to symbiosis; living together.
Of a relationship with mutual benefit between two individuals, organisms, or groups.
A Mexican dish of tortilla chips, covered in melted cheese and sometimes other ingredients.
e: Thumb Borrowed from nachos, from Nacho. Nacho is a common diminutive form of Ignacio (“Ignatius”) in Spanish. The Mexican creator of the dish, Ignacio Anaya (1895–1975), named it after himself in 1943: Nacho's Especiales.

s: The act of using a paddle.
An act of corporal punishment consisting of spanking the buttocks with a paddle.
A group of ducks (mallards, etc.) on the water.
A profitable product or scheme; something that brings in good money.
That splits into two or more directions, or parts.
Having forks (parts into which anything is furcated or divided).
A courgette; a variety of squash, Cucurbita pepo, which bears edible fruit.
The edible fruit of this variety of squash.
e: Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino, diminutive of zucca (“squash”). Ultimately related to courgette through the original Latin cucurbita. Compare Sicilian cucuzza.

s: A plant, Foeniculum vulgare, of the parsley family, which has a sweet, anise-like flavor.
The bulb, leaves, or stalks of the plant, eaten as a vegetable.
The seeds of the fennel plant used as a spice in cooking.
The quality or degree of being tight.
Having been enhanced by electronic, mechanical, or mechatronical parts; cyborg.
e: bio- + electronic. The superhuman sense is attributed to the TV shows The Six Million Dollar Man (1973–1978) and The Bionic Woman (1976–1978).

s: Of a rail vehicle, having a through brake pipe, without the vehicle having brakes operating from it.
To rotate, revolve, spin or turn rapidly.
To have a sensation of spinning or reeling.
To make something or someone whirl.
To remove or carry quickly with, or as with, a revolving motion; to snatch.
Something that whirls, such as a whirlwind.
One or both regions of the Earth where it snows the year round; the Arctic and/or Antarctic.
A musical wind instrument with a series of holes for the player to blow into, each hole producing a different note.
A toy instrument of strips of glass or metal hung on tapes, struck with hammers.
The act by which something is stifled.
A sheep that is losing or has lost its teeth.
Covered with gum or a substance resembling gum.
e: From gum (“(substance)”) + -y. The noun was influenced by gummi (from German).

s: Speech or writing that is unintelligible, incoherent or meaningless.
Needlessly obscure or overly technical language.
A language game, comparable to pig Latin, in which one inserts a nonsense syllable before the first vowel in each syllable of a word.
e: First attested mid-16th century. Origin Unknown. Possibly from *gibber, of onomatopoeic origin imitating to the sound of chatter, possibly from or influenced by jabber, ish denoting the name of a language (compare English, Finnish, Spanish, etc.). The verb gibber, first attested circa 1600, is usually regarded as a back-formation from gibberish.
Borrowed from Late Latin reprehensibilis, from Latin reprehendo; equivalent to reprehend + -ible.

s: The quality or state of being inferior.
The quality of being a competitive disadvantage.
Of, relating to or exhibiting misogyny.
A looking inward; specifically, the act or process of self-examination, or inspection of one's own thoughts and feelings; the cognition which the mind has of its own acts and states.
e: From Latin intrōspectiō, noun of action (with -iō) from past-participle (intrōspectus) stem of intrōspiciō (“to look into, look at, examine, observe attentively”), from intro- (“inward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look at”). introspect + -ion.

s: The act or motion of something that gushes.
A vehicle, generally pulled by an animal, which moves over snow or ice on runners, used for transporting persons or goods. (contrast "sled", which is smaller)
To ride or drive a sleigh.
e: From Modern Dutch slee, from Middle Dutch slede, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slidô. Doublet of sled and further related to slide.

s: The act of one who toys.
Darkened to the point of appearing black; as

e: Eye dialect form of a reduction of would have.

s: To compel (a person or persons) to leave.
To throw out or remove forcefully.
To compel (a sports player) to leave the field because of inappropriate behaviour.
To forcefully project oneself or another occupant from an aircraft (or, rarely, another type of vehicle), typically using an ejection seat or escape capsule.
To cause (something) to come out of a machine.
To come out of a machine.
an inferred object of someone else's consciousness
e: From Middle French éjecter, from Latin ēiectus, perfect passive participle of ēiciō (“to throw out”), or from ēiectō, the frequentative form of the same verb, from ē-, combining form of ex (“out”), + iaciō (“to throw”).
From Latin ēiectum (“(that which is) thrown out”), from ēiciō (“to throw out”) (see Etymology 1). Coined by W. K. Clifford by analogy with subject and object.

s: A small enclosed structure, often freestanding, open on one side or with a window, used as a booth to sell newspapers, cigarettes, etc.
A similar but unattended stand for the automatic dispensing of tickets, etc; an e-kiosk.
e: Earlier kiosque, from French kiosque, from Italian chiosco, from Ottoman Turkish كوشك, from کوشْک (“palace, portico”), from Middle Persian kwšk'.

s: To read or interpret in a new way.
The act of reading something again.
Having or exhibiting good taste; aesthetically pleasing or conforming to expectations or ideals of what is appropriate.
The act of putting anything into a bag.
Cloth or other material for bags.
Use of BVM to ventilate a patient.
A type of hammer with a larger-than-usual head made of wood, rubber or similar non-iron material, used by woodworkers for driving a tool, such as a chisel. A kind of maul.
A weapon resembling the tool, but typically much larger.
A small hammer-like tool used for playing certain musical instruments.
A light beetle with a long handle used in playing croquet.
The stick used to strike the ball in the sport of polo.
To beat or strike with, or as if with, a mallet.
Having the property of being a snob; arrogant and pretentious; smugly superior or dismissive of perceived inferiors.
Of a patient or child, stained or dirtied by defecation.
Having a specific or particular type of soil.
That has been fed or nourished with green fodder.
A person who (habitually) urinates in their bed (during sleep).
A wart, especially one that grows on the foot, caused by a human papilloma virus.
A sexine element similar to a wart.
Characteristic of a cretin; very stupid.
A self-contained page or group of pages meant to supplement a larger website.
A small area with distinctive ecological characteristics.
A carrier around a projectile in a firearm, cannon or other type of artillery piece that precisely holds the projectile within the barrel.
To enclose (a projectile) in a sabot.
e: Early 17th century, borrowed from Middle French sabot (see French sabot below). Doublet of sabaton, ciabatta.

s: A use of the mystical term ‘abracadabra’, supposed to work as part of a healing charm or a magical spell; any spell or incantation making use of the word.
Arcane and obscure language of occult rituals or mystical practices.
Mumbo jumbo; obscure language or technicalities; jargon.
Used to indicate that a magic trick or other illusion has been performed.
To unfasten by means of hooks.
To unfasten the bra of (its wearer).
Alternative spelling of anesthetist; an anaesthesiologist.
A type of undergarment worn by cheerleaders under their skirts in place of panties.
e: Shortened form of lollipop pants, which was the standard form in Rhode Island at least through the mid 1980s. It is not known when the shortened form became the standard term.

s: Having a rosy or pale red colour; ruddy.
In a blatant, vivid, or highly disorganized state.
Flourishing; in the bloom of health.
e: From French floride (“flourishing”), from Latin floridus (“flowery, blooming”). Doublet of Florida.

s: Referring to something that has been struck by vandalism
Having the ability to be bent easily.
Of a person, flexible; having the ability to bend easily; resilient.
Divided into diagonal bands of colour.
A field divided diagonally into several bends, varying in metal and colour.
e: From Middle English bendee, from Old French bendé. right|thumb|Bendy of six, or and gules.

s: Situated under one's foot or feet.
In the way; placed so as to obstruct or hinder.
In the way; situated so as to obstruct or hinder.
A storage compartment that sits below the deck of a boat.
To provide a footing beneath; to shore up or underpin.
To assign a column summary that is less than the sum of all the entries in that column.
e: From Middle English underfoote, underfote, equivalent to under- + foot. Cognate with Middle Dutch ondervoet (“underfoot”). Compare also Middle Low German undervôt (“pedestal, base”).

s: Tall, slim, and rather ungraceful or awkward.
Pertaining to, or suffering from, anorexia nervosa.
Having very little to no appetite (a symptom that occurs in various diseases).
Tending to talk excessively about oneself.
Believing oneself to be better and more important than others due to one's position, popularity, wealth, appearance, etc.
by confusion of the similar words
A lightweight, two-wheeled vehicle equipped with a small motor and pedals, designed to go no faster than some specified speed limit.
e: [[File:Honda Hobbit.jpg|thumb|Honda PA50 step-through moped (European market)]] Borrowed from Swedish moped.

s: In the form of coils; having coils.
Prepared and poised to act, like a snake that has coiled its lower body so it can strike.
The study of the skin and its diseases.
e: From Ancient Greek δέρμα (“skin, hide”) + -logy. Analysable as dermato- + -logy.

s: One who shows extreme love and admiration for themself.
An egoist; a person full of egoism and pride.
e: From Narcissus (“a character in Greek mythology who became obsessed with his own reflection”) + -ist.

s: A man who makes or sells butter.
A highly skilled and dedicated member of the police.

e: Unknown; possibly coined in the 19th century.

s: A person who is intoxicated, especially one who is habitually drunk.
To cause to be drunk; to intoxicate.
To disorder the senses of; to exhilarate, elate or stupefy as if by spirituous drink.
One who participates in proof of stake.

e: From Middle English trecher, from Old French trecheor (modern tricheur), from trechier, tricher (“to cheat, trick”). Compare English trick.

s: Under the astrological influence of the planet Jupiter.
In a jovial manner; jollily, merrily.
A dish of minced meat made up like a pudding, and boiled in a shape or mould.
To express contempt for (laws, rules, etc.) by word or action.
The act by which something is flouted; violation of a law.
e: Perhaps from Middle English flouten (“to play the flute”); compare with Dutch fluiten.

s: The short coarser fibers of flax or hemp; tow.
e: From Middle English herdes, hurdes, plural of herde (“piece of hards”), from Old English heordan (“hards of flax, tow”), weak feminine plural of heorde (“headhair”), from Proto-West Germanic *heʀdā, from Proto-Germanic *hezdǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to comb, card”).

s: In an arrogant manner; with undue pride or self-importance.
To be guilty of, or responsible for a crime etc; to commit.
e: From Middle English perpetrat (“committed, perpetrated”), from Latin perpetrātus, past participle of perpetrāre (“to carry through”).
From naive + -ity, English analogue of naïveté (naïf + -eté) borrowed from French.

s: A person who is addicted to or regularly uses crack cocaine.
Someone whose thinking makes no sense; a fool or an idiot; broadly, any contemptible person.
e: From crack + -head. First sense appears c. 1978. Second sense appears c. 1977 in Best Canadian Stories.

s: A person who fells trees; a lumberjack
A person who fells a seam.
An appliance to a sewing machine for felling a seam.
e: Variant of fellow that reflects the reduction of the last vowel to a schwa and its conflation with the endings -er/-ar.

s: That thieves; that steals; inclined to steal
Unable to be changed without exception.
Not able to be altered in the memory after its value is set initially.
A tool consisting of two blades with bevel edges, connected by a pivot, used for cutting cloth, or for removing the fleece from sheep etc.
The bedpiece of a machine tool, upon which a table or slide rest is secured.

An apparatus for raising heavy weights, and especially for stepping and unstepping the lower masts of ships. It consists of two or more spars or pieces of timber, fastened together near the top, steadied by a guy or guys, and furnished with the necessary tackle. Also sheers.
Anything resembling a pair of shears in shape or motion, such as a pair of wings.
A machine for applying size to warp yarns.
A horror movie with graphic blood and violence; a slasher movie.
A murderer in such a film.
One who writes slash fiction and/or supports male/male ships.
Like a bush in having many branches that spread out densely in all directions.
Of, relating to, or being the person or entity after which someone or something is named; serving as an eponym.
Of a thing: named after a person or entity.
e: From Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (“concerning giving one’s name to something; named in a significant manner; surnamed”) + English -ous. epi- + -onymous.

s: An assignment, project or task that a student is required to complete as part of a particular course, which is then assessed and counts towards the grade given.
The tinkling sound of light piano music.
The act by which somebody is dandled.
Failure to assert a legal right in a way that implies that it is being given up.
e: From Middle English taciturnite, or alternatively from taciturn + -ity; both ultimately from Latin taciturnitās.

s: Fat or puffed out in the cheeks.
The practice of forcing unwilling participants to vote, often several times over, for a particular candidate in an election.
To write or speak at length; to be copious in argument or discussion.
To range at large, or without restraint.
To expand; to spread; to extend; to diffuse; to broaden.
e: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).
From Middle English opprobrious, from Middle French opprobrieux and its etymon Late Latin opprobriōsus.

s: Expressing annoyance or irritation towards the mentioned thing.
clothing worn next to the skin; underwear.
To swell up (of water, waves etc.); to overflow, to surge (of bodily fluids).
To contribute to an advantage or disadvantage for someone or something.
To contribute to the honour, shame etc. of a person or organisation.
To reflect (honour, shame etc.) to or onto someone.
To attach, come back, accrue to someone; to reflect back on or upon someone (of honour, shame etc.).
To roll back; to be sent or driven back.
A coming back, as an effect or consequence; a return.
e: From Anglo-Norman redunder, Middle French redonder, and their source, Latin redundō, from red- + undō (“surge”), from unda (“a wave”).

s: Of or relating to love, especially sexual love.
e: From Latin amātōrius (“pertaining to love or a lover”), from amātor (“a lover”), from amō (“to love”).

s: A station, as for police, customs agents, palanquin-bearers, etc.
e: Borrowed from Hindi चौकी and Urdu چَوکی (“post, police station, etc.”).

s: A woodpecker of the eastern United States (of the genus Sphyrapicus) that feeds mainly on the sap of trees
Any woodpecker that punctures the bark of trees and feeds upon the sap.
A person, usually male, especially one who behaves in an objectionable or pitiable manner.
A man or child, especially an annoying one.
a shrub of species Kalmia angustifolia.

A competitive game in which the objective is to flick as many small discs (each called a tiddlywink or wink) as possible into a container (the pot) by pressing on their edges with a larger disc (a shooter or squidger), causing them to jump up from the surface on which they are placed.
Especially in the form to play tiddlywinks: a meaningless or unimportant activity.
An area of grassland available as pasture for cattle.
The exposing of linen in fields to air and light for bleaching purposes.
The covering of land with grass.
(by extension of sense 1, and by analogy to slang tasty) Sexually attractive.
Having a pleasing texture when bitten.
of a bicycle, horse, or the like
of a path, road, or the like
Fit to be traveled on bicycle, horseback, etc.
Any small vehicle, such as an electric scooter, designed to be used by a single person.
The act of one who hews or chops.
The act of making a tut sound in disapproval.
A modern street dance style in which dancers position body parts in angular positions, especially moving the hands and fingers in intricate ways (finger-tutting).
e: From the English nickname Tut for Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun, likening the geometric positions and right angles of the dance style to the perceived angularity of ancient Egyptian at.

s: To act or speak in a futile, ineffective, or nonsensical manner.
e: Unknown, 1847. Perhaps piddle + trifle, perhaps puff (“(onomatopoeia, puff of air)”) + -le (“diminutive”).

s: A worthless mixture, especially of liquors.
One who supports policy favouring war.
e: From the minced oath by jingo, which was used in a music hall song, written ca. 1878 by G. W. Hunt, that supported Britain's then belligerent attitude towards Russia. In this context, a euphemism for Jesus, influenced by the meaningless presto-jingo used by conjurors. A connection with the Basque jainko (“god”) has been suggested, but evidence is lacking.

s: A lottery in which the prize or prizes constitute all the money paid by the participants.
Any member of a class of molluscs (Gastropoda) that includes snails, slugs, and limpets; univalve mollusc.
In a tolerable manner; to an extent that can be tolerated.
not invited, requested or asked for
Who walks while dragging or shuffling the feet.
Clothes worn at nighttime or in bed, such as pyjamas
An expression of mild surprise or annoyance.
e: An alteration of earlier Gemini (“an expression of mild surprise or annoyance”); see there for more.

s: Injured, or not functioning properly (with respect to legs).
e: Origin obscure and uncertain. Possibly from the English dialectal (North Midlands) adjective game (“lame”), Welsh cam (“crooked”), or from Irish cam (“bent”), by way of. Compare also Old Occitan gambi (“lame, limping”), related to Old Occitan gamba (“leg”) (see also French jambe (“leg”), English gam).

s: A soft-bodied invertebrate of the phylum Mollusca, typically with a hard shell of one or more pieces.
To walk, move or stand unsteadily or falteringly; threatening to fall.
To be on the brink of collapse.
Having romantic feelings for; excited or enthusiastic about.
Of an egg: cooked so that the yolk remains runny and can be used for dipping.
To a great or impressive degree; very.
A cone-shaped tent traditionally used by many native peoples of the Great Plains of North America.
A conical formation of small flammable sticks leaning on each other, in roughly the shape of an Indian teepee, built over smaller tinder such as cotton or leaves.
e: From the word thípi (/ˈtʰipi/), which consists of two elements: the verb thí (“to dwell”), and pi, a pluralising enclitic (a suffix-like ending that marks the subject of the verb as plural), which means they dwell. Lakota verbs can be used as nouns and this is the case with thípi, which in practice simply means house.

s: of a word, shortened by syncope
of a rhythm, modified by syncopation
Not inclined; having a disinclination; being unwilling, reluctant.
A building providing sleeping quarters for workers or guests, especially in a rural setting.
Especially of a person: deserving of disgrace or dishonour; contemptible, despicable.
Causing or marked by disgrace or dishonour; disgraceful, dishonourable; also, humiliating, shameful.
The sound of walking with heavy footfalls.
A toy that rights itself when pushed over.
A short, plump person (especially a child).
A forward roll or sideways roll.
Synonym of tumbleweed; specifically, the prickly Russian thistle (Kali tragus or Salsola tragus).
A baked or steamed pudding made from suet pastry which is spread with fruit or jam (or occasionally other fillings) and then rolled up.

In full roly-poly bug: a small terrestrial invertebrate which tends to roll into a ball when disturbed, such as a woodlouse (suborder Oniscidea, especially a pill bug (family Armadillidiidae) or a sowbug (family Porcellionidae)) or a pill millipede (superorder Oniscomorpha).
A mischievous or worthless person; a scoundrel, a rascal.
An activity or game involving rolling.
A game involving people (usually children) rolling down a slope.
A game in which balls are rolled along the floor to knock down pins, or bowled into holes, or thrown into hats placed on the ground.
Moving with a rolling and swaying motion.
By rolling, so as to roll.
Without hesitating; directly; hence, in a thoughtless manner; indiscriminately.
e: The noun is apparently derived from roll (“to turn over and over”) + -y, reduplicated with a change of the initial consonant. Compare rolly (“having the ability to roll, rolling”), which is attested since the 19th century. (“mischievous or worthless person”) is possibly influenced by poll (“head; (archaic) scalp; (by extension) person”).

s: The topmost covering of a bed, often functioning as a blanket.
To breathe hard, and with an audible piping or whistling sound, as persons affected with asthma.
To convulse with laughter; to become breathless due to intense laughing.
To make a sound that resembles the sound of human wheezing.
A piping or whistling sound caused by difficult respiration.
An ordinary whisper exaggerated so as to produce the hoarse sound known as the "stage whisper"; a forcible whisper with some admixture of tone.
A sound that resembles a human wheezing.
e: From Middle English whesen, perhaps from Old Norse hvæsa (“to hiss”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwes- (“to pant”).

s: To give life or spirit to; to revive or animate.
To make more lively, cheerful or interesting.
In a fearful manner; characterized by fear.
Something difficult (e.g. a given puzzle) or unpleasant (e.g. negative review, nasty letter).
Any of several species of large Antarctic petrels which feed on blubber and carrion and have an offensive odour, such as the giant fulmar.
An eastern long-necked turtle (which emits a foul-smelling musk when threatened).
The act of pelting with eggs.
The act of gathering the eggs of wild birds.
The property of being lucid; lucidness.
The state of being aware that one is dreaming, i.e. being in a lucid dream.
A person who is not reputable.
The game played by throwing horseshoes toward a metal stake.
In the shape of a cup; concave.
The property of being unpleasant or disagreeable.
normally confined to the expression come a cropper
A fall, a tumble; a decided failure.
A breed of domestic pigeon with large crop.
A person who nurtures and gathers a crop.
A variety of plant producing a good harvest.
A machine for cropping, as for shearing off bolts or rod iron, or for facing cloth.
e: From crop + -er, in reference to a bird's crop.
From crop + -er or er, in reference to agricultural crops.
From Middle English chivalerous, from Old French chevalerous; see chivalry.

s: To give and receive reciprocally; to exchange.
To use or pass about casually.
To throw or strike reciprocally, like balls in sports.
A winter sport played on ice, from which ice hockey developed.
A club bent at the lower part for striking a ball at play; a hockey stick.
A carriage or cart used in India, especially one drawn by bullocks.
e: From French bander (“to bandy at tennis”), with -y, -ie added due to influence from Spanish and Portuguese bandear and/or Old Occitan bandir (“to throw”), from the same root as English band. Compare also with banter.
Probably from the verb bandy in the sense "toss/bat back and forth", or possibly from the Welsh word bando, most likely derived from the Proto-Germanic *bandją (“a curved stick”).

s: A large fire extending to many objects, or over a large space; a general burning.
A situation of great passion or emotion.
e: From Middle French, from Latin cōnflagrātiō (“burning, conflagration”).

s: Overly ostentatious; so colorful as to be in bad taste.
e: Unknown, possibly from obsolete Middle English gawren (“to stare”) which is of uncertain origin, probably from Old Norse gá (“to watch, heed”) or gaurr (“rough fellow”) (Proto-Indo-European *gʰow-rós, from *gʰew- (“to be angry”)). Compare with English gaw.

s: Possessing tact; able to deal with people in a sensitive manner.
The quality of being fit or suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended; suitability for particular circumstance or situation.
Pursuit of the course of action that brings the desired effect even if it is unjust or unprincipled.
A starchy food made from the cassava plant, used in puddings.
The cassava plant, Manihot esculenta, from which tapioca is derived; manioc.
e: Borrowed from Portuguese tapioca, from Old Tupi tapi'oka.

s: A device through which a liquid is passed for purification, filtering or separation from solid matter; anything (including a screen or a cloth) used to strain a liquid.
A perforated screen or openwork (usually at the end of a suction pipe of a pump), used to prevent solid bodies from mixing in a liquid stream or flowline.
in water that blocks the passage of solid objects.
In a cool, unpanicked or collected manner.
A separator for removing cream from milk to leave skimmed milk.
A nondairy product that adds a creamy texture to coffee.

A small thimble-sized or stick-shaped container of milk or cream, used as a standard individual "cream" or "milk" portion, typically provided by restaurants for cups of tea or coffee. In recent decades usually a disposable plastic container; in the mid-20th century often a tiny porcelain pitcher.
Of an animal; having a yellow underside or belly.
Giving strength, energy and vitality; quickening; stimulating.
Able to respond to external stimuli.
Able to be promoted to an excited state.
A motion by which something quivers or trembles.
An element or ornament resembling a rose, especially on a wall or other surface, mostly for decorative purposes.
An imitation of a rose made of ribbon or other material, worn as an ornament or symbol, especially
A rose-shaped arrangement awarded as a prize won in a competition (e.g., a horse show).
A rose-shaped badge of support or membership (e.g., of a political party).
A small rose-shaped ornament worn as a symbol of an honorific order or military decoration, typically presented with a medal or in place of a medal (e.g., as a lapel button).
A decorative inlay surrounding the sound hole of a guitar or a viol.
One or more whorls of leaves, clustered tightly at the base of a plant.
A plant growth form in which the plant grows outward in all directions for a short distance, producing a small round shape.
Any structure having a flowerlike form; especially, the group of five broad ambulacra on the upper side of the spatangoid and clypeastroid sea urchins.
A flowerlike color marking, as on the leopard.
A floral pattern in latte art.
A clustered formation of tumor cells.
A thin, cookie-like, deep-fried Scandinavian pastry, made using an iron, which resembles a rose blossom.
e: Borrowed from Middle French rosette (in) and (modern) French rosette. rose + -ette.

s: A person who buys and sells shares (stock) on a stock exchange on behalf of clients. May also provide investment advice and/or company information, depending on the level of service offered (or chosen by the client).
Pertaining to, or having the form, nature or habits of, a beast.
Similar to the nature of a beast; contrary to the nature and dignity of human beings.
Of computer hardware or motor vehicles etc.: ostentatiously powerful.
e: From Middle English bestely, bestly, equivalent to beast + -ly. Compare West Frisian bistachtich (“beastly”), Dutch beestachtig (“beastly”), German biestig (“beastly”).

s: To reside somewhere temporarily, especially as a guest or lodger.
e: From Middle English sojourne and sojournen, from Old French sojor, sojorner (modern séjour, séjourner), from (assumed) Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”), from Latin dies (“day”).

s: A mouth or aperture, such as of a tube, pipe, etc.; an opening.
One of the natural external openings of the human or animal body.
e: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).

s: An insane or very foolish person.
e: Shortened from lunatic, and likely also from loon + -y.

s: A sense of evil to come.
Of ominous significance; serving as an ill omen; foretelling of harm or difficulty.
e: From Middle English forbodyng, vorboding, equivalent to fore + bode + ing. Compare German Vorbote (“harbinger, omen”).
From the fact that ears made of cloth (for example, belonging to a stuffed toy) cannot hear.

s: The process or result of something being scooped.
A singing technique in which the singer begins by singing a note slightly below the desired pitch, and then slides up to it.
A tall building in an Indian, Burmese, or Thai style erected at Hindu or Buddhist temples in South and Southeast Asia, a stupa surmounted with a high point.
A multi-storey tower in a Chinese style used in various contexts across East Asia and Nepal, usually with upturned curving roofs above each storey.
Alternative form of pagod, an idol, chiefly in South and Southeast Asia.
A unit of currency, a coin made of gold or half gold, issued by various dynasties and colonial powers in southern India.
The quality of being brief in duration.
e: First attested in English in 1509; either: By surface analysis, brief + -ity.

s: To investigate something, or solve a problem using brainstorming.
To participate in a brainstorming session.
To think up (ideas); especially, to do so creatively.
A sudden thought, particularly one that solves a long-standing problem.
A session of brainstorming, investigating a problem to try to find solutions.
e: From brain + storm. In the sense of "problem-solve", devised as a method of group creative problem-solving by advertising executive Alex F. Osborn and his employees, who coined the term based on the image of using "the brain to storm a problem". First use appears c. 1945. In the sense of "seizure, convulsion, brain activity", from the unrelated idea that it resembles a storm in the brain.

s: One who is betrothed, i.e. a fiancé or fiancée.
A shot in billiards or snooker in which the cue ball strikes two other balls; a carom.
Pertaining to the game of billiards.
A dynamical system in which a particle alternates between motion in a straight line and specular reflections from a boundary.
1015, a thousand billion (long scale) or a million milliard.
To a reasonable or acceptable degree.
To study an animal's anatomy by cutting it apart; to perform a necropsy or an autopsy.
To study a plant's or other organism's anatomy similarly.
To analyze an idea in detail by delineating between its parts.
To decontextualize an idea, especially through overanalysis by delineating between its parts too strongly based on style, usually involving pedantry, at the expense of substance.
To separate muscles, organs, etc. without cutting into them or disrupting their architecture.
Of an infection or foreign material, following the fascia separating muscles or other organs.
e: Borrowed from Latin dissectus past participle of dissecare (“to cut asunder, cut up”), from dis- (“asunder”) + secare (“to cut”); see section.

s: A shaft in a multi-story building enclosing a stairway or staircase.
An action in which principles are compromised for personal gain.
A person who sells out, who compromises their principles for financial gain or some other advantage.
The selling of an entire stock of something, especially tickets for an entertainment or sports event.
A building; a structure; an architectural fabric, especially a large and spectacular one.
An abstract structure, such as a school of thought, an argument, a theoretical position, etc.
e: From Middle English edifice, from Old French edifice, a classical borrowing of Latin aedificium (“building”), derived from aedificāre (“to build, establish”) (whence also English edify).

s: A northerly wind (that is, a northern wind, which blows from the north or northerly).
Facing the north; directed towards the north.
In an northward direction or position; (towards the) north.
The act by which something is fetched.
Commonly believed or deemed to be the case; generally assumed.
Accepted by supposition rather than as a result of proof.
e: First attested c. 1432, from Middle French putatif, from Latin putātīvus (“supposed, purported”), from putātus (“thought”), from putō (“to think, to consider, to reckon”).

s: Able to be regretted, especially deserving of regret.
The act of one who peers; a looking around.
The act of carrying communications traffic terminating on one's own network on an equivalency basis to and from another network, usually without charge or payment.
Existing in or sunk to a low condition, position, or state; contemptible, despicable, miserable.
Of a person: cast down in hope or spirit; showing utter helplessness, hopelessness, or resignation; also, grovelling; ingratiating; servile.
A person in the lowest and most despicable condition; an oppressed person; an outcast; also, such people as a class.
To cast off or out (someone or something); to reject, especially as contemptible or inferior.
To cast down (someone or something); to abase; to debase; to degrade; to lower; also, to forcibly impose obedience or servitude upon (someone); to subjugate.
Of a fungus: to (forcibly) give off (spores or sporidia).
e: From Late Middle English abjecten (“to cast out, expel”), from abiect, abject (see etymology 1). Sense 3 (“of a fungus: to give off (spores or sporidia)”) is modelled after German abschleudern (“to give off forcefully”).

s: A person who is very sexually attractive.
Something newly released, such as a song or film.

e: A nineteenth-century Hiberno-English phonological overlay of the early medieval Irish Gaelic héis and Middle English aitch. Héis is a graphemic mapping of Classical Latin ha, borrowed into Irish Gaelic to represent the autochthonous phoneme. Middle English aitch derives from Old French ache, from Vulgar Latin *acca, from Classical Latin ha.

s: In a calm or quiet manner.
To move at full speed, especially in retreat.
e: From high + tail; refers to the behavior of fleeing animals, such as deer, that raise their tail when running away.

s: A heavy, waterproof sheet of material, often cloth or plastic sheet, used as a cover or blanket (often as weatherproofing, or to keep loose cargo from blowing off a lorry).
Canvas waterproofed with tar, used as a cover.
A hat made of, or covered with, painted or tarred cloth, worn by sailors and others.
e: From tar + pall (“heavy canvas”) + -ing. The sailor sense reflects that sailors of centuries past often wore garments made of tarred cloth (for weatherproofing).

s: Of hair, to form into a mass of tight curls.
To form into little burs, knobs, or tufts, as the nap of cloth.
To make (leather) soft and of even thickness by rubbing, as with pumice stone or a blunt instrument.
To fry, cook, or sear with a sizzling noise; to sizzle.
A mass of tightly curled or unruly hair.
e: From Middle English frysen, from Old French friser, frizer (“to frizzle, crisp, curl, ruffle, braid, touch lightly, graze, scratch”), of Proto-Germanic origin, perhaps via Old Frankish *fris (“curl”), from Proto-Germanic *frisaz (“frizzy, curly”).
From Middle English fryse, from the verb. See above.

s: A rope or cord tied up outdoors to hang clothes on so they can dry.
A structure with multiple cords for the same purpose, such as a Hills hoist.
The act of knocking a person over by striking his or her upper body or neck with one's arm, as if he or she had run into a low clothesline.
To knock (a person) over by striking them across the neck or upper body with an outstretched arm, mimicking the motion of running into a low clothesline.
A stream that flows out, such as from a lake or reservoir; an outflow; effluence.
Sewage or waste water discharged into a natural body of water.
A form of sexual bonding involving a permanent pair bond between two beings.
The practice of being married to one person as opposed to multiple.
e: From French monogamie, from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία. mono- + -gamy.

s: A good character in a story, often a hero.
Tangled, tangly, knotty, entangled, matted, snarled, unkempt, or uncombed.
Having the shape or form of a knot.
e: From Middle English knotted, iknotted, from the past participle of the verb knotten.

s: A form of cement, made from linseed oil and whiting, used to fixate panes of glass.
Any of a range of similar substances.
An oxide of tin, or of lead and tin, used in polishing glass, etc.
A fine cement of lime only, used by plasterers.
A golf ball made of composition and not gutta-percha.
Of, pertaining to, or resembling putty.
To fix or fill using putty.
e: Borrowed from French potée (“polishing powder", originally "the contents of a pot, potful”), from French pot (“pot”). More at English pot.

s: A device that is used to remove blockages from the drain of a basin or tub, by suction.
The internal piece of a syringe that pushes out or pulls in any contents.
The sliding activator of an exploder, an electrical generator used to trigger electrical detonators such as blasting caps.
The part of a cafetière that is pushed down to remove grounds from coffee.
A cafetière, through abbreviation of coffee plunger.
A horse that plunges, or throws itself suddenly forward.
A device similar to a piston but without a mechanism; a long solid cylinder used, instead of a piston or bucket, as a forcer in pumps.
The moving portion of a solenoid.
The spring-loaded assembly that propels the ball onto the table.
A boiler in which clay is beaten by a wheel to a creamy consistency.
The firing pin of a breechloader.
Tending to relay information and gossip.
The art or practice of successively outdoing a competitor.
A succession of instances of outdoing a competitor.
The property or trait of being a snob.
A low-mounted plumbing fixture or type of sink intended for washing the external genitalia and the anus.
A small horse formerly allowed to each trooper or dragoon for carrying his baggage.
Any bulbous plant of the genus Hyacinthus, native to the Mediterranean and South Africa.
A variety of zircon, ranging in color from brown, orange, reddish-brown and yellow; a jacinth.
e: From Middle English jacinth, partly from Old French jacincte, from Medieval Latin jacintus, and partly from Old English iacinþ, from Medieval Latin jacinthus, both from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (“any of several dark blue flowers”), ultimately from a non-Indo-European Mediterranean language. Re-Latinized in the 16th century.

s: Any of various small passerine songbirds, especially of the family Sylviidae (Old World warblers) and Parulidae (New World warblers).
Applied formerly to various other passerine bird families, such as the Australian Acanthizidae.
A device that makes a warbling sound.
Slightly drunk, fuddled, staggering, foolish as a result of drinking alcoholic beverages.
A dress, a piece of clothing, which consists of a skirt and a cover for the upper body.
An outer garment worn by priests and other clericals; a habit.
To grant to an officer the title and uniform of a rank he will soon be promoted to.
e: From Middle English frok, frokke, from Old French froc (“frock, a monk's gown or habit”), perhaps via Medieval Latin hrocus, roccus, rocus (“a coat”), from Frankish *hrokk (“skirt, dress, robe”), from Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz (“robe, jacket, skirt, tunic”), from Proto-Indo-European *kreḱ- (“to weave”).
From Middle English frock, froke, from Old Norse frauki (“frog”), related to Old English frocga (“frog”). More at frog.

s: A genre of folk music and dance native to Andalusia, in Spain.
A song or dance performed in such a style.
e: Borrowed from Spanish flamenco, from Middle Dutch vlaminc (“Fleming”) (> Dutch Vlaming).

s: A pole, garlanded with streamers held by people who dance around it to celebrate May Day.
A very tall girl or young lady.
A maypole-like structure of sticks placed about a sapling in the bowers of certain species of bowerbird.
A penis, especially a large one.
To dance or spin in a circle around something.
e: So called in reference to its use on May Day.

s: A small shoot or twig of a tree or other plant; a spray.
An ornament resembling a small shoot or twig.
One of the separate pieces of lace fastened on a ground in applique lace.
A brad, or nail without a head.
A small eyebolt ragged or barbed at the point.
To decorate with sprigs, or with representations of sprigs, as in embroidery or pottery.
To nail the sole onto a shoe.
e: From Middle English sprig, sprigge, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle Low German sprik, spricke (“a dry, easily broken twig that has fallen from a tree; sprig”). Compare also dialectal English sprag (“sprig, twig”), English spray (“branch”), Old English spræc (“a shoot”), Low German Spricke, Sprick (“dry branch, twig”).

s: A clairvoyant or clairaudient experience, such as a dream, which resonates with some event in the future.
A strong intuition that something is about to happen (usually something negative, but not exclusively).
e: First use appears c. 1533. From Anglo-Norman premunition, from Ecclesiastical Latin praemonitiōnem (“a forewarning”), form of praemonitiō, from Latin praemonitus, past participle of praemoneō, from prae (“before”) (English pre-) + moneō (“to warn”) (from which English monitor). Compare Germanic forewarning.

s: A person employed to obtain and maintain the storage of provisions, especially food.
A person or company hired to provide and serve food, usually for a large group and at a location separate from where the food is prepared.
Interesting enough to be reported as a news
In the 48 contiguous states or the District of Columbia.
In or to the United States.
In or to the 48 contiguous states or the District of Columbia.
An avocado-based greenish dip with onions, tomato and spices, common to Mexican cuisine and often served with tortilla chips.
e: Borrowed from Spanish guacamole, from Classical Nahuatl āhuacamōlli.

s: A form of clay containing iron and manganese.
A pigment with a reddish-brown colour.
e: From Italian terra di Siena (“earth of Siena”), Siena being the most notable Renaissance location of the clay.

s: A cultivar of chicory (Cichorium intybus var. foliosum) with red leaves and a slightly bitter taste, eaten as a salad vegetable or grilled.
A logical fallacy resulting from the use of multiple meanings of a single expression.
The use of expressions susceptible of a double signification, possibly intentionally and with the aim of misleading.
e: From Middle English equivocacion; from Old French equivocation; from Medieval Latin aequivocātiō; from aequivocō, from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”); from Latin aequus (“equal”) + vocō (“call”), a of Ancient Greek ὁμωνυμία..

s: A small cloth bag filled with drybeans, used as a toy or for exercising the hands.
A type of juggling ball usually made from leather or cloth stuffed with dry beans.
To shoot with a baton round consisting of a bag of shot.
A net used to catch fish.
A fabric mesh with an open diamond-shaped structure.
A wrestling move where the attacker puts their arm tightly round their opponent's head, from which the opponent cannot easily escape.
A person skilled in hygienics, but especially a dental assistant who cleans teeth etc
a lotion, gel, or liquid used after finishing shaving
A sauce, made of an acidic liquid such as vinegar or lemon juice; oil; and other ingredients, used as a salad dressing, or as a marinade for cold meats.
A small perforated box for holding aromatic vinegar contained in a sponge, or a smelling bottle for smelling salts
A small, two-wheeled vehicle, like a litter, to be drawn or pushed by a person. They were used in France until the late 18th century.
e: Borrowed from French vinaigrette. is a Semantic loan from Russian винегре́т, whence also the Doublet of vinegret.

s: The sport of racing or riding on go-karts (small racing cars with lightweight or skeleton bodies) around a track.
An old Saxon and Welsh form of tenure by which an estate passed, on the holder's death, to all the sons equally; also called gavelkind.
To divide or distribute according to the gavel system.
A wooden mallet, used by a courtroom judge, or by a committee chairman, struck against a sounding block to quieten those present, or by an auctioneer to accept the highest bid at auction.
The beginning or end of legal proceedings.
The legal system as a whole.
To begin or end legal proceedings
A small heap of grain, not tied up into a bundle.
e: From Middle English gavel, from Old English gafol, from Proto-West Germanic *gabul, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną (“to give”), equivalent to give + -el.

Thumb Origin obscure. Possibly an alteration of dialectal cavel, a variant of kevel (“a stone mason's axe with a flat face, a cleat or bollard”), from Middle English kevel (“a mason's hammer”), from Old Norse kefli (“a piece of wood, stick, cylinder, mangle”). Cognate with Norwegian kjevle (“rolling pin”).
From Old French gavelle (cf. Modern French javelle) probably diminutive from Latin capulus (“handle”), from capere (“to lay hold of, seize”); or compare Welsh gafael (“hold, grasp”). Compare heave.

s: The act by which someone or something is smothered.
Having the characteristics of a wimp; feeble, indecisive, cowardly.
Not in accord with the current fashion, standards, or mores of a particular group; not cool.
A sheep-like domesticated animal of the Andes, Vicugna pacos, in the camel family, closely related to the llama, guanaco, and vicuña.
Wool from the alpaca, with strong very long fibres and coloring from black to brown to white.
A garment made of such wool.
To squeeze, compress, or crush (especially something moist).
To make the sound of something being squeezed or crushed.
To proceed or make one’s way (somewhere) with the sound of something being squeezed or crushed.
The sound or action of something, especially something moist, being squeezed or crushed.
A political moderate; a moderate on a specific issue.
An effect in internal combustion engines which creates sudden turbulence of the air–fuel mixture as the piston approaches top dead center.
A continuum or progression between categories that are normally considered discrete.
A non-romantic and generally non-sexual infatuation with somebody one is not dating, or the object of that infatuation; a platonic crush.
e: Apparently an alteration of squash, influenced by obsolete squiss (“to squeeze”). Cognate with Scots squische, squies (“to crush, squeeze”). Compare also French esquicher, from Old Occitan esquichar (“to squeeze, squish”). See also squeeze and squelch. The noun is derived from the verb. The linguistic was coined in 1972 by the American poet and linguist John R.

s: To suffocate; stifle; obstruct, more or less completely, the respiration of something or someone.
To extinguish or deaden, as fire, by covering, overlaying, or otherwise excluding the air.
To reduce to a low degree of vigor or activity; suppress or do away with; extinguish
To cook in a close dish.
To breathe with great difficulty by reason of smoke, dust, close covering or wrapping, or the like.
to burn very slowly for want of air; smolder.
to perish, grow feeble, or decline, by suppression or concealment; be stifled; be suppressed or concealed.
To get in the way of a kick of the ball.

To get in the way of a kick of the ball, preventing it going very far. When a player is kicking the ball, an opponent who is close enough will reach out with his hands and arms to get over the top of it, so the ball hits his hands after leaving the kicker's boot, dribbling away.
To prevent the development of an opponent's attack by one's arm positioning.
That which smothers or appears to smother, particularly
The state of being stifled; suppression.
e: From Middle English smother, smorther (“a suffocating vapour, dense smoke”), from Old English smorþor (“smoke”), from smorian (“to suffocate, choke”) + -þor.

s: The state or quality of being weird.
The result or product of being weird.
A lavatory: a room used for urination and defecation.
A toilet: a fixture used for urination and defecation.
Of or relating to an ulcer
Expressing a sick or sickened feeling, or vomiting.
A mild oath expressing surprise or generally adding emphasis.
An instance, or action, of a person being blackballed.
Of, related to, or suffering from scrofula (form of tuberculosis tending to cause enlarged lymph nodes and skin inflammation).
A mischievous person, especially a child.
In a manner or to a degree that can not be repressed; in an irrepressible way.
Any of various medium-sized water birds of the genus Gallinula, of the rail family, that feed in open water margins.
A female red grouse, Lagopus lagopus scotica.
e: From Middle English morhen, perhaps from Old English *mōrhenn, an alteration of Old English worhenn (compare coordinate masculine term mōrhana, a possible corruption of worhana (“pheasant”)), equivalent to moor + hen.

s: Not expurgated, not having had anything objectionable removed
A person or animal (especially a horse) that prances.
a pom; a Briton; an Englishman.
e: From pomme + -y. right|thumb|Arms of Écromagny: Argent, pommy.

s: A concave-upward fold in rock strata
A person who supplies help or companionship.
A recreational problem in chess in which both sides cooperate to achieve a specific goal.
e: A folk-etymological alteration of helpmeet, by reanalysis as help + mate.

s: Limp, weak by nature; lacking strength.
Of a man: having effeminate qualities or characteristics perceived to be homosexual in nature.
A simple dessert made by cooking sweetened milk with cornstarch and vanilla.
A dish, eaten in the Middle Ages, generally consisting of chicken (or sometimes capon or fish), milk or almond milk, rice and sugar.
e: From Middle English blancmanger, blomanger, from Old French blanc mangier (“white food”). The pudding evolved from the chicken dish. Compare French blanc-manger.

s: A measure of weight containing a hundred pounds, variously understood as
A unit of measurement containing 100 avoirdupois pounds (about 45.4 kg).
A unit of measurement containing 112 avoirdupois pounds (eight stone or about 50.8 kg).
Synonym of quintal, a unit of measurement containing various amounts depending on the objects weighed.
Various units of ancient measurement systems consisting of 100 units usually translated as "pounds".
Contradiction, inconsistency, incompatibility, incongruity; an instance of such.
e: From Middle English repugnance,repugnaunce, from Old French repugnance,repugnaunce (French répugnance) and its etymon Latin repugnantia. Doublet of repugnancy.

s: An ungulate animal; a hooved mammal of the clade Euungulata.
A member of the now obsolete clade Ungulata.
e: From Late Latin ungulātus, from Latin ungula (“hoof”), see -ate. The noun was substantivized from the adjective through the associated taxon's name (Ungulata), see -ate.
