The room where a group of people (especially the board of a company or organization) conducts its meetings
Corporations or corporate management considered as a section of society

A cross with arms of equal length all bent halfway along at a 90° angle to the right or to the left, used as a religious symbol by various ancient and modern civilizations, but now mainly seen and used in the West (with arms angled to the right) as a symbol of Nazism and fascism.
e: Sanskrit स्वस्तिक, from सु- (“good, well”) + अस्ति, a verbal abstract of the root of the verb "to be", स्वस्ति thus meaning "well-being" — and the diminutive suffix क; hence "little thing associated with well-being", corresponding roughly to "lucky charm". First attestation in English in 1871, a Sanskritism that replaced the Grecian term gammadion.

s: smoothly, and swiftly; with supreme style.
Having a tendency to seek revenge when wronged, vengeful.
The motion of something that twitches.
Birdwatching by people (twitchers) who travel long distances to see rare species or add a new species to a personal list.
Using a horse team to pull logs.
One who sets something, such as a challenge or an examination.
Any of several long-haired breeds of hunting dog that set when they have scented game.
The player who is responsible for setting, or passing, the ball to teammates for an attack.
A function used to modify the value of some property of an object, contrasted with the getter.
A game or match that lasts a certain number of sets.
One who hunts victims for sharpers.
One who adapts words to music in composition.
A shill bidder at an auction.
To cut the dewlap (of a cow or ox), and insert a seton, so as to cause an issue.
e: From Middle English settere, equivalent to set + -er. Compare West Frisian setter, Dutch zetter, Low German Setter, German Setzer. The hunting dogs are so named because when they scent the game, they set (that is, strike a certain stance).

s: The place where a bird sleeps (usually its nest or a branch).
A group of birds roosting together.
The open cross-joists or inner roof of a cottage or living space.
A kick which causes the ball to travel a long distance.
To settle on a perch in order to sleep or rest.
To kick (a ball) a long distance.
e: From Middle English roste (“chicken's roost; perch”), from Old English hrōst (“wooden framework of a roof; roost”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrōst, from Proto-Germanic *hrōstaz (“wooden framework; grill”); see *raustijan. Cognate with Dutch roest (“roost”), Low German Rust (“roost”), German Rost (“grate; gridiron; grill”).

s: Without swerving or deviation from a course.
That one has not acquired possession of.
rice topping; any food eaten with rice as a part of a main course meal.
e: From Middle English vyaund, from Anglo-Norman and Old French viande, from Late Latin *vivanda, from Latin vīvenda, from the verb vīvō (“to live”). Compare victual, viando. The Philippines usage is an anglicization of Spanish vianda (which is ultimately from Latin via French), which is used to translate ulam in Tagalog. See also usage notes.
From Middle English be- + tide (“time”) + -s. Compare bietiede (“from time to time; now and then”), German beizeiten (“early; betimes”), Swedish bitti (“early (in the day)”).

s: To interrupt, to stop or cease temporarily or periodically; to suspend.
To disdain; to value at little or nothing; to treat or regard with contempt.
To commit an offence of contempt, such as contempt of court; to unlawfully flout (e.g. a ruling).
e: From Middle English contempnen, from Old French contemner, from Latin contemnō (“to scorn”). See also contempt.

s: In the APL programming language: the act of reshaping a variable into a vector.
The state or quality of being wishful.
In an unblushing manner, without shame, or shamelessly.
Of a variable in the APL programming language: which has been reshaped into a vector.
Of bread: made from flour and bran.
To disenchant; to break (someone) from a spell of (mental) captivation.
To free from slavery or captivation (thraldom).
Not disconcerted or embarrassed; not concealed; not eliciting shame.
To make ashamed; to embarrass; to destroy the self-possession of, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to disconcert; to discomfit.
To lose self-possession; to become ashamed.
(of speech or writing) Unpoetic; dull and unimaginative.
(of a person) Behaving in a dull way; boring, tedious.
The proprietor, manager or operator of a small store.
Somebody who is debauched; somebody who is dissolute and acts without moral restraint.
A person addicted to excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures.
The quality of being abstemious, temperate, or sparing, particularly in the use of food and strong drinks.
Originally, any of various green-coloured gems; later specifically peridot.
e: From Middle English crisolite, from Old French crisolite, from Medieval Latin crisolitus, Latin chrȳsolithus, from Ancient Greek χρῡσόλιθος, from χρῡσός (“gold”) + λίθος (“stone”). chryso- (“pertaining to gold”) + -lite (“pertaining to rocks, minerals”).

s: A group of illustrious or talented people, especially one with seven members.
e: Probably from the English Pleiades, divine sisters in Greek mythology who were believed to have been placed in the heavens as a well known group of seven stars.

s: The act of one who drowses.

e: A modification of earlier dissimuler (from Middle English dissimulour) after resemble and semblance; equivalent to dissemble + -er.

s: The act by which somebody is waylaid; an ambush.
The use of a longer expression instead of a shorter one with a similar meaning, for example "I am going to" instead of "I will".
Expressing a grammatical meaning (such as a tense) using a syntactic construction rather than morphological marking.
The substitution of a descriptive word or phrase for a proper name (a type of circumlocution).
The use of a proper name as a shorthand to stand for qualities associated with it.
A perennial flowering plant, Campanula rotundifolia, native to the Northern Hemisphere, with blue, bell-like flowers.
To embarrass (someone) greatly; to confuse; to perplex; to disconcert.
To defeat the plans or hopes of; to frustrate; disconcert.
e: From Middle English discomfiten, from Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire (“to undo, to destroy”), from des- (“completely”), from Latin dis- + Old French confire (“to make”), from Latin cōnficiō (“to finish up, to destroy”), from com- (“with, together”) + faciō (“to do, to make”).

s: A severe pang or spasm of pain, especially one experienced when the uterus contracts during childbirth, or when a person is about to die.
The pain of labour or childbirth; the suffering of death.
Any severe pang or spasm, especially an outburst of feeling; a paroxysm.
A hard struggle, especially one associated with the beginning or finishing of a task.
To cause (someone) to feel throes, as if in childbirth; to put in agony.
To feel throes; to struggle in extreme pain; to be in agony; to agonize.
e: The noun is probably derived partly: The current spelling of the word is a 16th-century variant of Middle English throu, throwe, perhaps to avoid confusion with throw (“act of turning or twisting; fit of bad temper or peevishness; look of anger, bad temper, irritation, etc., a grimace”). The verb is derived.
From Middle English fleschles, flechles, equivalent to flesh + -less. Compare West Frisian fleisleas (“meatless”), Dutch vleesloos (“meatless”), German fleischlos (“meatless”).

s: The act of one who tarries; a waiting or staying behind.
Obsolete spelling of dropped; Infl of drop.
To occur before an event or time; to exist further back in time.
To assign a date to a document or action earlier than the actual date.
To find earlier citational evidence for a term.
Prior date; a date antecedent to another which is the actual date.
A variety of light-green translucent quartz.
Causing something or someone to parch; extremely drying.
The process of parching or roasting something, such as corn.
The condition of being parched; absolute dryness.
To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor.
To make active; to rouse oneself.
e: From Middle English bestyrien, bestirien, from Old English bestyrian (“to heap up, pile up”), equivalent to be- + stir.
From Middle English elat, elate, from Latin ēlātus (“exalted, lofty”), perfect passive participle of efferō (“bring forth or out; raise; exalt”), see -ate.

s: To make (someone or something) heavy with drowsiness or sleepiness.
Followed by away: to pass (time) drowsily or in sleeping; also, to proceed (on a way) drowsily or sleepily.
To make (someone or something) dull or inactive, as if from sleepiness.
Often followed by away or off: to be drowsy or sleepy; to be half-asleep.
To be dull or inactive, as if from sleepiness.
An act, or a state, of being drowsy or sleepy.
A state of dullness or inactivity, as if from sleepiness.
e: The is either: The is derived from the verb.

s: In a way that is slightly lacking, that is scant of how much should be provided.

e: From gentle (“(archaic) well-born; of a good family or respectable birth”) + folk.

s: A seller of alcoholic liquors; keeper of a tippling-house or tavern.
A breed of domestic pigeon bred to participate in endurance competitions.
An open wagon with a tipping trough, unloaded by being inverted (used for bulk cargo, especially minerals). A minecart, a lorry.
One who works at a tipple.
Alternative form of tipple, a revolving frame or cage in which a truck or wagon is inverted to discharge its load.

e: From Medieval Latin pēnūriōsus. See penury from Latin penuria (“want”), related to paene (“scarcely”), c. 1400. Compare French pénurie.

s: Related to hempen ropes, i.e., to hanging as capital punishment.
e: From Middle English hempen, hempyn, from Old English *hænepen (“made of hemp, hempen”), from Proto-West Germanic *hanapīn (“hempen, made of hemp”), equivalent to hemp + -en. Cognate with West Frisian himpen (“hempen”), Dutch hennepen (“hempen”), Low German hempen (“hempen”), German hanfen, hänfen (“hempen”). More at hemp.

s: Lack of interest or care; indifference or apathy.
Freedom from worry or apprehensiveness; insouciance or nonchalance.
A pastor of the Dutch Reformed Church.
e: Alteration of domine, with spelling changed to reflect pronunciation. Doublet of dom, dominus, don.

s: A fine, transparent type of muslin, usually stiffened.
e: From French organdi, possibly derived from the French name of the city Urgench.

s: The state of a beggar; indigence, extreme poverty.
The fact or action of begging.
robbery on the high seas; piracy
Something that promotes growth or development; a nutrient.
e: Inherited from Middle English nutriment, from Latin nūtrīmentum.

s: The quality or state of being noble; nobility or grandeur.
Talk to little purpose; trifling talk; unmeaningful loquacity.
To talk much and to little purpose; to be loquacious; to speak foolishly.
e: From Middle English praten; either inherited from Old English prætt or borrowed via Middle Dutch or Middle Low German praten (from Old Saxon *pratt), all from Proto-West Germanic *prattu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“idle or boastful talk, deceit”), from Proto-Indo-European *bred- (“to wander, rove”).

s: Wearing an abbot's or bishop's mitre.
e: From Middle English mytred; equivalent to mitre (“pointed hat”) + -ed.

s: One who receives a legacy (an inheritance).
A divinity, especially a local or presiding god.
An influence or phenomenon at once mystical and transcendent.
To engage in badinage or playful banter.
e: Borrowed from French badinage, from the verb badiner (“jest, joke”) from badin (“playful”), from Occitan badar (“gape”). Distantly related to abash.

From Middle English woonted (“usual, customary”), from wont (“custom, habit, practice”), alteration of wone (“custom, habit, practice”), from Old English wuna (“custom, habit, practice; usual, wonted”), from Proto-Germanic *wunô (“custom, practice”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).

s: Out of bed; up and about.
In good season or time; early, especially in the morning; seasonably.
In a short time, soon; quickly, forthwith.
e: From Middle English betymes, from bi (“by”) + time + adverbial -s. en + betime + -s. Compare also betides.

s: A premonition; a feeling that something, often of undesirable nature, is going to happen.
e: From French pressentiment, from Middle French, equivalent to pre- + sentiment.

From Middle English fotles, from Old English *fōtlēas (only found as fēþelēas (“footless”)), from Proto-Germanic *fōtalausaz (“footless”), equivalent to foot + -less. Cognate with Dutch voetloos, German fußlos, Swedish fotlös, Icelandic fótalaus (“footless, legless”).

s: A light boat, traditionally propelled by sails, but sometimes a rowboat, and usually serving to carry messages among the larger ships of a fleet.
e: From Middle French pinasse, from Spanish pinaza, from pino (“pine”) + -aza.

s: An ambush; a trap laid for an enemy.
The place in which troops lie hidden for an ambush.
The body of troops lying in ambush.
To lie in wait for, or to attack from a covert or lurking place; to waylay.
e: From French embuscade, from Italian imboscata from the past participle of imboscare (“to ambush”), from Vulgar Latin *imbosco (“I hide, ambush”) (see there for more), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambush. More at bush.

s: Provided, cooked, or stuffed with truffles.
One of the two long pieces of wood, extending before a vehicle, between which a horse is hitched; a shaft.
The shallow stratum of underclay that lies under a seam of coal; the bottom of a coal-seam.
e: From Middle English thille, thylle, from Old English þille (“board; floorboard; plank; stake; pole”), from Proto-West Germanic *þilljā, from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ (“board; floorboard; deck”), from Proto-Indo-European *tel- (“plank; board”).

From Middle English live long, leve-long, lefe long (as in Alle the lefe longe daye), equivalent to lief + long. Compare Dutch heel den lieven langen dag (“all the livelong day”), German der liebe lange Tag (“the livelong day”) and German die liebe lange Nacht (“the livelong night”).

s: To make a humble request to (someone, especially a person in authority); to beg, to beseech, to entreat.
To ask or request (something) humbly and sincerely, especially from a person in authority; to beg or entreat for.
To humbly request for something, especially to someone in a position of authority; to beg, to beseech, to entreat.
A dense, plain woven cloth, usually made of cotton or a cotton blend.
A fine smooth-faced woolen cloth for men’s garments, usually of double width (i.e., a yard and a half); so called in distinction from woolens three quarters of a yard wide.
One who tenders (a bid, a contract, etc.).
A light strong fabric with woven stripes or squares.
e: From earlier dimite, from Middle English demit, demyt, from Medieval Latin dimitum, from Byzantine Greek δίμιτον, from Ancient Greek δίμιτος (“of double thread”).

s: Any of the flowering plants of the family Asphodelaceae, especially Asphodelus ramosus and Asphodelus albus; the flower of these plants.
The flower said to carpet Hades, and a favorite food of the dead.
e: Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος. Doublet of daffodil.

s: An American migratory songbird (Dolichonyx oryzivorus), resembling a blackbird with the bill of a finch.
e: Imitative of its song. Compare Bob Lincoln.

s: To chastize; to punish or reprimand for the sake of improvement.
e: From Middle English chastien, from Old French chastier (“punish”), from Latin castīgō. Doublet of chastise, castigate and related to chaste.

s: a person who pleads in court; an advocate
e: Partly from Middle English pleder, pledere, equivalent to plead + -er; and partly from Middle English pledour, plaidour, from Anglo-Norman plaidur, pledour, Old French plaidëor, pledëor.

s: Any of several passerine birds, of the families Leiothrichidae, Timaliidae and Paradoxornithidae (found in Asia and Africa), and Pomatostomidae (found in Australia).
A hound who is too noisy on finding a good scent.
A nocturnal insectivorous bird of North America (Antrostomus vociferus, syn. Caprimulgus vociferus), a type of nightjar, named after its characteristic call.
The distinctive call of the above bird.
The act of one who forestalls.
The act of one who scorns.
Superlative of minute Smallest, littlest, tiniest.
To tease (someone) by offering or showing them something desirable but leaving them unsatisfied.
To be teased by something desirable that is kept out of reach.
e: From Tantalus (Ancient Greek Τάνταλος) in Greek mythology, who was condemned to Tartarus in the underworld. There, he had to stand for eternity in water that receded from him when he stooped to drink, beneath fruit trees whose branches were always out of reach. Derived as Tantalus + -ize.

s: An orchid; now specifically, a plant of the genus Orchis.
e: Borrowed from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (“testicle”).

s: Of, or relating to a cherub; angelic.
Of, or like a baby; infantile
Of or relating to a seraph or the seraphim.
e: From Medieval Latin seraphicus, from Late Latin seraphīm, seraphīn, from Hebrew שָׂרָף (“seraph”). seraph + -ic.

s: Any monetary or other incidental benefit beyond salary.
A privilege or possession held or claimed exclusively by a certain person, group or class.
e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin perquisitum (“something acquired for profit”)

s: Without a date imprinted, assigned, or associated.
Having no date (meeting with a lover or potential lover).
e: Unknown. Perhaps derived from Old English þeatless (“thoughtless, without plan”). See also deedless.

s: A secondary mineral deposit of calcium carbonate or another mineral, in shapes similar to icicles, that hangs from the roof of a cave.
e: [[File:Estalactites Lapa Doce.JPG|thumb|A group of stalactites in Brazil.]] From New Latin stalactītēs, from Ancient Greek σταλακτός (“dripping; dropping”) + Latin -ītēs (modelled after the names of stones ending in -ites). Σταλακτός is derived from σταλάσσειν (“to drip; to let (something) drip”) + -τός.

s: One of the component parts of the calyx, particularly when such components are not fused into a single structure.
Payment for employment or an office; compensation for a job, which is usually monetary.
Material benefit, either direct or indirect.
e: From Middle English emolument, from Old French emolument, from Latin ēmolumentum.

s: A person who takes particular pleasure in fine food and drink.
e: From Epicurus, the name of an Ancient Greek philosopher who advocated such a lifestyle.

s: A straight section of a racetrack.
e: From straight + way. First attested in the sense of "directly".
Inherited from Middle English happely, hapliche, happeliche; equivalent to hap + -ly.

s: That which is spoken in a lisp.
A frustration or disappointment; a check.
Tending to thwart or impede; frustrating.
Causing one to pause or stop; disheartening.
That refuses to cooperate or fails to behave in the desired and expected manner.
That makes motions which attempt to deceive the opponent.

A liturgical vestment of the Christian Church in the form of a tunic of white linen or cotton material, with wide or moderately wide sleeves, reaching to the hips or knees, usually featuring lace decoration and embroidered bordures.
e: Inherited from Middle English surplys, from Old French surpeliz, from Medieval Latin superpelliceum, from Latin super (“over”) and pellis (“fur”).

s: In a quaint manner; oddly; strangely.
A male merchant (person engaged in trade).
A domestic rooster or cock, especially in fables and fairy tales.
To make the crowing sound of a cock.

e: From Middle English wheron, from Middle English wher>.

s: To render less lively; to diminish; to muffle.
To become less lively; to diminish (by itself).
e: From dead + -en. Compare Dutch doden (“to kill”), West Frisian deadzje (“to kill”).

s: Past participle of hew (alternative to hewn)
please; used to make a question or request more polite or more forceful.
The act of exulting; great joy at success or victory, or at any advantage gained; rapturous delight
e: From Middle English exultacion, borrowed from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, from exult, -ation.

s: Of or relating to the druids.
Having a particular type or colour of funnel.
Arrogantly superior; showing contemptuous indifference; haughty.
The sound made by a horse: an act or instance of the verb neigh.
Furnished with, or carrying, a quiver for arrows.
Of or relating to the body.
Of, relating to or resembling flesh; composed of flesh; having a lot of flesh.
Of or relating to pleasurable (often sexual) sensations.
Of or relating to non-spiritual or non-religious matters.
In a sensual way; in a sexual way; carnally.
e: From Middle English fleschly, from Old English flǣsċlīċ; equivalent to flesh + -ly.
From Middle English fleschly, from Old English flǣsċlīċe; equivalent to flesh + -ly.

s: A thrumming sound; a hum or vibration.
To cause a steady rhythmic vibration in (something), usually by plucking.
To make a monotonous drumming noise.
The ends of the warp threads in a loom which remain unwoven attached to the loom when the web is cut.
A fringe made of such threads.
Any short piece of leftover thread or yarn; a tuft or tassel.
A threadlike part of a flower; a stamen.
A tuft, bundle, or fringe of any threadlike structures, as hairs on a leaf, fibers of a root.
A bundle of minute blood vessels, a plexus.
Small pieces of rope yarn used for making mats or mops.
A mat made of canvas and tufts of yarn.
A shove out of place; a small displacement or fault along a seam.
Made of or woven from thrum.
To furnish with thrums; to insert tufts in; to fringe.
To insert short pieces of rope-yarn or spun yarn in.
e: From Middle English thrum, throm (> Anglo-French trome), from Old English *þrum (found in tungeþrum (“ligament of the tongue”)) from Proto-Germanic *þrumą. Cognate with German Trumm, Trümmer and Old Norse þrǫmr (“edge, brim”), and more distantly to Latin termen.
Apparently a reduced form of the stem of threepenny/threepence through a sequence such as /ˈθrɛp(ə)n-/ > /ˈθrʊp(ə)m-/ > /ˈθrʊm-/ (> /ˈθɹʌm-/).

s: A scale insect of the species Dactylopius coccus, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas, which lives on prickly pear cacti (genus Opuntia).
A vivid red dye made from the dried bodies of cochineal insects.
The vivid red colour of this dye.
Possessing a vivid red colour, as or as if produced from dyeing with cochineal dye.
Like diamond in lustre; bright, lustrous, shiny; also, of a lustre: like that of a mineral with a high refractive index such as diamond.
The quality of being artificial or produced unnaturally.
To cool (something) with water or another liquid.
To become mixed with water, so that a true chemical combination takes place.
To mix with water, so that a true chemical combination takes place.
Of a person: to become less energetic, to slacken in one's efforts.
To slacken; to become relaxed or loose.
To become less intense; to weaken, decrease in force.
To go out; to become extinct.
e: From Middle English slaken (“to render slack, to slake”), from Old English sleacian, from Old English slæc (“slack”). Unrelated to, but possibly influenced by, the Old Norse sløkkva (“to extinguish”), compare Swedish släcka in the phrase släcka sin törst (“quench one's thirst”), släcka elden (“put out the fire”), and släckt kalk (“slaked lime”).
Probably connected with Icelandic sleikja, "to lick", and German schlecken (“to lick”).

s: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility.
e: From Middle French stolide, from Latin stolidus (“foolish, obtuse, slow”).

s: To embody, exemplify; to represent by a form, image, model, or resemblance.
To serve as a typical or reference specimen of.

e: From Latin tremulus, from tremō (“to tremble, shake”) + -ulus. Doublet of tremor, tremble. tremulate + -ous.

s: A state or act of violating faith or allegiance; violation of a promise or vow, or of trust.
An illegitimate act of deception, such as using symbols like the Red Cross or white flag in a false claim of surrender to gain proximity to an enemy for purposes of attack.
A state or act of deceit.
e: From Middle French perfidie, from Latin perfidia from perfidus (“faithless, treacherous, false”), from fides (“faith”); related to, for example, English fidelity.

s: Treated with irreverence or without due respect.
e: From the past and past participle of the verb profane.

s: To grind (one's teeth) in pain or in anger.
A sudden snapping of the teeth.
The quality of being sage, wise, or able to make good decisions; the quality of being perceptive, astute or insightful.
e: From French sagacité, from Latin sagācitās (“sagaciousness”), from sagāx (“of quick perception, acute, sagacious”) (whence -acity), from sāgiō (“to perceive by the senses”). Equivalent to sagacious + -ity.

s: A singer in a choir; especially a child in a church or cathedral choir.
A director or leader of a choral group.
e: Derived from late Middle English queristre, from an Anglo-Norman variant of Old French cueriste, from cuer (see Middle French cuer). Equivalent to choir + -ster.

s: The quality of being pompous; self-importance.
During which no phase of the Moon is visible to provide light, whether because of cloud cover or because of a new moon.
Pertaining to the dawn; dawning, eastern, like a new beginning.
Pertaining to the aurora borealis or aurora australis.

e: Aphetized from Middle English arayment, borrowed from Anglo-Norman arraiement and Old French areement, from areer (“to array”). See array.

s: An underground system of tunnels and chambers with recesses for graves, used (in former times) as a cemetery; a tunnel system used for burying the dead, as in Paris or Ancient Rome.
e: From Middle English catacombe, from Old English catacumbe, catacumbas, from Late Latin catacumbae, name of the underground cemetery of St. Sebastian in Rome, of unclear origin. Perhaps a dissimilation (influenced by *cumbō (“to lie, recline”)) of Late Latin cata tumbās (from Ancient Greek κατά (“under”) and τύμβος (“tomb”)).

s: To annul (as a law, decree, ordinance, etc.) by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or their successor; to repeal.
To put an end to; to do away with.
To block a process or function.
e: From Middle English abrogat (“abolished”), from Latin abrogātus, perfect passive participle of abrogō (“repeal”) (see -ate and -ate), formed from ab (“away”) + rogō (“ask, inquire, propose”). See rogation.

s: The quality or state of being vivid.
The shield on which a coat of arms is displayed, or, by extension, the coat of arms itself.
A small shield used to charge a larger one.
The pattern of distribution of hair upon the pubic mound.
A marking upon the back of a cow's udder and the space above it (the perineum), formed by the hair growing upward or outward instead of downward. It was once taken as an index of milking qualities.
The part of a ship's stern where its name is displayed.
A decorative or protective plate or bezel designed to fill the gap between a switch, pipe, valve, control knob, etc., and the surface from which it protrudes.
The insignia around a doorknob's exterior hardware or a door lock's cosmetic plate.
The depression behind the beak of certain bivalves; the ligamental area.
e: From Middle English scochon, from Anglo-Norman escuchon, Old French escusson (French écusson), ultimately from Latin scutum (“shield”). Related to Doublet of scutum, scute, scudo, escudo, écu.

s: The act of one who alights.
Having the appearance of having been ravished.
The art or pseudoscience of deducing the predominant temper and other characteristic qualities of the mind from the outward appearance, especially from the features of the face.
The face or countenance, with respect to the temper of the mind; particular configuration, cast, or expression of countenance, as denoting character.
The art of telling fortunes by inspection of the features.
The general appearance or aspect of a thing, without reference to its scientific characteristics.
e: Inherited from Middle English phisonomie, from Anglo-Norman phisenomie, Middle French phisonomie et al., ultimately from Late Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (“physiology”), from φύσις (“physique, appearance”) + γνώμη (“means of knowing”).

s: Small cylindrical beads made from polished shells (especially white ones) which have been strung together, formerly used by Native American peoples of eastern North America for various purposes including as jewellery and money, and for record-keeping; one such bead.
Ellipsis of wampum snake (“the common kingsnake or eastern kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula)”).
e: Clipping of wampumpeag, probably borrowed from wampompeage (“string of white beads used as money”). Compare peag (“string of white beads used as money”), also a clipping of wampumpeag. (“common kingsnake”) is from the similarity of the snake’s appearance to a string of wampum.

s: Prior claim (on payment, or on purchasing something); the first rights to obtain a particular payment or product.
The fact of being pushed or advanced to a more favourable situation; furtherance, promotion (of a candidate, action, undertaking etc.).
Advancement to a higher position or office; promotion.
A position (especially in the Church of England) that provides profit or prestige.
The fact of preferring something; preference.
A mixture of flour, water and yeast that is allowed to ferment prior to another baking process.
Having or decorated with a plume or plumes.
Not capable of being sounded or fathomed.
A chant, hymn or song, especially a nonmetrical one, with words from a biblical text.
Any of the species of Somateria spp. and Polysticta stelleri or of the seaduck subfamily Merginae, which line their nests with fine down (taken from their own bodies).
e: From Icelandic æður, from Old Norse æðr, which see for more. The word appears in various European languages in the first half of the 18th century with the growth of the Icelandic eiderdown trade.

s: A large wave, swell, surge, or undulating mass of something, such as water, smoke, fabric or sound.
To surge or roll in billows.
e: From Middle English *bilwe, borrowed from Old Norse bylgja, from Proto-Germanic *bulgijō. Cognates include Danish bølge (“wave”); Norwegian bølge (“wave”), Norwegian bylgje (“wave”); Swedish bölja (“wave”); Low German Bulge, Bulg, Bülg (“billow, wave”); German Bulge (“billow, wave”). Compare bellow, bawl.

s: A small passerine bird, the common linnet (Linaria cannabina syn. Carduelis cannabina), in the finch family Fringillidae, native to Europe, western Asia, and north Africa.
A house finch (Haemorhous mexicanus), of North America.
e: From Old French linette, from lin (“flax”), from the bird's fondness for the seeds of flax, the source of linen and Old English līnete, līnetwige (“linnet”) (> dialectal English lintwhite).

s: An oath, pledge, plight, or promise.
A pledge or promise to marry someone.
The state of being thus pledged; betrothal, engagement.
One who plumps or swells out something else.
That which plumps or swells out something else.
A small ball or pad carried in the mouth to fill out the cheeks.
In elections, a vote given to one candidate only, when two or more are to be elected, thus giving the candidate an advantage over the others.
A voter who plumps their vote.
An obese woman, especially in pornography.
An intense, paroxysmal, involuntary muscular contraction.
An uncontrolled fit, as of laughter; a paroxysm.

e: From Middle English febly; equivalent to feeble + -ly, euphonically blending -le and -ly. Compare nimbly, nobly, and Latinate -ably and -ibly.

s: Any of various herbs of the family Gentianaceae found in temperate and mountainous regions with violet or blue flowers.
Dried roots and rhizome of European gentian (Gentiana lutea), used as a tonic.
e: Via Middle English from Latin gentiāna, which, according to Pliny the Elder, was named after Gentius (Ancient Greek Γένθιος), the last king of Illyria, who supposedly discovered the plant's medicinal benefits. This has been dismissed as folk etymology but the word may still ultimately be of origin, as -an is a common suffix in Illyrian words.

s: To flow with a bubbling sound.
e: Back formation from Middle English gurguling (“a rumbling in the belly”). Akin to Middle Dutch gorgelen (“to gurgle”), Middle Low German gorgelen (“to gurgle”), German gurgeln (“to gargle”), and perhaps to Latin gurguliō (“throat”).

s: Capable of being specified or shown.
Not suspected; not having raised suspicion.
The act of disparaging, of belittling.
A woman who flirts or plays with people's affections.
Any hummingbird in the genus Lophornis.
Of or relating to a feminine style of clothing involving ribbons, frills, and bows.
Having the lees or sediment disturbed; not clear. (of a liquid)
e: From Middle English turbide, borrowed from Latin turbidus (“disturbed”), from turba (“mass, throng, crowd, tumult, disturbance”).

s: To pay out, expend; usually from a public fund or treasury.
Capable of soothing or eliminating pain.
Noncontentious, blandly agreeable, unlikely to cause offence or debate.
Any medicine or other agent that relieves pain.
A source of relaxation or comfort.
e: From Middle English anodine, from Medieval Latin anōdynos (“stilling or relieving pain”), from Ancient Greek ἀνώδυνος (“free from pain”), from ἀν- (“without”) + ὀδύνη (“pain”). Adjective sense “noncontentious” probably through French anodin (“harmless, trivial”), of same origin.

From Middle English cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin, from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīn, cherūbīm, from Ancient Greek χερουβίν, χερουβείν, χερουβίμ, from Hebrew כְּרוּבִים, from כְּרוּב + ־ִים.

s: The act of one who covets.
A disease of horses characterized by coughing and difficult breathing; broken wind.
To bump into or brush against while in motion; to push aside.
To move through by pushing and shoving.
To be close to or in physical contact with.
To contend or vie in order to acquire something.
To pick or attempt to pick pockets.
The act of jostling someone or something; push, shove.
The action of a jostling crowd.
e: Originally justle (“to have sex with”), formed from Middle English jousten, from the Old French joster (“to joust”), from Latin iuxtā (“next to”), from iungō (“join, connect”), equivalent to joust + -le.

s: of a work of art, literature, etc.
Guaranteed not to be lost or forgotten due to its importance or conspicuous excellence.
With stiffness; lacking a smooth flow of movement, or lacking movement altogether.
An essential oil extracted from flowers.
A perfume made from this oil.
e: Borrowed from Persian عطر (“scent”), from Arabic عِطْر (“perfume”). Arabic ع ط ر.

s: The act of providing housing for military personnel, especially when imposed upon the home of a private citizen.
The method of capital punishment where a criminal is cut into four pieces.
The division of a shield containing different coats of arms into four or more compartments.
One of the different coats of arms arranged upon an escutcheon, denoting the descent of the bearer.
A series of quarters, or small upright posts.
The practice of docking 15 minutes' pay from a worker who arrived late (even by less than 15 minutes).
Searching for prey by traversing a space. From hunting for game, where dogs will run parallel to the wind in search of a scent, thereby 'quartering' the field.
A point on an arch calculated by measuring one quarter of the height along a line from the peak to the outer edge on the ground.
Coming from a point well abaft the beam, but not directly astern; said of waves or any moving object.
Coming from aft and to one side; having both a crosswind and tailwind component.
At right angles, as the cranks of a locomotive, which are in planes forming a right angle with each other.
Not noticeably; such that it cannot be detected, through being too small or too fast, etc.

e: From Anglo-Norman and Old French propicius, from Latin propitius (“favorable, well-disposed, kind”). Compare French propice, Portuguese propício and Spanish propicio.

s: An instance of this; a moment of being impertinent.
The fact or character of being out of place; inappropriateness.
Habitually lazy, procrastinating, or resistant to physical labor.
Causing little or no physical pain; progressing slowly; inactive (of an ulcer, etc.).
e: From French indolent or directly from Late Latin indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“hurting”), from doleo (“to hurt”). The later sense of “living easily, slothful” perhaps developed in French.

s: The sounding of a bugle or drum early in the morning to awaken soldiers.
e: From French réveillez, imperative form of réveiller (“to wake”).

s: The application of a tint or shade of color.
Stealthy, furtive, well hidden, covert (especially movements).
e: Borrowed from Latin surrēptīcius (“furtive, clandestine”), from surrēpō (“to creep along”).

s: To treat with great respect and deference.
To revere or hold in awe.
e: Borrowed from Latin venerātus, perfect active participle of veneror (“to worship, venerate”), see -ate.

s: A spiderweb, especially a large one, an old abandoned one covered with debris and dust or an asymmetrical one woven with an irregular pattern of threads.
One of a spiderweb's filaments; gossamer; anything flimsy and gauzy, intricately interconnected or otherwise like a cobweb.
An intricate plot to catch the unwary; something entangling or confusing.
Something thin and unsubstantial, or flimsy and worthless; valueless remainder.
A web page that either has not been updated for a long time, or one that is rarely visited.
The European spotted flycatcher, Muscicapa striata.
e: From Middle English copweb, coppeweb, coppewebbe, from Old English ātorcoppe (“spider”) + webb. Compare Middle Dutch kopwebbe, Low German Kobbenwebbe (Westphalian). en (“spider”) + cob + web.

s: To turn or become red or redder.
To turn or make red or redder.
The act by which one endeavors or strives; an attempt.
A wide fabric band worn as a necktie by men having long ends hanging in front.
A decorative fabric band or scarf worn around the neck by women.
A bandage resembling a cravat, particularly a triangular bandage folded into a strip.
To adorn with a cravat; to tie a cravat, or something resembling a cravat, around the neck.
e: From French cravate, an appellative use of Cravate (“Croat”), from Dutch Krawaat, from German Krawatte, from Serbo-Croatian Hr̀vāt/Хр̀ва̄т (“Croat”). The cravat is regarded as originating from a linen scarf worn by Croatian mercenaries which was adopted into French fashion in the 17th century. Doublet of Croat.

s: The sound of a hoot, or the occasion of producing this sound.
A strip of pleated fabric or paper used as decoration or trim.
A substance or material on the edge of something, resembling such a strip of fabric.
A wrinkled edge to a film.
Something extraneous or not essential; something purely for show or effect; a luxury.
The relatively extensive margin seen on the back of the heads of reptiles, with either a bony support or a cartilaginous one.
To provide or decorate with a frill or frills; to turn back in crimped plaits.
To shake or shiver as with cold (with reference to a hawk).
To cry (with reference to a bird of prey).
deft, dexterous, or skillful in handling challenges.
The situation of having a thirst for something.
Not violable; not to be infringed.
Not susceptible to violence, or of being profaned, corrupted, or dishonoured.
Incapable of being injured or invaded; indestructible.
e: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable..
Via Middle English debonaire from Old French de bon aire (“of good stock; noble”).
From Middle French malevolence, from Latin malevolentia (“malevolence”), derived from malevolēns (“malevolent”).

s: Having or showing confidence or trust in another person.
In confidence; as if with trust.
Of a bird, allowing the close approach of humans.
The telling of something in confidence.
Somewhat less than is needed in amplitude or extent.
To add or to interrupt at regular intervals.
Point-like; consisting of or marked with one or more points.
the suit of clubs; primarily childish.
Any of various colourful passerine birds, New World orioles of the genus Icterus (family Icteridae) and Old World orioles of the family Oriolidae.
e: A borrowing from Middle French oriol, from Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus, diminutive of aureus (“golden”). Doublet of aureole. First use appears c. 1776 in the writings of Thomas Pennant.

s: The act or state of vanishing away; disappearance.
The event of fading and gradually vanishing from sight.
Gerund of flit: the motion of something that flits.
The act of moving from one residence to another; moving house.
Brief, likely to be of short duration.
Never again; at no time in the future.
e: From Middle English nevermore, from the Old English phrase nǣfre mā. Equivalent to never + -more.

s: A papal decree prohibiting the administration of the sacraments from a political entity under the power of a single person (e.g., a king or an oligarchy with similar powers). Extreme unction/Anointing of the Sick is excepted.
To exclude (someone or somewhere) from participation in church services; to place under a religious interdict.
To forbid (an action or thing) by formal or legal sanction.
To impede (an enemy); to interrupt or destroy (enemy communications, supply lines etc).
e: From Middle English entrediten, from Old French entredire (“forbid”), from Latin interdīcō (“prohibit, forbid”), from inter- (“between”) + dīcō (“say”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-.

s: A large drinking vessel, sometimes of pewter, sometimes with a glass base, with one handle and often a hinged cover.
e: From Middle English tan(c)kard(e), denoting 'a large tub for carrying liquid', perhaps related to Dutch tanckaert, from Middle Dutch tanckaert, meaning the same thing, but of uncertain ultimate origin. The OED suggests an alteration of Medieval Latin *kantard, from Latin cantharus (“tankard”). Klein suggests French tant quart (“as much of a quarter”).

s: To reject something by pushing it away with the foot.
To waste; fail to make the most of (an opportunity)
To kick or toss up the heels.
An act of spurning; a scornful rejection.
A kick; a blow with the foot.
A body of coal left to sustain an overhanging mass.
e: From Middle English spurnen, spornen, from Old English spurnan (“to strike against, kick, spurn, reject; stumble”), from Proto-Germanic *spurnaną (“to tread, kick, knock out”), from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-.
Inherited from Middle English frekled; equivalent to freckle + -ed.

s: Showing no regard; careless or unconcerned.
To make a judgment (on a dispute) as an arbitrator or arbiter
To submit (a dispute) to such judgment
To assign an arbitrary value to, or otherwise determine arbitrarily.
e: From Latin arbitratus, past participle of arbitrari (“to be a witness, act as umpire”), from arbiter (“umpire”); see arbiter.

s: Somebody who is gay (in the sense of either homosexual or uncool).
A saint; a holy person; an apostle.
The relics or shrines of saints or non-Christian gods.
To shout, especially to urge on dogs for hunting.
e: Inherited from Middle English halwe (“a saint, holy thing, shrine”), from Old English hālga (“a holy one, saint”), from Proto-Germanic *hailagô (“holy one”), from *hailagaz (“holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, safe, hale”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“safe, unharmed”).

Inherited from Middle English halwen (“to hallow, sanctify”), from Old English hālgian (“to hallow, sanctify, make holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailagōną (“to make holy”), from *hailagaz (“holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, safe, hale”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“safe, unharmed”).
Inherited from Middle English halowen, from halow, from Old English ēalā (“O!, alas!, oh!, lo!”), probably conflated with Old French halloer.

s: The quality of being slow of understanding things.
The quality of being uninteresting; boring; humorless or irksome.
The lack of visual brilliance; want of sheen.
The quality of not perceiving or kenning things distinctly.
A person who sells (women's) apparel, accessories, and other decorative goods, especially those originally manufactured in Milan.
A person involved in the design, manufacture, or sale of hats for women.
To manufacture (women's apparel, specifically hats); also, to supply (someone) with women's apparel, specifically hats.
e: Thumb|A milliner at work. The noun is a variant of Milaner (“(obsolete) inhabitant or native of Milan”) (referring to the importation and sale of women’s apparel, etc., made in Milan: see), from Late Middle English Milener, Miloner (“native of Milan”), from Milan + -er(e). The verb is derived from the noun.

s: An ornamental headband worn as a badge of royalty.
Regal power; sovereignty; empire—considered as symbolized by the crown.
An arch rising from the rim of a crown (rarely also of a coronet), and uniting with others over its centre.
To adorn with a diadem; to crown.
e: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (“band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (“bind around”).

s: To spring forward on the hind legs.
To strut about in a showy manner.
e: From Middle English prancen, prauncen (“to prance”), variant of Middle English pranken (“to prank”), thus probably from the same ultimate root as prank. Cognate with prangezen, prangssen (“to put on airs”), pranzen (“to strut”).

s: A set of one or more steps surmounting a fence or wall, or a narrow gate or contrived passage through a fence or wall, which in either case allows people but not livestock to pass.
A vertical component of a frame or panel, such as that of a door, window, or ladder.
e: Thumb|A stile (sense 1) over a stone wall From Middle English stile,style,stiȝele, from Old English stiġel (“stile, set of steps for getting over a fence”), from Proto-West Germanic *stigilu, from Proto-Germanic *stigilō (“entry, entrance, overpass, device for climbing, stile”), equivalent to sty (“to ascend, climb”) + -le.

s: To change, mutilate or disfigure by cutting, tearing, rearranging, etc.
To modify (an identifier from source code) so as to produce a unique identifier for internal use by the compiler, etc.
A hand-operated device with rollers, for wringing laundry.
The mangle attached to wringer washing machines, often called the wringer.
Any of various trees of the genus Rhizophora, especially the red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle).
Preceded by a descriptive word: any of various shrubs or trees of genera other than Rhizophora which resemble plants of this genus in appearance and habitat.
e: From Middle English mangelen, manglen, from Anglo-Norman mangler, mahangler, frequentative of either Old French mangonner (“to cut to pieces”) or mahaigner (“to mutilate”), of origin, for which see mayhem.

Ca. 1700, from Dutch mangel, from Early Modern German Mangel (15th c.), enhanced form (by analogy with other tool names in -el) of Middle High German mange, from Medieval Latin manga, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον. Doublet of mangonel.
Borrowed from Spanish mangle, mangue, probably from an language (such as), or a language.

s: Without a clearly defined or identifiable shape.
Any plant of the family Cyperaceae.
Any plant of the genus Carex, the true sedges; perennial herbs with triangular jointless stems, a spiked inflorescence, and long grass-like leaves which are usually rough on the margins and midrib.
Any of various other plants resembling true sedges, such as Gentiana rubricaulis and Andropogon virginicus.
A dry fly used in fly fishing, designed to resemble a sedge or caddis fly.
A flock of herons, cranes, or bitterns.
e: From Middle English segge, from Old English seċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *sagi, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sak- (“marsh plant”). Cognate with Dutch zegge and German Segge, dialectal German Saher (“reeds”).

s: That exasperates, infuriates, annoys or irritates
Of or related to the metal lead, particularly
Resembling the color of lead, metallic or dark gray; dim, overcast.
Resembling the density of lead, heavy.
Resembling the ponderousness of lead, sluggish.
To make or become dull or overcast.
e: From Middle English leden, leaden, from Old English lēaden (“leaden, of lead”). Cognate with West Frisian leaden (“leaden”), Dutch loden (“leaden”). en + lead + en.

s: A tramp, i.e. a long and tiring walk.
To walk wearily with heavy, slow steps.
To trudge along or over a route etc.
e: Mid-16th century. Original meaning was somewhat idiomatic, meaning "to walk using snowshoes." Probably of Scandinavian origin, compare Icelandic þrúga (“snowshoe”), Norwegian truga (“snowshoe”) and dialectal Swedish trudja (“snowshoe”).

s: Injury or wear caused by friction.
To excite heat in by friction; to rub in order to stimulate and make warm.
To excite passion or anger in; to fret; to irritate.
To fret and wear by rubbing.
To rub; to come together so as to wear by rubbing; to wear by friction.
To have a feeling of vexation; to be vexed; to fret; to be irritated.
e: Inherited from Middle English chaufen (“to warm”), borrowed from Old French chaufer, from Latin calefacere, calfacere (“to make warm”), from calere (“to be warm”) + facere (“to make”). See caldron.

s: A burning serpent, often winged, with human hands and sometimes feet; one of God's entourage. On Earth, they strike with burning poison; in Heaven, with burning coal.
A six-winged angel; one of the highest choir or order of angels in Christian angelology, ranked above cherubim, and below God.
e: Back-formation of singular from plural seraphim, from Latin seraphim, from Hebrew שְׂרָפִים, plural form of שָׂרָף. The plural "seraphims" occurs in the King James Bible (Isaiah chapter 6). According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the singular "seraph" may have originated with John Milton, who used it in Book I of Paradise Lost (1667).

s: At any or all times in the future; forever.
The part of or interest in a deceased husband's property provided to his widow, usually in the form of a life estate.
Property given by a groom to his bride or her family, at or before their wedding, in order to legitimize the marriage
That with which one is gifted or endowed; endowment; gift.
To give a dower or dowry to.
e: From Middle English dower, dowere, from Old French doeire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dowry.

s: An officer who proclaims the orders or directions of a court, or who gives public notice by loud proclamation, such as a town crier.
e: From Middle English criour, cryour, crier, from Old French crieor (Modern French crieur), derived from the verb crier. cry + -er.

s: The action of something that ebbs.
An act or case of reckless boldness.
e: From Middle English temerite, temeryte, from Old French temerité, from Latin temeritās (“chance, accident, rashness”), from temere (“by chance, casually, rashly”). temerarious + -ity.

s: Having the qualities of a bog; i.e. dank, squishy, muddy, and full of water and rotting vegetation.
The act of one who trudges, or walks slowly and heavily.
An echo, or a series of overlapping echoes.
The reflection of light or heat; a reflection in, or as though in, a mirror.
An evolving series of effects resulting from a particular event; a repercussion.
e: From Old French reverberation, from Medieval Latin reverberātiō. Morphologically reverberate + -ion.

s: At all, in any degree, in any respect.
Of importance or consequence (in the phrase "of aught").
Form of Obsolete or dialectal form
Form of Obsolete or dialectal form.
e: From Middle English aught, ought, from Old English āht, āwiht, from ā (“always", "ever”) + wiht (“thing", "creature”). More at wight.

From Middle English aught (“estimation, regard, reputation”), from Old English ǣht (“estimation, consideration”), from Proto-West Germanic *ahtu. Cognate with Dutch acht (“attention, regard, heed”), German Acht (“attention, regard”). Also see ettle.
From Middle English ahte, from Old English eahta (“eight”). More at eight.

s: The fact or action of becoming or making into a god; deification.
exaltation; crediting someone or something with extraordinary power or status.
A glorified example or ideal; the apex or pinnacle (of a concept or belief).
The best moment or highest point in the development of something, for example of a life or career; the apex, culmination, or climax (of a development).
Release from earthly life, ascension to heaven; death.
The latent entity that mediates between a person's psyche and their thoughts. The id, ego and superego in Freudian Psychology are examples of this.
e: Borrowed from Latin apotheōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις, from verb ἀποθεόω (“deify”) (factitive verb formed from θεός (“God”) with intensive prefix ἀπο-) + -σις (“forms noun of action”). apo- + theo- + -sis.

s: In a state of complete and thorough satisfaction; having one’s appetite fully satisfied, by having enough of something.
To delay; to be late or tardy in beginning or doing anything.
To linger in expectation of something or until something is done or happens.
To abide, stay or wait somewhere, especially if longer than planned.
To wait for; to stay or stop for; to allow to linger.
e: From Middle English tarien, terien (“to vex, harass, cause to hesitate, delay”), from Old English tirian, tirġan, terġan (“to worry, exasperate, pain, provoke, excite”), from Proto-Germanic *terganą, *targijaną (“to pull, tease, irritate”), from Proto-Indo-European *derHgʰ- (“to pull, tug, irritate”).

s: A fine film made up of cobwebs, seen floating in the air or caught on bushes, etc.

e: From Middle English therfrom, þærfrom, þarvram (also as ther-fro, þer-fro, þarfra), equivalent to there + from. Cognate with Danish derfra, Swedish därifrån, Norwegian derfra, Norwegian derifrå, derfrå, Icelandic þarfrá.

s: Not used to an event or thing, not accustomed.
To which one is not accustomed, unfamiliar
One who, or that which, dulls.
A small, narrow opening, fissure, crevice, or chink, as in a wall, or other substance.
A tool for forming the necks of bottles, etc.
To break into, or become full of, crannies.
To haunt or enter by crannies.
A member of the East Indians, or mixed-race people, from among whom English copyists were chiefly recruited.
Absence of sound; silence or hush.
Absence of disturbance; calm, stillness or serenity.

A weasel found in northern latitudes (Mustela erminea in Eurasia, Alaska, and the Arctic, Mustela haidarum in Haida Gwaii, Mustela richardsonii in the rest of North America) whose dark brown fur turns white in winter, apart from the black tip of the tail.
The white fur of this animal, traditionally seen as a symbol of purity and used for judges' robes.
The fur of this animal, used as a heraldic tincture: a white field with a repeating pattern of stylized black spots.
Any of various moths, especially in the family Yponomeutidae
In blazon, of the colour ermine (white with black spots).
e: From Middle English ermine, ermin, ermyn, from Old French ermin, ermine, hermine.

s: To lessen in price or estimated value; to lower the worth of.
To decline in value over time.
e: Inherited from Middle English depreciaten, borrowed from Late Latin dēpretiātus / dēpreciātus, perfect passive participle of dēpretiō / dēpreciō (see -ate), from dē- + pretium (“price”) + -ō.

s: A perennial flowering plant (of the genus Crocus in the Iridaceae family). Saffron is obtained from the stamens of Crocus sativus.
Any of various similar flowering plants, such as autumn crocus and prairie crocus.
A deep yellow powder, the oxide of some metal (especially iron), calcined to a red or deep yellow colour.
e: Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (“crocus”), from an ancient language.

s: Showing or characterized by great respect or reverence; respectful.
e: From Middle English reverent, from Middle French reverent (from Old French reverent) and its etymon Latin reverēns. revere + -ent.

s: Carefully aware of all circumstances; considerate of all that is pertinent.
The act of disenchanting or the state of being disenchanted.
Freeing from false belief or illusions.
The devaluation of religion or mysticism apparent in modern society.
e: From dis- + enchantment. In the social sciences sense a Calque of German Entzauberung, as used by sociologist Max Weber.

s: The quality of being constant; steadiness or faithfulness in action, affections, purpose, etc.
An unchanging quality or characteristic of a person or thing.
with the upper part of the body forward and downward to a half-squatting position.
The act of one who stoops.
The state of being idle; inactivity.
The state of being indolent; indolence.
e: From Middle English ydelnesse, from Old English īdelnes, from Proto-West Germanic *īdlanassī, equivalent to idle + -ness. Cognate with Old Frisian īdelnisse (“idelness”), obsolete Dutch ijdelnis, Old Saxon īdalnussi (“idleness, vanity”), Old High German ītalnissa (“idleness, vanity, emptiness”).

s: The state or quality of being direct.
Casually careless or indifferent; showing a lack of concern; nonchalant.
beautiful, comely; gracious, pleasant and attractive in manner.
To set out the meaning of; to explain or discuss at length.
To make a statement, especially at length.
e: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone, expose.

s: To make a sound similar to a horse's cry.
e: Inherited from Middle English neyen, from Old English hnǣġan, from Proto-West Germanic *hnaijan, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną (“to neigh”). Cognate with dialectal Dutch neien, Middle Low German neigen, Swedish gnägga, Icelandic hneggja.

s: To formally revoke the validity of.
To dissolve (a marital union) on the grounds that it is not valid.
e: From Middle English annullen, from Old French anuller, from Latin annullō (“annihilate, annul”), from ad (“to”) + nūllus (“none, not any”).

s: Of a thing: done with evasive or guilty secrecy.
Of a thing: that has been acquired by theft; stolen; also taken stealthily.
Of a person or an animal: sly, stealthy.
Of a person, etc.: inclined to steal; pilfering, thieving.
e: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft; robbery”) (from fūr (“thief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -īvus.

s: A circle of individuals who associate with one another for a common purpose.
A communal burrow of prairie dogs.
An ornate silk fabric originating from Damascus.
Linen so woven that a pattern is produced by the different directions of the thread, without contrast of colour.
A heavy woolen or worsted stuff with a pattern woven in the same way as the linen damask; made for furniture covering and hangings.
The peculiar markings or water of such steel.
A grayish-pink color, like that of the damask rose.
Of a grayish-pink colour, like that of the damask rose.
To decorate or weave in damascene patterns
e: From Middle English damaske, from Medieval Latin damascus, named after the city Damascus, where the fabric was originally made.

s: Not perceptible, not detectable, too small in magnitude to be observed.
Beyond the purview of man; too great and all-encompassing to be perceived.
e: Inherited from Middle English imperceptible, from Middle French imperceptible and its etymon Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. im- + perceptible.

s: Animated, gay or vivacious; lively, spirited.
Of a person: full of life and vigour, especially with a light and springy step.
Especially of an older person: energetic and in good health; spry.
Of or relating to a sprite; ghostly, spectral.
In a lively and vigorous way; sprightlily.
A short invocation for help, blessing and guidance from God, said on behalf of another person or persons (sometimes at the end of a church worship service).
In the Anglican church, the ceremony used to institute an abbot, analogous to the consecration of a bishop.
A Roman Catholic rite by which bells, banners, candles, etc., are blessed with holy water and formally dedicated to God.
Help, good fortune or reward from God or another supernatural source.
e: From Middle English benediccion, from Ecclesiastical Latin benedictio, benedictionis, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”). Doublet of benison.

s: The fact of being betrothed; a mutual promise, engagement, or contract for a future marriage between two people.
Fated, predetermined, or doomed; something whose outcome has been set beforehand.
Any member of the species Lobophora halterata of geometrid moths.
e: From Latin seraphim, from Koine Greek σεραφείμ, from Hebrew שְׂרָפִים, plural of שָׂרָף (often translated as "fiery ones" although meaning is uncertain); perhaps related to the root שרף (“to burn”).

s: A low wagon or cart on small wheels, used to transport things.
A motion as of something moving upon little wheels or rollers; a rolling motion.
The sound made by an object being moved on wheels.
A lantern wheel, or one of its bars.
A spool or skein of golden thread (chiefly in the arms of the Embroiderers Company, now the Company of Broderers).
To cause (a round object) to roll; to bowl, to roll.
To cause (something which is held) to rotate; to spin, to twirl, to whirl; specifically, to spin (a mop) to remove water from it.
To cause (an object with one or more castors, wheels, etc.) to move (heavily) by pulling or pushing; to roll, to wheel.
To carry or transport (someone or something) using an object or vehicle with one or more castors, wheels, etc.
Of an object: to move by revolving or rolling; to revolve, to roll.
Of an object: to move (often heavily) on one or more castors, wheels, etc.; to roll.
To be carried or transported, or to travel, in a wheeled vehicle.
To sleep in a trundle bed or truckle bed; to truckle.
e: The is either: The is either: and are from the fact that such a ball used to be rolled on the ground. is a back-formation from trundle bed.

s: A thing or person of no worth or value; nil.
Not any quantity of number; zero; the score of no points in a game.
The figure or character representing, or having the shape of, zero.
To abase, to set at nought.
To no extent; in no way; not at all.
e: From Middle English nought, noght, noȝt, from Old English nōwiht, nāwiht, which in turn comes from ne-ā-wiht, which was a phrase used as an emphatic "no", meaning "not anything". Equivalent to ne + ought or ne + a + wight. Doublet of naught, not.

s: The state of being frank; candour; honesty.
A rebuke by an authority that one has erred and should not persist in one's actions.
e: From Middle English amonicioun, from Old French amonicion, from Latin admonitio, stem of admonere. The -d- was restored in English in the 17th century.

s: A musical composition, often based on a religious theme; similar to opera but with no costume, scenery or acting.
e: Borrowed from Italian oratorio (“oratorical”), from Latin ōrātōrius. Doublet of oratory.

s: A confused sound of a crowd of people shouting or speaking simultaneously; an uproar.
Noisy confusion; commotion, uproar; an instance of this; an ado, a commotion.
A sound of people making a battle cry or war cry.
To make a confused sound of a crowd of people shouting or speaking simultaneously; to cause a racket or tumult.
e: In early use, the is often mentioned as a cry by Irish people, and so is possibly borrowed from Irish; compare Irish ababú, abú (“used as a battle cry”), and Scottish Gaelic ub, ubub (“used to express contempt, etc.”), ubh ubh (“used to express disgust”). The is derived from the noun.
Used by New England colonists (17th–18th century) to the sounds hub, hub, hub cried by the players: see the 1634 quotation.

s: To what (future) cause, condition or state, reason, etc.; where, where next; also to what extent; how far.
To which place; also (after a noun denoting a place) to which.
To the place in or to which.
In or to any place to which; to whatever place; wherever.
A place to which someone or something goes; also, a condition to which someone or something moves.
To cause (someone) to hurry; to hasten, to hurry.
To throw (something) forcefully; to hurl; also, to beat, to thrash.
To move quickly, to rush, to whiz; also, to make a rushing sound; to whizz.
Of the wind: to blow loudly and vigorously; to bluster; also, of an animal, etc.: to make a loud noise; to bellow, to roar.
A state of rushed action; a haste, a hurry; also, a state of anger or excitement.
An act of shaking (vigorously); a shiver, a tremble; also, a slight bout of discomfort or illness.
e: From Middle English whider (“to what place?; into or to which; to what place, where; no matter where, to wherever”), from Old English hwider, hwæder (“to what place, where”), from Proto-Germanic *hwadrê (“to what place, where”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos (“what; which”), from *kʷ-.

The verb is borrowed from Scots whidder, whither (“(of the wind) to bluster; to move quickly”), a frequentative form of whid (“(of wind) to gust; to move quickly”), of Scandinavian/ origin, from Old Norse hviða (“gust of wind”). Related to Middle English hwiþa, whyȝt (“breeze; wind”), Old English hwiþa, hwiþu, hweoþu (“breeze”).

s: A cry of joy or pleasure.

e: From Middle English lystles, equivalent to list (“desire”) + -less. Compare German lustlos and Dutch lusteloos (“lethargic, listless”). Doublet of lustless.

s: A pitted, now usually metal, cup-shaped cap worn on the tip of a finger, which is used in sewing to push the needle through material.
As much as fills a thimble (sense 1); a thimbleful.
An object which resembles a thimble (sense 1) in shape or size.
A thimble or similar object used in thimblerig.
A socket in machinery shaped like a thimble.
A metal ring which a cable or rope intended for attaching to other things is looped around as a protection against chafing.
A ring- or tube-shaped component such as a ferrule.
A cool room in a domestic house where food is stored.
e: Inherited from Middle English larder, from Anglo-Norman larder and Old French lardier, from Latin lardārium. lard + -er.

s: Shy; not liking to be noticed; socially timid.
The reflexive of the royal or editorial we: myself (as used by one who is a monarch, writer or speaker when referring to oneself as we).
The reflexive of the generic we: oneself.
Reflexive of "we" referring to an individual person being addressed, especially a person in the speaker's care.
A small crown, such as is worn by a noble.
The ring of tissue between a horse's hoof and its leg.
The traditional lowest regular commissioned officer rank in the cavalry.
Any of several hummingbirds in the genus Boissonneaua.
Any member of the species Craniophora ligustri of moths.
e: From Middle French couronnette, from Old French coronete, diminutive of corone (“crown”), from Latin corona, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (“a type of sea-bird, perhaps shearwater; a crow; anything curved or hooked (like a door handle or the tip of a bow); a type of crown”).

s: A type of parchment paper made from the skin of a lamb, baby goat, or calf.
A writing paper of very high quality.
e: From Old French velin (French vélin), from Latin vitulinus (“of a calf”), as if derived from Old French veel (“veal”).

s: The quality of deserving applause, praiseworthiness; something worthy of praise.
The appearance of truth, especially when deceptive; speciousness.
The fact of being believable; believability, credibility.
Agent noun of juggle; one who either literally juggles objects, or figuratively juggles tasks.
A person who practices juggling (trick of throwing and catching balls or similar).
A person who performs tricks using sleight of hand, a conjurer, prestidigitator.
e: From Middle English jogeler, jogelour, iogular, partly continuing Old English ġeogolere (“juggler; magician; wizard”) and partly from Anglo-Norman jogelour, jugelur, Old French jongleur (“juggler”), equivalent to juggle + -er. Doublet of jongleur.

s: To survive on a minimum of resources.
To have ontological reality; to exist.
To retain a certain state; to continue.
To supply sustenance or subsistence to or for.
e: From Latin subsistō (“halt, stop”), from sub (“below”) + sistō (“stand, place”). Compare consist, desist, exist, insist, persist.

s: Any ailment or disease of the body; especially, a lingering or deep-seated disorder.
A moral or mental defect or disorder.
e: From Middle English maladie, from Old French maladie (“sickness, illness, disease”), from malade (“ill, sick”), from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”), 1st century AD. See also malice and habit.

s: To sketch out, draw or trace an outline.
To describe or depict with words or gestures.
e: Borrowed from Latin dēlīneātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīneo (“to sketch out, to delineate”) (see -ate and -ate), from dē- + līnea (“line”) + -ō. Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s: A bulbous plant of the genus Narcissus, with yellow flowers and a trumpet shaped corona, especially Narcissus pseudonarcissus, the national flower of Wales.
A brilliant yellow color, like that of a daffodil.
Of a brilliant yellow color, like that of a daffodil.
e: Variant of Middle English affodill (“ramson”), from Medieval Latin affodillus, from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος, of origin. The initial d- is perhaps from merging of the article in Dutch de affodil, the Netherlands being a source for bulbs (compare adder, apron, newt, nickname, orange and umpire for this rebracketing process).

s: or impossible to comprehend, fathom or interpret.
One who or that which is inscrutable; a person, etc. that cannot be comprehended.
e: Borrowed into late Middle English from Late Latin īnscrūtābilis, from in- (“not”) + scrūtō (“to examine”), corresponding to in- + scrutable.

s: in a bent bodily position, hunched
Conveyed without the use of words; unspoken or unsaid.
Unable or unwilling to speak; dumb, silent or inarticulate.
e: From Middle English wordles, equivalent to word + -less. Compare Dutch woordeloos (“speechless, inexpressible in words”), German wortlos (“silent, speechless”), Danish ordløs (“wordless”), Swedish ordlös (“wordless”), Icelandic orðlaus (“wordless, speechless”).

s: Someone who moves about in roving fashion looking for plunder.
Any person who or thing which marauds.
The vault of the heavens, where the clouds, sun, moon, and stars can be seen; the heavens, the sky.
The field or sphere of an activity or interest.
In the geocentric Ptolemaic system, the eighth celestial sphere which carried the fixed stars; any celestial sphere.
The abode of God and the angels; heaven.
A piece of jewellery worn in a headdress with numerous gems resembling stars in the sky.
A basis or foundation; a support.
The act or process of making firm or strengthening.
e: From Middle English firmament, furmament (“heaven; sky”), from Old French firmament (“firmament”), or from its etymon Latin firmāmentum (“support; sky”), from firmāre (“to strengthen”) + -mentum.

s: Able to be perceived, sensed, or discerned.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin perceptibilis, from Latin percipio.

s: To make a false show or pretence of; to counterfeit or simulate.
To imagine; to invent; to pretend to do something.
To make an action as if doing one thing, but actually doing another, for example to trick an opponent; to feint.
e: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”). Compare French feignant. Also compare feint, figment and fiction.

s: A short, simple verse or song.
A saying or utterance, especially one that is short and frequently repeated.
To sing; to warble a little tune.
e: From Middle English dite, ditee, from Old French ditie or dité, from ditier, from Latin dictāre (participle dictatus).

s: The extinction of any of several physical properties.
The rapid cooling of a hot metal object, by placing it in a liquid, in order to harden it.
A process in which a galaxy loses cold gas, thus strongly suppressing star formation.
The dissipation of energy from light in excess of what can be used for photosynthesis.
A method of representing a language or the sounds of language by written symbols; spelling.
A set of conventions for writing a language, including norms of spelling, capitalization, emphasis, hyphenation, punctuation, and word breaks.
The aspect of language study concerned with letters and their sequences in words; the study of spelling.
Correct spelling according to established usage; also pronunciation according to the spelling of a word.

A form of projection used to represent three-dimensional objects in two dimensions, in which all the projection lines are orthogonal or perpendicular to the projection plane; an orthographic projection, especially when used to draw an elevation, vertical projection, etc., of a building; also a drawi
To spell (words) or write (text) according to established usage.
e: The noun is derived from Late Middle English ortografie, ortographie (“spelling”), and then either: The English word is analyzable as ortho- + -graphy. The verb is derived from the noun. First use appears before c. 1460.

From Middle English alwey, from Old English ealneġ, ealne weġ (“always, perpetually”), from ealne + weġ, equivalent to al-#Etymology_1- (“all”) + way. Cognate with Scots alwayis (“always”). More at all, way.

s: The fruit of this tree; the pulp is used as spice in Asian cooking and in Worcestershire sauce.
Diploglottis australis, native tamarind, a rainforest tree of Eastern Australia.
Garcinia gummi-gutta, Malabar tamarind, native to Indonesia.
A dark brown color, like that of tamarind pulp (also called tamarind brown).
e: From Late Middle English thamarynde, from Old French tamarinde, from Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ.

s: Showing disrespect through a casual attitude, levity, and a lack of due seriousness; pert.
e: 1595, from Northern English dialectal flippand (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of flip (“to babble”), of origin. Cognate with Icelandic fleipa (“to babble, prattle”), Swedish dialectal flepa (“to talk nonsense”). Alteration of -and suffix (a variant of the participial -ing) to -ant probably due to influence from words in -ant.

s: Sparingly; not plentifully; not fully; in a scanty manner.

e: Probably the same word as nit, a louse's egg.

s: Extremely full of people, packed, chockablock.
Pertaining to or having the characteristics of prose.
Straightforward; matter-of-fact; lacking the feeling or elegance of poetry.
usually of writing or speaking but also figurative
Overly plain, simple or commonplace, to the point of being boring.
e: From Middle French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus (“in prose”), from Latin prosa (“prose”), from prorsus (“straightforward, in prose”), from Old Latin provorsus (“straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn, to bend”).

s: Avoidance of saying or reluctance to say too much; discretion, tight-lippedness; an instance of acting in this manner.
Followed by of: discretion or restraint in the use of something.
Often followed by to: hesitancy or reluctance (to do something).
To deliberately not listen or pay attention to; to disregard, to ignore.
e: The noun is borrowed from Middle French réticence (“act of keeping silent, silence; reserve; aposiopesis”) (modern French réticence (“tight-lippedness, reticence”)), or derived from its etymon Latin reticentia (“act of keeping silent, silence; aposiopesis”), from reticēns (“keeping silent, reticent, silent; keeping secret, concealing”) + -ia.

s: Drooping, typically due to lack of water.
To break up and smooth soil with a harrow.
e: From the brand name of a harrow maker.

s: An instance of scalding: a burn.
Synonym of escaline, the form circulated by Stephen de Fulbourn in Ireland as a debased form of the sterling silver penny, outlawed under Edward I of England.
e: From Old French escalin, from Middle Dutch schelling (“shilling”). Doublet of shilling.

s: A person who practices or performs necromancy.
e: An alteration of nigromancer after necromancy, equivalent to necromancy + -er.
From Latin magnanimus, from magnus (“great”) + animus (“soul, mind”). Displaced native Old English miċelmōd.

s: An itinerant seller of small goods.
A fake-news disseminator; A conspiracy-theory propagator.
e: From Middle English pedlere, pedlare, pedeler, alteration of Middle English peddere (“hawker, peddler”), of Uncertain origin. Compare Medieval Latin pedārius, from Latin pedāre (“to furnish with feet; prop up”).

s: The emotion usually following humor and accompanied by laughter.
e: From Middle English merth, myrthe, murhthe, from Old English myrgþ (“mirth, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgiþu (“briefness, brevity”); equivalent to merry + -th. Cognate with Middle Dutch merchte (“pleasure, joy, delight”).
From Middle English venquysshen, vaynquisshen, borrowed from a conjugated form of Old French veincre, from Latin vincō.

s: separable from the thing itself; inessential.
e: From French extrinsèque, from Latin extrinsecus (“from without, without, on the outside”), from *extrim, an assumed adverbial form of exter (“outer, outward”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

s: Probably; not falsifiably, based on available facts and general knowledge.
Unwilling to communicate; keeping one's thoughts and opinions to oneself; reserved or restrained.
Hesitant or not wanting to take some action; reluctant (usually followed by a verb in the infinitive).
e: Latin reticēns, present participle of reticeō (“to keep silence”).

s: That scintillates with brief flashes of light; sparkling.
Brilliantly or impressively clever, exciting, amusing or witty.
A great outcry or vociferation; loud and continued shouting or exclamation.
A continued public expression, often of dissatisfaction or discontent; a popular outcry.
e: Recorded in English since c. 1385, as Middle English clamour, from Old French clamor (modern clameur), from Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”). The verb sense "to silence" may have a distinct (unknown) etymology.

s: in, involving, or reflecting deep or serious thought.
Having the appearance of deep, often melancholic, thinking.
e: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

s: In a cordial, warm, friendly or heartfelt manner.
A horizontal architectural element of a building, projecting forward from the main walls, originally used as a means of directing rainwater away from the building's walls.
A decorative element applied at the topmost part of the wall of a room, as with a crown molding.
A decorative element at the topmost portion of certain pieces of furniture, as with a highboy.
An overhanging edge of snow on a ridge or the crest of a mountain and along the sides of gullies.
To furnish or decorate with a cornice.
e: From Middle French corniche or Italian cornice, possibly from either (1) Latin cornīx (“crow”) or (2) Latin coronis (“curved line, flourish in writing”), from Ancient Greek κορωνίς. See also corniche.

s: Not realized; possible to obtain or achieve, yet not obtained or achieved.
Not yet realized in cash; hypothetical.
A small light umbrella used as protection from the sun.
