A miniature paper umbrella used as a decoration in tropical-themed cocktails.
A sun umbrella for garden use etc., mounted on a stand; these can be foldable and demountable.
A roof or covering of a structure designed to provide cover from wind, rain, or sun.
Any of various Asian species of libellulid dragonfly of the genus Neurothemis.
To protect with, or as if with, a parasol; to shade.
e: From French parasol, from Italian parasole, from Italian parare + Italian sole.

s: Something that is supposed; an assumption made to account for known facts, conjecture.
The act or an instance of supposing.
e: From Middle English supposicioun, from Anglo-Norman supposicion, from Latin suppositiō, suppositiōnem (“supposition”), from sub- (“under”) + positiō, positiōnem (“position; theme”), from positus (“position”), from the perfect passive participle of pōnō, pōnere (“put, place”).

s: A group of attendants or servants, especially of someone considered important.
A group of warriors or nobles accompanying a king or other leader; comitatus.
e: From Middle English retenue, from Old French retenue, past participle of retenir (“retain”). Doublet of ritenuto.

s: To lessen the intensity of, to mitigate or relieve (hunger, emotion, pain, etc.).
To calm down, become less violent (of passion, hunger etc.); to subside, to abate.
e: From Middle English aswagen, from Old French asuagier (“to appease, to calm”), from Vulgar Latin *assuāviō (“to sweeten, to butter up, to calm”), derived from Latin ad- + suāvis (“sweet”) + -iō.

s: The act of rejecting or renouncing something as invalid.
The resignation of an ecclesiastical office.
The act by which a person abandons a right acquired, but without transferring it to another.
In the Anglican baptismal service, the part in which the candidate in person or by his sureties renounces the Devil and all his works.
Excessively particular, demanding, or fussy about details, especially about tidiness and cleanliness.
Overly concerned about tidiness and cleanliness.
Difficult to please; quick to find fault.
Having precise requirements for nutrition and environment (chemical and physical); especially, being difficult to culture because of those requirements.
e: Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus (“passive: that feels disgust, disdainful, scornful, fastidious; active: that causes disgust, disgusting, loathsome”), from fastīdium (“a loathing, aversion, disgust, niceness of taste, daintiness, etc.”), perhaps for *fastutidium, from fastus (“disdain, haughtiness, arrogance, disgust”) + taedium (“disgust”). Cf. French fastidieux.

s: of intense emotions arising from sexual love; ardent and passionate.
[of a streak, form, etc.]; impressive; hot.
Any of several varieties of thin cotton cloth.
Fabric made of cotton, flax (linen), hemp, or silk, finely or coarsely woven.
Any of a wide variety of tightly-woven thin fabrics, especially those used for bedlinen.
Woven cotton or linen fabrics, especially when used for items other than garments.
A mock-up of a garment pattern made of inexpensive fabric for the purpose of optimizing its fit on the wearer, before the garment is produced in more expensive fabric.
Any of several different moths, especially the muslin moth, Diaphora mendica.
Woman as sex object; prostitute, as in a bit of muslin.
e: From French mousseline, from Italian mussolina, from Mussolo (“Mosul”), that is Mosul in northern Iraq (compare 1875 Knight, Edward H., Knight's American Mechanical Dictionary, V2 p1502: "Muslins are so called from Moussol in India."). Doublet of mousseline.

s: A person in attendance at a royal court.
A person who flatters in order to seek favour.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the Asian genus Sephisa.
e: From Middle English courteour, from Anglo-Norman corteour, Old French cortoiier, from cort (“court”). court + -ier.

s: The state or quality of having value or merit.
The result or product of having value or merit.
The state or quality of being qualified or eligible.
The result or product of being qualified or eligible.
A small, narrow or enclosed, usually wooded valley.
e: From Middle English dingle (“a deep hollow; dell”), from Old English *dyngel, a diminutive of Old English dung (“dungeon; pit”), equivalent to dung + -le. Compare Dongel (“hollow tooth, cavity”), English dimble. Related to dungeon.

s: Not obtrusive; not blatant or noticeable; discreet, inconspicuous.
A kingfisher whose nesting by the sea was said, in classical mythology, to cause the Gods to restrain the wind and waves.
The dead body of such a bird, said in Tudor times to act as a weather vane when hung from a beam.
A tropical kingfisher of the genus Halcyon, such as the sacred kingfisher (Halcyon sancta) of Australia.
Pertaining to the halcyon or kingfisher.
e: Inherited from Middle English Alceoun, from Latin halcyōn, alcyōn (“kingfisher”), from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών.

s: A shining fabric used for ornamental purposes.
A silk or wool fabric with gold or silver thread woven into it; brocade.
A very thin, gauzelike cloth with gold or silver (or, later, copper) thread woven into it, or overlaid with thin metal plates.

A thin, shiny foil for ornamental purposes which is of a material made of metal or resembling metal; especially, narrow glittering strips of such a material, often strung on to thread, and traditionally at Christmastime draped on Christmas trees, hung from balustrades or ceilings, or wrapped around
Anything shining and gaudy; especially something superficially shiny and showy, or having a false lustre, and more pretty than valuable.
Of fabric: ornamented by being woven with gold or silver thread, or overlaid with thin metal plates; brocaded.
Apparently beautiful and costly but having little value; superficially attractive; gaudy, showy, tawdry.
To ornament (fabric, etc.) by weaving into it thread of gold, silver, or some other shiny material.
To deck out (a place or something) with showy but cheap ornaments; to make gaudy.
To give (something) a false or superficial attractiveness.
To cause (someone) damage or loss; also, to impose a fine on (someone); to mulct.
e: The noun is derived from Middle English tinsel (“cloth containing gold or silver thread”), probably from Anglo-Norman tincel, tincelle, tencele, and then: The English word is a Doublet of scintilla, scintillate, stencil. The adjective is from an attributive use of the noun; while the verb is derived from the noun.

s: A sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from various plants.
A plant or tree yielding such substance.
A flowering plant of the genus Impatiens.
Any member of the balsam family of flowering plants (Balsaminaceae), which includes genera Impatiens and Hydrocera.
Canada balsam, a turpentine obtained from the resin of balsam fir.
Any of various traditional European herbal liqueurs, originally used medicinally.
To treat or anoint with balsam.
e: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (“balsam”), of origin (Hebrew בושם (“spice, perfume”)); compare Old English balsam, balsamum (“balsam, balm”), Doublet of balm, desman. Not related to balsa.

s: The act by which a bell is tolled.
As if shining with a brilliant light; radiant.
One who means or intends something.
Thought, imagination, or conjecture, which may be based upon feeble or scanty evidence; suspicion; guess.
To imagine or suspect; to conjecture; to posit with contestable premises.
e: From Old French surmis, past participle of surmetre, surmettre (“to accuse”), from sur- (“upon”) + metre (“to put”).

s: Of speech or style: brief, concise, to the point.
Of manner or speech: abruptly or brusquely short; curt.
Burnished, polished; fine, smooth; neat, spruce.
e: From Latin tersus (“clean, cleansed, rubbed or wiped off; neat, spruce; terse”), perfect passive participle of Latin tergeō, tergō (“to clean, cleanse, rub, wipe, wipe off”).

s: To become too big in size or too mature in age or outlook to continue to want, need, use, experience or accept some object, practice, condition, belief, etc.
To grow faster or larger than.
A rheostat that is used to vary the intensity of a domestic electric light
A switch used to select between the low and high headlamp beam on a road vehicle. (usually as "dimmer switch", primarily in North America; elsewhere "dipswitch" or "dipper switch")
Not affected emotionally, or not showing emotion.

e: From Middle English kynnesman, from late Old English cinnes man, equivalent to kin + -s- + -man.

s: Conveying in demeanour the assumption of superiority; disdainful, supercilious.
A recess in some early churches in which the reserved sacrament, etc. was kept from Good Friday till Easter.
e: From Middle English sepulchre, sepulcre, sepulker, from late Old English sepulcer, Old French sepulchre, sepulcre, and their etymon Latin sepulchrum, sepulcrum (“grave, burial place”).

s: Very sad or distressed, sorely upset.

To convert a representation of language, typically speech but also sign language, etc., to a written representation of it. The term now usually implies the conversion of speech to text by a human transcriptionist with the assistance of a computer for word processing and sometimes also for speech rec
To make such a conversion from live or recorded speech to text.
To transfer data from one recording medium to another.
To adapt a composition for a voice or instrument other than the original; to notate live or recorded music.
To cause DNA to undergo transcription.
To represent speech by phonetic symbols.
e: Latin trānscrībere (“to write again in another place, transcribe, copy”).

s: To recall; to collect one's thoughts again, especially about past events.
e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin recollectus (“remembered, composed”), from Latin recolligo (“gather again, recover”).

s: Ostentatious display of wealth and luxury; plushness.

A cylindrical mechanical fastener which is supplied with a factory head at one end and is used to attach multiple parts together by passing its bucktail through a hole and upsetting its end to form a field head.
Any fixed point or certain basis.
A light kind of footman's plate armour; an almain rivet.
To attach or fasten parts by using rivets.
e: From Old French rivet (13th century), from the verb Old French river (“to fetter [a person]”) (12th century), from Old French rive (“rim, edge”) (ca. 1100), which is ultimately from Latin ripa (“riverbank”). Compare river, rival, riparian.

s: To execute (a person) by nailing to a cross.
To punish or otherwise express extreme anger at, especially as a scapegoat or target of outrage.
To thoroughly beat at a sport or game.
e: From Middle English crucifien, from Old French crucefier, from Late Latin crucificō, from Latin crucifigō.

[[File:Maelstrom-Clarke.jpg|thumb|An illustration from 1919 by Harry Clarke of a boat caught in a maelstrom (sense 1) for Edgar Allan Poe’s short story A Descent into the Maelström (1841).]] The word was originally the name of a giant whirlpool off Norway in the Arctic Ocean which was said to destroy all ships that came close to it, likely the actual tidal pool system of Moskstraumen in Lofoten.

s: To move suddenly, or be excited, on feeling alarm; to start.
To excite by sudden alarm, surprise, or apprehension; to frighten suddenly and not seriously; to alarm; to surprise.
To deter; to cause to deviate.
A sudden motion or shock caused by an unexpected alarm, surprise, or apprehension of danger.
e: From Middle English startlen (“to rush, jump”), from Old English steartlian (“to kick with the foot, struggle, stumble”), equivalent to start + -le. Cognate with Old Norse stirtla (“to hobble, stagger”), Icelandic stirtla (“to straighten up, erect”). Compare also Middle English stertil (“hasty”). More at start.

s: To raise a corner of the upper lip slightly, especially in scorn.
To utter with a grimace or contemptuous expression; to say sneeringly.
A facial expression where one slightly raises one corner of the upper lip, generally indicating scorn.
e: From Middle English sneren (“to mock, scoff at”), from Old English fnǣran (“to snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *fnāʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *fnesaną (“to pant, gasp”). Akin to sneere (“to scorn”), Middle High German snerren (“to chatter; gossip”), Danish snerre (“to growl, snarl”).

s: The mass of ordinary people; the populous or the masses.
A small, showy ornament, especially a piece of jewellery.
A thing of little practical and/or monetary value; a toy, a trifle.
A small item of food; a small dainty.
A small item forming part of a set of equipment; an accessory, an accoutrement.
An item used in a religious rite (also, a religious rite, belief, etc.) regarded as superfluous or trivial.
Often followed by out: to adorn (someone or something) with trinkets (noun).
A small vessel for drinking from; a cup, a mug, a porringer.
A small sail, specifically, a three-cornered sail formerly carried on a ship's foremast, probably on a lateen yard.
To act in a secret, and often dishonest, way; to have secret, and often dishonest, dealings; to intrigue, to scheme.
e: The origin of the noun is Unknown; the word is possibly related to Old French tryncle (“piece of jewellery”). The following have also been suggested: However, according to the Oxford English Dictionary, there is insufficient evidence of any shift of meaning from these words to the current meanings of trinket. The verb is derived from the noun.

Probably from French trinquet (“foremast; sail attached to a foremast”), from Italian trinchetto (“small sail, especially a foresail”), possibly from Latin triquetrus (“three-cornered, triangular”) (referring to a three-cornered sail), from tri- (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes (“three”)) + Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₁d- (“sharp”).
Possibly borrowed from Scots trinket, trincket; further origin Unknown, possibly related to.

s: In a royal manner; in a manner having to do with royalty.
A mournful or plaintive poem; a funeral song; a poem of lamentation.
A classical poem written in elegiac meter
e: From Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ, ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (“an elegiac song”).

s: Set into a surface in a decorative pattern.
of the surface of an item
A fine-grained white or lightly-tinted variety of gypsum, used ornamentally.
A variety of calcite, translucent and sometimes banded.
An off-white color, like that of alabaster.
Resembling alabaster; white, pale, smooth, translucent.
e: From Middle English alabastre, from Old French alabastre, from Latin alabaster (“box for perfumes or unguents”), from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος, from earlier ἀλάβαστος (“vase without handles for storing perfumes”). This may further derive from Egyptian ꜥj-r-bꜣstjt (“vessel of the Egyptian goddess Bast”).

s: To move back; to retreat; to withdraw.
To cede back; to grant or yield again to a former possessor.
e: Inherited from Middle English receden, from Middle French receder and its etymon Latin recedere (“to withdraw; to go back”), from re- + cedere (“to go”).

s: Measurement or estimation, with or as if with a gauge.
The addition of various materials to lime mortar.
An act of, or the process of, uttering.
An instance of that act or process: especially, something spoken (e.g., syllables, words, phrases); any such thing either spoken or written.
A sale made by offering to the public.
An act of putting in circulation.
The utmost extremity, especially of a fight; bodily harm or death.
e: From Middle English outraunce, utteraunce, from Old French outrance (see outrance).

s: To confuse or perplex (someone) completely; to bewilder, to confound, to puzzle.
To defeat, frustrate, or thwart (someone or their efforts, plans, etc.); to confound, to foil.
To dampen, muffle, restrain, or otherwise control (a fluid, or waves travelling through a fluid such as light or sound).
To expend effort or struggle in vain.
To argue or complain in a petty or trivial manner; to quibble.

A device used to dampen, muffle, restrain, or otherwise control the movement of a fluid, or waves travelling through a fluid such as light or sound; specifically, a surface positioned inside an open area to inhibit direct motion from one place to another without preventing motion altogether.
A lever for operating the throttle valve of a winding engine.
A device to prevent the spreading of sound or light.
A barrier designed to obstruct and confuse enemies, rendering them vulnerable.
An argument or objection based on an ambiguity of wording or similar trivial circumstance; a minor complaint; a quibble.
To publicly disgrace (someone); specifically, a recreant knight.
To treat (someone) with contempt; to disgrace; also, to speak of (someone or something) in contemptuous terms; to speak ill of, to vilify.
Intentional insult; affront; also, disgrace; an instance of this.
e: The origin of the verb is Uncertain; it is possibly: The noun is derived from the verb.

s: A soft crackling sound similar to the movement of dry leaves.
A movement producing such a sound.
To move (something) with a soft crackling sound.
To make or obtain in a lively, energetic way.
e: From Middle English rustelen, russelen, of uncertain origin, but probably from Old English hrūxlian, hristlan, hrystlan, hristlian (“to make a noise”). Compare also Scots reesle (“to crackle; rattle; rustle”), West Frisian risselje, Dutch ritselen (“to rustle”), Afrikaans ritsel (“to rustle”), German rascheln (“to rustle”).

s: The act of one who hurries; hasty motion.
Exceptional in importance or significance; special.
e: From Middle English especial, via Old French especial, from Latin specialis, from species (“appearance, form, beauty”), from specere (“to look”). Doublet of special. Related to species.

s: The space around the altar in a church or cathedral, often enclosed, for use by the clergy and the choir. In medieval cathedrals the chancel was usually enclosed or blocked off from the nave by an altar screen.
The entire end of the church in which the altar stands, including the apse and the ambulatory.
A certain central portion of that end of the church, excluding the apse and the ambulatory.
Any adversity; a trying period or event.
e: From Middle English tribulation, from Old French tribulacion, from Late Latin trībulātiō (“distress, trouble, tribulation, affliction”), from Latin tribulāre (“to press, probably also thresh out grain”), from trībulum (“a sledge consisting of a wooden block studded with sharp pieces of flint or with iron teeth, used for threshing grain”), from terēre (“to rub”); see trite.

s: Filled with grief or sadness; being in a state in which one mourns.
A porch, or a small space with a roof supported by columns, serving as the entrance to a building.
e: From Italian portico, from Latin porticus (“porch”), from porta (“gate”). Doublet of porch, portego, porticus.
Borrowed from French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir (“to be unconcerned”), from non- (“not”) + chaloir (“to have concern for”), from Latin non (“not”) + calēre (“to be warm”).

s: One who procrastinates or is lazy; one who does not do their fair share or pull their own weight.
A person lacking a sense of direction in life; an underachiever.
A member of a certain 1990s subculture associated with Generation X.
A person who seeks to avoid military service.
A user of the Slackware Linux distribution.
A vivid red synthetic pigment made of mercury sulfide, cinnabar.
A type of red dye worn in the parting of the hair by married Hindu women.
The red skin of the lips or its border with the skin of the face.
A scale insect of the species Dactylopius coccus.
The dye made from this insect.
Having the color of vermilion dye.
e: From Middle English vermelioun, vermyloun, vermylon, vermilun, from Old French vermeillon (“vermilion”), from vermeil, from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”), from vermis (“worm”), ultimately in reference to Kermes vermilio, a type of scale insect used to make a crimson dye. Displaced native Old English bōcrēad.

s: Of or relating to the grammatical aspect which expresses that a secondary action is occurring simultaneously to the primary action of the statement.
Something happening or existing at the same time.
An invariant homogeneous polynomial in the coefficients of a form, a covariant variable, and a contravariant variable.
e: First attested 1607; from Middle French concomitant, from Latin concomitāns, the present participle of concomitor (“to accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitor (“to accompany”), from comes (“companion”).

s: The inedible parts of a grain-producing plant.
Straw or hay cut up fine for the food of cattle.
Any excess or unwanted material, resource, or person; anything worthless.
Loose material, e.g. small strips of aluminum foil dropped from aircraft, intended to interfere with radar detection.
To use light, idle language by way of fun or ridicule; to banter.
To make fun of; to turn into ridicule by addressing in ironical or bantering language.
To cut up (straw or hay) for use as cattle feed.
e: From Middle English chaf, from Old English ċeaf, from Proto-West Germanic *kaf. Cognate with Scots caff, Sääf, West Frisian tsjêf, Dutch kaf, Low German Kaff, regional German Kaff.

s: Astuteness often marked by a certain sense of cunning or artful deception.
e: From Middle English gile, from Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile (“deception”), from Frankish *wīl (“ruse”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą, from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”). Cognate via Proto-Germanic with Doublet of wile.

s: A man in the context of his own wedding; one who is going to marry or has just been married.
e: From Middle English brydgrome, bridegome, from Old English brȳdguma, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô; equivalent to Old English brȳd (“bride”) + guma (“man”). Altered by folk etymology to end with groom, with it re-analyzed as or influenced by grom, grome (“attendant”), as guma was obsolete.

s: Intelligently analytical and concise. (of a person or mental process)
Accurate and sharply focused. (of an account)
Quickly proceeding to judgment and forceful in expression. (of an action)
Having the quality of incising, cutting, or penetrating, as with a sharp instrument; trenchant.
Of or relating to the incisors.
e: Late Middle English (in the sense), borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus, from incīdō (“to cut in, cut through”) + -īvus (“-ive”). Compare Middle French incisif.

s: State of owing money; being in debt.
The state of owing something or being under obligation to someone.
The state of being banished, exile.

Any of various small two-winged flies, for example, from the family Chironomidae or non-biting midges, the family Chaoboridae or phantom midges, and the family Ceratopogonidae or biting midges, all belonging to the order Diptera.
A small, short or insignificant person.
Any bait or lure designed to resemble a midge.
e: From Middle English mydge, migge, from Old English myġġ, myċġ (“midge, gnat, mosquito”), from Proto-West Germanic *muggju, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō, from Proto-Indo-European *mū-, *mu-, *mew- (“fly, midge”).

s: To require (something) as a condition of a contract or agreement.
To specify, promise or guarantee something in an agreement.
To acknowledge the truth of; not to challenge.
To ask for a contractual term.
Having stipules; that is, having outgrowths borne on either side of the base of the leafstalk.
e: From Latin stipulātus, perfect active participle of stipulor (“to demand a formal promise, stipulate”), see -ate.

s: To surround with a wall, fence, etc.
To insert into a container, usually an envelope or package.
e: From Middle English enclosen, inclosen, from Middle English enclos, from Old French enclose, feminine plural past participle of enclore, from Vulgar Latin *inclaudō, *inclaudere, from Latin inclūdō (Doublet of include), from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”).

s: A carpenter's tool for boring holes longer than those bored by a gimlet.
A snake or plumber's snake (plumbing tool).
A tool used to bore holes in the ground, e.g. for fence posts
A hollow drill used to take core samples of soil, ice, etc. for scientific study.
To use an auger; to drill a hole using an auger.
To proceed in the manner of an auger.
e: From a rebracketing of Middle English a nauger (seen as an + auger), from Old English nafugār (“nave drill”), from Proto-West Germanic *nabugaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz. Cognate with Dutch avegaar.

s: In a tender manner; gently; sweetly.
The act of one who skirts around something, or avoids it.
Astonishingly great or large; huge; enormous.
Of stunning excellence or degree; marvelous.
e: First attested from 1547, from Late Latin stupendus (“stunning, amazing”), from the verb stupeō (“(I) am stunned”). Doublet of stupend (which is obsolete), and related to stupor and stupid.

s: Formed into a row, or rows; having a specified number of rows.
The appearance or aspect of something, especially when expressive or distinctive.
e: From Middle English visage, from Anglo-Norman visage, from Vulgar Latin *vīsāticum, derived from Latin vīsus (“appearance, sight”), derived from vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision. See -age (“noun suffix”).

s: Why, for what reason, because of what.
An intent or purpose; a why.
e: From Middle English wherfor, wherfore, hwarfore, equivalent to where- (“what”) + for. Compare Dutch waarvoor (“what for, wherefore”), German wofür (“for what, what for, why”), Danish and Norwegian hvorfor (“wherefore, why”), Swedish varför (“wherefore, why”). More at where, for.

s: In a dim manner; not clearly.

e: From Middle French industrieux, from Late Latin industriosus (“diligent, active, industrious”), from Latin industria (“diligence, industry”); see industry.

s: Gerund of waver: a state of fluctuation or indecision.
A group of people crowded or gathered closely together.
A group of things; a host or swarm.
To crowd into a place, especially to fill it.
To crowd or press, as persons; to oppress or annoy with a crowd of living beings.
Filled with persons or objects; crowded.
e: From Middle English throng, thrang, from Old English þrang, ġeþrang (“crowd, press, tumult”), from Proto-Germanic *þrangwą, *þrangwō (“throng”), from *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from *þrinhwaną (“to press, to push; to force”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”). Cognate with Dutch drang, German Drang.

s: Clear enough to be read; readable, particularly of handwriting.
Written or phrased so as to be easy to understand.
e: From Late Latin legibilis (“that can be read”), from Latin legō.

s: The state of being sincere and open in speech; honesty in expression.
A single-masted sailboat with only one headsail.
A sailing warship, smaller than a frigate, with its guns all on one deck.
A sloop-of-war, smaller than a frigate, larger than a corvette.
Experiencing dazzlement; overcome by light or brilliance.
The property of being rough, coarseness.
Something that is rough; a rough spot.
A measure of how rough something is, such as a surface
e: Inherited from Middle English roughnes//roughnesse. rough + -ness. Compare Old English hrēohnes (“roughness”).

s: Partially or wholly deprived of the use of some part of the body, usually by wounding or injury.
Impaired or defective in some way.
That which girds, encircles, or encloses; a circumference.
A belt or sash at the waist, often used to support stockings or hosiery.
A garment used to hold the abdomen, hips, buttocks, and/or thighs in a particular shape.
The line of greatest circumference of a brilliant-cut diamond, at which it is grasped by the setting.
A thin bed or stratum of stone.
The removal or inversion of a ring of bark in order to kill or stunt a tree.
To gird, encircle, or constrain by such means.
To kill or stunt a tree by removing or inverting a ring of bark.
e: From Middle English girdel, gerdel, gurdel, from Old English gyrdel, from Proto-West Germanic *gurdil, from Proto-Germanic *gurdilaz (“girdle, belt”), equivalent to gird + -le.

s: Any of several plants of the genus Aster; one of its flowers.
A star-shaped structure formed during the mitosis of a cell.
e: From Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ. Doublet of star; related to estoile, étoile, stella, and stelo.

s: Characterized by rigorous self-denial or self-discipline; austere; abstinent; involving a withholding of physical pleasure.
One who is devoted to the practice of self-denial, either through seclusion or stringent abstinence.
e: First use appears c. 1646. From Medieval Latin asceticus, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητικός, from ἀσκητής (“monk, hermit”), from ἀσκέω (“to exercise”).

s: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
To say suddenly and with strong emotion.
e: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).

s: To waver or be unsteady; to weaken or trail off.
To stammer; to utter with hesitation, or in a weak and trembling manner.
To fail in distinctness or regularity of exercise; said of the mind or of thought.
To lose faith or vigor; to doubt or abandon (a cause).
To hesitate in purpose or action.
To cleanse or sift, as barley.
e: From Middle English falteren (“to stagger; be unsteady, tremble, quiver; to stammer; be entangled, get caught”), further origin Unknown. Probably from a source such as Old Norse faltrask (“to hesitate, be puzzled, be encumbered”). May also be a frequentative of fold, although the change from d to t is unusual.

s: An unsteady movement of the body in walking or standing as if one were about to fall; a reeling motion.
A disease of horses and other animals, attended by reeling, unsteady gait or sudden falling.
The spacing out of various actions over time.
The difference in circumference between the left and right tires on a racing vehicle. It is used on oval tracks to make the car turn better in the corners.
The horizontal positioning of a biplane, triplane, or multiplane's wings in relation to one another.
To sway unsteadily, reel, or totter.
In standing or walking, to sway from one side to the other as if about to fall; to stand or walk unsteadily; to reel or totter.
To cause to reel or totter.
To cease to stand firm; to begin to give way; to fail.
To begin to doubt and waver in purposes; to become less confident or determined; to hesitate.
To cause to doubt and waver; to make to hesitate; to make less steady or confident; to shock.
Have multiple groups doing the same thing in a uniform fashion, but starting at different, evenly spaced, times or places (attested from 1856).
To arrange (a series of parts) on each side of a median line alternately, as the spokes of a wheel or the rivets of a boiler seam.
To arrange similar objects such that each is ahead or above and to one side of the next.
e: From Middle English stageren, a variant of stakeren ("to walk unsteadily, stagger"; whence modern dialectal English stacker (“to totter, reel, stagger”)), from Old Norse stakra (“to stagger, sway, waver, swing, wobble”), frequentative of Old Norse staka (“to push, knock, bump into, stumble”).

s: In a state of hurry, panic or wild activity.
Of an event, happening at the appointed time.
Of a person, acting at the appointed time.
Existing as a point or series of points.
Expressing a momentary action that has no duration.
e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“relating to a point”), from Late Latin pūnctus (“point”) + -ālis.

s: Either of the two parallels of latitude 23°26′ north and south of the equator; the farthest points at which the sun can be directly overhead; the boundaries of the torrid zone or tropics.
The component of tone or rhetoric in a sentence.
Of, or relating to the tropics; tropical.
Having the quality of indirectly inducing a biological or chemical change in a system or substrate.
Pertaining to, involving, or of the nature of a trope or tropes.
e: From Late Latin tropicus (“of or pertaining to the solstice, as a noun, one of the tropics”), from Ancient Greek τροπικός (“of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic; tropical; etc.”), from τροπή (“turn; solstice; trope”).

s: Rent in tatters, torn, hanging in rags; ragged.
Dressed in tatters or rags; ragged.
Dilapidated; showing gaps or breaks; jagged; broken.
e: From Middle English tatered, tatird, from Old Norse tǫturr. Originally, it was derived from the noun, but it was later reanalysed as a past participle (tatter + -ed), whereafter the verb came into being. Compare tatter.

s: An inscription on a gravestone in memory of the deceased.
A poem or other short text written in memory of a deceased person.
To write or speak after the manner of an epitaph.
e: From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (“relating to a funeral”), from ἐπί (“over”) + τάφος (“tomb”). By surface analysis epi- + -taph. Compare epitaph.

s: An unhappy, unfortunate, or miserable person.
An unpleasant, annoying, worthless, or despicable person.
e: From Middle English wrecche, from Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, fugitive, warrior”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to track, follow”). Doublet of garçon, garson.

s: Ground ploughed and harrowed but left unseeded for one year.
The ploughing or tilling of land, without sowing it for a season.
Ploughed but left unseeded for more than one planting season.
Left unworked and uncropped for some amount of time.
To make land fallow for agricultural purposes.
Of a pale red or yellow, light brown; dun.
e: Thumb|alt=A photograph of a ploughed field.|A fallow field From Middle English falwe, from Old English fealh, fealg (“fallow land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgu (compare Falge, West Frisian falig, felling, Dutch valg, German Felge), from Proto-Indo-European *polḱéh₂ (“arable land”) (compare olca, Russian полоса́).

From Middle English falowen, falwen, from Old English fealgian (“to fallow; break up land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgōn (“to fallow”). Cognate with Dutch valgen (“to plow lightly; fallow”), Low German falgen (“to till; dig a hole”).
+ (color) thumb|alt=A photograph of a light brown deer.|A fallow deer.

s: The act of bequeathing or leaving by will.
The transfer of property upon the owner's death according to the will of the deceased.
That which is left by will; a legacy.
That which has been handed down or transmitted.
A person's inheritance; an amount of property given by will.
To give as a bequest; bequeath.
e: From Middle English biqueste, bequeste (“will, testament, bequest”), from be- + queste (“saying, utterance, testament, will, legacy”), from Old English *cwist, *cwiss (“saying”) (compare Old English andcwiss, ġecwis, uncwisse, etc.), from Proto-Germanic *kwissiz (“saying”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet- (“to say”).
From Middle English biquesten, from the noun (see above).

s: A place to moor a vessel.
The act of securing a vessel with a cable or anchor etc.
Something to which one adheres, or the means that helps one to maintain a stable position and keep one's identity - moral, intellectual, political, etc.
A container for arrows, crossbow bolts or darts, such as those fired from a bow, crossbow or blowgun.
A ready storage location for figurative tools or weapons.
A multidigraph, especially in the context of representation theory.
To shake or move with slight and tremulous motion.
e: From Middle English quiver, from Anglo-Norman quivre, from Old Dutch cocar (source of Dutch koker, and cognate to Old English cocer (“quiver, case”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kokar (“container”), said to be from, possibly from *kökexür (“leather vessel for liquids”); see there for more.
From Middle English quiver, cwiver, from Old English *cwifer, probably related to cwic (“alive”).
From Middle English quiveren, probably from the adjective.

s: Dull or dark in colour or brightness.
To make sombre or dark; to make shady.
e: Borrowed from French sombre (“dark”), from Old French sombre, from a verb *sombrer or Latin sub- + umbra. Compare Spanish sombra (“shade; dark part of a picture; ghost”).

s: Very baffling, confusing, or perplexing, often due to a very large choice being available.
e: From bewilder (“to confuse, disorientate, or puzzle someone, especially with many different choices”) + -ing.

s: To beg or plead for (something) earnestly or urgently; to beseech.
To beg or plead that (someone) earnestly or urgently do something; to beseech, to entreat.
Often followed by for (a thing) or of (a person): to express an earnest or urgent plea.
An act of begging or pleading earnestly or urgently; an entreaty, an imploration or imploring, a plea.
A member of the common people who holds no title or rank.
Someone who is not of noble rank.
A Member of Parliament in the House of Commons.
One eligible to be a member of the House of Commons.
A student who is not dependent on any foundation for support, but pays all university charges.
Someone who has a right over another's land. They hold common rights because of residence or land ownership in a particular manor, especially rights on common land. eg: centuries-old grazing rights
One sharing with another in anything.
a rankless or average player in Tycoon; not the tycoon, rich, poor, or beggar.
The underside of a roof that extends beyond the external walls of a building.
Something that extends over or projects beyond.
e: From eave + -s, from a misinterpretation of the -s ending of eaves as forming a plural.

s: One who adheres to the theory or method of impressionism.
A performer who does impressions; a mimic.
Having unlimited power, force or authority.
Describing a cell (especially a stem cell) that is capable of developing into any type of cell or forming any type of tissue (also called a totipotent cell).
e: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

s: A collection of live wild animals as an exhibition historically associated with the aristocracy and considered a precursor of modern zoos.
The enclosure where they are kept.
e: From French ménagerie, derived from ménager (“to keep house”), household. Housekeeping used to include taking care of domestic animals.

s: A light wind from the west.
Any light refreshing wind; a gentle breeze.
Anything of fine, soft, or light quality, especially fabric.

A type of soft confectionery made by whipping fruit and berry purée (mostly apple purée) with sugar and egg whites with subsequent addition of a gelling agent like pectin, carrageenan, agar, or gelatine.
To blow or move like a zephyr, or light breeze.
To blow or blow on gently like a zephyr; to cool or refresh with a gentle breeze.
e: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος. Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a Semantic loan from Russian зефи́р.

s: The rounding up and theft of animals, cattle in particular.
e: From Middle English *rustlynge, rustland, from Old English hrīstlende, *hrȳstlende, present participle of Old English *hrȳstlan (“to rustle”), equivalent to rustle + -ing.

s: By habit; in a habitual manner.
Making unwarranted presumptions or assumptions, often out of arrogance or excessive self-confidence, and thus exceeding appropriate or rightful limits.
e: From Middle English presumptuous, borrowed from Old French presumpcieus,presumptieus,presumptuos and its etymon Medieval Latin praesūmptuōsus.

s: An act in which something is plucked.
A fragment of something obtained by plucking.
The undesirable situation in which printed ink becomes detached from the paper.
Any of the poisonous umbelliferous plants, of the genera
Conium, either Conium maculatum or Conium chaerophylloides.
obtained from these Conium and Cicuta plants.
Any of several coniferous trees, of the genus Tsuga, that grow in North America; the wood of such trees.
e: From Middle English hemlok, hemeluc, from Old English hemlīc, hymlīc and hymlīce (“hemlock, bryony, convolvulus”), of Uncertain origin. Compare Old English hymele, Old English humele, Danish and Swedish humle (“hops”), Icelandic humall (“hops”).

s: A room or set of rooms in another person's house where a person lodges.
A furnished room or suite of rooms rented within a private house as a temporary or semi-permanent accommodation, often including a baseline of domestic service.
Any of many plants with thorny stems growing in dense clusters, such as many in the Rosa, Rubus, and Smilax genera.
Anything that is sharp or unpleasant to the feelings.
Tree heath (Erica arborea), a thorny Mediterranean shrub.
A pipe for smoking, made from the roots of that shrub.
e: [[File:Briar_rose_(3212229202).jpg|thumb|A sweetbriar (Rosa rubiginosa, syn. Rosa eglanteria). Mudgee, New South Wales.]] From Middle English brere, from Old English brēr [Old Mercian], brǣr (“briar, bramble”); further origin Unknown, perhaps related to Old French bruiere (“heather”) (French bruyère). Compare Old Norse brǫrr (“briar”), whence Icelandic brörr.
Thumb|A briar pipe (2) From French bruyère, assimilated with Etymology 1, above.

s: Accompanied by or uttered with a sigh.
The act, or an instance of, chirping.
A silicate mineral of aluminium and fluorine, usually tinted by impurities.
An often clear, yellowish-brown gemstone cut from this.
A yellowish-brown color, like that of the gemstone.
Or (gold or yellow), in blazoning by precious stones.
Either of two species of very large hummingbirds in the genus Topaza.
A ruby-topaz hummingbird, Chrysolampis mosquitus, the male of which has bright ruby feathers on the head and topaz on the throat
Of a yellowish-brown color, like that of the gemstone.
A black Catholic soldier in the British Army.
e: From Old French topace (compare French topaze), from Ancient Greek τόπαζος.
Various theories. Hobson-Jobson mentions as possibilities a corruption of Persian (from Turkish) top-chi, "gunner", or a connection with topee, from the hats they wore.

s: To take the dressing, or covering, from.
Partial or informal dress for women, as worn in the home rather than in public.
Informal clothing for men, as opposed to formal or ceremonial wear.
Now more specifically, a state of having few or no clothes on.
e: From Middle English undressen, equivalent to un- + dress. Compare Old English unsċrȳdan (“to undress”).

s: Lithe and agile when moving and bending.
Compliant; yielding to the will of others.
To make compliant, submissive or obedient.
e: From Middle English souple, from Old French souple, soupple (“soft, lithe, yielding”), from Latin supplic-, supplex (“suppliant, submissive, kneeling”), of uncertain formation. Either from sub + plicō (“bend”) (compare complex), or from sub + plācō (“placate”). More at sub-, placate.

s: To strip, deprive, or dispossess (someone) of something (such as a right, passion, privilege, or prejudice).
To sell off or be rid of through sale, especially of a subsidiary.
e: Alteration of devest, from Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

s: Sharp or keen to the senses.
Especially of a woman: fierce, loud, strident.
e: From Late Middle English schrille, shirle, shrille (“of a sound: high-pitched, piercing; producing such a sound”), possibly from the earlier shil, schille (“loud, resounding; high-pitched”), from Old English sċill (“sonorous sounding”), of Germanic origin and probably ultimately Onomatopoeic.

s: Having a crest, or ornamental tuft (on an animal) or plume (on a helmet).
Having a heraldic crest, badge, shield-like emblem, etc.
Any of various creatures having a crest.
The property of being short, of being small of stature or brief.
The result or product of being short.
The property of being short or terse.
e: From Middle English schortnesse, from Old English sċortnes, sċeortnys, equivalent to short + -ness.

s: To keep down by unjust force.
Physically to press down on (someone) with harmful effects; to smother, crush.
e: From Middle English oppressen, from Old French oppresser, from Medieval Latin oppressare (“to press against, oppress”), frequentative of Latin opprimere, past participle oppressus (“to press against, press together, oppress”), from ob (“against”) + premere, past participle pressus (“to press”); see press.

s: The act or ceremony of consecrating; the state of being consecrated; dedication.
A man or person skilled at hitting targets, as with a firearm, bow, or thrown object.
A thin fabric with a loose, open weave.
A similar bleached cotton fabric used as a surgical dressing.
A thin woven metal or plastic mesh.
To apply a dressing of gauze; to cover with gauze.
To mist; to make or become gauze-like.
Having been created through the sewing process.
Having no matter or substance; incorporeal.
Of the nature of the soul or spirit; spiritual.
Of no importance; inconsequential, insignificant, unimportant.
Having or seeming to have very little substance; insubstantial, slight.
Especially of evidence; chiefly followed by to: not associated in any way that is important or useful to the context being discussed; irrelevant.
A being or entity having no matter or substance.
A thing which is abstract or intangible; chiefly preceded by the: things which are abstract or intangible considered collectively.
A small mound or rounded hill.
A rounded, underwater hill with a prominence of less than 1,000 metres, which does not breach the water's surface.
To ring (a bell) mournfully; to knell.
To sound (something) like a bell; to knell.
To call (someone, to church) by sounding or making a knell (as a bell, a trumpet, etc).
To arrange related objects in parallel or at 90 degree angles.
e: From Middle English knol, knolle, from Old English cnoll (“summit”), from Proto-Germanic *knudan-, *knudla-, *knulla- (“lump”), possibly related to cnotta. Related to Old Norse knollr (found only in names of places), Dutch knol (“tuber”), Swedish knöl (“tuber”), Danish knold (“hillock, clod, tuber”) and German Knolle (“bulb”).
+ing Named after Knoll, a furniture fabrication shop, famous for its angular range of designer furniture.

s: Characteristic of, belonging to, or befitting a home; domestic, cosy.
Lacking in beauty or elegance, plain in appearance, physically unattractive.
On intimate or friendly terms with (someone); familiar; at home (with a person); intimate.
e: From Middle English homly, hoomly, hamely (“domestic, familiar, plain, unattractive”), from Old English *hāmlīċ (“of the home, domestic”), from Proto-West Germanic *haimalīk (“of or characteristic of home”), equivalent to home + -ly.

s: The state or quality of being eager; ardent desire.
The act or process by which something blossoms.
Examining one's own perceptions and sensory experiences; contemplative or thoughtful about oneself.
e: From Latin intro "inward, within" (see intro-) + Latin specere "look at".

s: A kind of firearm formerly carried by the infantry of an army, originally fired by means of a match, or matchlock, for which several mechanical appliances (including the flintlock, and finally the percussion lock) were successively substituted; ultimately superseded by the rifle.
e: First attested around 1210 as a surname, and later in the 1400s as a word for the sparrowhawk (Middle English forms: musket, muskett, muskete (“sparrow hawk”)), from Middle French mousquet, from moschetto (a diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca) used to refer initially to a sparrowhawk (given its small size or speckled appearance) and then a crossbow arrow.

s: Having suffered the death of a loved one.
Unhealthily thin, as from hunger or illness: drawn, emaciated, haggard.
Of a place or thing: bleak, desolate.
With a positive or neutral connotation: not overweight; lean, slender, slim.
Of a sound: suggesting bleakness and desolation.
e: From Middle English gaunt, gawnt, gawnte, gant (“lean, slender, thin, gaunt”); further etymology uncertain. Speculated origins include.

s: An attic or semi-finished room just beneath the roof of a house.
e: From Middle English garett, garite, from Old French garite, guerite (“watchtower”), from garir, guarir (“to defend, protect”) (compare English garrison), ultimately of origin (see English garage). Doublet of guerite.

s: The act or process by which something is threaded (in various senses).
An ancient Eastern method for removing hair by means of a thread, which is rolled over the hair in order to pluck it out at the follicle level; especially used in the context of eyebrows.
Appearance, especially the features and expression of the face.
To tolerate, support, sanction, patronise or approve of something.
e: From Middle English contenaunce, countenaunce, from Anglo-Norman countenance and Old French contenance, from the present participle of contenir, or from Late Latin continentia, and therefore a Doublet of continence.

s: A common true thrush, Turdus merula, found in woods and gardens over much of Eurasia, and introduced elsewhere.
A variety of New World birds of the family Icteridae (26 species of icterid bird).
A native of the South Pacific islands.
To enslave someone, especially through chicanery or force
e: From Middle English blakebird, blacbrid (“ouzel; Eurasian blackbird”), equivalent to black + bird.

s: A type of open shoe made up of straps or bands holding a sole to the foot
A long narrow boat used on the Barbary coast.
e: From Middle English sandal (“sandal”), from Old French sandale, from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον, diminutive of σάνδαλον (“sandal”), of unknown origin. Often mistakenly parsed as related to sand.

From Middle English sandal (“sandalwood”), from Medieval Latin sandalum, from Byzantine Greek σάνδανον, σάνταλον, from Arabic صَنْدَل, from Middle Persian (“sandalwood”), from Sanskrit चन्दन (“sandalwood”). Doublet of santalum.
From Arabic صَنْدَل, the same word as the shoe Doublet of sandal, just applied for boats of the shape of this shoe.

s: The process of subtracting a number from another.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin subtractio, subtractionis. Can be decomposed to subtract + -ion.

s: A person who lives in self-imposed isolation or seclusion from the world, especially for religious purposes; a hermit.
The place where a recluse dwells; a place of isolation or seclusion.
e: From Old French reclus, past participle of reclure, from Latin reclūdere (“to disclose, to open”), from re- + claudō (“close”).

s: The act of secluding, shutting out or keeping apart.
The state of being secluded or shut out, as from company, society, the world, etc.; solitude.
A secluded, isolated or private place.
The mature phase of the extratropical cyclone life cycle.
e: From Medieval Latin, from Latin seclusio, from secludere.

s: A period or condition when food is rare and hence expensive; famine.
Scarcity; a lack or short supply.
Dearness; the quality of being rare or costly.
To cause or produce a scarcity in something.
e: First attested at least as early as the late 1300s, and appearing in Tyndale’s Pentateuch (1530) as well as the Coverdale Bible (1535). From Middle English derth, derthe, derþe, probably from Old English *dīerþ, *dīerþu, from Proto-West Germanic *diuriþu, from Proto-Germanic *diuriþō (“costliness, preciousness, honour”); corresponding to dear + -th.

s: In a positive sense: marvellous, wonderful; extremely talented, especially at a young age.
In a negative sense: appalling, horrifying, shocking; abnormal, freakish, monstrous, unnatural.
Very big in extent, quantity, or size; abundant; intense; colossal, huge.
Having the nature of an omen or portent; ominous, portentous.
A simple brass instrument consisting of a horn with no valves, playing only pitches in its harmonic series
The sound of something that bugles.
A sort of wild ox; a buffalo.
To announce, sing, or cry in the manner of a musical bugle.
A tubular glass or plastic bead sewn onto clothes as a decorative trim.
A plant in the family Lamiaceae grown as a ground cover Ajuga reptans, and other plants in the genus Ajuga.
e: Thumb|A soldier playing a bugle. Inherited from Middle English bugle, from Anglo-Norman bugle (“young ox, heifer; bugle”), from Latin būculus (“young ox, steer”).
From Late Latin bugulus (“a woman's ornament”), probably from Latin būculus.
From Middle English bugle (“bugleweed”), from Anglo-Norman and Old French bugle, from Medieval Latin bugilla, probably related to Late Latin bugillo. thumb|common bugle (Ajuga reptans)

s: Having (selfishly) abandoned a person, group, or ideal.
Returning or having returned, especially repentantly, after such an abandonment.
A prodigal person; a spendthrift; a wastrel.
e: From Middle French prodigal, from Late Latin prōdigālis (“wasteful”), from Latin prōdigus (“wasteful, lavish, prodigal”), from prōdigō (“to consume, squander, drive forth”), from prōd- [from prō (“before, forward”)] + agō (“to drive”). Also see unrelated prodigy.

s: A little playful skip or leap; a brisk and lively movement.
The act of frisking, of searching for something by feeling someone's body.
To frolic, gambol, skip, dance, leap.
To search (someone) by feeling their body and clothing.
e: From Middle English frisk (“lively, frisky”), from Middle French frisque (“lively, jolly, blithe, fine, spruce, gay”), of origin, perhaps from Middle Dutch frisc (“fresh”) or Old High German frisc (“fresh”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *friskaz (“fresh”). Cognate with Icelandic frískur (“frisky, fresh”). Doublet of fresco, fresh. More at fresh.

s: Ready to accept instruction or direction; obedient; subservient.
Yielding to control or supervision, direction, or management.
e: From Middle English docyle, from Middle French docile, from Latin docilis, from docēre (“teach”). Compare Portuguese dócil ("docile").

s: (often with for) Missing one's home and family very much when away; nostalgic.
Joined as if in a marriage.
To move or act in a quick fashion.
To make someone speed up or make something happen quicker.
To cause some scheduled event to happen earlier.
Any of several North American plane trees, of the genus Platanus, especially Platanus occidentalis (American sycamore), distinguished by its mottled bark which flakes off in large irregular masses.
A large British and European species of maple, Acer pseudoplatanus, known in North America as the sycamore maple.
A large tree bearing edible fruit, Ficus sycomorus, allied to the common fig, found in Egypt and Syria.
e: Circa 1350 as Middle English sicamour, from Old French sicamor, from Latin sȳcomorus, from Ancient Greek σῡκόμορος, from σῦκον (“fig”) + μόρον (“mulberry”). Possibly influenced by Hebrew שִׁקְמָה (“fig-mulberry”).

s: Discontinued; having ceased or gone out of use.
Changed to a less valued condition or state; especially having lost one's religious faith.
By extension, having changed a (secular) belief or adherence.
Having passed from the original holder or authority; no longer claimed.
The act of blaming, criticizing, or condemning as wrong; reprehension.
A judicial or ecclesiastical sentence or reprimand; condemnatory judgment.
A judgment (either favorable or unfavorable); an opinion.
To form or express a judgment in regard to; to estimate; to judge.
e: From 1350–1400 Middle English censure, from Old French, from Latin censūra (“censor's office or assessment”), from censēre (“to consider, to assess, to value, to judge, to tax, etc.”).

s: To stray; to wander; to rove.
To go out of a straight line; to deflect.
To wander from any line prescribed, or from a rule or duty; to depart from what is established by law, duty, custom, or the like; to deviate.
To bend; to incline; to give way.
To climb or move upward by winding or turning.
To turn aside or deviate to avoid impact.
Of a projectile, to travel in a curved line
To drive in the trajectory of another vehicle to stop it, to cut off.
To go out of one's way to avoid; to snub.
A curve, bend, or deviation from a straight course or line (e.g. the winding path of a stream or a sudden change of direction to avoid an obstacle or collision.).
A deviation from duty or custom.
e: From Middle English swerven, swarven, from Old English sweorfan (“to file; rub; polish; scour; turn aside”), from Proto-Germanic *swerbaną (“to rub off; wipe; mop”), from Proto-Indo-European *swerbʰ- (“to turn; wipe; sweep”).

s: Making great demands; difficult to satisfy.
Of an action, task, etc., requiring precise accuracy, great care, effort, or attention.
Of a person or organization, characterized by exaction.
One who expounds, represents or advocates.
The number by which a value (called the base) is said to be raised to a power in exponentiation: for example, the 3 in 2^3=8.
The degree to which the root of a radicand is found, for example, the 2 in \sqrt[2]r=b.
A phonological manifestation of a morphosyntactic property; in layman's terms, the expression of one or more grammatical properties by sound.
The part of a floating-point number that represents its exponent value.
e: From Latin expōnēns, of expōnō (“to expose; to exhibit, display, set out; to explain”), from ex- + pōnō.

s: Appearing as if one side were cut away.
of one's reputation, name or word

A temporary mental state with a sudden onset, usually reversible, including symptoms of confusion, inability to concentrate, disorientation, anxiety, and sometimes hallucinations. Causes can include dehydration, drug intoxication, and severe infection.
favorable for life; livable; suitable for life.
e: Borrowed from Middle French hospitable, formed from the root of Latin hospitare with the suffix -able. Displaced native Old English cumlīþe.

s: A hat with a wide brim to shade the eyes from sunlight.
To experience an episode or an onset of some detrimental mental condition like agitation, anxiety, hallucination or dementia, daily at the approach of nightfall.
The willingness to carry out the wishes of others.
Reproduction in the exact form as the original.
A fax, a machine for making and sending copies of printed material and images by means of radio or a telephone network.
The image sent by the machine itself.
To send by means of a facsimile machine; to fax.
To make a copy of; to reproduce.
e: From Latin fac simile (“make like”), from fac (“make”) (imperative of facere (“make”)) + simile (neuter of similis (“like, similar”)).

s: At or in a distant but indicated place.
Syn of thither: to a distant but indicated place.
The farther, the more distant of two choices.
Who or which is over yonder, usually distant but within sight.
One who or which is over yonder, usually distant but within sight.
The vast distance, particularly the sky or trackless forest.
e: From Middle English yonder, yondre, ȝondre, ȝendre, from Old English ġeonre (“thither; yonder”), equivalent to yond (from ġeond, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz) + -er, as in hither, thither.

s: A person who carries out some task.
A component of a system that executes or runs something.
Someone appointed by a testator to administer their estate in accordance with their will; an administrator.
e: From Middle English executour, from Anglo-Norman executour, from Latin exsecūtor, agent noun of exsequor.

s: Someone living in the same house.
Taking place after one's own death.
In reference to a work, published after the author's death.
In reference to a musical opus, published or initially performed after the composer's death.
Born after the death of one's father.
e: From Latin posthumus, a variant spelling of postumus, superlative form of posterus (“coming after”), the ⟨h⟩ added by association with humus (“ground, earth”) referring to burial.

s: A physical exercise or cosmetic product intended to firm part of the body.
A thin chisel with a tang to enter the handle instead of a socket for receiving it.
An appearance of light, especially one which is indistinct or small, or short-lived.
An indistinct sign of something; a glimpse or hint.
A bright, but intermittent or short-lived, appearance of something.
A look of joy or liveliness on one's face.
Sometimes as hot gleam: a warm ray of sunlight; also, a period of warm weather, for instance, between showers of rain.
Chiefly in conjunction with an adverb: to cause (light) to shine.
To shine, especially in an indistinct or intermittent manner; to glisten, to glitter.
To be strongly but briefly apparent.
Of a hawk or other bird of prey: to disgorge filth from its crop or gorge.
e: From Middle English glem, gleam, gleme (“shaft of light; reflected light; radiance; something ephemeral”), from Old English glǣm (“gleam”), from Proto-West Germanic *glaimi (“brightness; splendour”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to shine”).
From Middle English glemen (“to shine; to glance, look”), from glem, gleme (see etymology 1) + -en. Cognate with Low German glemen (“to glow, shine”).

s: The act of enchanting or the feeling of being enchanted.
Something that enchants; a magical spell.
e: From Middle English enchauntement, from Old French enchantement.

s: Having been made less tight or more relaxed.
A cover to protect and hide the back panel of a computer or other office machine.
A frame worn underneath a woman's skirt, typically only protruding from the rear as opposed to the earlier more circular hoops.
To move busily and energetically with fussiness (often followed by about).
To teem or abound (usually followed by with); to exhibit an energetic and active abundance (of a thing).
e: From Middle English bustlen, bustelen, bostlen, perhaps an alteration of *busklen (> Modern English buskle), a frequentative of Middle English busken (“to prepare; make ready”), from Old Norse búask (“to prepare oneself”); or alternatively from a frequentative form of Middle English busten, bisten (“to buffet; pummel; dash; beat”) le.

s: Chilly in manner; lacking affection or zeal; impassive.
Sexually unresponsive, especially of a woman.
e: Borrowed from Latin frīgidus (“cold”), from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos.

s: To apply or make use of (someone or something); to employ, to use.
To apply (money) for some purpose; to expend, to spend.
To impart (something) gratuitously; to present (something) to someone or something, especially as a gift or an honour; to confer, to give, to accord; to render.
To place or put (someone or something) somewhere or in a certain situation; to dispose of.
To deposit (something) for safekeeping; to lay up (something) in store; to stow.
To provide (someone or oneself) with accommodation; to find quarters for (someone or oneself); to lodge, to quarter.
To behave or conduct (oneself); to acquit.
To give (someone or oneself) in marriage.
An act of presenting a thing to someone or something, especially as a gift or an honour; a bestowal.
A purplish-red pigment, made from dye obtained from the cochineal beetle; carminic acid or any of its derivatives.
A purplish-red colour, resembling that pigment.
Of the purplish red colour shade carmine.
e: From French carmin, from irregular Medieval Latin carminium, itself from Arabic قِرْمِز (“crimson, kermes”) from Persian *کرمست (*kermest), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kŕ̥miš (“worm”), plus or with influence from Latin minium. Compare crimson and kermes.

s: The act of inhabiting; state of inhabiting or dwelling, or of being inhabited; occupancy.
A place of abode; settled dwelling; residence; house.
A group, lodge, or company, as of the Primrose League.
e: From Middle English habitacioun, from Old French habitacion, abitacion (“act of dwelling”), from Latin habitātiōnem, accusative of Latin habitātiō.

s: The quality or state of being still.
e: From Middle English stilnesse, from Old English stilnes (“stillness, quiet; absence of noise or disturbance, release, relaxation; silence, abstention from speech; absence of disturbance or molestation, tranquility, peace, security; that which appeases”), equivalent to still + -ness.

s: The act of one who agonizes.
Full of zeal; ardent, fervent; exhibiting enthusiasm or strong passion, particularly in matters of religion.
e: From Middle English zelose, from Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus + -ōsus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (“zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (“to emulate, to be jealous”). zeal + -ous. Doublet of jealous.

s: So angry that one turns pale; very angry; furious; liverish.
e: From Middle English livid, livide, from Old French livide, from Latin līvidus (“bluish, livid; envious”), from līveō (“be of a bluish color or livid; envy”), from Proto-Italic *sliwēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sliwo-, suffixed form of *(s)leh₃y- (“bluish”).

s: Sweet and pleasant; delicious; juicy, succulent.
e: From earlier lushious, lussyouse (“luscious, richly sweet, delicious”), a corruption of lustious, from lusty (“pleasant, delicious”) + -ous. Shakespeare uses both lush (short for lushious) and lusty in the same sense: "How lush and lusty the grass looks" (The Tempest ii. I.52).

s: In excess of what is required or sufficient.
e: From Middle English superfluous, from Latin superfluus (“superfluous”) + -ous, from superfluō (“overflow”), from super (“above, more than, over”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare mellifluous and fluid, also from Latin. Literally corresponds to overflow, which is from Germanic, rather than Latin. super- + -fluous.

s: The most extreme or furthest point of something.
e: From Middle English extremite, from Old French extremité, from Latin extrēmitātem (“extremity; border, perimeter; ending”), from extrēmīs (“furthest, extreme”) + -itās (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts; see extreme.

s: Either salty or spicy, but not sweet.
Any of several Mediterranean herbs, of the genus Satureja, grown as culinary flavourings.
The leaves of these plants used as a flavouring.
e: From the Middle English savory, savourie, from Old French savouré, from Old French savourer, from Late Latin sapōrāre, from Latin sapor (“taste, flavour”), from sapiō, sapere (“taste of, have a flavour of”).
Thumb|Savory (herb) From Middle English saverey, possibly from Old English sæþerie, from Latin satureia, influenced by or via Old French savereie.

s: Extremely happy; full of joy; experiencing, indicating, causing, or characterized by bliss.
Uneven, with many furrows and prominent points, often in reference to the skin or hide of animals.
ended; having passed over or passed by
Of any metre rhythmically intermediate between ordinary speech (or prose) and song (or poetry), typically combining dactyls and trochees.
e: From Latin logaoedicus, from Ancient Greek λογᾰοιδῐκός, from λόγος (“speech, prose”) + ἀοιδή (“song”) + -ῐκός (“-ic”).

s: A trip out on horseback to inspect a ranch etc.
To displace one from one's housing or shelter.
To take a house away from.
Causing or caused by dimness of sight.
To be blear; to have blear eyes; to look or gaze with blear eyes.
To make (usually the eyes or eyesight) blurred or dim.
e: From Middle English blere, related to Low German bleeroged (“bleareyed”), Middle High German blerre (“double vision”), German Blerre (“double vision”). Perhaps also related to blur.
From Middle English bleren, from Old English *blerian.

From Middle English bleren, from Old English *blǣran, related to West Frisian blearje (“to bleat, shout”), Dutch bleren, blaren (“to bellow, bleat”), Low German blaren, blarren (“to blare, howl, shriek”), German plärren (“to howl, shriek, blare”).

s: That makes childless: that takes the lives of children (and thus leaves their parents childless).
Able to be moved or set in motion.
Able to be made as a motion.
Any member of the species of the genus Aria (formerly subgenus Sorbus subg. Aria), native to Eurasia, especially common whitebeam (Aria edulis).
e: From Middle English witbeam, equivalent to white + beam (“tree”) – see Old English bēam (“tree”). In the name, white refers to the color of the leaves, when emergent and later the undersides.

s: The thick, voluminous, and shiny soil turned over by a plow.
e: Revived by Gerard Manley Hopkins in his 1877 (published posthumously in 1918) poem The Windhover; ultimately related to French sillon (“furrow”).

s: Not hampered or hindered; without encumbrance.
Like a brick, a helpful or reliable person.
A beach lying along the sea.
An act of pillage or plunder.
A large, powerful horse used for pulling drays.
Someone who undergoes or underwent many a hardship, who suffers some great burden; a burdened, beleaguered, downtrodden man.
A pale or withered forest; a ghostly wood, implying decay or melancholy.
One leaf at a time; leaf by leaf.
A feed or meal, particularly for animals, consisting chiefly of decayed vegetable matter, especially leaves.
Fallen or decaying leaves; leaf litter

e: From Middle English ertheles, erþeles, equivalent to earth + -less. Cognate with West Frisian ierdleaze, German erdlos.

s: To bend to excess; to bend farther than the desired or intended amount.
To increase the tension on a string at the fret, causing the note to sharpen.
To overblow or overdraw in order to create a note that is sharper; to move the point in the mouth where airflow is narrowest forward.
The portion of a pipeline that curves downward from a higher level to the inflection point where the surface holding the upper part is no longer supporting the pipe.
An instance of overbending (bending too far).
The amount by which a material has been overbent.
A note that is played sharp due to overbending.
A note that is played sharp due to overbending.
Filled or overrun (with moving objects or beings).
Resembling or characteristic of a dragon.
Wastefully reckless in the use of money or resources.
The property of lasting; duration, permanence.
Not having a full complement of workers.

e: From heart + sore. Compare Haatseer (“heartache”), West Frisian hertsear (“heartache”), Dutch hartzeer (“heartache”), Low German Hartsehr (“heartache”).

s: Having curds of a specified kind.
An analysis of past events; retrodiction or review.
An analysis of past meteorological data to determine what the weather was like at a previous time.
Resembling or characteristic of a lion.

e: From up- + roll. Compare Dutch oprollen (“to roll up”), German aufrollen (“to roll up”).

s: Several daisy-like flowers in various genera
Any of a genus of composite plants (Buphthalmum spp.), with large yellow flowers.
A titmouse, especially the great titmouse (Parus major) or the blue titmouse (Parus caeruleus).
A fish of species Boops boops (bogue, box)
e: From ox + eye. Apparently in some senses, specifically Buphthalmum, translated from Calque of Arabic عَيْن الْبَقَر, as also the case for French œil-de-bœuf.

s: Any plant of the taxonomic genus Fumaria of annual herbaceous flowering plants in the family Papaveraceae, native to temperate Europe and Asia.
e: From late Middle English fumyter (with remodelling of suffix), from Old French fumeterre, from Latin fūmus terrae (“literally, smoke of the earth, referring to the plant's aroma”).
From Middle English honysoke, from Old English huniġsūce, huniġsūge; equivalent to honey + suck.

s: Made of twine; having the appearance of twine.
Of or pertaining to a caesura.
A coat of arms; an armorial bearing or bearings.
The specialized language used in blazoning arms.
A musician who plays the rhythm.
So as to wave; with a waving motion.
A board that shows the direction (and often distance) to a named place; especially one of several attached to a milepost.
Marked or connected with a hyphen.
An inversion of the usual or logical order of words or phrases, for emphasis or poetic effect.
Adding a word or thought to a sentence that is already semantically complete, thus drawing emphasis to the addition.
e: Borrowed from Latin hyperbaton, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπερβατόν (“overstepping”), from ὑπερβαίνω, from ὑπέρ + βαίνω (“walk”).

s: Especially of the fur or skin of animals: having a patchy or streaky pattern, usually brown or grey in colour; brindled.
e: From Middle English brend (“burnt, branded”), from bren (“burned, branded”), from the past participle of brennen (“to burn”), from Old English bærnan (“to burn”). Also compare Old Norse brǫndóttr, Icelandic bröndóttr (“brindled”).

s: Covered with a lattice-like pattern of diagonally interlaced bendlets and bendlets sinister.
Any action, carried out onstage during a performance, apart from the main action.
The next-to-last syllable of a word.
The next to the last in a series.
Not having confessed to a priest.
A foot containing any pattern of three short syllables and one long syllable.
Which has the characteristics of a tower.
Wood, often in the form of splinters, suitable for making matches.
A horse or other animal having a docked tail.
Of horses, having a docked tail.
A euphemism for the word cunt
betrothed or engaged to be married
A piece of ceramic from pottery, often found on an archaeological site.
e: [[File:Poshuouinge potsherds.jpg|thumb|Potsherds from Poshuouinge, a large ancestral Pueblo ruin on U.S.

s: Containing or relating to an autograph.
Addiction to or obsession with sensual pleasures or affairs.
The doctrine that gratification of the senses is the highest good.
The doctrine that all knowledge not only originates in sensation, but are transformed sensations, copies or relics of sensations; sensationalism.
An associate with whom one shares a mess (eating place) on a ship.
Any of various eucalypts with rough bark, specifically Eucalyptus obliqua.
The process by which fabrics, etc. are beetled, or beaten with a mallet.
Jutting or protruding, especially of a person's brows.
To spot; to stain; to blur.
Marked with spots or maculae; blotched.
e: First attested during the last quarter of the 15th century, in Middle English; Inherited from Middle English maculaten (“to spoil, polute”), borrowed from Latin maculātus, perfect passive participle of maculō (“to spot”), see -ate and -ate.

s: The act by which something is hallowed.
A piece of music composed for six voices or six instruments; a sextet or sestuor.
The last six lines of a sonnet, forming two stanzas of three lines each.
Any elevated object on land which serves as a guide to mariners, such as a hill or steeple.
A beacon, buoy, etc. placed in the sea to aid navigation.
A trip on a horse outside an enclosed area, a trip on a horse in the open.
To ride a horse, bicycle, etc. better than (someone); to surpass in riding.

A student at secondary school or university who has been awarded an exhibition. The exhibition usually involves a financial prize and may include the right to wear a distinctive gown, especially at the University of Oxford.
An eight-line poem whose rhyme scheme is ABaAabAB and whose lines are in iambic tetrameter.
Having bells (especially around the neck of an animal). right|thumb|A falcon belled.
Having a thicker hollow end, for example to allow pipes to plug into each other.
A rough surface finish, as of a plaster or stucco wall.
A mixture of pebbles or similar material used to finish a plaster or concrete wall.
To shape crudely; to form in its first rudiments, without correction or polish.
To apply a roughcast finish to.
A reading of a religious text; a lesson to be read in church etc.
e: Borrowed from Old French lection, from Latin lēctiōnem, form of lēctiō, from legō (“to read; to gather”). Doublet of lesson.

s: The act of one who gambols.
To plunder, pillage, rob, pirate, or remove.
To deprive (a person) of something through theft or violence.
e: From Middle English reven, from Old English rēafian, from Proto-West Germanic *raubōn. Germanic cognates include West Frisian rave, Old English rēaf (“spoils, booty”)), and Old English past participle rofen (“torn, broken”), Norwegian rjuva, German rauben, Danish røve, and Swedish röva.
Alteration of rive by confusion with the above.

s: The act of taking a jaunt.
The act by which something is poised.
Of a person: deprived of comfort; uncomforted.
Of a thing: offering no comfort; uncomforting.
A lark, Lullula arborea, the only member of the genus Lullula, found in western Eurasia and northern Africa.
A small wheel; a caster or pulley.
To roll or move upon truckles, or casters; to trundle.
To sleep in a truckle bed.
To act in a submissive manner; to fawn, submit to a superior.
e: From Middle English trokel, trocle, trookyl, from Anglo-Norman trocle, from Medieval Latin trochlea (“a block, sheaf containing one or more pulleys”); or from a diminutive of truck (“wheel”), formed with -le, equivalent to truck + -le.

s: To boast of; to make a vain display of; to display with ostentation.
An instance of vaunting; a boast.
e: From Middle English vaunten, from Anglo-Norman vaunter, variant of Old French vanter, from Latin vānus (“vain, boastful”).

s: A landscape of an indoor setting.
The distinctive design that constitutes individual identity; a concept derived by Gerard Manley Hopkins from the ideas of the medieval philosopher Duns Scotus.
Lacking tone or pitch, have the neutral tone.

e: From Middle English housel, from Old English hūsl (“housel, Eucharist, the Host, a sacrifice”), from Proto-Germanic *hunslą (“sacrifice”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwen- (“holy”). Cognate with Icelandic húsl (“housel”), Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌽𐍃𐌻 (“sacrifice, offering”), *svętъ (“holy, sacred”) (OED).

From Middle English houselen, from Old English hūslian (“to administer the sacrament”), from Proto-Germanic *hunslōną (“to sacrifice, offer”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwen- (“holy”). Cognate with Icelandic húsla (“to housel”), Old Swedish húsla (“to administer the Eucharist to”), Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌽𐍃𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 (“to offer, sacrifice”).

s: regimen; government; the rules governing the syntax, rules of agreement of a language.
e: From Latin rectio, from regere (“to rule, to govern”).

s: The quality of being malign or malignant; badness, evilness, monstrosity, depravity, maliciousness.
e: From Middle English malignete, malignitee, malignyte, malyngnite, from Middle French maligneté, from Latin malignitās. malign + -ity.

s: A stylized flower or leaf with five lobes.
A particular knot of five crossings.
Having the characteristics of a rush (the plant); rushlike.
e: From Middle English russhy, russhi, resshi, equivalent to rush (“a plant”) + -y.

s: Not penitent; specifically, not repenting of one's sins; unrepentant.
To engage in a noisy or drunken social gathering.
e: From Middle French carousser (“to quaff, drink, swill”), from German gar aus, from gar austrinken (“to drink up entirely, guzzle”). Compare German Garaus.

s: Disobedient, contrary, unmanageable; difficult to deal with; with an evil disposition.
e: From Middle English froward, fraward, equivalent to fro + -ward. Compare Old English fromweard, framweard (“turned away, having the back turned”).

s: A free#Adjective peasant (as opposed to a serf) of the low#Adjective rank#Noun, below an earl and a thane; a freeman; also, a person#Noun without royal#Adjective or noble#Adjective status; a commoner#Noun.
A rough#Adjective, surly, ill-bred person; a boor.
A countryman, a peasant, a rustic#Noun.
A person who is stingy, especially with money; a selfish miser, a niggard#Noun.
A freedman, rank#Verb below a thane but above a thrall#Noun.
e: Inherited from churle (“person not of the nobility or clergy; serf, servant, simpleton, fellow”), from Old English ċeorl (“freeman ranking below a thane but above a thrall; commoner, peasant; countryman, husbandman; man; husband”), from Proto-West Germanic *kerl, from Proto-Germanic *karilaz (“elder; man”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂- (“to grow old; to mature”).

s: A sketch or mark made in pencil.
Now chiefly in "bounden duty": made obligatory; binding.
To be obliged; to be under a duty or obligation (to do something).
e: From bound + -en, the archaic past participle of bind.

s: Of or pertaining to accent; characterized or formed by accent.
Designating verse rhythms based on stress accents.
The state of being poorly illuminated, almost dark.
e: From Middle English dymnes, dymnesse, from Old English dimnes, dymnys, dimness (“dimness, darkness, obscurity”), equivalent to dim + -ness.
