s: An act by which somebody is wronged.
The act of altering for the better, or correcting what is erroneous or faulty; correction; improvement.
Alteration by editorial criticism, as of a text so as to give a better reading; removal of errors or corruptions from a document.
An intentional change in the spelling of a scientific name, which is usually not allowed.
e: From Middle English emendatioun, from Latin ēmendātiō; equivalent to emend + -ation..

s: festive, relating to a festival or feast
Pressure or an act of applying pressure.
Of a word's sound or of a language, without any stress (accent).
Of a person's speech, not pronounced with a distinctive accent.
Of a written word, having no accent marks.
Of a written word, having no diacritical marks of any kind.
Of, related to, or abounding in palm trees.
Made out of palm leaves or palm sap.
The state or period of infancy.
The state or characteristic of being wanton; recklessness, especially as represented in lascivious or other excessive behavior.
The state of being lighthearted, joyous, cheerful, without a care.
An amusement or item of a pleasant but inconsequential nature.
The state or fact of being quaint; having old-fashioned charm.
The quality of having great value or price.
of a node in a graph
The act or process of slightly burning.
e: From Middle English *sengynge, sengeand, from Old English *senġende, *senċġende, *sænċġende, from Proto-West Germanic *sangijandī, present participle of *sangijan (“to singe”), equivalent to singe + -ing.

s: A short nail with a thick head, typically used in boot soles.
To tread down roughly, as with hobnailed shoes.
e: From hob + nail. The oldest attestation is in William Shakespeare, but he likely did not coin the term.
From a variation of splot (“a spot”) (compare blotch, from blot). More at splot.

s: Having been renounced, forsworn or rejected.
A pronunciation of letters and syllables which is pleasing to the ear.
The tendency to make phonetic change for ease of pronunciation.
e: From French euphonie, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία, from εὐ- + φωνή (“sound; (human) voice; discourse, speech”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to say, speak”)) + -ῐ́ᾱ. The English word is analysable as eu + phony.

s: Expressing a wish or a choice.
Related or pertaining to the optative mood.
A mood of verbs found in some languages (e.g. Sanskrit, Old Prussian, Tamil and Ancient Greek, but not English), used to express a wish.
A verb or expression in the optative mood.
e: From Middle French optatif, from Late Latin optātīvus, a calque of Ancient Greek εὐκτική (“related to wishing”), from Latin optātus, past participle of optāre.

s: Having the same sound; being homophones.
Having a single, accompanied, melodic line.
Resembling a pillow: soft and fluffy
Friendliness, especially easy approachability owing to a cheerful and pleasant disposition.
The beginning of the day, or first appearance of light; the dawn; daybreak.
e: From Middle English dai spring, equivalent to day + spring.

s: In a boisterous manner, energetically and noisily.
To cause irritation, bitterness or acrimony.
A festering, embittering object or condition, either mental, or a physical sore or ulcer.
e: From Middle English ranklen, ranclen, from Old French rancler, räoncler, draoncler (“to ulcerate, to form a boil”), from Old French draoncle (“a boil”), from Latin dracunculus (“little serpent”), diminutive of Latin dracō (“serpent, dragon”).

s: A guide or escort, especially one who rides in advance.
One who rides out on horseback to inspect a ranch etc.
In a manner that is tedious, repetitious or lacking in variety.
In a droning manner, that does not change pitch.
A droplet of water formed as dew.
A plant of species Dalibarda repens.
e: From Middle English deu drop, dew droppe, dewe droppe, equivalent to dew + drop. Compare Dutch dauwdruppel (“dewdrop”), German Tautropfen (“dewdrop”), Danish dugdråbe (“dewdrop”), Swedish daggdroppe (“dewdrop”), Faroese døggdropi (“dewdrop”).

s: The condition of being plain (in all senses)
The product or result of being plain
Of or relating to a residue; residual; left over, when the main portion has been removed.
With respect to a will, relating to the portion of an estate which was not disposed of in the will, or for which the directions in the will could not be carried out.
One who receives the residue of an estate.
The part of a person's hairstyle which covers the forehead.
The part of a horse's (or similar animal's) mane that lies on its forehead.
A wedge pushed through a hole at the end of a bolt to hold it in place.
To fix in place with a forelock (wedge)
e: From Middle English *forelock, *forelok, from Old English forelocc, equivalent to fore- + lock.

s: The sky which appears to an observer on the Earth as a dome in which celestial bodies are visible; the firmament.
The upper atmosphere occupied by clouds, flying birds, etc.
The place above the Earth where God or other deities live; heaven.
e: Inherited from Middle English welkne (“weather; heavens; (earlier) cloud”), from Old English wolcnu (“sky, heavens”), plural form of wolcn (“cloud”), from Proto-West Germanic *wolkn (“cloud”), from Proto-Germanic *wulkną (“cloud”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥ɡ-no-m, from *welg- (“damp; wet”).

s: Relatively small writing paper used for writing notes or letters; often provided with matching envelopes.

e: From Middle English pitous, from Old French piteus, pitus, ultimately from Latin pietās. (“piety, compassion”).

s: To put (something such as a knife or sword) into a sheath.
To encase (something) with a protective covering.
Of an animal: to draw back or retract (a body part) into the body, such as claws into a paw.
To thrust (a sharp object like a sword, a claw, or a tusk) into something.
To provide (a sword, etc.) with a sheath.
To relieve the harsh or painful effect of (a drug, a poison, etc.).
e: From Late Middle English shethen (“to put (a sword or knife) into a sheath, sheathe; to provide with a sheath; (figuratively) to have sexual intercourse”), then.

s: A person who distributes alms, especially the doles and alms of religious houses, almshouses.
A person who dispenses alms on behalf of another person.
A hospital official responsible for patient welfare and aftercare.
e: From Middle English aumener, aulmener, from Old French almosnier, from almosne (“alms”), from Latin eleemosyna. See alms, Almosen.

s: A small passerine bird, Fringilla coelebs, of the finch family, found throughout Europe and eastward to Iran and eastern Mediterranean coastlands.
e: Right|thumb|197px|A male chaffinch From Middle English chaffynch, chaffynche, caffynche, equivalent to chaff + finch. However, more recently the first element has been argued to derive from the same root as Old English cæfed (“ornamented”) and cæfing (“hair-ornament”), thus meaning "ornamented finch, colourful finch".

s: The planet Venus as the morning star.
e: From Middle English daysterre, from Old English dæġsteorra, equivalent to day + star. Cognate with Scots daystern (“morningstar; daystar”).
From Middle English plowman, ploghmon, plouȝman, equivalent to plough + man. Compare Middle Dutch ploechman.

s: The common good; public wellbeing or prosperity.
e: From Middle English comun wele, commen wele, comune wele, equivalent to common (“public”) + weal (“well-being”). By the 1520s used by some authors as the equivalent of res publica (republic), alongside commonwealth from about the same time.

s: A mottled marking, usually in clusters.
An animal with a mottled or spotted skin or coat.
Having a mottled or spotted skin or coat, dappled.
To mark or become marked with mottling or spots.
e: Uncertain. The adjective is first attested circa 1550 though the first element is already attested in dapple-grey as early as 1386, in Middle English, and later as dappled circa 1400; the OED suggests either: The noun and verb are both later attested likely as back-formations. See also Norwegian eplut and Russian в яблоках.

s: Of or pertaining to calling; used in calling or vocation.
Used in address; appellative; said of the case or form of the noun, pronoun, or adjective by which a person or thing is addressed.
A word in the vocative case
Something said to (or as though to) a particular person or thing; an entreaty, an invocation.
e: From Late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French vocatif, from Latin vocātīvus (“for calling”); a calque of Ancient Greek κλητῐκή (“for calling; vocative case”) – from vocāre (“to call”), from Proto-Indo-European *wokʷ-, o-grade of *wekʷ- (“give vocal utterance, speak”). See Latin vōx.

s: The use of small dots that give the appearance of shading; the dots thus used.
To use small dots to give the appearance of shading to.
e: Probably from Dutch stippel (“small dot”), originally applied to the dots themselves and later to the technique.

s: In a lusty manner: vigorously, loudly, enthusiastically.
A more distinct or prominent form.
Act of accentuating; applications of accent.
Pitch or modulation of the voice in reciting portions of the liturgy.
e: From Late Latin accentuatio. Compare French accentuation. Equivalent to accentuate + -ion.

s: An element, often triangular, to which the strings of a violin, guitar, etc. are attached at the lower end of an instrument.
A short joist between a header and a wall.
The part of a telescope containing the adjusting device for the eyepiece, etc.
The part of a lock that transmits motion from the hub to the latch bolt.
An ornamental design at the end of a chapter or page.
A leafy herb, Anthriscus cerefolium, resembling parsley.
Leaves from the plant, used as an herb in cooking, which have a mild flavor of anise.
e: From Middle English chervell, from Old English cerfille, from Anglo-Norman chervele (compare Jèrriais chèrfi), from Latin caerefolium, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον.

s: Swelling or swollen into large waves; full of billows or surges; resembling billows.
A tree of the genus Carpinus, having smooth grey bark and a ridged trunk, the wood being white and very hard, found in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Especially, the American hornbeam (Carpinus caroliniana), which is common along the banks of streams in the United States.
Especially, the common hornbeam or European hornbeam (Carpinus betulus).
The wood of these trees or one species of them; a sample of such wood.
A beam or ray of light emanating from the head of a deity like a horn.
e: From Late Middle English hornbeme, hernbem, hernebem (“European hornbeam (Carpinus betulus)”), from horn (“antler or horn of an animal; etc.”) + bem (“tree; piece of metal, wood, etc.”) (referring to a tree with wood as hard as horn): horn + beam (“only in compounds: tree”).
From horn + beam (“principal stem of the antler of a deer; ray of light”).

s: Of, pertaining to, or obtained by construction.
To punish or reprimand someone severely.
To execrate or condemn something in a harsh manner, especially by public criticism.
To revise or make corrections to a publication.
e: First attested in the beginning of the 17 century; Borrowed from Latin castīgātus, perfect passive participle of castīgō (“to reprove”) (see -ate and -ate), from castus (“pure, chaste”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱes- (“to cut”). Doublet of chastise, chasten, taken through Old French. See also chaste.

s: In an intolerable manner; beyond endurance.
Not having been created, thus not existing.
That exists without having been created.
Earth which grass has grown into the upper layer of; greensward, sod, turf; a portion of such earth.
An expanse of land covered in grass; a lawn or meadow.
The upper layer of the ground, especially when vegetation is growing on it.
The rind of bacon or pork; also, the outer covering or skin of something.
Of ground, etc.: to be covered with sward; to develop a covering of sward.
A particular region defined by its weather or climate.
The context in general of a particular political, moral, etc., situation.
e: Borrowed from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (“(zone of) latitude”), from κλίνω (“to slope, incline”). See also climate.

s: A ship riding at anchor and displaying a light for the guidance of sailors, in a position where a fixed lighthouse structure would be impracticable.
e: From light + ship. Cognate with Middle Low German lüchteschip (“lightship”), Dutch lichtschip (“lightship”).

s: The state or quality of being odd.
The result or product of being odd.
A behavior or way of thinking that is characteristic of a person or a group.
A peculiar individual reaction to a generally innocuous substance or factor; a risk factor.
A peculiarity that serves to distinguish or identify.
e: First attested in 1604, in modern sense since 1665, from Ancient Greek ἰδιοσυγκρασία (“one’s own temperament”), from ἴδιος (“one’s own”) + σύν (“together”) + κρᾶσις (“temperament”). idio- + syn- + -crasy.

s: The profession or skill of being a soldier.
A state of physical condition; kilter or trim.
Sand used to line a furnace.
A seam line left by the meeting of mould pieces.
A person's mood or state, often assuming the worst.
To sort out, to fix, to mend, to repair.
To make preparations; to put things in order; to do trifling business.
To line the hearth of a furnace with sand prior to pouring molten metal.
To be upset or in a bad mood.
To remove (as by sanding) the seam lines left by the meeting of two molds.
To machine away seam lines or more generally to make small adjustments to a component or machine to improve its fit or operation.
e: From Late Middle English fetlen (“(verb) to bestow; to fix, prepare, put in place; to prepare (oneself) for battle, gird up; to shape; to be about to, or to ready (oneself) to stay; (adjective) shaped (well or poorly)”), which possibly: Compare Old English ġefetelsod (“provided with a belt; trimmed, polished, ornamented”).

s: By a factor of one hundred.
To increase to one hundred times as much; to multiply by a hundred.
A narrow tube through which a jet of air is directed onto a flame; used in the analysis of minerals etc and in jewelry manufacture.
A weapon through which darts may be shot by blowing; a blowgun.
A long narrow pipe, rotated in the hands, upon which glassware is blown.
To direct air through a blowpipe.
To shoot with a blowpipe (a weapon).
A verbal or written description of a coat of arms.
A formalized language for describing a coat of arms.
A coat of arms or a banner depicting a coat of arms.
Ostentatious display, verbal or otherwise; publication; description; record.
To describe a coat of arms.
To make widely or generally known, to proclaim.
To deck; to embellish; to adorn.
e: From Middle English blason, blasoun (“shield”), from Old French blason (“shield”).

s: To move or vibrate (something) with a buzzing sound.
To make a sibilant buzzing or droning sound.
To cause (something) to make such a sound.
(of a panther) To make a vibrating sound in its throat when contented, much like the domestic cat’s purr.
A sibilant buzz or vibration; the sound of something in rapid motion.
A bustle of noise and excitement.
The vibrating sound made by a panther in its throat when contented.
e: From Middle English whirren, probably from Old Norse: compare Danish hvirre, virre, Norwegian kvirre, Old Norse hvirfla (“to whirl, spread”).

s: In the nature of a conjecture, or based on a conjecture.
Something that is conjectural; a conjecture.
A measure of particle flux (or that of a pulse of electromagnetic radiation)
A magical or mysterious force; hypnotic power; energy.
To propel or throw (something) hard or violently; to fling, to hurl.
To cause (someone or something) to collide with or hit another person or thing; or (two people or things) to collide with or hit each other.
To attack or criticize (someone) verbally or in writing.
To move rapidly, violently, or without control, especially in a noisy manner.
An act of colliding with or hitting; a collision.
A rapid or uncontrolled movement; a dash, a rush.
A sound of clashing or colliding; a clattering, a rattling.
To make (something, such as a surface) bright, shiny, and smooth by, or as if by, rubbing; to polish, to shine.
Of a stag: to remove the velvet from (its antlers) by rubbing them against something; to velvet.
To make (someone or something) appear positive and highly respected.
To become bright, glossy, and smooth; to brighten, to gleam, to shine forth.
A shine of something which has been polished; a lustre, a polish.
A shiny layer applied to a surface or other thing.
The making of something bright, shiny, and smooth by, or as if by, rubbing; an instance of this; a burnishing, a polishing, a shining.
Of a person's body: to grow large or stout; to fatten, to fill out.
Of a thing: to increase in size; to expand, to spread out, to swell.
The act by which a vessel founders.
Of or relating to a dialect.
Peculiar to a (nonstandard) variety or lect.
A small domed cap that covers the area from the forehead to just above the back of the neck.
The calvaria, the top part of the skull, covering the cranial cavity containing the brain.
Any of several species of flowering plants of the genus Scutellaria, in the Lamiaceae family.
A torture device for compressing the skull.
A person who regularly attends sermons; a devout listener.
To be uncertain or unable to make a decision; to vacillate, hesitate, or delay.
To apply an algorithm to digital data to minimize the effects of quantization
To use dot patterns in an image or graphic to simulate colors or shades not in the system palette.
To intentionally add noise to a signal to remove artifacts caused by digitization.
The state of being undecided; indecision; vacillation.
Any algorithm applied to digital data to minimize the effects of quantization
A form of noise intentionally added to remove artifacts caused by digitization.
The use of dot patterns in an image or graphic to approximate colors not available in the system palette.
e: Variant of didder, from Middle English dideren (“to tremble”). Compare Middle English bididren, bididdren (“to seduce, deceive”), from Old English bedidrian, bedyderian (“to deceive, trick”). Alternatively, perhaps with expressive voicing from *titeren, from Proto-Germanic *titrōną.

s: A delphinium: any plant of the genus Delphinium, especially Delphinium ajacis and other plants of the subgenus Delphinium subg. Consolida
e: From lark + spur, so named for the spur's shape, which resembles the hind toe of a lark.

s: Resembling or made of a thin film; gauzy.
Covered by (or as if by) a film; hazy.
e: From film + -y. Cognate with Middle Dutch velmich, vilmich (“filmy, membranous”)..

s: to irreversibly damage the shape or structure of something, negatively affecting its appearance or functionality without completely destroying it.
Someone who constantly brags or boasts.
e: From Middle French bragard (“bragging, flaunting, vain", also "a showy, arrogant individual”), from braguer (“to boast, brag”). No firm relation to English brag has been established.

s: The quality of being wrong; error or fault.
Wrong or reprehensible things or actions.
The hair of a horse, especially from the mane and tail, used for upholstery.
e: From Middle English hors her, horshere, hors-here, hors heer (also hors-hore), equivalent to horse + hair. Compare Old Norse hross-hár (“horsehair”).
From Middle English prophetesse, from Old French prophetesse, from Late Latin prophetissa. prophet + -ess.

s: Superlative of utter; situated at the most distant limit; farthest, outermost.
utmost; of the farthest, greatest, or highest degree.
The utmost; the highest or greatest degree; the farthest extent.
e: From Middle English, alteration of uttermest. Compare inmost and innermost.

s: A state of melancholy or depression; low spirits, the blues.
The act of humbling or abasing oneself.
e: From Old French dejection, from Latin dejectio (“a casting down”). deject + -ion.

s: The act by which something is lanced.
A planet or other large environment that is dominated by water.
A word or phrase within parentheses.
A descriptor or modifier enclosed within parentheses and put, indented, in a line of dialogue to describe how it should be acted or directed onscreen.
e: From Medieval Latin parentheticus (from Late Latin parenthesis or Ancient Greek παρένθετος, + -icus) al. par- + en- + thetical.

s: Subject to legal discovery; able to be requested by an opposing party through a legal process such as a subpoena.
Causing, feeling, or expressing regret or sorrow, especially in a wry or humorous way.
A cheeky or disrespectful girl; a woman showing inappropriate or improper behavior.
A case or bag for needles, thread, etc.
e: From earlier hussive, hussif, the regular evolution of Middle English houswyf (“housewife”), equivalent to house + wife.

s: A person who makes manual copies of works such as manuscripts or paintings.
Used to mark a beloved person mentioned in conversation as being deceased.
A pointed stick used to make a fence.
A fence made of galvanized sheeting.
A strong chest or box used for keeping money or valuables safe.
An ornamental sunken panel in a ceiling or dome.
A temporary watertight structure used during underwater construction of bridges, causeways, ships, etc.
A supply or store of money, often belonging to an organization.
A trench dug in the bottom of a dry moat, and extending across it, to enable the besieged to defend it with raking fire.
To put money or valuables in a coffer.
To decorate something, especially a ceiling, with coffers.
To panel, frame, or border with a raised protective trim.
e: From Middle English cofre, coffre, from Old French cofre, coffre, from Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (“basket”). Doublet of coffin. Cognate with German Koffer (“a suitcase”) and Dutch koffer (“a suitcase, luggage compartment”).

s: Possessed of great wrath; very angry.
Mental or sensory distinctness; clarity of understanding, perception etc.
The state of being free from obscurities or opacity; distinctness of light, colour etc.
The state of being free from obstruction or interference.
Written or marked with a pencil.
Marked with fine lines, as if with a pencil.
A person aboard ship who is in charge of various maritime affairs.
The officer (or warrant officer) in charge of sails, rigging, anchors, cables etc. and all work on deck of a sailing ship.
The petty officer of a merchant ship who controls the work of other seamen.
A kind of gull, the jaeger.
e: From Middle English botswain, botswein, bote-swayn, from late Old English bātsweġen, from bāt (“boat”) + sweġen (“swain”), the latter element a borrowing from sveinn (“boy”); equivalent to boat + swain (“boy, servant”).

s: The situation where something is overruled.
The state or characteristic of being childish.
Having a specified number of members.
Having legs of a different tincture from that of the body.
Skill in, and knowledge of, the work of navigating, maintaining, and operating a vessel at sea.
Not heeded; not listened to; ignored
Agile; flexible; able to move fluidly and gracefully.
Skilled at argumentation; mentally skillful; quick-witted.
e: From dexter (“right, ready”) + -ous. Displaced native Old English handcræftiġ.

s: Of a book or other work: the end.
e: From Middle English finis, from Latin fīnis (“end; limit”). Doublet of fin, fine, finish.

s: To wake or rouse from sleep.
To awaken; to cease to sleep; to be awakened; to stir.
e: From Middle English waknen, from Old English wæcnan, from Proto-Germanic *waknaną.

s: Covered with short, dense, greyish white hairs.
e: Possibly from Middle English *hori (suggested by horilocket (“hoary-locked, having hoary locks or curls”)), equivalent to hoar + -y. Alternatively, Middle English horilocket may represent Middle English hor + ilocket (“locked”) rather than hori (“hoary”) + locket (“locked”).

s: The study of rhythm, intonation, stress, loudness and related attributes in speech.
The suprasegmentals produced when prosodic elements of speech extend across more than one segment.
The study of poetic meter; the patterns of sounds and rhythms in verse.
e: From Middle French prosodie, from Latin prosōdia, from Ancient Greek προσῳδία (“song sung to music; pronunciation of syllable”), from πρός (“to”) + ᾠδή (“song”).

s: An attempt to assume or exhibit what is not natural or real; false display; artificial show.
e: From Middle French affectation and its etymon Latin affectātiōnem, from affectō (“to feign”). affect + -ation.

s: An offer made; something proposed for acceptance by another; a tender.
To offer for acceptance; to propose to give; to make a tender of.
To attempt or essay of one's own accord; to undertake or propose to undertake.
A person who maintains the health and balance of horses' feet through the trimming of the hoofs and fitting of horseshoes.
To practise as a farrier; to carry on the trade of a farrier.
e: Borrowed from Middle French ferrier, from Old French ferrier, from Latin ferrārius, from ferrum (“iron”).

s: Having a barrel or specified number of barrels.
The cognomen given to the oldest son prior to his taking his father's title.
A vampire who was turned by another vampire (the childe's sire) in a particular way.
Having a lilt; with energy, spirit and sprightliness; lively and cheerful.
A type of lively singing without any musical accompaniment, where the tune itself is sung, often to nonsense syllables.
Things that happened in the past.
To understand (something) as meaning, to take to mean.
To interpret (something) to another or publicly, explain the meaning of (something, usually language).
To analyze the grammatical structure of a clause or sentence; to parse.
e: From Middle English construen, from Late Latin construo, construere (“to relate grammatically”), from Latin construo (“pile together”); Doublet of construct.

s: The act or process of perusing, or an instance of it.
Studying something carefully; a careful study.
Giving something a cursory scan; a cursory scan.
In the manner of a sister, behaving as one would expect of a sister; as a sister, as sisters.
The act of, or occurrence of capsizing or overturning.
e: Attested since 1788. Origin unknown. Possibly related to Spanish chapuzar (“to sink by the head”).

s: A cord or tendon of the body.
A cord or string, particularly as of a musical instrument.
Muscular power, muscle; nerve, nervous energy; vigor, vigorous strength.
That which gives strength or in which strength consists; a supporting factor or member; mainstay.
To knit together or make strong with, or as if with, sinews.
The work of a soldier; military action.
Of, relating to, or consisting of a syllable or syllables.
Designating a sound that is or can be the most sonorant segment of a syllable, as a vowel or a resonant. In the word riddle ([ɹɪdl̩]), the two syllabic sounds are [ɪ] and [l̩].
Of, or being a form of verse, based on the number of syllables in a line rather than on the arrangement of accents or quantities.
e: From Medieval Latin syllabicus, from Ancient Greek συλλαβικός, from συλλαβή (“syllable”).

s: Overdeveloped at the expense of essential organs.
e: Borrowed from Latin lūxuriāns, present participle of lūxuriō, itself from lūxuria (“luxury, excess”). Equivalent to luxury + -ant.

s: The middle section of the human torso, from below the chest to above the waist; the abdomen and its back part.
e: From Middle English midref, mydrif, from Old English midrif, midhrif (“the midriff; diaphragm”), from Proto-West Germanic *middjahrif. Equivalent to mid- + riff.

s: Either of two poles with footrests that allow someone to stand or walk above the ground; used mostly by entertainers.
A tall pillar or post used to support some structure; often above water.
Any of various wading birds of the genera Himantopus and Cladorhynchus, related to the avocet, that have extremely long legs and long thin bills.
to raise on stilts, or as if on stilts
to apply unnecessary pomp or formality
e: From Middle English stilte, stulte, from Old English *stilte, *stylte, from Proto-Germanic *stiltijǭ, *staltijǭ, *stultijǭ (“stilt”), from Proto-Germanic *stelt- (“to be stiff”). Akin to Danish stylte, Dutch stelt, German Stelze.

s: The posture of someone who slouches.
Any bird that spends most of its time in coastal waters or over the oceans.
The time of day or night when the moon begins to rise over the horizon.
Having a mottled or spotted skin or coat, dapple.

e: From Middle English bitwixe, from Old English betweox, from Proto-Germanic *twiskaz (“twofold, double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, doubly; in two”). be- (“by, near, around”) + twixt (“between”). Compare twiske (“between”), Dutch tussen, German zwischen.

s: Without a hard, smooth, permanent surface.
Situated within the hull of a vessel.
Positioned nearer to the centre line of a vessel.
An engine located within the hull of a ship.
A boat with such an engine.
To discount a product in order to increase sales.
The principles and practices of an ascetic; extreme self-denial and austerity.
An instance of wafting; the action of something that wafts.
Having the appearance of cords or furrows.
Wound about with a cord or cords of a specified tincture.
to make a slight involuntary movement because of pain, distress, or embarrassment.
to make a slight involuntary movement because of pain, distress, or embarrassment.
The act by which someone winces; a grimace.
A flat fold; a doubling, as of cloth; a pleat.
A braid, as of hair or straw; a plat.
To fold; to double in narrow folds; to pleat
To interweave the strands or locks of; to braid
e: From Middle English pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (compare Old French ploit), from Latin plectō, which is akin to Old Norse flétta (Danish flette), Russian плести́ and also to Old English fleohtan, which it displaced. Doublet of plight, pleat.

s: Yarn made from long strands of wool.
The fine, smooth fabric made from such wool yarn.
e: Inherited from Middle English worstede, worsted, from Worstede (now Worstead; Old English *Wurϸestede), a town in Norfolk, England.

s: To bewail; to weep bitterly over; to feel sorrow for.
To condemn; to express strong disapproval of.
To regard as hopeless; to give up.
e: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.

s: An act of jostling; a push or shove.
The quality of being distinctive, individual or discrete.
Something which distinguishes something from anything else.
To cause to become limber; to make flexible or pliant.

A two-wheeled vehicle to which a wheeled artillery piece may be attached for transport. (Some versions have built-in storage bins for ammunition. Either the limber itself or the ammunition box may also be called a caisson.)
The shafts or thills of a wagon or carriage.
Gutters or conduits on each side of the keelson to allow water to pass to the pump well.
To prepare an artillery piece for transportation (i.e., to attach it to its limber.)
e: Unknown; possibly related to limb or limp -er, as seen in clever, slipper (“slippery”), waker (“alert”), etc.
Thumb|a limber attached to a field artillery piece and an artillery tractor For the obsolete limmer, from Old Norse limar (“branches”), plural of lim.
From Middle English wherof; equivalent to where + of. Compare the parallel formations of Swedish varav and Dutch waaraf.

s: The act of a character speaking to themselves so as to reveal their thoughts to the audience.
A speech or written discourse in this form.
e: 1595–1605; From Late Latin sōliloquium in the title of St. Augustine's Soliloquiorum libri duo ("Two Books of Soliloquies"), from sōlus (“only, sole”) + loquor (“to speak”).

s: A musical instrument in the harpsichord family.
e: From Middle English virginal, from Middle French virginal, from Latin virginālis. The musical instrument is probably so called from being played by young girls.

s: A song for a small number of unaccompanied voices; from 13th century Italy.
A polyphonic song for about six voices, from 16th century Italy.
A short poem, often pastoral, and suitable to be set to music.
Excessively nervous, excited, tense, angry, anxious, or upset; overemotional; very uneasy.
Thinking beforehand or in advance, planning; prior or previous consideration.
e: From Middle English forethouht, forethoght, from Old English *foreþōht (“forethought”); equivalent to fore- + thought. See also forethink.

s: Burning slowly, producing smoke but no flame.
The act by which something smoulders; residual heat.
Cold and damp, usually referring to hands or palms.
The quality of normal skin signs, epidermis that is neither diaphoretic nor dry.
e: From enm:clam (“viscous, sticky; slimy”) + -y, from Old English clǣman (“to smear, bedaub”). Compare German klamm (“clammy”) and klemmen (“to be stuck, stick”). See also clam.

s: Causing sorrow, distress or regret; deplorable, pitiful or distressing.
e: From Middle English lamentable, from Middle French lamentable, from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”). lament + -able.

s: Clumsy, unwieldy, or slow, especially due to weight.
Dull, boring, tedious; long-winded in expression.
Characterized by or associated with pondering.
The state or quality of being wild.
In a careful manner, with scruple; done with careful attention to detail.
e: From scrupulous + -ly, from Middle French scrupuleux, from Latin scrūpulōsus (“careful, scrupulous”), from scrūpulus (“anxiety, uneasiness”), diminutive from scrūpus (“sharp stone; anxiety”) + -ulus.

s: The punctuation mark ";", which is used to separate two sentences, the latter of which qualifies the former; to separate a series of related clauses or sentences; to separate items in a list where the items themselves include commas; etc.
e: From the fact that the mark is a colon (“:”) with the lower half replaced by a comma (“,”).

s: Someone who roleplays or describes themselves as being a bird or bird-like animal character with human characteristics.

A size of paper (7.5"-10" x 10"-12.5" or 190-254 x 254-312 mm). Formed by folding and cutting one of several standard sizes of paper (15"-20" x 20"-25" or 381-508 x 508-635 mm) twice to form 4 leaves (eight sides).
Quarto writing paper (10 inches x 8 inches)
A book size, corresponding to the paper size.

A board game for two players in which the players each have a set number of pieces (typically 12 or 20, depending on the rule set), known as men, and the object is to capture each of the opponent's pieces by jumping one's own pieces over the opponent's pieces.
Neutral in opinion or allegiance; centrist
A set of two things, particularly.
A pair of lines, typically with rhyming end words.
A pair of one-way streets which carry opposing directions of traffic through gridded urban areas.
A pair of two mutually exclusive choices in a dichotomous key.
In the way it sounds, particularly: written to describe the sound rather than the dictionary spelling.
To that point, end, or result.
The farther, the other and more distant.
e: From Middle English thider, from Old English þider, an alteration (probably by analogy with hider (“hither”)) of earlier þæder (“to there”), from Proto-Germanic *þadrê.

s: A spool or cylinder around which wire is coiled.
In a sewing machine, the small spool that holds the lower thread.
The little rounded piece of wood at the end of a latch string, which is pulled to raise the latch.
A fine cord or narrow braid.
e: Borrowed from French bobine, recorded in English since 1530.

s: A group of houses standing together in the country; a hamlet; a village.
e: From Middle English thorp, throp, from Old English þorp, þrop (“farm, village”), from Proto-West Germanic *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą, *þrepą (“village, farmstead, troop”), from Proto-Indo-European *trab-, *treb- (“dwelling, room”). Doublet of dorf, dorp, and possibly also of Doublet of troop, troupe.

s: Mercilessly or impudently violent or cruel, savage.
Like a barbarian, especially in sound; noisy, dissonant.
e: Late Middle English, from Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (“foreign, strange”).

s: The property of being lovely, of attractiveness, beauty, appearing to be lovable.

e: From Middle English needeful, nedeful, from Old English nēodful (“necessary; earnest; zealous”). Equivalent to need + -ful. Cognate with Dutch noodvol, German notvoll.

s: To inhabit a place in unpleasantly large numbers; to plague, harass.
To invade a host plant or animal.
e: From Middle English infesten, from Old French infester (“to infest”), from Latin īnfestō (“assail, molest”), from īnfestus (“hostile”), of uncertain origin.

s: A fragment or shaving that has been pared.
The cutting off of the surface of grassland for tillage.
An act of remembering long-past experiences, especially positive or pleasant ones, often fondly.
e: From Late Latin reminīscentiae (“remembrances”), from Latin reminīscēns, present active participle of reminīscor (“remember”); see reminiscent.

s: Each circle, volution or equivalent in a pattern of concentric circles, ovals, arcs, or a spiral.
A circle of three or more leaves, flowers, or other organs, about the same part or joint of a stem.
A volution, or turn, of the spire of a univalve shell.
Any volution, as for example in the human ear or fingerprint.
A flywheel, a weight attached to a spindle.
To form a pattern of concentric circles.
Streaked or mixed with grey; grizzly; griseous.
The state or condition of being naked; nudity; bareness; defenselessness; undisguisedness.
e: From Middle English nakednesse, from Old English nacodnes (“nakedness”); equivalent to naked + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian neakenens (“nakedness”).

s: The state or condition of being irregular, or the extent to which something is irregular.
An object or event that is not regular or ordinary.
Irregular bowel movement (e.g. diarrhea or constipation).
e: From Middle French irrégularité, from Medieval Latin irregularitas. Morphologically irregular + -ity.

s: The state of being happy or merry.
To avoid; to shun, to shy away from.
e: From Middle English eschewen, from Anglo-Norman eschiver, (third-person present eschiu), from Frankish *skiuhijan (“to dread, shun, avoid”); thus a Doublet of skew. For the pronunciation with /ʃ/, compare the development of marshal from Middle English marschal (/marsˈt͡ʃaːl/) or Middle English myssheve, variant of myschef (“hardship”).
From Middle English poetical, possibly equivalent to poet + -ical.

s: Of a grammatical case: in an inflected language (such as Greek or Latin), expressing that a thing denoted by a word is related to a thing denoted by another word as its origin or possessor; and in an uninflected language (such as English), expressing origin or possession; possessive.
Of, pertaining to, or used in the genitive case.
Of or pertaining to the generation of offspring; generative, procreative, reproductive.
A word inflected in the genitive case, and which thus indicates origin or possession.
Feeling pain or sorrow on account of one's sins or offenses; feeling sincere guilt.
One who repents of sin; one sorrowful on account of their transgressions.
One under church censure, but admitted to penance; one undergoing penance.
One under the direction of a confessor.
e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin paenitēns, poenitēns (“penitent”), present participle of paeniteō, poeniteō (“to cause to repent; to regret, repent”). Doublet of penitente.
From drudge (“person who works in a low servile job”) + -ery.

s: The quality of being forgetful; proneness to let slip from the mind.
Loss of remembrance or recollection; a ceasing to remember; oblivion.
Failure to bear in mind; careless omission; inattention.
Having a pleasant melody or sound; tuneful.
e: Inherited from Middle English melodious, from Middle French melodieus, melodieux. en + melody + ous.

s: Of two or more people or things
Apart or separate from each other.
Into separate parts or pieces, often due to some violent action.
Apart from other people; individually, separately; specifically, in private, privately.
Chiefly in the form to know asunder: in a manner distinguishable from other similar things.
To set apart (one or more people or things) from other people or things; to put asunder, to separate, to sunder.
To reduce to half the original amount.
To join two pieces of timber etc. by cutting away each for half its thickness at the joining place, and fitting together.
In match play, to achieve a tie or draw on.
e: From Middle English halven, helven, from Old English hilfan, helfan, *hielfan (“to halve, divide in two”), from Proto-West Germanic *halbijan, from Proto-Germanic *halbijaną (“to halve”), from Proto-Germanic *halbaz (“half”). Cognate with Middle Dutch halven (“to halve”), Middle High German halben, helben (“to halve”).

s: A quantity of the stalks and ears of wheat, rye, or other grain, bound together; a bundle of grain or straw.
Any collection of things bound together.
A bundle of arrows sufficient to fill a quiver, or the allowance of each archer.
A quantity of arrows, usually twenty-four.

An abstract construct in topology that associates data to the open sets of a topological space (i.e. a presheaf) in such a way so as to make the local and global data compatible, generalizing the situation of functions, fiber bundles, manifold structure, etc. on a topological space. Formally, a pres
If two sections over U agree under restriction to every U_i, then the sections are the same.
Given a family of sections s_i \in \mathcal{F}(U_i) such that all pairs (s_i, s_j) agree under restriction to U_i \cap U_j, there is a (unique) section s over U whose restriction to U_i is s_i.
To gather and bind into a sheaf; to make into sheaves.
To collect and bind cut grain, or the like; to make sheaves.
e: From Middle English scheef, from Old English sċēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaub, from Proto-Germanic *skauba- (“sheaf”). Akin to West Frisian skeaf (“sheaf”), Dutch schoof (“sheaf”), German Schaub, Old Norse skauf (“a fox's tail”). Compare further Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐍆𐍄 (“hair of the head”), German Schopf (“tuft”).

s: To flinch as if in pain or distress.
To wash (cloth), dip it in dye, etc., with the use of a wince.
To kick or flounce when unsteady or impatient.
A sudden movement or gesture of shrinking away.
A reel used in dyeing, steeping, or washing cloth; a winch. It is placed over the division wall between two wince pits so as to allow the cloth to descend into either compartment at will.
A battleship, especially of the World War I era, in which most of the firepower is concentrated in large guns that are of the same caliber.
Any type of warship heavier in armour or armament than a typical battleship.
One that is the largest or the most powerful of its kind.
A type of acoustic guitar with a very large body and a waist that is less pronounced than on other guitar shapes, producing a deep, bold sound.
A garment made of thick woollen cloth that can defend against storm and cold.
e: Named after HMS Dreadnought, the first battleship finished of this type, itself named for Etymology 2.

s: The act of one who strides; a long step.
A technique for propelling forward that appears similar to walking, where a foot slides forward on the opposite side of a pole being planted to provide a location to apply force.
e: From Middle English strydyng, stridende, strydand, from Old English strīdende, from Proto-Germanic *strīdandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *strīdaną (“to endeavour; stand tall; withstand; take long steps”), equivalent to stride + -ing.

s: The nurturing of a child by its mother.
The protective behavior of a mother towards her child.
Nurturing or protective behavior reminiscent of that performed by a literal mother.
A dramatic performance, often performed at court as a royal entertainment, consisting of dancing, dialogue, pantomime and song.
Words and music written for a masque.
At fault; failing to fulfill responsibility, duty, or obligations.
Not energetic or exact in duty or business; careless; tardy; slack; hence, lacking earnestness or activity; languid; slow.
e: From Middle English remisse, remysse, from Latin remissus (“languid, negligent”), perfect passive participle of remittō (“remit”).

s: The act by which something is unwound.
Not winding or meandering; straight, direct.
One who keens at a funeral.
Someone who is excessively keen or eager, possibly making others look bad; a brown-noser.
A small flat-bottomed open boat with a pointed bow and square stern.
Any of various types of boats small enough for sailing or rowing by one person.
A light, fleeting shower of rain or snow, or gust of wind, etc.
A (typically light) dusting of snow or ice (or dust, etc) (on ground, water, trees, etc).
To fall lightly or briefly, and lightly cover the ground (etc).
An act of slightly pruning tea bushes, placing new leaves at a convenient height without removing much woody growth.
To cut (a tea bush) to maintain the plucking table.
e: From Middle English skif, from Middle French esquif, from schifo (“small boat”), from skif (“boat”), from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“boat, ship”). Doublet of ship.

From Scots skiff (“light shower of rain or snow”), from skiff (“move lightly”); compare the derivative skiffle (whence English skiffle) and (English skift (“light dusting of snow”) from) Scots skift (“light shower of snow”), from skift (“move lightly”), perhaps related to shift/Old Norse skipta, or perhaps an onomatopoeic formation.

s: Feeling, expressing, or caused by despair; hopeless.
A mood or display of despair.
Terrified; struck with amazement; showing signs of terror or horror.
e: From Middle English agast, agasted, past participle of agasten (“to terrify”), from Old English a- (compare with Gothic 𐌿𐍃-, German er-, originally meaning "out") + gæstan (“to terrify, torment”): compare Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (“to terrify”); akin to Latin haerere (“to stick fast, cling”). a- + ghast/gast. See gaze.

s: The act of staying at a place throughout the winter.
To convey, imply, or profess (often falsely or inaccurately).
e: From Middle English purporten, from Anglo-Norman purporter and Old French porporter (“convey, contain, carry”), from pur-, from Latin pro (“forth”) + Old French porter (“carry”), from Latin portō (“carry”).

s: The act of indenting or state of being indented.
A notch or recess, in the margin or border of anything.
A recess or sharp depression in any surface.
The act of beginning a line or series of lines at a little distance within the flush line of the column or page, as in the common way of beginning the first line of a paragraph.
A measure of the distance from the flush line.
A division unit of a piece of law distinguished by its indentation or by a dash.
An area in a large body of water with many shallow areas.
The symbol "‐", typically used to join two or more words to form a compound term, or to indicate that a word has been split at the end of a line.
Something which links two things of greater significance than itself.
An enclosed walkway or passage that connects two buildings.
Someone who belongs to a marginalized subgroup, and can therefore described by a hyphenated term, such as "German-American", "female-academic", etc.
To separate or punctuate with a hyphen; to hyphenate.
Used to emphasize the coordinating function usually indicated by the punctuation "-".
e: Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔φέν (“in one, as a single word”), of ῠ̔φ’ ἕν (“under one”), from ῠ̔πο- + ἕν, neuter of εἷς (“one”).

s: A ray of sunlight; especially, a demarcated, narrow, and intense (relative to ambient light) ray of sunlight (as revealed by, for example, its diffraction among dust particles).
Any of various lycaenid butterflies of the genus Curetis.
Any hummingbird of the genus Aglaeactis.
An item of cutlery or crockery laid out on a table, but not used, and which can be returned to the drawer without being washed.
e: From Middle English sonnebem, sonnebeem, from Old English sunnbēam, sunnebēam (“sunbeam”), equivalent to sun + beam.

s: Having a spiral on the interior of a gun bore to make a fired bullet spin in flight to improve range and accuracy.
On the side sheltered from the wind; in that direction.
Away from the direction from which the wind is blowing; downwind.
Divinity or godhood, divine essence or nature.
An admired or influential person or entity.
e: Inherited from Middle English godhede, equivalent to god + -head (“-hood”). First attested in the Ancrene Wisse (ca. 1225). Doublet of godhood. Compare Dutch godheid, German Gottheit.

s: (of rain) To fall suddenly and forcefully, as if a squall.
A sudden, windy storm, such as is found in a squall line.
A squall line, multicell line, or part of a squall line.
e: From Middle English *squalen and squelen (“to cry, scream, squall”), from Old Norse skvala (“to cry out”), probably ultimately Onomatopoeic with influence from squeal and bawl. Cognate with Swedish skvala (“to gush, pour down”), Norwegian skval (“sudden rush of water”). The noun is probably from the verb.

s: The act of one who wallows.
Any of the many species of arching shrubs and climbing vines of the genus Lonicera in the Caprifoliaceae family, many with sweet-smelling, bell-shaped flowers.
A light yellow color inspired by the color of honeysuckle blossoms.
Any of several species of superficially similar plants from Australia.
e: From Middle English honysokel, honisokel, honysocle, hunisuccle, perhaps an alteration of Middle English honysoke, honysouke (“honeysuckle”) (whence honeysuck), from Old English huniġsūce, huniġsūge (“honeysuckle”); equivalent to honey + suck + -le, or honeysuck + -le.

s: The act by which somebody is tormented.
Open land that has an acidic peaty soil and is mostly covered with heather or bracken.
e: From Middle English morelond, equivalent to moor + land. Compare Old Norse mýrlendi (“moorland”).

s: Required to justify one's actions (to somebody); accountable, responsible.
Of an argument: capable of being answered or refuted; admitting a satisfactory answer.
Lacking faith; lacking belief in something.
Not believing in God, religion, or a comparable ideology.
Unfaithful (said of people, towards their partners)
Not observant of promises or covenants.
Not true to allegiance, duty, or vows
Extremely costly; so expensive as to cause financial ruin.
Characterized by ruin; ruined; dilapidated; as, an edifice, bridge, or wall in a ruinous state.
e: From Middle English ruynous, from Old French ruinos, ruineus, from Latin ruīnōsus. ruin + -ous.

s: The crime of knowingly presenting forged documentation.
A dense, but generally small, growth of shrubs, bushes or small trees; a copse.
A dense aggregation of other things, concrete or abstract.
The collection of many small linked files created when a document is saved in HTML format by some word processors and web site creation software.
e: Inherited from Middle English *thikket, from Old English þiccet, from þicce (“thick”) + Old English nominal suffix -et. Compare similar German Dickicht (“thicket”), which is first attested in the 17th century, however.

s: Determined to do as one pleases, and not as others want.
Full of woe; sorrowful; distressed with grief or calamity.
e: From Middle English woful, waful, equivalent to woe + -ful. Compare Old English wālīċ (“woeful”), Old English tēonful (“woeful”).

s: Confused, agitated noise as made by a crowd.
A violent commotion or agitation, often with a confusion of sounds.
To make a tumult; to be in great commotion.
e: From Old French tumulte, from Latin tumultus (“noise, tumult”).

s: The act of committing a sin.
Superlative of holey; most full of holes.
Rotting flesh of a dead animal or person.
The flesh of a living human body; also, sinful human nature.
A dead body; a carcass, a corpse.
An animal which is in poor condition or worthless; also, an animal which is a pest or vermin.
Pertaining to, or made up of, rotting flesh.
Of the living human body, the soul, etc.: fleshly, mortal, sinful.
The practice of constructing vaults, or a particular method of such construction.
A vaulted structure; such structures treated as a group.
The sport of gymnastics and dance routines performed on horseback, and on the longe line.
The condition quality of being frail, physically, mentally, or morally; weakness of resolution; liability to be deceived.
A fault proceeding from weakness; foible; sin of infirmity.
e: From Middle English frelete, frailte, from Old French fraileté, from Latin fragilitās. frail + -ty. Doublet of fragility.

s: Choice and use of words, especially with regard to effective communication; the effectiveness and degree of clarity of word choice and expression.
Having a specified form of flesh or body.
Being one or more complete laps behind the leader in a race.
The act of something that wells, or issues forth like water.
Some flowering plants of the genus Lychnis.
Any flowering plant of the genus Silene.
e: Old French la Likely from Middle English campion, a variant of champioun; see Doublet of champion. In classical times, the rose campion was fitted in garlands used to crown victors.

s: With the head first or down.
Rashly; precipitately; without deliberation; in haste, hastily.
e: From Middle English hedlong, alteration of hedling, heedling, hevedlynge (“headlong”), assimilated to long. More at headling.

s: or characteristic of winter; cold, stormy.
e: From winter + -y; compare Old English wintriġ (a parallel formation).

s: To collect (fruit, grain, or other produce) from a field, an orchard, etc., after the main gathering or harvest.
To collect fruit, grain, or other produce after the main gathering or harvest.
Of an animal, especially a bat or a bird: to feed by picking up or plucking prey, mainly arthropods such as insects, from various places.
A collection of something made by gleaning.
The afterbirth or placenta of an animal, especially a cow or sheep.
Of an animal, especially a cow or sheep: to deliver its afterbirth or placenta.
e: Possibly a variant of clean (“(UK, dialectal; noun) the afterbirth of a cow or sheep; (verb) of a cow or sheep: to bring forth the afterbirth”), possibly from clean (“to remove dirt from an object or place”), referring to an animal’s uterus being cleaned out by the delivery of the afterbirth.

s: To sexually assault or sexually harass.
e: From Middle English molesten, from Old French molester, from Latin molestō (“to trouble, annoy, molest”), from molestus (“troublesome”), from moles (“a burden, difficulty, labor, trouble”); see mole.

s: A tree-branch, usually a primary one directly attached to the trunk.
In a single or unaccompanied manner; without a companion.
Without partners, companions, or associates; single-handed.
To waste, lavish, splurge; to spend lavishly or profusely; to dissipate.
To wander at random; to scatter.
e: Earliest uses (late 16th c.) "to spend recklessly or prodigiously", also "to scatter over a wide area". Of Unknown. Perhaps a scatter + wander. Compare Danish skvætte (rare)/skvatte (“to splash”) (nominalised: skvæt), Icelandic skvetta (“to squirt”), Swedish skvätta (“to splash”), Norwegian skvette.

s: To swing or wave, especially in the air, wind, etc.; to flutter.
To move without purpose or a specified destination; to roam, to wander.
To sway back and forth, as if about to fall; to reel, to stagger, to totter.
To cause (someone or something) to move back and forth.
To cause (someone) to begin to or show signs of weakening in resolve; also, to weaken in resolve due to (something).
An act of moving back and forth, swinging, or waving; a flutter, a tremble.
A state of beginning to weaken or showing signs of weakening in resolve; a falter.
A state of feeling or showing doubt or indecision; a vacillation.
One who waves their arms, or causes something to swing or wave.
A person who specializes in treating hair to make it wavy.
A tool used to make hair wavy.
In full waver roller: a roller which places ink on the inking table of a printing press with a back and forth, waving motion.
A sapling or other young tree left standing when other trees around it have been felled.
e: The verb is derived from Middle English waveren (“to move back and forth, swing; to move unsteadily, totter; to shake, tremble; to wander; (figurative) to be changeable or unstable; to deviate”), and then possibly: both from Proto-Germanic *webaną (“to weave”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to braid, weave”). Doublet of wave. The noun is derived from the verb.

Uncertain, possibly from waive (“(obsolete) to disregard, overlook”). According to the Oxford English Dictionary the early forms waiver, wayver, weaver indicate that the word is probably not derived from wave.

s: A female lion (famous person regarded with interest and curiosity).
A female visitor to a student at Oxford, especially during commemoration week.
e: From Middle English leonesse, lyonesse, from Old French leonesse, lionesse; equivalent to lion + -ess.

s: The relics or remains of a saint, or the shrines in which they are kept.
Often followed by out: to squeeze or twist (something moist) tightly so that liquid is forced out.
Often followed by from or out: to extract (a liquid) from something wet by squeezing, twisting, or otherwise putting pressure on it.
To hold (someone or something) tightly and press or twist; to wrest.
To bend or strain (something) out of its position; to wrench, to wrest.
To contort or screw up (the face or its features).
To twist or wind (something) into coils; to coil.
Of a thing (such as footwear): to pinch or press (a person or part of their body), causing pain.
To cause (someone or something) physical harm, injury, or pain; specifically, by applying pressure or by twisting; to harm, to hurt, to injure.
To slide (two ultraflat surfaces) together such that their faces bond.
To be engaged in clasping and twisting (especially the hands), or exerting pressure.
To twist the body in or as if in pain; to writhe.
Of a lode: to be depleted of ore; to peter or peter out.
To make a way out with difficulty.
A powerful squeezing or twisting action.
Followed by down: the product of wringing, such as cider or wine.
A sharp physical pain, especially in the abdomen; also, mental pain or distress.
e: From Middle English wring, wringe, wringen, wryng, wrynge, wryngen, wryngyn, from Old English wringan (“to wring”), from Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, twist, wring”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrenǵʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”).
From Middle English wring, wringe, wrynge (“a press, especially for olives or wine”), from Old English wringe, from wringan: see further at etymology 1.

s: The act of one who bawls or shouts.
A task; an assigned item of work.
From the urban musical genre called grime.
Morally corrupt, malicious, vile, or selfish; base or dirty; rotten.
Of a beat or song, darkly atmospheric; having affinities with the style of the East Coast hip hop of the 90s, especially that of New York.
Capable of being understood; clear to the mind.
e: From Middle French intelligible, from Old French, from Latin intelligibilis.
From Middle English a-fresche, equivalent to a- + fresh. Compare Old English afersċean (“to freshen; become fresh”).

s: Of or like glass, especially in being smooth and somewhat reflective.
Lacking any chop; smooth and mostly flat.
e: From Middle English glasy, equivalent to glass + -y. Compare glääsich (“glassy”), Dutch glazig (“glassy”), Low German glasig (“glassy”), German glasig (“glassy”).

s: only used in the phrase hither and thither
e: From Middle English hider, from Old English hider, from Proto-Germanic *hidrê. Cognate with Latin citer.

s: To make such a sudden, unsteady movement.
To swallow or eat greedily; to devour; hence, to swallow up.
To evade by stooping; to lurk; lie in wait; go about in a sneaking way.
To take by surprise; to unexpectedly detain.
An old game played with dice and counters; a variety of the game of tables.
A double score in cribbage for the winner when their adversary has not yet pegged their 31st hole.
To defeat in the game of cribbage with a lurch (double score as explained under noun entry).
To leave someone in the lurch; to cheat.
e: Originally a nautical term, found in lee-larches (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of Unknown origin. Possibly the same as lurch (“to move stealthily, evade by stooping”) (see below), or from French lâcher (“to let go”).

From Middle English *lurchen (recorded only in Middle English lurcare, lurcard (“glutton”)), from Old French *lurcher, from Latin lurcō (“eat greedily, guzzle”), of Uncertain origin. Compare Middle High German slurken (“to slurp”) (whence German schlurken).
From Middle English lorchen, variant of Middle English lurken (“to lurk”). More at lurk.

From Middle English *lurche (implied in derivative lurching), from Old French lourche (“deceived, embarrassed; also the name of a game”), from Proto-West Germanic *lort (“left; left-handed; crooked; bent; warped; underhanded; deceitful; limping”). Cognate to English lirt.

s: A building for soldiers, especially within a garrison; originally referred to temporary huts, now usually to a permanent structure or set of buildings.
A primitive structure resembling a long shed or barn for (usually temporary) housing or other purposes.
Any very plain, monotonous, or ugly large building.
A (structure with a) movable roof sliding on four posts, to cover hay, straw, etc.
To house military personnel; to quarter.
To jeer and heckle; to attempt to disconcert by verbal means.
To cheer for or support a team.
e: Vulgar Latin qsb-ibe Borrowed from French baraque, from Spanish barraca or Catalan barraca, which is of uncertain origin. It is probably either a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *barra (“bar”), of unclear origin, or a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *barrum (“clay, mud”) from or.

s: The particular character or essence of someone or something; individuality.
A piece of land owned by someone; someone's property.
More generally, something owned by someone; a possession.
The fact of possessing something; ownership.
Suitability, fitness; the quality of being appropriate.
Correctness in behaviour and morals; good manners, seemliness.
e: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. en + proper + iety. Doublet of property.

s: A kind of coarse woollen cloth or stuff with a shaggy or tufted (friezed) nap on one side.
To make a nap on (cloth); to frizz.

The portion of an architectural entablature situated between the architrave and the cornice, consisting of a flat surface that may be continuous or articulated by triglyphs and is often decorated with sculptural figures and ornamental details.
Any sculptured or richly ornamented band in a building or in rich pieces of furniture.
A banner with a series of pictures.
e: Frieze (textile) Late Middle English, from French and Middle French frise, probably from Medieval Latin Frisia (“Frisian (wool)”) due to import via Northern ships. Or, from French friser (“to curl”)..

s: A marine gastropod of the family Strombidae which lives in its own spiral shell.
The shell of this sea animal.
A musical instrument made from a large spiral seashell, somewhat like a trumpet.
The semidome of an apse, or the apse itself.
To refine the flavour and texture of chocolate by warming and grinding, either in a traditional concher, or between rollers.
To play a conch seashell as a musical instrument, by blowing through a hole made close to the origin of the spiral.
Crudely or roughly assembled; put together in an improvised way (as in "cobbled together").
Exhibiting lust (in the obsolete sense meaning "vigor"); strong, healthy, robust; vigorous; full of sap or vitality.
Hearty, merry, gleesome, enthusiastic, lively, stirring.
Given to experiencing lust; enjoying physical sensations; lustful.
e: From Middle English lusty (“mirthful, pleasant, delicious, delightful”), equivalent to lust + -y. Compare lustich (“amusing”), West Frisian lustich (“amusing, funny”), Dutch lustig (“cheerful”), German lustig (“amusing”), Danish lystig (“merry”), Swedish lustig (“funny”).

s: A blemish or smear, especially a dark or sooty one.
Dense smoke, such as that used for fumigation.
A heap of damp combustibles partially ignited and burning slowly, placed on the windward side of a house, tent, etc. to keep off mosquitoes or other insects.
in the phrase "smudge stick"  "stick of incense"
A quantity of herbs used in suffumigation.
To obscure by blurring; to smear.
To soil or smear with dirt.
To use dense smoke to protect from insects.
To stifle or smother with smoke.
To burn herbs as a cleansing ritual (suffumigation).
To subject to ritual burning of herbs (suffumigation, smudging).
e: Derived from the verb (see below). Doublet of smutch.

From Middle English *smogen (attested in the gerund smogynge (“soiling, smudging”)), of Uncertain origin. Compare Middle English besmudded, bismuddet (“filthy”), Middle English smod (“filth, obscene behaviour”), Middle Dutch smoddich (“filthy, dirty”), German schmutzig (“dirty, filthy”).

s: Someone who observes or beholds; an observer or spectator.
A fictional monster in roleplaying games, a floating orb of flesh with a large mouth and many eyes on stalks.
e: From Middle English behalder, be holdar, beholder, beholdere, biholdar, biholdere, byholdere; equivalent to behold + -er.

s: A person who comforts someone who is suffering.
A padded cover for a bed, duvet, continental quilt.
e: From Middle English comfortour et al, from Anglo-Norman confortour, from Old French conforter. See comfort.

s: A mixture of a powdered mineral substance (often slaked lime (containing calcium hydroxide), chalk (calcium carbonate), or both) and water which is used for painting surfaces such as fences and walls bright white.

A thing used to hide mistakes, or to create an appearance of honesty, propriety, etc.; also, an act of hiding mistakes or creating an appearance of honesty, propriety, etc.; especially, a campaign, investigation, etc., which intentionally hides or overlooks unfavourable facts.
An act of clearing a person's debts, especially through a declaration of bankruptcy by a court.
A complete victory or series of victories without suffering any losses; a clean sweep; also, a victory or series of victories by a very large margin.
The most basic type of thickening agent, consisting of flour blended with water to make a paste.
A preparation for making the skin look lighter.
Any of several medicinal preparations for treating skin diseases consisting of a mixture of a metallic compound (such as one of lead, sulfur, or zinc) and water.
White wine, especially Madeira or sherry, drunk after dinner or after taking claret and port; a glass of such wine.
To paint (a building, a wall, etc.) a bright white with whitewash.
To make (the face, etc.) look lighter with makeup or a similar preparation.
To paint bright white with whitewash.
To have debts cleared through a declaration of bankruptcy by a court.
Of bricks: to become encrusted with a white layer of soluble salts due to efflorescence.
e: [[File:Whitewash (3915197412).jpg|thumb|A young man in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, painting with whitewash.]] The is derived from white + wash. is a Calque of New Latin lōtiō alba. The is derived partly from white + wash, and partly from the noun.

s: To thrust oneself in; to come or enter without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass.
Of large magnitude, either good or bad, and sometimes both.
Full of burls or knots; knotty.
Extremely bad; very unpleasant; used as an intensifier.
Made or done in pieces or one stage at a time.
Piece by piece; in small amounts, stages, or degrees.
To divide or distribute piecemeal; dismember.
e: From Middle English pecemele, from pece (“piece”) + mele (from Old English mǣlum (“at a time”), dative plural form of mǣl (“time, measure”), taking the place of Old English styċċemǣlum (“in pieces, bit by bit, piecemeal; to pieces, to bits; here and there, in different places; little by little, by degrees, gradually”); equivalent to piece + -meal.

s: Such a man employed as harem guard or in certain (mainly Eastern) monarchies (e.g. late Roman and Chinese Empires) as court or state officials.
A man who is not inclined to marry and procreate.
e: From Middle English eunuk, from Middle French eunuque, from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος, from εὐνή (“bed”) + ἔχω (“to have, keep”). Originally probably used to refer to a bed chamber attendant.

s: Tending to destroy, devastate, overwhelm or cause complete destruction.
Tending to make someone feel small; scornful in a mortifying way.
The process by which something withers.
Having a powerful effect; forceful, telling, strong, convincing, effective.
e: From Middle English forcible, forsable, from Old French forcible, from forcier (“to conquer by force”), equivalent to force + -ible.

s: A comprehensive summary of, or treatise on a subject, especially theology or philosophy.

The eldest son of the king of France. Under the Valois and Bourbon dynasties, the Dauphin of France, generally shortened to Dauphin, was heir apparent to the throne of France. The title derived from the main title of the Dauphin, Dauphin of Viennois.
e: Inherited from Middle English Dauphin, from Middle French dauphin, from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς; the modern pronunciation is sometimes remodelled on Modern French. Doublet of dolphin.

s: Lack of care; the state or quality of being careless.
e: From Middle English *carelesnes, *carlesnesse, from Old English carlēasnes (“freedom from care, security, carelessness”), equivalent to careless + -ness.

s: Not defensible; not capable of being defended.
Not capable of being justified or excused.
Charming; likely to put one at ease.
Of or pertaining to volume or volumes.
Consisting of many folds, coils, or convolutions.
Of great volume, or bulk; large.
Having written much, or produced many volumes.
e: From Late Latin voluminosus, from volumen, from volvō (“roll, turn about”) + -men. Related to volume.

s: One of the hairs which grows along the edge of eyelids.
The rise and fall of the voice in speaking.
Emotive stress used to increase the power of delivery in speech.
A sound made by, or resembling that made by, a musical instrument.
Singing or playing in good tune or otherwise.
Reciting in a musical prolonged tone; intonating or singing of the opening phrase of a plain-chant, psalm, or canticle by a single voice, as of a priest.
e: From French intonation, from Medieval Latin intonatio, from intonō + -tiō.

s: A reel; a device around which thread, wire or cable is wound, especially a cylinder or spindle.
One of the rotating assemblies of a gas turbine engine, composed of one or more turbine stages, a shaft, and one or more compressor or fan stages.
A temporary storage area for electronic mail, etc.
A splinter caught in the skin.
To wind on a spool or spools.
To send files to a device or a program (a spooler or a daemon that puts them in a queue for processing at a later time).
A small swimming pool that can be used also as a spa.
e: From Middle English spole (possibly via spole, espole), from Middle Dutch spoele, from Old Dutch *spōla, *spuola, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ (“spool”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to cleave, split”).

s: A feast, or an occasion on which people or animals feast
Lying beyond the proton or neutron drip line; having a negative particle separation energy; capable of decaying by the spontaneous exothermic emission of one or more nucleons.
To split or sever something with, or as if with, a sharp instrument.
To break a single crystal (such as a gemstone or semiconductor wafer) along one of its more symmetrical crystallographic planes (often by impact), forming facets on the resulting pieces.
To make or accomplish by or as if by cutting.
(chemistry) To split (a complex molecule) into simpler molecules.
Of a crystal, to split along a natural plane of division.
Flat, smooth surface produced by cleavage, or any similar surface produced by similar techniques, as in glass.
A cut (slash) or a cut location, either naturally or artificially.
Followed by to or unto: to adhere, cling, or stick fast to something.
e: From Middle English cleven, from the Old English strong verb clēofan (“to split, to separate”), from Proto-West Germanic *kleuban, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- (“to cut, to slice”). Doublet of clive.

From Middle English cleven, a conflation of two verbs: Old English clifian (from Proto-West Germanic *klibēn, from Proto-Germanic *klibāną) and Old English clīfan (from Proto-West Germanic *klīban, from Proto-Germanic *klībaną), both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gleybʰ- (“to stick”). Cognate with Dutch kleven, German kleben (“to stick”).

s: The pear-shaped fruit of a small tree of the rose family, Cydonia oblonga.
The deciduous tree bearing such fruit, native to Asia.
A soft yellow colour, like that of a quince.
e: From Middle English quynce, coince, a variant of coins, coin (“quince”), from Old French cooing (modern coing), from Late Latin cotōneum, from Latin mālum cotōneum, a variant of mālum Cydonium (“Cydonian apple”), translating Ancient Greek μηλοκυδώνιον.

s: Characterized by violence and agitation; wild; stormy.
e: From Middle English boistres, an alteration of Middle English boistous (“crude, unrefined”), of Uncertain origin. Likely from Anglo-Norman boystous, bustous (“rough, in a crude state, disabled, paralysed, unable to walk, lame”), Old French boitous (“limping; having a rough, uneven surface”).

s: Undisciplined, unruly; not able to be controlled.
Capricious, reckless of morality, justice etc.; acting without regard for the law or the well-being of others; gratuitous.
An overly playful person; a trifler.
A self-indulgent person, fond of excess.
A lewd or immoral person, especially a prostitute.
To rove and ramble without restraint, rule, or limit; to revel; to play loosely; to frolic.
To waste or squander, especially in pleasure (most often with away).
To act wantonly; to be lewd or lascivious.
e: From Middle English wantoun, wantowen, wantoȝen, wantowe (“uneducated; unrestrained; licentious; sportive; playful”), from wan- (“not, un-, mis-”) + towen, i-towen (“educated”), from togen, ġetogen, past participle of tēon (“to train, discipline”), equivalent to wan- + towed.

s: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.
Exhibiting advanced skills and aptitudes at an abnormally early age.
e: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”). Doublet of apricot.

s: an instance of gallant behaviour or speech.
A burning pain in the chest that is caused by stomach acid entering the gullet.
e: From Middle English hertbryne, herte-bren (“lust", also "heartburn”), equivalent to heart + burn. Compare also Middle English herte-brennyng (“anger, bitterness, heartburn”). Compare also Ancient Greek καρδιαλγία, from καρδία (“heart”) + ἄλγος (“pain”). From being a burning sensation near the location of the heart in the chest.

s: The act or operation of removing the fleece from a sheep, llama etc. with shears or a shearing machine
The removal of nap from cloth.
The material cut off in this way.
Deformation by forces acting in opposite directions.
The act or operation of reaping.
The act or operation of dividing with shears.
The process of preparing shear steel; tilting.
The process of making a vertical side cutting in working into a face of coal.
of or relating to a spouse, spouses; to the relationship between spouses
e: From Middle English spousaille, from Old French esposaille, espousaille, espousalle, Anglo-Norman (e)spusaille, esposalie, sposale, spousaille.

s: The action of perverting someone or something; humiliation; debasement.
The state of being perverted; depravity; vice.
or corruption of the original course, meaning or state of something.
A sexual practice considered abnormal; sexual deviance; immorality.
A junction or joining of ropes made by splicing them together.
The electrical and mechanical connection between two pieces of wire or cable.
That part of a bat where the handle joins the blade.
Bonding or joining of overlapping materials.
The process of removing intron sequences from the pre-messenger RNA, and then joining together exons.
To unite, as two ropes, or parts of a rope, by a particular manner of interweaving the strands, the union being between two ends, or between an end and the body of a rope.
To unite, as spars, timbers, rails, etc., by lapping the two ends together, or by applying a piece which laps upon the two ends, and then binding, or in any way making fast.
To remove intron sequences from the pre-messenger RNA, and then join together exons.
To add, remove and/or replace several array/data elements in one operation.
e: Circa 1525, borrowed from Middle Dutch splissen (Modern Dutch splitsen); akin to Middle Dutch splitten (“to split”), German spleißen (“to split, splice”), Spliss (“split ends, hair breakage”), French épisser (also from Dutch).

s: Emergency intervention to save a patient's life.
To be overwhelmed by emotion, especially infatuation.
To overwhelm with emotion, especially infatuation.
To make a moan, sigh, or some other sound expressing infatuation or affection.
e: From Middle English swoune, swone, from the verb (see below).

s: having the surface cooked and crispened (particularly by cooking on a grill or pan)
The smoldering or glowing remains of a fire, smoldering ash.
Of a person or animal: large but not obese.
A narrow valley; a cleft in a hillside; a ravine, glen, or gorge.
A sluice used in returning water to a channel after depositing its sediment on the flooded land.
The cleft or fork of a tree; crotch.
e: From Middle English clough, clow, cloȝ, from Old English *clōh, from Proto-West Germanic *klą̄h (“cleft, sluice, abyss”), of Uncertain origin, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to form into a ball”).

s: A reflection after an act; a later or subsequent thought, action, or expedient.
Something additional to the original plan or concept.
e: From after- + thought, probably modelled on forethought. Compare also the verb afterthink.

s: Semi-formal trousers which are less formal than those that are part of a suit but nowadays are considered suitable casualwear in most offices.
To satisfy, especially a literal or figurative thirst.
To extinguish or put out (as a fire or light).
To cool rapidly by direct contact with liquid coolant, as a blacksmith quenching hot iron.
To terminate or greatly diminish (a chemical reaction) by destroying or deforming the remaining reagents.
To rapidly change the parameters of a physical system.
To rapidly terminate the operation of a superconducting electromagnet by causing part or all of the magnet's windings to enter the normal, resistive state.
The act of quenching something; the fact of being quenched.
The abnormal termination of operation of a superconducting magnet, occurring when part of the superconducting coil enters the normal (resistive) state.
A rapid change of the parameters of a physical system.
e: From Middle English quenchen, from Old English cwenċan, from Proto-Germanic *kwankijaną.

s: Bad weather involving blowing winds and snow, or blowing winds and heavy snowfall amount.
Giving the appearance of carelessness; relaxedly.
Done without care or attention; inattentively.
Any of several local officials, with varying responsibilities.
The president of a township or municipal district council.
