A set of three se-tenant postage stamps that form a composite picture.
Any set of three closely connected ideas or objects.
e: From Ancient Greek τρίπτυχος (“consisting of three layers, threefold”), from τρι- + πτυχή (“a fold”).

s: Silica based glass extruded into fibers that possess a length at least 1000 times greater than their width.
A composite material made from fine fibres of spun glass held together with resin.
A movement in the arts in which the artist did not depict objective reality, but rather a subjective expression of their inner experiences.
A somewhat analogous genre in early 20th century music.
The act by which something is wreaked.
A bag carried on the back or shoulder, supported by straps.
Expressing a hope or intention but not creating a legally binding obligation.
Someone who reefs sails, especially a midshipman.
A reefer jacket; a close-fitting jacket or short coat of thick cloth.
A refrigerated, insulated trailer, ship or shipping container.
e: Uncertain. Perhaps from grifa (“cannabis”)/Central American Spanish grifo (“someone who smokes cannabis”), or from the rolled-up appearance of a marijuana cigarette resembling a reefed sail..
From reef + -er. # A miner that works on a reef (large vein of auriferous quartz).

s: An ornamental garment worn under a doublet.
A sleeveless, collarless garment worn over a shirt and under a suit jacket.
The external female genitalia of humans and other placental mammals, which includes the clitoris, labia, and vulval vestibule/vulvar opening.
A protrusion on the side of a nematode.
e: Latin vulva, earlier volva (“womb, female sexual organ”), probably from volvō (“to turn, wrap around”). Akin to Sanskrit उल्ब॑ and उल्व॑ (“womb”) or English valve, valva and other descendants of the Latin term (evolve, involve, revolve).

s: A form of exercise, designed to enhance one's cardiovascular fitness, normally performed to music.
The quality of being immediate, of happening right away.
A herb of the mint family, Origanum vulgare, having aromatic leaves.
Other herbs with a similar flavor, including other species in the genus Origanum, and Mexican oregano, Lippia graveolens.
The leaves of these plants used in flavouring food.
e: 18th century, from Spanish orégano (“wild marjoram”), from Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὀρίγανον. Doublet of origanum.

s: A person who does small tasks and odd jobs, especially building repairs and the like.
To work as a handyman; to do odd jobs.
A leisurely stroll; a recreational walk in the countryside.
A rambling; an instance of someone talking at length without direction.
A bed of shale over the seam of coal.
A section of woodland suitable for leisurely walking.
To move about aimlessly, or on a winding course.
To walk for pleasure; to amble or saunter.
To lead the life of a vagabond or itinerant; to move about with no fixed place of address.
To talk or write incessantly, unclearly, or incoherently, with many digressions.
To follow a winding path or course.
Very miserable, wretched, unhappy, measly, forlorn.
A water sport involving travelling or racing in canoes or kayaks.
When a cigar, cigarette, or joint burns unevenly, burning more on one side.
Overly bossy, domineering, arrogant, forceful, intense, or annoying.
To hang loosely with the ability to swing.
The action of performing a move or deke with the puck in order to get past a defender or goalie; perhaps because of the resemblance to dangling the puck on a string.
To hang or trail something loosely.
To put forth as a possibility.
Of a patient: to be positioned with the legs hanging over the edge of the bed.
To position (a patient) in this way.
An agent of one intelligence agency or group who pretends to be interested in defecting or turning to another intelligence agency or group.
The action of dangling; a series of complex stick tricks and fakes in order to defeat the defender in style.
e: Uncertain, but likely of origin, akin to Danish dingle, dangle, Swedish dangla (“to swing about”), Norwegian dangla, perhaps via dangeln; all possibly related to Old Norse dengja (“to hit”).

s: Of, like, or suitable for a child.

A device using gunpowder and other chemicals which, when lit, emits a combination of coloured flames, sparks, whistles or bangs, and sometimes made to rocket high into the sky before exploding, used for entertainment or celebration.
e: From fire + work. Compare Fjuurwierk (“firework”), West Frisian fjoerwurk (“firework”), Dutch vuurwerk (“firework”), Low German Füürwark, Füerwark (“firework”), German Feuerwerk (“firework”), Danish fyrværkeri (“firework”), Swedish fyrverkeri (“firework”), Faroese fýrverk (“firework”).

s: An instance of using a club.
A thickening of the ends of fingers and toes.
The development of clubroot in a plant.
A strip of fabric worn around the head.
A hair accessory, made of a flexible material and curved like a horseshoe, for holding one's hair back.
A strip of fabric attached to the top of the spine of a book; used as decoration and reinforcement.
A thin slip of iron on the tympan of a printing press.
e: From Middle English *hedband, from Old English hēafodbænd, hēafodbend (“headband”), equivalent to head + band. Cognate with Old High German houbitbant (“headband”), Dutch hoofdband (“headband”).

s: Any powder (originally containing gypsum plaster and glue) that when mixed with water forms a plastic paste, which is used to fill cracks and holes in plaster.
A plastic paste meant for filling cracks and holes in plaster.
A paste-like substance that fills a gap.
To fill or repair with a plastic paste.
To fill cracks or holes with a spackle.
To fill gaps with something, as if spackling; to speckle
e: From Spackle, originally a brand name, perhaps based on German Spachtel which is ultimately from Latin spatula. Doublet of spatula.

s: The act of fraternizing or uniting as brothers.
Having a friendly relationship with the enemy.
any type of disallowed, supposedly unethical and unprofessional, social or intimate contact between employees, especially between different gender, class or rank.
To injure, e.g. tissues, by force or by thermal, chemical or other agents.
A semi-hard cheese made of whole milk from cows. It comes primarily from Southern Italy.
To an extent or in a way that cannot be, or could not have been, imagined.
Uncommunicative; unwilling or hesitant to give information.
e: Initially US colloquial, of Unknown origin. A connection with the behavior of caged prisoners (wary and closed-lipped) and caged animals (wary) has been speculated. If so, en + cage + -y.

s: A generic snack product consisting of an oblong yellow cake with a creamy white filling.
An actor, actress, or public figure regarded primarily for their physical attractiveness rather than for substantive talent, achievement or contribution.
A Georgian or North Carolinian, particularly one from the pine forests of the Sandhills region.
A foolish, simple, or amusingly silly person.
To drip or slather; to apply a gooey substance to a surface.
An act of washing or cleaning the inside of something.
An appliance designed to wash out the inside of something.
The erosion of a relatively soft surface by a sudden gush of water; also, a channel produced by this action.
A breach in a railway or road caused by flooding.
A sporting fixture or other event that cannot be completed because of rain.
The aerodynamic effect of a small twist in the shape of an aircraft wing.
A trainee who drops out of a training programme.
A period between clinical treatments in which any medication delivered as the first treatment is allowed to be eliminated from a person's body before the second treatment begins.
The cleaning of matter from a physiological system using a fluid; also, the fluid used for such cleaning; or the matter cleaned out from the system.
The action whereby falling rainwater cleans particles from the air.
A place in a mine where ore has been washed away by a flow of water.
A large marine fish with a long, pointed bill, Xiphias gladius.
A sudoku technique involving possible cell locations for a digit, or pair, or triple, in uniquely three rows and three columns only. This allows for the elimination of candidates around the grid.
e: From Middle English swerdfysche, from Old English *sweordfisċ. Equivalent to sword + fish.

s: A beard trimmed to grow only at the center of the chin.
e: From goat + -ee, referring to the tuft of hair on the chin of many domestic goats.

s: Beginning something by leading the way, e.g. being the first batter in an inning
Not able to be reduced or lessened.
Not able to be brought to a simpler or reduced form.
Unable to be factorized into polynomials of lower degree, as (x2 + 1).
Whose numerator and denominator share no common factor greater than 1.
Unable to be factored into smaller integers; prime.
of an element of a ring
Whose only divisors are units and associates.
Inexpressible as the union of two proper algebraic subvarieties.
Not containing a sphere of codimension 1 that is not the boundary of a ball.
Impossible to divide further into representations of lower dimension by means of any similarity transformation.
An act of disrespect or impiety towards something considered sacred.
The preparing of a medicine, food or other substance out of many ingredients.
A mixture prepared in such a way.
The act of digesting in the mind; rumination.
An abatement of a morbid process, such as a fever, and a return to a normal condition.
The act of perfecting or maturing.
Unwilling or unable to forgive or show mercy.
Having no allowance for error or weakness.
The act or means by which something is anchored or made firm.

The tendency of people to place subsequently refined answers to a given question close to the initially estimated answer, giving undue weight to the initial answer, such as adjusting an initial estimate of 20% to 30% when 90% would be more appropriate.
To perform or speak without prior planning or thought; to act in an impromptu manner; to improvise.
To adapt, improvise, or devise action or speech in an impromptu or spontaneous manner.
Having a greater than normal sexual appetite
The act of one who snickers.
One who heckles; somebody who insults, makes fun of, or teases.
An aircraft flying attack missions at night.
In an unbearable manner, not bearably, in a way unable to be borne.
Standing elevated, on or as if on the tips of one's toes.
Moving carefully, quietly, warily or stealthily, on or as if on the tips of one's toes.
To walk quietly with only the tips of the toes touching the ground.
e: From Middle English tipto, typto; equivalent to tip + toe. Compare fingertip.

s: Girded, steeled, resolvedly prepared (for a challenge).
Wearing, or provided with a shroud.
Concealed or hidden from sight, as if by a shroud.
An agent or drug that sedates, having a calming or soothing effect, or inducing sleep.
e: Inherited from Middle English sedatif, from Anglo-Norman sedatif, from Medieval Latin sēdātīvus, which itself likely influenced the modern spelling. sedate + -ive.

s: (of a meeting) Having a quorum; having the minimum number of people necessary to conduct business and to cast votes.
That does not deviate, veer or turn aside; unswerving.
To officially charge someone in a court of law.
To call to account, or accuse, before the bar of reason, taste, or any other tribunal.
Free from guile; honest but naive.
Befitting the status or skill of a magister or master; authoritative, masterly.
Of or pertaining to a master, magistrate, the magisterium, or one in authority.
Pertaining to, produced by, or of the nature of, magistery.
The act by which something is chafed.
A face mask with an integrated filter or filters to keep out harmful dusts, fumes, and mists.
A person who restores peace, especially by settling disputes; one who engages in peacemaking.
e: peace + maker. First attested in the Tyndale Bible from 1526, as a translation of Koine Greek εἰρηνοποιοί, a hapax legomenon found in the New Testament. (The Wycliffe Bible from 1395 instead uses "pesible men", to translate Latin pacifici from the Vulgate)

s: A place where the bodies of dead people are cremated.
Free from blame; without fault; innocent.
Not meriting blame or censure; undeserving of reproof.
Synonym of leper: a person suffering from Hansen's disease; a person suffering any contagious disease requiring similar isolation.
Synonym of leprous: afflicted by Hansen's disease; afflicted by any contagious disease requiring similar isolation.
e: From Middle English lazare, from Old French lazare, from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), an antonomasia from Lazarus, from Koine Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος, the given name of the Biblical figure found in Luke 16, from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר (“Eleazar”), a given name shared by various figures in the Hebrew Bible and literally meaning "God has helped".

s: The state or quality of being immoral; vice.
The application of a substance (lubricant) between moving surfaces in contact in order to reduce friction and minimize heating.
An absurd, grotesque, misrepresentative or grossly inferior likeness or imitation.
A pastiche, parody, or stylistic imitation; a burlesque literary or artistic imitation (typically of a more serious work).
An appalling event, situation or outcome (especially in relation to another outcome to which it is grossly inferior).
To make a travesty of; to parody.
Intimidated or overwhelmed by a nagging or overbearing matriarch, wife, or girlfriend.
Incompetently performed; ruined through incompetent action; botched up.
The act by which somebody is avenged.

e: From Old French latimier, latinier (“interpreter”), etc. and directly from Vulgar Latin latimarus, from Latin latinarius (“interpreter, speaker of Latin”), from lingua Latina + -arius (“-ary”). Equivalent to Latin + -er and compare Latiner.

s: In a just or fair manner; rightfully.
With a just or fair use of language; with good reason, properly.
Someone who hates women; a misogynist.
In a confiding manner; in a matter that confides.
To free from misconception, deception or error.
An act of procrastination of vacillation.
An opera glass with a handle.
e: Borrowed from French lorgnette, from lorgner (“to take a sidelong look at”) (from Middle French lorgne (“crosseyed”)).

s: To signify by some visible object; show by signs or tokens.
To foreshow by present signs; indicate something in the future by that which is seen or known.
e: From Middle English bitoknen, bitacnen, from Old English betācnian (“to betoken, signify, designate”), from Proto-West Germanic *bitaiknijan. Equivalent to be- + token.

s: A surveyor's instrument for measuring distances, consisting of a wheel that rolls over the ground, along with a clockwork apparatus and a dial plate upon which the distance travelled is shown by an index.
To cause (something) to occur; to bring about.
To conduct or lead (someone or something).
To advantage or benefit (someone or something).
To carry on or continue (an activity).
To contribute or lead to a specific result.
To be advantageous to; to advantage, to benefit.
A band fastened around a hat.
A British or Irish coin worth two (old or new) pence.
A cost or value of two pence.
One who pretends to cure; a quacksalver.
One who salves or saves goods, etc. from destruction or loss.
A tray used to display or serve food or other items (such as a visiting card).
e: From Middle English salver (attested only in the sense of "ointment box"), from Old English *sealfere (“salver, one who anoints”), equivalent to salve + -er. Cognate with Dutch zalver (“salver”), German Salber (“salver”).

Thumb From Middle English salver (“serving platter”), from Spanish salva (“a testing of food or drink to test for poison”), from salvar (“to save, taste food for one's master”), from Latin salvō (“save”). More at save.

s: Not gentlemanly; not adhering to the high moral standards expected of a gentleman; impolite, unchivalrous, or indecent.
In a manner not befitting a gentleman.
The outermost liturgical vestment worn by clergy for celebrating Eucharist or Mass, equivalent to the phelonion of the Eastern tradition.
e: From Middle English chesible, from Old French chesible, from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).

s: A stand with three short legs, especially for cooking over a fire.
A stand, sometimes with short, stumpy feet, or a mat used to support hot dishes and protect a table; a coaster.
A weaver's knife used to cut out the wire that was used to form a pile.
e: From Middle English trevet, from Old English trefet, borrowed from Latin tripēs, tripedis (“tripod”).

s: Impossible to achieve or overcome or be negotiated.
An act of insolent and shameless audacity.
e: From late 17th century French effronterie, from effronté (“shameless, insolent”), from Old French esfronté, from Vulgar Latin *exfrontātus. Compare Latin effrōns (“barefaced”), from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”) (English: front)..

s: In Africa, a teacher of the Qur'an.
The quality of being trivial or unimportant.
Something which is trivial or unimportant.
Incapable of being altered, or of changing.
of an ideal <math>i</math> in a noetherian ring <math>r</math>
Such that its height is equal to the height of every associated prime of the quotient R/I as a module over R.
In a cheerful manner; with a cheery demeanour.
In an ostentatious manner; extravagantly or flamboyantly.
A hole through which a button is pushed to secure a garment or some part of one.
A flower worn in a buttonhole for decoration.
So shaped that it can be worn on a buttonhole or it is similar to a buttonhole.
A small slotlike cut or incision, made for example by an accident with the scalpel.
The mouth, nose or eyes of a tiny appearance.
To detain (a person) in conversation against their will.
To cut one or more buttonholes (in).
To make a small slot-like incision in (intentionally or unintentionally).
To apply a flowery formation in.
To attain buttonhole-like formations on cutting.
e: Originally buttonhold (“a loop of string to hold a button down”), but changed by folk etymology by influence of hole. button + hole.

s: One who has a negative view of the entire human race.
Someone who distrusts or avoids other people.
e: From Ancient Greek from μισέω (“I hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (“man; human”); compare miser.

s: Having a lot of space inside; roomy.
e: From capāx (“wide, spacious, large; capable”) + -ious. Displaced native Old English numol.

s: Unconsciousness or incapacity resulting from a cerebral hemorrhage or stroke.
Gross hemorrhage into a cavity or into the substance of an organ.
A state of intense anger; uncontrollable fury so intense as to have effects like a stroke.
e: Late Middle English from Old French apoplexie, from Late Latin apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (“madness; apoplexy, paralysis”), from ἀποπλήσσω (“to cripple by a stroke”) + -ία. See plague.

s: In a disrespectful manner; with a lack of respect.
Causing ecstasy or rapture; enrapturing; charming.
The process by which somebody is entranced.

e: From Middle English ripenesse, rypenesse, rijpnesse, from Old English rīpness, equivalent to ripe + -ness.

s: Contrary to religious beliefs and practices.
In a manner that involves luxury; in an expensive or indulgent manner.
That cannot be currently found, put in an obscure place, lost - often temporarily.
Not giving the truth; providing untrue facts; lying.
Showing scorn or disrespect; contemptuous; scathing; withering.
e: Inherited from Middle English scornful; equivalent to scorn + -ful.

s: A willingness to believe in someone or something in the absence of reasonable proof; credulousness.
Faith, credence; acceptance or maintenance of a belief.
e: Inherited from Middle English credulite (“faith, belief”), borrowed from Middle French credulité (French crédulité), from Latin crēdulitās. Corresponding to credulous + -ity (compare credulosity).

s: Inclined to waste resources or behave extravagantly.
An abandoned person; one openly and shamelessly vicious; a dissolute person.
An overly wasteful or extravagant individual.
Alt of profligated: profligated: routed, overcome, driven away.
e: The adjective is first attested in 1535, the verb in 1542; Borrowed from Latin prōflīgātus, perfect passive participle of prōflīgō (“to strike down, cast down”) (see -ate and pro-), from prō- (“forward”) + flīgō (“to strike, dash”) + -ō. Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s: The state of being calm, stable and composed, especially under stress.
e: From French équanimité, from Latin aequanimitās (“calmness, equanimity”), from aequus (“even; calm; fair”) + animus (“mind, soul”) + -itās. en + equ + animus + ity.

s: Of or pertaining to a lack of attention; not paying attention; careless.
To utter suddenly and unadvisedly; to speak quickly or without thought; to divulge inconsiderately.
e: Possibly Onomatopoeic, or possibly an alteration of Middle English blurden (“to wail, cry out, threaten”), or possibly from Middle English *blerten, *blarten, *blorten, from Old English *blǣrettan, a frequentative or emphatic form of *blǣran (“to blear, bellow, roar”). If so, equivalent to blear + -t.

s: A rigid bracelet or anklet, especially one with no clasp.
To beat about or beat down, as corn by the wind.
To waste away little by little; squander carelessly; fritter (away).
To beat about in the air; flutter: said of a hawk which does not rise steadily and then swoop down upon its prey.
To flap or hang down loosely, as a hat brim or an animal's ear.
The cut branch of a tree; a large, rough stick; the largest piece of wood in a bundle of twigs.
e: Apparently from bang + -le, perhaps ultimately connected with Proto-Germanic *bangilaz. Compare Dutch bengel, German Bengel.

s: Feeling desire; eagerly wishing; eager to obtain.
e: From Middle English, from Old French desirrous, from desirrer + -ous.

s: Through evil fate or chance; wretchedly.
e: From Middle English onhappily, unhappili, unhappily, unhappyly; equivalent to un- + happily or unhappy + -ly.

s: An individual or a corporation who has the right of use of something of value, gained through a lease agreement with the real owner of the property.
The entity to whom a lease is given, or who takes an estate by lease.
Someone who is allowed to use a house, building, land etc. for a period of time in return for payment to the owner.
e: From Anglo-Norman lessié, past participle of lessier (“to permit, to let”).

s: A rule or principle, especially one governing personal conduct.
A written command, especially a demand for payment.
An order issued by one local authority to another specifying the rate of tax to be charged on its behalf.
A tax rate set by such an order; the tax thus collected.
To act as a preceptor; to teach a physician-in-training by supervising their clinical practice.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin praeceptum, form of praecipiō (“to teach”), from Latin prae (“pre-”) + capiō (“take”).

s: Such as to be greater than usual; particularly; exceptionally.
To greater degree than is usual.
In a manner that is greater than usual.
Such as to be strange or odd.
In a strange or perverse manner; strangely.
Such as to be strange or odd.
Acting in strange or perverse way.
Strongly associated with; in a manner that is peculiar or restricted to some person or place.
A contorted facial expression, often expressing contempt or pain.
To make grimaces; to distort one's face; to make faces.
e: From French grimace, from Middle French grimace, from Old French grimace, grimuche, from grime (“mask”) (with the pejorative suffix -ace, from Latin -āceus), from Frankish *grīma, *grīmō (“mask”), from Proto-Germanic *grīmô (“mask, helmet”). Cognate with Old English grīma (“mask, visor, helmet, spectre, apparition”). More at grime.

s: An act of being disloyal; a betrayal, faithbreach.
Not written clearly enough to be deciphered.
Making an unpleasant reading experience, e.g. because it is dull or upsetting.
Not able to be accessed or played by some technical device.
That serves to demonstrate, show or prove.
Given to open displays of emotion.
That specifies the thing or person referred to.
e: From Middle English demonstratif, from Middle French démonstratif, from Latin dēmōnstrātīvus. Equivalent to demonstrate + -ive.

s: Someone who habitually expects the worst outcome; one who looks on the dark side of things.
To refer to something indirectly or by suggestion; to invoke it by implication rather than mention.
e: From Middle French alluder, from Latin alludere (“to play with or allude”), from ad + ludere (“to play”). See also al-#Etymology_2.

s: Dictating, the process of speaking for someone else to write down the words.
An activity in school where the teacher reads a passage aloud and the students write it down.
The act of ordering or commanding.
Orders given in an overbearing manner.
e: From Late Latin dictātiō, noun of action from dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō. dictate + -ion.

s: Of a boy or man, exhibiting behavior or mannerisms considered typical of a woman or unmasculine.
e: From Middle English effeminat, effemynat, from Latin effēminātus, past participle of effēminō, from fēmina (“woman”).

s: To shout, or to call with a loud voice.
e: From Middle English halou, halow, halloo, representing Old English hēlā, ǣlā, ēalā (“O!, alas!, oh!, lo!”), equivalent to hey + lo.

s: The act of burying a dead body; burial.
e: From Middle English enterement, interment, from Old French enterrement. inter + -ment.

s: A pain or ache in a tooth.
e: From Middle English toth-ake, from Old English tōþeċe (“toothache”). tooth + ache.

s: The act of guarding, protecting or guiding.
The state of being under a guardian or a tutor; the care or protection enjoyed; being a ward or a tutee.
Instruction; teaching; guidance; being a tutor.
e: From la:tūtēla (“a watching, guardianship, protection”) + -age, from tuērī (“to watch, guard”). See tuition.

s: Unable to be retracted or reversed; final.
e: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.

s: An expression of comfort, support, or sympathy offered to the family and friends of somebody who has died.
e: From condole + -ence, or from Middle French condoléance, or formed from the root of Latin condoleō (“to sympathize”), from con- (“together, with”) and doleō (“to hurt, suffer, have pain”).

s: The quality which the sense of taste detects; also, a specific flavour or taste, especially one different from the predominant one.
An appealing or appetizing flavour, especially one which is savoury or strong.
A distinctive sensation like a flavour or taste, or an aroma or smell.
A particular quality, especially a small amount of it; a hint or trace of something.
A quality which is appealing or enjoyable; merit, value.
Enjoyment or taste for something; appreciation; pleasure; relish; an instance of this.
To detect (a flavour or taste, or food or drink); to taste; specifically, to enjoy or linger on (a flavour or taste, or food and drink); to relish.
To give (food or drink) flavour; to flavour, to season.
To detect (an aroma or smell, especially an appealing one); to smell.
Of a thing: to give off a (specified) aroma or smell.
Of food or drink: to have a specified (especially appealing) flavour or taste.
e: From Middle English savour, from Anglo-Norman saveur, savor, savour, and Old French saveur, savor, savour (modern French saveur), from Latin sapor, from sapiō (“to taste of (something); to have a flavour”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁p-, *sep- (“to taste; to try out”)) + -or. Doublet of sapor.

From Middle English savouren, savour, from Anglo-Norman savorer, savourer, Middle French savorer, savourer, and Old French savorer, savourer (modern French savourer), from Late Latin sapōrāre, the present active infinitive of sapōrō (“to give flavour, make tasty; to give pleasure”), from Latin sapor (see etymology 1) + -ō.

s: A piece of furniture for the storage and display of books.
Food miraculously produced for the Israelites in the desert in the book of Exodus.
Any boon which comes into one's hands by good luck.
The sugary sap of the manna gum tree which oozes out from holes drilled by insects and falls to the ground around the tree.
e: From Middle English, from Old English, from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα, from Hebrew מן (“'manna”).

s: An act or state of being sentimental.
e: From sentimental + -ity The music sense is a calque of German Empfindsamkeit.

s: A person, thing or name typifying a certain quality or idea; an embodiment or exemplification.
An artistic representation of an abstract quality as a human.
The process of creating such a representation: a literary device or other artistic method in which an inanimate object or an idea is given human qualities.
A condition of heartburn, nausea, or other stomach-related pain, sometimes caused by eating too quickly.
e: From Middle English indigestioun, from Old French indigestion, from Late Latin indigestio, in- + digestion.

s: Of or pertaining to heresy or heretics.
Contrary to mainstream or accepted opinion.
e: From Middle English, Borrowed from Middle French eretical and from Medieval Latin haereticālis, from haereticus, equivalent to heretic + -al. See heretic.

s: To make depressed, sad or bored.
To cause a depression or a decrease in parts of the economy.
To bring down or humble; to abase (pride, etc.).
To reduce (an equation) in a lower degree.
e: From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) + premō (“to press”).

s: The feeling or experience of being astonished; great surprise.
Loss of physical sensation; inability to move a part of the body.
Loss of mental faculties, inability to think or use one's senses.
Loss of composure or presence of mind.
A woman paid to educate children in their own home.
To work as governess; to educate children in their own home.
e: From Middle English governesse, a contracted form of governeresse, from Old French governeresse (“female ruler or administrator”). In later senses, equivalent to governor + -ess.

s: Having an excessively favourable opinion of one's abilities, appearance, etc.; egotistical and vain.
Having an ingenious expression or metaphorical idea, especially in extended form or used as a literary or rhetorical device.
A sharp or witty reply, or one which turns an argument against its originator; a comeback.
To say something sharp or witty in answer to a remark or accusation.
To make a remark which reverses an argument upon its originator; to return, as an argument, accusation, censure, or incivility.
To throw back; to reverberate; to reflect.
A flask with a rounded base and a long neck that is bent down and tapered, used to heat a liquid for distillation.
An airtight vessel in which material is subjected to high temperatures in the chemical industry or as part of an industrial manufacturing process, especially during the smelting and forging of metal.
e: From Middle English retorte, from Latin retortus, from retorquēre (“to be forced to twist back”).

s: In a way worthy of admiration.
In a fluent manner, as expressing oneself easily, especially in a foreign language.
In a fluent manner, as having graceful movements.
In a fluent manner, as literally flowing.
Marriage; the state of being married.
A particular solitaire card game using two decks of cards.
e: From Old French matremoine, from Latin mātrimōnium (“marriage, wedlock”), from mātri(s) (“mother”) + -mōnium (“obligation”). en + matri + mony. Compare patrimony.

s: A striking and vivid representation or scene; a picture.
A vivid graphic scene of a group of people or objects arranged as in a painting or bas relief sculpture.
An arrangement of actors in static positions on stage, having the effect of pointing up a particular moment in the drama, conventionally revealed by opening tableau curtains (known as "tabs").
A two-dimensional array or table of data, usually numbers, of various specific kinds.
A table that shows constraint violations of a list of candidates given an input and a constraint ranking.
Mostly in solitaire card games, but also in other card and board games, the main area, where random cards can be arranged.
A unit of a play, an opera or a ballet with change of stage setting.
e: French tableau, from Old French tablel (“a surface which is used primarily for painting”).

s: Not inhabited, especially by a tenant
Not being used; vacant or free
Not employed on a task; idle
Not occupied by foreign troops etc
The process of refreshing; a means of restoring strength, energy or vigour.
That which refreshes, such as a light snack or drink.
e: Recorded since 1665; either directly or via Middle English refreschement, from Old French refrescher (12th century; modern French rafraîchir), itself from re- (“again”) + fresche (“fresh”) (modern French frais; from a Germanic source, cognate with Old High German frisc, modern German frisch, Dutch fris, etc.)

s: An indirect reference; a hint; a reference to something supposed to be known, but not explicitly mentioned.
e: From Latin allūsiōnem, accusative singular of allūsiō (“the act of playing with”), from allūdō (“play with; allude”), from al-, combining form of ad (“to”), + lūdō (“play”): compare French allusion.

s: A mild rebuke, or an implied criticism.
To disgrace, or bring shame upon.
e: From Middle English reprochen, from Old French reprochier (Modern French reprocher).

s: The quality of being unhealthful or diseased, sometimes including the cause.
The quality of being morbid; an attitude or state of mind marked by gloom.
The incidence of a disease, as a rate of a population which is affected.
An occurrence of illness or disease, or a single symptom of that illness.
Adverse effects caused by a medical treatment such as surgery.
The sickness rate of a population.
e: Recorded since 1721; from morbid + -ity, from Latin morbidus (“diseased”), from morbus (“disease”), from the root of morī (“to die”) or from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to rub, pound, wear away”).

s: In a metaphorical manner; not literally; by means of metaphor.
Used to draw attention that what follows is a metaphor, not to be taken literally
The action of the verb to sprinkle.
A small thinly distributed amount, e.g. of some liquid, powder or other fine substance that is sprinkled on to something.
Not pleased or happy with something.
The act of one who ventures.

e: Late 14th century, from Old French inquisitif, from Late Latin inquisitivus, from Latin inquisitus, past participle of inquirere. See also inquire.

s: So much better than another as to be beyond comparison.
Something beyond compare; a thing with which there is no comparison.
e: From Middle English incomparable, from Middle French incomparable, from Old French, from Latin incomparābilis. en + in + comparable.

s: The condition of being amazed; a state of overwhelming wonder, as from surprise or sudden fear, horror, or admiration; a feeling of intense astonishment or awe, as from witnessing something incredible and impressive.
A particular feeling of wonder, surprise, fear, or horror.
The quality or condition of being too numerous.
A person employed to litigate, a lawyer skilled in arguing in court.
A telephone with a microphone and loudspeaker separate from those in the handset.
A loudspeaker on a telephone that broadcasts the sound, in order to use it hands-free.
A feature on a phone that reroutes audio through its external speaker, rather than the earpiece.
An audio feature in a car that connects a communication device to the car so as the sound projects from the car's speaker systems.
A mason’s tool, used in spreading and dressing mortar, and breaking bricks to shape them.
A gardener’s tool, shaped like a scoop, used in taking up plants, stirring soil etc.
A tool used for smoothing a mold.
To apply (a substance) with a trowel.
To pass over with a trowel.
To apply something heavily or unsubtly.
e: From Middle English trowell, trouel, truel, from Middle French truelle, from Late Latin truella, from Classical Latin trulla, the diminutive of trua (“ladle”). Doublet of trullo.

s: Knocked out; temporarily confused or unconscious due to a blow to the head.
A very intelligent and usually studious, erudite person.
e: brain + maniac, with influence from ENIAC, the name of an early computer. The term was coined as the name of the fictional supervillain Brainiac in the Superman series and first appeared in Action Comics comic book #242 in July, 1958. brainy + -ac.

s: Characterized by a lack of care; not caring.
The herb absinthium Artemisia absinthium (grande wormwood); essence of wormwood.
A distilled, highly alcoholic, anise-flavored liquor originally made from grande wormwood, anise, and other herbs.
e: Both from Middle French absinthe, from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (“wormwood”). Doublet of absinthium.

s: At or nearest the top of something.
A plant of the species Eutrema japonicum, cultivated for its edible root.
A pungent green Japanese condiment made from the plant Eutrema japonicum (syn. Wasabia japonica).
An imitation of this condiment made from horseradish with green dye.
Obligated to provide, display, or do something for another; indebted, obliged for a bounden duty.
e: From Middle English biholden (“beholden, obligated”), past participle of biholden (“to behold, look at”), though that verb does not mean "to bind, obligate".

s: Quickness of perception or discernment; penetration of mind; the faculty of nice discrimination; acuity of mind.
A sharp, tapering point extending from a plant.
A bony, often sharp, protuberance, especially that of the ischium.
Pertaining to or resembling a frog or toad.
e: From New Latin Batrachia, former name of the zoological order Anura, from Ancient Greek βατράχεια, neuter plural of adjective from βάτραχος (“frog”).

s: One who wanders aimlessly, who roams, who travels at a lounging pace. One who walks to observe and enjoy rather than to get somewhere.
To wander aimlessly or at a lounging pace. To walk to observe and enjoy rather than to get somewhere.
Of, being, pertaining to, or resembling a sheep; also, of an animal: from the genus Ovis.
Resembling a sheep in character; acquiescent, easily influenced, passive, or willing to follow a leader blindly.
An animal from the genus Ovis; a sheep.
A person regarded as resembling a sheep in character; one who is acquiescent, easily influenced, passive, or willing to follow a leader blindly; a sheep.
e: Thumb|An ovine (Ovis aries, noun sense 1), in this case a Welsh Mountain sheep.

s: Any artiodactyl ungulate mammal which chews cud in the suborder Ruminantia, such as cattle or deer.
e: From Latin rūmināns, rūminantem, present participle of rūminārī (“to chew the cud, ruminate”), from rūmen (“throat, gullet, rumen (first stomach of a ruminant)”).

s: Of, pertaining to, or being a pig.
Overweight to the extent of resembling a pig; severely obese.
A porcine animal: a pig, hog, boar, or related wild animal.
e: From Middle English porcine, partly from Middle French porcin (from Old French) and partly from its etymon, Latin porcīnus, from porcus (“pig”).

s: Of or pertaining to apes and monkeys.
Bearing resemblance to an ape or monkey; apelike or monkeylike.
An ape or monkey, especially an anthropoid (infraorder Simiiformes).
e: From Latin sīmia (“ape, monkey”), from Ancient Greek σιμός (“snub-nosed”).

s: An auditory tone of low pitch or volume.
An implicit message perceived subtly alongside, but not detracting noticeably from, the explicit message conveyed in or by a book, film, speech or similar (contrast with overtone); an undercurrent.
A pale colour, or one seen underneath another colour.
A low state of the physical faculties.
To say or speak in an undertone.
To present as less important, noticeable or prominent.
The act of exasperating or the state of being exasperated; irritation; keen or bitter anger.
Increase of violence or malignity; aggravation; exacerbation.
Of or relating to the class Amphibia.
Capable of operating on both land and water; amphibious.
An animal of the Amphibia; any vertebrate that does not have amniotic eggs, typically living both on land and in water.
A vehicle which can operate on both land and water.
A person with two distinct characters, qualities or identities.
e: Latin amphibius [from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος, from ἀμφίς (“of both kinds”) + βίος (“life”)] an.

s: To live, last or remain longer than.
General inflammation of the elbow or knee.
Any of various small finches in the genus Serinus, with largely yellow plumage.
A piece of verse with a simple, songlike rhythm.
An informal gathering at which songs are sung; a singing session.
A drawling or monotonous tone, as of a poorly executed song.
Of or relating to a piece of singsong; simple and melodic, varying in pitch.
To utter in a singsong voice.
Literal interpretation or understanding; adherence to the exact letter or precise significance, as in interpreting or translating.
The style of art portraying a subject as literally and accurately as possible.
The person who writes a libretto.
Presented without a source or reference.
Indulging in or characterised by sensual pleasures to a degree perceived to be morally harmful; corrupted; immoral; self-indulgent.
A crisp, smooth woven fabric made from silk or synthetic fibers.
e: From Late Middle English, from Old French taffetas, from Medieval Latin taffata, from تافته, from تافتن.

s: To interpret, view, or portray something in a romantic (unrealistic, idealized) manner.
To think or act in a romantic manner.
Indiscreet; not using clear and sound judgment.
Mindless, lacking conscious thought or the capacity for it.
e: From Middle English witles, from Old English witlēas (“senseless; witless”), from Proto-Germanic *witjalausaz (“witless”), equivalent to wit + -less. Cognate with Swedish vettlös (“senseless; witless; wild”), Icelandic vitlaus (“senseless; witless; foolish; mad”).

s: A person who is not suited to employment.
Based on deference; based on the doctrine, ideology, or wishes of others rather than one's own conclusions.
Of or relating to the vas deferens.
e: From deference (or its Latin type *dēferentia) al; compare essence, essential; prudence, prudential, etc. Coined by Q79025.

s: A male reporter; a male person in the profession of providing news.
A small refrigerator in a hotel room, containing drinks and snacks that the guest may choose to purchase during their stay.
The derivation of sexual satisfaction by watching unsuspecting people secretly, especially when those being watched are undressed or undressing, toileting, or engaging in sexual activity.
The derivation of satisfaction by obsessively watching or following sensational or sordid subjects.
To make furious or mad with anger; to fill with fury.
Filled with, characterized by or expressing fury.
e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin infuriātus (“enraged”), perfect passive participle of infuriō (“to enrage”) (see -ate), from Latin furia (“rage, fury, frenzy”); perhaps via Italian infuriato.

s: By reflex, automatically, without conscious thought.
Of fluid motion, smooth and regular, flowing as though in different layers.
In, or consisting of, thin plates or layers.
In the form of thin flat electronic circuits, usually flexible
Describing the layer of capillaries in the choroid of the eye
Of or pertaining to atmospheric pressure.
Made or done with a barometer.
To crouch or cringe, or to avoid or shy away from something, in fear.
To cause to cower; to frighten into submission.
To be a coward; to hide away or refuse to face opposition due to fear.
e: From Middle English couren, cowre, from Middle Low German kûren (“to lie in wait; linger”) or from (Icelandic kúra (“to doze”)); according to Pokorny, all are ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, bend”), see also Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“shell, pod”).

s: Not deterred or put off; undiscouraged.
Cast out; rejected or excluded from a group.
An outcast; someone cast out of a group or society.
The act by which something (a computer, a TV series, etc.) is rebooted.
A broadcast of the news; a news report that is transmitted over the air for television, radio, etc.
In a manner that is not measurable, in a way that cannot be measured.
To feel with or use the hands; to handle.

To search or attempt to find something in the dark, or, as a blind person, by feeling; to move about hesitatingly, as in darkness or obscurity; to feel one's way, as with the hands, when one can not see.
To touch (another person) closely and (especially) sexually.
To intentionally and inappropriately touch or rub against another person, in such a manner as to make the contact appear accidental, for the purpose of one's sexual gratification.
To examine; to test; to sound.
An act of groping, especially sexually.
An iron fitting of a medieval cart wheel.
e: From Middle English gropien, from Old English grāpian, related to grīpan (whence English gripe); compare also grip.

s: That has been cleared from a sin or an offence.
In a manner that is not ambiguous; leaving no doubt; clearly.
Marked by courage, determination or boldness in the face of difficulties or danger; having guts.
From the gut; deep and often coarse.
The nerve gas O-isopropyl methylphosphonofluoridate, used as a chemical weapon.
e: Named after the initials of its creators, Gerhard Schrader (1903–1990), Ambros, Rüdiger and Van der Linde.

s: Characterized by or resembling stealth or secrecy.
The act of marking off a boundary or setting a limit, notably by belligerents signing a treaty or ceasefire.
A limit thus fixed, in full demarcation line.
e: First recorded c.1752, from Spanish línea de demarcación and/or Portuguese linha de demarcação, the demarcation line laid down by the Pope on May 4, 1493, dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal on a line 100 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.

s: The formal charging of a defendant with an offense; in many jurisdictions it includes their response in the form of a plea, typically as guilty, not guilty, or no contest.
The act of disowning or disinheriting a child.
The act of abdicating; the renunciation of a high office, dignity, or trust, by its holder.
The voluntary renunciation of sovereign power.
The renunciation of interest in a property or a legal claim; abandonment.
The action of being deposed from the seat of power.
e: First attested in 1552. From Latin abdicātiō (“renunciation”), from abdicō. abdicate + -ion.

s: A market activity in which a security, commodity, currency or other tradable item is bought in one market and sold simultaneously in another, in order to profit from price differences between the markets.
To engage in arbitrage in, between, or among
A mound, pile, or stack of stored hay.
A standing wave in a rapid.
The text string within which another string is searched for. (see: needle in a haystack)
Any place or collection of items through which one searches for something that is rare and hard to find.
A dish composed of a starchy food (rice, tortillas, crackers, etc.) topped by a protein (beans, cheese, meat, etc.) in combination with fresh vegetables, assembled on the plate by the diner.
e: From Middle English haystak, haystake, hey stak, equivalent to hay + stack.

s: A person with a scarred face.
Of, relating to, or in accordance with scripture.
A person who writes the lyrics of a song.
To disparage, depreciate, or minimize the importance, value, merit, or significance of someone or something.
complimentary; in the nature of a compliment.
An act or instance of retracting.
A statement printed or broadcast in a public forum which effects the withdrawal of an earlier assertion, and which concedes that the earlier assertion was in error.
A continuous function from a topological space onto a subspace which is the identity on that subspace.
Of a person: lacking reverence for God; of an action: not in accordance with God's will or religious teachings.
In an impious, irreverent, or ungodly manner; ungodlily.
e: From Middle English ungodli, from un-, + godli (“belonging to God; resembling God, godlike”). Godli is derived from Old English godlīċ (“divine, godlike; godly”), from god (“god”) + -līċ (“suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘characteristic of, pertaining to’”).

From Middle English ungodli (“cruelly, maliciously, wickedly; unfairly, unlawfully, wrongly; discourteously, rudely”), from un-, + godli (“excellently; pleasingly, splendidly; courteously, graciously; gladly, willingly; righteously; properly, rightly; at all, possibly; much”).

s: adorned with starshaped emblems, especially as spangles woven into fabric or other material; identifying the United States flag or another star-based design that resembles the United States flag.
quintessentially American; displaying feelings of patriotic pride in American identity.
representing, upholding, or believing in traditional American values and the moral purpose of American society and culture.
e: Best-known from Francis Scott Key's 1814 poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry": "O! say does that star-spangled Banner yet wave, / O'er the Land of the free, and the home of the brave?" "Defence of Fort M'Henry" was set to music with the title "The Star-Spangled Banner" and was officially designated as the national anthem of the United States in 1931.

s: A female member of the House of Representatives.
The tendency to reduce a religion to its most fundamental tenets, based on strict interpretation of core texts.
A rigid conformity to any set of basic tenets.
The belief that fundamental financial quantities are the best predictor of the price of a financial instrument.

A Christian movement that started in the late 19th and early 20th centuries among British and American Protestants, which emphasizes literal interpretation of the Bible, and came up as a reaction to liberal theology and cultural modernism
e: From fundamental + -ism. First used in the 1910s by American Christians.

s: Excessive arrogance or pride, or presumption; originally toward the gods; a feeling of overwhelming and all-encompassing pride.
The duration during which a radio or television program (or part of one) is transmitted.
The duration spent talking during a conversation.
The chargeable use of a mobile phone, either in minutes or in units dependent on the use or traffic.
The period of freefall after jumping.
The period during which a person riding a rollercoaster or similar ride experiences a feeling of weightlessness.

e: Borrowed from French inexpérience, from Late Latin inexperientia.

s: Radio-frequency electromagnetic waves, usually used in the context of wireless communication; radio waves.
The act of transmitting and/or receiving sexually suggestive text messages and/or photographs between cell phones equipped with text messaging.
The practice of forming blisters on the skin, to promote blood flow and aid healing.
The act of cutting or tearing into shreds.
That which is cut or torn off; a piece.
A style of very fast and very complex guitar playing.
The state, quality, or condition of being self-centered; concern only for oneself.
A device which binds together sheets of paper by driving a thin metal staple through the sheets and simultaneously folding over the ends of the staple against the back surface of the paper.
Any device for stapling with (small or large) staples, including any office stapler, staple gun, or hammer tacker.
One employed to sort wool according to its staple.
The remains after gutting a fish.
The act by which somebody is gutted.
Thriving, prosperous, successful; growing rapidly or vigorously.
Capable of being searched, especially something that has an automated search function included.
Something that can be searched, or searched for.
To knowingly and willfully make a false statement of witness while in court.
To cause to violate an oath or a vow; to cause to make oath knowingly to what is untrue; to make guilty of perjury; to forswear; to corrupt.
To make a false oath to; to deceive by oaths and protestations.
The list of a newspaper's or another periodical's main staff, contributing writers, publisher, circulation, advertising rates etc.
The title (normally in a large and distinctive font, and at the top of the front page) of a newspaper or another periodical.
The publication itself, or the rights to publish it.
The logo of a broadcaster used in an ident.
To send to the masthead as a punishment.
To furnish (a newspaper) with a masthead.
To say or write something with different wording.
Any of several games played by arranging domino tiles on a flat surface.
A sterile container for holding fluid used in a vaginal douche.
A jerk or asshole; a mean or rude person; someone seen as being arrogant, snobby or obnoxious.
Any social misfit: a doofus, dork, nerd or loser.
Gaudy, superficial; offering attraction without depth.
Characteristic of an insider; especially, reflecting an insider perspective.
Having the characteristics of a pig.
The sound of a small object falling into liquid.
Searching for, and digging up truffles.
The act or result of egesting
e: From Old French egestion, from Latin ēgestiōnem, accusative of ēgestiō (“emptying, voiding”), action noun from the perfect passive participle of ēgerō (“to carry out”), from ex- + gerō.

s: Not having been arrested (taken in by police etc.).
To hug and snuggle simultaneously: gesture of tender non-sexual affection.
A hug while snuggling: gesture of tender non-sexual affection.
e: Frequentative of hug: hug + -le. Perhaps also influenced by snuggle.

s: Gerund of rejig: an act of rearranging or tweaking.
Like poo; crappy, of low quality.
A situation that is bad or mismanaged in every way.
e: From omni- + shambles. Introduced by the television show The Thick of It in 2009.

s: Easily flicked; thus, light and fast.
Resembling or characteristic of a flick.
A gelatinous mass of frogs' eggs, laid in ponds and ditches.
A motorized platform installed in a stairway, which traverses the stairs when activated and can be ridden by those for whom the stairs are a barrier.
action of the verb to backslap
a vertical post from which a gate is hung/attached.

e: From Middle English ikil, ykle, from Old English *ġicol, ġiċel (“icicle, ice”), from Proto-West Germanic *jekul, *jikil, from Proto-Germanic *jekulaz (“piece of ice”), diminutive of *jekô (“lump of ice”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁yeg-.
Alteration of Spanish vamos (“we go”) or vámonos (“let's go”). Doublet of namous.

s: A pal, buddy, mate, friend; often used in direct address by one male to another.
A sweet consisting of a small block of hard caramel covered in chocolate.
e: Uncertain. Perhaps from Yiddish חבֿר (“friend, comrade”), from Hebrew חבר (“friend”), possibly via Dutch gabber; alternately, perhaps from the British dialectal term cob (“take a liking to”), or a conflation of both.

s: The act of a man inserting his scrotum in another person's mouth, in a similar motion as when a tea bag is juiced into a mug.
The act of simulating the above sex act in a video game (usually by crouching).
Sexual activity in a public lavatory, especially homosexual activity between men.
A seasonal activity involving a prolonged stay at one or more cottages; similar to visiting, but typically for a longer duration and at a seasonal home that one owns or rents.
The hole at the bottom of a bath, sink or tub, which can be blocked using a plug; a drain (US)
Any of various diving ducks of the subfamily Aythyinae (genera Aythya and Netta), especially the common pochard, Aythya ferina.
e: Apparently originally from poach (“to poke”) + -ard. Compare poker.

s: Having a weak or indecisive character; ineffectual or dim-witted.
The act by which something is quaffed; a drinking.
That echoes; having an echoing quality.
A nonce word in Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky
A strip of paper coated with a sticky, often poisonous, substance that catches and kills flies that land on it.
To cause something to become stuck with, or as if with, flypaper.
A person who or a device which calls, summons loudly, or hails.
Of a plant or part of a plant: pale and weak because of sunlight deprivation or excessive exposure to sunlight.
Of a plant: intentionally grown in the dark.
Of an animal or person: having an ashen or pale appearance; also, haggard or thin; physically weak.
The surface of coal exposed by mining, or a part of a coal seam that is currently being mined.
The end of a drift, entry, or room in a coal mine.
A place where difficult or strenuous work is done.
A place where more tangible, practical, or direct work of an activity is done, as opposed to theoretical or managerial work.
A soft Italian sourdough brioche from Milan, with candied fruit, usually prepared for Christmas as a dessert.
e: Borrowed from Italian panettone, from panaton, an augmentative of pan (“bread”).

s: An odd, eccentric or insane person.
A bag filled with nuts, especially one that is hung outdoors to act as a bird feeder.
A frumpy person, somebody who is unattractive, drab or dowdy.
To insult; to flout; to mock; to snub.
To assume a countenance or demeanor indicating irritation, ill-humor, or disapproval.
e: Probably a contraction of late Middle English frumpylle (“wrinkle”), from Middle Dutch verrompelen, originally equivalent to for- + rump + -le.

s: Inclined to swear; characterised by bad language.
The young of various species of fish, especially herrings, sprats or smelts
Food prepared from such fish, often deep fried and served as a starter or snack.
Able to be thought or imagined; conceivable.
Something that can be thought about.
A flexible pipe for carrying water or other liquids.
To film with erratic panning movements of the camera.
A kind of marble used in games, originally made of clay, baked hard and oiled.
A piss: an act of urination.
(Often followed by about or around): to act or work ineffectually and wastefully.
Syn of peck: to attack or eat with a beak.
Syn of nibble: to pick at or toy with one's food, to eat slowly or insubstantially.
e: Unknown. Compare regional German piddlen, pitteln, pütteln, pühteln (“to pick at something, pick at one's food”), dialectal German Pitzel (“small effort, small task”). Alternatively, perhaps originally from paw or put + -le. The noun derives from the verb.

s: The act by which something is sluiced; a copious wetting; a drenching.
A kind of ellipsis, introduced by an interrogative, where (usually) everything except the interrogative is elided from the clause.
The action of the verb moo; a mooing sound.
Synonym of answering machine, especially one built into a telephone.
A dogmatic decree or command, especially issued by one who rules without popular consent.
A harsh penalty or settlement imposed upon a defeated party by the victor.
e: Borrowed from German Diktat, from Latin dictātum (“that which has been dictated”), from the perfect passive participle of dictō (“dictate”). Doublet of dictate#Noun, ditty. Originally used with reference to Germany's penalties as dictated by the Treaty of Versailles.

s: A restaurant specializing in roast meat, particularly roast beef and Sunday roasts.
The station within a buffet where such food is served.
A meal consisting of such food.
To walk unsteadily, as a small child does.
To walk or travel in a carefree manner.
A carefree or aimless gait; a stroll.
e: Of Unknown origin. Possibly a byform of totter.

s: An isolated or secluded place; a hideaway or hideout.
Spin applied to a ball in order to slow it, change its flight, or stop it when it lands.
To spin (a ball) with this motion.
To play a section of a record in reverse, as a disc jockey; to apply spinback.
A long, thick log held upright at one end and tossed in the Highland games.
Gerund of curry: the technique of converting a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument; an instance of using this technique.
e: . Curry is Named after Haskell Curry (1900–1982) who further developed the technique based on earlier work by the German logician and mathematician Gottlob Frege (1848–1925) and the Germany-based Russian logician and mathematician Moses Schönfinkel (1888–1942). It is not known who coined the term.

s: The state or quality of being interconnected

e: Unknown; the synonym ninnyhammer appears around the same time. Possibly related to innocent or Italian ninno (“small child”).

s: or difficult to pronounce or articulate.
Something, especially an ingredient, that is difficult or impossible to pronounce.
In a limp manner, without support or resistance.
Whatever person or persons (as object of a verb or preposition): emphasised or elaborated form of whomever.
e: From Middle English whom so evere, whom soever, whom-so-ever, whom-so-evere, whomsoever, whom-so-evyr. whom + so + -ever.

s: one who comes to humbly ask or petition
A device attempting to authenticate itself to an 802.11 network.
e: From Latin supplicans (“supplicating, bowing down”), from supplicō, from sub- + plicō.

s: A board used as a target for throwing darts.
The focus of one's attraction or attention
e: First attested from 1515, from Middle English lode (“guide”) + stone. From use as a guide tool by mariners. See also: lodestar.
From problem + humorous -o suffix to imitate Spanish, the intended word being problema (still masculine, as it is derived from Greek).

s: In flowering plants, a male reproductive structure in a flower that produces pollen, typically consisting of an anther and a filament.
e: From New Latin stāmen, from Ancient Greek στη̃μα. [https://www.etymonline.com/word/stamen].

s: A device placed in arid regions to catch water for wildlife to drink from.
In a cheeky or impudent manner.
Of the shape of a cube.
A person skilled at locating the causes of problems and rectifying them.
A software program or routine that attempts to diagnose a problem with the system.
e: From trouble + shooter, circa 1905. Whence troubleshoot, shoot trouble and troubleshooting as back-formations.

s: The practice of making very small loans, especially to poor people to promote self-employment; microlending.
To censor, to black out or remove parts of a document while leaving the remainder.
To black out legally protected sections of text in a document provided to opposing counsel, typically as part of the discovery process.
To reduce to form, as literary matter; to digest and put in shape (matter for publication); to edit.
To draw up or frame a decree, statement, etc.
To bring together in one unit; to combine or bring together into one.
To gather or organize works or ideas into a unified whole; to collect, order, or write in a written document or to put into a particular written form.
To insert or assimilate into a written system or scheme.
To bring an area of study within the comprehension capacity of a person.
To reduce to a particular condition or state, especially one that is undesirable.
To reduce something physical to a certain form, especially by destruction.
e: From Old French redacter, from Latin redactus, perfect passive participle of redigō (“drive, lead, collect, reduce”), from re- (“back”) + agō (“put in motion, drive”)..

s: Something used for taking hold or holding; a catch, loop, button.
The action of the verb to butter
The application of butter to something.
The action of a rider having to butter in an acrobatic maneuver.
Any garment worn underneath others, especially one worn next to the skin; an item of underwear.
Temple garments worn by the followers of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
Something that is reiterated or restated.
The form that backs or perfects paper already printed on one side.
A clause using existential "there" with a verb other than a form of "be", as in "There followed a brief silence".
A satellite navigation system; the navigation that is done via the use of such a system.
e: . Such formation from initial syllables is also alternatively classified as clipping of the compound type (producing a clipped compound), and it is sometimes categorized as blending (but blending stricto sensu involves initial and terminal parts of words that may be delimited by reanalysis).

s: Restricted to one's home, as by physical infirmity.
A benign tumour of the uterus that is composed of either fibrous connective tissue or muscle.
A period of associating with people or engaging in activities with a status below one's own.
A fibrous material used for tying plants, originating from the leaves of raffia palm trees (genus Raphia).
In the fourth place; fourth in a row.
A sheet, a piece of cloth cut and finished as bedlinen.
e: From Middle English bedeschette, bedshete, bed shete, equivalent to bed + sheet.

s: A point-counting card game for two players, with variants for three or four players; the cribbage board used for scoring to 61 or 121 points in numerous small increments is characteristic.

A variety of pocket billiards that, like the card game, awards points for pairs that total 15. A player who pockets a ball of a particular number must then immediately pocket the companion ball that brings the number to 15.
A point scored in this variety of pocket billiards.
e: From crib + -age. Named from the "crib" consisting of certain cards laid aside by each player.

s: A short staff, a club; a cudgel.
A baton, or military staff of command, now especially the stick carried by a police officer.
A fragment or piece broken off from something, especially a broken-off piece of a spear or lance.
A stout stem, as of a tree, with the branches lopped off, to produce rapid growth.
e: From Middle English tronchoun, from Old French tronchon (“thick stick”), from Late Latin *troncionem, from Latin truncus.

s: To replace the traction-providing surface of a vehicle that employs tires, tracks or treads.
To renew the tread of a tyre, providing a cheaper alternative to buying a new tyre, but potentially introducing a risk of premature failure if performed improperly.
A used tire whose surface, the tread, has been replaced to extend its life and use.
A person who re-entered military service in World War II after serving in World War I.
To tread again, to walk along again, to follow a path again.
A return over ground previously covered; a retraversal or repetition.
e: From re- + tread (“grooves carved into the face of a tire”)

s: A South Asian snack consisting of a deep-fried triangular turnover filled with vegetables (especially potatoes) or meat.
e: Borrowed from سموسہ / समोसा, from سنبوسه, from Middle Persian *sambōsag. Doublet of sambusa, sambusak, sambuseh, sambuusa, samsa.

s: A machine which reproduces documents by photographing the original over a glass plate and printing duplicates.
A bird of the genus Coloeus, similar in appearance to crows and found within the same family; traditionally associated with church towers and ruins, where it frequently likes to nest.
e: Compound of jack + daw. The first element, also present in Low German (North Saxon) Jöker (“jackdaw”), may refer either to its characteristic call, often represented as tchak-tchak, maybe influenced by association with the name Jack. The second element means “jackdaw” in itself, from Old English *dāwe, from Proto-West Germanic *dāhwā.

s: Incapable or unlikely of being elected to political office, especially due to a lack of suitable qualities or policies.
A person who is unable, unlikely, or unfit to be elected to office.
To relax; to be laid back.
e: chill out + relax. First use appears c. 1994. See cite below.

s: A high-ranking nobleman in Spain or Portugal.
e: Borrowed from Spanish grande, from Latin grandis (“large, great”). Doublet of grand, grande.

s: Tending to avoid commitment; lacking certainty or decisiveness; reluctant to give out information or show one's feelings or opinion.
Failure to commit to a decision or course of action.
A voter etc. who has not yet committed to a decision.
To disembowel; to remove the viscera.
To destroy or make ineffectual or meaningless.
To remove a bodily organ or its contents.
To protrude through a surgical incision.
e: From Latin ēviscerātus, past participle of ēviscerāre (“to disembowel”), from e- (“out”) + viscera (“bowels”), equivalent to e- (“out”) + viscera + -ate.

s: The act of one who grovels.
A large and deep armchair with a cushion.
A variety of long-grain rice, notable for its fragrance.
The area immediately around a grave.
A person obsessed with their own (supposed) importance.

e: Borrowed from French svelte, from Italian svelto (“stretched out”), past participle of svellere (“to pluck out, root out”), from Vulgar Latin *exvellere, from ex + vellere (“to pluck, stretch”).

s: A strong vertical post of timber or iron, fixed to a wharf, dock or the deck of a ship, to which the ship's mooring lines or towlines are secured.
A similar post preventing vehicle access to a pedestrian area, to delineate traffic lanes, or used for security purposes.
e: From Middle English bollard, probably from Middle English bole (“tree trunk”), from Old Norse bolr (“stump, trunk”), equivalent to bole + -ard.

s: To spend too much money; especially, to spend more than one earns.
The amount by which someone or something is overspent.
Inanely stupid; vacantly silly; content in one's foolishness.
A wasting of time in idleness or trifles.
A sexual relationship, not serious but often illicit.
e: From Middle English daliaunce et al., from dalien (“to exchange pleasantries, to chat; to flirt”), from Old French dalier, dailer. dally + -ance.

s: The cutting made by the hewer at the side of the face.
Lit by a candle or candles.
Marked by extreme anger or fury.
e: From French apoplectique, from Late Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός, from ἀπόπληκτος, from ἀποπλήσσω, from ἀπό (“of, from”) + πλήσσω (“I strike”).

s: A traitor; one who turns against a previous affiliation or allegiance.
To act as a turncoat; to betray
e: A turn + coat, reportedly derived from the sometime military practice of wearing uniform coats that were lined in material of a contrasting color, and which could be worn inside out to present a different appearance.

s: A mixture of fruit, spices and suet used as a filling for mince pies.
A badly cut-up body or parts of a body.
e: An alteration of earlier minced meat; equivalent to mince + meat.

s: Plural of mouth-breather; Alternative spelling of mouth breather.
The amount that a room can hold, especially the number of people that can fit into a room.
The people in a room, considered as a group.
Abounding with room or rooms; roomy.
Not able to be impeached or reproached.

e: Possibly from shambles + -o- + -ic, in which the interconsonantal -o- avoids the /mbl/ consonant cluster. Possibly influenced by symbolic. Alternatively, possibly a shambles + symbolic.
Either from frump or from Middle English frumple + -y.

s: To crumple and squeeze to make more compact.
To contract the muscles of one's face so as to draw their facial features together, out of pain, discomfort, uncertainty, etc.
e: Attested since about 1800. Probably an intensive form of crunch; ultimately derived from the onomatopoeia of a crumpling sound; or perhaps a squeeze + crunch.

s: To remove water from; to dry up.
To lose water from one's body; to become dehydrated.
Existing or happening outside the frame of the cinema or television screen.
Outside the frame of the cinema or television screen.
One who, or that which, nips.
Any of various devices (as pincers) for nipping.
A child aged from 5 to 13 in the Australian surf life-saving clubs.
A boy working as a navvies' assistant.
One of four foreteeth in a horse.
A pickpocket; a young or petty thief.
The claws of a crab or lobster.
A machine used by a ticket inspector to stamp passengers' tickets.
One of a pair of automatically locking handcuffs.
One of the gloves or mittens worn by fishermen to protect their hands from cold and abrasion.
Any agent used to make dough rise or to have a similar effect on baked goods.
Anything that induces change, especially a corrupting or vitiating change.
To cause to rise by fermentation.
To temper an action, decision, attitude, characteristic, etc.
To imbue; to infect; to vitiate.
To rise or become larger; to prove.
e: From Middle English levayn, borrowed from Old French levain, from Vulgar Latin *levāmen, a noun based on Latin levō (“raise”).

s: Related to a topic of discussion or consideration.
Any organic derivative of this compound.
e: A variant form of german (“having the same parents; related”), adapted in this sense in allusions to its use in Shakespeare's Hamlet (see quotations at germaine).

s: The pole that holds up a light so it can illuminate a wide area, such as holds up a streetlight.
In a weary manner; feeling weary.
In a weary manner; causing weariness.
A group of children who meet together for supervised play.
A group of gamers who meet together, especially for role-playing games.
An informal organised group providing care and activities for preschool children.
One who advocates a certain course of action, often of political or social concern, and often with the naive conviction of their own moral superiority.

e: From thus + -ly, dating from the 19th century, seemingly coined by educated writers to make fun of uneducated persons trying to sound genteel, with a false inference that thus is not an adverb.

s: The index finger: the first finger next to the thumb.
e: Mid-15th century, from Middle English forefynger; equivalent to fore- + finger.

s: Of or pertaining to or resembling tin.
Pertaining to the thinness and cheapness of tin or similar-looking metals, in contrast to a heavier, more valuable metal.
Pertaining to a thin, unpleasant sound recalling that of tin being rapped.
(of changes within physical environments) Abruptly, perilously, sharply, steeply, severely.
(of events in general) Abruptly; with no notice or ceremony: in a sudden or hasty manner, instantly, quickly.
(of actions involving intentionality) Done with a lack of proper decorum, or without adequate thought, care or concern for consequences.
Closely familiar; current; having frequent interaction.
Familiar or acquainted by use or study; well-informed; versed.
e: From Old French conversant, present participle of converser.

s: of a spear, axe, dagger, etc
Having a shaft (or handle) of a specified tincture, typically different from the head.
Not specially prepared or designated for skiing, hence viewed as more exciting but also more dangerous.
Deviating from what is seen as correct, usual or conventional.
Placed in a bin (of various kinds).
An incision into the colon to allow for drainage.
The opening produced in such incision.
A tool which projects a controlled stream of a highly flammable gas over a spark in order to produce a controlled flame.
A very rapidly moving object, especially one that is thrown.
A surprising or unusually pointed, humorous and impressive insult or insulting quip.
An event that when experienced leaves the witness dazed, either physically or metaphorically.
An outstanding, energetic and surprising thing or person.
A piece of food or drink that is tart and stimulating.
A thatched frame covering blocks or tiles of dried china clay, to protect them from the rain while permitting free ventilation.
An Asian plant, Solanum melongena, cultivated for its edible purple, green, or white ovoid fruit; eggplant.
The fruit of this plant, eaten as a vegetable.
e: French aubergine, from Catalan albergínia, from Arabic اَلْبَاذِنْجَان (“the aubergine”), from بَادِنْجَان, from بَاتِنْگَان, from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (“the plant that cures the wind”), from, ultimately from Proto-Dravidian *waẓVtV. Cognate with Malayalam വഴുതനങ്ങ, Hindi बैंगन. Doublet of brinjal, malidzano, melongene.

s: The act of one who stammers.
Having the characteristics of a sheep, as meekness, shyness, or docility.
The act by which something is overheard.
The act of one who scoffs; derision; mockery.
To destroy (older) data by recording new data over it.
To cover in writing; to write over the top of.
To write in an unnecessarily complicated or florid way; to produce purple prose.
The operation of destroying older data by recording new data over it.
The act of one who pities.
A confection made from a paste of almonds, sugar and egg white as a binder.
A similar confection made using another nut, such as peanut or hazelnut.
A piece of such a confection.
e: Borrowed from German Marzipan, from Italian marzapane, Venetian marzapane. Believed to be, with influence from pane (“bread”), derived from Arabic مَرْطَبَان (“spice box”) which comes from the name of a Burmese port known for its spice exports, Martaban, now called in Burmese မုတ္ထမ.

s: That returns rapidly to its original form (as a spring does) after being bent, compressed, stretched, etc.
Of land, having many springs (of water).
Pornography that does not contain depictions of explicit sexual penetration.
Less intense, committed or aggressive than hardcore.
A very direct or quick path or trip.
A dynamite fuse made with a small quantity of dynamite powder along its length, so that the spark travels quickly and at a specific known rate.
To travel in a straight line, ignoring established paths of travel.
e: From bee + line, due to the belief that a bee returns to its hive in a straight course, originally an Americanism.

s: suicide by disembowelment, as by slicing open the abdomen with a dagger or knife: formerly practised in Japan by the samurai when disgraced or sentenced to death.
An act against one's own interests.
e: Borrowed from Japanese 腹切り, ultimately from 腹 (“belly”) + 切る (“to cut”).

s: full of energy or strength; refreshed and revitalized
Not frightened or hesitant; undaunted; not put off; unimpressed.
The ordinal form of the number thirty.
The person or thing in the thirtieth position.
One of thirty equal parts of a whole.
e: From earlier thirteth, from Middle English thrittithe, threttiþe, thrittyde, from Old English þrītigoþa; equivalent to thirty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.

s: A food item prepared very sweet, frequently decorated in fine detail, and often preserved with sugar, such as a candy, sweetmeat, fruit preserve, pastry, or cake.
The act or process of confecting; the process of making, compounding, or preparing something.
The result of such a process; something made up or confected; a concoction.
An artistic, musical, or literary work taken as frivolous, amusing, or contrived; a composition of a light nature.
Something, such as a garment or a decoration, that is very elaborate, delicate, or luxurious, usually also impractical or non-utilitarian.
A preparation of medicine sweetened with sugar, honey, syrup, or the like; an electuary.
A medicinal preparation of any kind, a compound of drugs.
To make into a confection, prepare as a confection.
e: From Middle English confescioun, borrowed from Old French confeccion (French confection), borrowed from Latin cōnfectiōnem, from cōnfectus, past participle of cōnficiō (“prepare”), from con- (“with”) + faciō (“to make, do”). confect + -ion. Originally "the making by means of ingredients"; sense of "candy or light pastry" predominant since 1500s.

s: The act of something that froths.
A plant of various species, chiefly cruciferous. The leaves have a moderately pungent taste, and are used as a salad and antiscorbutic.
e: From Middle English cresse, crasse, from Old English cressa, cærse (“cress”), from Proto-West Germanic *krassjō, from Proto-Germanic *krasjô (“cress”). Cognate with West Frisian kers (“cress”), Dutch kers (“cress”), German Kresse (“cress”), Danish karse (“cress”), Swedish krasse (“cress”), Icelandic krassi (“cress”).
