From Ancient Greek κλέπτω (“I steal”) (from Proto-Hellenic *klépťō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *klep-) maniac.
From the pronunciation of "taser": the 's' is pronounced as a 'z'.

e: Unknown. s: Any of many elongated arthropods, of the class Diplopoda, with cylindrical bodies that have two pairs of legs for each one of their 20 to 100 or more body segments.

In a manner that is radiant; glowingly.
A wuss; a person who refuses to perform a particular task due to an unreasonable fear.
e: 1960s: probably an alteration of pussy, perhaps a wimp + pussy, or short for pussy-wussy (reduplication of pussy). Compare later wuss.

s: A small, hat-shaped explosive device, used to breach a door or wall.
Anything potentially explosive, in a non-literal sense.
To attack or blow a hole in (something) with a petard.
e: From Middle French petard; see Modern French pétard (“firecracker”).

s: The state of being dissident; dissent

A prehistoric enclosure in the form of a circle or circular arc defined by a raised circular bank and a circular ditch usually running inside the bank, with one or more entrances leading into the enclosed open space.
e: Back-formation from Stonehenge, although it is not strictly a ME henge.

s: Indicative of or afflicted with gangrene.
Gloomy, mournful or dismal, especially to an exaggerated degree.
e: Borrowed from Latin lūgubris (“mournful; gloomy”), with the suffix -ious.

s: One who eats food very quickly, without decorum.
A loud electric alarm or horn, especially as used in automobiles in the early 20th century.
To produce a loud, siren-like wail.
e: {| class="floatright" style="width: 20%" |- | [[File:Sign on rural road in United States (1920).jpg|thumb|A warning sign on a rural road in the United States advising drivers to “sound klaxon”]] |- | |} From the trademark Klaxon, based on Ancient Greek κλάζω (“make a sharp sound; scream”).

s: Of or pertaining to growth that is likely to develop into cancer.
To make (more) fit for domestic life.
To adapt to live with humans.
To adapt to live with humans.
To make a legal instrument recognized and enforceable in a jurisdiction foreign to the one in which the instrument was originally issued or created.
To amend the elements of a text to fit local culture.
An animal or plant that has been domesticated.
e: Either Borrowed from Middle French domestiquer (Modern French domestiquer) or directly from Medieval Latin domesticātus, perfect passive participle of domesticō (“to domesticate”), see -ate. domestic + -ate.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin domesticātus (“domesticated”), see Etymology 1 and -ate.

s: Lacking strength or vitality; feeble, powerless, impotent.
Hanging from, or as if from, a support.
Having branches etc. that bend downwards; drooping or weeping
Goner; someone who is done for.
A small annual plant in the family Asteraceae, Centaurea cyanus, usually with bushy blue flowers which grows natively in European cornfields (i.e. wheatfields).
A plant of the species Cichorium intybus.
Synonym of cornflower blue, a shade of blue similar to that of the usual cornflower.
Offensive to good taste, tactless, overzealous, excessive.
Characterised or marked by fullness; abundant, copious.
e: From Middle English fulsom, equivalent to full + -some. The meaning has evolved from an original positive connotation "abundant" to a neutral "plump" to a negative "overfed". In modern usage, it can take on any of these inflections. See usage note.

s: The military punishment of placing somebody on the back of another person, or on a wooden horse, etc., to be flogged.
A waxy substance secreted by the ear.
e: From Middle English erewax, from ere + wax. Equivalent to ear + wax.

s: In an epic manner; in the style of an epic.
To pour off (a liquid) gently, so as not to disturb the sediment.
To pour from its original vessel into one intended for a different use or appearance.
To remove (a clone or other artificially-gestated baby) from its chamber, vat, or artificial womb.
To rehouse people while their buildings are being refurbished or rebuilt.
A portion of perfume unofficially sold in a smaller bottle.
e: From French décanter, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from dē- + canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).

s: The action of the verb ruffle
Fire that spreads quickly through dry vegetation.
A piece of timber or steel laid horizontally, or nearly so, to which the planks of the floor, or the laths or furring strips of a ceiling, are nailed.
To fit or furnish with joists.
e: From Old French giste, feminine of gist, the past participle of gesir (“to lie down”).

s: The sound made by something that jingles.
An old parlour game in which blindfolded players within a ring attempted to catch another player to whom a bell was tied.
Someone who stingily avoids spending money.
Someone who does not give freely.
Any of the suborder Vermilingua of New World mammals with long, narrow snouts, notable for feeding on ants and termites using their long tongues.
Any of various other not closely related mammals that feed on ants, including pangolin (scaly anteater), echidna (spiny anteater), aardvark (African anteater) and numbat (banded anteater).
A gardener; a person interested in or practicing horticulture.
Of, or relating to art of topiaries.
Of a tree or shrub, trimmed in artistic shape.
Art or practice of trimming shrubs or trees in artistic or ornamental shapes, e.g. of animals.
A garden decorated with such art.
e: From Latin topiarius (“of or relating to ornamental gardening; an ornamental garden, an ornamental gardener”), from Latin topia (“ornamental gardening, landscape painting”), from Ancient Greek τόπια (“artistic representation in which natural or artificial features of a place are used as the medium”), plural of Ancient Greek τόπιον (“field, landscape”), from τόπος (“place”).

s: The act or process of desensitizing, of reducing or eliminating sensitivity.
An invertebrate animal of the phylum Arthropoda, characterized by a chitinous exoskeleton and multiple jointed appendages.
e: From New Latin Arthropoda, from Ancient Greek ἄρθρον (“joint”) + πούς (“foot”), equivalent to arthro- + -pod.

s: A marking made by a postal service on a delivery, usually indicating the place where and the date and time when the item was received or processed for the first time, mostly serving to cancel a postage stamp.
Part of the seat of a chair that is designed to support the arm.
Any of many kinds of birds of the family Muscicapidae, of Africa, Europe, and Asia, that catch insects in flight; an Old World flycatcher.
Any of many kinds of similar birds of various families, such as Tyrannidae (the New World flycatchers of the Americas), Tityridae, Stenostiridae, Monarchidae, Petroicidae, etc.
The act by which somebody is quizzed, or teased; banter, raillery.
An organism that feeds chiefly on plants; an animal that feeds on herbage or vegetation as the main part of its diet.
An act of giving (sometimes sexual) pleasure.
Boldness of enterprise; aggressiveness or initiative.
Energy of body and mind, enthusiasm.
e: Borrowed from Scots gumption (“common sense, shrewdness; drive, initiative”); further etymology unknown, possibly connected with Middle English gome (“attention, heed”), from Old Norse gaumr (“attention, heed”), from Proto-Germanic *gaumō. English cognates include gaum (“to comprehend, understand”) and goam (“to recognize, see”).

s: A prank in which a person's underpants are pulled up sharply from behind in order to wedge the clothing uncomfortably between the person's buttocks.
A situation where a person's underpants are stuck uncomfortably between their buttocks.
A basketball stuck between the rim and the backboard following a field goal, free throw, rebound, or block attempt.
To play the wedgie prank on.
To swing back and forth, especially if with a regular rhythm.
To vacillate between conflicting opinions, etc.
To vary above and below a mean value.
e: Borrowed from Latin ōscillātus, perfect passive participle of Latin ōscillō (“to swing”) (see -ate), from ōscillum (“a swing”), usually identified with ōscillum (“a little face or mask hung on a tree that sways with the wind”), diminutive of ōs (“mouth, face”). See also osculate.

s: A type of aromatic resin obtained from the trees of the genus Boswellia, family Burseraceae, used in incense and perfume.
homosexuality; the state of a woman being sexually attracted to other women.
Being the subject of cultural buzz.
Using a large number of buzzwords.
Of, or relating to the hypodermis, the layer beneath the dermis.
A hypodermic syringe, needle or injection.

A marine sport in which one stands on a floating board (typically 2 - 3 meters in length) to which a sail is attached. The board is steered by tilting the sail or banking the board. Some windsurfers use large waves to perform jumps and other stunts.
A proponent or supporter of creationism.
A type of warm headgear covering the neck, head, and often part of the face, with apertures left as necessary, often made out of wool.
A ski mask with holes for the eyes and, sometimes, the nose and mouth, which may be rolled up and worn like a toque or pulled over the face for greater protection.
e: From the city of Balaklava in Crimea, from Ottoman Turkish بالقلاوه (modern Turkish balıklava), alteration of بالقلاغه (“fishing ground”). During the Crimean War the British troops suffered from cold due to improper clothing.

s: To discharge through pores or incisions, as moisture or other liquid matter; to give out.
To flow out through the pores.
To give off or radiate a certain quality or emotion, often strongly.
e: Latin exudāre, exsudāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- (“out, out of”) + sudāre (“to sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

s: Any squid-like cephalopods (marine mollusks) of the order Sepiida that have eight arms, two retractable tentacles, and a calcareous internal shell, and can eject a dark ink when threatened.
In the sociology of Erving Goffman, an action or utterance that signals the meaning of interaction to participants.
The input of text or data by means of a keyboard.
A form of vandalism performed by scratching paint with a key
A rounded cooking pot of various designs, commonly pot-bellied, with or without tripod, handles, lid etc; originally earthenware but currently more commonly of cast iron or other metals.
A red-brown resinous material, the dried sap of a tree of the genus Commiphora, especially Commiphora myrrha, used as perfume, incense or medicine.
e: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα, from. Compare Arabic مُرّ (“myrrh”), Hebrew. Compare מרור: maror.

s: A heavy fabric, usually made of cotton, with vertical ribs.

A pattern on snow resulting from the use of a snow groomer to pack snow and improve skiing, snowboarding and snowmobile trail conditions. Corduroy is widely regarded as a good surface on which to ski or ride.
Of a road, path, etc., paved with split or round logs laid crosswise side by side.
To make (a road) by laying down split logs or tree-trunks over a marsh, swamp etc.
e: Origin Uncertain. Probably from cord + duroy (“a 17th century coarse fabric made in England”). Probably not from French *corde du roi (“cloth of the king”), which is unattested in French, where the term for the corduroy is velours côtelé.

s: In a useful manner; in a way that achieves something.
An instrument located within the dashboard of a vehicle that measures and indicates the current speed of the vehicle.
Such a device incorporating an odometer.
A tropical tree or shrub of the myrtle family, Psidium guajava.
Its yellowish tropical fruit, globular or pear-shaped with thin, yellow, green or brown skin, is often made into jams and jellies.
A medium reddish-pink color, like that of guava flesh (also called guava pink).
e: Recorded since 1555, from Spanish guayaba, from *wayaba. Doublet of guayaba, which is now rare or obsolete.

s: A displeasing sight; something prominently ugly or unsightly.
e: From Middle English eye sor, eie-sor, eyen soore, eæge-sare, equivalent to eye + sore.

s: One who suffers an inability or difficulty sleeping; a sufferer from insomnia.
Suffering from or pertaining to insomnia.
The act of recording an individual's fingerprints.
A test made to establish and confirm the properties of a material or components.
Death due to lack of oxygen.
An executioner responsible for hanging criminals.
Someone responsible for hanging pictures and other artworks in a gallery, museum etc.
A guessing game where one has to guess the word an opponent is thinking of by guessing one letter at a time, and involving the gradual drawing of a stick figure hanging from the gallows.
e: Inherited from Middle English hangman, hongman, hangeman, equivalent to hang + -man.

s: The act of one who dogs or harasses.
The practice of having sexual intercourse in public places, especially parks, deliberately taking the chance of being watched.
The job of killing wild dogs and dingos in a rural area.
The act of riding a bicycle.
Alternative form of of light bulb.
An uninvited third person joining a couple's date who prevents or hinders romantic interactions.
e: Calque of Cantonese, as though the third person is a light bulb in the background.

s: A soft, chewy candy made from boiled sugar, molasses, or corn syrup and butter.
e: Probably related to tafia (“a type of rum”).

s: An iron or steel bar, often with a flattened end which may also be hook-shaped, to be used as a lever to manually force things apart.
An electrical circuit that prevents an overvoltage from causing damage.
A type of cocktail made with only Crown Royal whiskey and lemon lime soda.
To force to move, usually with a crowbar; to prise.
e: From crow (“crow (bird)" also "metal lever, crowbar”) + bar, probably because the forked end looks like a crow's foot.

s: The nerve-dense, retractable fold of skin which covers and protects the glans of the penis in humans and some other mammals.
To sexually stimulate by manipulating the foreskin.
e: From fore- + skin, a loose Calque of Latin praepūtium. Compare German Vorhaut, etc...

s: In a funny or amusing manner.
In a strange or unexpected manner, especially of a coincidence.
The examination of the colon using a colonoscope.
Any tree of the genus Anacardium.
A tree, Anacardium occidentale, native to northeastern Brazil, now widely grown in tropical climates for its cashew nuts and cashew apples.
e: Reanalysis of French acajou as a + cajou, from Old Tupi akaîu. Doublet of acajou.

s: The act of aggravating, or making worse; used of evils, natural or moral; the act of increasing in severity or heinousness; something additional to a crime or wrong and enhancing its guilt or injurious consequences.
An extrinsic circumstance or accident which increases the guilt of a crime or the misery of a calamity.
A feeling of being provoked by irritation and annoyance; the feeling of being riled up or increasingly irritated.
A long, slender, chiefly terrestrial amphibian of the order Caudata, superficially resembling a lizard.
A creature much like a lizard that is resistant to and lives in fire (in which it is often depicted in heraldry), hence the elemental being of fire.
A metal utensil with a flat head which is heated and put over a dish to brown the top.
A small broiler (North America) or grill (Britain) that heats the food from above, used in professional cookery primarily for browning.
Solidified material in a furnace hearth.
A portable stove used to heat or dry buildings under construction.
A fire-eater (performer who pretends to swallow fire).
To use a salamander (cooking utensil) in a cooking process.
e: From Middle English salamandre, from Anglo-Norman salamandre, from Latin salamandra, from Ancient Greek σαλαμάνδρα, of uncertain origin (per Beekes, likely); possibly of origin, see Persian سمندر for more information.

s: A deciduous tree (Pistacia vera) grown in parts of Asia for its drupaceous fruit.
The nutlike fruit of this tree.
A pale green colour, like that of a pistachio seed.
e: From Italian pistacchio (1590s), from Latin pistācium (“pistachio”), from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον, from πιστάκη (“pistachio tree”), of origin.

s: An infant that is still being breastfed (being suckled) by its mother.
A young mammal not yet weaned and still being fed milk by its mother.
e: From Middle English sukling, sukeling, sokeling, equivalent to suck + -ling. Cognate with Middle Dutch sogelinc (“suckling”), Dutch zuigeling (“suckling”), German Säugling (“suckling”).

s: a herbaceous annual plant of species Montia fontana, in the family Montiaceae, formerly included in the purslane family (Portulacaceae).
Arousing or meriting strong dislike, aversion, or intense displeasure.
e: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).

s: To twist one's body with snakelike motions.
To twist in discomfort, especially from shame or embarrassment.
To evade a question, an interviewer etc.
A twisting, snakelike movement of the body.
e: First recorded 1690's, originally used of eels; cognate with Scots squimmer (“to wriggle, squirm”). Of Uncertain origin. Compare dialectal quirm, whirm (“to disappear quickly, vanish suddenly and mysteriously”), Norwegian kverva (“to turn around, take away, remove, shrink”), from Old Norse hverfa (“to turn, vanish”).

s: A halogenated hydrocarbon, trichloromethane, CHCl3; it is a volatile, sweet-smelling liquid, used extensively as a solvent and formerly as an anesthetic.
To treat, or to render unconscious, with chloroform.
e: Borrowed from French chloroforme, portmanteau of terchloride (tertiary chloride, trichloride) and formyle (CH, an obsolete radical of formic acid) by Jean-Baptiste Dumas, from 1834. chloro- + -form.

s: The branch of medicine that focuses on the design, manufacturing and installation of prostheses.
Unravelled; worn at the end or edge.
(figurative) Exhausted, strained, beleaguered, or suffering from stress.
e: From fray + -ed, from Old French froiier (“to rub against, scrape; thrust against”), from Latin fricare (“to rub, rub down”).

s: The ordinal form of the number one hundred.
The person or thing in the hundredth position.
One of a hundred equal parts of a whole.
e: From Middle English hundred (“hundredth”); equivalent to and remodelled after hundred + -th, displacing Old English hundtēontigoþa.

s: Occurring in the middle point of one's life, usually considered about 45.
The middle period of one's life.
Sequoiadendron giganteum, a coniferous evergreen tree formerly in the genus Sequoia, now placed in Sequoiadendron.
Sequoia sempervirens, a coniferous evergreen tree, the only living species of the genus Sequoia.

e: From Middle English overdon, from Old English oferdōn, equivalent to over- + done.

s: Any of several common, often asymptomatic, sexually transmitted diseases caused by the microorganism Chlamydia trachomatis.
Any of various coccoid microorganisms of the genus Chlamydia that are pathogenic to humans and other animals.
e: From New Latin chlamydia, from Ancient Greek χλαμύδιον (“small cloak”), from χλαμύς (“cloak”).

Borrowed from Welsh corgi, a compound of cor (“dwarf”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”)) + gi (the soft mutation of ci (“dog”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ (“dog”), perhaps from *peḱ- (“livestock; wealth”)). The rare plural form corgwn is borrowed from Welsh corgwn.

s: The buildings forming the border of such a courtyard.
A burrowing crab of the genus Gelasimus, of many species. The male has one claw very much enlarged, and often holds it in a position similar to that in which a musician holds a fiddle.
The common European sandpiper (Actitis hypoleucos); so called because it habitually wags its tail up and down resembling the back and forth movement of a fiddler.
A large species of cicada, Macrotristria angularis, of eastern Australia; cherry nose.
A coin of little value: a sixpence or a farthing.
e: From Middle English fithelere, from Old English fiþelere, from *fiþele. en + fiddle + er.

s: Any of several Old World birds of prey of the genus Buteo with broad wings and a broad tail.
Any scavenging bird, such as the American black vulture (Coragyps atratus) or the turkey vulture (Cathartes aura).
In North America, a curmudgeonly or cantankerous man; an old person; a mean, greedy person.
The insignia of a colonel, or a petty officer within the navy.
A military discharge (due to the military discharge certificate).
e: From Middle English bosart, from Anglo-Norman buisart, from Old French busart, busard, a derivative (-ard) of Old French buison, buson (French buse), possibly from Latin būteō (“hawk”).

s: An instrument consisting of a tube containing mirrors and loose, colourful beads or other objects; when the tube is looked into and rotated, a succession of symmetrical designs can be seen.
A constantly changing series of colours or other things.
To move in shifting (and often attractive or colourful) patterns.
e: The noun is derived from Ancient Greek καλός (“beautiful, lovely”) + εἶδος (“form, image, shape”) + English -scope, Coined by David Brewster (1781–1868) in his 1817 patent for the invention: see the quotation. The verb is derived from the noun.

s: Involving marriage to one person at a time.
Of a relationship, characterized by mutual sexual and romantic exclusivity.
Of a person, exclusively engaging in a mutually exclusive sexual or romantic partnership.
Having only one sexual partner at a time.
Monogamic; having a simple flower with united anthers.
A small fleet of warships (usually of the same class), or a fleet of small ships.
A small group of things or people
A spaceship made of one or more central mutually stabilizing overweight spaceships flanked by lightweight, middleweight, or heavyweight spaceships that prevent the formation of destructive eggs.
e: From Spanish flotilla, diminutive of flota (“fleet”), from French flotte.

s: The trefoil leaf of any small clover, especially Trifolium repens, or such a leaf from a clover-like plant, commonly used as a symbol of Ireland.
Any of several species of small clover-like plant species, with trefoil leaves, especially Trifolium repens.
e: From Irish seamróg, from Old Irish semróc, diminutive of semar, semair (“clover”), from Proto-Celtic *semarā, *semaris (compare uisumaris (“clover”)), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *semh₁r-, *smeh₁r-. Related to Old Norse smári (“clover”) and possibly Georgian სამყურა (“clover”).

s: A plant of the genus Allionia.

A kind of jam made with citrus fruit, distinguished by being made slightly bitter by the addition of the peel and by partial caramelisation during manufacture. Most commonly made with Seville oranges, and usually qualified by the name of the fruit when made with other types of fruit.
A cat having orange- or ginger-colored fur.
e: Borrowed from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (“quince jam”), from marmelo (“quince”), from Latin melimēlum (“sweet apple”), from Ancient Greek μελίμηλον. A false folk etymology claims that this comes from the French phrase “Marie est malade” (“Mary is ill”), referring to Mary, Queen of Scots, falling ill and being given marmalade to feel better.

s: An instance or period of roaming.
emission of ionizing radiation as a consequence of a nuclear reaction, or directly from the breakdown of an unstable nucleus.
The radiation so emitted; including gamma rays, alpha particles, neutrons, electrons, positrons, etc.
Plural of environ: the environment, the surroundings.
A nonmetallic chemical element (symbol Se) with an atomic number of 34, used mainly in glassmaking and pigments and as a semiconductor.
e: From French sélénium, the name coined by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1818 from Ancient Greek σελήνη (“moon”) in reference to original confusion with the similar element tellurium.

s: The act of ejecting or suddenly throwing fluid or some other substance from a duct or other body structure.
A reflex in human beings and other mammals in response to sexual stimulation involving the forcible ejection from the urethra of, in males, semen; and, in females, vaginal fluid.
The act of throwing or darting out with a sudden force and rapid flight.
The uttering of a short, sudden exclamation or prayer, or the exclamation or prayer uttered.
Any of various large, venomous rays, of the orders Rajiformes and Myliobatiformes, having a barbed, whiplike tail.
A device that simulates a cell tower, used to intercept cell phone communications.
Arranged or groomed with a comb.
Serving to caution or warn; admonitory
Tending to cause discomfort, uneasiness or alarm.
Of or concerning the devil: devilish, satanic.
Crazy, wild (sometimes especially due to being unexpected or surprising).
By means of symbols or a symbol.
Something which shoots off or separates from a main stem or branch of a plant.
Something which develops from something else.
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; effected by insects, birds, bats and the wind etc.
Requiring secret or mysterious knowledge to understand.
Extremely old (e.g. interpretation or knowledge), and possibly irrelevant.
e: Borrowed from Latin arcānus (“hidden, secret”), from arceō (“to shut up, enclose”); cognate with Latin arca (“a chest”).

s: Faded creases around the crotch of blue jeans. Can be added artificially or created by daily wear over the lifetime of a garment.
The sound made by a telephone when ringing.
A customizable tone used to indicate an incoming call on a telephone, especially a mobile phone.
Of a telephone: to play a ringtone.
Constructed from, or decorated with tiles.
Of a lodge, having been sealed against intrusions from unauthorized people.

The inner layer of a diaper or menstrual pad that directly touches the wearer's skin, concealing the ADL and absorbent layers below; usually made from hydrophobic material so that the liquid wicks through.
A bumper car in an amusement park.
A complication of chronic filariasis, in which nematode worms block the lymphatic vessels, usually in the legs or scrotum, causing extreme enlargement of the infected area.
e: From Latin elephantiasis or directly from Ancient Greek ἐλεφᾰντῐ́ᾱσῐς.

s: To impose again, a further time.
A soft membraneous spot on the head of a baby due to incomplete fusion of the cranial bones.
A structural component of some woodwind instruments, such as recorders and shawms, resembling a barrel with holes bored into it, designed to protect the keywork and to allow the sound to project.
e: Borrowed from French fontanelle, from Old French fontenelle, a diminutive of fontaine (“fountain, spring”) + -elle, from Late Latin fontāna, from Latin fontānus, from fōns + -ānus. font + -an + -elle.

s: A subgenre of reggae and dancehall influenced by hip hop and digital production techniques such as sampling.
e: Clipping of raggamuffin, variant of ragamuffin (“troublemaker”), influenced by reggae.

s: Demonstrating good sportsmanship, behaving in an honorable and appropriate manner.
in combination, preceded by a number
A member of a group that forms a specified percentage of a population.
e: From percent + -er or -er; the sense of "agent" relates to a percentage of profits being charged as a fee.

s: In a facetious or flippant manner; in a manner that treats serious issues with deliberately inappropriate humor.
In a pleasantly humorous or playful fashion.
A Norway lobster, a langoustine (Nephrops norvegicus).
The battered or breaded tails of this species, usually served with chips.
Any member of a similar species of genus Nephrops or similar prawns.
The act by which a baby, or a container of fermenting substance, is burped.
A procession of riders, vehicles, ships, etc.
A trail ride, usually more than one day long.
An often dramatic series or chain of events or things.
To move as part of a series or group, such as marchers in a parade or snow in an avalanche, especially in large numbers or in a chaotic or dangerous fashion
e: From French cavalcade, from Old French cavalcade, from cavalcata, from cavalcare (“to ride on horseback”), from Medieval Latin caballicō, from Vulgar Latin caballus (“horse”). Doublet of chevauchee.

s: An area where a fair (an event for public entertainment) or other public event is held; a showground.
A commercially-operated collection of rides, games and other entertainment attractions; an amusement park.
To ruin many or all things over a large area, such as most or all buildings of a city, or cities of a region, or trees of a forest.
To destroy a whole collection of related ideas, beliefs, and strongly held opinions.
To break beyond recovery or repair so that the only options are abandonment or the clearing away of useless remains (if any) and starting over.
To greatly demoralize, to cause to suffer intense grief or dismay
The waterfront of a seaside town.
A disease of sheep, with great heat and itchiness.
Of a long-barrelled firearm, having had the stock sawn off.
A speaker placed inside or held near to the ear.
A receiver of a telephone to hold near to one's ear.
The arm on a pair of glasses that hooks over the ear to hold them in place.
The floodgates of heaven, regarded as holding back the rain.
e: From Late Middle English cataractes, cataractis, cateractes, used to translate καταρράκται (“(probably) floodgates, sluices”) in the Septuagint and cataractae (“floodgates, sluices”) in the Vulgate versions of the Bible.

From Middle Low German paltrig (“ragged, rubbishy, worthless”), from palter, palte (“cloth, rag, shred”), from Old Saxon *paltro, *palto (“cloth, rag”), from Proto-Germanic *paltrô, *paltô (“scrap, rag, patch”). Of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *polto- (“cloth”), see also *poltьno (“linen”).

s: The chemical element (symbol Ar) with an atomic number of 18. The third most abundant gas in the Earth's atmosphere, it is a colourless, odourless, inert noble gas.
e: From Ancient Greek ἀργός (“idle, lazy”), because of its inertness, + -on, used for all noble gases.

s: Any of various types of footwear with thick soles, often used to elevate the foot, especially wooden clogs.
One of various wooden attachments used to lift a shoe above wet or muddy ground.
A circular wooden plank attached to a horse's foot to prevent it from sinking into a bog while plowing.
An iron hoop attached to a person's boot in cases of hip-joint disease.
e: From Middle English patyn, patin, pateyn, from Old French patin, from patte (“paw, hoof”), from Latin patta, of Onomatopoeic origin.

s: Empty of all the air or gas that was or could be inside.
Disappointed; depressed, especially after having been hopeful or in high spirits.
Adjusted downward to compensate for inflation.
Having been removed or cut off.
Made up of various disparate elements mixed together; of disorderly composition.
Having many sexual partners, especially if indiscriminate in choice of sexual partners.
The mode in which a network interface card gathers all network traffic instead of getting only the traffic intended for it.
A place where something is deposited, as for storage, safekeeping or preservation.
e: From Medieval Latin dēpositōrium, from Latin dēpositum, past participle of dēpōnō. deposit + -ory.

s: Short trousers for men, or more usually boys.
An article of clothing worn as underpants by women.
e: Recorded since 1845 in the plural, meaning “drawers for men”, a derogatory diminutive of pants (the shortening of pantaloons); meaning “underpants for women or children” first recorded 1908.

s: Not providing help or assistance; not helpful.
Characteristic of a plagiarist; of, relating to, or characterized by plagiarism.
The quality of being fractious; trouble-making; unruliness.
In a fragile way or manner.
The state or quality of being inconsequent.
Low, indistinct (of a sound); reminiscent of a murmur.
A square piece of cloth for washing the face and body.
As much as a pit will hold.
With the playful, innocent, eager-to-please or energetic qualities of a puppy.
In an abstracted manner; separately; in the abstract.
Relating to or carried out while sleepwalking.
The act of reasoning earnestly in order to dissuade or remonstrate.
e: From Latin expostulātiōnem, accusative singular of expostulātiō (“complaint, expostulation”), from expostulō (“demand, expostulate”), from ex (“out of, from”) + postulō (“demand or claim”). See expostulate.

s: Of, resembling, characteristic of, or pertaining to ants; formic.
A lampoon, originally as published in public; a satire or libel on someone.
To satirize (someone) by using a pasquinade.

s: At or along a shore or coast.
At or along a shore or coast.
Inconsiderate of the feelings of others.
In a lingering manner, persistently, tending to remain.
In a way or to an extent that challenges.

e: From Late Middle English fruiterē̆r (“fruit grower; fruit dealer”), from fruitē̆r (“fruit dealer; household official having charge of fruit”) + -er (it is unclear why the second suffix was added).

s: Without paint: unpainted (of an object), not involving paint (of a finishing process), or whose paint has worn off (of an object).
The front part of a shirt.

A pitch that is easy to bat on.
A head-on charge aimed at bumping an opponent to the ground.
An attractive facade applied only to the front of a house.
To confront in a threatening manner.
The characteristic or quality of being gruff

e: From prodigal + -ity, from Old French prodigalite, from Late Latin prodigalitas.

s: A small antelope native to eastern and southern Africa having a dense, brown, speckled coat (Oreotragus oreotragus).

s: Pretension in appearance; looking overly and distastefully adorned.
In an understanding manner; with empathy.
In a way that can be understood; intelligibly.

e: Anglicization of caravanserai, influenced by -ary, -ery, as if meaning “place of caravans” by reanalysis as caravan + -s- + -ary, -ery.

s: In an indistinguishable manner; so that separate components or differences cannot be discerned.
In a tactless manner; in a manner intentionally inconsiderate of another's feelings.
A room with pool tables where pool can be played, usually for a fee.
A room in a house or other domestic dwelling set up with a pool or snooker table.
The involuntary repetitive echoing of words or phrases spoken by another person; either immediate or delayed.
An infant's repetitive imitation of vocal sounds spoken by another person, occurring naturally during childhood development.
Any apparently meaningless, repetitious noises, especially voices.
e: From echo- + -lalia; echo- ultimately from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (“reflected sound, echo”), -lalia from λαλιά (“talk, chat”).

s: In a wan or pale manner.
Lacking energy, drive, motivation or emotion. Enervated.
To stay beyond or longer than.
The state of being substantial; substantialness.
The extent to which something is substantial.
A table containing a basin and a pitcher of water for washing.
In a stable or garage, a place in the floor prepared so that carriages or automobiles may be washed there and the water run off.
Void of essence, or real being.
In an unutterable manner; inexpressibly; so bad or otherwise extreme that one cannot talk about it.
In an alert manner; with alertness.
A table designed for work of a specific type.
A small table used by ladies for doing needlework.
The characteristic of being bulky, or of having bulk.
A printing process by which the paper is rolled through intaglio cylinders.
A print made by such a method.
e: From German Rotogravur, derived from the Berlin printing firm Rotogravur Deutsche Tiefdruck Gesellschaft, the name of which is conjectured to be a portmanteau of Rotophot and Deutsche Photogravur.

s: An eye doctor: either an ophthalmologist or an optometrist.
The state or quality of being suggestive.
The result or product of being suggestive.
Possessed or controlled by a demon.
Of or pertaining to demons; demonic.
Someone who is possessed by a demon.
e: From Middle English demoniak et al., from Old French demoniaque, from Late Latin daemoniacus.

s: In a genial manner; gaily; cheerfully.
In an airy, showy, or affected manner.
In a dapper or stylish manner.
In a peremptory manner; in a commanding tone, brooking no delay.
Suspended from above or from the top.
A woman's tailored blouse, buttoned down the front.
Not recoverable; incapable of being recovered
That cannot be recovered from or made good; irremediable.
e: From Middle English irrecoverable, from Middle French irrecovrable. Attested earlier than recoverable. en + ir + recoverable.

s: In an inept or incompetent manner.
Strictly attentive to detail; meticulous or fastidious, particularly to codes or conventions.
Precise or scrupulous; finicky or nitpicky.
e: From punctilio (“fine point in exactness of conduct”) + -ous.

s: The state of being senseless; unsense.
Pertaining to or having the characteristics of wine.
Having the colour of red wine.
Affected by the drinking of wine.
e: From Late Middle English vinous, vinose (“consisting of, containing, or made of wine”), from Latin vīnōsus (“fond of wine; wine-flavoured”), from vīnum (“wine”) + -ōsus.

s: Men's or boys' baggy knee breeches, of a type particularly popular in the early 20th century.
e: From Knickerbocker + -s, after the short breeches worn by Diedrich Knickerbocker in George Cruikshank's illustrations of Washington Irving's 1809 A History of New York.

s: In a haughty manner; with excessive or unwarranted pride.
A back door or gate, side entrance, or other entrance distinct from the main one, especially one that is private or not obvious.
A hidden or secret exit or tunnel of a fortification such as a castle, city wall, or fort.

The back or rear part of a thing.

The state or characteristic of being wistful.
Designed and equipped for use on ocean voyages.
A blanket used as a bed covering, usually quilted.
e: From Middle English coverlite, from Anglo-Norman cuver-lit, formed on cuvrir (“to cover”) + lit (“bed”). Cognate with Catalan cobrellit.

s: Intentionally delaying (someone or something), intended to cause delay, gain time, or adjourn decision.
e: From Middle English dilatorie, from Old French dilatoire, from Latin dīlātōrius (“extending or putting off (time)”), from dīlātor, from differō. Not etymologically related to delay.

s: A labourer on an oil rig or in the oilpatch, either skilled or semiskilled.
A dirty or low-paid worker, a labourer; an ironworker in an ironworks or a steelworker in a steelworks.
Someone with rough manners; a rowdy or uncouth person.
To work as a laborer on an oil rig.
e: From rough + neck, originally "someone who works a manual labour job".

s: Relating to an orgy; uncontrolled, wild.
e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀργιαστικός (“exciting”), from ὀργιαστής (“orgy celebrator”), from ὀργιάζειν (“to celebrate orgies”), from ὄργια.

s: Trembling, or prone to trembling and shaking.
The act of something that quavers.
Certainly; without the possibility of argument or debate.
In a guilty manner; as if guilty.
A room before, or forming an entrance to, another; a waiting room.
e: From ante- + room, as a Calque of French antichambre or its model Calque of Italian anticamera.

s: An enclosure where pigs are kept, either a building or part of one.
A dirty or very untidy place.
A lack of similarity or a lack of likeness in appearance to something else.
Not violated; free from violation or hurt of any kind; secure against violation or impairment.
A blank leaf at the front or back of a book.
Especially, the free portion of an endpaper.
To skim the surface of a body of water while moving at high speed.

For a car or similar vehicle to slide along the road on a thin film of water between the road and the tyres. A specific type of motorboat used exclusively for racing.

The wing of a submarine, used to help control depth
Untrustworthy as a result of being incompetent at the job.
Destitute of shifts or expedients; lacking proper means.
Not capable of being discerned or perceived.
Not capable of being distinguished from something else.
Something which is incapable of being discerned.
In the manner of a sage, with wisdom, wisely; sagacious.
Resembling or characteristic of a sage.
From an external source; not innate or inherent, foreign.
Developing in an unusual place or from an unusual source.
e: From Medieval Latin adventītius (“coming from abroad, extraneous”), a corruption of Latin adventīcius (“foreign, strange, accidental”), from adventus (“arrival, coming, approach, advent”) + -īcius, from adveniō (“to arrive”) + -tus.

s: An animal, especially a calf, born prematurely or abortively.
A slough, a low, wet, miry place. (Compare slank.)
e: From an allusive sense of slink (“to bring forth young prematurely”).
Compare slank (“low place, especially one which fills with water”), dialectal slonk (“depression, hollow, slough”).

s: In an obliging manner; so as to oblige another; as a favour to another.

e: From Middle French explicable, from Latin explicabilis, from explicō (“unfold, explain”).

s: The process of supporting or securing something with a wedge.
A woman who engages in sports; a female athlete.
Dashingly, carelessly, or sportingly unconventional or stylish; jaunty; characterized by a devil-may-care unconventionality; having a somewhat disreputable quality or appearance.
In such a way as to achieve a desired result; effectively; so as to have an effect.
Eager or quick to argue, fight or start a conflict.
e: First attested circa 1540, from Middle French, from Latin truculentus (“fierce, savage”), from trux (“fierce, wild”).

s: The act of one who marvels; amazement.
The announcement of a forthcoming marriage (legally required for a church wedding in England and Wales and read on the three Sundays preceding the marriage).
Any public announcement of an upcoming event.
A boat used to ferry passengers, vehicles, or goods across open water, especially one that runs to a regular schedule
A failed or reverse climax, particularly
An unsatisfying resolution to a narrative, usually owing to a deus ex machina or similarly trivial resolution of the main conflict.
An abrupt descent (either deliberate or unintentional) from the dignity of the idea which the speaker or writer appeared to be aiming for.
In a languid manner, without force or effort, in a manner requiring little energy or exertion.

The fighting of hawks with each other.

The state or property of being insincere, lacking sincerity or truthfulness.
A visible substance believed to emanate from the body of a spiritualistic medium during communication with the dead.

The outer granule-free layer of cytoplasm.
e: From ecto- (“outside”) + plasm or -plasm, referring to the fact that ectoplasm is believed to emanate from and materialize outside of the medium's body.

s: Precluding debate or expostulation; not admitting of question or appeal.

e: From Anglo-Norman peremptorie, parentorie et al. (Modern French péremptoire), and its source, Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; precluding debate, decisive”), from perimō (“destroy, thwart”), from per- (“thorough”) + emō (“to obtain, buy”).

s: A usually small indoor receptacle for items that are to be discarded; a rubbish bin.
Any region or grouping that is worthless or meaningless.

Gerund of broil: the act of broiling.
A container designed to keep its contents at a constant humidity; especially such a box for storing cigars.
A torn-up piece of turf, especially by a golf club in making a stroke or by a horse's hoof.
A disruption in an otherwise smooth contour.
A drop in a graph between two linear portions ([https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/0004-6256/151/2/31 example])
To tear up pieces of turf from, especially with a golf club in making a stroke.

s: A dull banging sound; a thud.

e: From Middle English corpulent, from Old French corpulent, from Latin corpulentus.

s: Of, relating to, or having the nature of, a portent.

Arrogant or grand in an affected manner; pompous, pretentious.
One who is illegally a producer and/or trader of goods, especially of alcohol.
One who breaks intellectual property laws by reproducing protected works without permission.
e: From bootleg + -er. Originally a nickname given to smugglers in King George III's reign, derived from the smugglers' custom of hiding packages of valuables in the legs of their large sea-boots when dodging the king's coastguardsmen.

s: An inhabitant of a place; one who dwells in a certain place.

To grant rights of citizenship to; to naturalize.

e: From Middle English denisein, from Old French denzein, from deinz (“within”) + -ein, from Late Latin dē intus (“from within”), whence French dans.

Without point; in a pointless manner; so as to lack purpose or importance.
A refreshing drink flavored with aromatic herbs, especially mint, and sometimes alcohol.

e: From Middle English, from Old French julep, from Medieval Latin julapium, via Arabic جُلَاب from Persian گلاب (“rosewater”), from گل (“rose”) + آب (“water”).

The state or condition of being a girl.

Lack of reality or real existence.

Having or consisting of a higher population than can be sustained.

A tendency to talk excessively about oneself.
A belief that one is superior to or more important than others.
The result or product of being egoistic.
by confusion of the similar words
Egoism (belief that behavior should be directed towards one's self-interest).
e: From Latin ego (“I”) + -t- (perhaps modelled on dogmatism, despotism, idiotism) + -ism.

s: Fragrant or aromatic; having a sweet scent.
Having the smell of the article in question.
e: From Middle English redolent (first attested in 1400), from Old French redolent, from Latin redolentem, present participle of redoleō (“to emit a scent”), from red- + oleō (“to smell”).

s: A very loud low-pitched horn, used especially in lighthouses and on large boats.
To shout or bellow in a loud, deep voice
clothing made of flannel; especially trousers and underwear.
A women's hairstyle in which the hair is swept upwards from the face and worn high over the forehead.

A pattern for silk, with leaves and flowers in pink, blue, and gold.
A member of the 56th (West Essex) Regiment of Foot, an infantry regiment in the British Army, active from 1755 to 1881.
To style hair into a pompadour
e: From French Pompadour, after Madame de Pompadour (1721–1764), mistress of Louis XV.

s: Causing mental trouble or anguish; upsetting; making uneasy.
The act by which someone or something is disquieted.
Distended beyond the natural state by some internal agent, especially fluid, or expansive force.
Of a river, inundated with excess water as from a flood; swollen.
Overly complex and difficult to understand; grandiloquent; bombastic.
The idle behaviour of somebody who loafs.
Clothed, dressed, wearing clothing, often of a specified type.

Of, relating to or resembling weeds.
Characteristic of a plant that grows rapidly and spreads invasively, and which grows opportunistically in cracks of sidewalks and disturbed areas.
feeling or showing no shame, embarrassment or remorse

e: Borrowed from French convivial, from Latin convīvium (“a feast”), combined form of con- (“together”) + vīvō (“to live”).

To back out in a mean way.
e: . Unknown, but probably of imitative origin (compare dialectal Italian squacco (“small-crested heron”) and English quack).

Of an argument, excuse, etc.: used so often that it is no longer effective or interesting; banal, clichéd, trite.
An argument or assertion with little in the way of substance or supporting evidence.

Substitution of one thing for another; interchange.

The change to a lesser penalty or punishment by the State
Substitution, as a means of discriminating between phonemes.
The reversal of an electric current.
A passing from one state to another; change; alteration; mutation.
The act of giving one thing for another; barter; exchange.
The process or habit of journeying to and from work on a regular basis; commuting.

Without the use of forms or templates.

One of an ancient religious sect of Alexandria, whose adherents believed that the body of Christ was incorruptible, and that he suffered hunger, thirst, and pain only in appearance.

s: Being in or facing towards the sea.

From Middle English aschen, asshen (“ash-colored; pale; lifeless”). en (“remains”) + ash (“made or consisting of”) + en.

s: A shop that sells cooked or prepared foods ready for serving.

From German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), at the time also spelled Delicatesse(n), from French délicatesse, from délicat (“fine”), from Latin delicatus (“alluring”). Material used for making pockets for clothing.

A planting of shrubs; a wide border to a garden where shrubs are thickly planted; or a similar larger area with a path winding through it.
abundance; the state of being profuse; a cornucopia

or inability to believe; doubt about the truth or verisimilitude of something; disbelief.

The remaining portion of a partially suppressed sideband.

e: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

Having an edge or border marked with semicircles.
Cooked gratin; baked in a typical type of sauce, usually with cheese, as a casserole, e.g. scalloped potatoes; scalloped corn
e: From scallop + -ed. In culinary sense, originally referred to a seafood dish baked and served in a scallop shell, but now used more generally.

s: The yard associated with or surrounding a barn.
Of food or drink, having an earthy flavor.
In context of possibility of being heard; in an audible manner.
Not capricious or impulsive; sedate, serious, sober.
Always fixed in the same location; stationary.
e: From an obsolete spelling of stayed, the past participle of stay, used as an adjective.

s: Existing or occurring without interruption or end; ceaseless, unending.
e: From Middle English interminable, from Middle French interminable and its etymon Late Latin interminābilis. in- + terminable.

s: Pleased, satisfied, or gladdened, especially by the fulfillment of a certain desire or wish.
A lightness of manner or speech, frivolity; flippancy; a lack of appropriate seriousness; an inclination to make a joke of serious matters.
The state or quality of being light, buoyancy.
e: Coined in 1564, from Latin levitās (“lightness, frivolity”), from levis (“lightness (in weight)”). Cognate to lever, and more distantly, light.

s: In an unnatural manner; to an unnatural extent.
e: From Middle English unnaturelly, equivalent to unnatural + -ly and/or un- + naturally.

s: Not in accord or harmony; conflicting, incompatible.
Of people: disagreeing with each other; dissenting, quarrelsome.
Of sounds: harsh, jarring; specifically, of musical notes or tunes: not in harmony; dissonant, inharmonious.
Of a rock formation or other land feature, or its alignment: cutting across or transverse to neighbouring features.
Of a coastline: having bands of different types of rock running transversely to the coast, leading to the formation of alternating bays and headlands.
Of two similar subjects, especially twins: differing in some characteristic.
Of figures, etc.: having opposite signs (for example, positive and negative).
A thing which is not in accord or harmony with one or more other things.
Having gotten off one's horse, or been removed from its usual mounting, as with a statue off its pedestal, a framed picture from a wall, or a chandelier hanging from a ceiling.
A ballroom dance with a slow-slow-quick-quick rhythm.
A pace with short steps, as in changing from trotting to walking.
To repeat the strokes quickly on (bells) so as to produce a loud clang.
e: From Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”).

s: That with which something is laced.
The tied or threaded laces that form a netlike pattern.
A beating as punishment; a hiding.
Lagging, or cross-pieces placed to prevent ore from falling into a passage.
The cords by which the boards of a book are fastened to the back.
The knee of the head, or lace-piece, a piece of compass or knee timber secured to the back of the figurehead.
A hinged bridge which can be raised (to prevent its being crossed, as across a moat, or to allow watercraft to travel beneath it).
A tendency to provide only limited access.
Spoken of in a private manner.
The condition of being homogeneous: having uniformity of constituent content.
Happy and ready to do favours for others.
Incalculably, exceedingly, or immeasurably minute; vanishingly small.
Of or pertaining to non-zero quantities whose magnitude is less than any positive rational number.
A non-zero quantity whose magnitude is smaller than any positive number (by definition it is not a real number).
In a blank manner, especially showing no emotion or expression.
To pass through the pores or interstices of; to penetrate and pass through without causing rupture or displacement; applied especially to fluids which pass through substances of loose texture
To enter and spread through; to pervade.
A watery by-product of milk production.
Liquid that has passed through a filtration system.
e: Borrowed from Latin permeātus, perfect passive participle of permeō (“to pass through”), see -ate and -ate.

s: Foamy or churned to the point of becoming infused with bubbles.
Highly speculative; having high risk and high return.
Being a pretense, simulation, or counterfeit, or something false or fraudulent.
A Hindu prince or ruler in India.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genus Charaxes.
e: Borrowed from Hindi राजा and Urdu راجا, from Sanskrit राजन् (“king, prince”), from *Hrā́ȷ́ā (“king”), from *Hrā́ȷ́ā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵ-ō, from *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler, king”). Doublet of Rex, rex, roy.

s: (typically in a negative way) or obtrusive.
Vigorous; making strides; forceful in a positive way.
One of a class of s-like fricatives produced by an airstream directed at the upper teeth.
e: From French strident, from Latin strīdēns, present active participle of strīdō.

s: One's personal budget or financial capacity; the amount one can afford.
A small book, particularly a paperback or notebook able to fit into a pocket (of any genre, from reference work to fine art).
A romance novel published as a small paperback.
e: 1610s, from pocket + book, popularized in its sense as a paperback by the success of Pocket Books in the United States after its 1939 launch.

s: Having the shape of or resembling a bulb, bloated.
Growing from a bulb or producing bulbs.
Produced by abortion; born prematurely and therefore unnatural.
Coming to nothing; failing in its effect..
Imperfectly formed or developed; rudimentary; sterile.
Cutting short; acting to halt or slow the progress (of a disease).
Having a short and mild progression, without pronounced symptoms.
Made from the skin of a still-born animal.
Someone or something born or brought forth prematurely; an abortion.
A medicine that causes abortion, an abortifacient.
A medicine or treatment acting to halt or slow the progress of a disease.
To cause an abortion; to render without fruit.
e: First attested in 1382, with the meaning "causing stillbirth or miscarriage". From Middle English abortif, from Old French abortif, from Latin abortīvus (“causing abortion”), from aborior (“miscarry, disappear”), from ab (“amiss”) + orior (“appear, be born, arise”). abort + -ive.

s: A passageway covered by an arch, particularly one made of masonry.
A doorway with a semilunar-shaped top.
The action or process of perspiring.
e: Borrowed from late Middle French perspiration, from perspirer (“perspire”), from Latin perspirare (“to blow or breathe constantly”), from per (“through”) + spirare (“to breathe, blow”). Morphologically perspire + -ation.

s: A waterproof coat to be worn in the rain; any coat or jacket with this purpose.
A piece of deckwork; a deck.
The material from which a deck is made.
Healthful; having a disposition to promote healing.
e: From Middle English laudable, from Old French laudable or directly from Latin laudabilis; equivalent to laud + -able.

s: Lasting only a short time; temporary.
Of an action: that may be brought in any county
e: From Middle French transitoire, from Old French, from Latin trānsitōrius.

s: Of, pertaining to, or involving a contribution.
Tending to contribute to a result.
A person or thing that contributes.
e: From earlier contributary, from Middle English contributarie, from con- + tributarie after Middle French contributaire.

s: An inn or similar establishment situated beside a road beyond the jurisdiction of a town or city. In the centuries before motor vehicles, such inns were places for travellers to stop at night during multi-day journeys, besides being public houses for their local countryfolk.
A truck stop located in a remote area, with basic accommodation facilities.
In a profitable manner, in a way that achieves profit or gain.
Having a nose that is short and turned upward at the tip.
Moving in a chaotic, undulating fashion, as in a flow of water or a flag blowing in the wind.
A motion or sound that ripples.
Impoverished rural farm workers, either as serfs, small freeholders or hired hands.
Ignorant people of the lowest social status; bumpkins, rustics.
The condition of being a peasant; the position, rank, conduct, or quality of a peasant.
Immoderate; not restrained or held in check; inordinate (literary).
Yielding to the touch, and easily moved or shaken; hanging loose by its own weight; lacking firmness; flaccid.
Having a slight lack of acidity; having mild sweetness.
Which forms a surjection from the domain to every open subset of the codomain.
e: From a variant of flappy, from flap (“to hang loose”).

A variant of dialectal scranny (“thin; lean; scraggy; poor; scanty; of inferior quality”), perhaps from Old Norse skran (“rubbish; junk”) y. Compare Norwegian skran (“lean, thin, skinny”), English scrannel (“lean; meager; poor; worthless”). Alternatively, perhaps from Old Norse skrælna (“to be shrivelled”).

s: The act of condescending; a manner of behaving in an outwardly polite way that nevertheless implies superiority to another; patronizing courtesy toward inferiors.
Courtesy, affability of a superior towards an inferior.
tempting, especially that which is beyond reach.
The foam made by rapidly stirring soap and water.
Foam from profuse sweating, as of a horse.
To form lather or froth, as a horse does when profusely sweating.
e: From Middle English lather, from Old English lēaþor (“a kind of nitre used for soap, soda”), from Proto-West Germanic *lauþr, from Proto-Germanic *lauþrą (“that which is used for washing, soap”), from Proto-Indo-European *lówh₃trom (“that which is used for washing”), from *lewh₃-, *lowh₃- (“to wash, bathe”).
From Middle English letheren, from Old English līeþran, from Proto-West Germanic *lauþrijan, from Proto-Germanic *lauþrijaną (“to soap, wash”). Cognate with Old Norse leyðra (“to wash, lather”).

s: Any of various fan palms of the family Arecaceae, especially Sabal palmetto or the saw palmetto, Serenoa repens.
A hat made of palmetto leaves.
A native or resident of the US state of South Carolina.
e: From Spanish palmito, diminutive of palma (“palm tree”), from Latin palma. Doublet of palmite, palmito.

s: A physical activity involving yachts, such as racing sailing boats, cruising to distant shores, or day-sailing along a coast.
The act of sailing along a coast, or from port to port.
The act of disengaging the gears of a moving vehicle and rolling along without the use of engine power.
A progression of symptoms after treatment, before gradual improvement begins.
Drinking nolo drinks so as to imbibe less alcohol while still enjoying tippling.
In a vicarious manner; indirectly; as, by, or through a substitute; by proxy.
Not held firmly in position; physically unstable.
Inconstant in purpose, or volatile in behavior.
e: From un- + steady. Like steady, the word first appeared in English around 1530. The word is comparable to Old Frisian onstedich, Low German unstadig, etc.

s: Having no material body, immaterial; incorporeal or insubstantial.
Of a body part, separated from the body.
Brought into being by one's begetter(s).
Pertaining to the astrological influence of the planet Jupiter; having the characteristics of a person under such influence (see sense 1).
Insulting in manner or words, particularly in an arrogant or insubordinate manner.
e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin īnsolēns (“unaccustomed, unwanted, unusual, immoderate, excessive, arrogant, insolent”), from in- + solēns, present participle of solēre (“to be accustomed, to be wont”).

s: A period of experimentation with or interest in a particular idea or activity.
A dry red wine produced in the Bordeaux region of France, or a similar wine made elsewhere.
A deep purplish-red colour, like that of the wine; Bordeaux.
Of a deep purplish-red colour, like that of claret.
e: From Middle English claret, from Middle French claret, from Medieval Latin clārātum vīnum, from clārus. Compare tent (“Spanish red wine”), also from color. Doublet of clairet.

s: The act of something becoming darker.
Of or relating to spectroscopy or to a spectroscope.
Furnished with a rail or railing.
In a wild, uncontrolled, or savage manner.
Marked with, bearing, or wearing the sign of the cross.
An inflammation of the vermiform appendix.
Whatever person or persons: emphasised or elaborated form of whoever.
Under a spell; subject to an act of witchcraft.
(Of a person) entranced, charmed, fascinated, as though subject to a magical influence.
An object, such as a cloth or a purpose-made soft and puffy pad or mitt, used for dusting surfaces etc.
A revolving wire-cloth cylinder which removes the dust from rags, etc.
A blowing machine for separating the flour from the bran.
A dry drillhole, one that does not produce oil or gas.
A type of loose dress worn at home as well as within the vicinity of one's home.
A block of felt strips, shaped ergonomically, used to remove chalk from a chalkboard.
A high pitch toward the batter.

e: Ancient Greek ληθαργικός, from λήθαργος (“forgetful, lethargic”), from λήθη (“a forgetting, forgetfulness”) (from which Lethe (“river in Hades”)) + ἀργός (“not working”). lethargy + -ic.

s: A lightweight, balanced plain-woven sheer fabric, or gauze, like gossamer, woven of alternate S- and Z-twist crepe (high-twist) yarns made of silk, polyester, or cotton.
Any purely ornamental accessory on a woman's dress, such as a bunch of ribbon, lace, etc.
e: Borrowed from French chiffon, from Middle French chiffe (“cloth, old rag”), from Old French chipe (“rag”), from Middle English chip, chippe (“chip, shard, fragment”), from Old English ċipp (“chip, splinter, shaving”); see chip.

s: A work of art, music or literature.
A substantial or complete corpus of works produced by an artist, composer, or writer.
e: From French œuvre, from Old French uevre, from Latin opera (plural of Latin opus), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”). Doublet of opera, opus, ure.

s: Appealing to the senses, or to sensual gratification.
Of or relating to the senses; sensory.
A dark blue neckerchief with white spots, each having a dark-blue spot in the centre.
e: Named after James Belcher (1781–1811), a famous English boxer.

s: The state or condition of being restless; an inability to be still, quiet, at peace or comfortable; a feeling of discomfort with stillness causes by anxiety, boredom or other emotions.
Liable to perish, especially naturally subject to quick decomposition or decay.
That which perishes or is short-lived.
Food that does not keep for long.
e: From Middle English *persishable, perysabyl, equivalent to perish + -able. Compare Old French perissable (and modern French périssable).

s: Painted with the temporary paint whitewash.
Having had any controversy or potential for scandal removed, ignored or downplayed.

Having been subjected to racial whitewashing: made to be or seem more white (Caucasian); for example, having been made to appear whiter via makeup, or by being illustrated in pictures or portrayed in films as white (despite originally or properly being nonwhite).
A person of color perceived as having assimilated at the expense of their own racial or cultural identity.
Covered or decorated with flowers, or images of flowers.
Having a fever, an elevated body temperature.
Lacking respect; not having or not showing respect for or seriousness towards something that is usually treated with respect; going against conventional precepts.
Very showy or ornamented, now especially when excessive, or in a tasteless or vulgar manner.
One of the large beads in the rosary at which the paternoster is recited.
A reunion held by one of the colleges of the University of Oxford for alumni, normally during the long vacation.
e: From Middle English gaudi, from Old French gaudie, from Medieval Latin gaudia. equivalent to gaud (“ornament, trinket”) + -y.

s: An instruction to play gradually more loudly, denoted by a long, narrow angle with its apex on the left (<), by musicians called a hairpin.
A gradual increase of anything, especially to a dramatic climax.
The climax of a gradual increase.
To increase in intensity; to reach or head for a crescendo.
Gradually increasing in force or loudness.
e: Borrowed from Italian crescendo, gerund of crescere (“to grow, to increase”).

s: The act by which things are confounded, or confused.
The process by which an apparent association between an exposure and an outcome is actually explained by another factor.
In a satisfactory manner, in a manner adequate to requirements.
Affected by dampness or mould; damp, mildewed, mouldy.
Having an odour or taste of mould; also, having a stale or unfresh odour or taste.
Characteristic of or relating to mould or mouldiness.
Of attitudes, ideas, writing, or other abstract things: no longer fresh or interesting; outdated, stale.
Of a person: boring and unadventurous; also, old-fashioned, stuck in the past.
A type of snuff with a musty flavour (adjective sense 2).
To turn musty (adjective sense 1 or 2); to must.
Of a male animal such as a camel or an elephant: in musth.
e: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English musty; further origin Uncertain, possibly from one of the following: Compare Middle French moisi (“mouldy”), an adjective use of the past participle of moisir (“(to cause) to go mouldy, to moulder”) (modern French moisir), from Latin mūcēre, the present active infinitive of Old Latin mūceō (“to be mouldy or musty”): see above.
From musth (“time during which male elephants exhibit increased levels of sexual activity and aggressiveness”) + -y.

s: Pitifully sad, wretched, miserable; lonely, especially from feeling abandoned, deserted, forsaken.
A member of a forlorn hope.
e: From Middle English forlorn, forloren, from Old English forloren (past participle of forlēosan (“to lose”)), from Proto-Germanic *fraluzanaz (“lost”), past participle of *fraleusaną (“to lose”), equivalent to for- + lorn.

s: Of a proportionate or similar measurable standard.
Describing a crystal in which every atom or molecule is placed in the same relative position
Describing two numbers within the same Archimedean class, so that neither is infinitely larger than the other.
To reduce to a common measure.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin commēnsūrātus, from com- (“together, with”) + mēnsūrātus, perfect passive participle of mēnsūrō (“to measure, to estimate”), (see -ate and -ate), from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”) + -ō.

s: A horse for riding or driving on the road.
A bicycle, or tricycle, adapted for common roads, rather than for the racing track, usually of classic style and steel-framed construction.
One who drives much; a coach driver.
A hunter who keeps to the roads instead of following the hounds across country.
An open automobile having a front seat and a rumble seat.
A person who lives along the road.
a sea-going vessel riding at anchor in a road or bay.
A clumsy vessel that works its way from one anchorage to another by means of the tides.
Separated or disconnected; withdrawn; removed; apart.
Separated from matter; abstract; ideal, not concrete.
Inattentive to surrounding objects; absent in mind; meditative.
Of, relating to, or appropriate to a villain.
offensive, or reprehensible in nature or behaviour; nefarious.
e: From Middle English vileinous, from Old French vileneus. villain + -ous.

s: Depicted with shading, as if showing areas in shadow.
Furnished with a shoulder-shaped joint or protrusion.
Having or pertaining to (a specific kind of) shoulders.
The fine particles (dust) created by sawing wood or other material.
Food that is unpleasantly powdery and tasteless.
the state or quality of being soft-minded.
A pantomime fool, typically dressed in colorful checkered clothes, used as a stock character in commedia dell'arte and other genres.
Any of various riodinid butterflies of the genera Taxila and Praetaxila.
Brightly colored, especially in a pattern like that of a harlequin clown's clothes.
To remove or conjure away, as if by a harlequin's trick.
To make sport by playing ludicrous tricks.
Having a specified kind of hair.
The act of something that simmers.
In an irregular manner; without rule, method, or order.
The state of being preoccupied or an idea that preoccupies the mind; enthrallment.
The act of occupying something before someone else.
e: Borrowed from Middle French préoccupation, from Latin praeoccupātiō. pre- + occupation or preoccupy + -ation.

s: Out of breath, gasping for air; breathing rapidly, or given to becoming short of breath.
Under the influence of marijuana, usually at a relatively high dose.
The amount that a spoon will hold, either level or heaped.
Active strength or force of body or mind; a capacity for exertion, physically, intellectually, or morally; energy.
Strength or force in animal or vegetable nature or action.
e: From Middle English vigour, from Old French vigour, from vigor, from Latin vigor, from vigeō (“thrive, flourish”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be lively”). Related to vigil, vegetable, vajra, and waker.

s: Not accurately determined, not determinable, or both.
Not definitively or precisely determined, because of the presence of infinity or zero symbols used in any of several improper combinations.
With no genetically defined end, and thus (1) ongoing, and (often) sprawling, as well as (2) theoretically limitless.
Not topped with some form of terminal bud.
Designed to allow the incorporation of future changes whose nature is not yet known.
A symbol that resembles a variable or parameter but is used purely formally and neither signifies nor is ever assigned a particular value; a variable.
A gallery, platform, or balcony, usually roofed and often partly enclosed, extending along the outside of a building.
e: An word of origin, from Portuguese varanda (“balustrade; balcony”). Further etymology is Unknown and disputed.

s: Quick, smart; sharp, active, brisk or nimble; lively.
A short line of horsehair, gut, monofilament, etc., by which a fishhook or lure is attached to a longer (and usually heavier) line.
To tie a hook to the end of a fishing line with a snell knot.
e: Inherited from Middle English snell (“quick, fast”) from Old English snell, snel (“lively, quick”) from Proto-West Germanic *snell, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, swift, brisk”).

s: The state of being calm; tranquillity; silence.
the state of being luminous, or a luminous object; brilliance or radiance
the ratio of luminous flux to radiant flux at the same wavelength; the luminosity factor
The rate at which a star radiates energy in all directions.
e: Borrowed from French luminosité or else a native formation from luminous + -ity.

s: In an involuntary manner; done without conscious thought.
To be active, but not excessively busy, at a task or a series of tasks.
One who pushes the small wagons in a coal mine, to transport the coal mined by the getter.
A golf club specifically intended for a putt.
A person who is taking a putt or putting.
To produce intermittent bursts of sound in the course of operating.
In a manner without pause or stop, especially to the point of annoyance; not ceasing.
The action of the verb crouch.
Not personal; not representing a person; not having personality.
of a verb or other word
Not having a subject, or having a third person pronoun without an antecedent.
e: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.

s: A feeling of dislike, aversion or antipathy.
Aversion of the taste; dislike, as of food or drink; disrelish.
To be distasteful; to taste bad
To offend; to disgust; to displease.
To deprive of taste or relish; to make unsavory or distasteful.
Shrivelled, shrunken or faded, especially due to lack of water.
To confirm or support something with additional evidence; to attest or vouch for.
e: Borrowed from Latin corrōborātus (“strengthened”), perfect passive participle of corrōborō (“to support, corroborate”) (see -ate and -ate), from con- (“together”) + rōborō (“to strengthen”), from rōbur, rōboris (“strength”). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English, otherwise archaic.

s: The act of making something straight.
The craft or business of upholstering furniture.
The materials used in upholstering furniture.
e: First recorded in 1597; from upholster or upholsterer + -ery or -y.

s: The motion by which someone or something thrusts.
The act of squeezing curd by hand, to expel the whey.
The white whey, or that which is last pressed out of the curd by the hand, and of which butter is sometimes made.
from constraints of the material world.
That which surpasses or is supereminent; something excellent.
An extravagant or eccentric piece of music, literature or drama, originally associated with Victorian England.
An instance of fantastical, unrestrained, lavish, or chaotic behaviour or conduct.
e: From Italian stravaganza under influence from English extravagance.

s: Lacking a definite form or clear shape.
Being without definite character or nature.
In the non-crystalline solid state of, or being a non-crystalline counterpart to, a crystalline solid.
Infinite and not the disjoint union of two infinite subsets.
e: From Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (“without form, shapeless, deformed”) (itself from ἀ- (“without”) + μορφή (“form”) -ous. a- + -morphous.

s: A small box or tin (can) with a lid for holding dried tea leaves used to brew tea.
A (usually small) box, chest, or tin with a lid, and often with partitions, used to keep things in.
A small lidded bin for food waste.
A movable tray or other mechanism for holding (sometimes within a piece of equipment or machinery), securing, and transporting a removable component.
A lightweight wheeled cart; specifically, one attached to a bicycle as a conveyance for a child, or pulled by hand and used to transport groceries away from a shop.
Chiefly followed by for: Alternative spelling of caddie (“to serve as a caddy (noun sense) for a golfer”)
e: An alteration of catty (“(unit of) weight used in China, equivalent to 1⅓ pounds avoirdupois (about 0.605 kilograms)”), borrowed from Malay kati (“weight used in China, Indonesia, and Japan”), from Tamil கட்டி (“measure of weight; clod, lump”), from கட்டு (“to coagulate, congeal, or consolidate (into a concretion); to harden”).

s: Rapid back-and-forth or up-and-down waving or oscillation of, e.g. wings or a vibrating engine; the condition of engaging in such an action.
The action of atrial flutter, in which the upper chambers of the heart beat too rapidly.
A feeling of internal shifting, as with indigestion, nervous flutters, etc.
To rise and fall as a wave; to be tossed up and down the waves.
Tossed up and down the waves.
e: Borrowed from Latin flūctuātus, perfect passive participle of flūctuō (“(of the sea) to surge, swell; (of man) to waver, fluctuate”), see -ate and -ate.

s: The process by which something hardens.
Subject to irregular changes in quantity or quality.
A silent person; a person who does not talk.
A figure of a person or animal used by a ventriloquist; a puppet.
Something constructed with the size and form of a human, to be used in place of a person.
A person who is the mere tool of another; a man of straw.
A deliberately nonfunctional device or tool used in place of a functional one.
A pacifier; a plastic or rubber teat used to soothe or comfort a baby.
A player whose hand is shown and is to be played from by another player.
A word serving only to make a construction grammatical.
A feigned pass or kick or play in order to deceive an opponent.
A bodily gesture meant to fool an opposing player; a feint.
A newborn animal that is indifferent to stimulus and does not voluntarily move.
A fairy chess piece that cannot move or capture, but can be captured and used to skip moving another piece.
e: From dumb + -y. Pacifier sense from dummy teat where dummy is in the sense of a nonfunctional replica.

s: To show or demonstrate clearly; to manifest.
e: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex-) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.

s: A head of real or synthetic hair worn on the head to disguise baldness, for cultural or religious reasons, for fashion, or by actors to help them better resemble the character they are portraying.
To put on a wig; to provide with a wig (especially of an actor etc.).
To act in an extremely emotional way; to be overly excited, irritable, nervous, or fearful; behave erratically.
e: Clipping of periwig, itself an alteration of French perruque. The meaning of "to reprimand" perhaps came from this being something a bigwig would do or perhaps from the expressions to flip one's wig, wigs on the green, or dash my wig!

s: A ceremonial form of this weapon.

A long baton used by some drum majors to keep time and lead a marching band. If this baton is referred to as a mace, by convention it has a ceremonial often decorative head, which, if of metal, usually is hollow and sometimes intricately worked.
An officer who carries a mace as a token of authority.
A knobbed mallet used by curriers to make leather supple when dressing it.
To hit someone or something with a mace.
A spice obtained from the outer layer of the kernel of the fruit of the nutmeg.
Tear gas or pepper spray, especially for personal use.
To spray in defense or attack with mace (pepper spray or tear gas) using a hand-held device.
To spray a similar noxious chemical in defense or attack using an available hand-held device such as an aerosol spray can.
An old money of account in China equal to one tenth of a tael.
An old weight of 57.98 grains, approximately 3.8 grams.
e: From Middle English mace, borrowed from Old French mace, mache, from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea, matia, (compare Italian mazza, Spanish maza), probably from Proto-West Germanic *mattjō (“cutting tool, hoe”).
From Middle English, from re-interpretation of macys as a plural (as with pea); from Latin macir. Doublet of macir.

From the name of one brand of the spray, Mace. Pepper spray may be derived from cayenne pepper, but not from mace (etymology 2 above), which is a different spice; rather, it was named after the weapon (etymology 1).

s: To be more than an ample reward for.
To restore consciousness, vigor or life to.
e: From Latin resuscitātus, past participle of resuscitō (“to raise up again, revive”), from re- (“again”) + suscitō (“to raise up”), from sub- (“up, under”) + citō (“to summon, rouse”).

s: A large flightless bird of the order Struthioniformes.
The most widespread species of that order, known as the common ostrich (Struthio camelus).
One who buries their head in the sand instead of acknowledging problems.
The hypothetical completion of a hole five strokes under par (a quintuple birdie, quadruple eagle, triple albatross, or double condor).
Unwilling to do work or make an effort; disinclined to exertion.
