A 1639 borrowing, perhaps from Dutch bles or Middle Low German blesse, bles, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *blasī, from Proto-Germanic *blasį̄, from *blasaz (“white, pale (of animals)”) + *-į̄, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“shiny, white”). Cognate with German Blesse, Swedish bläs. The verb is from the noun.
From Middle English blasen (“to blow”), from Old English *blǣsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan, from Proto-Germanic *blēsaną (“to blow”). Related to English blast.

s: A sequence of states representing an encoded message in a communication channel.
Any variation of a quantity or change in an entity over time that conveys information upon detection.
A sign made to give notice of some occurrence, command, or danger, or to indicate the start of a concerted action.
An on-off light, semaphore, or other device used to give an indication to another person.
of a radio, tv, telephone, internet, etc.
An electromagnetic action, normally a voltage that is a function of time, that conveys the information of the radio or TV program or of communication with another party.
An action, change or process done to convey information and thus reduce uncertainty.
A token; an indication; a foreshadowing; a sign.
A simple interprocess communication used to notify a process or thread of an occurrence.
To indicate; to convey or communicate by a signal.
To communicate with (a person or system) by a signal.
Standing above others in rank, importance, or achievement.
e: From Old French segnal, seignal or Medieval Latin signāle; noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum; verb use from 1805, as a shortened from signalize (1650s). Doublet of signum, sign.
From Middle English snelly, snellych, snellik, snellich, from Old English snellīċe (“rapidly, quickly, with activity”), from snellīċ (“moving quickly; swift”), equivalent to snell + -ly.

s: A non-auger posthole digger of a hand tool type with hinged operation.
To stay or remain in a place or situation, especially as if unwilling to depart or not easily able to do so.
To remain alive or existent although still proceeding toward death or extinction; to die gradually.
To consider or contemplate for a period of time; to engage in analytic thinking or discussion.
e: From Middle English lengeren, frequentative of lengen (“to stay, dwell, tarry”), from Old English lenġan (“to lengthen, delay, extend”), from Proto-West Germanic *langijan, from Proto-Germanic *langijaną (compare West Frisian lingje (“to linger”), Dutch lengen, German längen, Icelandic lengja (“to lengthen”)), related to the root of English long.

s: To evoke, educe (emotions, feelings, responses, etc.); to generate, obtain, or provoke as a response or answer.
To draw out, bring out, bring forth (something latent); to obtain information from someone or something.
To use logic to arrive at truth; to derive by reason.
Elicited; drawn out; made real; open; evident.
A young man; a boy, a lad; specifically, one regarded as of low social status; a ragamuffin.

A person engaged to run errands such as carrying goods and messages; a commissionaire, an errand boy or errand girl, a gofer; specifically, a member of an organized group of such persons working in large Scottish cities and towns in the early 18th century.
A person hired to assist a golfer by carrying their golf clubs and providing advice.
Chiefly followed by for: to serve as a caddie (noun) for a golfer.
e: The noun is borrowed from Scots caddie (“military cadet; young man; ragamuffin; person engaged to run errands; person hired to assist a golfer”), from French cadet (“army cadet; younger sibling”), from capdet (“captain; chief”) (Gascony, archaic), from Late Latin capitettum, from Latin caput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“head”).
Borrowed from Latin expendō (“to weigh; to pay out”). Doublet of spend.

s: A large group of musicians who play together on various instruments, usually including some from strings, woodwind, brass and/or percussion; the instruments played by such a group.
A semicircular space in front of the stage used by the chorus in Ancient Greek and Hellenistic theatres.
The area in a theatre or concert hall where the musicians sit, immediately in front of and below the stage, sometimes (also) used by other performers.
To turn (someone) away from a privilege, right, job, etc.
To reject, put off (a request, demand etc.).
To ward off (a malignant influence, attack etc.).
To drive back (an assailant, advancing force etc.).
To force away by means of a repulsive force.
To cause repulsion or dislike in; to disgust.
e: From Middle English repellen, a borrowing from Old French *repeller, from Latin repellere (“to drive back”), from re- (“back”) + pellere (“to drive”). Doublet of repeal.

s: A chair with a rotating seat, typically used in an office or at a computer.
To give up, abandon or retire from something; to trade away.
To let go (free, away), physically release.
To metaphorically surrender, yield control or possession.
To accept to give up, withdraw etc.
e: From Middle English relinquisshen, from the inflected stem relinquiss- of Middle French relinquir, from Latin relinquere, itself from re- + linquere (“to leave”). Compare also Sanskrit रिणक्ति (“to leave”).

s: A seabird of the genus Larus or of the subfamily Larinae.
Any of various pierid butterflies of the genus Cepora.
A breach or hole made by the force of a torrent; fissure, chasm.
A channel made by a stream; a natural watercourse; running water.
To sweep away by the force of running water; to carve or wear into a gully.
e: Inherited from Middle English gulle, from a language (compare Breton gouelan, Welsh gwylan and Cornish golan), from *gwuɨlann, from Proto-Celtic *weilannā (“seagull”). Cognate with Old Irish foílenn, Scottish Gaelic faoileag. Compare French goéland, a borrowing from Breton.
Perhaps from an obsolete term gull (“to swallow, guzzle”), from Middle English golen (“to make swallowing motions, gape”), from Middle English gole (“throat”).

From Middle English gole (“a whirlpool, narrow inlet of the sea, ditch or stream”), from Middle Low German goel, gȫl, gȫle (“swamp, marshy lowland”), related to Old Dutch gulla (“pool, puddle”), Old French goille (“pool, puddle, pond”), all ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *goli, *golljā (“puddle”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *guljaz, *guljǭ.

s: A piece or point of land, extending beyond the adjacent coast into a sea or lake; a promontory; a headland.
A sleeveless garment or part of a garment, hanging from the neck over the back, arms, and shoulders.
To incite or attract (a bull) to charge a certain direction, by waving a cape.
To head or point; to keep a course.
To skin (an animal, or particularly the head and shoulders of an animal, especially a deer), for taxidermy.
To defend or praise, especially that which is unworthy.
To cover (as) with or like a cape.
e: From Middle English cape, gappe, cap, from Old French cap (“cape, headland”), from Latin caput (“head”). Compare Old Norse kobbi (“islet, small cape”). Doublet of capo, caput, chef, chief, and distantly with Doublet of head, Howth.

From French cape, from Old Occitan capa, from Late Latin cappa (“cape”). The second sense ("superhero") is metonymic from the fact that many superheroes wear capes. Likewise, the verb sense "defend, praise" alludes to the stereotypical depiction of superheroes wearing capes when they come to people's defense. (Compare caped crusader.) Doublet of capa, cappa.

s: An act of revisiting; a second or subsequent visit.
e: From Middle English revisite, from Middle French revisiter and Latin revīsitāre. re- + visit.

s: To bring back into a particular place or condition; to restore.
To cause (something) to turn around a central point.
To orbit a central point (especially of a celestial body).
To move in order or sequence.
To ponder on; to reflect repeatedly upon; to consider all aspects of.
To read through, to study (a book, author etc.).
The rotation of part of the scenery within a theatrical production.
e: From Middle English revolven (“to change direction”), borrowed from Old French revolver (“to reflect upon”), from Latin revolvere (“turn over, roll back, reflect upon”), from re- (“back”) + volvō (“roll”); see voluble, volve.

s: as written; used to indicate, for example, that text is being quoted as it is from the source.
Used in the manner of scare quotes
To mark with a bracketed sic.
To incite an attack by, especially a dog or dogs.
To set upon; to chase; to attack.
The letter ص in the Arabic script.
Debased, corrupt; seeking personal gain by dishonourable means.
Taking part in promiscuous sexual activity, licentious; (later, chiefly as attributive use of noun) that is a prostitute.
Any person (especially a woman) who has sexual intercourse or engages in other sexual activity for payment, especially as a means of livelihood.
A woman who has sexual intercourse or engages in other sexual activity for payment, especially as a means of livelihood.
A person who does, or offers to do, a demeaning or dishonourable activity for money or personal gain; someone who acts in a dishonourable way for personal advantage.
To offer (oneself or someone else) for sexual activity in exchange for money.
To sacrifice (oneself, one's talents etc.) in return for profit or other advantage; to exploit for base purposes.
e: From Latin prōstitūtus, past participle of prōstituō, from prō̆ (“for, before”) + statuō (“to set up, to erect”).

s: An outdoor area or a building where cars may be parked.
A rectangular section, usually marked by painted lines, designated for the parking of a single car.
A road with serious traffic congestion preventing the movement of vehicles.
Founded in law; legal; valid; not defective.
Yes; used to show agreement or understanding.
A sensation perceived by the ear caused by the vibration of air or some other medium.
A vibration capable of causing such sensations.
A distinctive style and sonority of a particular musician, orchestra etc.
Earshot, distance within which a certain noise may be heard.
A segment as a part of spoken language, the smallest unit of spoken language, a speech sound.
e: From Middle English sound, sund, isund, ȝesund, from Old English sund (“sound, safe, whole, uninjured, healthy, prosperous”), from Proto-West Germanic *sund, from Proto-Germanic *sundaz (“healthy”), merged with synonymous Old English ġesund, from Proto-West Germanic *gasund.
Displaced native Middle English swei, from Old English swēġ, from Proto-Germanic *swōgiz.

From Middle English sound, sund (“body of water; swimming; air bladder of a fish”), from Old English sund (“the power, capacity, or act of swimming; swimming; sea; ocean; water; sound; strait; channel”), Old Norse sund (“channel, inlet, strait”), from Proto-Germanic *sundą (“swimming; sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *swem- (“swimming; sea”).

From Middle English sounden, from Old French sonder, from sonde (“sounding line”) of origin, compare Old English sundgyrd (“a sounding rod”), sundline (“a sounding line”), Old English sund (“water, sea”). More at Etymology 3 above.

s: A person who or a type of aircraft that flies at high elevations.
An ambitious person, especially one who takes risks or has an extravagant lifestyle.
A vertical pole used in commercial fishing to locate the beginning and end of a long fishing line.
A glamorous stock that potentially offers high returns to investors.
The process of making woven material on a loom.
An unsteady back and forth motion.
The uncontrolled crossing of multiple streams of traffic in the same general direction.
Each of the flashing lights on each side of a vehicle which is used to indicate the vehicle is moving left or right.
A player of the game of tiddlywinks.
A telegraph that automatically prints transmitted messages in letters rather than Morse code or other symbols, typically resembling a typewriter in appearance.
A telegram produced by this device.
An early input/output device for mainframe computers, resembling a typewriter.
e: From tele- (“far, distant, telegraph”) + type (“text, typewriter”), q.v. In the United States, chiefly understood as a genericization of the Morkrum or Teletype Corporation's branded teletype machines. Doublet of telotype.
The noun is from dog + -o, perhaps after the adverb. The adverb is probably of the same origin.

s: An expression of pleasure or enjoyment, mostly from rapid physical motion.
To excite; to arouse; to energize.
To separate or reduce into atoms.
To make into a fine spray.
To fragment; to break into small pieces or concepts.
To deprive of community and political capital.
The milk-secreting organ of female humans and other mammals which includes the mammary gland and the nipple or teat; a breast; an udder.
An accessory cloud like a mammary in appearance, which can form on the underside of most cloud genera.
A protective mat, usually heat-resistant, placed under a single person's tableware (including cutlery) at the dining table.
A goblin, imp, bogeyman, bugbear or similar a frightful being or phantom.
A Jamaican dance move that involves raising and lowering the arms while moving the body in a waving motion.
e: Uncertain; possibly cognate with English bug, or Derived from Welsh bwgwly.

s: of a ball in cricket, tennis, etc.
To rebound unexpectedly or unusually slowly, due to backward spin on the ball or imperfections of the ground.
To hold or bear in a suspended or inclined manner or position instead of erect.
To cause (something) to be suspended, as from a hook, hanger, hinges or the like.
To kill (someone) by suspension from the neck, usually as a form of execution or suicide.
To be executed by suspension by one's neck from a gallows, a tree, or other raised bar, attached by a rope tied into a noose.
To loiter; to hang around; to spend time idly.
To apply (wallpaper or drywall to a wall).
To remain persistently in one's thoughts.
To prevent from reaching a decision, especially by refusing to join in a verdict that must be unanimous.
To stop responding to manual input devices such as the keyboard and mouse.
e: From hang sangwich, Irish colloquial pronunciation of ham sandwich.
Alteration of dang, itself a minced oath of damn.

s: A powerful synthetic analgesic drug which is similar to morphine in its effects but less sedative and is used as a substitute drug in the treatment of morphine and heroin addiction.
A handcrafted sailboat with a motor or lateen sails, resembling a dhow, that is used in the Maldives.
Any of many subspecies of bee, in seven species of genus Apis, often kept commercially for honey, beeswax, and pollination of crops.
A conical vascularized body forming the extremity of the penis.
A fold of skin that surrounds and protects the clitoris, homologous with the male foreskin; the female prepuce.
A light boot, fitted with a blade, used for ice skating.
A sudden hit or blow; a glancing blow.
To skim or slide along a surface.
To slip, such as on ice.
To move swiftly; to move in leaps and bounds.
To pop, to quickly or briefly make a trip to.
To drink a large amount of alcohol.
e: From Middle English skit, from Old Norse *skitr, older form of skítr (“dung, faeces”), from Proto-Germanic *skitiz. Cognate with Old English sċite (“dung”).
Inherited from Middle English skiten, from Old Norse skíta, from Proto-Germanic *skītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skéydt.
Inherited from Middle English *skiten, from Old Norse skýt-, present singular stem of skjóta (“to shoot”), from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd-. Doublet of shoot.

s: The quality of being amusing, comical, funny.
A mood, especially a bad mood; a temporary state of mind or disposition brought upon by an event; an abrupt illogical inclination or whim.
Any of the fluids in an animal body, especially the four "cardinal humours" of blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm that were believed to control the health and mood of the human body.
Either of the two regions of liquid within the eyeball, the aqueous humour and vitreous humour.
e: From Middle English humour, from Old French humor, humour, from Latin hūmor, correctly ūmor (“liquid”), from hūmeō, correctly ūmeō (“to be moist”). The h in these words, which was silent in late Classical Latin, is folk etymological, due to the erroneous association with the word humus (“soil”).

s: A cloth-covered frame used for protection against rain or sun.
Anything that provides similar overarching coverage of a range of concepts, purposes, groups, etc.
A strategy in which five players in the offensive zone form an umbrella-shaped formation around the opposition's goal net.
The main body of a jellyfish, excluding the tentacles.
An umbrella-shaped reflector with a white or silvery inner surface, used to diffuse a nearby light.
To cover or protect, as if by an umbrella.
To form the dome shape of an open umbrella.
e: Borrowed from Italian ombrella (“parasol, sunshade”), from Late Latin umbrella (influenced by umbra (“shadow, shade”)), from Latin umbella, from umbra + -lus.

s: A coarse kind of linen made from hards (also called hurds).
A whirlwind that forms over water, not associated with a mesocyclone of a thunderstorm (contrary to a true tornado).
A true tornado that passes over a body of water.
A plume of water rising from the surface of a body of water as the result of an explosion or impact.
A channel through which water is discharged, especially from the gutters of a roof; downspout; drainpipe.
A gate in the form of a grating which is lowered into place at the gateway of a castle, a fort, etc.
An old English coin from the reign of Elizabeth I, minted for the use of the East India Company, and bearing the picture of a portcullis on the reverse.
To obstruct with, or as with, a portcullis; to shut; to bar.
e: From Middle English portcolyse, from Old French porte colëice, from porte (“door”) + feminine of colëiz (“sliding”), ultimately from Latin colāre.

s: A difficulty that has to be resolved or dealt with.
An addiction, other substance use disorder, or comparable psychological challenge.
A question to be answered, schoolwork exercise.
Difficulty in accepting or understanding or refusal to accept or understand.
A set of moves required to complete a climb.
Of a person or an animal, difficult to train or guide; unruly.
e: From Middle English probleme, from Middle French probleme, from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (“anything thrown forward, hindrance, obstacle, anything projecting, a headland, promontory”), from προβάλλω (“to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward”), from προ- (“in front of”) + βάλλω (“to throw, to cast, to hurl”).

s: To bite something persistently, especially something tough.
To produce excessive anxiety or worry.
To corrode; to fret away; to waste.
e: From Middle English gnawen, gnaȝen, from Old English gnagan, from Proto-West Germanic *gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą (“to gnaw”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʰnēgʰ- (“to gnaw, scratch”). Cognate with Dutch knagen, German nagen, Danish gnave (“to gnaw”), Norwegian gnage, Norwegian gnaga, Swedish gnaga.

s: A convoy or procession of travellers, their cargo and vehicles, and any pack animals, especially camels crossing a desert.
A furnished vehicle towed behind a car, etc., and used as a dwelling when stationary.
A group of camels, especially when used as beasts of burden carrying people and merchandise.
To travel and/or live in a caravan (vehicle).
e: From Middle French caravane, from Old French carvane, from Persian کاروان, from Middle Persian kʾlwʾn', from Old Persian 𐎣𐎠𐎼 (“people, subjects”). The word was used to designate a group of people who were travelling by camel or horse on the Silk Road. Doublet of Kairouan.

s: Any contest or trial of strength or skill, or to determine superiority.
A competitive sporting event such as a boxing meet, a baseball game, or a cricket match.
Equality of conditions in contest or competition.
A pair of items or entities with mutually suitable characteristics.
Someone with a measure of an attribute equaling or exceeding the object of comparison.
Equivalence; a state of correspondence; a counterpart.
A perforated board, block of plaster, hardened sand, etc., in which a pattern is partly embedded when a mould is made, for giving shape to the surfaces of separation between the parts of the mould.
To agree; to be equal; to correspond.
To agree with; to be equal to; to correspond to.
To equal or exceed in achievement.
To make a successful match or pairing.
To unite in marriage, to mate.
To fit together, or make suitable for fitting together; specifically, to furnish with a tongue and groove at the edges.
e: From Middle English macche, mecche, from Old English mæċċa, ġemæċċa (“companion, mate, wife, one suited to another”), from Proto-West Germanic *makkjō, *gamakkjō (“partner, equal”), from Proto-Germanic *makô, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, work”). Compare Danish mage (“mate”), Icelandic maki (“spouse”).
From Middle English macchen (“to marry; be paired with”), from the noun (see above).

From Middle English macche, mecche (“wick (of a candle)”), from Old French mesche, meische, from Vulgar Latin micca (compare Catalan metxa, Spanish mecha, Italian miccia), which in turn is probably from Latin myxa (“nozzle, curved part of a lamp”), from Ancient Greek μύξα (“lamp wick”).

s: A tall glass tumbler used for highballs, usually holding 240350 mL.
The act of speaking in a quiet voice, especially without vibration of the vocal cords; the sound thus produced.
A faint trace or hint (of something).
A low rustling sound, like that of the wind in leaves.
A private message to an individual in a chat room.
A projection of intention and influence caused by sending thoughts or desires outward through softly-spoken words or subtle mental or energetic means.

To speak softly or under one's breath, so as to be heard only by one near at hand; to utter words without sonant breath; to talk without that vibration of the vocal cords which gives sonorous, or vocal, sound.

To say (something) softly or under one's breath, so as to be heard only by one near at hand; to utter (something) without sonant breath, without that vibration of the vocal cords which gives sonorous, or vocal, sound.
To mention privately and confidentially, or in a whisper.
To make a low, sibilant sound.
To speak with suspicion or timorous caution; to converse in whispers, as in secret plotting.
To address in a whisper, or low voice.
To prompt secretly or cautiously; to inform privately.
To send a private message to an individual in a chat room.
To exercise skill in taming or training a creature.
To project intention and influence events by sending thoughts or desires outward through softly-spoken words or subtle mental or energetic means; to subject someone or something to this influence.
e: From Middle English whisperen, from Old English hwisprian (“to mutter, murmur, whisper”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwisprōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwisprōną (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweys-, *ḱwey- (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”). Cognate with Dutch wisperen (“to whisper”), German wispern (“to mumble, whisper”).

s: To act in a manner such that one has fun; to engage in activities expressly for the purpose of recreation or entertainment.
especially with 'with'; see also play with
To toy or trifle; to act with levity or thoughtlessness; to be careless.
To perform in (a sport); to participate in (a game).
Specifying a particular sporting role or position.
To compete against, in a game.
in the scoring of games and sports
To be the opposing score to.
To contend or fight using weapons, both as practice or in real life-or-death combats; to engage in martial games; to joust; to fence
To act or behave in a stated way.
To give a false appearance of being; to pretend to be.
To portray (a character) in (a film or theatre).
To produce sound (especially music), moving pictures or theatrical performance.
To produce music using a musical instrument.
To operate (a device or media) so as to cause sound (especially music) or moving pictures to be produced.
To render (a musical title, compositional style, film title, etc.) using a musical instrument or device.
e: From Middle English pleyen and Middle English pleye, from Old English plegian and plegan, plagian (“to play, exercise, etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *plehan (“to care about, be concerned with”) and Proto-West Germanic *plegōn (“to engage, move”), of uncertain origin.

s: A room in a home or hotel set aside for the use of visiting guests.
The angle by which an aircraft's nose is pointed upwind of its groundtrack to compensate for crosswinds during an approach and landing.
A vehicle, usually a car, that may be hired for single journeys by members of the public, particularly one with an automated meter to calculate the fare.
An aircraft used for practicing ground manoeuvres.
The movement of an aircraft across an airport's surface under its own power; a phase of aircraft operation involving this movement.
To move an aircraft on the ground under its own power.
To transport by taxicab, or in a way suggesting a taxi service.
e: Shortened from taximeter cab, taximeter (“automatic meter that records distance and fare”) from French taximètre, from German Taxameter (whence also English taxameter), coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”). More at tax, task.

s: A maneuver which rotates an object end over end.
A complete change of direction, decision, movement etc.
A whit or jot; the tiniest amount.
A hairstyle popular among boys in the 1960s–70s and 2000s–10s, in which the hair goes halfway down the ears, at which point it sticks out.
The purchase of an asset (usually a house) which is then improved and sold quickly for profit.
The tendency of a gun's barrel to jerk about at the moment of firing.
To throw so as to turn over.
To put into a quick revolving motion through a snap of the thumb and index finger.
To win a state (or county) won by another party in the preceding elections.
To turn state's evidence; to agree to testify against one's co-conspirators in exchange for concessions from prosecutors.
To induce someone to turn state's evidence; to get someone to agree to testify against their co-conspirators in exchange for concessions.
To go berserk or crazy; to get extremely angry.
To go berserk or crazy; to be extremely thrilled or enthusiastic.
e: Alteration of earlier fillip, from Middle English filippen (“to make a signal or sound with thumb and right forefinger, snap the fingers”), an attenuated variation of flappen (“to flap, clap, slap, strike”). Cognate with Dutch flappen (“to flap”), German flappen (“to flap”).
Compare English dialect flip (“nimble, flippant, also, a slight blow”).

s: A place where prescription drugs are sold or dispensed.
The science of medicinal substances, inclusive of pharmaceutics, pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacology, phytochemistry, and forensics.
The role or occupation of a pharmacist.
A collection, group or set of drugs or similar products; a set of drugs taken.
e: From Middle English pharmacy, borrowed from Middle French pharmacie (“the art of creating drugs; a drug, especially a laxative”), from Old French farmacie, from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (“the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (“a drug, charm, enchantment”), of uncertain but likely origin. Attested since late 14th century.

s: An unusually large payment due at the end of the term of a loan agreement.
e: So called because the debt becomes inflated like a balloon as a result of the compound interest accumulating on the large sum.

s: A raised rib in knitted goods or fabric, especially corduroy.
The texture of a piece of fabric.
A horizontal ridge or ledge on the outside planking of a wooden ship, such as a gunwale or a chainwale.
A horizontal timber used for supporting or retaining earth.
A timber bolted to a row of piles to secure them together and in position.
A ridge on the outside of a horse collar.
A ridge or streak produced on skin by a cane or whip.
To strike the skin in such a way as to produce a wale or welt.
To beat a person, especially as punishment or out of anger.
To give a surface a texture of wales or welts.
Something selected as being the best, preference; choice; choosing.
e: The noun is from Middle English wāle (“planking, welt”), from Old English walu (“ridge, bank; rib, comb (of helmet); metal ridge on top of helmet; weal, mark of a blow”), from Proto-Germanic *waluz (“stick, root”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, wind, roll”). Akin to Low German wāle; Old Norse vala (“knuckle”).

From Middle English wale, wal, from Old Norse val (“choice”), from Proto-Germanic *walą, *walō (“desire, choice”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, want”). Akin to Old Norse velja (“to choose”), Old High German wala "choice" (German Wahl "choice"), Old English willan (“to want”). More at will.

s: A black person with light skin with yellow undertones.
Of a black person, having a light skin tone.
e: After the golden-yellow skin tone of some multiracial people. "High" is usually considered a reference to a social class system in which skin color (and associated ancestries) is a major factor, placing those of lighter skin (with more white ancestry) at the top and those of darker skin at the bottom.

s: To remain in a particular place, especially for a definite or short period of time; sojourn; abide.
To continue to have a particular quality.
To prop; support; sustain; hold up; steady.
To support from sinking; to sustain with strength; to satisfy in part or for the time.
To stop; detain; keep back; delay; hinder.
To cause to cease; to put an end to.
To put off; defer; postpone; delay; keep back.
To bear up under; to endure; to hold out against; to resist.
To remain for the purpose of; to stay to take part in or be present at (a meal, ceremony etc.).
To stop; come to a stand or standstill.
To come to an end; cease.
e: From Middle English stay, from Old English stæġ (“stay, a rope supporting a mast”), from Proto-West Germanic *stag, from Proto-Germanic *stagą (“stay, rope”), from Proto-Indo-European *stek-, *stāk- (“stand, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”).
From Middle English *steȝe, from Old English *stǣġe, an apocopated variant of stǣġel (“steep, abrupt”), from Proto-West Germanic *staigil (“steep”), see sty.

s: A large room, especially one used to receive and entertain guests.
A gathering of people for a social or intellectual meeting.
An art gallery or exhibition; especially the Paris salon or autumn salon.
A beauty salon or similar establishment.
e: Borrowed from French salon (“reception room”), from Middle French, from Italian salone (“large hall”), augmented form of sala (“hall”), from sala (“room, house, entrance hall”), from Proto-Germanic *salą (“dwelling, house, hall”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“human settlement, village, dwelling”).

s: A slideshow: a set of slides for a presentation, either digital or physical.
An item of casual clothing: a top with no sleeves.
The top of a ship's bilge tank, usually the lowest horizontal surface on board.
e: The upper part of a tank suit worn by female swimmers in modester times when swimming pools were called swimming tanks.

s: The growth of the economic output of a country.
A student at a military school who is training to be an officer.
A younger or youngest son, who would not inherit as a firstborn son would.
Junior. (See also the heraldic term cadency.)
A young man who makes a business of ruining girls to put them in brothels.
A young gentleman learning sheep farming at a station; also, any young man attached to a sheep station.
e: Borrowed from French cadet, from Gascon capdet, from Late Latin capitellum (“small head”). Attested in English from 1634. Doublet of caddie, cadeau, cadel, capital, capitellum, caudillo.

s: Used preceding a name as a title for a mother.
Used as a (respectful) term of address for a woman, especially an older one.
A dominant female partner, often used as a term of address.
A woman regarded as sexually attractive or promiscuous.
Often preceded by oh: used to express approval, joy, surprise, etc.
Used as a (respectful) term of address for one's mother.
e: The origin of the is Uncertain; it is probably a of ma, thought to be a sound made by babies when breastfeeding.
Borrowed from Xhosa umama and Zulu umama, sometimes only distinguishable from English mama (see etymology 1) by the context and pronunciation.

s: A secluded religious community in Eastern Orthodox Christianity which is a dependency of, and generally less physically substantial than, a monastery, generally consisting of living quarters and a church.
e: From ecclesiastical (medieval) Ancient Greek σκήτη, which is either from a place name in Egypt Σκήτις, Coptic Ϣⲓϩⲏⲧ, or via aphesis from ἀσκητής (“ascetic; monk, hermit”).

s: A vehicle for hire, typically smaller than a bus, taking passengers on a fixed or semi-fixed route without timetables, departing when all seats are filled.
Nut-shaped; of or relating to a nucule — a section of a compound (usually hard) fruit.
e: Respelling representing a mispronunciation of nuclear by and epenthesis or by association with nuke.

s: In a dejected manner, in a dispirited way.
A bag in which nuts are carried or stored.
A silly, crazy or stupid person.
A special ornamental typographical symbol, such as a bullet, an arrow, a pointing hand etc.
An architectural style of apartment building, where the second storey overhangs an area for parking cars.
A kind of word puzzle involving pictures or typography that hint at the solution.
Anything that can be thrown or swung with force against something else.
A small device or gadget, the correct term for which is forgotten or unknown.
e: Unknown, US mid 19th century. The word-puzzle sense comes from the board game Dingbats, which is based on these puzzles. In the sense of a miscellaneous gadget, probably influenced by dingus or its etyma.

s: A poem or other text in which certain letters, often the first in each line, spell out a name or message.
A poem in Hebrew in which successive lines or verses start with consecutive letters of the alphabet.
A kind of word puzzle, whose solution forms an anagram of a quotation, with its initial letters often forming the name of the person quoted.
A kind of word puzzle in which a series of words are clued, and individual letters from the clued word spell out one or more additional words.
e: Borrowed from Middle French acrostiche, acrostique (“acrostic”) (modern French acrostiche), and its etymon Late Latin acrostichis, from Ancient Greek ἀκροστιχίς, from ἄκρο- + στῐ́χος (“row or file of soldiers; line of poetry, verse”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steygʰ- (“to climb, go”)).

s: Suggesting or characterized by hippie attitudes.
A somnambulist; one who walks, or is active, while asleep.
One in a state of magnetic or mesmeric sleep; someone in a hypnotic trance.
A person from whom a voodoo practitioner (a bocor) has taken over control of their mind, making them a zombie who must do the bocor's bidding.
One who goes though life in a state of obliviousness.
To remove the regulations, or legal restrictions, from.
To adjust; to optimize; to rebuild.
A blue blazer, part of the school uniform at Harrow School.
e: From blue + -er (“Oxford -er”). Used at Harrow School in London, United Kingdom.

s: a person who studies oceanography, the science of oceans
A freshwater turtle of the eastern United States of the genus Pseudemys.
e: Borrowed from cootuh (“turtle”), from an African language, e.g. kuta (“turtle”). Attested in English from the 19th century.
Uncertain. Possibly identical to Etymology 1, above; compare clam, beaver. Alternatively, compare cooch from hootchy-kootchy.

s: The ordinal form of the number forty.
The person or thing in the fortieth position.
One of forty equal parts of a whole.
e: From earlier fourteth, from Middle English fourtithe, fourtiþe; equivalent to forty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.

s: A crack or fissure in a glacier or snowfield; a chasm.
A breach in a canal or river bank.
A discontinuity or “gap” between the accounted variables and an observed outcome.
In a theatrical or dramatic manner.
In theaters, or in terms of the theater.
The result of disfiguring; the state of being disfigured.
An X-ray picture of the breasts (mammaries), used to screen for breast cancer.
One who squats; one who sits down idly.
One who occupies a building or land without title or permission.
A poor vagrant; a hobo or beggar; one suffering from extreme poverty.
The act of assigning a caption.
A step that is wrong, a false step.
To make an error or mistake.

e: From French laitue romaine, and direct borrowing of French romaine, from its supposed association with Rome.

s: A cosmetic product intended to give the skin a temporary bronzed colour resembling a suntan.
To approve; to permit to proceed.
To approve or requisition the harming or death of; to put a hit out on.
A large hairy humanoid creature of western North America.
A theory that views environment, rather than heredity or culture, as the important factor in the development of an individual or group.
A political and social ideology that seeks to prevent the environment from degradation by human activity.
A mostly herbivorous sirenian of the genus Trichechus, having a paddle-like tail and nails on their flippers, found in tropical regions.
e: Borrowed from Spanish manatí, from a -language term meaning ‘breast’, ultimately from *manatɨ; compare manaty, manatï, manaty, manatï, manatü, manatî.

s: The act of one who blackmails.
Breeding between members of a relatively small population, especially one in which most members are related.
A humorous play on words; such plays on words collectively.
A witty verbal exchange; such exchanges collectively.
The part of a cryptic clue that indicates but does not define the solution.
To bring about by urging or encouraging.
To goad or urge (a person) forward, especially to wicked actions.
e: Borrowed from Latin īnstīgātus, perfect passive participle of īnstīgō (“to instigate”), see -ate.

s: Taking a direct object or objects.
of a relation on a set
Having the property that if an element a is related to b and b is related to c, then a is necessarily related to c.
Such that, for any two elements of the acted-upon set, some group element maps the first to the second.
Such that, for any two vertices there exists an automorphism which maps one to the other.
Of a set of dice: not having the intransitive property.

e: Abbreviation of dreadlocks. Sense of “Rastafarian person” by synecdoche.

s: The state of being bold; courage.
The relative weight of a font; the thickness of its strokes.
e: From Middle English boldnesse, equivalent to bold + -ness. Cognate with Scots baldness, bauldness (“boldness”).

s: To speak (words) with a spasmodic repetition of vocal sounds.
To expel a gas with difficulty.
A speech disorder characterized by stuttering.
Containing fangs; full of sharp teeth.
A person who lacks brains; an idiot.
Having the traits of a vampire; vampiric.
To apply insecticides or insect repellents to, in order to be sure that no lice or other parasites are present.
To remove malicious software, such as viruses, trojans, spyware, or worms, from.
A state of being that is not life (but may resemble it).
Resembling vomit in colour, texture, etc.
In a manner portending future disaster, devastation and doom.
A person who, or thing which cripples.
A corrugated board used to grain leather.
A sighting of an extraordinarily rare bird, such that it almost has an paralysing effect on the birder.
Suitable for munching; characteristic of a snack.
Lacking vigor or decisiveness; spineless; wishy-washy.
One who is insipid, sentimental or weak.
Talk or writing which is weakly sentimental or affectedly pretty.
e: From the poem Namby-Pamby (1726) by Henry Carey, a satire on the sentimental pastorals of the poet Ambrose Phillips. The word is a satirical distortion of Phillips' name.

s: A utensil, as a bucket or cup, used in bailing; a machine for bailing water out of a pit.
A delivery that heads towards the bails after pitching.
A delivery in which the ball hits one or both bails but does not dislodge them.
Having a specified kind or number of garages.
To prevent troops from entering (an area).
To return (an area) to civilian control, after military control.
A child. Often used lovingly or in an affectionate way.
A rag baby; a puppet made of cloth.
A disease characterized by headache, chills, fever, and soreness of muscles, caused by the presence of nematodes of genus Trichinella in the intestines and muscular tissues.
The edible root of the yam bean (Pachyrhizus erosus) used in salads in Central America and as a snack in Mexico.
e: Borrowed from jícama, from Classical Nahuatl xīcama, form of xīcamatl.

s: A valved, lip-reed brass aerophone—typically pitched in B-flat—characterized by a predominantly conical bore, cup mouthpiece, and three piston valves, which produces a darker, mellower timbre than the trumpet or cornet.
Infl of liquefy; Alternative spelling of liquifying.

e: Diminutive of Cupid; originally a brand name.

s: To look or stare with anger.
That which glows or emits light.
e: From an alteration (possibly Scots) of glore, from Middle English glōren, glouren (“to gleam; to glare, glower”); or from glow (“to stare”) (obsolete), and ultimately from a Scandinavian (North Germanic) language. Cognate with Low German gloren (“to flicker; to glimmer”), Dutch gloren, Icelandic glóra. glow + -er. See more at glare.

s: That cannot be tolerated or endured.
That cannot be supported; that cannot be demonstrated or proved. (of a statement, claim, argument, etc.)
e: From Middle French insupportable, from Late Latin insupportabilis. See also in- + supportable.

s: something, such as a substance or medicine, that purges; laxative
A slow-witted, unresponsive, or inept person (usually male).
The process of putting text in boldface.
A four-sided spinning top, inscribed with the four Hebrew letters נ, ג, ה, and ש (or פ) on each side, often used to play a traditional game during the Jewish festival of Hanukkah.
A gambling game played using this top.
A dockworker involved in loading and unloading cargo, or in supervising such work.
To load or unload a ship's cargo.
Of or pertaining to an individual who suffers from kleptomania.
The state or quality of being special.
A place of shabby lodging, particularly a filthy hotel or run-down apartment.
A mammal whom the speaker dislikes.
Having lustful desires; characterized by lewdness.
Of or relating to the libido.
e: From Middle English libidinous, borrowed from Latin libīdinōsus.

s: Any small crawling animal such as a spider, insect or worm that is unpleasant.
e: A partial appellativization of Kreepy Krauly, a brand name, from Etymology 1.

s: The act of one who simpers.
A woman or girl employed to care for children.
To tend to as a nursemaid.
To care for or look after.
The act by which something is flayed.
A blanket, especially one used as a security blanket.
An informal, festive performance by folk singers, often including audience participation with the use of acoustic instruments.
A placeholder word for a nonspecific or forgotten thing.
e: Unknown; potentially Scottish. Use is tied to the Appalachian culture in the US.

s: The act of watching a location or people, generally covertly.
One who commits blasphemy; a person who mocks or derides a deity or religion, or claims to be God.
e: From Middle English blasfemour, from Old French blasfemeor; equivalent to blaspheme + -er.

s: A person who fights a duel.
Pertaining to, full of, or characteristic of moles (burrowing insectivores).
A kind of coconut curry from Madras.
Resembling or characteristic of a skank (disreputable woman).
Resembling or characteristic of the skank dance.
A brook; an occasional small waterway: a ditch, a gutter or drain; a ravine.
e: From Middle English sich, siche, from Old English sīċ (“a watercourse; sike”), from Proto-West Germanic *sīk, from Proto-Germanic *sīką (“slow flowing water; a trickle”).

s: A green chalcedony that is sprinkled with red spots or veins of hematite.
e: From blood + stone, from the fact that the red inclusions in the stone resemble blood.

s: The study of demons, especially the incantations required to summon and control them.
The supply and purchase arrangement engaged in by an outgrower.
One who whines about perceived problems; a complainer.
One who chats or talks to excess.
Having a high tendency to melt.
In the state of being melted.
A rope used to retain the bars of the capstan in their sockets while it is being turned.
A rope used to encircle a boat longitudinally, to strengthen and defend her sides.
The forward shroud of a lower mast.
To tighten (e.g. slack standing rigging) by bringing the opposite shrouds nearer.
A wavy underline used to indicate an error in text or source code.
Having the style of a cartoon.
One who practices taxidermy, the stuffing of animals.
Deception by the use of trickery, quibbling, or subterfuge.
An individual act of trickery or deception.
The quality of being inclined to trickery or deceitfulness.
e: From French chicanerie (“trickery”), from chicaner, from Middle French chicaner, borrowed from Middle Low German schicken, from Old Saxon *skikkian, from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan (“to order, arrange”). Related to German schicken (“to send, ship”), Middle English skekken (“to send forth, issue”).

s: The act of creating a croon.

e: From Middle English gravere, graver, gravoure, from Old English græfere, grafere (“graver; engraver; sculptor”), equivalent to grave (“to engrave”) + -er. Cognate with Dutch graveur, German Graveur, Danish gravør, Swedish gravör, Icelandic grafari.

s: Of food or drink: containing sugar.
A contagious fungal infection of the skin, characterized by ring-shaped discolored patches, covered by vesicles or scales.
e: From Middle English ringworm (“ringworm; intestinal worm”), from Old English rengwyrm (“maw-worm, intestinal worm”), equivalent to ring + worm.

s: To treat gently or with great care.
To cook slowly in hot water that is below the boiling point.
To exercise excessive or damaging authority in an attempt to protect. To overprotect.
An Irish dish comprising layers of roughly sliced pork sausages and bacon rashers with sliced potatoes and onions.
e: Probably from caudle. Compare British dialect caddle (“to coax, spoil, fondle”) and cade.

s: Not diluted or mixed with other substances.
Pure; unadulterated; free from extraneous elements.
Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of witches; witchlike.
To sing (a song) in such a way that the voice fluctuates rapidly between the normal chest voice and falsetto.
The place to which one's spirit descends upon death, conceived as below the surface of the earth.
The locale of the spirit world or afterlife, whether deemed to be situated below the world of the living or not.
Specifically, a location of punishment in the afterlife; a hell.
A hidden, shadowy, or sinister subculture, such as that of organized crime.
A small, decorative, somewhat weighty object placed on one or more pieces of paper to keep them from fluttering away.
Any object used for this purpose.
The act of making a blunder.
A stick used to play drums.
The second joint of the legbone of a chicken or other fowl, especially as an item of food.
The moringa or drumstick tree, Moringa oleifera, especially its slender, cylindrical pods.

Physical exercises with the participation of a multitude of muscles and often minimal equipment (thus, usually bodyweight exercises); strength training aspects and cardio aspects are both involved, and stamina is often a focus.

e: Of cow, which see for more.

s: A holy candelabrum with seven branches used in the Temple of Jerusalem.
A candelabrum with nine branches, used in Jewish worship on Hanukkah.
e: Borrowed from Hebrew מְנוֹרָה. From the same Proto-Semitic root *nūr- (“light”) as minaret.

s: Changeable, dynamic, evolutive; inclined to change, evolve, mutate.
Having a value that is changeable during program execution.
Being one of the signs Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius and Pisces, associated with adaptability, flexibility and sympathy.
Something mutable; a variable or value that can change.
e: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). muta- + -able.

s: Lacking sufficient staff or people, as for normal or efficient operations.
Having, or occurring during an interval with, fewer than a full complement of players, often as the result of a penalty.
Having fewer than the standard number of players.
A way of catching fish at night with torchlight and spear.
To lend money at exorbitant rates of interest.
e: From the character Shylock in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (1600).

s: A desire for bloodshed and carnage, often aroused in the heat of battle and leading to uncontrolled slaughter and torture.
The quality or degree of being bad.
A type of glove or garment that covers a hand with a separate sheath for the thumb, but not for other fingers, which are either enclosed in a single section or left uncovered.
The paw of a cat or dog that is of a different color from the main body.
A romantic rejection; dismissal of a lover.
To dress in mittens; to put a mitten on.
e: From Middle English myteyne, from Old French mitaine (Modern French mitaine), of unclear origin; possibly from mite, miste (“playful name for cat”) + -aine.

s: A kiss, especially that which is on the cheek.
Someone who easily agrees to give oral sex.
e: Perhaps from a dialectal variation of smack. Compare also Low German smok (“a kiss, a smouch/smooch”), Schmutz, Schmützle (“a kiss, a smooch”).
The interjection is an application of the noun.

s: A mythological creature generally depicted as a bird-of-prey with the head of a maiden, a face pale with hunger and long claws on her hands personifying the destructive power of storm winds.
One who is rapacious or ravenous; an extortioner.
Any of a number of eagle-like birds of prey of the subfamily Harpiinae, especially the species Harpia harpyja.
The European moor buzzard or marsh harrier (Circus aeruginosus).
e: Ultimately from Middle French harpie, from Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ, from ἁρπάζω (“to snatch, seize”). Compare rapacious. Middle English had arpie.

s: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging.
The removal of bones from a carcass; filleting.
The arrangement of bones in a corset.
The fertilization of a field with bone meal.
The process or result of leveling using a boning rod.
Placement of a curse by pointing with a bone, practiced by Australian aborigines; an act of pointing the bone.
The process of passing something through a funnel.
A jerk; a person who is unlikable, detestable, or contemptible because they are stupid, foolish, clumsy, oafish, inept, malicious, or unpleasant.
Best; the best of the best.
Best; the best of the best.
(by extension) A field of corn: maize, wheat or other cereal crop.
Hypocritically or self-righteously pious; sanctimonious; smugly morally superior.
e: From Isaiah 65:5 in the Bible (King James Version; spelling modernized): “Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou”; from Hebrew קְדַשְׁתִּיךָ.

s: The act or process of using formulas and/or usually rhyming words, sung or spoken, with occult ceremonies, for the purpose of raising spirits, producing enchantment, or creating other magical results.
A formula of words used as above.
e: From Middle English incantacioun, from Old French incantation, from Latin incantatio. More at enchant.

s: An unseen ghost which makes noises and causes disruption, especially by causing physical objects to move or fly about.
e: German Poltergeist, from poltern (“to rumble”) + Geist (“ghost”), cognates with English boulder and ghost, respectively.

s: To designate a date earlier than the actual one; to move a date, appointment, event, or period of time to an earlier point (contrast "postdate".)
To exist or to occur before something else; to antedate.
A publication, such as a newspaper or magazine, that is issued with a printed date later than the date of issue.
A type of settee having a seat at each end at right angles to the main seats.
Pertaining to antithesis, or opposition of words and sentiments; containing, or of the nature of, antithesis; contrasted.
To fit or clasp together securely.
A safety device that prevents activation in unsafe conditions.
To obtain by pulling or violent force.
To distort, to pervert, to twist.
To tune with a wrest, or key.
The act of wresting; a wrench or twist; distortion.
A key to tune a stringed instrument.
Ellipsis of saw wrest; a saw set.
A partition in a water wheel by which the form of the buckets is determined.
A metal (formerly wooden) piece of some ploughs attached under the mouldboard (the curved blade that turns over the furrow) for clearing out the furrow; the mouldboard itself.
e: Possibly a variant of wrist: see the quotation. Wrist is also derived from *wrīþaną (“to weave, twist”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *wreiḱ-, *wreyḱ- (“to bend, twist”), *wreyt- (“to bend”).
A misspelling of rest, probably influenced by wrest (etymology 1, verb and noun).

s: Accepting of one's legal or moral obligations and willing to do them well, and without complaint.
Pertaining to one's duty; demonstrative of one's sense of duty.
The state or condition of being dismembered.
Removal from membership; detachment from an organization, group, etc.
The act of giving a prod.
Cut in the edge into points or inequalities, like teeth; dented on the surface; jagged; notched; stamped in.
Having an irregular, uneven border; sinuous; undulating.
Notched like the part of a saw consisting of the teeth; serrated.
Bound out by an indenture; apprenticed; indentured.
Notched along the margin with a different colour, like the feathers of some birds.
Excessive; unreasonable or inappropriate in magnitude.
e: From Middle English inordinat, from Latin inōrdinātus (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ōrdināre (“to arrange, order”).

s: Having a taste of hops; heavily flavoured with hops.
Tending to jump; full of jumps.
Inconsistent with established standards of good form or taste.
e: From Middle English unsemli, probably a Old Norse úsǽmiligr; equivalent to un- + seemly. Cognate with Icelandic ósæmileg (“offensive”), Norwegian usømmelig (“unseemly”), Danish usømmelig (“unseemly”), German unziemlich.

s: A long pin, normally made of metal or wood, used to secure food during cooking.
A scenario in which a piece attacks a more valuable piece which, if it moves aside, exposes a less valuable piece.
To attack a piece which has a less valuable piece behind it.
e: From Middle English skeuier, skuer, likely a variant of Middle English *skever, *skiver (compare Modern English skiver), probably of origin, compare Icelandic skífa (“to slice”), Norwegian skive, Swedish skiva, Swedish skifer (“a slate”).

s: Of a tournament: in which the favorites win, or expected to win, most of the games.
The state of being a mother.
Erroneous in date; containing an anachronism; in a wrong time; not applicable to or not appropriate for the time.
The act of conveying from one place to another; the act of transferring or the fact of being transferred.
The process by which emotions and desires, originally associated with one person, such as a parent, are unconsciously shifted to another.
Any of several deciduous trees of the genus Prosopis found in America, and used as forage, which have long, beige seed and bean pods which may be dried and ground into a sweet, nutty flour.
The wood of these trees, used for smoking food, or charcoal made from this wood.
Country or land dominated by mesquite trees.
e: Borrowed from Spanish mezquite, mizquite, from Nahuatl mizquitl (“the mesquite tree”).

s: with emphasis; so as to make a point, especially with criticism.
A swampy, soggy area of ground.
A perilous, mixed up and troubled situation; a hopeless tangle.
To embroil (a person, etc.) in complexity or difficulty.
e: Recorded since 1579, from quag + mire. The sense “perilous, mixed up and troubled situation” has been recorded since 1775. Alternatively, the word may apparently be a variation of the earlier quakemire, from quake + mire.

s: The art of performing acrobatic gymnastic feats.
The brink of a dangerous situation.
e: First attested in 1598, from Middle French precipice, from Latin praecipitium (“a steep place”), from praeceps (“steep”), from prae + caput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“head”).

s: To breathe during sleep with harsh, snorting noises caused by vibration of the soft palate.
The act of snoring, and the noise produced.
An extremely boring person or event.
e: From Middle English snoren, fnoren (“to snore loudly; snort”), from Middle English snore, *fnore (“snore; snort”), from Old English fnora (“snort; sneezing”), from Proto-Germanic *fnuzô, from Proto-Indo-European *pnew- (“to breathe; snort; sneeze”).

s: To loot or plunder by force, especially in time of war.
e: From Old French pillage, from piller (“plunder”), from an unattested meaning of Late Latin piliō, probably a figurative use of Latin pilō (“to remove (hair)”), from pilus (“hair”).

s: an evil spell; a curse or hex
The vibrato system of an electric guitar, or just its lever (whammy bar)
Stimulated by uplift to renewed erosive activity.
Developed with steep slopes inside a district previously worn down nearly to base level.
Pertaining to, resulting from, or characterised by association; capable of associating; tending to associate or unite.
Such that, for any operands a, b and c, (a * b) * c = a * (b * c); whose multiplication operation is associative.
Addressable by a key more complex than an integer index.
Calling attention; flashy; standing out to the eye.
Making a striking or aesthetically pleasing display.
Inclined to showing (by conveying an impression so that events are described in the narrative), instead of telling (by explicitly stating facts).
Any of the medium-sized to large feliform carnivores of the family Hyaenidae, native to Africa and Asia and noted for the sound similar to laughter which they can make if excited.
A man that performs ritualized sex acts with recently widowed women and menarchal girls.
e: From Middle English hiena, variant of hyene, from Old French hiene, from Medieval Latin hyēna, from Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα. Displaced native Old English nihtgenġe.

s: Excited or full of energy, especially to excess.
Synonym of pure and virtuous, particularly
Sexually pure, abstaining from immoral or unlawful sexual intercourse.
Synonym of celibate, abstaining from any sexual intercourse.
Synonym of virginal, innocent, having or providing no sexual knowledge or experience.
Synonym of modest, particularly in reference to behavior expected of sexually pure women.
Synonym of austere, plain, unextravagant, particularly demure, sexually discreet.
e: From Middle English chaste, from Old French chaste (“morally pure”), from Latin castus (“pure”).

s: One who or that which divides or separates.
A physical object for dividing up a space.
A piece of card placed in a ring binder to separate groups of documents.
An electronic device for separating a signal, frequency, etc., into two or more parts.
A device resembling a drawing compass and used to transfer measurements of length.
The median or central reservation of a highway or other road where traffic in opposite directions are kept separated.
A plant, principally of Medicago sativa, grown as a pasture crop.
A type or breed of this plant.
e: From Spanish alfalfa, from Old Spanish alfalfez, from Arabic الْفَصْفَصَة (“alfalfa, lucerne”).

s: Having qualities resembling those of steel, especially hardness and resoluteness.
Any of the trailing or climbing vines producing fruit with a hard rind or shell, from the genera Lagenaria and Cucurbita (in Cucurbitaceae).
A hard-shelled fruit from a plant in Lagenaria or Cucurbita.
The dried and hardened shell of such fruit, made into a drinking vessel, bowl, spoon, or other objects designed for use or decoration.
Any of the climbing or trailing plants from the family Cucurbitaceae, which includes watermelon, pumpkins, and cucumbers.
e: From Middle English gourde, from Anglo-Norman gurde, gourde, from Latin cucurbita. Doublet of cucurbit.

s: To make subservient; to strip one of freedom; enthrall.
Of exaggerated importance; too heavily emphasized, hyped, etc.
A shrub, Lawsonia inermis, having fragrant reddish flowers.
A reddish plant substance, prepared from the dried leaves of this plant, used for temporary tattoos and hair coloring. Hair colorings range from bright red to earth brown to near black.
To dye or tattoo with henna.
e: Borrowed from Arabic حِنَّاء, the name of the tree used to make the dye, probably from Middle Persian (“to smear, anoint”). Doublet of alkanet.

s: Of, concerned with, or preoccupied with a world different from the tangible world, especially a fantasy, imaginary, or mystical world.
Odd and unfamiliar; strange, uncanny, weird.
Of, concerned with, or preoccupied with spiritual matters.
Of or relating to the imagination or intellect.
e: Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- From other world (“a world beyond death; a world other than the everyday world”) + -ly.

s: The tendency to undergo change, characteristic of both animal and vegetable organisms, and not restrained or checked by the environment.
The tendency to activity of muscular tissue, including the voluntary muscles, when in a state of healthful vigour and refreshment.
Being easily influenced (especially of young people).
e: From French impressionnable, equivalent to impression + -able. See also impressible.

s: The act by which something is unleashed.
To feel a prickling or mildly stinging sensation.
To cause to feel a prickling or mildly stinging sensation.
To cause to feel an ASMR response.
To ring; to tinkle or twang.
To cause to ring, to tinkle.
A prickling or mildly stinging sensation; frisson.
A tingling sound; a chime or tinkle.
A nail of the very smallest size; a tack.
A patch that covers a hole in something that needs to be watertight, such as a roof or a boat.
An attachment in the middle of a long guide line to keep it from sagging.
To fasten with a tingle; to tack.
To patch with a tingle; to cover a hole in something that requires it to be watertight.
To secure the middle of a guide line by means of a tingle.
e: From Middle English tinglen, of Uncertain origin. Possibly from Middle English tingen (“to tink”) + -len, equivalent to ting + -le. Alternatively, possibly a variant of Middle English tinclen or from Old English tinclian (“to tickle”). More at tinkle. Compare also West Frisian tingelje (“to tinkle”), Dutch tingelen (“to tinkle, jingle”).

s: A mechanical control device consisting of a handgrip mounted on a base or pedestal and typically having one or more buttons, used to control an aircraft, computer, or other equipment.
To maneuver by means of a joystick.
e: From joy + stick. First attested around 1910 (as joy-stick) as the control stick on an airplane. Its relation to the word joy is Unknown.

s: The act of one who lounges.
A red compound deposited during wine making, mostly potassium hydrogen tartrate; wine stone — a source of cream of tartar.
A hard yellow deposit on the teeth, formed from dental plaque.
A fearsome or angrily violent person.
e: From Old French tartre, from Medieval Latin tartarum, from Byzantine Greek τάρταρον, said to be from Arabic دُرْدِيّ, though it is already found in Pelagonius’s Ars veterinaria 46 in the adjective tartarālis, if the reading is correct.

s: Characterized by, or performed with, cleverness or contrivance; clever, ingenious.
Exhibiting or using much art or skill; dexterous; skilful.
Skilful at using dishonest or unfair means to achieve a purpose; crafty, cunning.
Knowledgeable about the liberal arts; learned, wise.
e: From art (“skill that is attained by study, practice, or observation”) + -ful.

s: To reduce to nothing, to destroy, to eradicate.
To react with antimatter, producing gamma radiation and (for higher-mass reactants, especially composite particles such as protons) lighter particles (such as pions, muons, and neutrinos).
To treat as worthless, to vilify.
To render null and void; to abrogate.
To cause to become zero by means of an annihilator operator.
e: Borrowed from Latin annihilātus, perfect passive participle of annihilō (“to reduce to nothing”) (see -ate), from ad (“to”) + nihil (“nothing”) + -ō. See also an-#Etymology_4.

s: Having been changed to fit in with a particular context or to be in sync with a phenomenon.
Lacking a soul (inherently or from death)
As if without a soul; insensitive, unfeeling.
e: From Middle English souleles; equivalent to soul + -less. Compare Old English sāwollēas; the Middle English word likely is a re-formation.

s: The state or condition of being a woman.
All of the women of a given place, area or subgroup regarded collectively.
The idealized nature of a woman: all of the characteristics traditionally and ideally ascribed to womanliness regarded collectively.

The self-concept of a woman with respect to her possession of the various qualities traditionally and ideally ascribed to womanliness; a woman's sense or view of herself as being more or less womanly.
The female genitalia, especially the vulva.
The one weakness of something or someone that is otherwise invulnerable.
To expose to, or attack with, kryptonite.
To destroy, wreck, or ruin; to affect adversely, as Superman is affected by kryptonite.
e: From a fictional radioactive element, kryptonite, that has a detrimental effect on the otherwise invulnerable character Superman. Formed from Superman's home planet Krypton + -ite, which was named after the chemical element krypton.
Borrowed from Middle French férocité, from Latin ferocitas, from ferox (“fierce”), from ferus (“wild, savage, fierce”).

s: That is able to, or is designed to, ventilate.
Tutoring; extra lessons in a specific subject outside of school hours.
That has been converted from analog to digital.
To follow (in time), to be subsequent to.
To occur afterwards, as a result or effect.
e: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre); see sequel.

s: in scope, effect, application or influence to a prior time or to prior conditions.
Very fast or quickly; a directive for the musician(s) to play in a very quick tempo.
Used by magicians when performing a trick; ta-da; voilà.
A pair of fives as a starting hand in Texas hold 'em.
To strike down or kill with godly force.
To put to rout in battle; to overthrow by war.
To afflict; to chasten; to punish.
To strike with love or infatuation.
A heavy strike with a weapon, tool or the hand.
e: From Middle English smiten, from Old English smītan (“to daub, smear, smudge; soil, defile, pollute”), from Proto-West Germanic *smītan, from Proto-Germanic *smītaną (“to sling; throw; smear”), from Proto-Indo-European *smeyd- (“to smear, whisk, strike, rub”).

s: A male fan who is obsessive about a particular subject (especially, something or someone in popular entertainment media).
To worship, support, drool over the object of affection; to be a fanboy.
Of a vehicle: having the height reduced by lowering the body with respect to the frame rails.
Sunken below the surface, resulting in a rounded channel.
Unhallowed; defiled by something unholy, either physically by an objectionable substance, or morally by guilt or sin
Unchaste; obscene (not according to or not abiding by some system of sexual morality)
Lively and often cheerful and enthusiastic.
A burn on the skin caused by excess exposure to the sun's rays.
A burn on the tissue of crop plants or their fruits (especially if they are rich in water like tomatoes, grapes, apples, gooseberries) caused by excess exposure to the sun's rays.
To burn or tan (someone's skin) by the sun; to allow (a part of one's body) to become sunburnt.
e: From Middle English *sunne burnen, *sonne brennen, *sunne brennen (suggested by derivatives sonne brennynge, sunne brennynge (“sunburn”) and sunne brente (“sunburnt”), equivalent to sun + burn.

s: The act of one who socializes.
The quality of being impatient; lacking patience; restlessness and intolerance of delays; anxiety and eagerness, especially to begin something.
e: Inherited from Middle English impacience, from Old French impacience (modern French impatience), from Latin impatientia. im- + patience.

s: A destructive capacity that exceeds that needed to destroy an enemy; especially with nuclear weapons.
Destruction beyond what is necessary to kill, especially in murder.
An unnecessary excess of whatever is needed to achieve a goal.
An unnecessary excess of disposal because of too high criteria of inspection.
To destroy something with more (nuclear) force than is required.
To dispose of too many items because of too-high criteria of inspection.
To do something excessive to achieve a goal.
Undeservedly; in a way that is not warranted.

e: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα, of Unknown ultimate origin.

s: Loud enough to cause temporary or permanent hearing loss.
The process by which something is deafened.
Linked, locked, or fitted closely together.
An arrangement of signal apparatus that prevents conflicting movements through a set of intersecting tracks, such as junctions or crossings.
A state of turmoil or agitated excitement.
To spin or swirl like the water in a whirlpool.
e: From earlier whirlpoole, whirlpole, apparently from Middle English *whirlpole, potentially coalescing Old English hwierfel (“whirlpool”) and Old English hwierfepōl (“whirlpool”). Equivalent to whirl + pool. Cognate with Scots quhirlepole, whirle-pule (“whirlpool”). Compare also English whirlpit.

s: The state or act of keeping faith.
Consistency; exactness in copying or following.
A Levantine Arab dip made of chickpea paste with various additions, such as olive oil, fresh garlic, lemon juice, and tahini, often eaten with pitta bread, or as a meze.
e: Borrowed from Arabic حُمُّص, an alternative pronunciation of حِمِّص.

s: A large drinking cup, often having a stem and base and used especially for formal occasions and religious ceremonies.
A kind of water-cooled pipe for smoking cannabis.
e: From Middle English chalis, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French chalice, collateral form of calice, borrowed from Latin calix, calicem (“cup”), of uncertain etymology. In view of skalçeta (“sacrifical vessel”), perhaps from a Proto-Italic *(s)kalik-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel-.

s: A small unspecified object; bric-a-brac (in plural).
A freestanding set of shelves on which ornaments are displayed; an etagere.
A confederacy or band of people.
A formal group or assembly of witches.
In fantasy fiction, a family, group or assembly of vampires.
A clique that shares common interests or activities.
e: From Middle English covent, from Anglo-Norman covent, cuvent, from Old French covent, from Latin conventum, from conveniō, from cum (“with”) and venio (“to come”). Doublet of convent.

s: The act or art of creating puns.
Any of various species of damselfly of the genus Lestoidea (not to be confused with superfamily Lestoidea), endemic to Australia.
The act of performing a wassail.
A new or recent member of a Greek monastic religious order; a caloyer.
A monk who lives in a religious community, rather than in solitude.
A torturous demon creature made famous by the Hellraiser series.
e: From Old French cenobite or Ecclesiastical Latin coenobīta, from coenobium, from Ancient Greek κοινόβιον (“community life, convent”), from κοινός (“common”) + βίος (“life”).

Borrowed from Yiddish באָבע (“grandmother”), and then either from a language or from eastern Middle High German bābe (“old woman”), both from *baba (“old woman”) and ultimately imitative of a child’s babbling. Doublet of baba.

s: Someone or something that can be persuaded.
To change the tone or pitch of the voice when speaking or singing.
To vary the form of a word to express tense, gender, number, mood, etc.
To be varied in the form to express tense, gender, number, mood, etc.
someone or something that causes or produces an effect.
The speech of one who tattles.
To alternate between scenes from one sequence and scenes from another film sequence, often with the sequences to be perceived as simultaneous.
An alternating sequence of this kind.
Something that is blurted, or spoken hastily without thinking.
To shoot again, especially of video recording.
Using, or characterised by, hacks: poorly designed workarounds.
Short and interrupted, broken, jerky; hacking.
Hackneyed (lacking significance through having been overused; unoriginal and trite)
A device used to stir. (Cardinal types include wood or plastic strips (for beverages) and magnetic objects that react to a spinning magnet nearby (for chemistry beakers).
A person who spreads rumours or causes agitation.
One who stirs or moves about, as after sleep.
A thick stew of European origin made throughout the Upper Midwestern United States, based on a broth of meat bones to which vegetables are added.
Entertainment involving naked people, especially women.
Any of several large North American hares of the genus Lepus.
To make a sudden, rapid movement
A person who engages in wild, wanton behavior: one who raises hell.
To confuse or overcome with glamour or showiness; to dazzle.
Powdered and perfumed talc for toilet use.
e: From talc + -um, from Medieval Latin talcum, from Arabic طَلْق.

s: A rank in the classification of organisms, below kingdom and above class; also called a divisio or a division, especially in describing plants; a taxon at that rank
A large division of possibly related languages, or a major language family which is not subordinate to another.
e: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (“tribe, race”).

s: Someone who advocates defeatism, or has such an attitude.
Having a hump or humps, or, in combination, a hump or humps of the specified number or type.
To make human; to give or cause to have the fundamental properties of a human.
To convert into something human or belonging to humans.
To make (an AI-generated text) seem as though it was written by a human.
Neuralgia of the sciatic nerve, characterised by pain radiating down through the buttocks and the back of the thigh.
e: Late Middle English, from Late Latin sciatica, feminine of sciaticus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός, the adjective of ἰσχίον (“hip”).

s: Of or relating to atheists or atheism.
One who acts in a practical or straightforward manner; one who is pragmatic; one who values practicality or pragmatism.
One who acts in response to particular situations rather than upon abstract ideals; one who is willing to ignore their ideals to accomplish goals.

One who belongs to the philosophic school of pragmatism; one who holds that the meaning of beliefs is the actions they entail, and that the truth of those beliefs consists in the actions they entail, successfully leading a believer to their goals.
To make a fundamental change to the behaviour or habits of.
To shift funds appropriated for one government program to a different government program.
To treat someone, or something roughly or badly.
To administer an incorrect treatment to a patient.
The act of, or a period of, working on the side (at a secondary job), often in the evening or during the night, either openly or secretly.
Something printed on paper, usually a copy generated by a printer (machine).
A brief media report of something that has recently taken place.
Introduces an obvious fact of which the person addressed is ostensibly not aware.
Of or pertaining to two races.
A person belonging to two races.
A composite particle that comprises two or more quarks held together by the strong force and (consequently) can interact with other particles via said force; a meson or a baryon.
e: Coined by Lev Okun in a plenary talk at the International Conference on High Energy Physics.

s: A relatively weak shaking movement; the condition or state of weakly shaking.
depictions of scantily-clad female bodies in motion, especially in action media genres.
To shake something gently; to rattle or wiggle.
An expression or motion that pouts; a pout.
A fish in the cod family (Gadidae), Trisopterus luscus.

A hollow muscular organ of the neck of mammals situated just below where the tract of the pharynx splits into the trachea and the oesophagus. It is involved in breath control and protection of the trachea, and, as it houses the vocal cords, sound production.
e: Borrowed from New Latin larynx, from Ancient Greek λᾰ́ρῠγξ (“larynx; windpipe; gullet, throat”).

s: A group of four, a quartet or a game (such as golf) played by four players, especially by two teams of two.
A sex act between four people.
A failure to fit well; unsuitability, disparity.
A badly adjusted person; someone unsuitable or set apart because of their habits, behaviour etc.
The daughter of one's spouse from a previous relationship.
e: From Middle English stepdoughter, stepdoghter, steopdohter, from Old English stēopdohtor (“stepdaughter”), from Proto-Germanic *steupaduhtēr (“stepdaughter”), equivalent to step- + daughter.

s: Having the specified kind of bark.
Anas platyrhynchos, a common and widespread dabbling duck, natively found throughout the Northern Hemisphere, whose male has a distinctive dark green head.
The meat of this bird, eaten as food.
e: From Middle English malard, mawlard, from Old French malard, malart, mallart (“male wild duck”), from Old French male, masle (“male”) + -ard, -art. Cognate with Medieval Latin maslardus, mallardus.

s: Pertaining to or having the nature of fire; containing fire; resembling fire.
Resulting from, or produced by, great heat. With rocks, it could also mean formed from lava or magma.
One who, or that which, gets.
A function used to retrieve the value of some property of an object, contrasted with the setter.
A material which is included in a vacuum system or device for removing gas by sorption.
A miner who dug coal, contrasted with the putter, who took it to the surface.
To remove gas by sorption, using a getter.
Something consisting of two or more elements combined together.
An artistic work that consists primarily of parts borrowed from other works, or features a mixture of genres.
A remix created by combining two or more songs from different artists into one piece of music.

A derivative work consisting of two or more pieces of (generally digital) media joined together, such as a video clip with a different soundtrack applied for humorous effect, or a map overlaid with user-supplied data.
A Web application that combines data or functionality from more than one source.
e: From mash (“to convert into a mash; to mix thoroughly”) + up.

s: Any of several forms of particle accelerator in which two opposing beams of particles collide.
A node in a causal graph that has at least two incoming edges.
A model of the shape of an object for purposes of collision detection.
Something which is free; a giveaway or handout.
Having not been filtered (e.g., coffee grounds).
The linguistic phenomenon of morphological variation, whereby words take a number of distinct forms in order to express different grammatical features.
Any specific type of morphological variation, which applies to a given word class.
An affix representing a given variation.
