Any specific morphological form of a particular word, such as the principal parts for any given stem; any of the declined or conjugated forms that constitute its declension or conjugation.
A change in pitch or tone of voice.
A change in curvature from concave to convex or from convex to concave.
A turning away from a straight course.
e: From older inflexion, borrowed from Middle French inflexion, itself borrowed from Latin inflexiōnem (“alteration”). The English spelling with ⟨ct⟩ is due to influence from inflect or related words like correction.

s: The act or product of one who sculpts; sculpture.
Fitted or furnished with a poop.
Having had a wave come over the stern from abaft.
Holding to one's own opinion obstinately and unreasonably.
Infused with opinions rather than wholly objective.
Enforcing one particular approach instead of offering options and flexibility.
The property of all possible outcomes being equally likely.
A type of circumstance or event that is described by a probability distribution.
A measure of the lack of purpose, logic or objectivity of an event.
Any of several species of large bee in the genus Bombus.
A mid yellow, sometimes slightly orange.
A layered drink with ice whose main ingredients are orange juice and espresso coffee.
e: 1520s from bumble + bee, replacing Middle English humbul-be. Merged with Middle English bombeln (“to boom, buzz”), in the late 14th century. The name of the drink is a Semantic loan from Ukrainian джміль.

s: To prove to be false or erroneous; to confute; to refute.
e: From Middle English disproven, dispreven, from Old French desprover, from des- + prover, equivalent to dis- + prove.

s: Squeezed into a compact mass by irregular folds.
Rising to a point or head; conical; pointed; crested.
The act of spending the night as a guest in another's house, especially when the participants are children.
A curved depression or natural amphitheatre, especially one in a mountainside at the end of a valley.
Something in the shape of a circle or ring.
e: Borrowed from French cirque (“circular arena; cirque”), from Latin circus (“circle, ring”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (“circle, ring; racecourse, circus”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend; to turn”). Doublet of circus.

s: The act by which something is bailed.
Used to indicate that what follows is to be taken as a figure of speech, not literally.
To an extreme or excessive degree; absurdly.
Overly excessive or flashy ornamentation or decoration.
e: First attested in the 1930s, of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to French fanfaron (“boasting”).

s: A hollow tube partially filled with pebbles or beans, and with small pins or thorns arranged helically on its inner surface, so that it produces a rain-like sound when upended.
In an incorporeal manner; without physical form.
To punish by dragging under the keel of a ship with the intent of causing painful injuries.
Discomfort, especially uneasiness associated with awkwardness, embarrassment, or self-consciousness.

e: Popularized by the 2002 television series Firefly.

s: The trade or traffic in old clothes.
The place where old clothes are sold.
Hence: secondhand finery; cheap and tawdry decoration; affected elegance.
e: From French friperie, from Old French fripier (“to rub up and down, to wear into rags”). Compare fripper.

s: A peasant, farmer or agricultural laborer in the Middle East and North Africa.
e: Borrowed from Arabic فَلَّاح (“peasant”), from Classical Syriac ܦܠܚܐ (“worker; peasant”). Attested since 1743.
Representing an eye dialect pronunciation of fellow.

s: To cover the eyes with, or as if with, a hood; to blindfold.
To deceive using a disguise; to beguile, dupe, mislead.
An act of hiding from sight, or something that cloaks or hides another thing from view.
The game of blind man's buff.
e: The verb is derived from hood (“head covering attached to a larger garment such as a jacket or cloak”) + wink (“to close one’s eyes”). (< C16 'to blindfold'). The noun is derived from the verb.

s: A soft, percussive sound, as of tiny feet, or of rain on a rooftop; patter.
Which ingratiates; which attempts to bring oneself into the favour of another, often with flattery or insincerity; smarmy; unctuous; oily.
Characterized by or constituting (any kind of) irony.
Given to the use of irony; sarcastic.
Feigning ignorance; simulating lack of instruction or knowledge; exhibiting Socratic irony.
Alternative spelling of re-attached, the past participle of re-attach.
Of an age suitable for marriage; marriageable (principally of a young woman).
Sexually attractive (especially of a young woman).
A woman of marriageable age; a sexually attractive young woman
e: From French nubile, from Latin nūbilis (“marriageable”), from nūbō (“marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ- (“to marry, to wed”). Possibly cognate with Ancient Greek νύμφη (“bride, young wife, nymph”) (English nymph), but this is disputed.

s: The act by which something is freshened.
To obtain illegally, as by con game.
To obtain money immorally or through deceitful means.
e: American criminal underworld slang, 1906 (noun), 1915 (verb), alteration of Doublet of graft, alteration perhaps influenced by similar sounding words, e.g. drift, etc., probably ultimately from Middle Dutch graft (“digging, ditch, canal, trench”) (modern Dutch gracht), related to Dutch graven (“to dig”), English grave (“to dig”).

s: That which consists of many previously separate parts.
An instance of conglomerating, a coming together of separate parts.
That prays frequently; characterised by prayer, devout, reverent.
An excess of what is needed or is appropriate.
Disagreeable, stubborn, and troublesome to deal with; cantankerous.
Troublesome to deal with in a good way; mischievous, prankish, teasing.
Ordinary, commonplace; hence, inferior, plain-looking, unpleasant.
e: A contracted or dialectal pronunciation of Doublet of ordinary. (“ordinary, commonplace”) was the earliest sense; the meaning of the word then shifted to “inferior, plain-looking, unpleasant”—presumably due to ordinariness—and finally to (“disagreeable, stubborn, and troublesome to deal with”).

s: Methodical and efficient, in a way that would be advantageous to a business or businessperson.
Earnest and practical without being distracted or enthusiastic.
Of speech or writing, communicative through the use of as few words as possible.
Of a speaker or writer, communicating through the use of as few words as possible.
e: + phrase From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (“Laconian”). Laconia was the region inhabited and ruled by the Spartans, who were known for their brevity in speech.

s: Indication of surprise or amazement; jinkies.
A lawspeaker: a declarer of the law.
One of 12 magistrates in certain Danish boroughs of England empowered with soc and sac over their own households.
The presiding justice of the supreme court.
A man of the law: a lawyer.
An officer of the law: a law-enforcement officer.
e: From Middle English laweman, laȝaman (as a man's name, Laȝamon, Layamon), from Old English lahmann, borrowed from Old Norse lǫgmaðr. In present use as a law-enforcement officer, law + -man.

s: Of or pertaining to a vestige or remnant; like a trace from the past.
Not fully developed in mature animals.
Of a vestigial structure; that has lost all or most of its original function in the course of evolution.
A small, degenerate, or imperfectly developed part or organ which has been more fully developed in some past generation.
Having a sex; being male or female.
Having had its sex determined; having undergone sexing.
Having a quantifiable libido or particular sex drive.
In a generous or overlarge quantity.
A person who lies or deceives.
e: Inherited from Middle English deceyvour, from Anglo-Norman decevour; deceive + -er. Displaced native Old English swica.

s: One who is not married; a bachelor or a spinster.
To go out and engage women in order to pick them up.
e: From sergeant, q.v. In reference to PUA slang, Coined by Q2375193 after the behavior of his cat Sarge.

s: A type of coloured marble from Belgium. Rance is red and often has white or blue graining.
A round or spreader between the legs of a chair.
The quality of being religious or pious, especially when zealous.
The act of one who cusses, or uses bad language.
Someone who creates black MIDI music.
Material sucked up by a vacuum cleaner.
A break between stages of a journey.
Having well-developed muscles with minimal bodyfat.
An instance of blocking or obstructing.
of a person or an animal
Sturdy; solidly built; heavy and compact.
A person who is subject to an indenture.
Any communication to get somebody's attention.
To call out one or more words.
Alternative form of hollow (narrow valley between mountains).
e: American variant of holla, hallo or hollo.

s: Brought to lie as near to the windward as it can to get out to sea, and thereby held steady.
Listening secretly to the private conversations of others.
The act of one organism listening for another's calls, so as to exploit them.
A skirmish involving an exchange of gunfire.

e: Recorded since 1890; possibly a derived from a ruction (“disturbance”) + rumpus (“disturbance, fracas”) - potentially with influence from raucous (“rowdy, hoarse”), from Latin raucus (“rough, hoarse”).

s: To give power, strength, or vigour to (oneself or someone, or to something); to strengthen.
To support (one's or someone's opinion, statement, etc.) by producing evidence, etc.; to confirm, to corroborate.
To increase the nutritional value of (food) by adding ingredients, especially minerals or vitamins.
To make (something) structurally strong; to strengthen.
To add spirits to (wine) to increase the alcohol content.
To install fortifications or other military works; also, to put up a defensive position.
To undergo, or cause to undergo, fortition.

e: From Spanish panatela, the name of a long thin biscuit, from the Italian diminutive panatella, which ultimately derives from Latin pānis (“bread”).

s: A fictional motor car that hovers a short distance above the ground.
In the manner of pleasing rhythmic music, as would make one tap one's toes.
e: From tap one's toes. Also from toe-tapping.

s: A robot designed to kill; a robotic assassin.
A device that allows the wearer to watch video material as if immersed in the world being shown.

e: From Yiddish תּחת (“buttocks”), in turn from Hebrew תַּחַת (“buttocks”).

s: self-determination (in the context of African-American culture)

e: From Quranic Arabic جالُوت, proper name equivalent to English Goliath, giant warrior of the ancient Philistine ethnicity; cf. connotations of derogatory uses of English Philistine. Doublet of goliath.

s: An upward movement of part of the Earth's crust.
Capable of or fit for being smoked (as tobacco, etc.).
A human or another living creature with flesh in its composition.
e: From meat + bag. The use as a slur for organic lifeforms – as opposed to robots or AIs – originated with the robot Bender from the animated TV series Futurama, but it became still more popular with its use by killer droid HK-47 from the Star Wars fictional universe.

s: To divide an image into pixels, or to display an image in pixels.
To transform an image (or a portion thereof) into large pixels, especially in order to hide details.
Too many to be counted (either by reason of being infinite or for practical constraints).
In a way that is incapable of being put into one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers or any subset thereof.
Syn of dorodango: a ball of dirt, especially one that is polished in a popular outdoor activity done by Japanese schoolchildren.
Like a tramp or homeless person.
A socialist ideology of cooperation and collective advancement that formed the basis of socioeconomic policies in Tanzania in the 1960s.
A village built according to this ideology, with central homes and school surrounded by communal farmland.
e: Borrowed from Swahili ujamaa (“brotherhood, extended family”), from jamaa (“family”), from Arabic جَمَاعَة (“group (of people)”).

s: The branch of medicine dealing with the pathology of the colon, rectum, and anus.
The branch of medicine dealing with the surgery of the colon, rectum, and anus.
Colorectal surgery as a specialty inside proctology.
The department or the building of the hospital or clinic.

e: From Middle English splendiferous, from Medieval Latin splendiferus + -ous, from Late Latin splendōrifer, from Latin splendor + -fer (“bearing”). Reintroduced humorously into English.

s: A paper card that is timestamped by a time clock to record the times when an employee starts and stops work.
A digital record representing the same concept.
An object, especially a gadget, whose name the speaker currently cannot recall.
The quality or state of being stupid.
The result or product of being stupid.
That cannot, or should not, be named.
An act of turning inside out.
The state of being turned inside out.
The condition of being turned outward.
To love; to like a lot.
e: From an expressively lengthened pronunciation of love ([lʌːv]~[lɜːv]~[lɐːv]). The spelling is based on non-rhotic English.

s: Technical or scientific language used to convey a false impression of meaningful technical or scientific content.
From the point of view of the layperson, technical and scientific literature not understood.
To calm (a person or animal) or put them to sleep using a tranquilizer dart.
To dart (a person or animal) with a sedative
Any small house, structure or fold used to house a cat.
A person or device that produces a great deal of noise, especially one used in a celebration or sporting event.

A device comprising a handle with a ratchet at one end, with the ratchet end contained within a box that serves as an echo chamber, so that swinging or moving the device causes the ratchet to rotate within the box, creating a series of loud clicking sounds
Any of various animals having ten legs or similar appendages, especially mollusks such as squid and cuttlefish.
Any crustacean of the order Decapoda, such as crabs or lobsters.
A nickname for either the 0-10-0 or 2-10-0 train configurations.
Mentally or physically infirm due to old age; senile.
A shaking or trembling movement, as of old age.
A person who is (very) drunk or intoxicated.
An artwork created using blots of ink or paint.
To become or cause to become (very) drunk or intoxicated.
To be annihilated or destroyed; to be blotted out.

A reagent made from non-fat dry milk, phosphate buffered saline, and sodium azide, which is used to block protein binding sites for laboratory techniques such as blots and the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
On Sulawesi: a hollowed-out tree trunk used as a boat.
e: From blot + -o. The verb sense “to be annihilated or destroyed” may be related to blot out.

s: A tool for cutting sheet metal.
A fish of the sea chub subfamily Girellinae.
A program for copying floppy disks at a low level (typically one bit at a time) to circumvent protection systems.
Articles of clothing or jewelry which hang from or around the neck.
Something that is tough, or difficult.
Someone or something that is strong and resilient.
A tough; Someone or something that acts as a thug or bully.

e: Probably a scummy + fuzzy 1960s, US, colloquial, expressive coinage, with influence from scum, fuzzy, lousy, sleazy.

s: An exclamation of accordance; okay, OK.
A single cigarette, especially one sold individually.
A track that is not part of an album.
To suffer violent involuntary contractions of the muscles, causing one's body to contort.
To be beset by political or social upheaval.
To cause (someone) to suffer such contractions, especially as a result of making them laugh heartily.
e: From Latin convulsus, past participle of convellere (“to pluck up, dislocate, convulse”), from com- (“together”) + vellere (“to pluck, pull”). Doublet of convel.

s: That which was done that should not have been, ranging from any sin or moral offense to various degrees of crime.
e: From Middle English misdede, from Old English misdǣd (“misdeed”), from Proto-West Germanic *missadādi, from Proto-Germanic *missadēdiz (“misdeed”); equivalent to mis- + deed.

s: Any substance used to whiten something; a bleach.
A person employed to whiten or bleach.
A powder added to tea or coffee in place of milk. A "non-dairy creamer".
Any germ or contaminant, real or imagined, especially from the opposite gender (for pre-pubescent children).
A nest-building female American coot (counterpart to cooter).
A sideswiper, a type of telegraph key.
e: Probably from Malay kutu (“flea, louse”) (and/or Tagalog/Maori). First attested in English in 1917 as British army slang during World War I.

s: The practice and sport of fishing for catfish using the bare hands.
Carried out at very low temperatures, near absolute zero.
Having little ambition for success or achievement
In a manner that leaves one stunned and horrified.
To interpret erroneously, to understand incorrectly; to misunderstand.
The science and technology of the production of very low temperatures.
The scientific study of low-temperature phenomena.
Cranky, disagreeable, or stubborn, especially if prone to odd whims or fancies.
e: From crotchet + -y, using crotchet in the 16th-century sense of a whim or fancy.

s: Any small monkey, now specifically a Central and South American monkey of the genera Callithrix, Mico, Cebuella, and Callibella, with claws instead of nails, and a rather primitive layout.
e: Borrowed from Middle French marmouset (“a gargoyle; a small child”), probably from marmouser (“to mumble”), of imitative origin.

s: A horizontal frame with wires stretched across it for drying paper.
A fictional alien creature in Star Trek, a fast-breeding, cooing ball of fur.
e: Unknown. The Century Dictionary suggests possibly a corruption of cribble (“sieve”).
Probably invented for alliteration with trouble; the creatures first appeared in an episode called "The Trouble with Tribbles".

s: Conforming tightly to the body, snug against the skin.
An explosive manufactured from a variety of materials, including nitroglycerine, wood meal and nitrates.
An explosive composed of nitrobenzene, saltpetre, sulfur and kieselguhr.
A naturally occurring carbonaceous material formed from coal, natural coke.
A thousand trillion (logic: 1,000 × 1,0004): 1 followed by fifteen zeros, 1015.
A million trillion (logic: 1,000,0004): 1 followed by twenty-four zeros, 1024.
Any very large number, exceeding normal description.

e: From Yiddish קלאָץ; cognate to German Klotz (“block, lump”). Doublet of clot, clod.

s: A session in which something is binged, such as food or television.
Any of several plants, of genus Echinacea, having pinkish-purple flowers.
A herbal medicine extracted from the roots and seeds of such plants.
The act of one who yodels.
Darker-skinned than white, but lighter-skinned than tawny; tan.
e: Alteration of obsolete swarty, from swart + -y, from Old English sweart (“black”).

s: The violent, criminal acts that are associated with thugs, and/or the fashion, manner of speaking, and demeanor associated with them.
A male lover, especially a young one.
The chemical element (symbol Cs) with an atomic number of 55. It is a soft, gold-colored, highly reactive alkali metal.
e: From Latin caesius (“sky-blue”), in reference to the radiation spectra, -ium.

s: To dig out of the ground; to take out of a place of burial; to disinter.
To uncover; to bring to light.
e: From Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

s: Of, relating to, being, or having the quality of felony.
Done with intent to commit a crime.
e: From Middle English *felonious (implied in feloniously; compare felonous); equivalent to felony + -ous.

s: A Chinese dumpling, often stuffed with varieties of meat or seafood and vegetables.

e: Originally reflecting a Scottish pronunciation. Compare Scots onyhoo, onyhow (“anyhow”).

s: A phrase used (by a stage magician, etc.) as a magical incantation to bring about some change: abracadabra, hey presto.
Some ineffectual action or speech, especially if intended to divert attention; nonsense.
Religious or supernatural phenomena one holds to be nonsense or mere trickery; superstitious mumbo-jumbo.
Some action carried out to bring about change as if by magic; a trick; sleight of hand, trickery.
To play tricks or practise sleight of hand (on someone); to cheat, to deceive.
e: . The interjection and noun are derived from pseudo-Latin magical incantations used by conjurers (formerly called “jugglers”) such as “hocus pocus, tontus talontus, vade celeriter jubeo” (by a particular 17th-century conjurer who allegedly adopted the moniker Hocus Pocus) and “hax pax max Deus adimax”.

s: Someone who is thick-skulled, stupid or stubborn.
A member of a neo-Nazi, white supremacist and antisemitic offshoot of the skinhead subculture.
A cocktail of rum, lemon or lime juice and sugar, sometimes with fruit added.
e: First use appears c. 1920. From daiquiri, named after a beach on the south coast of Cuba, from.

s: The act by which something is foiled; prevention of success.
The track of game, such as deer, in the grass.
Any human, the only members of the family Hominidae as traditionally defined.
Any anthropoid of the taxonomic family Hominidae, which includes all the great apes (chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans) as well as humans.
To invest with dignity or honour.
To treat as worthy or acceptable; to indulge or condone by acknowledging.
e: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”). See deign and fact.

s: To leave in a hurry; to go away.
To shut down (a nuclear reactor or, by extension, some other thing) for safety reasons, usually because of an emergency.
Of a nuclear reactor or some other thing: to shut down, usually because of an emergency.
A shutdown of a nuclear reactor (or, by extension, some other thing), often done rapidly due to an emergency.
The device used to shut down a nuclear reactor; also, the button or switch used to initiate a shutdown.
To scratch (something) with claws or fingernails; to claw.
To mine for ore on a small scale, especially from mines previously been worked on where most of the ore is believed to have been removed.
A scratch, especially caused by claws or fingernails.
A mine previously worked on where most of the ore is believed to have been removed, but which is still being mined on a small scale.
Of one's body or limbs: to become numb or stiff due to cold, lack of movement, etc.
To be weakened by an accident, a disease, starvation, etc.
e: Uncertain; the verb is possibly derived from etymology 1. It has been suggested that the word is an acronym for phrases like “safety control rod actuator mechanism”, “safety cut rope axe man”, “safety control rod axe man”, and “safety control rods activation mechanism”, but these are most likely backronyms. The noun is probably derived from the verb.

The verb is a variant of dialectal English scramb, possibly related to Dutch schrammen (“to graze, scratch”) and German schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”); see etymology 1. The noun is derived from the verb.

s: The act of going in quest of something.
A short skirt with its hemline well above the knees, generally at mid-thigh level.
The flower Camellia sasanqua, native to Japan and nearby islands.
e: From Yule (“Germanic Winter Festival”) + -tide (“period around a festival, season”); compare Swedish juletid.

s: Having insufficient power for its operation.
The likelihood that something will sell; market appeal.
A sweet cake or biscuit (crumbly leavened bread) typically made with flour, sugar, salt, butter, milk or cream, and sometimes eggs, and leavened with baking powder or baking soda.
A dessert made with such a cake, typically having layers of cream and fruit.
The cytopharynx of a ciliate, through which food is ingested.
The space between the teeth of a saw blade.
A preparatory cut or channel in excavations, of sufficient width for the passage of earth wagons.
The wide space under the pommel of a saddle; the hollow over the withers of a saddled animal.
e: From Middle English golet, borrowed from Old French goulet, from Latin gula.

s: An extragalactic object, starlike in appearance, that is among the most luminous and (putatively) the most distant objects in the universe.
e: quasi- + stellar, from quasi-stellar radio source. Coined by Hong-Yee Chiu in an article in Physics Today. quasi- + -ar.

s: A knit fabric similar to velvet, but usually somewhat coarser.
Of or pertaining to a janitor.

A cannon that combines certain characteristics of field guns and mortars, delivering projectiles with medium velocities, usually with relatively high trajectories; normally a cannon with a tube length of 20 to 30 calibers.
e: Borrowed from Dutch houwitser, from German Haubitze, from Middle High German haufniz, from Czech houfnice, which was derived from houf (“flock, crowd”) + -nice. The Czech noun houf comes from Middle High German hufe (“heap”), from Old High German hūfo.

s: The act of one who frolics.
having characteristics associated with being male, such as strength; exhibiting masculine traits to an exaggerated degree such as strength, forcefulness or vigor.
Possessing high sexual drive and capacity for sexual intercourse.
Pertaining to a grammatical gender used in plurals of some Slavic languages, corresponding to the personal masculine animate nouns.
e: From Middle French viril, from Latin virīlis, from vir (“man”, “male human”) + -īlis.

s: Scratched or marked by contact with another object.
Poorly made or done; of low quality.
The state or quality of being sterile.
Bearing cones, as the pine and cypress.
Of, or pertaining to, a conifer.
e: From Latin. cone + -i- + -ferous (“bearing”), or conifer + -ous (“pertaining to”), as reflected in the meanings.

s: A place of intense hatred, misery, or turmoil.

An apparatus composed of a wheel which spins inside of a frame (gimbal) and causes the balancing of the frame in any direction or position. In the form of a gyroscopic stabilizer, used to help keep aircraft and ships steady.
e: Borrowed from French gyroscope, coined in 1852 by physicist Leon Foucault, equivalent to gyro + scope, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (“circle”) and σκοπός (“watcher”).

s: The sound of one who whimpers; a whimper; a feeble complaint.
The quality or skill of giving an engaging or compelling performance; a stage presence.
A twisting turning battle between two or more military aircraft, especially between fighters.
A fight between dogs, especially as part of the blood sport of dogfighting.
To engage in a battle between fighter planes.
The act or actions of one who rampages.
Any of several trees, genus Durio, of Southeast Asia.
The spiky edible fruit of this tree, known for its strong taste and very strong, unpleasant odor.
A deep, rich yellow colour, like that of durian flesh (also called durian yellow).
e: From Malay durian, ultimately from *duRi (“thorn”). Doublet of iwi, from Māori.

s: A person who sympathizes (with a political cause, a side in a conflict, etc.); a supporter.
A person who has, shows or expresses sympathy (with another person or people); a person who enters into the feelings of another.
The philosophical belief that prioritizes happiness, particularly sensual pleasure as the highest good in life.
A general devotion to the pursuit of pleasure.
The placing of one thing on top of another.
The deposition of one stratum over another; the principle that in a series of sedimentary strata, the lower strata are the older.
The situation in quantum mechanics where two or more quantum states are added together (superposed) to yield another valid quantum state.
Something, generally a food or drug, having such an effect.
e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀφροδισιακός (“venereal”), from Ἀφροδίσιος (“pertaining to Aphrodite”).

s: Formed of a mass of small, tight, wiry curls; unruly or extending in all directions.
A small amount of unkempt, curly hair
An inexpensive waterproof covering used especially for floors, made from solidified linseed oil over a burlap or canvas backing, or from its modern replacement, polyvinyl chloride.
e: From Latin līnum (“flax”) + oleum (“oil”). Coined by Q907886 and used as a trade name but never registered as a trademark. It was the first product whose name was ruled to be genericized.

s: Having the consistency, feel, or texture of leather.
The act or process by which something is squared (in various senses).
An imaginary creature reputed to be mischievously inclined, for example, to damage or dismantle machinery.
Any mysterious, unknown source of mischief or trouble, or the problem created thereby.
A young, inexperienced surfer or skateboarder, regarded as a nuisance.
A person regarded as similar to a fictional gremlin, in particular: mischievous, troublesome, short, or annoying.

e: Back-formation from mutation on the basis of -ate, ultimately from Latin mūtō (“to exchange; to change, to vary”). Doublet of moult.

s: Any of several species of macropod marsupials; usually smaller and stockier than kangaroos.
To attribute or credit something to something; to impute.
To consider, think, esteem, reckon (a person or thing) to be, or as being, something
e: From Old French reputer, from Latin reputō (“to count over, reckon, calculate, compute, think over, consider”), from re- (“again”) + putō (“to think”).
Variant of an other, another, rebracketed as a nother. Compare Middle English a noþer.

s: A person of low moral standards.
A man who is sexually aggressive or forward with women to the point of causing disgust.
To act or progress in a sleazy manner.
e: Back-formation from sleazy, originally used to describe the thinness and low quality of cloth.

s: Shaped like an octagon, in having eight sides and eight angles.
A moist sausage of soft, even texture and flavor, often made from mechanically recovered meat or meat slurry.
e: From German Frankfurter, the demonym of Frankfurt. Specifically, a reference to Frankfurt-am-Main.

s: The liberation of hydrogen from an overcharged battery due to electrolysis of the electrolyte.
The process of passing cotton goods between two rollers and exposing them to numerous minute jets of gas to burn off the small fibres.
Of the giant Gargantua or his appetite.
e: From French Gargantua, a giant with a very large appetite in Rabelais's The Inestimable Life of Gargantua. Rabelais derived Gargantua from the Portuguese and Spanish garganta (“throat”).

s: Plural of shaving; those particles or pieces left after or created by shaving.
The motion of something that squirms.
The tendency to squirm or be restless.
The act of putting someone into danger, or the condition of being in danger.
The exposure of someone, especially a child, to danger or harm.
A wax secreted by bees from which they make honeycomb; or, the processed form of this wax used in the manufacture of various goods.
The targeting by men of overweight or obese women for sexual encounters, not due to sexual attraction but for amusement, or to take advantage of low self-esteem.
Taking up too much of something so others cannot use it.
Making a rough cut to quickly remove material
Drooping at the ends; arching; in distinction from sagging.
A taste of something that persists when it is no longer present.
The persistence of the taste of something no longer present.
A machine or robot designed to follow a precise sequence of instructions.
A person who acts like a machine or robot, often defined as having a monotonous lifestyle and lacking in emotion.
A formal system, such as a finite-state machine or cellular automaton.
A toy in the form of a mechanical figure.
The self-acting power of the muscular and nervous systems, by which movement is effected without intelligent determination.
e: From Ancient Greek αὐτόματον, neuter of αὐτόματος (“self moving, self willed”). Doublet of automat.

s: A formal demand made by one state or government upon another for the surrender or extradition of a fugitive from justice.
A notarial demand for repayment of a debt.

A formal request by a doctor or other clinician, usually on a standardized form, for specific medical tests or procedures to be performed on a patient by a third party, such as a laboratory or imaging center
A demand by the invader upon the people of an invaded country for supplies, as of provision, forage, transportation, etc.
A formal application by one officer to another for things needed in the public service.
That which is required by authority; especially, a quota of supplies or necessaries.
A call; an invitation; a summons.
To demand something, especially for a military need of staff, supplies or transport.
e: From Middle English requisicion, from Old French requisicion, from Medieval Latin requisitio. en + requisite + ion.

s: The condition of being impure; because of contamination, pollution, adulteration or insufficient purification.
A component or additive that renders something else impure.
A state of immorality or sin; especially the weakness of the flesh: inchastity.
e: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.

s: One who discovers: a person who has discovered something.
e: From Middle English discoverour, dyscowerer, partly from Middle French descouvreur and partly equivalent to discover + -er.

s: To grow too quickly in an uncontrolled way.
e: From Middle English overheten. Cognate with German überheizen, überhitzen (“to overheat”), Swedish överhetta (“to overheat”). en + over- + heat.

s: Not fit for people (or other living things) to live in; not able to be inhabited.
A liquid used to clean one's mouth.
To clean one's mouth with mouthwash.
An outlet from a liquid/fluid main often consisting of an upright pipe with a valve attached from which fluid (e.g. water or fuel) can be tapped.
e: An irregular formation: hydr + ant, originally US English. hydrate + -ant.

s: A morbid condition, characterized by yellowness of the eyes, skin, and urine.
A feeling of bitterness, resentment or jealousy.
To affect with jaundice; to color by prejudice or envy; to prejudice.
e: From Middle English jaundis, jaunis, from Middle French jaunisse, from jaune (“yellow”) + -isse (“-ness”). Jaune, from Old French jalne, from Latin galbinus (“yellowish”), from galbus (“yellow”).

s: An animal without vertebrae (i.e., without a backbone).
Having a certain type or number of pockets.
Of or relating to the members of the class Reptilia (reptiles).
Cold-blooded, treacherous, unavoidably selfish and hostile.
A reptilian person, especially a Jew.
A reptilian alien, especially of a shapeshifting race alleged to secretly control the world.
Of a country, region, etc., surrounded by land (having no borders with the sea).
Living in freshwater, such as landlocked salmon.
Of a property or parcel, surrounded by other property and having no access to a public road.
e: From land + locked (i.e. "locked-in by land on all sides").

s: To step or turn aside; to deviate; to swerve; especially, to turn aside from the main subject of attention, or course of argument, in writing or speaking.
To turn aside from the right path; to transgress; to offend.
A palpable depiction of a (usually sensational) vision of the future.
e: A generalised application of Futurama, the name of an exhibit-cum-ride at the 1939–40 New York World’s Fair that presented a possible model of the world twenty years thence (1959–60).

s: A sexually-provocative dance, involving the performer thrusting their hips back from a low squatting stance and shaking their buttocks.
The act of one who twerks.
A stonen coffin, often with its exterior inscribed, or decorated with sculpture.
The cement and steel structure that encases the destroyed nuclear reactor at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Chernobyl, Ukraine.
A type of wine cooler shaped like a sarcophagus (sense 1).
A kind of limestone used by the Ancient Greeks for coffins, so called because it was thought to consume the flesh of corpses.
To enclose (a corpse, etc.) in a sarcophagus (noun sense 1).
Permanently frozen ground, or a specific layer thereof.
Particularly of pigs or pork: infected with larval tapeworms or trichinae (parasitic roundworms).
Of a person: infected with measles.
(Fabric, cordage, etc made of) aramid fiber, an exceptionally strong, light, man-made fibre used to strengthen cables and sheet materials, e.g. in stab-resistant vests.
A piece of personal protective equipment made from Kevlar, such as a helmet or a vest.
e: Genericization of the trademarked name Kevlar, itself of obscure origin.

s: A cycle with three wheels, powered by pedals and usually intended for young children.
An autorickshaw; A motorized cycle rickshaw (usually a roofed motorcycle with sidecar, often available for hire in the manner of a taxi)
One who performs in a silly or ridiculous fashion; a clown or fool.
e: From Middle French bouffon, from Italian buffone (“jester”), from buffare (“to puff out the cheeks”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Middle High German buffen ("to puff"; > German büffen), Old English pyffan (“to breathe out, blow with the mouth”). More at English puff.

s: Endurable, survivable, suitable for living in, inhabitable.
To make the sound of water boiling on a hot surface.
To cook (something) in a manner which causes that sound.
The sound of water boiling on a hot surface.
The process of being cooked which involves that sound.
e: Probably a derivative of Middle English sissen (“to hiss; buzz; hum”), equivalent to siss + -le; Ultimately imitative.

s: A sweet, stretchable chewing gum designed for blowing bubbles.
A type of pop music marked by sweetness, pep and charm (rather than depth or complexity).
A light pink colour, the hue in which bubblegum is traditionally coloured.
typical of, or in the style of, pop music.
An inflamed (raised and colored) spot on the surface of the skin that is usually painful and fills with pus.
To mark, cover or disfigure (something) as with pimples.
e: Early Modern English pimple, pumple, from Middle English pymple, pympyl, of Uncertain origin but probably a nasalized variant of Old English *pipel, *pypel, from Old English piplian, pyplian (“to break out in pimples, show eruptions”), probably related to Latin papula (“pimple, pustule”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pap- (“pock mark, nipple”)).

s: Any of the diluted remedies used in homeopathy.
The state of being geometrically normal, at a right angle.
The state of being normal; the fact of being normal; normality.
e: From normal + -cy. The original sense was mathematical. The broader sense was popularized in the United States by its use by President Warren G. Harding.[https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=normalcy].

s: An official who is part of a bureaucracy.
A user on a wiki with the right to change users' access levels.
Capable of being raised to an upright position.
Capable of filling with blood and becoming rigid.
e: From French érectile, from Latin erectus, past participle of erigere, equivalent to erect + -ile.

s: Occurring across a single galaxy, interstellar.
Small square parcels of pasta filled with meat, cheese, spinach etc.
by analogy, similar dishes/pastas from non-Italian cuisines.
Synonym of dumpling, dishes similar to Italian ravioli, stuffed doughs and pastries.
Any bird of the genus Nucifraga in the crow family.
A bootleg mixed drink made from a blend of alcohols and fruit juices.
Something that is difficult to figure out; a puzzle.
Thirsty for blood: inexorably violent or eager for bloodshed; murderous.
Of a book, film, etc.: depicting much violence; gory, violent.
Of a mosquito, tenaciously seeking to draw blood.
e: From blood + thirsty. Cognate with West Frisian bloeddorstich (“bloodthirsty”), Dutch bloeddorstig (“bloodthirsty”), German blutdürstig (“bloodthirsty”), Danish blodtørstig (“bloodthirsty”), Swedish blodtörstig (“bloodthristy”), Norwegian blodtørstig (“bloodthirsty”).

s: A rapid-firing small-calibre cannon used especially as an anti-aircraft gun.
Arousing little or no interest; boring or uneventful.
A ball of minced or ground meat, seasoned and cooked.
An easy pitch to hit, especially thrown right down the middle of the plate.
A menu icon of three horizontal dots.
A restaurant that bakes and sells pizzas.
Of computer-generated animations: based on models with simulated bones or joints.
Beset with unfortunate circumstances that seem difficult or impossible to overcome; in imminent danger.
Having had the bones removed before cooking.
of a garment such as a corset or basque
Having the legs straightened during a trick.
Gerund of munch: the action of one who munches.
The sound of one who munches.
The stems and leaves of the coriander plant, Coriandrum sativum, used as a seasoning and garnish in cooking.
e: From Spanish cilantro, possibly from an unattested regional Vulgar Latin variant (with a front vowel) of Late Latin coliandrum, from Latin coriandrum (“coriander”). Doublet of coriander, culantro.

s: To collect into an assembly or assemblage; to bring into one place, or into a united body.
To come together; to assemble; to meet.
One who advocates for the protection of the environment and biosphere from misuse from human activity through such measures as ecosystem protection, waste reduction and pollution prevention.
One who holds the view that environment, rather than heredity or culture, is the primary factor in the development of an individual or group.
To restrict (someone or something) to a particular scope or area; to keep in or within certain bounds.
To have a common boundary with; to border on.
e: From Middle French confiner, from confins, from Medieval Latin confines, from Latin confinium, from confīnis.

s: The restoration to atmospheric pressure of a person who has spent time under higher pressure (such as a diver).
A mode of operation of some internal combustion engines which reduces the engine's compression ratio, making it easier to start but significantly increasing fuel consumption.
The relief of pressure on a body part by surgery.
The science of the dynamics of bodies moving relative to gases, especially the interaction of moving objects with the atmosphere.
The aerodynamic properties of a particular object (typically a car or aircraft).
e: From aero- + dynamics. Compare French aérodynamique, German Aerodynamik, and Italian aerodinamica.

s: In proportion; in due degree; adapted relatively.

A substance made by bees (clade Anthophila) primarily from beeswax which has hexagonal cells to hold their larvae, and for storing pollen and honey to feed the larvae and themselves when other food is scarce; it is also eaten by humans as part of comb-honey; a single sheet made up of two layers of t
Something resembling honeycomb in having numerous cells or small holes.
A space-filling packing of polytopes in three- or higher-dimensional space.
Something resembling honeycomb in sweetness; hence, something desirable or pleasant.
Used as a term of endearment: honey, sweetheart.
A crumbly confection usually made by boiling together golden syrup, sugar, bicarbonate of soda, and water.
To riddle (something) with small holes, especially in a pattern resembling a honeycomb; also, to cause (something) to become hollow or weakened in this way.
To bore cavities or tunnels inside (something).
To decorate (something) with a honeycomb pattern.
To make way deeply into (something) so as to weaken it; to undermine.
To ornament (a ceiling) with honeycomb work (see).
To become riddled with small holes, especially in a pattern resembling a honeycomb; also, to become hollow or weakened in this way.
e: {|class="floatright" | | |} The noun is derived from Middle English honycomb, from Old English huniġcamb, from huniġ (“honey”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kn̥h₂ónks (“honey”)) + camb (“comb”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“peg; tooth; row of teeth”)). The English word is analysable as honey + comb.

s: Impossible (unable) to avoid or escape; not escapable.
to make something inactive or no longer effective
to prevent the action of a biochemical agent (such as an enzyme)
to remove a person or piece of hardware from active military service
A partial obscuring of data points.
Going or moving back or further away from a previous position; gradually diminishing.
The action of something that recedes.
Cruel, abusive, unfair, or thoughtless treatment of a person or animal (or rarely an object).
Of two objects, at right angles; perpendicular to each other.
Of a pair of vectors: having a zero inner product; perpendicular.
Of a square matrix: such that its transpose is equal to its inverse.
Of a linear transformation: preserving its angles.
Of grid graphs, board games and polyominoes: vertical or horizontal but not diagonal.
Of a pair of elements in an ortholattice: each less than or equal to the orthocomplement of the other.
Statistically independent, with reference to variates.
Of two or more aspects of a problem, able to be treated separately; of a design, exhibiting consistency and composability.
Of two or more problems or subjects, independent of or irrelevant to each other.
e: From Middle French orthogonal, in turn from Medieval Latin orthogōnālis and Latin orthogōnius (“right-angled”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρθογώνιος (“rectangular”). ortho- + -gon + -al.

s: A difficult question or riddle, especially one using a play on words in the answer.
A difficult choice or decision that must be made.
e: A word of Unknown origin with several variants, gaining popularity for its burlesque imitation of scholastic Latin, as hocus-pocus or panjandrum.

s: A traditional Jewish greeting or farewell.
e: Borrowed from Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (“peace, well-being; Hello, good-bye”). Doublet of salaam, the same word via Arabic.

s: A woman employed in a shop.
The quality associated with home; domesticity.
In a vacant manner; inanely or foolishly.
In a mournful manner; as if in mourning for something.
An illustration that is on the page before the title page of a book, a section of one, or a magazine.
The title page of a book.
A façade, especially an ornamental one.
A small ornamental pediment, especially at the top of a window or door.
e: From Middle French frontispice, from Italian frontespizio or Medieval Latin frontispicium, from Latin frōns (“forehead”) + speciō (“to watch”) + -ium. Spelling altered due to folk etymology, influenced by piece.

s: Plain and unfashionable in style or dress.
To press the crust into the filling during baking, to allow the juices to caramelize on top.
e: First appears c. 1581. Origin Uncertain, probably literally "little poorly dressed woman," formed from doue, "poorly dressed woman". Possibly also related to the Scots dow, meaning to "fade".

s: possessed by an organism at birth.
The act of something that billows; a billow.
Affectedly modest, decorous or serious; making a show of gravity.
e: Inherited from Middle English demure, demwre, an abbreviation of Anglo-Norman de mure port (“with a mature demeanor”) (compare Old French meur from Latin mātūrus)

s: In an impulsive manner; with force; by impulse.
The act of one who strays; deviation or sin, often sexual infidelity.
In a heated manner; intensely or vehemently.
e: From Middle English *hotly, *hatliche, from Old English hātlīċe (“ardently, fervently”); equivalent to hot + -ly.

s: Alternative case form of Clarissa: a nun of the Order of Saint Clare.
e: Borrowed from Italian clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa; see there for more. Doublet of Clarisse, Clare, Clarist.
From Middle English torplen, of obscure origin. Compare torfel and topple.

s: A puzzle box solved with a passcode.
e: cryptology + codex, coined in The Da Vinci Code (2003); see quotations.

s: Clumsy, oafish, or socially awkward; unattractive or unkempt.
e: From schlub + -y; schlub is derived from Yiddish זשלאָב, perhaps from Polish żłób (“manger, trough; furrow, large groove in the soil”).

s: An act of abandoning a person in a remote, deserted place.
Habitually during the night; every night at night.
To grope, to make snatches at.
Of or pertaining to a romantic tendency or character.
A soft Italian cheese from Lombardy.
e: Borrowed from Italian taleggio, from a place name.

s: To snort, grunt; breathe or inhale noisily.
e: From Dutch snorken or Middle Low German snorken, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *fnoʀukōn (“to snore, snort”).

s: Messages, left by leaving a trail of smoke from an airplane, that are visible from the ground.
A device used to scan prepared forms used for multiple-choice and true-or-false testing.
A prepared form for use in such a device.
e: . By genericization of Scantron (from scan + -tron), a manufacturer and brand name of the devices.

s: Prepared in an Italian style with wine, mushrooms, spices and tomatoes.
A meal prepared in this style.
A board set up to windward in a boat, to keep out water.
A public commission charged with overseeing water quality in a particular area.
To subject to waterboarding, to pour water over a cloth covering the face and breathing passages of an immobilized captive.
e: From Middle English water boarde, waterbord, equivalent to water + board. Compare West Frisian wetterboard (“waterboard”), Dutch waterbord (“waterboard”), German Wassertafel (“waterboard”), Danish vandbræt (“waterboard”), Swedish vattenbräda (“waterboard”), Icelandic vatnsbretti (“waterboard”).

s: A person employed to perform all sorts of duties.
A large decorative printing block with a central space into which any letter can be inserted, used to mark the beginning of a chapter of a book in early printing.
A person having many diverse activities or responsibilities.
e: From Medieval Latin domine fac tōtum (“O Lord, do everything”), also with substition of nominative dominus for vocative domine.

s: The act of making a shush sound to silence somebody.
The first compartment of the stomach of a ruminant, the rumen.
The contents of this stomach in a slaughtered animal, viewed as food or a byproduct.
The belly of a human, especially a large, fat protruding one.
The thickened rim of a bell, struck by the clapper.
To remove the internal organs of a ruminant, prior to eating.
e: From Middle English paunche, from panche, Old French pance (French panse), from Latin pantex.

s: of a liquid, semisolid, or other substance
Having the nature or properties of an unguent or ointment; greasy, oily.
Having fat or oil present; fatty, greasy, oily.
Of an aroma or taste, or a beverage (such as coffee or wine) or food (such as gravy, meat, or sauce): having layers of concentrated, velvety flavour; lush, rich.
Profusely polite, especially in an insincere and unpleasant manner.
e: From Late Middle English unctuous, borrowed from Medieval Latin ūnctuōsus (“greasy, oily, unctuous”), from Latin ūnctum (“ointment; rich banquet; rich savoury dish”) + -ōsus. Ūnctum is a noun use of the perfect passive participle of unguō (“to anoint; to smear with oil, to grease or oil”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to anoint; to smear”).

s: of tools or objects, especially suturing needles
Having no eye: having no hole.
e: From Middle English eyles, eieles, equivalent to eye + -less. Compare West Frisian eachleas (“eyeless”), Dutch oogloos (“eyeless”), German augenlos (“eyeless”), Swedish ögalös (“eyeless”), Icelandic augnalaus (“eyeless”).

s: An Italian liqueur made from elderberries and flavoured with licorice, traditionally served with 3 coffee beans that represent health, wealth and fortune (or past, present and future).
An ancient form of triangular harp having a very sharp, shrill tone.
An ancient type of ship-borne siege engine.
e: Thumb|sambuca served over ice as a chasse-café Borrowed from Italian sambuca, from Latin sambūcus (“elder tree”), due to a similar 19th century liquor flavored with elderflower. Modern sambuca, which doesn't necessarily have elderberry, started being marketed in 1971.
+ (instrument),+ (siege engine) From Latin sambūca, from Ancient Greek σαμβύκη, ultimately from Aramaic סַבְּכָא.

s: The act of spreading needless fear; exaggerating purported threats in order to incite fear.
Having the quality called stank, i.e. jazzy, funky, good.
One of the wooden targets used in skittles.
(sometimes with out) To rapidly bowl out a succession of batsmen.
e: Origin Unknown. Perhaps of origin, from Old Norse skutill (“bolt, harpoon”), related to skjóta (“to shoot”), but the OED dismisses this connection as conjecture. The Old Norse word is related to Swedish and Danish skyttel (“shuttle, child's toy”). Compare also Old English sċytel (“a dart, bolt”). More at shuttle.

s: The practice of creating a fake profile on a social media platform in order to deceive people.
An urban style of acrobatic street dance that originated in the hip hop culture of New York City in the late 20th century.
e: From break + dancing. Influenced by breakdown (the percussion break of songs chosen by a DJ for use in hip-hop music) -- breakdancers were originally those who danced to a breakdown.

s: Eating utensils; cutlery, such as forks, knives and spoons.
Plates, dishes and other relatively flat crockery.
Alternative form of napa (Chinese cabbage or napa leather)
A decorative Native American object in the form of a hoop and net with attachments such as feathers, traditionally believed by the Ojibwa to “filter out” bad dreams.
The water used in a bath (bathtub).
A complaint, a grumble, a fit of ill-humor.
One who is grumpy or irritable.
To be grumpy or irritable; to complain.
e: From Middle English grouchen, variant of grucchen (“to complain, mumble, murmur”). See grutch.

s: A board with a corrugated surface against which laundry may be rubbed.
Such a board used as a simple percussion instrument.
A board fastened along a ship's gunwale to prevent splashing; a splashboard.
A stretch of ripples or bumps on a dirt or gravel road caused by interaction between traffic and road surface.
To produce a rippled texture on a surface.
To move up and down or back and forth across the surface of a hive, possibly to lay down a layer of propolis and wax.
Ilex paraguariensis, a species of holly native to southern South America; or the dried leaves and twigs of this plant, used to make the caffeine-rich beverage maté.
Any of various luxury forms of camping.
e: glamorous + camping. Of UK origin, first appears c. 2005 in The Guardian, adopted in the U.S. by 2007.

s: An annoying person or someone who is difficult to get along with.
One of the five basic tastes, the savory taste of foods such as seaweed, cured fish, aged cheeses and meats.
e: From Japanese 旨味, うまみ, from 旨い (“delicious”) + み (“-ness”), which describes the quality of a pleasant, savory taste.

s: The act of something that bottoms; the point at which something bottoms (in various senses).
Material used to line the bottom of something.
A substance used to prepare a material for dyeing.
Residue left at the bottom of something.
The contouring of the wooden seat of a chair.
The act of thoroughly cleaning something.

e: From Middle English meteles, from Old English metelēas (“foodless”), equivalent to meat + -less.

s: A wilt, especially one that affects multiple plants
Something that blinds, literally or figuratively.
A bag or cloth put over the head of a difficult horse while it is being handled or mounted.
A screen attached to a horse's bridle preventing it from being able to see things to its side.
Something that impairs visual or mental perception in a way figuratively compared to horses' blinders.
A bright light used to blind the audience temporarily during a scene change.
Dry and flaky due to excessive evaporation of water from its surface.
Having chaps, or jaws, of a specified kind.
A man funded by women who find him attractive, particularly
A hired escort or dancing partner.
A male prostitute with female clients.
To work or act as a gigolo.
To provide (someone) with the services of a gigolo.
To offer (oneself or someone else) to someone as a gigolo.
A card game resembling chemin de fer with many forms, usually entailing the player(s) betting against two or three hands dealt, and also bearing some similarities to blackjack.
e: . Borrowed from French baccarat, baccara, likely named after the French town Baccarat (noted for glassmaking) in Grand Est, of ultimately Unknown (. (uncertain)).

s: The member of staff at a restaurant who keeps the wine cellar and advises the guests on a choice of wines; a wine steward / stewardess, a wine waiter / waitress / server.
e: Borrowed from French sommelier (“originally, a person in charge of the beasts of burden carrying wine”), from somme (“pack”) + -ier. somme is from Vulgar Latin *sauma, from Latin sagma (“packsaddle”).

s: The set of pedal movements to be performed when playing a piano or organ.
A foolish or silly person or animal.
A pill or tablet containing a pharmaceutical which has hypnotic or intoxicating effects, especially a barbiturate.
The act or process of endearing, of causing (something or someone) to be loved or to be the object of affection.
The state or characteristic of being endeared.
Of or relating to the genitals or sexual intercourse.
Of a disease: sexually transmitted; of or relating to, or adapted to the cure of, a venereal disease.
Pertaining to the astrological influence of the planet Venus; lascivious, lustful.
Of or relating to copper (formerly called Venus by alchemists).
e: From Middle English venereal, venerealle (“of or relating to sexual intercourse”), from Latin venereus, venerius (“of or relating to sexual love”), from Venus (“Roman goddess of love”) (from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”)) + -eus, -ius.

s: A fantasy-fiction criminal or evildoer, often with supernatural powers or equipment, in popular children's and fantasy literature who can present a credible challenge for a superhero.
The action of the verb to rib; teasing.
A rib, or the collective ribs, on an object.
e: From rib (“tease”) + -ing; from the common practice of tickling the ribs to cause laughter.

s: A one-wheeled attachment to the side of a motorcycle to allow for a separate seat for a passenger or cargo space.
A cocktail made with cognac (or brandy), triple sec liqueur and lemon juice.
A software component that runs in a separate process from the rest of the software, to provide isolation and encapsulation.
Items that have been or are about to be ejected from a boat or balloon to lighten the vessel.
The act of throwing goods overboard to lighten a ship or aircraft in distress.
To eject from a boat, submarine, aircraft, spaceship or hot-air balloon, so as to lighten the load.
To let go or get rid of as being useless or defective.
e: From Anglo-Norman getteson, from Old French getaison, from geter, jeter (modern French: would be *jetaison like pendaison); possibly from a Vulgar Latin *iectātiō, from *iectātus iectāre, from Latin iactō. Doublet of jetsam.

s: Any of the sweet herbs of genus Stevia, native to tropical and subtropical regions of South America and western North America.
A sweetener, many times sweeter than an equal amount of sugar, extracted from Stevia rebaudiana, that can be substituted for sugar for some purposes.
e: Borrowed from Stevia, after 16th century Spanish botanist Pedro Jaime Esteve (latinized as Petrus Jacobus Stevus).

s: A small, spineless cactus (Lophophora williamsii) found from southwest United States to central Mexico that produces buttonlike tubercles that can be chewed for their psychedelic effect, primarily from the drug mescaline.
A mescal button produced by the plant.
A collection of writings on various subjects or topics; an anthology.
The condition of being miscellaneous, of being a hodgepodge.
e: Borrowed from French miscellanées, from Latin mīscellānea, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

s: An athletic contest consisting of ten events which includes sprinting, hurdling, jumping, and throwing over a span of two days.
A contest in science and math proving skill.
e: From dec- + -athlon, coined for the 1912 Summer Olympics in analogy to the word pentathlon.

s: The act of sliding downhill, or transporting something, on a sled.
Before now, until now, up to the present time; from the beginning to this point.
Previously within the present text; earlier herein.
e: From Middle English heretoforn, equivalent to here (“here”) + toforn (“before”), from Old English tōforan (“before”). More at here, tofore.

s: A small galley or cookhouse on the deck of a small vessel.
A small sand-filled container used as an oven on board ship.
The last car on a freight train, consisting of cooking and sleeping facilities for the crew; a guard’s van.
The person or team in last place.
A youngest child who is born after a long gap in time.
e: From Dutch kabuis, kombuis (“galley, kitchen”) or Low German Kabüüs (“galley”), from Middle Dutch cabûse and Middle Low German kabûs, kabûse respectively. Cognate with German Kabüse, Kombüse, Danish kabys, Swedish kabyss, French combuse (kabuys). Probably related to English boose (“a stall or shed”).

s: The large, mature form of the crimini mushroom (Agaricus bisporus)
e: In use by 1985. Uncertain origin. Possibly a marketing name; possibly from dialectal Italian pratarolo (“meadow mushroom”), ultimately from Latin pratum (“meadow”). It has also said to be named after Portobello Road in London, which originally led to the Porto Bello House.

s: To bid more than (somebody else) in an auction.
Within the walls; within one institution, particularly a school.
Within the substance of the walls of an organ.
A (usually sports) competition between teams belonging to the same school.
The part of a projecting stone or brick inserted in a wall.
The lighter parts of grain separated from the seed by threshing and winnowing; chaff.
A prolongation of current in a telegraph line, due to capacity in the line and causing signals to run together.
The act or process of briefly submerging or immersing an object or person in a liquid, as in dunking a cookie in milk, or dunking a playmate in the swimming pool.
A forceful thrust of the ball through the basket from above.
The act of one who domineers.
A one-piece garment for an infant or small child, generally worn over a diaper.
A one-piece fashionable streetwear worn mostly by teenagers.
e: From the Gerber Childrenswear brand name Onesies, which became reinterpreted as a plural. Equivalent to one + -sie.

s: The abnormal lateral curvature of the spine.
e: From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (“twisting; torsion”).

s: Similar to, or tasting like beef.
One or to whom a pledge is delivered as security one who takes anything in pawn.
A contagious disease caused by the Mumps virus of the genus Rubulavirus, mostly occurring in childhood, which causes swelling of glands in the face and neck.
e: Circa 1600, from mump (“grimace”), compare mump, most likely referring to the painful difficulty in swallowing.

s: The genitalia; those body parts that are not normally displayed; private parts.
(expletive) (A) hell of a; extremely or very.
e: Written form of a reduction (relaxed pronunciation) of hell of a.

s: The secretion of milk#Noun from the mammary gland of a female mammal.
The process of providing the milk to the young; breastfeeding.
The period of time that a mother lactates to feed her young; a lactation period.
One of the ingredients in an alloy.
An alloy of mercury used to fill tooth cavities.
e: From Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (“emollient poultice or unguent for sores”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (“emollient; malleable material”), from μαλάσσω (“to soften”), from μαλακός (“soft”). Doublet of malagma. For the verb, compare French amalgamer.

s: A small burrowing rodent native to North and Central America, especially in the family Geomyidae (pocket gophers).
e: Perhaps an adaptation of Cajun French gaufre, based on the analogy of holes in the ground to the indentations in a honeycomb or a waffle (Doublet of waffle). Alternatively, from.

s: To fit (an animal) with a microchip.
To cause microscopic chips (abrasions) in a material.
A tropical American evergreen tree, Carica papaya, having large, yellow, edible fruit.
An orange colour, like that of papaya flesh.
e: Borrowed from Spanish papaya, from papáia. Doublet of pawpaw.

s: A kitchenware utensil for cutting ball-shaped pieces of foods.
A person employed to divide molten metal into separate balls before it is hammered out.
One who plays basketball (US) or association football (UK).
One who has swag and lives an extravagant lifestyle.
Very cool, especially due to extravagance.
e: From ball + -er. The sense referring to extravagance comes from NBA b-ballers being wealthy.

s: Deprived of the opportunities and advantages of others, usually through no fault of one's own.
A deprived person; deprived people (normally used as a plural).
To schedule again or at a different time.
To reclassify; to change the schedule (division into which something is classified) of.
Someone, especially a romantic partner, with whom one is exceptionally or uniquely compatible or has a special, almost spiritual connection.
e: From soul + mate. First attested as soul-mate in an 1822 letter by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Not in common usage before the 1980s.

s: The area between the tee and the green, where the grass is cut short.
Any tract of land free from obstacles.
A channel either from offshore, in a river, or in a harbor that has enough depth to accommodate the draft of large vessels. (JP 4-01.6)
A navigable channel in a harbour, offshore etc; the usual course taken by vessels in such places.
A close-range shot in which the shooter banks the ball off the backboard from a few feet away.
The state of being laid up.
A track used to store train cars.

A side track, tunnel, or elevated structure where idle trains park during off-peak hours, overnight, or on weekend; a targeted spot because the stationary trains give them enough time to paint large pieces.
A train car sitting in storage (laid up), often overnight.
The process of applying alternate layers of a material and a binding agent to form a composite material.
An objectionable person; a bastard; a jerk.
A marsupial of the family Didelphidae of the Americas; an opossum.
A marsupial of several families of the order Diprotodontia, found in Australia and neighboring islands.
To play possum; to feign sleep, illness, or death.
Implied, but not made explicit, especially through silence.
Not derived from formal principles of reasoning; based on induction rather than deduction.
e: Borrowed from late Middle French tacite, or from Latin tacitus (“that is passed over in silence, done without words, assumed as a matter of course, silent”), from tacere (“to be silent”).

s: A traditional Japanese T-shaped, wrapped-front garment with square sleeves and a rectangular body, now generally worn only on formal occasions.
A long robe-like garment in Western fashion, which may be open at the front, loosely inspired by the Japanese garment.
e: Borrowed from Japanese, which is from 着 (“wearing”) +.

s: Any loud noise, such as from an elephant.
crude; unrefined or insensitive; lacking discrimination or taste.
e: From Middle English cras, craas, from Old French cras, from Latin crassus (“dense, thick, gross, fat, heavy”). Doublet of grease.

s: very busy; having too much to do
Having or showing keenness or sharpness of perception, insight, understanding, or intuition.
A supposed organ of the brain, dealing with concrete observations of reality.
The act of joining with rivets.
The act of spreading out and clinching the end, as of a rivet, by beating or pressing.
A set of rivets; rivets collectively.
An Indian soup having a meat base and curry seasoning.
An individual male who prefers voluptuous buttocks in a female.
An excess amount provided in one area in an effort to overcome a perceived lack in another area.
Excessive pay or reward provided for work performed.
A farm worker who looks after pigs.
A doctor specializing in the colon, rectum, and anus; an expert in proctology.
A type of woolen cloth with a diagonal ribbed texture on one side.
A similar fabric, made from cotton.
A yellow robe that Jews in England were compelled to wear in the year 1189 as a mark of distinction.
A step in a protocol in which information is exchanged between computing processor devices; often as part of the initiation process for communications.
A full or complete view; a good look.
A remarkable sight or a very attractive person.
Enough material to fill one's eye.
A brief period of sleep; forty winks.
Filling or attractive to the eye; visible; remarkable.
An edible mushroom (Boletus edulis), prized for its flavor.
One who puts meat on a spit.
A young deer whose antlers are beginning to shoot or become sharp.
Someone who spits out semen during oral sex.
A small shower (of rain), a spatter.
An improvised and portable spittoon, typically a beverage bottle repurposed.
The pronged plater used in frogging (transferring cells to another plate).
A person interested in frogs; a herpetologist who specialises in frogs; a frog enthusiast.
To dodge traffic while navigating across a busy road.
A person who engages in froggery.
e: From Frogger, a 1981 arcade game developed by Konami, in which the player directs frogs across a busy road and other hazards.

s: A piece of cloth used to cover the head; a bandana.
e: From Middle English keverchef, coverchef et al., from Old French couvrechief, from couvrir (“to cover”) + chief (“head”). Compare curfew.

s: An informal greeting, especially when answering the phone.
In a callous manner; done without regard to others' sensitivities.
A smooth tool that assists in putting the foot into a shoe, by sliding the heel in after the toe is in place.
Anything by which a transaction is facilitated; a medium.
Anything which draws on or allures; an inducement.
To force (something) into (a tight space); to squeeze (something) into (a schedule, etc); to exert great effort to insert or include (something); to include (something) despite potent reasons not to.
To force some current event into alignment with some (usually unconnected) agenda, especially when it is fallacious.
A studious or learned man; a scholar; a student of books.
One who sells or publishes books; a bookseller.
e: From Middle English bocman, from Old English bōcmann (“bookman, a holder of bookland”), equivalent to book + man.

s: A possible world, as a starting point for reasoning.
A baked Italian turnover made of pizza dough and stuffed with tomato, cheese and other toppings.
Expectancy; a condition when an ownership of real property is undetermined; lapse in succession of ownership of estate, or title.
Expectancy of a noble or armigeral title, its right in existence but its exercise suspended.
e: First attested in 1528. From Anglo-Norman abeiance (“legal expectation”), from Old French abeance (“desire”) from abeër (“to gape at, aspire after”), abaer, abair (“to desire”), from a (“to”) + baër (“to gape”), bair (“yawn”), from Medieval Latin batō (“to yawn”).

s: A fishing boat with identical bow and stern.
e: From peter (“a safe, cash box”) + man (the former being 17th-century slang, still in use).
After the apostle Peter, a fisherman.

s: In a greedy manner; with keen or ardent desire.
e: From Middle English gredyly, gredily, from Old English grǣdiglīce, grǣdelīce; equivalent to greedy + -ly.

s: A person, especially an entertainer, who practices ventriloquism.
A thick creamy soup made from fish, shellfish, meat or vegetables.
A form of unglazed earthenware; biscuit.
Of a pale pinkish brown colour.
To prepare ceramics in the bisque style.
An extra turn, free point or some other advantage allowed.
A free turn in a handicap croquet match.
A free point in a handicap real tennis match.
Exemption from work or other duty on a particular day.
A day's leave an employee may take without warning or reason and not be counted as annual leave.
Permission for an MP to be absent from a vote, granted by the whips when the absence is not likely to affect the outcome.
e: Borrowed from French bisque, of unknown origin; Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française, suggests a comparison with Spanish bisca (“gambling house, gambling den”).

s: That which overflows; the excess or side effect.
The spread of infectious disease between different species of animal and particularly to humans.
Of or pertaining to a lens system used to produce an enlarged image of a distant object.
A photograph taken through a telephoto lens.
Of, relating to, or designed for, or being children between the ages of approximately 10 and 12.
A child between approximately 10 and 12 years of age, at the onset of adolescence.
Full of, covered with, or similar to gravel or pebbles.
Of a voice: unpleasantly harsh or rasping.
Full of or covered with sand; sandy.
The tenderest part of a loin of meat, especially of pork or beef.
A district of a city where corruption is common, often because the district is devoted to questionable businesses (peep shows, etc) which are easy for police to blackmail and extort.
To free, disengage, loosen, or untangle.
To free from intricacies or perplexity.
e: Borrowed from Latin extrīcātus, past participle of extrīcō. Compare intricate.

s: A medicine which preserves or defends against disease; a preventive.
Any device or mechanism intended to prevent harmful consequences.
Serving to prevent or protect against an undesired effect, especially disease or pregnancy.

e: From Middle English wetnes, wetnesse, from Old English wǣtnes (“moisture, wetness”). wet + -ness.

s: Slowed or weakened, as by drink, sleepiness, etc.
Of a horse: bearing wholly on its heels when trotting.
Stranded and helpless, especially on a beach
A small recessed area set off from a larger room.
The geographical and geological term for a steep-sided hollow in the side of an exposed rock face or cliff of a homogeneous rock type, that was water eroded.
To furnish (something) with an alcove or to form an alcovelike recess.
e: From French alcôve, from Spanish alcoba or Portuguese alcova, from Arabic القُبَّة (“vault, chamber with vaulted roof”). Doublet of qubba.

s: Information (the story [on something], the truth [about something]), especially inside information and especially a summary of it that glosses over its minor details.
down low; purporting to be heterosexual while engaged in sex with men.
Unfairly; dishonourably; in a deceitful or mean manner.
e: Compound adjective of low + down in the sense of "humble" recorded in the 1540s, in the sense of "vulgar, far down the social scale" in 1888. Recorded as a noun in 1915 in the slang sense of secret or inside information.

s: Someone who tips; someone who gives a gratuity.
A goods vehicle with a tippable body, used for carrying loose materials such as gravel or rubble; a tipper truck, tipper lorry or dump truck.
A device for loading goods such as coal by tipping them.
One who gives private hints about racing or financial speculation, etc.; a tipster.
A cutting tool used to cut off or trim the horns of livestock; a horn tipper.
A person who tips or discharges a load, or dumps waste (especially illegally with the latter).
A kind of ale brewed with brackish water obtained from a particular well.
e: So called from the first brewer of it, one Thomas Tipper.

s: Reduced in size as a result of shrinkage; shrivelled.
A salad of finely shredded raw cabbage and sometimes shredded carrots, dressed with mayonnaise (white slaw) or a vinaigrette (red slaw).
e: Borrowed from Dutch koolsla (mentioned in English as the Dutch name by at least in 1794), from kool (“cabbage”) + sla (“salad”).

s: The act of glorifying or the state of being glorified.
Specifically, the ascension (of Christ or humans) to the glory of heaven.
The worshiping of a deity; extolment or laudation.
The portrayal of something as being ideal; idealization.
e: From Middle English glorificacion,glorificacioun, from Middle French glorification and its etymon Latin glōrificātiō. glorify + -ication.

s: That part of the skull consisting of the bones enclosing the brain, but not including the bones of the face or jaw.
The upper portion of the skull, including the neurocranium and facial bones, but not including the jawbone (mandible).
e: From Medieval Latin crānium (“skull”), from Ancient Greek κρᾱνίον (“skull”). crani- + -um.

s: To make (someone or something) physically dirty or unclean; to befoul, to soil.
To make (someone or something) morally impure or unclean; to corrupt, to tarnish.
To act inappropriately towards or vandalize (something sacred or special); to desecrate, to profane.
To cause (something or someone) to become ritually unclean.
To cause uncleanliness; specifically, to pass feces; to defecate.
To march in a single file or line; to file.
To march across (a place) in files or lines.
A narrow passage or way (originally, one which soldiers could only march through in a single file or line), especially a narrow gorge or pass between mountains.
An act of marching in files or lines.
A single file of soldiers; any single file.
An act of defilading a fortress or other place, or of raising the exterior works in order to protect the interior.
e: The verb is borrowed from French défiler (“to march; to parade”), from dé- + one or both of the following: The noun is borrowed from French défilé (“parade, procession”), a noun use of the past participle of défiler; see above.

The verb is borrowed from French défiler (“to arrange soldiers or fortify (something) as a protection from enfilading fire; to unthread”) (compare Middle French desfilher (“to unthread”)), from dé- + enfiler (“to rake with gunfire, enfilade; to string on to a thread; to thread (a needle)”) (from en- + filer or file; see etymology 2). The noun is derived from the verb.

s: The condition or state of being (or becoming) bald.
A young actress with a promising career ahead of her.
An accomplished and important supporting player in a sports team.
A house where insane persons are confined; an insane asylum.
Of a person: having a pleasing appearance; attractive; handsome.
Of a person: having a pleasant manner; amiable, friendly.
Being a legal person and thus able to maintain a plea in court, or to hold some property or right.
e: From Late Middle English personable, personabil (“having a pleasing appearance, handsome”), and then from both of the following: person + -able.

s: An added touch; an ornamental addition; a flourish.
An interaction between two parties in which information is/was not communicated as desired.
The process of passing urine, that is, of eliminating liquid waste from the body.
Turned or twisted to one side.
A storehouse for maturing wine, a winery.
A store specializing in Hispanic groceries.

Any small or medium-sized shop with a unique facade in a shopping center plaza, usually located in the center or the sides of the plaza. (Does not include the anchor tenant of the shopping center, as they are usually referred to as the anchor.)
e: Borrowed from Spanish bodega, from Latin apothēca (“storehouse”), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (“storehouse”). Doublet of apotheke, apteka, boutique. In New York, it was popularized by the Puerto Rican community.

s: The act by which something is flaunted.
In an irrevocable manner; in a manner which prevents the ability to be reverted, repealed, or undone.
Associated with or causing one or more sudden sharp increases.
The act by which something is spiked.
A thick, creamy soup or stew.
A stew, particularly fish or seafood, not necessarily thickened.
e: Probably borrowed from French chaudière, from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”). Related to English cauldron. Possibly from older English jowter (“fish monger”).

s: An artist who makes nudes: nude paintings, sculptures, photographs, etc.
