(usually attributive) Relating to, or reserved for, nudists and nudism.
Representing the sound of a large dog barking.
The action or motion of something that cascades.
A two-wheeled carriage pulled along by a person.
To move someone by means of a rickshaw.
e: Borrowed from Japanese, a clipping of, from 人力 (“human power”) + 車 (“cart”) (compare Mandarin 人力車).

s: having a specified form of wit (intellectual ability)
e: From Middle English witted, ywitted, equivalent to wit + -ed. Compare Old English witod (“appointed, ordained, assured, certain”).

s: One who, or that which, injects something.
One who injects (himself or herself with) psychoactive drugs.
Any of various devices that are used to inject something, as
An object that realizes a dependency injection.
Something which requires two hands to handle, such as
A food item requiring two hands to eat.
A play, film or television programme with only two main characters.
The act of shrinking, or the proportion by which something shrinks.
The loss of merchandise through theft, spoilage, and obsolescence: the shrinking of inventory.
The reduction in size of the male genitalia when cold, such as from immersion in cold water.
The unlawful taking of personal property as an attempt to deprive the legal owner of it permanently.
An individual instance of such a taking.
e: Coined in Middle English (as larceni) between 1425 and 1475 from Anglo-Norman larcin (“theft”), from Latin latrocinium (“robbery”), from latro (“robber, mercenary”), from Ancient Greek λάτρον (“pay, hire”). Doublet of latrociny.

s: To cause an erection of the penis or other physical signs of sexual arousal, such as fluid secretion.
To wake from sleep or stupor; to rouse.
In a cruel manner; with cruelty.
To a degree that is cruel.
To have a strong desire for something or to do something; to long for or to do something.
To long for something in the past with melancholy or nostalgia.
Of music, words, etc.: to express strong desire or longing.
To have strong feelings of affection, love, sympathy, etc., toward someone.
To be distressed or pained; to grieve; to mourn.
Often followed by out: to perform (music) which conveys or say (words) which express strong desire or longing.
To have a strong desire or longing (for something or to do something).
To cause (someone) to have strong feelings of affection, love, sympathy, etc.; also, to grieve or pain (someone).
A strong desire or longing; a yearning, a yen.
Of milk: to curdle, especially in the cheesemaking process.
Of cheese: to be made from curdled milk.
To curdle (milk), especially in the cheesemaking process.
A structure made up of layers.
A method of plant propagation by rooting cuttings.
A choice that has been permitted.
A rhetorical device in which a thing is predicated on the decision of one's opponent.
e: Possibly derived from French permis or Latin permissus; might also be a back-formation from permissible,permission,permissive.

s: Of, pertaining to, or in the style of cubism.
Resembling or characteristic of a bird.
In set theory, a semiset is a proper class that is a subclass of a set.
Of or pertaining to an internal skeleton, usually of bone (an endoskeleton).
Relating to, or having the form of, a worm.

e: Probably from *lunk (perhaps an alteration of lump; compare hunk & hump), a diminutive of lump + head.

s: A place where spacecraft can dock.
A relatively small spacecraft, usually capable of atmospheric transport.
The state or quality of being assured.
Of or pertaining to a supposed analogue of electronics using positrons
e: From positron + -ic. The science fiction sense was Coined by Isaac Asimov in his short story "Liar!".

s: The characteristic of being devious; sneakiness; underhandedness.
To bend the knee, as in servitude.
To briefly enter a position that touches one knee to the ground in a manner that is typically associated with formal homage or religious worship.
To behave in a servile manner; to grovel.
e: From around 1620–1630 from Medieval Latin genūflectō (“to bend the knee”) equivalent to the Latin genū (“knee”) + flectō (“to bend”).

s: A fictional futuristic handheld device used for scanning, which may be specialized for medical, technical or other purposes.
A real-world advanced handheld medical scanner.
e: The name of such a device in Star Trek, from tri- (referring to its three input keys, which by default cover geological, meteorological, and biological functions) + (re)corder.

s: A shell or other outer protective layer.
An outer protective covering such as the feathers or skin of an animal, a rind or shell.
The outer layer of an ovule, which develops into the seed coat.
Of or pertaining to a torus
The date on which a television or radio program is broadcast.
The rabble; crowds; people of a low, disreputable or undesirable class or position.
e: From Old French rif et raf (“one and all”), of origin. The first word is from rifler (“to scrape off”) and the last is from raffler, related to rafler (“to plunder”).

s: A North American mammal, Antilocapra americana, that resembles an antelope.
Of a shape similar to a squashed sphere.
A solid of revolution generated by rotating an ellipse about its major (prolate), or minor (oblate) axis.
A base (for trading, military operations, etc.) located in space, among the stars.
A visible mark left on a surface by the contact of a hand, not limited to fingerprints.
Unsure how to act or respond; bewildered, perplexed.
e: {| class="floatright" |- | | |}Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- From nonplus (“state of bewilderment or perplexity”) or nonplus (“to bewilder or perplex (someone)”) + -ed. Nonplus is derived from Latin nōn plūs (“no further, no more”), from nōn (“not”) + plūs (“additionally, more; further”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”)).

s: To place side by side, especially for contrast or comparison.
e: Borrowed from French juxtaposer, corresponding to juxta- + pose, derived from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to”) + pōnō (“place”).

s: The point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, etc., where it is nearest to the Sun.
The highest point or state; the peak, zenith.
In a sober manner; temperately; coolly; calmly; gravely; seriously.
That deserves, evokes or can be given pity; pitiful.
e: From Middle French, from Old French piteable. pity + -able.

s: To fill to satisfaction; to satisfy.
To satisfy to excess. To fill to satiety.
Filled to satisfaction or to excess; satiated, satisfied.
e: In Middle English; Borrowed from Latin satiātus, perfect passive participle of satiō (“to fill full, satiate, satisfy”) (see -ate and -ate), from satis (“sufficient”).

s: To end up; to set on end.
To destroy, invalidate, overthrow, or defeat.
Someone with an extraordinarily high capability of sensing the emotions of others.
Someone who does so through psychological talent or training, thus having an unusually good level of empathy.
Someone who does so through psychicness, telepathy, etc: that is, through either supernatural powers or neurotechnological powers.
The state or quality of being sentient; possession of consciousness or sensory awareness.
e: From sentient, from Latin sentiēns, present participle of sentiō (“feel, sense”). Compare with sentence, its equivalent formation from Classic Latin sententia (for *sentientia).

s: As though the situation is normal and not unusual; not dramatically or fancifully.
The behaviour of one who moralizes.
A room that provides holographic simulations for recreation, training, etc.
e: From holo- + deck, coined in the television series Star Trek: The Next Generation.

s: A Russian movement in modern art characterized by the creation of nonrepresentational geometric objects using industrial materials.
A style of modern architecture that flourished in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and early 1930s.
A philosophy that asserts the need to construct a mathematical object to prove it exists.
A psychological epistemology which argues that humans generate knowledge and meaning from their experiences.
A school of studying international relations that prioritises the way the behaviour of polities and agents in geopolitics is constructed by norms and identities.
A word (pronoun, pronominal adjective, or adverb) implying interrogation, or used for asking a question: why, who, when, etc.
floating in a river or sea, in particular fragments from a shipwreck.
e: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.

s: A person who intentionally causes the destruction of property in order to hinder the efforts of their enemy.
e: Borrowed from French saboteur See also saboter and the discussion of the etymology in.

s: Pertaining to only one direction, e.g.: where all component parts are aligned in the same direction in space.
Not subject to change or reversal of direction.
A fabric in which the majority of fibers run in the same single direction.
In a wry or sarcastic manner; ironically.
Walking on two feet or two legs; biped.
The wobbling motion of the axis of a spinning body when there is an external force acting on the axis.
The slow gyration of the earth's axis around the pole of the ecliptic, caused mainly by the gravitational torque of the sun and moon.
Any of several slow changes in an astronomical body's rotational or orbital parameters.
e: From Middle English precessioun, precession, from Medieval Latin prēcessiōn-, prēcessio, from Latin praecēdō.

s: Consisting of, or limited to, letters and/or numbers, especially the characters A to Z (lowercase and uppercase) and 0 to 9.
Consisting of these characters plus punctuation and other special characters.
Unlimited power; commonly attributed to a deity or deities.
e: From Late Middle English omnipotens, from Old French omnipotence, from Latin omnipotentia, from omnipotēns + -ia. omnipotent + -ence or omni- + potence.

s: To unstick; to get something unstuck
A member of a ship's crew who is responsible for steering.
Defective and impossible to materially correct or set aright.
Unmanageable; impervious to correction by punishment or pain.
Unchangeably established in a belief or habit.
Intrinsically incapable of being corrected; impossible to disprove, by its very nature.
e: From Middle English incorrigible, from Middle French incorrigible (1334), or directly from Latin incorrigibilis (“not to be corrected”), from in- (“not”) + corrigō (“to correct”) + -ibilis (“-able”), equivalent to in- + corrigible. Recorded since 1340.

s: To evoke an intense interest or attraction in someone.
To make someone hold motionless; to spellbind.
To be irresistibly charming or attractive to.
e: Borrowed from Latin fascinātus, perfect passive participle of fascinō (“to enchant, bewitch, fascinate”) (see -ate), from fascinum (“a phallus-shaped amulet worn around the neck in Ancient Rome; witchcraft”) + -ō, itself of obscure origin.

s: A section of code, called by the main body of a program, that implements a task.

e: The adjective is first attested in the first part of the 15 century, in Middle English, the verb in 1525; Inherited from Middle English procreat(e) (“(construed as past participle) begotten, procreated”), borrowed from Latin prōcreātus, perfect passive participle of prōcreō (“to beget”), see -ate; pro- + create. Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s: The quality or state of being irrational.
The state of being illogical or absurd.
The property of being an irrational number.
The state of being incapable of reason or abstract thought.
Something that is irrational; the result of an illogical or absurd thought or action.
e: From irrational + -ity. May also be analyzed as ir- + rationality.

From French sardonique, from Latin sardonius, from Ancient Greek σαρδόνιος, alternative form of σαρδάνιος (“bitter or scornful laughter”), which is often cited as deriving from the Sardinian plant (Ranunculus sardous or possibly Oenanthe crocata), known as either σαρδάνη or σαρδόνιον.

s: A major change in appearance or form; a metamorphosis.
A change that exalts or glorifies.
superposition of one or more ideal-elements in comparison with other real ones, often through imagination but sometimes at the risk of confusing when not clearly realized.
e: From Middle English transfiguracioun, from Old French transfiguracion, Anglo-Norman transfiguraciun, and Latin transfigūrātio.

s: Not burdened with worries, cares or responsibilities.
To make untidy, to make a mess

A greeting gesture in which the thumb and little finger are extended while curling the three middle fingers in a semi-fist, used to express a variety of positive meanings including all right, hello and goodbye.
e: Origin Uncertain. Shaka is not a word in the Hawaiian language, which lacks the /ʃ/ sound.

s: Not subjected to discipline, control or correction; uncorrected.
An isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron in each atom -.
e: From deutero + ium. Coined by Q179777, from Ancient Greek δεύτερος (“second”).

s: Of, or pertaining to, the Apocrypha.
Of doubtful authenticity, or lacking authority; not regarded as canonical.
Of dubious veracity; of questionable accuracy or truthfulness; anecdotal or in the nature of an urban legend.
Not knowable; not able to be known.

The fundamental force of attraction which exists between all matter in the universe that tends to draw bodies towards each other, due to matter causing the curvature of spacetime. It is the weakest of the four fundamental interactions, and possesses a gauge boson known as the graviton.

e: From Middle English trayterous, traytrous, (also Middle English traytours, treytours), from Anglo-Norman traiterous, traitourous and Old French traitros.

s: A place or situation of chaotic uproar, and where confusion prevails.
An insane person; a lunatic; a madman.
e: From Bedlam, alternative name of the English lunatic asylum, Bethlem Royal Hospital (royal hospital from 1375, mental hospital from 1403) (earlier St Mary of Bethlehem outside Bishopsgate, hospice in existence from 1329, priory established 1247), since used to mean “a place or situation of madness and chaos”. Bedlam as name of hospital attested 1450.

s: To seize and hold or use (powers, an office, a coat of arms, a right or copyright, etc) from another, without right (usually by illegitimate means).
To take the place of someone or something else; to supplant.
e: From Middle English usurpen, from Old French usurper, from Latin ūsūrpō.

s: of an approach to problem solving, learning, or discovery
That employs a practical method not guaranteed to be optimal or perfect; either not following or derived from any theory, or based on an advisedly oversimplified one.

That provides a useful, but not optimal, solution to a problem. Such algorithms are typically employed either because the only known algorithms that provide optimal solutions use too much time or resources, or else because there is no known algorithm that provides an optimal solution.
That reasons from the value of a method or principle that has been shown by experimental investigation to be a useful aid in learning, discovery and problem-solving.
The art of applying heuristic methods.
e: Irregular formation from Ancient Greek εὑρίσκω (“I find, discover”) (compare the proper Greek term εὑρετικός).

s: A word hybridizing Ancient Greek and Latin or other heterogeneous roots.
An error in language use within a single word, such as a mispronunciation.
A name or title by which someone is addressed or identified; a designation.
A geographical indication for wine that describes its geographic origin.
e: From late Middle English appellacion, from Old French apellatiun, from Latin appellātiō (“a naming”).

s: Something that inverts, or causes inversion.
Not belonging to, or dependent upon, a thing; without or beyond a thing; foreign.
e: From Latin extrāneus (“from without, strange”). Doublet of strange. Cognate with estrange, Spanish extraño.

s: Of or pertaining to cosmology, or to the overall structure of the universe.
Notched or cut like a saw.
Having a row of sharp or tooth-like projections.
To cause to move (suddenly), as by pushing or shoving; to give a (sudden) start to.
To divert to a less important place, position, or state.
To move data in memory to a physical disk.
To divert electric current by providing an alternative path.
To move a train from one track to another, or to move carriages, etc. from one train to another.
To have a minor collision, especially in a motor car.
To divert the flow of a body fluid.
To turn aside or away; to divert.
To carry on arbitrage between the London stock exchange and provincial stock exchanges.
An act of moving (suddenly), as due to a push or shove.
A connection used as an alternative path between parts of an electrical circuit.
The shifting of the studs on a projectile from the deep to the shallow sides of the grooves in its discharge from a shunt gun.
An abnormal passage between body channels.
A passage between body channels constructed surgically as a bypass; a tube inserted into the body to create such a passage.
A switch on a railway used to move a train from one track to another.
e: From Middle English schonten, schunten (“to jerk, swerve; to dodge, escape”), either: As regards the noun sense, compare Middle English shunt (“swerve; sudden jerk”), derived from the verb.

s: The four-dimensional continuum of the three spatial dimensions plus time.

An n-dimensional continuum consisting of dimensions of both space and time. Normally spacetime is considered as having 4 dimensions (x, y, z, t), but higher-dimensional spacetimes are often encountered in theoretical physics, e.g. the 5-dimensional spacetime of Kaluza-Klein theory or the 11 dimensio
A specific region of the universe with mathematically different properties than the surrounding spacetime. Synonymous with "metric" within the context of general relativity.
e: From space + time, as a Calque of German Raumzeit, introduced in this sense by Hermann Minkowski. First appears in print c. 1893 in the Philosophical Review.

s: The identity and nature of one's parents, and in particular, the legitimacy of one's birth.
The social quality of one's class in society.
e: From Middle French, from Old French parentage.

s: An elementary particle that is classified as a lepton, and has an extremely small but nonzero mass and no electric charge. It interacts with the surroundings only via the weak force or gravitation, making it very difficult to detect.
e: Coined by Enrico Fermi from neutron + the Italian diminutive suffix -ino; neutro- + -ino.

s: Honors. From the Ancient Greek practice of crowning victors with bays, sacred to Apollo.
A double-ended fire-fighting tool, usually long-handled, and having an ax-blade on one side and a mattock-blade on the other.
e: Named from Edward C. Pulaski (1866-1931), the American ranger who designed it.

s: Of, or relating to a chemical reaction brought about by electricity.
Of, or relating to electricity produced by a chemical reaction, e.g. in a battery.
A reducing to heads or articles; a formal agreement.
The act of capitulating or surrendering to an enemy upon stipulated terms; the act of ceasing to resist an opponent or an unwelcome demand.
The instrument containing the terms of an agreement or surrender.
An enumeration of the main parts of a subject.
e: From Middle French capitulation; equivalent to capitulate + -ion. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-.

s: A person or thing that fails to make a profit.
A clash; the sound or action of clashing; violent collision.
conflicting, contrasting, or contrary; inconsonant, incompatible, or irreconcilable
mismatched, inharmonious, discordant or dissonant, not fitting well together (especially in regards to aesthetics, colors, clothing, or sounds)
adverse or antagonistic; disagreeing or opposing
Producing a clash or series of clashes.
A fleet of starships; a space navy.
At or near the speed of light.
An artificial channel that is constructed to convey water from one location to another.
A structure carrying water over a river or depression, especially an ancient structure.
A structure conveying fluid, such as the cerebral aqueduct or vestibular aqueduct.
e: Adapted borrowing from Latin aquaeductus (“conveyance of water”), from aqua (“water”) + dūcō (“to lead”, “to bring”); compare the French aqueduc.

s: A form of indoctrination that forces people to abandon their beliefs in favour of another set of beliefs by conditioning through various forms of pressure or torture.
e: Calque of Chinese 洗腦. First use appears c. 1950.

s: Carefully attentive to details; studious; diligent in performing a process or procedure.
The application of careful and attentive effort.
To overturn from the foundation; to overthrow; to ruin utterly.
To pervert, as the mind, and turn it from the truth; to corrupt; to confound.
To upturn convention from the foundation by undermining it (literally, to turn from beneath).
e: From Middle English subverten, from Old French subvertir, from Latin subvertō (“to overthrow”).

s: A deadlock or stalemate situation in which no progress can be made.
The state of nonexistence; the condition of being nothing.
The quality of inconsequentiality; the lack of significance.
Large and impressive in size, scope or extent.
e: From French grandiose, from Italian grandioso, from Latin grandis (“great, grand”) (English grand). Possibly from grand + -ose, though to be debated. Doublet of grandioso.

s: In a thoughtful or pensive manner.
In a way that shows kindness or consideration for others.
Embodied in flesh; given a bodily, especially a human, form; personified.
To embody in flesh; to invest with a bodily, especially a human, form.
To gain full existence (bodily or otherwise).
To incarn; to become covered with flesh; to heal over.
To make carnal; to reduce the spiritual nature of.
To put into or represent in a concrete form, as an idea.
e: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, see -ate and Etymology 1 for more.

s: Of or relating to the cranium, or to the skull.
Having been overused such that it has lost its meaning; trite; banal.
Small dumplings of Eastern European origin, filled with meat or cheese and served usually in soup.
e: From Yiddish קרעפּלאַך, a regional plural form of קרעפּל (“meat dumpling”).

s: A radioactive metallic transuranic chemical element (symbol Md) with atomic number 101, which is artificially produced in a particle accelerator.
e: From a modified version of Mendeleev + -ium, named in honour of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev (1834–1907) who formulated the periodic law and created an early version of the periodic table of elements.
Originated in the 1948 novelty song “Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo”, used in the 1950 film Cinderella.
From tuchus, from Yiddish תּחת, from Hebrew תַּחַת (“underside, buttocks”).

s: The act or process of satisficing.
A crazy, irrational, or eccentric person.
An exotic atom (specifically, an onium) consisting of a positron (antielectron) and an electron, as a particle–anti-particle bound pair with no nucleus.
A soldier with remarkable strength, stamina, etc., especially if assisted by technology or genetics.
Of rocks: forced, while in a plastic or molten state, on to the Earth's surface to lie atop existing rocks.
Rock which has been formed through volcanic extrusion.
A hostile taunt, often repeated in a singsong voice.
By the use of axioms; in the form of an axiom.
To mouth words so that they can be heard over noise (or later so that they cannot be overheard), originally in the cotton industry of Lancashire.
e: Probably an affectionate alteration of mama or reduplication of maw (“mother”).
From Italian schifo (“disgust, nausea”) plus English suffix -y. Compare Italian schifoso (“disgusting, loathsome”).

s: Not arguable; certain, incontestable or incontrovertible.
Exclamation indicating a successful trick or prank.
Exclamation indicating a successful outcome or sudden realization.
A thingamabob, a placeholder word for any unknown or nonspecific object.
e: Probably from zing. Appears to originate from the X-Files season 7 episode "Hollywood A.D." Popularized as the catchphrase of the character Sheldon Cooper on the American sitcom The Big Bang Theory.

s: Not able to be supported or endured.
Located in the frontal lobes above the orbits of the eyes.
The inability to speak, be it from psychological or physical cause.
e: From French mutisme, from Latin mutus (“mute”), equivalent to mute + -ism.

s: Any of many thick Italian vegetable soups.
A hobby or recreational or leisure pursuit.
That which calls one away from one's regular employment or vocation.
Pursuits; duties; affairs which occupy one's time; usual employment; vocation.
The calling of a case from an inferior to a superior court.
e: From Latin āvocātiō (“a distraction”), from āvocō (“to call off, distract”).

s: Able to be diagnosed; having a cause which can be determined.
Of, pertaining to, or causing perturbation

e: From a corruption of *hindie, for *behindie (“behind, rear end, hindward parts”), equivalent to hind + -ie. Perhaps influenced in some way by Heinie (“a German”).

s: Marked by or resulting from extraordinary ability to recall detailed and vivid mental images of visual images.
Of or relating to the essential forms of a phenomena.
e: From German eidetisch, from Ancient Greek εἰδητικός, from εἶδος (“form”).

s: A child who attends a kindergarten.
A person who teaches at a kindergarten.
e: From kindergarten + -er, with spelling influenced by German Kindergärtner (“kindergarten teacher”).

s: The removal of the penis, testicles, and scrotum of (a male person or animal).
The act of depriving of virility, or the state of being so deprived; castration.
The act of depriving, or state of being deprived, of vigour or effectiveness.
A Scandinavian pastry, a variety of pretzel.
e: From Danish kringle, ultimately from Old Norse kringla (“ring, circle”).

s: An assistant waiter; one who clears plates from and cleans tables.
(An instance of) meaningless nonsense with an outward appearance of being impressive and legitimate.
(An instance of) excessively contrived, hackneyed, or sentimental material in a film, television programme, theater production, etc.
A film, television programme, theater production, etc., containing excessively contrived, hackneyed, or sentimental material.
A genre of blues song or music, often characterized by sexual innuendos or satire.
e: Uncertain; first attested as US theater slang, possibly a hocus-pocus + bunkum.

s: to touching other people with one's hands, especially in an inappropriate or sexual manner.
Moving the hands and wrists excessively when making a stroke or swing.
A failure to understand something; an illusion, misconception or misunderstanding.

An eating utensil shaped like a spoon, the bowl of which is divided into tines like those of a fork, and so has the function of both implements; some sporks have a serrated edge so they can also function as a knife.
To move or impale (food etc.) with a spork.
A supreme and most powerful enemy.
Viscid, coagulated; jelly-like, unusually thick (of a liquid).
To set off, get going; to start a journey.
To go off quickly: to hurry up.
To amble; to walk or proceed in a leisurely manner.
e: Unknown. Originally attested in Southern US dialects. Suggested origins include.
From moss + -y (apparently reflecting Middle English open vowel lengthening).

s: A fried pastry from Spain, typically eaten as a dessert and with chocolate beverage.
Of or pertaining to neurobiology, the biological study of nerve and brain function.
Describing rocks, such as silicate minerals, magmas, and volcanic and intrusive igneous rocks, which contain relatively high concentrations of magnesium and iron.
A pathological attraction to dead bodies.
e: From necro- (Ancient Greek νεκρός (“corpse, dead”)) + -philia (Ancient Greek φιλία (“affection”)), after German Nekrophilie (in Krafft-Ebing 1887).

s: Occurring or arising between species; interspecific.
The top layer of the cerebral hemispheres in the brain of mammals; part of the cerebral cortex.
Having relationships with multiple partners, with the knowledge and consent of all involved; engaging in polyamory.
Open to having such relationships, regardless of one's experience or current practices.
e: From a 1990 article by Morning Glory Zell-Ravenheart, A Bouquet of Lovers, formed poly- + amorous or polyamory + -ous.

s: Of, pertaining to, or using microfluidics or a microfluid
A newborn baby's bed, traditionally woven with reeds or straw; a (wicker) cradle.
e: From French bassinet (“small basin”), equivalent to basin + -et. Ernest Klein, however, suggests derivation from French bercelonnette (“cradle”), with influence from bassin(et), to account for the English sense's semantic specialization.

s: A noxious atmosphere or emanation once thought to originate from swamps and waste, and to cause disease.
A noxious atmosphere or influence, an ominous environment.
e: First attested in 1665. From Ancient Greek μίασμα (“stain; pollution”).

s: Used to express surprise or dismay.
Of eyes or people/animals: blinking repeatedly, prone to blink.
flickery, prone to flicker or flash (of lights, shining objects)
in digital photography, a flashing pixel.
Not having an outer layer of skin or skinlike material, or with such a layer removed.
e: From Middle English skynles, equivalent to skin + -less. Cognate with Old Norse skinnlauss (“skinless”).

s: consistently accurate; not missing a target.
Whilst not being seen or observed.
To populate again; to breed among a group in order to keep the population up.
To reintroduce a species into (an area).
To fill with data again; to refresh.
A person who lives in the slums of cities.
e: From slum + dog; first appeared in the 2008 British romantic comedy film Slumdog Millionaire.

s: A small ornament of glass or china.
The act, or the result of zeroing
An inauthentic or inadequate substitute or imitation.
Something made in imitation; an effigy or substitute.
A person who participates in a conversation.
A person skilled in general conversation.

A property of a system such that an output value is not a strict function of the corresponding input, but also incorporates some lag, delay, or history dependence, and in particular when the response for a decrease in the input variable is different from the response for an increase. For example, a
Magnetic friction in dynamos, by which every reversal of magnetism in the iron causes dissipation of energy.
e: Coined by Sir James Alfred Ewing from Ancient Greek ὑστέρησις (“shortcoming”), from ὑστερέω (“I am late, fall short”), from ὕστερος (“later”)..

s: So as to be highly visible or obvious; so as to attract notice or attention.
Short and thick, like something truncated; blunt; obtuse.
(Slang) The quality of being made of nips.
A muscle whose contraction narrows a vessel or passage or compresses an organ.
In part; part of the way; some of the way.
A sequence of gradual, successive stages; a systematic progression.
A passing by small degrees from one tone or shade, as of color, to another.
The act of gradating or arranging in grades.
Any degree or relative position in an order or series.
A gradual change within one parameter, or an overlapping of two blocks of sound.
A biologist whose speciality is microbiology.

e: Unknown; the word was popularized by the Irish-American cartoonist Thomas Aloysius (“Tad”) Dorgan (1877–1929), who started using it in cartoons on March 9, 1922. Maybe from Irish mallachtóireacht or Greek μαλακίες.

s: A seasoned smoked cut of beef, traditionally made from a navel cut.
e: Borrowed from Yiddish פּאַסטראַמע, from Romanian pastramă, from Ottoman Turkish باصدرمه (modern Turkish pastırma), a variation of bastırma (“dried meat”), from root bas- (“to press”). It is sometimes claimed that the origin of the Turkish word is Greek παστώνω (“I salt”), from Ancient Greek παστός (“sprinkled with salt, salted”).

s: Of something highly offensive; causing aversion or disgust.
An imitation of something, particularly a well-known product, usually of lower quality and price than the original.
A device in a knitting machine to remove loops from the needles.
Any of several short-lived herbs or shrubs of the Erysimum genus with bright yellow to red flowers.
Gastrolobium grandiflorum, a poisonous bushy shrub, endemic to Australia.
A person who does not dance at a party, due to shyness or unpopularity; by extension, anyone who is left on the sidelines while an activity takes place.
Any person who is socially awkward, shy, or reserved.
To stand shyly apart from a dance, waiting to be asked to join in.
An astronaut, especially a Russian or Soviet one.
e: Borrowed from Russian космона́вт, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (“universe”) + ναύτης (“sailor”). cosmo- + -naut.

s: Undergarments worn on the legs, such as socks, stockings, and pantyhose.
The business or art of a hosier; the practice of making hose.
An instrument or device for domestic use, especially in the kitchen.
Specifically, a eating utensil (fork, table knife, or spoon); a piece of flatware or cutlery.
A useful small tool, implement, or vessel.
e: From Middle English utensyl, from Old French utensile, from Latin ūtēnsilis (“useful, usable”).

s: The act of consummating, or the state of being consummated; the state of being completed; completion.
The first act of sexual intercourse in a relationship, particularly the first such act following marriage.
Termination; the end (as of the world or of life); an end or resulting state.
The date at which the mortgager becomes contractually obligated to the mortgagee in a real estate transaction.
Experiencing or expressing phobia (strong fear and/or dislike).
A person who has a phobia.

e: From Ancient Greek ἀξιωμᾰτικός (“employing logical propositions”), from ἀξίωμα (“self-evident principle”) + -ικός (“of or pertaining to, -ic”), equivalent to axiom + -atic.

s: Of metal, coated with zinc as a form of protection against rust.
Having been subjected to galvanism; electrified.
Whether desired or not; without regard for consequences or wishes of those affected; whether willingly or unwillingly.
That happens whether willingly or unwillingly.
e: . From will I, nill I (“whether I want to or not”), reflecting the old (viz. pre-Great Vowel Shift) pronunciation of I as ee, not yet as eye. Conflated with will he, nill he (with silent h) and will ye, nill ye (with yod dropping), meaning likewise.

s: A term of address for someone, usually used to instruct, to make a statement, or to draw attention.
Very foolish; failing to exercise intelligence or judgement or rationality.
Characteristic of an ass (an asshole): objectionably inconsiderate or jerky.
Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of donkeys.
e: From Latin asinīnus (“of a donkey or ass”).

s: Undergoing a sharp drop in blood pressure when changing posture between lying, sitting and standing.
To bother, harass, or annoy persistently.
e: In the senses of “overcrowd (a place)” and “impede (a person)”: from Middle French and Old French empestrer (“encumber”), influenced by English pest. The modern sense is an extension of the sense “infest”. Comparable to English construction pest + -er (used to form frequentative verbs).

s: A person who is or tries to be excessively proper, especially one who is easily offended by matters of a sexual nature.
e: From French prude, from Old French prude, prode, feminine of prou, prod, prud (“good, excellent, brave”), from Latin prōde. Related to proud but unrelated to prudent.

s: The act of attaching something with glue.
A connection between the edges of two planes, or between the points at the ends of two lines.
Any of various processes for producing some structure (e.g. a sheaf or scheme) by combining smaller structures that are in some way compatible with each other.
Inequality in marriage; marriage with an inferior.
To match unequally; to degrade or dishonor.
To dishonor by a comparison with what is inferior; to lower in rank or estimation by actions or words; to speak slightingly of; to depreciate; to undervalue.
e: From Middle English disparage, disparagen, from Old French desparage, desparagier, from des- (“dis-”) + parage (“equal rank, rank”).

s: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters.
Existing only in theory, not proven in reality.
e: English theory + -etic, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός.

s: An act in which something is dabbled in
Characterized by percussion; caused by or related to the action of striking or pounding something.
Produced by striking organs together, for example, smacking the lips or gnashing the teeth.
A neurotransmitter found in the locus coeruleus which is synthesized from dopamine.
Something, generally a device or gadget, whose real name is unknown or forgotten.
The scientific study of nerve and brain function in people and animals: the biological extent of neuroscience.
The act by which something is shunned; avoidance.
Used to affirm, indicate agreement, or consent.
The division of a cell nucleus in which the genome is copied and separated into two identical halves. It is normally followed by cell division.
e: From German Mitose, from Ancient Greek μίτος (“thread”) + -osis, probably in reference to the thread-like chromatin seen during mitosis.

s: A point designated for pedestrians to cross a street.
A mapping between equivalent elements (fields) in different database schemas.
To map equivalent elements (fields) in different database schemas.
Sounding dull and without resonance or freedom of sound.
e: From tub + -y. False cognate with chubby, even though they are often interchangeable.

s: Of or pertaining to a cataclysm; causing great destruction or upheaval; catastrophic.
Designed to be collapsed, especially so as to be more compact when not in use.
Any object that can be collapsed to save space.
A kind of boat that can be collapsed for greater portability.
A display element that can be collapsed to hide it from view.
The portion of a hammer containing the metal striking face (also including the claw or peen if so equipped).
Any organism with head shaped like that of a hammer
Any shark of the family Sphyrnidae, which only includes the genera Sphyrna and Zygaena, with eyes set on projections from the sides of the head.
A hogsucker, a fresh-water fish of species Hypentelium nigricans, in the sucker family Catostomidae.
A hammer-headed fruit bat, a fruit bat of species Hypsignathus monstrosus, with a large blunt nozzle.
A hammerkop, a bird of species Scopus umbretta.
A turn-around; a parking area constructed in a subdivision for initial access and construction.
A kind of ribozyme; hammerhead ribozyme.

A semiaquatic monotreme from eastern Australia with a bill resembling that of a duck, that has a mole-like body, a tail resembling that of a beaver, a waterproof pelt, and flat webbed feet (Ornithorhynchus anatinus).
e: From New Latin Platypus (originally a genus name already in use for a type of beetle), from Ancient Greek πλατύπους (“flat-footed”), from πλατύς (“flat”) + πούς (“foot”)..

s: Alternative form of meemaw, i.e. mamaw (grandmother).
To silently make exaggerated movements with the mouth so as to be understood in environment with loud noise, such as that of machinery.
An exaggerated mouthing of a word.
The two-tone wailing of a siren.
To make the two-syllable wailing noise of a siren.

A type of diminutive, solitary fairy or sprite, traditionally depicted as a small, bearded man wearing a green coat and hat, often found repairing a single shoe; they typically possess hidden treasure, such as a pot of gold hidden at the end of a rainbow, and can be forced to reveal its location if
e: From Irish leipreachán, luprachán, from Middle Irish luchrupán, from Old Irish luchorpán. See also Irish lucharachán. The word's further etymology is disputed; it is traditionally explained as a compound containing lú (“small”) + corp (“body”).

s: One who, or that which, accumulates.
A collective bet on successive events, with both stake and winnings being carried forward to accumulate progressively.
A system of elastic springs for relieving the strain upon a rope, as in deep-sea dredging.
A vessel containing pressurized hot water ready for release as steam.
A container which stores hydraulic power for release, in the form of a pressurized fluid (often suspended within a larger tank of fluid under pressure).
A register or variable used for holding the intermediate results of a computation or data transfer.
A derivative contract under which the seller commits to sell shares of an underlying security at a certain strike price, which the buyer is obligated to buy.
One who takes two higher degrees simultaneously, to reduce their length of study.
e: From Latin accumulātor, agent noun of accumulō (“pile up”), accumulate + -or.

s: A form of trapshooting using clay targets to simulate birds in flight.
A hand consisting of a 9, a 5, a 2, and two other cards lower than 9.
A young working-class person who may be loud, disruptive and poorly educated.
A scoop with a long handle, used to wash the sides of a vessel and formerly to wet the sails or deck.
To wet the sails or deck of a vessel.
to spy through the front windows of somebody else's house
A post on the Bluesky social media platform.
e: Pseudo-archaic alteration of shoot, perhaps with reference to Old Norse skjóta; compare Scots skite (“to dart, to shoot”). The name for a form of trapshooting is attested from the 1920s, see quotations below. Senses related to ejaculation of semen likely derive from this, but compare also squirt, skite, or scoot.
Unknown. Compare Icelandic skeið (“spoon”), from Old Norse skeið (“a sheath”). Attested from the 15th century; see quotation below.
Unknown. Compare Manx skeetagh (“nosy”). Compare also English peek (“to look slyly; a quick glance”) or skit (“to caper; to be skittish”).
sky + tweet, from the resemblance to tweets posted on Twitter. Strongly discouraged by CEO Jay Graber.
From Latin et cetera (“etc.: and the other things”).

s: That sinks or droops from wear or its own weight.
A scientist whose speciality is neuroscience.
Uninterested; exhibiting little passion or eagerness; lukewarm.
e: Borrowed from Latin tepidus. Cognate with Sanskrit तप्, *teplъ.

s: Pertaining to a gland or glands.
Having the characteristics or function of a gland.
A food supplement made from glands.
The ability of a system or living organism to adjust its internal environment to maintain a state of dynamic constancy; such as the ability of warm-blooded animals to maintain a stable temperature.
Such a dynamic equilibrium or balance.
e: From ὅμοιος (“similar, the same”) + -stasis, from Ancient Greek στάσις (“standing, state”).

s: Alternative form of of post mortem.
Alternative form of of post mortem.
The support about which a lever pivots.
A crux or pivot; a central point.
e: Borrowed from Latin fulcrum (“bedpost, foot of a couch”), from fulciō (“prop up, support”).

s: A particle with totally symmetric composite quantum states, which exempts them from the Pauli exclusion principle, and that hence obeys Bose-Einstein statistics. They have integer spin. Among them are many elementary particles, and some (gauge bosons) are known to carry the fundamental forces.
e: From Bose + -on. Named after Satyendra Nath Bose; Coined by Paul Dirac in a lecture titled Developments in Atomic Theory.

s: In such a manner that is capable of being demonstrated, shown, or proved (without doubt).
An Italian variant of ice cream made from milk and sugar, combined with other flavourings. The ingredients are supercooled while stirring to break up ice crystals as they form.
e: Borrowed from Italian gelato (“ice cream”), from Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

s: Someone who finds suitable dates or marriage partners for other people.
Someone who arranges professional boxing matches.
A service that matches up players for multiplayer game sessions.

One thousand (10³) watts, an amount of power large enough to power such things as a typical home appliance (e.g., a microwave oven, a toaster, or a hair dryer). (Consuming 1 kilowatt during a duration of 1 hour consumes 1 kilowatt-hour of energy.)
The coexistence of opposing attitudes or feelings (such as love and hate) towards a person, object or idea.
A state of uncertainty or indecisiveness.
e: Borrowed from German Ambivalenz (“simultaneous conflicting feelings”), from Latin ambi- (“both”) and valentia (“strength”), from the verb valere (“to be strong”) (see valiant); spelled on the model of French-origin words ending in -ence. The German term was Coined by Eugen Bleuler in 1910; by 1929, it had taken on a broader literary and general sense.

s: Of, pertaining to or situated in the anterior part of the frontal lobe.
Of, pertaining to or situated in front of the frontal bone.
A place set apart, as with a sanctum sanctorum; a sacred or private place; a private retreat or workroom.
A member of a mob or Mafia.
Each one of the two regions of the brain, located as a pair in the medial temporal lobe, believed to play a key role in processing emotions, such as fear and pleasure, in both animals and humans.
e: Latin amygdala (“almond, amygdala”), from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (“almond”), named as such due to its shape. Doublet of almond, amygdale, mandorla.

s: A dish of ground meat (usually made from ground beef, although lamb, pork, veal, venison, poultry and seafood are also used) formed into a loaf shape, mixed with egg and breadcrumbs, then baked or smoked, and usually served in slices.
Of a stimulus, below the limen or threshold of conscious perception, especially if still able to produce a response; also, below the threshold where a response can be produced.
Of an advertisement, a message, etc.: conveyed in a manner that the viewer is unaware of being influenced by it.
Without directed awareness or thought; subconscious (dated), unconscious.
Chiefly preceded by the: something which is below the limen or threshold of conscious perception.
An advertisement, a message, etc., which is conveyed in a manner that a person is unaware of being influenced by it.
An audio or video recording, often consisting of ambient music or white noise with hidden affirmations, intended to produce physical or psychological changes in the listener through repetition.
Chiefly preceded by the: the subconscious (dated) or unconscious self.
e: From sub- + liminal (from Latin līminālis, from līmen (“doorstep, threshold; doorway, entrance; beginning, commencement”). The noun is derived from the adjective. The English word is a borrowing from German subliminal or a German unterschwellig.

s: An aromatic hydrocarbon of formula C6H6 whose structure consists of a ring of alternate single and double bonds.
Sometimes used in place of the phenyl group.
e: A technical term in chemistry, adopted in English in 1835 as benzine (benzene from 1872), from German Benzin, which was coined in 1833 by Eilhardt Mitscherlich based on Benzoesäure (“benzoic acid”), plus the technical ending -ene (German -in) denoting hydrocarbons.

s: An absence of symmetry or proportion between the parts of a thing, or a distinction that produces such a lack of symmetry.
The lack of a common measure between two objects or quantities; incommensurability.
e: From Ancient Greek ἀσυμμετρία, from ἀσύμμετρος + -ία, from ἀ- + σύμμετρος; equivalent to a- + symmetry.

s: The combining capacity of an atom, functional group, or radical determined by the number of atoms of hydrogen with which it will unite, or the number of electrons that it will gain, lose, or share when it combines with other atoms, etc.
The number of binding sites of a molecule, such as an antibody or antigen.
The number of arguments that a verb can have, including its subject, ranging from zero to three or, less commonly, four.
A one-dimensional value assigned by a person to an object, situation, or state, that can usually be positive (causing a feeling of attraction) or negative (repulsion).
The value which a person places on something.
For a correspondence T on a curve: a number k such that the divisors T(P)+kP are all linearly equivalent.
A pilot partner of another; a pilot who flies in the same wing or squadron.
A friend or associate who accompanies one to offer (or receive) support, especially in flirting with love interests.
A player positioned on the wing.
To act as a wingman for (someone); to accompany in order to provide support.
Having the form or shape of a larva.
The removal or lessening of something's value.
The intentional or deliberate lowering of a currency's value compared to another country's currency or a standard value (e.g. the price of gold).
Not even or balanced; not the same on one side as on the other.
biased; not balanced between points of view
The simultaneous execution of multiple tasks (programs) under the control of an interrupt-driven operating system.
The practice or capability of handling more than one task at the same time.

e: From Middle English resuscitacion, from Old French ressuscitacion and Latin resuscitātio. Equivalent to resuscitate + -ion.

s: Having at most one instruction associated with any given internal state.
For a given particular input, always producing the same output through the same sequence of states.
To combine two or more things to produce a new product.
To be combined producing a new, more complex product.
To produce a substance by chemical synthesis.
To be produced by chemical synthesis.
An act of endearment; any act or expression of affection; an embracing, or touching, with tenderness.
To touch or kiss lovingly; to fondle.
To affect as if with a caress.
e: From French caresse, from Italian carezza (“dear”), from Latin cārus (“dear”), from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂-, akin to Sanskrit काम (“love”). Doublet of karezza.

s: Repressed or suppressed, especially of emotions or impulses.

e: Learned borrowing from New Latin fōrma Doublet of form.

s: Small candy or sugar pieces that are sprinkled over other confections.
A section of a road or path that crosses over an obstacle, especially another road, railway, etc.
To pass above something, as when flying or moving on a higher road.
To exceed, overstep, or transcend a limit, threshold, or goal.
To disregard, skip, or miss something.
The trade of manipulating materials in order to construct, install, and/or repair buildings or other structures.
The trade of cutting and joining wood, timber, or lumber; woodworking.
A collection of timber connected by being framed together, as the pieces of a roof, floor, etc.; work done by a carpenter.
e: From Middle English carpentrie, from Anglo-Norman carpenterie, from (compare French charpenterie). See carpenter.

s: A person of uncommon strength or endurance (like that of a thoroughbred horse).
Any of various echinoderms (not in fact fish) with usually five arms, many of which eat bivalves or corals by everting their stomach.
Any many-armed or tentacled sea invertebrate, whether cnidarian, echinoderm, or cephalopod.
A woman (or, less commonly, a gay man) who reluctantly takes part in sexual intercourse, and lies on the back while spreading the limbs.
To assume a splayed-out shape, like that of a starfish.
To form into a splayed-out shape, like that of a starfish.

e: Taken from a gibberish word (supposedly meaning "A big, dumb, balding North American ape with no chin and a short temper") used in the 1990 episode "Bart the Genius" of the TV show The Simpsons.

s: Characteristic of snitches or snitching; tell-tale
A mock-Polynesian hors d'oeuvre, usually made from water chestnuts and pieces of duck or chicken liver wrapped in bacon and marinated in soy sauce and either ginger or brown sugar.
e: Unknown; possibly related to Japanese 春巻き (“spring roll”).

s: The obscene manner of speaking of a person who is foul-mouthed.
A boneless rib sandwich, usually with BBQ sauce and deboned pork ribs.
A manufactured product, that is conform to the living required standards in a zone.
To fail or refuse to conform; to differ.
A form of contract bridge in which only goulash hands are played.
e: From goulash + -ie, with spelling influenced by unrelated ghoul.

s: The face (front part of the head).
The act of taking, or an action taken against someone or something, ostensibly in retaliation for another act that has not yet been committed; pre-emptive action characterized as revenge.
A puzzleheaded person, one having a mind full of confused notions.
A person who enjoys solving puzzles.
To bind or tie; to unite.
To solve an arithmetic problem concerning proportions by means of alligation; to associate as having the same ratio.
Having the same proportion or ratio.
e: From Latin alligatus (“tied, bound”), past participle of alligo (“to bind”), from ad + ligo (“to bind”). Doublet of alloy.

s: To bring out of a tent.

e: By dissimilation of mn to ml, followed by epenthesis of b.

Borrowed from Middle French caligineux (“misty; obscure”), or directly from its Latin etymon cālīginōsus (“misty; dark, obscure”). Cālīginōsus is derived from cālīgō, cālīginis (“fog, mist, vapour; darkness, gloom”)) + -ōsus.

s: A ball of dough, prepared as food or as fishing bait.
A metric verse (form), modeled after the rondeau, in two rhymes over seven lines, the first (in four syllables) being repeated as third and refrain (final one), each other line having eight syllables
A disease of the lungs, allegedly caused by inhaling microscopic silicate particles originating from the eruption of a volcano.
e: Coined by Q5417062, President of the National Puzzlers' League, at their convention in 1935 as a deliberately long word. An extension of the medical term pneumonoconiosis (pneumono- + coniosis) with ultramicroscopic + silico- + volcano inserted between the two elements.

s: A person who is very annoying; a pest, a nag, a jerk.

e: A humorous, intentionally morphologically opaque neologism and nonce word Coined by Q455743 for “Lisa the Iconoclast”, a 1996 episode of the animated sitcom The Simpsons. The ending resembles corpulent, temulent and other Latinate adjectives (derived from -ulentus (“full of, abounding in”)).

s: A ball of mucus ejected from the mouth.
A person who plays a trombone.

e: From the Yiddish; one of several words Anglicized and popularized by the original writer of MAD Magazine, Harvey Kurtzman. The word comes from shlogn ("to hit") with the prefix far- which often indicates the one so described is taking on the quality named. Thus, in Yiddish it means something that is old, battered, or junky.

s: A difficult or disagreeable person, especially a child.
e: Alteration of Welsh mochyn (“pig, greedy or immoral person”). Of disputed origin.

s: A type of knot which is useful for shortening a rope or taking up slack without cutting it.
To shorten (a rope) using a sheepshank knot.
e: Originally sheepshank knot or sheepshanks knot, from sheep + shank (“part of the leg between the knee and ankle”); the connection between the knot and a sheep’s leg is unclear.

s: A person who is easily taken advantage of.
A dingbat (ornamental typographical symbol), especially one from the Wingdings font.
e: After the Wingdings font developed by Microsoft in 1990. Its name was presumably derived from dingbat and earlier senses of wingding.

s: One who is under official protection.
A wick of a lamp, usually an oil lamp.
Material for making wicks for lamps.
A plant of species Phlomis lychnitis.
Focused on the phallus, especially as a symbol of male dominance; characterised by male attitudes, focused on men.
An aircraft in which lift is provided by unpowered rotating wings and thrust is provided by a conventional propeller.
e: From auto- and gyro-, from latinized forms of Ancient Greek αὐτο- (“self-”) and γῦρος (“circle, gyre”), a variant of earlier Spanish autogiro.

s: One who makes dire predictions about the future; one who predicts doom.
A small towel, hand or face wipe, either dry or more commonly impregnated with water or a cleansing fluid.
A donut in the form of a twisted ring.
To stage (a production) again; to bring (a production) to the stage again.
To stage (a disease, especially a cancer) again; to revise the staging of a case as its course varies.
To release from the hand; to let go.
Any of several bipedal dinosaurs, of the genus Oviraptor, from the late Cretaceous period.
e: From scientific Latin Oviraptor (genus name), from Latin ōvi- (“ovi-”) + raptor (because it is believed to have fed on the eggs of other dinosaurs).

s: A rectangular flap mounted near the wheel of a motor vehicle (especially a truck) to prevent mud or rocks from being thrown up (by the wheel), either onto the body panels or into the path of vehicles following behind.
A man of Asian ethnicity who is heavily influenced by hip-hop culture.
A vulgar insult for a contemptible Chinese (or, more generally, East Asian) man.
A young working-class person from Hobart, Tasmania
Used to describe someone or something that shows commitment; committed, attractive, cool.
e: From for + the Popularized by the Canadian sitcom Letterkenny.

s: The obsequious behavior of a toady; sycophancy.
A set of matching briefs and top (usually a sleeveless shirt or T-shirt) themed after a superhero or other fictional character, popular with children in the 1980s.
Tending to cause a scandal; scandalous.
slightly painful, akin to being pinched
nonce word for an action that impacts on something, especially if it is sudden.
An ordinary person with nothing to recommend them.
Used for emphasis or to express that one is impressed.
Onomatopoeic, accompanying or describing a yank, swipe, or snatch.
To take or win (something that others want).
e: Coined by writer George Meyer for the TV show The Simpsons; perhaps from yank, or imitative of the sound effect (a quick upward slide on a violin) that accompanies something being snatched in classic comedies.

s: Having the quality of a smart aleck; rude, disrespectful.
Playing badly because one is nervous; having the yips.
An extra or unexpected gift or benefit, such as that given to customers when they purchase something.
e: Borrowed from lagniappe, from Spanish la ñapa, a variant of yapa (“small gift or additional quantity given to a valued customer”), from Quechua yapa (“addition, increase, supplement; lagniappe”), yapay (“to add, to increase”).

s: A fritter (with a fruit or vegetable filling).
A Louisiana-style fried doughnut or fritter covered in powdered sugar.
e: Borrowed from French beignet, ultimately of Frankish origin.

s: A coat of paint or other material applied onto a surface before that of a topcoat; an undercoat.
An action to recover personal property unlawfully taken, especially that seized by way of distraint; the writ or procedure of such action.
e: Anglo-Norman, from Old French replevir (“recover”), from re- + plevir (apparently from a Germanic word which was also the source of English pledge).

s: A pointed tool, shaped like an awl, used for breaking ice.
A type of narrow and deep atrophic (indented) acne scar that resembles a puncture in the skin.
To break or stab with an icepick.

e: Alteration of US and British dialectal crawdab (“crayfish”).

s: Verbal impudence or argumentative discourse, given in response.
To respond to in an aggressively disputatious, often sarcastic or insolent manner.
Lacking the suitable qualifications for a particular job.
Exclamation of surprise or dismay.; gosh!, darn!
e: Borrowed from Spanish caramba, a euphemism for the real expletive carajo.

s: A chicken; a chick (a young bird, especially a young chicken).
Affectionate term of address for a pet, child, etc.
A person who kills his or her mother.
e: From French matricide, from Latin mātricīda (“person who kills his own mother”) and mātricīdium (“the murder of one's mother”). matri- + -cide.

s: Jagged, as if torn or lacerated.
e: The verb is first attested in 1425, the adjective in 1514; Inherited from Middle English laceraten, Borrowed from Latin lacerātus, perfect passive participle of lacerō, see -ate and -ate.

s: A script formatted like a screenplay for cinema, but written to be made into an episode of a television show.

e: From Middle English carnalitee, carnalyte, carnalite, from Latin carnālitās, equivalent to carnal + -ity. Compare Old French charnalité.

s: A cannabis blunt rolled inside a Dutch Masters cigar.
A fast food pastry, being a square doughnut with raisins and glaze.
A large cooking pot; a Dutch pot; a Dutch oven.
e: From Dutch + -ie. It is unclear whether the sense of a cannabis joint comes from an earlier meaning of cannabis blunt rolled using a Dutch Masters cigar or whether it instead derives from the song, which is itself based on the song (where kouchie in the title refers to koutchie (a pipe for smoking cannabis)).

s: A male member of a jazz band.
Men's or boys’ traditionally white briefs.
Characteristic of sludge; slimy or mucky
A form of investment in which, on the death of an investor, his share is divided amongst the other investors.
e: From French tontine, named after Lorenzo de Tonti, who introduced the scheme into France in around 1653. Thus, from Tonti + -ine.

s: One million (106, or 1,000,000) bits or 1,000 kilobits. Equals 125,000 bytes (125 kilobytes).
A beer produced by a small local brewery, or microbrewery.
To produce beer on a small scale, as a microbrewer.
to unfasten (the buckle of (a belt, shoe, etc))
To make deaf, either temporarily or permanently.
e: From deaf + -en. Compare Middle English deven, deaven (“to make deaf”), Old English ādēafian (“to deafen”) and Old English ādȳfan, Dutch verdoven (“to stupefy, deafen”), German betäuben (“to stun, stupefy, deafen”).

s: A support on which to rest the feet.
The act of one who hectors, or acts blusteringly.
A carriage; a vehicle, now chiefly in French contexts.
e: Borrowed from French voiture, from Latin vectūra. Doublet of vecture, vettura.

s: A contagious bacterial skin disease forming pustules and yellow crusty sores, chiefly on the face and hands. It is common in children and infection is often through cuts or insect bites.
The principles of a freethinker; free thought.

e: Unknown, but was popularized (as Kowa-Bunga) by Chief Thunderthud on the American children's show Howdy Doody in the late 1940s or early 1950s, and became associated with American surfing culture.

s: A person who lives in a Gaeltacht area of Ireland.
A person who exhibits Münchausen syndrome; a person who feigns a disorder.
e: An anglicisation of Irish muintir na hAite.

s: A bullfighter, especially one on horseback.
e: From Spanish toreador, from torear (“to fight bulls”), from toro (“bull”), from Latin taurus.
According to one theory, from Cree. An alternative etymology, perhaps a folk etymology, attributes the name to their peculiar, wavy flight.

s: The state of being greedy; greed.
e: From Middle English gredynesse, from Old English grǣdiġnes; equivalent to greedy + -ness.

s: An energy weapon in the form of a pistol.
One who partakes in clubbing: one who frequents nightclubs.
One who clubs: one who hits (something or someone) with a club.
The act of one who besets or attacks.
The act of handling something with care or skill.

e: Borrowed from Italian imbroglio (“tangle, entanglement, muddle”) (im-, alternative form of in- + broglio (“confusion; intrigue, fraud, rigging, stuffing”); see also imbrogliare (“to tangle”)), cognate with and probably from an earlier form of French embrouiller (“to embroil, muddle”) (em- (“em-”), a form of en- (“en-”) + brouiller (“to confuse, mix up”)).

s: An idiot; a stupid or contemptible person.
e: From Ned + -y, Ned being a diminutive of Edward.

s: Any of the wild species of apple tree, genus Malus, which generally yield small, bitter fruit (in comparison to domestic apples, Malus domestica).
An unpleasant person; a person who is crabby.
To create (a small ornamental handicraft also called a scrimshaw) by carving or engraving on bone (originally whalebone or whales' teeth), ivory, or other materials.
To carve or engrave (bone, ivory, or other materials) with ornamental designs.
To carve or engrave (ornamental designs) on bone, ivory, or other materials.
To make a handicraft of scrimshaw.

A small ornamental handicraft created by carving or engraving bone (originally whalebone or whales' teeth), ivory, or other materials, formerly produced by sailors on whaling ships to pass the time on long voyages.
The manufacture of small ornamental handicrafts by carving or engraving bone, ivory, or other materials, formerly by sailors on whaling ships to pass the time on long voyages.
e: The origin of the verb is Unknown, but it has possibly been influenced by the surname Scrimshaw. Various etymologies have been proposed (for example, that it derives from scrimshank (“(Britain, military slang) to be idle, to shirk duty”)), but the Oxford English Dictionary does not consider any of them convincing.

s: A short, or deliberately shortened tail.
An animal that has a bobtail, such as certain canines or nags.
A tractor which performs without its trailer.
A tractor-trailer that is relatively short in length.
The tractor unit of a semi-truck without a trailer.
An open-ended straight or four flush.
To drive a tractor without its trailer.
To drive a truck or other vehicle without its trailer.
Having one or more sharp points.
Acting in a violent and/or deranged manner.
Prone to commit an act of stabbing.
Weakened; reduced to a powerless state.
Excessively fed; given too much to eat; having had too much to eat.
A heart-shaped cherry with a very dark skin.
Any of various plant diseases that cause darkening of the central tissue.
A type of malleable cast iron with minimum tensile strength of 350 N/mm2.
A brawl or fracas; a scene of chaos.
e: Named from Donnybrook Fair, a notoriously disorderly event, held annually from 1204 until the middle of the 19th century. The town of Donnybrook comes from the Irish Domhnach Broc (“The Church of Saint Broc”).

s: A dirty, shabbily-clothed child; an urchin.
e: From the Middle English Ragamuffyn. Of uncertain origin, according to Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable: A muffin is a poor thing of a creature, a ‘regular muff’; so that a ragamuffin is a sorry creature in rags.

s: One who underachieves, i.e. performs less well than expected.
The act of cutting oneself open, usually on the forehead, to draw blood and make the fight more spectacular.
The fact or legal status of being a territory.
The pattern of behaviour in animals that defines and defends a territory.
A pattern of human behaviour characterised by defence of a particular territory or area of interest.
History that emphasizes the role of women, or that is told from a woman's (or from a feminist) point of view.
Any historical writing by or about women.
e: Wordplay: her + history, derived as though the first syllable in history were his, the male determiner.

s: A fruit that falls from the tree, rather than being picked.
A part which acts by falling, such as a stamp in a fulling mill, or the device in a spinning machine to arrest motion when a thread breaks.
An assimilatory process whereby a vowel is pronounced more like a following vocoid that is separated by one or more consonants.

The umlaut process (as above) that occurred historically in Germanic languages whereby back vowels became front vowels when followed by syllable containing a front vocoid (e.g. Germanic lūsiz > Old English lȳs(i) > Modern English lice).
The diacritical mark (¨) placed over a vowel when it indicates a (rounded) front vowel
To place an umlaut over (a vowel).
To modify (a word) so that an umlaut is required in it.
e: Borrowed from German Umlaut in the 19th century, from um- or um (“around, re-, trans-”) + Laut (“sound”), from Old High German hlūt. More at loud.

s: To decisively put a stop to or terminate (someone or something).
Chiefly preceded by the: fashion, style.
e: The origin of the is Uncertain; the following etymologies have been suggested: The is derived from the noun.

Probably a irrespective + regardless. The word may also be analysed as ir- + regardless, as it is possible that the prefix ir- was added to amplify the negative in regardless just as plain negatives often did at the time the word came into use (and still do in dialects).

s: Containing a great deal of dialogue or talking in general
To criticize or malign, especially unfairly or spitefully.
e: Calque of a term, perhaps Calque of or Calque of, which entered English via. Compare Japanese, which is a compound of and.

s: look, listen; see here, pay attention; the thing is, to be honest
behold!; look at that; look here or there; look!
Of, pertaining to, containing, or characteristic of malt

e: From Middle English quoth, quath, from Old English cwæþ (first and third person past indicative of cweþan (“to say, speak to, address, exhort, admonish”)), from Proto-Germanic *kwaþ (first and third person past indicative of Proto-Germanic *kweþaną (“to say”)). Unrelated to quote.

s: An inexperienced person; a novice, beginner or newcomer.
e: Inherited from Middle English grene horn, which is attested for “horn of a recently killed animal” and as the name of a horse. It may also have been used of young horned animals. In all cases “green” refers to the idea of “fresh, young, recent”, taken from plants and used in Middle English for all kinds of things irrespective of their colour, e.g. wounds, leather, fish, cheese (see green cheese).

s: An expression of joy or excitement, commonly associated with cowboys.
To shout yee-haw, or exclaim in a similar manner.
Of or relating to cowboys or the southern United States.
e: From gee and haw, words used to instruct a horse to turn in different directions.

s: A pain in the abdomen, often caused by indigestion, usually lower than the stomach and related to the intestines.
A woman's nightgown or nightdress for wearing to bed.
Synonym of juvenile hall (a youth detention centre).
A minor (youth); especially, Synonym of juvenile delinquent.
e: From juvenile + -ie with elision; morphologically analogous to bougie#Etymology 2 = bourgeoisie + -ie/-y.

s: An annoying, contemptible, or worthless person.
e: Compound of ass + wipe. First use appears c. 1947 in the writings of Mari Sandoz.

s: The state of lacking meaning; the quality of being meaningless.
an upward current of air, especially a strong one

e: First attested in the 1910s in the US Northeast. Likely from German nit, dialect form of nichts (“nothing”), or Yiddish ניט, dialect form of נישט (“no”), although some dictionaries give the alternative etymology nit (“louse egg; something very small”) + wit.

s: Easily excited; set off by the slightest excuse; easily enraged or inflamed.
Incapable of burning; not easily set on fire. From in- + flammable, via backformation.
e: From Middle French inflammable, from Medieval Latin īnflammābilis, from Latin īnflammāre (“to set on fire”), from in (“in, on”) + flamma (“flame”). inflame + -able.

s: A charitable institution where poor or homeless people are lodged.
A type of loose shorts which look like a skirt; a divided skirt.
Any device or object used to halt the motion of a door, as a large or heavy object, a wedge, or some piece of hardware fixed to the floor, door or wall.
A large book, which by implication could be used to stop a door.
An interview with a politician or other public figure (apparently informal or spontaneous but often planned), as they enter or leave a building.

A headphone-like device designed to cover a person's ears for protection against cold or noise. They consist of a thermoplastic or metal head-band, that fits over the top of the head, and a pad at each end, to cover the external ears.
A univalent functional group consisting of a carbonyl and a hydroxyl functional group (-CO.OH); characteristic of carboxylic acids.
A kind of small, ring-shaped pasta, stuffed with meat, cheese, etc; and eaten with a sauce or in a soup.
The act of one who slobbers.
A very strong and instant glue, generally cyanoacrylate.
e: From super- + glue, a held by Super Glue Corporation.

s: Ribbons of pasta, cut from a sheet, not as wide as tagliatelle.
A removable protective shield separating the inner workings of a machine from operator and observer.
A rigid flat surface that has an active role in the interaction of a device with an operator or user.
A transparent window forming part of a helmet directly in front of the wearer's face, allowing them to see out.
One who is prone to anger or who actively seeks out conflicts and confrontations.
One who reacts or responds rapidly without engaging in careful deliberation.
e: From hot + head. Compare English hot-brain (“a hothead”); Middle English hot-heorte, hat-heorte (“anger”), Old English hātheort (“furious, angry, irascible, passionate, ardent”).

s: A type of men's garment popular in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: a close-fitting collarless jacket, with or without sleeves.
A sleeveless jacket, usually leather; a long waistcoat.
e: First recorded in early 1500s. Possibly related to Dutch jurk (“dress”), itself of unknown origin and not attested before the 17th century. Derivation from Old French jornee (“day”) has been suggested.

s: Having (at least) two sides of equal length, used especially of a triangle or trapezoid.
e: Borrowed from Latin īsoscelēs, from Ancient Greek ἰσοσκελής (“equal-legged”), from ἴσος (“equal”) + σκέλος (“leg”) + -ής. See also iso-.

s: The state of being jobless or unemployed.
The phenomenon or level of unemployment in an economy.
To reclaim ownership of property for which payment remains due.
The burrow in the ground where a fox lives.
A small pit dug into the ground as a shelter for protection against enemy fire.
To dig a military foxhole into, or convert into a foxhole by digging.
To drive into a military foxhole.
e: From Middle English foxhol, from Old English foxhol, equivalent to fox + hole.

s: To broadcast, or be broadcast, by television.
Device used with muzzleloaders to push the projectile up against the propellant.
Ranch or trail foreman, usually the first or second person in charge. The person responsible for getting the work done.
The mass of grape solids that floats on the surface during the fermentation of wine.
The text at the start of a numbered section of a legal document that appears directly beside the section number, ahead of any numbered subsections.
A passage of introductory text appearing in a treaty that broadly defines its principles, objectives, and background.
well done, bravo; a verbal representation of a hat tip
e: Borrowed from Middle French chappeau. The interjection is after Modern French chapeau in similar use, originally short for chapeau bas.

s: Any tall-stemmed plant principally from genus Solidago (also Oligoneuron), usually with clusters of small yellow flowers.
A golden-yellow colour, like that of the goldenrod plant.
Of a golden-yellow colour, like that of the goldenrod plant.
Someone who takes care of the upkeep of grounds (gardens, a playing field, woodlands, etc.)
An imitation of the sound of gagging, used to express disgust or disdain.
To have the vomiting reflex triggered.
A metal sheet used to cover stovetop burners on Shabbat to allow food to be kept warm without violating the prohibition against cooking.
A participant in a spelling bee.
A book used to learn how to spell properly.
One who engages in bullfighting; a toreador or matador.
A type of distilled alcoholic beverage (liquor), often with a herbal or fruit flavoring, typically drunk neat as an apéritif or digestif.
Of or pertaining to an entrance or threshold.

Pertaining to or in a state that is in-between or transitional between two (or more) other states, while belonging to neither; pertaining to or in a state such as to be neither definitively in a particular other state or category nor definitively outside it.
Of or pertaining to a beginning or first stage of a process.
Of an empty environment that evokes a surreal blend of nostalgia, comfort, and unease; see liminal space.
e: From Latin līmināris, from līmen (“doorstep, threshold; doorway, entrance; beginning, commencement”) + -ālis. Līmen is possibly derived from līmus (“askew; sideways”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l- (“to bend, bow; elbow”)) + -men (from Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥).

s: Having a gender identity which matches the sex one was assigned at birth; or, pertaining to such people.
e: From cis- (“on this side of”) + gender, by analogy with transgender.. Compare slightly earlier cisgendered (1994).

s: Falsely earnest, smug, ingratiating, or pious.
Unctuous, greasy, as hair from pomade.
e: From smarm + -y. Apparently coined by "B.R.L., of Brighton" with sense "saying treacly things which do not sound genuine" in a competition for neologisms in The Academy (London) published on 14 January 1899.

s: A coward; a person who is easily frightened or high-strung and easily scared.
One who performs parlor tricks, sleight of hand.
One who conjures; one who calls, entreats, or charges in a solemn manner.
One who conjectures shrewdly or judges wisely; a man of sagacity.
A cooking appliance comprising a pot (large or small) with a gridiron wielded beneath it, like a brazier, used for cooking methods such as broiling.
e: From Middle English conjurer, from Anglo-Norman conjurour (“conjurer, conspirator”). Equivalent to conjure + -er.
From Italian bordello. Distantly related to brothel, through Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carve, cut, split, rub”). Doublet of bordel. la:borda + it:-ello (“diminutive”).

s: Any salt or ester of benzoic acid.
A person who is deficient in intelligence.
A gadget, device, or object whose name is either unknown, forgotten, or omitted for the purpose of humor.
A foolish, incompetent, or silly person.
e: Probably of multiple origins. Partially a borrowing from Dutch dinges (“thingamajig, thingy; whatshisname, whatshername”), ding (“thing”). Probably also partially a borrowing from Afrikaans in view of its South African occurrence. The spelling dingus is a to look like a Latin word ending in -us.

s: The act of one who rags or teases.
An initiation in educational institutions (e.g. universities) usually involving harassment by seniors.
Suffering from sickness, nausea or dizziness due to the motion of a ship or boat at sea.
e: From Middle English see seke, equivalent to sea + sick.

s: Someone or something that earns or makes money; anything lucrative or profitable.
(usually a woman's) butt, ass, rear end
A spherical or nearly spherical structure.
A lump in the throat; the sensation of having such a lump present.
Ellipsis of globus oculi: the eyeball.
e: Borrowed from Latin globus. Doublet of globe and perhaps glob.

s: A portion of a recording (a take) that is not included in the final version of a film or a musical album, often because it contains a mistake.
A complete version of a recording or film that is dropped in favour of another version, reject.
An opening for outward discharge; a vent.
e: From Middle English outtaken (“to take out”), equivalent to out- + take.
From Middle English outtake, outtaken, from the past participle of outtaken (“to take out”). See above. Compare earlier Middle English outnime, out-neme (“except, except for”).

s: Having a range of physical powers as specified.
A person who has no disability.
A sugary, gelatinous material used to make candies.
A candy made of this material.
e: From German Gummi (“brand name of German candy”), from Gummi (“India rubber”).

s: A long sled without runners, with the front end curled upwards, which may be pulled across snow by a cord or used to coast down hills.
A similar sled of wood, pulled by dogs, possibly with steel runners, made to transport cargo.
