A concealed aperture through which an occupant of a building can surreptitiously listen to people talking at an entrance to the building.
The act of intentionally hearing a conversation not intended to be heard.
e: From eaves + drop; the "listening" sense derives from the notion of the listener standing in the area denoted by the physical sense.

s: A tool used to carry the woof back and forth between the warp threads on a loom.
The sliding thread holder in a sewing machine, which carries the lower thread through a loop of the upper thread, to make a lock stitch.
A transport service (such as a bus or train) that goes back and forth between two or more places.
Such a transport vehicle; a shuttle bus; a space shuttle.
Any other item that moves repeatedly back and forth between two positions, possibly transporting something else with it between those points (such as, in chemistry, a molecular shuttle).
A shutter, as for a channel for molten metal.
To go or send back and forth between two places.
To transport by shuttle or by means of a shuttle service.
e: From a merger of two words: The name for a loom weaving instrument, recorded from 1338, is from a sense of being "shot" across the threads. The back-and-forth imagery inspired the extension to "passenger trains" in 1895, aircraft in 1942, and spacecraft in 1969, as well as older terms such as shuttlecock.

s: To prod or jab with an object such as a finger or a stick.
To stir up a fire to remove ash or promote burning.
To rummage; to feel or grope around.
To modify the value stored in (a memory address).
To put a poke (device to prevent leaping or breaking fences) on (an animal).
To thrust at with the horns; to gore.
To notify (another user) of activity on social media or an instant messenger.
To thrust (something) in a particular direction such as the tongue.
A device to prevent an animal from leaping or breaking through fences, consisting of a yoke with a pole inserted, pointed forward.
The storage of a value in a memory address, typically to modify the behaviour of a program or to cheat at a video game.
A notification sent to get another user's attention on social media or an instant messenger.
e: From Middle English poken, perhaps from Middle Dutch poken or Middle Low German poken, both from Proto-West Germanic *pukōn or similar, which is itself of uncertain origin, but may be from an Onomatopoeic Proto-Germanic root *puk-. Doublet of poach#Etymology 2.
From Middle English poke, from Anglo-Norman poke (whence pocket), from Frankish *poka. More at pocket. Doublet of pouch.
Clipping of pocan or directly Borrowed from pocan. See pocan for more.

s: To prescribe or administer medication to.
To have a medicinal or healing effect on a person, body part, or ailment; to act on.
To determine the value of (a variable or expression).
To relate a statement (called a predicate) to a given set using a quantifier—either for all (denoted ∀) or there exists (denoted ∃).
e: From Medieval Latin quantifico (introduced by Sir William Hamilton in logic).

s: The act or craft of producing a carved object.
A burger made with goose meat.
The amount that a pocket would hold.
To welcome in a friendly manner, either in person or through another means such as writing.
To arrive at or reach, or meet.
e: From Middle English greten, from Old English grētan, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōtijaną. Cognate with Dutch groeten, German grüßen, grüssen.

From a blend of two Old English verbs, grētan, grǣtan (itself from Proto-West Germanic *grātan); and of Old English grēotan (itself from *greutan), both meaning "to weep, lament". Possibly reinforced in Northern England and Scotland by Old Norse gráta, whence also Danish græde, Norwegian gråte, Swedish gråta, all meaning "to cry, to weep".

s: A term of endearment, especially for a young girl or a female relationship partner.
The sound of something wet and gooey; splat.
A gooey mess; a splash or splatter.
The relocation of goods when transferring one's household, business, etc., to another location
To batter; to clobber; to conk.
e: Uncertain. Perhaps short for whangdoodle (“gadget, doodad”), or from whang, a dialectal form of thong (“strip of leather”). Compare wong.

s: A person or thing that spews.

e: From screw + -y. 1820, original meaning “tipsy, slightly drunk”; meaning “crazy, ridiculous” first recorded 1887.
From an Internet meme and YouTube Poop sample of a line in the television series Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog, spoken by the character Dr. Robotnik: "Snooping as usual, I see?".

s: A human or human body, as opposed to a robot or incorporeal being.
Produced or effected by force; not spontaneous; unnatural.
e: From Middle English violent, from Old French violent, from Latin violentus, from vīs (“strength”). Displaced native Old English stræc. For the verb, compare French violenter.

s: A small genital opening in the female of some insects etc.
A kernel of corn, usually from a can.
A small piece of something, especially of snack food.
A robot in female or feminine form.
A docile, unthinking and conformist woman.
e: female + -bot. Coined by screenwriters Arthur Rowe and Oliver Crawford in the television series The Bionic Woman (1976–1978), specifically in "Kill Oscar" (season 2, episode 5) first broadcast on October 27, 1976.

s: A Japanese art form in which earth and water are moulded to create a delicate shiny sphere resembling a billiard ball.
To bark with a sharp, high-pitched voice.
e: Possibly from dialectal yip (“to cheep like a bird”), from Middle English ȝyppe, probably imitative.

s: One who meddles or interferes in something not of their concern.
To relax in a hot tub.
Experienced, especially used to indicate a veteran of the naval services; salty dog (from salt of the sea).

Pertaining to the Sardinian language and those dialects of Catalan, spoken in the Balearic Islands and along the coast of Catalonia, that use definitive articles descended from the Latin ipse (“self”) instead of the Latin ille (“that”).
e: Equivalent to salt + -y. Compare soaltig (“salty”), West Frisian sâltich (“salty”), Dutch zoutig (“salty”), Low German soltig (“salty”), German salzig (“salty”). (coarse; irritated, annoyed) Referencing the sharp, 'spicy' flavor of salt. (indignant) Perhaps implying the person is a crybaby, shedding salty tears, or derived from the preceding.

s: Mischievous; tending to misbehave or act badly (especially of a child).
Sexually provocative; now in weakened sense, risqué, cheeky.
Decadent, had as indulgence, especially an unhealthy one.
e: Old English gmw-pro From late Middle English noughti, naughty (“evil, immoral, wicked”), from nought (“evil, immoral”) + -ī̆. Analysable as naught + -y.

s: To force or trick someone to go somewhere or do something against their will or interest, particularly
To press-gang sailors, especially for shipping or fishing work.
To trick a suspect into entering a jurisdiction in which they can be lawfully arrested.
To transfer a serviceman against their will.
To commandeer, hijack, or otherwise (usually wrongfully) appropriate a place or thing.
A breed of chicken with large bodies, long legs, and feathered shanks.

A kind of dart game in which players are gradually eliminated ("shanghaied"), usually either by failing to reach a certain score in 3 quick throws or during a competition to hit a certain prechosen number and then be the first to hit the prechosen numbers of the other players.
e: 1871, from the important Chinese port Shanghai, as a verb with reference to the former practice by some shippers on the West Coast of the United States of press-ganging crews for fishing or shipping in the Pacific Ocean.
From Scottish shangan, from Scottish Gaelic seangan, influenced by the Chinese city.

s: A bicycle or motorcycle trick where the front wheel is lifted off the ground while riding.
A diet where someone eats only one type of food.
Any fish of the family Monodactylidae.
Monaural or monophonic; having only a single audio channel.
e: Shortenings, ultimately from the prefix mono- (“one, single”).

s: The anus; often in reference to anal intercourse.
One who poops out on an activity; one who dampens the mood by lack of participation or negative attitude. Mostly used in the phrase party pooper.
A selection in a slot machine game that ends the picking bonus.
One who poops; or, poops well.
A hunt for foxes, usually with dogs.
A hunt for radio transmitters; radiosport.
To hunt foxes, usually with dogs.
To shake or tremble as one moves, especially as of old age or childhood; to totter.

Any of about 100–170 species of yellow, orange or red (rarely green) parasitic plants of the genus Cuscuta. Formerly treated as the only genus in the family Cuscutaceae, it is now placed in the morning glory family, Convolvulaceae.
e: Early 17th century, variant of dialectal dadder, from Middle English daderen (“to quake, tremble”), ultimately from the root of dither. Compare Norwegian dudra (“to tremble”).

From Middle English doder (“flax dodder”), from Middle Dutch doder, from Old Dutch *doder, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *dodr (viz. theories of origin). Cognate with Middle Low German doder, dodder.

s: A unit of length equal to 10−10 meters (that is, one ten-billionth of a meter), approximately the size of an atom, and denoted by the symbol Å, used especially to measure the wavelength of electromagnetic radiation or distances between atoms.
e: Borrowed from Swedish ångström, Named after Anders Jonas Ångström.

s: Complete in every detail, perfect, absolute.
Supremely skilled and experienced; highly accomplished; fully qualified.
To bring (a task, project, goal etc.) to completion; to accomplish.
To make perfect, achieve, give the finishing touch.
To make (a marriage) complete by the spouses' first engaging in sexual intercourse.
To become perfected, receive the finishing touch.
e: Either Inherited from Middle English *consummaten or directly Borrowed from Latin consummātus, see -ate and Etymology 1 for more.

s: A pancake fried in oil, usually made from potatoes and sometimes also onions, traditionally served on Hanukkah.
e: Borrowed from Yiddish לאַטקע, from either Russian ла́тка (“pastry, patch”) or Ukrainian оладка (“pancake, fritter”). In Polish łatka (“patch”) or placek, placki (“fritter, fritters”).

s: A string or flat strip of pasta or other dough, usually cooked (at least initially) by boiling, and served in soup or in a dry form mixed with a sauce and other ingredients.
An object which is long and thin like a noodle (sense 1).
A dumpling cooked by boiling and served in soup; a knaidel or knödel.
A long and slender dragon, usually an eastern dragon.
A person with poor judgment; a fool.
To engage in frivolous behavior; to fool around or waste time.
To hum or sing (a tune) at a low pitch or volume.
To play (a musical instrument or passage of music) or to sing (a passage of music) in an improvisatory or lighthearted manner; also, to play (a series of ornamental notes) on an instrument.
To play a musical instrument or to sing in an improvisatory or lighthearted manner; also, to play a series of ornamental notes on an instrument.
An improvised passage of music played on an instrument; also, a series of ornamental notes played on an instrument; a trill.
e: Borrowed from Dutch noedel (“noodle”), or from its etymon German Nudel (“piece of pasta, noodle”); further etymology uncertain, probably a variant of Knödel (“dumpling”), from Middle High German knödel (“dumpling; small knot”), and then either.
The origin of the noun is uncertain; it is possibly a variant of noddle (“the head”). The verb is derived from the noun.

The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly derived: The word was probably also influenced by doodle (“to draw or scribble aimlessly”). The noun is probably derived from the verb, though the verb is first attested later. The noun was probably also influenced by doodle (“small mindless sketch”).
Unknown; perhaps related to guddle (“to catch (fish) with the hands”).

s: The state of being unable to do something.
e: From Middle French impossibilité, from Latin impossibilitās. im- + possibility and impossible + -ity.

s: A person who shares star billing with another.
A person who slightly lacks the status to be considered a star.
To perform with the billing of a costar.
To feature (a number of star performers) jointly.
A flower; a small bouquet; a nosegay.
A verse of poetry, especially a motto or an inscription on a ring.
policies and rules and their application and enforcement
muscles or parts of the body
Painful or more rigid than usual as a result of excessive or unaccustomed exercise.
Having a dense consistency; thick; Difficult to stir.
of whipping cream or egg whites
Beaten until so aerated that they stand up straight on their own.
Of an equation, for which certain numerical solving methods are numerically unstable, unless the step size is taken to be extremely small.
Of a shot, landing so close to the flagstick that it should be very easy to sink the ball with the next shot.
Delivered more forcefully than needed, whether intentionally or accidentally, thus causing legitimate pain to the opponent.
An average person, usually male, of no particular distinction, skill, or education.
e: From Middle English stiff, stiffe, stif, from Old English stīf, from Proto-West Germanic *stīf, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *steypós. See also West Frisian stiif, Dutch stijf, Norwegian stiv, German steif; also Latin stīpes, stīpō, from which English stevedore.

s: The jaw, jawbone; especially one of the lateral parts of the mandible.
A fold of fatty flesh under the chin, around the cheeks, or lower jaw (as a dewlap, wattle, crop, or double chin).
The cheek; especially the cheek meat of a hog.
A cut of fish including the head and adjacent parts
To knock, bump, strike against; hit, strike; peck at.
To jolt or shake roughly; shake up, mix together.
The tolling of a bell; knell.
e: From Middle English jawle, chawl, chavel (“jaw, jawbone”), from Old English ċeafl (“jaw, cheek”), from Proto-West Germanic *kafl (“jaw, cheek”). The modern form (for expected chavel, chawl; still found dialectally) is influenced by Doublet of jaw, which it is a partial doublet of.
From Middle English jollen, chollen (“to knock, strike, batter; stagger”). Related to jow (“to knock, bump, ring”).

s: A short period of excessive consumption, especially of food, alcohol, narcotics, etc.
A compressed period of an activity done in excess, such as watching a television show.
To engage in a short period of excessive consumption, especially of excessive alcohol or media consumption.
e: From Leicestershire and Northamptonshire dialect, binge (“to drink deeply", also "to soak, steep, drench", specifically "to swell a leaky wooden vessel by filling it with or plunging it into water”), of unknown origin.

s: An enclosure for livestock, especially a circular one.
An enclosure or area to concentrate a dispersed group.
A circle of wagons, either for the purpose of trapping livestock, or for defense.
To place inside of a corral.
To make a circle of vehicles, as of wagons so as to form a corral.
A lever operated by one's foot that is used to control or power a machine or mechanism, such as a bicycle or piano.
an orthopedic structure or a footlike part.
An effects unit, especially one designed to be activated by being stepped on.
The ranks of pipes played from the pedal-board of an organ.
To operate a pedal attached to a wheel in a continuous circular motion.
Of or relating to the foot.
e: Borrowed from French pédale, itself borrowed from Italian pedale, from Latin pedālis. ped- + -al.
Latin pedālis. Cognate with French pédal (doublet of the pédale mentioned in § Etymology 1). Same surface analysis as in § Etymology 1.

s: The state of adverse conditions; state of misfortune or calamity.
An event that is adverse; calamity.
e: From Old French adversité, from Latin adversitātem, the accusative singular of adversitās, from adversus, the perfect passive participle of advertō (“to turn toward”).

s: An imagined superior type of human being representing a new stage of human development; an übermensch; (loosely), a man of extraordinary powers.
Someone likened to the comics character Superman; a man of seemingly superhuman powers.
e: A Calque of German Übermensch; super- + man. The German word was introduced by the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) in his work Also sprach Zarathustra (Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 1883), and rendered in English as superman by Irish playwright George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950) in the play Man and Superman (1903) and by Thomas Common (1850–1919) in his 1909 translation of Nietzsche’s work.

s: At no time; on no occasion; in no circumstance.
Not at any other time; not on any other occasion; not previously.
Negative particle (used to negate verbs in the simple past tense; also used absolutely).
A statement of disbelief or amazement
e: From Middle English nevere, navere, nævere, from Old English nǣfre (“never”), equivalent to ne + ever.

s: To repeatedly remind or complain to (someone) in an annoying way, often about insignificant or unnecessary matters.
To bother with persistent thoughts or memories.
To bother or disturb persistently in any way.
A persistent, bothersome thought or worry.
e: From Middle English nagg, nage, nagge (“horse, small riding horse, pony”), cognate with Dutch negge, neg (“horse”), German Nickel (“small horse”). Perhaps related to English neigh.

Probably from a source; compare Swedish nagga (“to gnaw, grumble”), Danish nage (“to nag, bother”), Icelandic nagga (“to complain”). Compare typologically fret, Bulgarian глождя, Russian глода́ть, грызть, по́едом есть, е́дкий.

s: A scoundrel, rascal, or unprincipled, deceitful, brutal and unreliable person.
To play the ruffian; to rage; to raise tumult.
A predisposition or natural inclination, propensity, or a predilection; especially, a strong disposition or bent.
A journey or effort in pursuit of a goal (often lengthy, ambitious, or fervent); a mission.
A task that a player may complete in order to gain a reward or advance the story.
The act of seeking, or looking after anything; attempt to find or obtain; search; pursuit.
A request; a desire; a solicitation.
A group of people conducting a search or inquiry.
An inquest; a jury of inquest.
To seek or pursue a goal; to undertake a mission or job.
To search for something; to seek.
To locate and attach to a host animal.
e: From Middle English quest, queste; partly from Anglo-Norman queste, Old French queste (“acquisition, search, hunt”), and partly from their source, Latin quaesta (“tribute, tax, inquiry, search”), noun use of quaesita, the feminine past participle of quaerō (“to ask, seek”). Doublet of question.
quiz + test, to avoid using the word test.

s: Any of certain freshwater fish of the subfamily Serrasalminae, native to South America; they are characterized by razor-sharp teeth and a reputation of being ferocious predators (despite most species being omnivorous).
Someone, especially a critic, who appears to be part of a swarm and attacks someone when they are vulnerable, as if in a feeding frenzy.
e: . The term entered English either via Portuguese piranha or Spanish piraña, from Old Tupi pirãîa.

s: One trillion (1012, or 1,000,000,000,000) bytes or 1,000 gigabytes.

A musical art form rooted in West African cultural and musical expression and in the African American blues tradition, with diverse influences over time, commonly characterized by blue notes, syncopation, swing, call and response, polyrhythms and improvisation.
The substance or makeup of a thing; unspecified thing(s).
Something of excellent quality, the genuine article.
A red-skinned variety of eating apple.
To dance to the tunes of jazz music.
To enliven, brighten up, make more colourful or exciting.
To have sex for money, to prostitute oneself.
To move (around/about) in a lively or frivolous manner; to fool around.
e: Unknown. First attested around 1912 in a discussion of baseball; attested in reference to music around 1915. Numerous references suggest that the term may be connected to jasm and jism.

s: A brushy, rural area or location.
A shot that strikes a squopped wink and sends it flying far away.
To camp in a dry brushy location.
To stay in a self-contained recreational vehicle without connections to water, electricity, or sewer services, especially in a remote location.
To strike a squopped wink and send it flying far away.
e: 1910s during or around the Philippine–American War after the Spanish–American War, from Tagalog bundok (“mountain”), adopted by occupying American soldiers serving in the mountains or rural countryside of the American-occupied Philippines under the United States Military Government of the Philippine Islands.

s: A type of biscuit (cookie), popular in Britain, traditionally made from one part sugar, two parts butter and three parts flour.
The crown or uppermost branches of a tree.
A person whose job is to publicize information or events; a publicity agent; a public relations agent or worker.
A journalist, often a commentator, who focusses on politics.
A scholar, of public or international law.
A receptacle which serves as a place to discard waste materials.
Merry, joyous, full of mirth; later especially, frolicsome, sportive, full of playful mischief.
To make merry; to have fun; to romp; to behave playfully and uninhibitedly.
An employee's action outside their job description for which the employer is not liable; a frolic of his own
e: From Dutch vrolijk (“cheerful”), from Middle Dutch vrolijc, from Old Dutch frōlīk, from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz. Compare German fröhlich (“blitheful, gaily, happy, merry”).

s: A deity or other supernatural being said to have been worshipped by certain West African peoples; an idol.
Any object of superstition; religious words and/or actions which are seen as superstitious or fraudulent.
Any confusing or meaningless speech; nonsense, gibberish.
e: Probably from maamajomboo (“mask; masked dancer”); or perhaps from /l/-vocalization in the words mumble and jumble.

s: A robe, gown, or other article of clothing worn as an indication of office.
Any of the special articles of clothing worn by members of the clergy etc., especially a garment worn at the celebration of the Eucharist.
An article of clothing, especially an outer garment.
e: From Middle English vestement, vestment, from Old French vestement, from Latin vestīmentum. vest + -ment. Compare French vêtement.

s: One who tills the earth; a farmer, a husbandman, a ploughman.
e: From Middle English erthling (“farmer, ploughman”) (in glossaries), from Old English ierþling, eorþling (“farmer, husbandman, ploughman”), from eorþe (“ground; dirt; planet Earth”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er- (“earth”)) + -ling. The English word is analysable as earth + -ling.

s: To travel, often instantaneously, from one point to another without physically crossing the distance between the two points.
To move (an object) in this fashion, as by telekinesis.
A course of violent, frenzied action.
Wild partying, typically a drinking binge
To move about wildly or violently.
e: From Scots rampage, equivalent to ramp + -age. Perhaps influenced by Middle English rampnen (“to force, ram”), from Old English *hrampian, from Proto-West Germanic *hrampōn (“to obstruct, hinder”), see ramp.

s: A building that is rented to multiple tenants, especially a low-rent, run-down one.
Any form of property that is held by one person from another, rather than being owned.
e: From Middle English tenement, from Anglo-Norman tenement (“holding”), from Old French tenement, from Medieval Latin tenimentum, from Latin teneō (“hold”).

s: The dry, leafy or stringy exterior of certain vegetables or fruits, which must be removed before eating the meat inside.
Any form of useless, dried up, and subsequently worthless exterior of something.
The supporting frame of a run of millstones.
An infection in cattle caused by a species of Dictyocaulus or lungworm
To say huskily, to utter in a husky voice.
e: From Middle English huske, husk (“husk”). Perhaps from Old English *husuc, *hosuc (“little covering, sheath”), diminutive of hosu (“pod, shell, husk”), from Proto-West Germanic *hosā, from Proto-Germanic *husǭ (“covering, shell, leggings”), from Proto-Indo-European *kawəs- / kawes- (“cover”). If so, equivalent to hose + -ock.
Partly Onomatopoeic, partly from Etymology 1, above, influenced by husky.

s: One who hunts whales; any person employed in the whaling industry.
A seagoing vessel used for hunting whales.
Something of unusually great size, a whopper, a whacker.
Any shark of the family Carcharhinidae; a requiem shark.
A sundowner; one who cruises about.
e: From whale + -er. In sense 1, displaced Old English hwælhunta.

s: A thin, shaved off slice of wood, metal, or other material.
The action of having a shave.
To move with irregular, back and forward or side to side motions; to shake or jiggle.
To move with shaking or jiggling.
A rapid movement in alternating opposite directions, not necessarily regular.
A dish that combines seafood and peas in a cream-based sauce.
e: From Middle English wiglen, probably from Middle Dutch wigelen (“to wiggle”) and perhaps Middle Low German wigelen, frequentative of wiegen (“to rock”), from wiege (“cradle”). See wain, and Dutch wieg (“cradle”). Cognate to Dutch wiggelen (“to wiggle”), Low German wiggeln (“to wiggle”).

s: A proclamation of law or other authoritative command.
e: From Middle English edycte, borrowed from Latin edictum; earlier form edit, from Old French edit, from the same Latin word.

s: An unconventionally modern style of fashionable dress originating in England in the 1960s, characterized by ankle-length black trenchcoats and sunglasses.
A 1960s British person who dressed in such a style and was interested in modernism and the modern music of the time; the opposite of a rocker.
An end user-created package containing modifications to the look or behaviour of a video game.
A moderator, for example on a discussion forum.
Used to express a wish of removal or, often hyperbolic, harm (as opposed to a literal request to moderators).
A module (file containing a tracker music sequence).
Moderations: university examinations generally taken in the first year.
To modify (an object) from its original condition, typically to individualize and/or enhance the performance of the object.
To install or create a mod.
To moderate; to silence or punish (a rule-breaking user) on a forum, especially when done by a moderator.
e: Probably reflecting a Jamaican pronunciation of.

s: Having deteriorated, degraded or fallen from normal, coherent, balanced and desirable to undesirable and typically abnormal.
Having lost good or desirable qualities; hence also having bad character or habits, base, immoral, corrupt.
Having multiple domain elements correspond to one element of the range.
Qualitatively different, usually simpler, than typical objects of its class.
Having the same quantum energy level.
One who is degenerate, who has fallen from previous stature; an immoral or corrupt person.
To lose good or desirable qualities.
To cause to lose good or desirable qualities.
e: From a substantivation of the above adjective, see -ate for more. Compare French dégénéré.
From degenerō + -ate. Compare Italian degenerare, French dégénérer (and its older (and now obsolete) English cognate from Middle French, degener). de- + generate.

s: A three-dimensional image of an object created by holography.
e: From holo + gram, from Ancient Greek ὅλος (“whole”) + γρᾰ́μμᾰ (“that which is written or drawn”), Coined by Dennis Gabor, the Nobel prize winner in physics in 1971 for his work in holography.

s: To produce an image or copy of.
To generate or propagate offspring or organisms sexually or asexually.
To bring something to mind; to recall.
A fitful movement similar to a twitch or jerk.
To dance in a sexually-provocative way using hip thrusts in a low squatting stance while shaking the buttocks; to take part in twerking.
A puny or insignificant person, generally male; a twerp.
An abrupt call, such as that made by the California quail.
e: twitch + jerk. The "sexually-provocative dance" sense was particularly popularized since c. 2000 by hip-hop from the United States of America, and again in 2013 by singer Miley Cyrus.
twerp + jerk, found primarily in the 1930s-era works of Walter Dumaux Edmonds.
Onomatopoeic, possibly coined by Roger Tory Peterson.

s: A short promotional video, particularly one showing off the work of a videographer or animator.
A personal feeling of fear or embarrassment that stops one behaving naturally.
The process of stopping or retarding a reaction.
A writ from a higher court to an inferior judge to stay proceedings.
e: From Middle English inhibicioun, inhibicione from Old French inibicion, from Latin inhibitio. Morphologically inhibit + -ion.

s: The infliction of severe pain or anguish, especially as an interrogation technique or punishment; (usually in the plural) a technique, method, or device which is designed to inflict such anguish.
Sexual activity involving the infliction of pain to a certain body part or in a certain manner.
Severe pain or anguish, of mind or body.
An unpleasant sensation or its infliction: embarrassment, heartache, etc.
To intentionally inflict severe pain or suffering on (someone), usually with the aim of forcing confessions or punishing them.
e: From Middle English torture, from Old French torture, from Late Latin tortūra (“a twisting, writhing, of bodily pain, a griping colic;” in Medieval Latin “pain inflicted by judicial or ecclesiastical authority as a means of persuasion, torture”), from Latin tortus (whence also tort), past participle of torquēre (“to twist”).

s: Singular of ravioli: A single, large parcel of pasta with a filling, served with a sauce. Alternative form of ravioli.
A decorative wooden figurine, traditionally German, shaped like a soldier, king, or other figure, known for its large jaw operated by a lever to crack nuts; usually associated with Christmas decor.
A ball made of pieces of soft fabric, tinsel, plastic, or paper streamers, tied together in the middle and left loose at the ends, used as decoration or as a showy prop for cheerleading.
e: Alteration of pompon, from French pompon (“ornamental tuft”); of unknown origin, perhaps related to Old French pomp.

s: A black flag with a solid orange circle, used to summon a damaged car to the pits for repairs.
A white flag with a solid red circle and sixteen red rays radiating from the central circle, used as a symbol of Imperial Japan.
To chew with a grinding, crunching sound, and with the mouth closed.
To eat vigorously or with excitement.
A location or restaurant where good food can be expected, or an instance of eating at such a place.
A casual meeting for those interested in BDSM, usually at a restaurant, bar or pub.
Someone who easily agrees to give oral sex.
e: From Middle English monchen, a variant of mocchen, mucchen ("to munch (food); chew audibly"; > Modern English dialectal Doublet of mouch), probably Onomatopoeic in origin (compare English crunch; German mampfen).

s: The gases surrounding the Earth or any astronomical body.
The air in a particular place.
The conditions (such as music, illumination, etc.) that can influence the mood felt in an environment.
The apparent mood felt in an environment.
A unit of measurement for pressure equal to 101325 Pa (symbol: atm), approximately the atmospheric pressure at sea level.
Extras in a scene who have no spoken lines.
e: Borrowed from French atmosphère, from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (“steam”) + σφαῖρα (“sphere”); corresponding to atmo- + -sphere.

s: The outer covering of a fruit or seed.
To remove the outer covering of a fruit or seed.
The body or frame of a vessel, such as a ship or plane.

The smallest set that possesses a particular property (such as convexity) and contains every point of A; slightly more formally, the intersection of all sets which possess the specified property and of which A is a subset.
To drift; to be carried by the impetus of wind or water on the ship's hull alone, with sails furled.
To hit (a ship) in the hull with cannon fire etc.
e: From Middle English hul, hulle, holle (“seed covering, hull of a ship”), from Old English hulu (“seed covering”), from Proto-Germanic *hul-, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide”); or possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kal- (“hard”).

From Middle English holle, hoole (“hull, hold of a ship, ship”), of Uncertain origin. Possibly a variant and special use of Etymology 1 above, conformed to hull. Alternatively, a variant of Middle English hole, hoole, holle (“hiding place, lair, den, shelter, compartment”), related to Middle Dutch and Dutch hol (“hole, ship's cargo hold”). More at hole.

s: A girl or an unmarried young woman.
A man with no experience of sex, especially because of deliberate abstention.
An unmarried woman, especially an older woman.
A racehorse without any victory, i.e. one having a "virgin record".
A horse race in which all starters are maidens.
A Scottish counterpart of the guillotine.
of a female, human or animal
Like or befitting a (young, unmarried) maiden.
Being a first occurrence or event.
e: From Middle English mayden, meiden, from Old English mæġden (“girl”), originally a diminutive of mæġeþ (“girl”) via diminutive suffix -en, from Proto-West Germanic *magaþ, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs. Equivalent to maid + -en.

s: To fill pores or spaces with a substance.
Imbued, saturated, permeated or filled with.
e: The adjective is, the verb in 1605; Borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate and -ate. Doublet of impregn; participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

s: A guarantee that a certain outcome or obligation will be fulfilled; security.

A legal agreement that was a real covenant and ran with the land: The grantor of a piece of real estate held in freehold, and their heirs, were required to officially guarantee their claim and plead their case for the title. If evicted by someone with a superior claim (paramount title), they were al

A covenant, also called the covenant of warranty, whereby the grantor assures the grantee that he or she will not be subject to the claims of someone with a paramount title, thereby guaranteeing the status of the title that is being conveyed.

A legal agreement, either written or oral (an expressed warranty) or implied through the actions of the buyer and seller (an implied warranty), which states that the goods or property in question will be in exactly the same state as promised, such as in a sale of an item or piece of real estate.

A written guarantee, usually over a fixed period, provided to someone who buys a product or item, which states that certain repairs and/or replacement parts will be provided free of charge in case of damage or a defect.
A stipulation of an insurance policy made by an insuree, guaranteeing that the facts of the policy are true and the insurance risk is as stated, which if not fulfilled renders the policy void.
Justification or mandate to do something, especially in terms of one’s personal conduct; warrant.
e: From Middle English warantye, warantie, from Anglo-Norman warrantie, an variant of Old French guarantie (Modern French garantie). Doublet of guarantee, guaranty. More at warrant.

s: A sudden, often uncontrolled movement, especially of the human body.
A person with unlikable or obnoxious qualities and behavior, typically mean, immoral, self-centered or disagreeable.
A stupid person; an idiot or fool.
A lift in which the weight is taken with a quick motion from shoulder height to a position above the head with arms fully extended and held there for a brief time.
An act of satirizing behavior that is, to an extent, common in a community, especially in circlejerk subreddits.
A dance, popular in Western culture in the 1960s, in which the head and upper body is thrown forwards regularly to the beat of the music.
The rate of change in acceleration with respect to time.
To make a sudden uncontrolled movement.
To give a quick, often unpleasant tug or shake.
To satirize behavior that is, to an extent, common in a community, especially in circlejerk subreddits.
To throw with a quick and suddenly arrested motion of the hand.
e: Probably from Middle English yerk (“sudden motion”) and Middle English yerkid (“tightly pulled”), from Old English ġearc (“ready, active, quick”) and Old English ġearcian (“to prepare, make ready, procure, furnish, supply”). Cognate with Scots yerk (“to jerk”). Equivalent to yare (“ready”) + -k. Doublet of yark.
+ (cooking), itself Borrowed from Spanish charqui, from Quechua ch'arki.

s: Insensate: unable to feel, or unconscious.
A substance administered to reduce the perception of pain or to induce numbness for surgery and may render the recipient unconscious.
e: From an- + esthetic, or Latinized form of grc:ἀναίσθητος + -ic, from ἀν- (“un-”) + αἰσθητικός (“perceptible”).

s: The reticulum (the second stomach of a ruminant).
A form of ceiling ornamentation (especially of an arch or dome) made up of small vaulted arches, especially in Moorish architecture.
Any type of natural structure or decoration consisting of a honeycomb pattern, or designed to resemble a honeycomb.
Something thought to bring good luck.
Something, especially a person or animal, used to symbolize a sports team, company, organization or other group.
A person engaged by an organization to portray its mascot in costume.
A personality type characterized by reliance on humor and positivity to wish away conflicts and attempt to defuse potentially violent situations.
e: Borrowed from French mascotte, from Occitan mascòta (“sortilege”), feminine diminutive of masca (“witch”), from Old Occitan masca, from Medieval Latin masca (“specter, nightmare”). More at mask.

s: A type of flowering plant, genus Tulipa.
e: Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- From Middle French tulipe, from earlier tulipan, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (“cheesecloth”), from دلبند (“turban”). Doublet of turban.

s: A body of forces equipped for war.
All the cannon and small arms collectively, with their equipments, belonging to a ship or a fortification.
The process of building up military capacity.
A sandal consisting of a rubber sole fastened to the foot by a rubber thong fitting between the toes and around the sides of the foot.
A change of places; an inversion or swap.
An instance of flip-flopping, of repeatedly changing one's stated opinion about a matter.

A bistable; an electronic switching circuit that has either two stable states (switching between them in response to a trigger) or a stable and an unstable state (switching from one to the other and back again in response to a trigger), and which is thereby capable of serving as one bit of memory.
The sound of a regular footfall.
A person or inhabitant of the Middle East, or a Muslim nation, particularly Afghanistan.
To alternate back and forth between directly opposite opinions, ideas, or decisions.
e: Onomatopoeic. Most probably an imitation of the sound produced when walking in them.
From weird + -o (“person with characteristic”)., in American English. The similar word weirdie (“odd, unconventional person”) is attested from earlier, in 1887; in Scottish English.

s: One of the two magistrates who originally administered the census of citizens, and by Classical times (between the 8th century and the 6th century) was a high judge of public behaviour and morality.
A high-ranking official who was responsible for the supervision of subordinate government officials.

An official responsible for the removal or suppression of objectionable material (for example, if obscene or likely to incite violence) or sensitive content in books, films, correspondence, and other media.
A college or university official whose duties vary depending on the institution.
An algorithm that approves or rejects something on grounds of taste or morality etc.

To review for, and if necessary to remove or suppress, content from books, films, correspondence, and other media which is regarded as objectionable (for example, obscene, likely to incite violence, or sensitive).
A hypothetical subconscious agency which filters unacceptable thought before it reaches the conscious mind.
e: The noun is borrowed from Latin cēnsor (“magistrate; critic”), from cēnseō (“to give an opinion, judge; to assess, reckon; to decree, determine”) + -sor (variant of -tor). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱens- (“to announce, proclaim; to put in order”).
From an incorrect translation of German Zensur (“censorship”).

s: A member of a society or class who herd animals from pasture to pasture with no fixed home.
Syn of wanderer: an itinerant person.
A person who changes residence frequently.
A player who changes teams frequently.
A dragonfly of Afroeurasia, Sympetrum fonscolombii.
e: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (“roaming, wandering, esp. to find pasture”), from Ancient Greek νομός (“pasture”). Compare Numidia.

s: A large, lush, undeveloped, humid forest, especially in a tropical region, thick with vegetation and wildlife; a tropical rainforest.
Any uncultivated tract of forest or scrub habitat.
A place where people behave ruthlessly, unconstrained by law or morality.
An area where hobos camp together.
A style of electronic dance music and precursor of drum and bass.
A dense mass of pubic hair.
(Of musical beat, rhythm, etc.) resembling the fast-paced drumming of traditional peoples of the jungle.
e: Borrowed from (Hindi जंगल / Urdu جَن٘گَل), from 𑀚𑀁𑀕𑀮, from Sanskrit जङ्गल (“arid or sterile region, desert”), from a language. First appears c. 1776 in a translation by Nathaniel Halhed.

s: A small brownish or reddish pigmentation spot on the surface of the skin.
Any small spot which has a different colour from its background.
A small sweet consisting of a flattish mound of chocolate covered in hundreds and thousands.
To cover (someone; or something, such as the skin) with freckles (and).
Pertaining to a current or recent time and style; not ancient.
Pertaining to the modern period (c.1500 to contemporary times), particularly in academic historiography.
Pertaining to specifically the period c.1800 to contemporary times (in contexts when the period c.1500 to 1800 is considered early modern).
Pertaining to modernism or its associated era (c.1880 to 1945).
Someone who lives in modern times.
e: From Middle French moderne, from Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (“measure”); hence, by measure, "just now". See also mode.

s: To mark with blotches of different color, or shades of color, as if stained; to spot; to maculate.
Any of several species of genus Logania of butterflies, found from Burma to the Philippines and New Guinea.
An artificial lens, especially one of a pair.
A large, landlocked stretch of water or similar liquid.
A small stream of running water; a channel for water; a drain.
To leap, jump, exert oneself; to play.
To subject biological cells to repeated cycles of freezing and thawing until lysis.
A kind of fine, white linen.
In dyeing and painting, an often fugitive crimson or vermilion pigment derived from an organic colorant (cochineal or madder, for example) and an inorganic, generally metallic mordant.
In the composition of colors for use in products intended for human consumption, made by extending on a substratum of alumina, a salt prepared from one of the certified water-soluble straight colors.
e: From lake, lak, lac (also laik, layke; Southern loke), from Old English lāc (“play, sport, strife, battle, sacrifice, offering, gift, present, booty, message”), from Proto-West Germanic *laik, from Proto-Germanic *laikaz (“game, dance, hymn, sport”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“to bounce, shake, tremble”).

From Middle English lake, from Old English *lacen or Middle Dutch laken; both from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“linen; cloth; sheet”). Cognate with Dutch lake (“linen”), Dutch laken (“linen; bedsheet”), German Laken, Danish lagan, Swedish lakan, Icelandic lak, lakan.
From French laque (“lacquer”), from Persian لاک, from Hindi लाख, from Sanskrit लाक्षा. Doublet of lac, lacquer.

s: A person with an ugly face.
A dislikable person, a disagreeable person.
A freshwater and marine fish of the family Centropomidae in the order Perciformes.
Any of various other ray-finned fishes in several families.
A disrespectful gesture, performed by placing the tip of a thumb on one's nose with the fingers spread, and typically while wiggling the fingers back and forth.
To lurk; to lie in ambush.
e: From Dutch snoek (“pike, Esox”). Doublet of snoek; perhaps more distantly related to snake.
From the 19th century. Uncertain origin, but probably a variant of snoke. Compare also sneck (“nose”). These words are partly, given the similarity to snoot, snout, sniff, sneeze etc.
A euphemistic substitution for the expletive bloody.

s: Something which is awesome, cool or spectacular.

A vibrant, chaotic, and heavily meme-driven aesthetic from the late 2000s to early 2010s; characterized by surreal, random, and ironic humor; often pairs MS Paint-style graphics and 80s airbrush motifs with neon colors, space galaxies, cats, or junk food.
e: From awesome + sauce. Usage of the term might be after earlier weaksauce.

s: To damage or vandalize something, especially a surface, in a visible or conspicuous manner.
To void or devalue; to nullify or degrade the face value of.
To alter a coat of arms or a flag by adding an element to it.
e: From Middle English defacen, from Old French defacier, desfacier (“to mutilate, destroy, disfigure”), from des- (“away from”) (see dis-) + Late Latin facia.

s: The small, young seedling of a plant used as a visual flavor accent and occasionally as salad greens.
A short preliminary statement or remark, especially an explanatory introduction to a formal document or statute.
To speak or write a preamble; to provide a preliminary statement or set of remarks.
e: From Middle English preamble, from Old French preambule (French préambule), from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from praeambulō (“to walk before”).

s: A machine for moistening animal skins with water.
e: Extended form of sam, of same meaning and doubtful origin, a quotation possibly pointing to derivation from some word with the prefix sam-.

s: A girl or woman, especially a masculine one.
A cowboy's wife, or a woman who moves out west with the intention of marrying a cowboy.
A girl or woman who is noted for being tough or capable.
A dull person (especially an old man) who is behind the times, holding antiquated, over-conservative views.
e: Borrowed from Scots foggie, fogie, perhaps derived from Scots foggie (“covered with moss or lichen; mossy", hence "old, antiquated, decrepit”), from Scots fog (“moss; lichen”), equivalent to fog (“moss”) + -y. Further origin Uncertain. More at fog.

s: Marked by low quality; inferior; inadequate.
Raunchy or perverted in nature; tastelessly sexual.
e: Unknown. Possibly a corruption of silesia. Silesia was formerly the most important location of Germany’s weaving industry.

s: Indicative of unkind or malevolent intentions; harsh, cruel.
Unpropitious, unkind, faulty, not up to reasonable standard.
in terms of health or physical condition; sick.
Sublime, with the connotation of being so in a singularly creative way.
Extremely bad (bad enough to make one ill). Generally used indirectly with to be.
e: From Middle English ille (“evil; wicked”), from Old Norse íllr, ílla, ílt, from Proto-Germanic *ilhilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁elḱ- (whence Latin ulcus (“sore”), Ancient Greek ἕλκος (“wound, ulcer”), Sanskrit अर्शस् (“hemorrhoids”)).

s: A prolonged, loud cry, like the sound of an animal; a wail; a howl.
To express by yowling; to utter with a yowl.
e: From Middle English youlen, goulen, from Old Norse gaula (“to low, bellow, howl, scream”), related to Icelandic gaula (“to yell, howl, roar”), Faroese geyla (“to bawl, squall, shout, yell, bellow”), Norwegian gaule (“to roar, howl, whine, weep noisily”), dialectal Swedish gjöla, Scots gowl (“to howl, yell, roar”), Shetlandic Scots gjol.

s: Having an unregulated body temperature; ectothermic.
Of a type of horse: tall and muscular, usually good-natured and suitable for heavy work.
Of an engine or vehicle: difficult to start; runs poorly until warmed up.
A polite form of address for a woman or lady.
A woman who runs a brothel, particularly one that specializes in finding prostitutes for rich and important clients.
A hated or contemptuous woman; used as a general term of abuse
To be a madam; to run (a brothel).
e: From Middle English madame, from Old French madame, from ma (“my”) + dame (“lady”), from post-classical Latin mea domina. Doublet of Madonna.

s: A serving of Cincinnati chili with spaghetti and cheese.
e: The sense referring to a serving of Cincinnati chili was coined in the 1920s by Tom and John Kiradjieff, Slavic-Macedonian immigrants to Cincinnati, for their Empress Chili chain. Doublet of trivia.

s: An exclamation denoting surprise or frustration.
e: A minced oath from the word Jesus.
From fear + monger (“dealer in a specific commodity; (by extension) person promoting something undesirable”).

s: of an electronic component, or software algorithm: generic, standard, vanilla, easy to find
Pigments ritually applied to the face and/or body (originally and still especially of a Native American warrior) prior to going into a battle.
Any fish of the order Siluriformes, mainly found in fresh water, lacking scales, and having barbels like whiskers around the mouth.
The meat of such a fish, popular in the Southern U.S. and Central Europe.
Someone who creates a false profile on a social media platform in order to deceive people.
To create and operate a fake online profile to deceive (someone).
e: From cat + fish. Likely so named for its prominent barbels like a cat's whiskers. Compare West Frisian katfisk (“catfish”), Dutch katvis (“catfish”). Compare also German Seekatze (“catfish”).
From the 2010 documentary Catfish, supposedly inspired by the practice of fishermen keeping cod active by storing them with catfish (see sense 1) which nip at their tails.

s: A possible or hypothetical situation or proposition.
The act of transporting, or the state of being transported; conveyance, often of people, goods etc.
A means or manner of conveyance; a system of conveyance.
Punishment by sending to a penal colony, such as Australia.
To carry or bear from one place to another; to remove; to convey.
To deport to a penal colony.
To move (someone) to strong emotion; to carry away.
The state of being transported by emotion; rapture.
A vehicle used to transport (passengers, mail, freight, troops etc.)
The system of transporting passengers, etc. in a particular region; the vehicles used in such a system.
A device that moves recording tape across the read/write heads of a tape recorder or video recorder etc.
e: Inherited from Middle English transporten, a borrowing from Old French transporter (“carry or convey across”), from Latin trānsportāre (“to carry over, take across, carry, convey, remove, transport”), from trāns- + portō. trans- + port.

s: A male member of a council, often a city council or town council.
Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis, a kind of Chinese cabbage.
e: From Napa, California, where the process of making napa leather was created.

s: A mode of school bullying involving holding a person upside down over a toilet bowl, submerging their head, then flushing water.
The act of concealing oneself and lying in wait to attack or kill by surprise.
An attack launched from a concealed position.
The concealed position or state from which a surprise attack is launched.
The troops posted in a concealed place, for attacking by surprise; those who lie in wait.
To station in ambush with a view to surprise an enemy.
To attack by ambush; to waylay.
e: From Middle English enbuschen, from Old French enbuscier, anbuchier (whence Middle French embusche), from Old French en- + Vulgar Latin boscus (“wood”) (whence also bouquet), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambuscade. The change to am- from earlier forms in en- is unexplained. More at bush.

s: six-pack (highly developed set of abdominal muscles)
The lowest or last position in a rank.
A garment worn to cover the body below the torso.
The lowest part of a container.
Spirits poured into a glass before adding soda water.
The second half of an inning, the home team's turn at bat.
The bass or baritone instruments of a band.
The working portion of a moldboard-style plow.
The remotest or innermost part of something.
The fundamental part; a basic aspect.
Low-lying land; a valley or hollow.
-lying land near a river with alluvial soil.
The bed of a body of water.
e: From Middle English botme,botom, from Old English botm,bodan (“bottom, foundation; ground, abyss”), from Proto-West Germanic *butm, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz, *budmaz (“bottom; ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”).

s: A male magic-user; a male equivalent of a witch.
A plant belonging to the genus Mimosa usually found in tropical climates, their leaves are usually prickly and sensitive to touch or light, and have small white or pink flowers.
Certain plants of the genus Albizia (silk tree, pink siris).
Certain plants of the genus Acacia.
A cocktail consisting of half champagne and half orange juice.
e: From New Latin mimosa, from Latin mimus (“mime, actor”), referring to Mimosa pudica and its habit of shrinking back when touched. The cocktail is named after the bright yellow, fragrant flowers of the mimosa Acacia dealbata.

s: Unable to see, or only partially able to see.
Failing to recognize, acknowledge or perceive.
Closed at one end; having a dead end; exitless.
Having no openings for light or passage; both dark and exitless.
Able to be fixed without access to one end.
Unconditional; without regard to evidence, logic, reality, accidental mistakes, extenuating circumstances, etc.
Using blinded study design, wherein information is purposely limited to prevent bias.
(Of a pimple) not having a well-defined head.
failing to produce flowers or fruit.
A movable covering for a window to keep out light, made of cloth or of narrow slats that can block light or allow it to pass.
A destination sign mounted on a public transport vehicle displaying the route destination, number, name and/or via points, etc.
e: From Middle English blynd, from Old English blind, from Proto-West Germanic *blind, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz. Cognate with blind, blindur.

s: To push someone over by heading straight over them. Often used in conjunction with "over".
To push into a heap, as a bulldozer does.
To shoot down an idea immediately and forcefully.
To intimidate; to restrain or coerce by intimidation or violence; used originally of the intimidation of black voters in Louisiana.
e: From earlier bulldose, equivalent to bull + dose or bullwhip + dose, as black voters were intimidated through whipping in the lead-up to the 1876 U.S. presidential election.

s: A small figure resembling a human being that is used as a toy.
A transgender woman or transfeminine person, especially one that has a highly sexual and feminine personal style.
A transgender woman or transfeminine person, in general.
A good-natured, cooperative or helpful person.
The smallest or pet pig in a litter.
A short signal post mounted on a bracket mounted on the main signal post, or on a signal gantry.
A pixel art depiction of a person, typically customized from a base template.
A temporary barrier used in horse racing.
To place a barrier in front of (a section of the course that is to be omitted from a horse race).
To warm moderately; to make tepid; to mull.
e: From Doll, pet form of the given name Dorothy. was and popularized by Coined by Jacqueline Susann through her book Valley of the Dolls (1966) and the film adaptation Valley of the Dolls (1967).

s: Any strategy devised to reach a given objective.
e: From the strategies used in sports.

s: Remarkably great, big, vast in an often unpleasant way; (of behaviour) Highly or conspicuously offensive.
Excluding any deductions; including all associated amounts.
Seen without a microscope (usually for a tissue or an organ); at a large scale; not detailed.
Lacking refinement in behaviour or manner; offending a standard of morality.
Lacking refinement; not of high quality.
Heavy in proportion to one's height; having a lot of excess flesh.
Difficult or impossible to see through.
Not sensitive in perception or feeling.
The total amount (of goods, money, etc) before taxes, expenses, exceptions, tares, or similar deductions are subtracted.
To earn money, not including expenses.
e: From Middle English gros (“large, thick, full-bodied; coarse, unrefined, simple”), from Old French gros, from Latin grossus (“big, fat, thick”), of uncertain further origin but perhaps related to Proto-Celtic *brassos.

s: Of the skin, to split or flake due to cold weather or dryness.
To cause to open in slits or chinks; to split; to cause the skin of to crack or become rough.
A cleft, crack, or chink, as in the surface of the earth, or in the skin.
A division; a breach, as in a party.
One of the jaws or cheeks of a vice, etc.
e: From Middle English chappen (“to split open, burst, chap”), of Uncertain origin. Compare Middle English choppen (“to chop”), Dutch kappen (“to cut, chop, hack”). Perhaps related to chip.
From Northern English chafts (“jaws”). Compare also Middle English cheppe (“one side of the jaw, chap”).

s: To wiggle or twitch; to move the body, especially the fingers, around nervously or idly.
To cause to fidget; to make uneasy.
A nervous wriggling or twitching motion.
A person who fidgets, especially habitually.
An object, such as a tool or toy, intended to be fidgeted with.
e: From fidge (“to fidget”), possibly from Middle English *-ten, from Old English -ettan.

s: A state legislature (of one of the fifty United States), or government generally.
A house built and operated by the government, usually of relatively low price and lived in by people on low incomes.
The fruit of the hazel, especially of species Corylus avellana, which is grown commercially.
A light tan color inspired by the color of hazelnut.
e: Equivalent to hazel + nut; from Middle English haselnote, from Old English hæselhnutu (“hazelnut”). Cognate with West Frisian hazzenút (“hazelnut”), Hoaselnuute (“hazelnut”), Dutch hazelnoot, German Haselnuss.

s: To be witness of the authenticity of a document and its accompanying signatures in one's capacity as notary public.
To split from or to withdraw from membership of a political union, an alliance or an organisation.
To split or to withdraw one or more constituent entities from membership of a political union, an alliance or an organisation.
The quantity or amount by which anything falls short.
A part by which a figure or quantity is wanting or deficient.
To abandon or turn against; to cease or change one's loyalty, especially from a military organisation or political party.
To desert one's army, to flee from combat.
To flee one's country and seek asylum.
e: Borrowed from Latin defectus (“a failure, lack”), from deficere (“to fail, lack, literally 'undo'”), from past participle defectus, from de- (“of, from”) + facere (“to do”).

s: A male ballet dancer; Synonym of ballerino.
The pointed head, or end, of a spear.
Something or somebody leading or initiating an activity (such as an attack or campaign).
The leading military unit in an attack.
A player who initiates attacking moves.
To drive or campaign ardently for (an effort, project, etc.); to direct.
A lighter-than-air aircraft that can be propelled forward through the air as well as steered.
A police air unit, a police helicopter.
A high ranking official of the RAF, viewed as arrogant and distant.
A small, light vehicle with runners, used recreationally, mostly by children, for sliding down snow-covered hills; no draft animal pulls it.
A vehicle on runners, used for conveying loads over the snow or ice, and often pulled by sled dogs.
A car (automobile) or truck, usually called so with the implication of sledlike traits: heavy, low-slung, and prone to going fast but not braking or cornering particularly well.
A piece of exercise equipment, used in American football training etc., that provides resistance as it is moved over a flat surface.
e: From Middle English sledde, from Middle Dutch sledde or Middle Low German sledde (compare Dutch slee, slede, Low German Sleden), from Proto-Germanic *slidô (compare sliede, German Schlitten, Norwegian slede). Doublet of sleigh; also related to slide.

s: An educational institution for young children, usually between ages 4 and 6; a nursery school.
The elementary school grade before first grade.
The two levels between nursery and prep; the second and third years of preschool.
Refinement; cleanliness in performance or presentation.
To shine; to make a surface very smooth or shiny by rubbing, cleaning, or grinding.
To apply shoe polish to shoes.
To become smooth, as from friction; to receive a gloss; to take a smooth and glossy surface.
To refine; to wear off the rudeness, coarseness, or rusticity of; to make elegant and polite.
e: From Middle English polishen, from Old French poliss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of polir, from Latin polīre (“to polish, make smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive, strike, thrust”), from the notion of fulling cloth.

s: To charge an electric battery after its power has been consumed.
To invigorate and revitalize one's energy level by removing stressful agents for a period of time.
To reload a gun with ammunition.
To add or restore water to an aquifer.
To charge or accuse in return.
Water that has percolated from the ground surface to an aquifer.
The process of charging (an electrical device) again.
The process of revitalizing one's energy level by removing stressful agents for a period of time.
e: From Old French rechargier, from Old French re- + Old French chargier.

s: A small nocturnal insect pest of humans, of species Cimex lectularius (common bedbug) and Cimex hemipterus (tropical bedbug) that feeds on the blood of humans during sleep.
Any similar insect of family Cimicidae, that feeds on the blood of humans and certain other warm-blooded animals.
Someone who looks after the maintenance and cleaning of a public building.

A caretaker or custodian; someone who maintains a school building specifically and may serve other administrative roles (the term caretaker is also used in Hong Kong, particularly in ESF and independent British schools).
A moderator for a discussion forum.
The caudal appendage of an animal that is attached to their posterior and near the anus or cloaca.
An object or part of an object resembling a tail in shape, such as the thongs on a cat-o'-nine-tails; a strand of material hanging from something.
The back, last, lower, or inferior part of anything.
The feathers attached to the pygostyle of a bird.
The rear structure of an aircraft, the empennage.
The visible stream of dust and gases blown from a comet by the solar wind.
The latter part of a time period or event, or (collectively) persons or objects represented in this part.
The part of a distribution most distant from the mode.
The lower order of batsmen in the batting order, usually specialist bowlers.
The lower loop of the letters in the Roman alphabet, as in g, q or y.
The side of a coin not bearing the head; normally the side on which the monetary value of the coin is indicated; the reverse.
All the last terms of a sequence, from some term on.
The penis of a person or animal.
e: From Anglo-Norman, probably from a shortened form of entail.

s: To submerge briefly in a liquid.
To put the ball directly downward through the hoop while grabbing onto the rim with power.
To put down on social media.
The act or instance of dunking, particularly in basketball.
e: From dunke, from Middle High German dunken, from Old High German dunkōn (“to dip, submerge, dunk”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunkōn (“to make wet”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *þunkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to moisten, wet”). Cognate with German tunken (“to dunk”), Latin tingō (“to wet, moisten”), Ancient Greek τέγγω (“to wet, moisten”).

s: To rule over or control arbitrarily or arrogantly; to tyrannize.
A large floor, usually made of hardwood, used primarily for dancing.
To express one’s sympathetic pleasure or joy to the person(s) it is felt for
To consider oneself fortunate in some matter.
e: Borrowed from Latin congrātulātus, the perfect active participle of Latin congrātulor (“to wish joy, rejoice (with); to congratulate”) (see -ate), from con- + grātulor, from grātus (“grateful, pleasing, agreeable, beloved”) + -or. con- + gratulate.

s: Of a speech: meandering, long and digressing.
A long meandering talk with no specific topic or direction.
To allow or permit without explicit approval, usually if it is perceived as negative.
e: Borrowed from Latin tolerātus, the perfect passive participle of tolerō (“to endure”), see -ate. Cognate with Old English þolian (“to tolerate, suffer, bear”) and French tolérer. More at thole.

s: To show or display in a bad light; to portray unfavorably.
Clip of submarine sandwich: a sandwich made on a long bun.
Clipping of subroutine (sometimes one that does not return a value, as distinguished from a function, which does)
Clipping of subscription (or a subscriber) to an online channel or feed.
A small, light, and usually savory first course in a meal.
Something that creates or increases excitement for what is to follow.
Anything that improves the condition of something.
Someone who trains athletes or racehorses.
An agricultural machine that crimps and crushes newly cut hay to promote faster and more even drying.
To move the lips with the mouth closed; to mumble, as in sulkiness.
To beg, especially if using a repeated phrase.
To deprive of (something) by cheating; to impose upon.
To cheat; to deceive; to play the beggar.
e: Perhaps borrowed through obsolete Dutch mompen (“to cheat, swindle, deceive”), according to Kroonen, a derivative of Proto-Germanic *mump- (“to stain”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mm̥bʰ-neh₂- Also akin to German mimpfeln (“to mumble”), Icelandic mumpa (“to take into the mouth”). See also English mum.

s: To attest to (a fact) as the truth.
To authenticate or verify in writing.
To attest that a product, service, organization, or person has met an official standard.
To inform; to tell (a person) that something is true.
To assure (oneself) of something; to ascertain.
e: From Old French certefier (“confirm, assure, make certain”). Compare French certifier.

s: Belonging or pertaining to an individual person, group of people, or entity that is not the state.
Relating to an individual or group of individuals outside of their official roles; often, sensitive or personal.
Not publicly known or divulged; secret, confidential; intended only for a specific person or group.
Protected from view or disturbance by others; secluded; not publicly accessible.
Not in governmental office or employment.
Of a room in a medical facility, not shared with another patient.
Financially reliant on fees rather than government funding.
Accessible only to the class itself or instances of it, and not to other classes or even subclasses.
Of the mind or language, not in principle experienceable, knowable, or understandable by others.
A soldier of the lowest rank in the army.
A doctor working in privately rather than publicly funded health care.
A secret message; a personal unofficial communication.
e: From Middle English privat (“individual, exclusive, private”), from Latin prīvātus (“bereaved, deprived, set apart from, release”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive, release”) (see -ate for more), from prīvus (“private, one's own, proper”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per; compare prime, prior, pristine.

s: To apply a fragrance to; to perfume.
e: Borrowed from French fragrance, from Middle French fragrance, from Old French fraglance, from Late Latin frāgrantia. See fragrant.

s: A dummy, or life-size model of the human body, used for martial arts training or the fitting or displaying of clothes.
A jointed model of the human body used by artists, especially to demonstrate the arrangement of drapery.
An anatomical model of the human body for use in teaching of e.g. CPR.
e: Borrowed from French mannequin, Derived from Old French (“little man, figurine”), Derived from Middle Dutch mannekin or mannekijn (see English manikin), diminutive of man (“man”). man + -kin. Compare ramequin/ramekin. Doublet of manakin, manikin.

s: A computer application for organization, analysis, and storage of data in tabular form.
A document created with such an application.
A sheet of paper, marked with a grid, in which financial data is recorded and totals calculated manually.
To model or compute by means of a spreadsheet.
A worker who runs errands; an errand boy.
e: From go + ferfor>, as in “go for coffee” or “go for that document” etc. Possibly also a pun on the rodent gopher, animals known for both their vast tunneling and their hoarding activities.

s: a silicone rubber wristband (originating as a basketball sports wristband)
e: From baller + band. Popularized by sports brands like Nike, Inc., particularly initially for basketball.

s: One who, or that which, bleaches.
A stand of tiered planks used as seating for spectators, often outdoors.
The tiered seating provided for the audience at a television filming.
e: From Middle English blechere, equivalent to bleach + -er. Compare Dutch bleker, Swedish blekare. The seating was so named because the boards were bleached by the sun.

s: Carbonated water (water impregnated with pressurised carbon dioxide, originally made with sodium bicarbonate).
A glass, bottle or can of this drink.
The first card in the dealing box in the game of faro, which is discarded to leave 51 cards in play.
A day that is an exact number of years (to the day) since a given significant event occurred. Often preceded by an ordinal number indicating the number of years.
Such a day that commemorates a wedding.
(loosely) A day subsequent in time to a given event by some significant period other than a year (especially as prefixed by the amount of time in question).
Lasting for or completed in a year.
To mark, commemorate, or celebrate the anniversary of (something).
To mark, commemorate, or celebrate an anniversary, especially a wedding anniversary.
To pass the anniversary of (something), in the context of a company’s yearly financial report.
e: From Middle English anniversary,annyversarie,annyverary,annyversarye,anyversarye, from Anglo-Norman aniversarie,anniversarie and aniversaire,anniversaire (modern French anniversaire) and their etymon Classical Latin anniversārius (“yearly”), from annus (“year”) + vertō (“to turn”). The verb is from the noun.

s: To apply lipstick to; to paint with lipstick.
A type of Mexican flatbread made out of cornmeal or flour.
Spanish omelette; a type of omelette containing potatoes and onions.
Lack of difficulty; the ability to do something easily.
Comfort, a state or quality lacking unpleasantness, particularly
Freedom from pain, hardship, and annoyance, sometimes idleness, sloth.
Freedom from worry and concern; peace; sometimes indifference.
Freedom from financial effort or worry; affluence.
Freedom from embarrassment or awkwardness; grace.
Relief, an end to discomfort, particularly
Followed by of or from: release from or reduction of pain, hardship, or annoyance.
Release from constraint, obligation, or a constrained position.
Additional space provided to allow greater movement.
To free (something) from pain, worry, agitation, etc.
e: From Middle English ese, eise, aise, from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (“elbow room; opportunity”), of Uncertain and obscure origin. Apparently related to Provençal ais, Italian agio and asio, Sicilian aciu and Portuguese azo.

s: A Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla wrapped around a filling of meat and/or beans, cheese etc.
To wrap someone or something up like a burrito.
e: Borrowed from Spanish burrito, diminutive of burro (“donkey”), from burrico (“donkey”), from Latin burricus (“small horse”), from burrus (“red-brown”), from Ancient Greek πυρρός (“flame-colored”), from πῦρ (“fire”). A possible origin is due to its resemblance to a rolled up pack as typically carried by donkeys, making it an example of synecdoche.

s: A person who practices swinging (sex with different partners).
A bet in which the bettor must correctly pick two runners to finish in any of the places in any order.
A performer of swing music or whose style is influenced by swing.
A passenger on a motorcycle's sidecar who athletically moves from one side to the other to alter the weight distribution.
Anything very large, forcible, or astonishing.

An area of wet (water-saturated), spongy (soft) land, often with trees, generally a rich ecosystem for certain plants and animals but ill-suited for many agricultural purposes. (A type of wetland. Compare marsh, bog, fen.)
A place or situation that is foul or where progress is difficult.
The alleged corruption, cronyism, inefficiency, and entrenched interests in the federal government, especially in Washington, DC.
To drench or fill with water.
To overwhelm; to make too busy, or overrun the capacity of.
To plunge into difficulties and perils; to overwhelm; to ruin; to wreck.
To clear (a road or an area) of brush, particularly so as to create a path for loggers to be able to access trees.
e: Early attestations (starting in 1624) are from North America, but the term was probably in local use in Britain earlier.

s: A hot sandwich consisting of a patty of cooked ground beef or a meat substitute, in a sliced bun, usually also containing salad vegetables, condiments, or both.
Ingredients used in this type of sandwich
The patty used in such a sandwich.
Ground beef, especially that intended to be made into hamburgers.
An animal or human, or the flesh thereof, that has been badly injured as a result of an accident or conflict.
Describing the shape of a rectangular piece of paper folded in half so that it forms a short rectangle.
To badly injure or damage (a fleshy part of the body).
e: Shortening of Hamburger sandwich, Hamburger steak, etc., the first element borrowed from German Hamburger (“native of Hamburg”), equivalent to Hamburg + -er.

s: A physically attractive man who lacks intelligence; the male equivalent of a bimbo.
e: him + bimbo, first recorded in 1988 and likely influenced by sex scandals in the US politics around the time.

s: Alternative form of of jet ski.
Alternative form of of jet ski.

Chinese-American variant of the spring roll (春卷); food made made by wrapping a combination of chopped vegetables, possibly meat, and sometimes noodles, in a sheet of dough, dipping the dough in egg or an egg wash, then deep frying it.

A thin crispy biscuit roll similar to the Spanish barquillo, Dutch kniepertjes, and Norwegian krumkake. Usually made from coconut milk, eggs, flour, sugar, and oil. This food item has many names: in Malay, kuih/kueh/kue kapit/sepit/sapit/semprong (literally "clamped/tongs/roll cake/snack"); in Chine
An African snack resembling a Scotch egg.
An instance of the egg rolling tradition.
e: (food) From egg + roll. In, uncertain. In, a direct transliteration of the Chinese 蛋卷.

s: A game played on a rectangular court between two teams of two to six players which involves striking a ball back and forth over a net.
The inflated ball used in such a game.
A small hole, opening or piece of glass, especially in a door, through which one can look without being seen.
An organized search for a criminal or enemy.
A variant of hide and seek in which a player who is caught by the seeker themselves becomes a seeker, and the final player remaining is declared the winner.
Alternative form of all right; satisfactory; okay; in acceptable order.
Used to indicate acknowledgement or acceptance; OK.
A generic greeting; hello; how are you.
e: From all + right Compare Old English eallriht (“all-right, just, exactly”) (from eall + riht), equivalent to al-#Etymology_1- (“all”) + right.

s: Not able to be dated; that may be not be ascribed a date (or age).
Not dateable; unsuitable for romantic outings; unattractive.
A person who is unsuitable to be dated, or taken on a romantic outing.

e: Onomatopoeic for the sound of urination.

s: In mammals, a sheet of muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen, contracted and relaxed in respiration to draw air into and expel air from the lungs.
Any of various membranes or sheets of muscle or ligament which separate one cavity from another.
A contraceptive device consisting of a flexible cup, used to cover the cervix during intercourse.
A flexible membrane separating two chambers and fixed around its periphery that distends into one or other chamber as the difference in the pressure in the chambers varies.
In a speaker, the thin, semi-rigid membrane which vibrates to produce sound.
A thin opaque structure with a central aperture, used to limit the passage of light into a camera or similar device.
A floor slab, metal wall panel, roof panel or the like, having a sufficiently large in-plane shear stiffness and sufficient strength to transmit horizontal forces to resisting systems.
To reduce lens aperture using an optical diaphragm.
To act as a diaphragm, for example by vibrating.
e: From Middle English diafragma, Ancient Greek διάφραγμα (“partition”), from διά (“across”) and φράγμα (“barrier”), from the verb φράσσω..

s: Any of various cobras of the genus Naja that can spit venom.
A booth on a toll road or toll bridge where the toll is collected.
The traditional municipal building of a Scottish town or burgh, usually including a meeting-hall, court, prison and (eponymically) a place for the receipt of taxes, duties and fines.
To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).
To steep; to cause to absorb liquid.
e: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

s: A legal document, signed by both parties before marriage, stating the legal claims on each other's estate upon a subsequent divorce.
To provoke someone to do wrong, especially by promising a reward; to entice.
e: From Middle English tempten, from Old French tempter (French: tenter), from Latin temptare, from tentare (“to handle, touch, try, test, tempt”), frequentative of tendere (“to stretch”). Displaced native English costning (“temptation”).

s: Able to be exchanged, one for the other, especially
Able to undergo conversion (i.e., inversion) without falsehood.
Able to be turned into a different thing, especially
A convertible car: a car with a removable or foldable roof able to convert from a closed to open vehicle and back again.
A convertible security: a stock, bond, etc. that can be turned into another (usually common stock) under certain set terms.
A computer able to be converted between laptop and tablet form factors.
e: From Old French convertible, from Late Latin convertibilis (“interchangeable”), from Latin convertere (“to turn back, to turn over, to turn around, to turn upside down”), from con- (“with, together”) + vertere (“to turn”), + -ibilis (“-ible: able to”). Equivalent to convert + -ible.
