To compel a supernatural entity to cease haunting a place, often by ritual or prayer; to exorcise or banish (a spirit or ghost).
To prepare (a plan, project etc.); to set out, establish (a law, principle).
To install certain building materials, laying one thing on top of another.
To produce and deposit (an egg or eggs).
To bet (that something is or is not the case).
To deposit (a stake) as a wager; to stake; to risk.
To put the strands of (a rope, a cable, etc.) in their proper places and twist or unite them.
To place and arrange (pages) for a form upon the imposing stone.
To place (new type) properly in the cases.
To impose (a burden, punishment, command, tax, etc.).
e: Inherited from Middle English leyen, leggen, from Old English leċġan (“to lay”), from Proto-West Germanic *laggjan, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną (“to lay”), causative form of Proto-Germanic *ligjaną (“to lie, recline”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie, recline”).
Inherited from Middle English lay, laye, laie, ley, leye, which may have multiple origins: All of these theories make it a Doublet of loch, Looe, lough.
Inherited from Middle English lay, from Old French lai, from Latin lāicus, from Ancient Greek λαϊκός. Doublet of laic.

Inherited from Middle English lay, from Old French lai (“song, lyric, poem”), from Frankish *laih (“play, melody, song”), from Proto-Germanic *laikaz, *laikiz (“jump, play, dance, hymn”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“to jump, spring, play”).
From Middle English lay, laye, laiȝe, leyȝe, from Old English lǣh, lēh, northern (Anglian) variants of Old English lēah (“lea”). More at lea.

Inherited from Middle English lay, lai, laye, ley, lei, borrowed from Old French lei (“law”). Possibly also from or influenced by the etymologically unrelated Middle English lawe (“law”) (with variants including laige, laiȝh, læȝe), from Old English lagu (“law”). More at law.
Semantic loan from Yiddish לייגן (“to put, lay”).

s: A pitch thrown on a count of three balls and two strikes.
My Lord (used to address peers temporal, judges, etc).
Repeated so often that it has become stale or commonplace; hackneyed.
A small, chocolate-covered, creme-filled pastry puff in a general oblong shape, typically larger than the miniature French version.
In the style of a negligee; revealing, titillating.
A woman's lightweight gown of the eighteenth century.
A necklace of beads, pearls etc.
A state of careless undress or very informal attire.
A woman's loose-fitting nightgown, especially when short, lacy or revealing; a nightie.
e: From French négligée, from French négligé (“underdressed; loose garment”), past participle of négliger (“to neglect”), from Latin negligere.

s: Valerianella locusta, a small dicot annual plant of the family Caprifoliaceae often cultivated as a salad green or herb.
Lo, there it is; ta-da; presto; behold!
A smaller dish served before the main course of a meal.
The main course or main dish of a meal.
The act of entering somewhere, or permission to enter; admittance.
Sought out and chosen with care; choice; exquisite.
Exotic; of rare quality, elegance, attractiveness, etc.
e: French recherché; more at French rechercher. Doublet of ricercata.

s: A type of cooperative society whereby all members pay a regular sum of savings, or through which goods can be paid for in installments.
A group of people in a sexual relationship; especially, such a group that live together; the relationship itself.
e: Borrowed from French ménage; compare Middle English menage, a parallel borrowing from an earlier form of the French word.

s: A ritualistic ceremony where people try to communicate with the spirits of dead people, usually led by a medium and often with the goal of getting the spirits cause physically observable phenomena.
The sitting of an assembly to discuss a matter.
To hold a séance (communication with spirits).
A man whose identity is unknown or forgotten (especially when better-known to the listener).
A passing (male) acquaintance of no importance or relevance.
A brilliant or successful effect; brilliance of success or effort; splendor; brilliant show; striking effect; glory; renown.
e: Borrowed from French éclat, from éclater (“to burst out”). Akin to Old English slītan (“to split”). More at slice, slit. Doublet of slate, slat. Middle French fro.

s: or with the fronts facing each other.
Looking frontwise, or toward the viewer.
e: Borrowed from French affronté, past participle of affronter (“to confront, face”).

s: The fifteenth birthday and particularly the celebration and ceremony surrounding it for a young Latina woman.
e: Borrowed from quinceañera, feminine of quinceañero, from quince años (“fifteen years”) + -ero.

s: used as a filled pause to indicating thinking or pondering, but allowing hearer to participate
A soft type originating in France, often formed in a cylinder.
Something, most often a phrase or expression, that is overused or used outside its original context, so that its original impact and meaning are lost. A trite saying; a platitude.
having the characteristics of a cliché.
To use a cliché; to make up a word or a name that sounds like a cliché.
Rice wine; a drink made from filtered fermented rice.
e: Borrowed from Japanese 酒 (“rice wine”), where the final e is accented to indicate that it is pronounced where it would usually remain silent in other senses of sake, as well as to differentiate it. Likely influenced by French saké.

s: To benefit by having two things which are mutually incompatible (such as eating a piece of cake and yet still possessing that piece for future use).
A coffee shop; an establishment selling coffee and sometimes other non-alcoholic beverages, simple meals or snacks, with a facility to consume them on the premises.
A small restaurant of any genre.
A smooth and continuous bending of the knees
A kind of corded or ribbed fabric made from cotton, rayon, or silk.
A movement in which the raised, pointed foot of the working leg is lowered so that it pricks the floor and then either rebounds upward or becomes a supporting foot.
A kind of fermented dark Assam green tea (C. sinensis var. assamica).
e: Shortened from pu'er tea, from the pinyin romanization of the Mandarin pronunciation of Chinese 普洱茶.

s: A building for the porter(s) near the gate of a castle, college, etc., formerly used as a place of punishment for the staff.
An equivalent room near the gate of a college, chiefly used as a mailroom.
A pale pink wine made by removing the dark grape skins at the required point during fermentation.
used to express the possibility of something occurring in the past as condition to another non-occurring past event
used to express uncertainty about a past event
A Spanish term of address equivalent to Mrs., used alone or capitalized and prefixed to the name of a married, divorced or widowed woman
An acknowledgement of the validity, appropriateness or superiority of an opponent's argument or statement in a discussion.
e: Borrowed from French touché, past participle of toucher (“to touch”). More at touch.

s: A miniature house used by children as a toy for recreating domestic settings.

A nonpossessory interest in land which grants the legal right to enter onto another person's real property (real estate) for the purpose of taking from its soil, mines and minerals, natural produce or flora and fauna.
A fabric made from gold or silver threads and silk, wool or cotton.
The electrically conductive jacket worn by foil and sabre fencers.
An expression of one's own physical pain.
An expression in sympathy at another's pain.
A reply to an insult seen as savage (frequently one that is tongue-in-cheek or joking).
Expressing surprise at the high price of something.
Something that causes discomfort or pain.
To exclaim "ouch!" in discomfort or pain.
e: Uncertain. Some sources say the interjection is attested since 1838 (and specifically in American English) and derives ultimately from German autsch, perhaps specifically via outch (“cry of pain”), as early attestations of the interjection are from Pennsylvania.

s: strength, force or influence held by a person or group.
Used to indicate a desired past action that was not done.
Used to indicate conditional or possible actions; would perhaps/maybe.
Used concessively to admit something before making a more accurate or important statement; although
Used in polite requests for permission.
e: From Old English meahte and mihte, inflections of magan, whence English may.

s: A brooch or clasp for fastening a piece of clothing together, especially when set with jewels or valuable.
e: From Middle English ouche, from nouche, which in phrases like a nouche was re-analyzed as an ouche. From Anglo-Norman nusche and Old French nusche (with metanalysis), from a source; compare German Nusche, Proto-Germanic *hnuts.

s: The act of one who fools; foolish behaviour.
An accumulation of angular, coarse-grained fragments (particles of sand and gravel) resulting from the chemical and mechanical weathering of crystalline rocks.
The condition or feeling of being safe; security; certainty.
A safety lock or safety catch: a mechanism on a weapon or dangerous equipment designed to prevent accidental firing or operation.
An instance of a player being sacked or tackled in the end zone, or stepping out of the end zone and off the field, resulting in two points to the opposite team.
Any of the defensive players who are in position furthest from the line of scrimmage and whose responsibility is to defend against passes as well as to be the tacklers of last resort.
A safety shot or sequence of such shots.
To secure (a mechanical component, as in aviation) to keep it from becoming detached even under vibration.
to secure a firing pin, as in guns, to keep the gun from firing
e: Inherited from Middle English savete, from Old French sauveté, from earlier salvetet, from Medieval Latin salvitās, salvitātem, from Latin salvus.

s: To pay (someone) less than the value of their work; to pay (someone) insufficiently.
To pay less than is due for (something).
A person with poor judgment or little intelligence.
A jester; a person whose role was to entertain a sovereign and the court (or lower personages).

A stock character typified by unintelligence, naïveté or lucklessness, usually as a form of comic relief; often used as a source of insight or pathos for the audience, as such characters are generally less bound by social expectations.
Someone who has been made a fool of or tricked; dupe.
Someone who derives pleasure from something specified.
An informal greeting akin to buddy, dude, or man.
A particular card in a tarot deck, representing a jester.
To act in an idiotic manner; to act foolishly.
To make a fool of; to make act the fool.
A type of dessert made of puréed fruit and custard or cream.
e: From Middle English fol (“fool”), from Old French fol (cf. modern French fou (“mad”)) from Latin follis. Doublet of fals, follis. Displaced native Old English dwæs.
Attested since 1917, apparently a back-formation from detoxify. (attested since 1905). Equivalent to toxic + -ify.

s: A northern shoveler (Spatula clypeata, formerly Anas clypeata).
A person with a chronic illness or disability.
e: Unknown. Possibly related to the phrase born with a silver spoon in one's mouth.
From the spatulate shape of the bill.
From spoon (“unit of limited personal energy”) + -ie. See spoon theory.

s: The act of putting up a barricade.
A large pot used for processing jars when preserving food, either in a boiling water bath or by capturing steam to elevate the pressure and temperature.
Someone who lives off container deposit refunds from recycling.
An animal yielding inferior meat best suited to canning.
e: From Middle English canner (“maker of cans”), originally from the noun canne and equivalent to can + -er. The modern senses reflect other meanings of the suffix -er.

s: Designed to perform a specific task.
Of devices, closely or tightly coupled.
Having a fixed placement (on a screen format for example).
Having made a belief or a pattern of behavior or a habit.
To beget (of a man); to bear or conceive (of a woman).
To give existence to, to produce (living creatures).
To bring into existence (a situation, quality, result etc.); to give rise to, cause, create.
To assume form; to come into existence; to be caused or produced.
To endow with gender; to create gender or enhance the importance of gender.
e: From Middle English engendren, from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.

s: The act of keeping something safe; protection from harm, damage, loss, or theft.
The storage of assets in a protected area.
The act or process of not returning checks; a system wherein banks keep checks (cheques) that people write, rather than returning them to the account holder with their monthly statement.
The portion of a communications link used for the transmission of signals from a ground station to a satellite or to an airborne platform.
The communication path from a mobile device to a base station, a consumer to the network backbone, a client device to a server, etc.
Data transmission from a data station to the headend.
To transmit a signal by means of an uplink.
One who spoons; one who engages in spooning.
A person who engages in kissing and petting.
A person who lies nestled against their partner in bed, back-to-front on their sides
A transparent screen made of glass, located at the front of a vehicle in order to protect its occupants from the wind and weather.
A cover for a microphone to exclude airy noises such as wind and breathing.
A lightweight aerodynamic fairing mounted on the nose of an armor-piercing shell to reduce drag and increase range.
A draught screen at the side of a passenger train doorway.
Characterised by causing feelings of embarrassment; embarrassing.
To give in or be swayed; to become less hard, harsh, or cruel; to show clemency.
To lessen, make less severe or intense.
To become less rigid or hard; to soften; to yield, for example by dissolving or melting
A stay; a stop; a delay.
e: From Middle English relenten, from Anglo-Norman relentir, from Latin re- + lentare (“to bend”), from lentus (“soft, pliant, slow”). Earliest recording dates to 1526. The noun is from the verb.

s: A plant of species Glycyrrhiza glabra, or sometimes in North America, the related American licorice plant Glycyrrhiza lepidota.
A type of candy made from that plant's dried root or its extract.
A black color, named after the licorice.
A flavoring agent made from dried root portions of the aforementioned plant.
A supposed aphrodisiac made in the past from dried roots of Glycyrrhiza glabra and Glycyrrhiza echinata.
e: From Middle English lycorys, from Old French licoresse, from Late Latin liquiritia, alteration of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα: γλυκύς (“sweet”) + ῥίζα (“root”) (English glucose, English rhizome). Doublet of glycyrrhiza.

s: A close friendship in a group of friends or teammates.
A spirit of familiarity and closeness, especially when expressed somewhat boisterously.
e: French camaraderie.. Recent American pronunciations such as /ˌkɑməˈɹɑdəɹi/ and /ˌkɑmˈɹɑdəɹi/ are influenced by the cognate comrade.

s: A framework on a post, with holes for the hands and head, used as a means of punishment and humiliation.
To subject to humiliation, scorn, ridicule or abuse.
e: From Middle English pilory, pillorie, from Old French pilori, pellori, which is either from Old Occitan espilori or Latin pīla (“pillar”).

s: One who herds cattle; a cowboy.
e: From Middle English couherde, from Old English cūhierde, equivalent to cow + herd (“herder”). Doublet of Coward (the surname). Cognate with German Kuhhirte (“cowherd”). Compare shepherd, goatherd, swineherd, etc.

s: Someone who supervises workers, especially one who imposes hard or burdensome work.
A source of hard work or responsibility.
Someone who is capable of performing many tasks; a multitasker.
To marry a second or subsequent time (the same spouse or a different one) after the end of a marriage.
A style of Afro-Caribbean music that originated in Trinidad and Tobago during the early to the mid-19th century and spread to the rest of the Caribbean Antilles and Venezuela by the mid-20th century.
A song in this style of music.
A bulbous bog orchid of the genus Calypso, Calypso bulbosa
e: Originally Trinidad English, an alteration of kaiso, perhaps ultimately of African origin; Allsopp 1996 suggests ka iso (“come on”), used to urge dancers on. The spelling reflects a later folk-etymological assimilation with the mythological name Calypso.
From Latin, itself from Ancient Greek Καλυψώ (“name of a sea nymph”)

s: Either of two very large amounts
A billion billion: 1 followed by eighteen zeros, 1018; one million million million.
A million quadrillion: 1 followed by 30 zeros, 1030.
Any very large number, exceeding normal description.
Items thrown overboard from a ship or boat in distress in order to lighten its load.
Discarded or leftover odds and ends.
e: From Middle English jetteson, from Anglo-Norman getteson. Doublet of jettison.

s: The act of making, or condition of being, cluttered.
A speech disorder characterized by fast, jerky, or irregular speech, which often sounds like stuttering.

e: From Middle French inhumanité, from Latin inhumanitas, equivalent to inhuman + -ity.

s: Incapable of suffering detriment or injury.
Unable to suffer, or feel pain.
A state of not knowing what to decide; a state of difficulty or perplexity; a state of uncertainty, hesitation or puzzlement; a dilemma, a difficult decision or choice.
e: 16th century. Origin Unknown; perhaps a dialectal corruption (simulating a word of Latin origin with suffix -ary) of wandreth (“evil, plight, peril, adversity, difficulty”), from Middle English wandreth, from Old Norse vandræði (“difficulty, trouble”), from vándr (“difficult, requiring pains and care”).

s: Enamored in a silly or sentimental way; having a crush (on someone).
A foolish, simple, or silly person.
A guard, particularly on duty at the entrance to a military base.
Sentry duty; time spent being a sentry.
A form of drag to be towed underwater, which on striking bottom is upset and rises to the surface.
An animal like a marmot tasked with alerting the pack to danger.
e: From earlier sentrie, sentery, of uncertain origin. Perhaps an alteration of Doublet of sentinel or sanctuary; or perhaps from Old French senteret (“a path”), diminutive of sentier, from Medieval Latin semitarius (“a path”).

s: Something assumed without proof as being self-evident or generally accepted, especially when used as a basis for an argument. Sometimes distinguished from axioms as being relevant to a particular science or context, rather than universally true, and following from other axioms rather than being an a
A fundamental element; a basic principle; a priori.
To assume as a truthful or accurate premise or axiom, especially as a basis of an argument.
To appoint or request one's appointment to an ecclesiastical office.
To request, demand or claim for oneself.
Alt of postulated, Infl of postulate.
e: Borrowed from Latin postulātum See -ate for more. Cognate with French postulat.
From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate for more. Cognate with French postuler.
From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate for more.

s: To bring something out of shape, to misshape.
To give a false or misleading account of; pervert.
e: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).

s: allowing little light to pass through.
of a subset <math>s</math> of a topological space <math>t</math>
Such that its closure in T is T.
to comprehend; of low intelligence. (of a person)
e: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς).

s: The flat, horizontal upper surface of a table.
A fixed item resembling a table, used for performing skateboarding tricks.
A photograph of an object or product placed on a table.
Suitable for use on top of a table.
Taking place on top of a table.
To make a whimpering or sniffing sound when breathing, because of a runny nose.
To utter with a whimpering or sniffing sound.
The act, or the sound of sniffling; the condition of having a runny or wet nose, as from a cold or allergies.
A trap (especially one made from a loop of wire, string, or leather).
A loop of cord used in obstetric cases, to hold or to pull a fetus from the mother animal.
A similar looped instrument formerly used to remove tumours etc.
A set of stiff wires held under tension against the bottom head of a drum to create a rattling sound.
To catch or hold, especially with a loop.
To play (a snare drum, or a beat on or as if on a snare drum).
e: From Middle English snare, from Old English sneare (“snare, noose”), from Proto-West Germanic *snarhā, from Proto-Germanic *snarhǭ (“a sling; loop; noose”). Cognate with Old Norse snara. Also related to German Schnur and Dutch snaar, snoer.

s: The stroke of a brush, as in painting.
To take the place of; replace.
e: From Middle English bistad; equivalent to be- + Old Norse staddr (“placed”), later assimilated to Etymology 1, above.

s: Incapable of being passed over, crossed, or negotiated.
Incapable of being overcome or surmounted.
The cardinal number occurring after ten and before twelve. Represented as 11 in Arabic digits.
A cricket team of eleven players. Hence first eleven - the team of best cricket players (at a school), second eleven - the "B" team, etc.
A football team of eleven players; the starting lineup.
A number off the charts of a hypothetical scale of one to ten.
An exceptional specimen, a physically attractive person.
A very high level of intensity.
e: From Middle English elleven, enleven, eleven, from Old English endleofan; from Proto-Germanic *ainalif (“one left”) (i.e., one left over after having already counted to ten), a compound of *ainaz and *-lif, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, remain”).

s: To connect components by means of permanent electrical wires.
To implement a feature in hardware rather than in software so that it cannot easily be changed.
To make a pattern of behaviour automatic.
Any game suitable for playing on a table or other flat surface.
Having become actual; having been realized or made real.
The accumulation of sticky ink on a plate.
That which is scummed off; skimmings; scum.
The strategy of collecting easy rewards in unchallenging areas, e.g. when a high-level character visits levels suitable for low-level characters in roguelike games.
The act of restoring a game's save file, or restarting the game, for the purpose of continuing play with a better outcome than was obtained the first time.
e: Probably from skimming, modified by the derogatory sense of scum.

s: A person with an abnormally small head.
Like or characteristic of a butch.
A stupid person; someone who is empty-headed or oblivious.
A navy hard hat or salvage diver.
A piece of armor for the hips and thighs: one of a set of plates (each being of one piece or segmented) hanging from the bottom of the breastplate or from faulds.
e: Inherited from Middle English tasse (“armor plate protecting the hip”), Derived from Old French tasse, tasche (“purse; pouch”), Derived from Frankish *taskā (“pouch”), Derived from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Cognate with Old High German tasca (“pouch”), German Tasche (“pocket; pouch; bag”), Dutch tas (“bag”).

s: A hospital for the mentally ill.
Drinking glasses that have a stem, such as wine glasses or champagne flutes.
A person who engages in necrophilia.
A term of endearment for a young woman.
A shout or whistle expressing dislike, especially from a crowd or audience; a jeer, a boo.
A shout, whistle, or comment of a harassingly sexual nature, usually made toward a passing woman, causing distress and trauma.
A whistle blown by a theatre-goer to express disapproval.
In the Eiffel programming language, a run-time error caused by use of the wrong data type.
e: From the resemblance to cats' nocturnal cries. From cat + call.
Short for change availability or type + call.

s: Lacking coverage over the area of the crotch.
A dealer in ribbons, buttons, thread, needles and similar sewing goods.
A member of the Worshipful Company of Haberdashers, a livery company.
The use of the lips, facial muscles, tongue, and teeth when playing a wind instrument.
The mouth of a river or valley.
e: From French embouchure, from emboucher (“to put in one’s mouth”), from en- (“in”) + bouche (“mouth”), from Latin bucca (“cheek”).

s: Alternative spelling of whoopsy (in all senses).
An exceptionally good-looking and sexually attractive person, particularly a man.
Anything considered highly desirable for its kind, especially a car.
A second or subsequent emergence after being hidden, suppressed, etc.
Anything that is difficult to digest.
Experiencing the influence of an ingested mind-altering substance.
A plant of the genus Ambrosia, native to North America and a common invasive species elsewhere, particularly noted for producing pollen that triggers hay fever.
A summer cypress, mock cypress (Bassia scoparia).
e: Alteration of earlier; presumably, with "rag" referring to the tattered appearance of the plant's leaves. Compare Middle English ragwed (“butcher's broom”), of uncertain linguistic relationship.

s: To make (something, such as an abstract idea) possible to be perceived by the senses.
To treat (someone) as a mere (usually sexual) object; to sexually dehumanize (someone).
An impromptu fight with the fists, usually between only two people.
Bare-knuckled boxing, a form of boxing done without boxing gloves or similar padding.
A craft involving pulling yarn, thread, or floss through a canvas mesh to produce a decorative design.
An object made using that craft.
To produce a decorative design by this means.
A person with whom one shares a prison cell.
A light, porous form of concretionary limestone (or calcite) deposited from solution, and sometimes quarried for building.
The practice of cooking and preparing ready-to-eat meat products, especially pork.
Cured meat that is ready to be eaten, especially pork.
A shop or part of a shop specialising in cured meat.
The hootchy-kootchy, a type of erotic dance.
In a manner relating to evolution or slow development.
The action of the verb quake.
Shaking uncontrollably, especially due to fear or awe; trembling or shivering.
e: From Middle English quakinge, quakyng, from Old English cwacung (“quaking, trembling”), equivalent to quake + -ing.
From Middle English quakynge, quakand, from Old English cwaciende (“quaking”), present participle of Old English cwacian (“to quake, tremble”); equivalent to quake + -ing.

s: Gerund of waltz: the motion of one who waltzes.
A contest in which cake was offered for the best dancers.
The style of music associated with such a contest.
The dance, or strutting style of dance, associated with such a contest.
Something that is easy or simple, or that does not present a great challenge.
e: From cake + walk. Originally an African-American form of dance and music that developed after the Civil War, later popularised by minstrel shows. It was danced at social events, with the best dancers often receiving cake as a prize. It derives from dance competitions by plantation slaves in which the style of dance lampooned the ballroom dances of the slaveowners.

s: A Mexican dish of cornmeal dough shell filled with various ingredients (e.g. chopped beef, pork, sweet filling) then steamed in corn husks.
e: Back-formation from the plural tamales, from Latin American Spanish tamales, plural of tamal, Derived from Nahuatl tamalli, Derived from *tïmaL-. Compare cemait (“tortilla”), tuma (“stone griddle for cooking corn flatbread”), tʉ'ma- (“to roast under ashes”).

s: A person possessing ambiguous sexual organs or characteristics.
Cosexual: an organism possessing both types of gonads; a flower possessing both stamens and pistils.
Dichogamous: an organism which begins its life as one sex and changes its sex over its life cycle.
A person or thing possessing two opposing qualities.
A farm wagon convertible to multiple purposes.
An armoured fighting vehicle having features of both male tanks and female tanks.
Having ambiguous sexual organs or characteristics.
Having both ovaries and testes or both stamens and pistils.
e: From Hermaphroditus, the mythical son of Hermes and Aphrodite, who merged bodies with a naiad, thereafter having both male and female qualities.

s: Alternative spelling of halter (rope, cord, or similar thing that fastens around the neck).
Able to be won or achieved.
Of or pertaining to necrosis, particularly of tissue.
To act or speak in an unduly threatening manner.
To blow in strong or sudden gusts (refers to winds).
e: From Middle English blusteren (“to wander about aimlessly”); however, apparently picking up the modern sense from Middle Low German blüstren (“to blow violently”; compare later Low German blustern, blistern). Related to blow, blast. Compare also bloasje (“to blow”), bruusje (“to bluster”).

s: Small pieces of wood and twigs used to start a fire.
The act by which something is kindled.
To dislodge or remove (someone) from a seat, especially on horseback.
To remove (someone) from an office or position, especially a political one; to dethrone.
To cause (something) to be removed or replaced in its role; to displace, to overturn.
To upset the composure of (someone); to astound, to shock, to unsettle.
To come off or out of a seat.
e: Proto-Indo-European *sed- From un- + seat (“to provide with a place to sit”).

s: The top surface of a counter, for preparation of food, etc.
Any epidemic disease that is highly contagious, infectious, virulent and devastating.
Anything harmful to morals or public order.
e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin pestilentia (“plague”), from pestilens (“infected, unwholesome, noxious”); equivalent to pestilent + -ence.

s: To check or adjust by comparison with a standard.
To mark the scale of a measuring instrument.
To measure the caliber of a tube or gun.

With a negative connotation: the process of declining from a state of moral virtue, prosperity, etc., to a worse state; decay, deterioration; also, the bad state which has been reached; an instance of this.
An age or period of time when art, literature, etc., is regarded as having declined.
With a positive connotation: the quality of being luxuriously enjoyable or self-indulgent, especially of food; luxuriousness, richness.
The process or state of falling down or falling off.
e: Proto-Indo-European *ḱad-, from Medieval Latin decadentia (“act of decaying, decay”), from Latin *decadens (“decaying”) + -ia. *Decadens is the of *decadere, from dē- + cadere (the present of cadō (“to fall, fall out; to decay; etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱad- (“to fall”), possibly related to *ḱeh₂d- (“anger; hatred”)).

s: Absent or reduced sensitivity to cutaneous stimulation.
Inability or reduced ability to experience emotion.
Lying beneath, or conceived as lying beneath, the Earth’s surface.
To bring or thrust down; bring or make low; lower; abase; humble.
To constrict; straiten; confine; restrict; suppress; lay low; keep under; press in upon; vex; harass; oppress.
To pinch or stunt with cold or hunger; check in growth; shrivel; straiten.
To shrink or huddle, as with cold; be shivery; tremble.
Oppression; stress; a withering or stunting influence.
A trouble; a fault or dislocation in a seam of coal.
e: From Middle English nether, nethere, nithere, from Old English niþera (“lower, under, lowest”), from niþer, niþor (“below, beneath, down, downwards, lower, in an inferior position”), from Proto-West Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, *niþra (“down”), from Proto-Indo-European *ni-, *nei- (“in, down”).

Alteration of earlier nither, from Middle English nitheren, from Old English niþerian (“to depress, abase, bring low, humiliate, oppress, accuse, condemn”), from niþer (“below, beneath, down, downwards, lower, in an inferior position”). See above.

s: An ecclesiastic title bestowed on some Roman Catholic clerics by the Pope.
e: From Italian monsignore, from signore under influence from Middle French monseigneur. Doublet of monseigneur, monsieur.

s: The simplest aldehyde, HCHO, a colourless gas that has many industrial applications; it dissolves in water to give formol (10%) and formalin.
A long piece cut or rent off; a sharp, slender fragment.
Specifically, a splinter caught under the skin.
A strand, or slender roll, of cotton or other fiber in a loose, untwisted state, produced by a carding machine and ready for the roving or slubbing which precedes spinning.
Bait made of pieces of small fish.
A small amount of something; a drop in the bucket; a shred.
To cut or divide into long, thin pieces, or into very small pieces; to cut or rend lengthwise; to slit.
e: From Middle English slivere, sliver from Middle English sliven (“to cut, cleave, split”), from Old English slīfan (as in tōslīfan (“to split, split up”)).

s: To transform data in an undefined or unexplained manner, as for example when data wrangling requires nonsystemic or nonsystematic edits.
To add a spamblock to (an email address).
To corrupt a record about a person by erroneously merging in information about another person.
e: Variant of mung; likely a misconstructed back-formation from munging, munged or munger.

s: At any time in the future.
e: From Middle English evermore (written as two words before 14th century), equivalent to ever + -more.

s: An instance of remembering something incorrectly.

e: From the adjective. Equivalent to renāscor (“to reborn”) + -ate.

s: One who scribbles; a hasty or untalented writer or artist.
A machine for coarse carding or teasing of wool.
A ruled notebook or exercise book, especially in grade school.
A small room, next to a kitchen, where washing up and other domestic chores are done.
e: Inherited from Middle English squylerie, from Anglo-Norman squillerie (“office of the servant in charge of plates”), from escuele (“bowl, dish”) + -erie (equivalent to English -ery), from Latin scutella.

s: The act by which something is tarnished.
Lacking variety or excitement; dull; boring.
The quality of lacking variety or excitement.
Stimulating disgust or detestation; offensive; shocking.
A female domestic worker responsible for cleaning a house.
To wait on someone hand on foot, to watch them.
That which has been scribbled, written in a scrawled or careless hand.
The carding of wool or cotton.
Having been tempted; Finding something enticing.

e: From Middle English permanence, permanens, from Middle French permanence, from Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).

s: Lacking a voice, without vocal sound.
Without a vote; having no input into a decision.
Spoken without vibration of the vocal cords; unvoiced, surd, breathed. Examples: [t], [s], [f], [m̥], [u̥].
Modest and having no pretensions or ostentation.
Of or pertaining to autohypnosis; self-hypnotizing.
A denial of knowledge, relationship, or responsibility towards something or someone.
The practice or character trait of deliberately drawing attention to oneself.
The practice or character trait of deliberately displaying one's genitals, female nipples, or buttocks in public for sexual gratification.
Any formal system of reasoning that arrives at a truth by the exchange of logical arguments.
A contradiction of ideas that serves as the determining factor in their interaction.
development by way of overcoming internal contradictions
Dialectal (of or relating to a dialect).
e: From Old French dialectique, from Late Latin dialectica, from Ancient Greek διαλεκτική (“the art of argument through interactive questioning and answering”), from διαλεκτικός (“relating to dialogue”), from διαλέγομαι (“to participate in a dialogue”), from διά (“through, across”) + λέγειν (“to speak”).

s: The state or quality of being peak, the state of having excellent quality.
A female comember of a gang.
Of or relating to the institutions and practices that privilege or value heterosexuality, heterosexual relationships, and traditional gender roles as fundamental and "natural" within society.
e: From hetero- + normative The word was popularized by the American social theorist Michael Warner (born 1958) in a 1991 journal article: see the quotation.
From Middle English beautevous, bewteose, beautuous, boyteous, beuteus, beuteowse, bewtyvows, equivalent to beauty + -ous and/or beauty + -eous.

s: A motion or action that sloshes.
A sexually mature person below, or appearing to be below, the legal age of consent, who is regarded, usually by an adult, as being sexually attractive and/or seductive.
The box in which shoes are sold.
A small, cramped residence or similar space.
Of, pertaining to, or being an empath, having an extraordinary level of empathy of others emotions.
Doing so through psychological talent or training.
Doing so through psychicness, telepathy, etc: that is, through either supernatural powers or neurotechnological powers.
The reflexive form of they, the third-person singular personal pronoun. The single person previously mentioned, as the object of a verb or following a preposition (also used for emphasis).
e: From Middle English theimself. Equivalent to them + -self. Reinforced by analogy with the singular-plural distinction between yourself and yourselves.

s: A synthetic opioid narcotic analgesic, C22H28N2O, with pharmacological action similar to morphine that is administered transdermally as a skin patch and in the form of its citrate, C22H28N2O·C6H8O7, is administered orally or parenterally (as by intravenous or epidural injection); N-phenyl-N-[1-(2-ph

A garnish of vegetables cut into long, thin strips.
To prepare (a food) by cutting in this way.
e: From French julienne (1722), from the given name Jules or Julien, presumably from an otherwise unknown chef of that name. Originally used in potage julienne (“Julienne potage, a soup in the manner of Jules or Julien”), meaning “soup made from thin slices”; this sense is now known as chiffonade.

s: Reduced to a level of simplicity that omits, suppresses, or misrepresents material complexities, qualifications, causal relationships, or relevant evidence.

s: One who conceptualizes, designs, builds, programs, and experiments with robots.
e: Coined by Isaac Asimov. robot + ic + -ist. Coined in his short story "Robbie" (initially published under the title "Strange Playfellow").

s: Something that is particularly outstanding, unusual, or exceptional.
e: US origin, perhaps a hummer (“something that moves fast”) + dinger (“something outstanding”). First attested in a newspaper article in the Daily Enterprise of June 4, 1883, at Livingston, Montana.

In a courteous manner; with obliging civility or condescension; politely.
Used to evoke spiritual unity and interpersonal harmony, with varying degrees of sincerity or sarcasm, as referring to the folk song.
e: From. Apparently a corruption of the English phrase “come by here” in a spiritual song.

A person who behaves with the reckless bravado expected of someone who would duel with guns.

e: From Middle English unwittinge, unwitand, from Old English unwitende (“unwitting; not knowing; unaware; unconscious”), from Proto-Germanic *unwitandz (“not knowing”), equivalent to un- + witting. Cognate with West Frisian ûnwittend, Dutch onwetend, Low German unwetend, German unwissend and unwissentlich, Icelandic óvitandi.

s: Reasonable and convincing; based on evidence.
Appealing to the intellect or powers of reasoning.
e: From French cogent, from Latin cōgēns, present active participle of cōgō (“drive together, compel”), from cō + agō (“drive”).

e: From Middle English bulwerk, from Middle Dutch bolwerk, bolwerc and Middle Low German bolwerk, equivalent to bole (“tree trunk”) + work. Cognate with German Bollwerk, Danish bolværk, Swedish bålverk, Dutch bolwerk.

s: An inhabitant of a specific place; an inhabitant or denizen.
Used too much, or too often.

To make an activity profit-generating, particularly in computer and Internet-related activities.

A woman who identifies with cowboy culture, including clothing such as the cowboy hat.
A playing card of queen rank.

Any of the twelve Companions of the court of Emperor Charlemagne.
e: Borrowed from French paladin, from Italian paladino, from Late Latin palātīnus (“palace officer”), derived from palātium (“palace”). Doublet of palatine.

From Old French charnel, from Latin cardinālis (“relating to a hinge”); related to French charnière.

s: The enacting part of a statute.
Scope or range of interest or control.

Influenced by view and its etymological antecedents.

indecency, or offensive behaviour or material.

From crab (“to be ill-tempered; to complain or find fault”) + -er.

In the novel series, as well as its television adaptation Game of Thrones, the character Daenerys Targaryen uses dracarys (drakarys in the television series) to command her dragons to breathe fire. The language creator chosen for Game of Thrones, David J.

s: One who ceremonially fills and hands out the cups in which a drink is served.
The quality of state of being rash; inconsiderate or presumptuous haste
Any of several poisonous perennial herbs of the genus Aconitum.

Back formation from septic acid (nitric acid), so named because nitrogen appeared to be the cause of putrefaction.

s: Of high social standing as a result of having been born a member of an upper-level social class.
Born a member of an upper-level social class (although not necessarily retaining high social standing)
Of, pertaining to, or befitting people of high social standing.

A stone or gem having magical powers in relation to dragons.
A type of jagged rock full of crevices, commonly used in aquascaping.

The undesirable situation where the separate missiles from a MIRV interfere with each other as they explode.

From Middle English fratricide, from Middle French fratricide or its etymon Latin frātricīda.

The course a river shapes through a landscape.

From Middle English kyngly, from Old English *cyninglīċe (“kingly, royally”), equivalent to king + -ly. Compare Old English cynelīċe (“kingly, royally, publicly”).

From French brasier (“pan of hot coals”), from Middle French braisier, from Old French brasier, from brese (“embers, hot coals”), of origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *brasō. See braise.

s: In a meek manner; quietly and humbly.

From Scots bicker, from Middle English biker. Doublet of beaker.

Compare wuttelje (“to waddle”), Old High German wadalōn (“to roam; wander”), Middle High German wadelen, wedelen (“to wander; rove”), German wedeln (“to waggle”). First known use in English in a version of the Song of Roland around the year 1400.

Equivalent to obsolete feal#Etymology 4 + -ty. Doublet of fidelity.
