One who slits the throat of another; a murderer.
An unscrupulous, ruthless or unethical person.
A three-player pocket billiards game where the object is to be the last player with at least one ball still on the table.
Of or relating to a card game where everyone plays for him or herself rather than playing with a partner.
An absolving of sins from ecclesiastical penalties by an authority.
The forgiveness of sins, in a general sense.
The form of words by which a penitent is absolved.
An absolving, or setting free from guilt, sin, or penalty; forgiveness of an offense.
An acquittal, or sentence of a judge declaring an accused person innocent.
e: From Middle English absolucion, absolucioun, from Old French absolution, from Latin absolūtiōnem, accusative singular of absolūtiō (“acquittal”), from absolvō (“absolve”). See also absolve.

s: Pertaining to or characteristic of flowers.
Decorated with or abundant in flowers.
Of a speech or piece of writing: overly complicated or elaborate; with grandiloquent expressions; marked by rhetorical elegance.
A drinking vessel, typically of glass or metal, consisting of a bowl supported on a stem and foot; especially one with a relatively large, rounded bowl and a substantial stem.
e: From Middle English goblet (= Middle Low German gobelet, kobelet (“goblet”)), from Old French gobellet, diminutive of gobel, from or related to the verb gober (“to ingest”).

s: The quality or state of being perpetual; endless duration; uninterrupted existence.

A limitation intended to be unalterable and of indefinite duration; a disposition of property which attempts to make it inalienable beyond certain limits fixed or conceived as being fixed by the general law.
An annuity in which the periodic payments begin on a fixed date and continue indefinitely.
e: From Middle English perpetuitee, perpetuite, perpetuyte, from Old French perpetüité, ultimately from Latin perpetuitās.

s: A vessel, vat, or cistern in which things are steeped.
The stem of a shrub or small tree in a hedgerow, often laid by being partially cut through at the base in the process of laying a hedge.
Filled with, or showing, spite; having a desire to annoy or harm.
Burning fiercely; in a blaze; on fire.
Radiant with bright light and color.
In a state of glowing excitement, ardent desire, or other strong emotion.
Lit up brightly and with color, gleaming.
In a state of glowing excitement or ardent desire.
The act by which something is dyed.
A woman with religious duties and responsibilities in certain religions.
A female Christian priest or minister, typically in a Protestant, Old Catholic, or independent Catholic denomination.
To oversee (a pagan ceremony, etc.) as priestess.
Adopted; granted citizenship; belonging after being introduced.
A person who talks, especially one who gives a speech, or is loquacious or garrulous.
Any creature or machine that talks.
A stripped-down version of a MUD which is designed for talking, predating instant messengers; a kind of early chat room.
An augmentative and alternative communication device.
Treated with excessive attention and care; spoiled or overindulged.
Prevented from growing or developing fully and hence shorter and stockier that usual.
Of a person: shorter than usual for one's age.
In a thorough manner; in manner free of defect or deficiency.
e: From Middle English soundly, soundely, from Old English ġesundlīċe (“safely, prosperously, gladly”), equivalent to sound + -ly. Originally meaning "safely", the present sense came in the 16th century.

s: To be more in number than somebody or something.
To make solid; convert into a solid body.
To become solid; to freeze, set.
To transform an open compound into a closed compound (solid compound).
A tumour that is caused by malignancies in precursor cells or blasts.

e: Both orthopod and orthoped are of jocular origin in the informal jargon of medicine; the first is a play on -pod (as in gastropod) and the second is a play on -pede (as in centipede). Each trades on the humorous portrayal of colleagues in other specialties (as opposed to one's own specialty) as strange critters (as if odd ducks).

s: The surgical removal of a portion of the tongue.
The state or condition of being loopy; craziness.
The quality of being a simpleton.
To remove a sense of personal identity or individual character from something; to anonymize.
To present (something) as an impersonal object.
To suffer an episode of depersonalization.
In an elective manner; by choice.
The removal of fluid from the pericardium for therapeutic or diagnostic purposes
The reattachment of a severed body part (for example, an avulsed tooth or fingertip).
A form of spina bifida characterized by protrusion of the spinal meninges.
To do the inverse or opposite of breaking: to mend, restore, heal or fix; to make no longer broken.
e: From un- + break, popularised in songs sung by The Alarm ("Unbreak the Promise") and Toni Braxton ("Un-Break My Heart").

s: Of or relating to the xiphoid process (also called xiphisternum).
A benign tumour of fibrous connective tissue.
A popular condiment in many countries, usually mayonnaise-based.

e: From Middle English fethirles, fedyrles, equivalent to feather + -less. Cognate with Dutch veerloos, German federlos, Swedish fjäderlös.

s: The surgical procedure to remove all or part of the large intestine or colon.
Finicky; overly critical; concerned with insignificant details.
Plural of preemie (a perinatal child with fewer than 37 weeks gestation).
Either of the upright posts on either side of a door, which together support a lintel.
dirty, disgusting, foul, revolting, yucky, grotesque.
e: From groady, apparently a clipping of grotesque y (intervocalic /t/ and /d/ are similar in American English). Compare British, of the same origin, and gro. Popularized by Moon Unit Zappa in song "Valley Girl" (1982) in phrase "grody to the max", as archetypal Southern California Valleyspeak; song also popularized "gag me with a spoon".

s: Causing trouble; acting in a disruptive way
A lethal birth defect involving the abscence of a major portion of the brain and parts of the skull; absence of the encephalon.
A benign or malignant tumour, especially of the gonads, that arises from germ cells and consists of different types of tissue such as skin, hair, or muscle.
Not threatening; not presenting a threat.
Water that dishes and cooking utensils have been washed in.
Anything dull and lacking interest or flavour.

Of a medium, substance, object, etc.: to deflect the course of (light rays), esp. when they enter the medium, etc., at an oblique angle; to cause refraction of (light, other electromagnetic radiation, or sound or other wave phenomena).
To mediate; to alter; to distort.
To cause (light) to change direction as a result of entering a different medium.
To measure, and often also to correct with lenses, the refractive error of (an eye) or the eyes of (a person).
e: From Latin refrāctum, neuter form of refrāctus, the past participle of refringō, itself from re- (“again”) + frangō (“to break”).

s: The complete exon content of an organism or individual; the subset of the genome that excludes introns.
The opening of a vein, either to withdraw blood or for letting blood; venesection.
e: From Old French flebothomie (French phlébotomie), from Late Latin phlebotomia, from Ancient Greek φλεβοτόμος (“that opens a vein”), from φλέψ (“vein”). phlebo- + -tomy.

s: A stoppage in the flow of blood in a vessel, caused either by the insertion of a tampon or by outside constriction.
To plug or stop with a tampon.
A system of therapy that avoids synthetic drugs and surgery, while emphasizing the use of natural remedies (plants and the elements) and physical means (massage, acupuncture) to treat illness.
The surgical procedure for removing a part of the skull, called a bone flap, prior to a treatment. The bone flap is replaced at the end of the operation.
The act of taking care or taking charge of something.
A female adulterer, a married woman or wife who commits adultery.
e: From adulter + -ess. In later use typically apprehended as the female equivalent corresponding to adulterer instead.

s: Used to request quiet; similar to shh.
To be quiet; to keep quiet.
The spine of a shish kebab structure.
A tool for basting meat with fat or gravy.
The surgical procedure of making an incision into the chest, normally as a first step to gain access to the thoracic organs, such as the heart, the lungs, and the esophagus.
Any of the muscles of the buttocks, gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
The sense of the position of parts of the body, relative to other neighbouring parts of the body.
e: From proprioceptor, from proprius (“one's own”) + reception. Coined by Charles Scott Sherrington.

s: A form of psychotherapy in which a patient acts a role in a context devised by a psychotherapist.
A dramatic work focusing on the psychology of its characters
A surgery in which part or all of the stomach is removed to treat conditions such as stomach cancer, severe ulcers, or obesity.
e: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: gastr- + -ectomy, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ.

s: A person who is easily made to bleed, or who bleeds in unusually large amounts, particularly a hemophiliac.
A blood vessel that requires cauterization etc. to stop it from bleeding during surgery.
Anything that saps a resource produced by something else.
A valve designed to release a small amount of excess pressure from a system.
A troublesome fellow or thing; a blighter.
A person who menstruates (used in the context of transgender inclusivity).
Any drug that lowers the blood pressure.
A drug that lowers the blood pressure as its principal intended effect; a drug taken to treat hypertension.
The final fused vertebrae at the base of the spine; the coccyx.
The condition of having a slow heartbeat, defined as under 60 beats per minute for an adult.
A pestilent or predatory ground-borne animal, especially one that kills or harasses a farmer's animals or crops.
e: Dialectal form of vermin, derived from Latin vermis (“worm”), c. 1530–1540s. Perhaps influenced by Latin vargus, though the pronunciation in /ɑː(ɹ)/ is more likely due to the same lowering of /ɛr/ > /ar/ found in carve kerven and starve sterven. The final syllable is probably altered after -ment; compare parchment parchemyn.

s: One who, or that which, retracts.
In breech-loading firearms, a device for withdrawing a cartridge shell from the barrel.
A chess puzzle in which a number of moves are retracted and the solver is challenged to reach an alternate outcome.
A surgical instrument used to hold apart the edges of an incision or wound.
A bandage to protect soft parts of the body from injury by a surgical saw.
A muscle serving to draw in any part.
Located or occurring below the arachnoid mater, often specifically between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater.
The festivities held after a wedding meal.
Fighting or arguing off the ball or when play has stopped.
An after-hours drinking session in a public house.
Of or pertaining to both the heart and the chest
A block of buildings in a Roman town.
A structure of the human brain located within the sylvian fissure.
A tumour that arises from glial cells in the brain or spinal cord
In an improbable manner; without probability.
A second or subsequent evaluation or rating
A small bag, especially a small, clear, plastic bag.
Alternative form of baggy (bag filled with marijuana)
A general medical examination to assess a person's health and fitness.
All the additional procedures and reactions carried out after the main chemical reaction to obtain the desired product.
A period of training or preparation, typically for a specific operation.
An unfinished or unfinalized version; a draft, prototype.
A spouse who has sex with a non-spouse.
Someone who cheats on their spouse or monogamous significant other.
Able to be forgiven; worthy of forgiveness.
Of a loan, or a portion of it: such that repayment may be deferred for a period, or canceled, by the lender, if the borrower meets certain obligations.
e: From forgive + -able. Partially displaced non-native Middle English pardonable (“capable of being pardoned, forgivable”) from Old French pardonable (“forgivable”).

s: Capable of surviving an attack, especially a nuclear strike.
Of or pertaining to a septum.
Separating compartments in a burial chamber.
Relating to an Irish clan or sept.
To cut or otherwise divide something into pieces.
e: From Middle English, from Old French desmembrer, from des- (“de-”) + membre (“limb”) + -er (“verbal suffix”).

s: To go too far beyond (a limit); especially, to cross boundaries or exceed norms or conventions.
To take a step in which the foot touches ground too far forward.
To move with a gait such that the hind foot touches the ground forward of the point where the front foot touches the ground.
A gait in which the hind foot touches ground in front of where the front foot touches the ground.
A movement in which one oversteps.
A decision or action that goes too far.
e: From Middle English *oversteppen, from Old English ofersteppan, from Proto-Germanic *uberstapjaną (“to step over; overstep”). Cognate with Dutch overstappen, Low German överstappen, German überstapfen, überstepfen. Cf. transgress. en + over + step.

s: In a longing manner, with desire, yearningly.
A party to celebrate moving into a new home.
The act of welcoming a person/family to their newly purchased or newly rented home.
A person or animal that steps, especially energetically or high.
A dancer in a step show.
A kind of electric motor that advances in steps rather than smoothly.
A device used in the manufacture of microcircuits to apply a photolithographic image repeatedly, at regular intervals (by imaging, moving a step and repeating).
Anything that moves or advances in steps.
A shoe, especially a fashionable or attractive shoe, or one used for step-dancing.
The feet of anthropomorphic animals, especially paws.
A kind of driving rhythm or drumbeat in reggae music.
The archaic practice of treating illness by removing some blood, believed to be tainted, from the stricken person.
The diminishment of any resource with the hope that this will lead to a positive effect.
A circumstance, such as a battle, where a large amount of blood is likely to be spilled through violence.
A musical organ, consisting of steam whistles played with a keyboard. Often used with merry-go-rounds.
e: From Ancient Greek Καλλιόπη (“Calliope, the muse of poetry”), from καλός (“beautiful”) + ὄψ (“voice”).

s: Not changeable; incapable of being changed or of changing; immutable.
e: Inherited from Middle English unchaungeable; equivalent to un- + changeable.

s: broken down so that its elements are placed in its most specific subset available
The act by which things are likened; a comparison.
To declare something holy, or make it holy by some procedure.
To commit (oneself or one's time) solemnly to some aim or task.
e: First attested in the late 14 century, in Middle English; Inherited from Middle English consecraten (“to dedicate, consecrate (an altar, church); to ordain (a bishop), anoint (a king, a pope); to devote one to religious life”), from consecrat (“consecrated”) + -en, borrowed from Latin cōnsecrātus, perfect passive participle of cōnsecrāre, see -ate.

First attested in the late 14 century, in Middle English; Inherited from Middle English consecrat(e) (“consecrated”), used as the past participle of consecraten (“to dedicate, consecrate (an altar, church); to ordain (a bishop), anoint (a king, a pope); to devote one to religious life”); see Etymology 1 and -ate for more. Regular participial usage up until Early Modern English.

s: The state of being free from the effects of gravity (the force).
An experience or instance of being weightless.
An abnormally increased acidity of the blood.
Not capable of being denied, challenged, or disputed; closed to questioning.
The act by which something is slit.
A perennial herb, the wormwood species Artemisia dracunculus, from Europe and parts of Asia.
The leaves of this plant (either fresh, or preserved in a vinegar/oil mixture) used as a seasoning.
e: Borrowed from Middle French targon (cf. modern estragon), from Medieval Latin tragonia, from Arabic طَرْخُون, ultimately from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (“dragonwort, Dracunculus vulgaris”), from δράκων (“dragon, serpent”). Doublet of estragon.

s: In an innate manner, referring to a property that is possessed merely by its nature.
Of or pertaining to both the heart and the lungs.
A small dried grape, usually the Black Corinth grape.
The fruit of various shrubs of the genus Ribes, white, black or red.
e: Latin grc Borrowed from French raisin de Corinthe. Cognate with Dutch krent. Doublet of Corinth.

s: A vertical panel, either plain or upholstered, attached to the head of a bed.
A panel, usually of metal, attached to the head of a fore-and-aft sail for additional strength.
A board on the front of a train, carrying the train's name or that of the service it is on.
A grave marker made of wood.
The disease or disorder of abnormally low blood pressure.
To have a sudden, pinching or sharp pain in a specific part of the body, like a twitch.
To pull and twist (someone or something); to pinch, to tweak, to twitch, to wring.
To affect or torment (someone, their mind, or part of their body) with one or more sudden, pinching or sharp pains; to irritate.
A sudden, pinching or sharp pain in a specific part of the body, especially one lasting for a short time.
A sudden, sharp feeling of an emotional or mental nature, as of guilt or sadness; a pang, a paroxysm, a throe; also, a prick of the conscience.
A sudden, sharp occurrence of something; a nip.
An act of pulling and twisting; a pinch, a tweak, a twitch.
Lacking motivation, without impetus to strive or excel.
For which there is no motive, or no apparent rational motive.
The introduction of a tube into an organ to keep it open, as into the larynx in cases of croup.
e: Probably coined in 1880–1884 by Joseph O'Dwyer, M.D.; in widespread publication in 1887.

s: To make more beautiful and attractive by adding ornamentation; to decorate.
To enhance by adding something not strictly integral or necessary.
To make something sound or look better or more acceptable than it is in reality; to distort, embroider, or even misrepresent or lie.
e: From Middle English embelishen, from Old French embellir, from em- + bel.

s: Wire used to bind bales of hay.
Roughly-made, unsophisticated, decrepit (from the use of haywire for temporary repairs).
Behaviorally erratic or uncontrollable, especially of a machine or mechanical process.
To attach or fix with haywire.
e: From hay + wire. The original meaning of “likely to become tangled unpredictably or unusably, or fall apart”, as though only bound with the kind of soft, springy wire used to bind hay bales comes from usage in New England lumber camps circa 1905 where haywire outfit became the common term to refer to slap-dash collections of logging tools.

s: The side of a coin that bears an image of the Irish harp.
The act of one who labors; toil; work done.
Of, relating to, or using laparoscopy or a laparoscope.
One who fancies; a person with a special interest, attraction or liking for something.
A person who breeds or grows a particular animal or plant for points of excellence.
In accordance with the science of physiology.
In a manner pertaining to an organism's physiology.
Of, like, or abounding in pith; spongy or having small holes or pits.
A swelling of blood, usually clotted, which forms as a result of broken blood vessels.
e: From hemato- + -oma. Among the many words derived from -oma that are in current common use, this word is one of only a few that do not denote a neoplasm; another is granuloma.

s: Those organs of the body that are essential for life.
Those parts of a system without which it cannot function.
A Middle Eastern food in the form of balls made from chickpeas or broad beans and other ingredients, often served in a pita.
A pita with falafel balls as a filling.
The anadromous form of the rainbow trout, Oncorhynchus mykiss.
Possessing the ability to cure, to heal or treat illness.
A substance that acts as a cure.
of a verb, conveying the meaning "the agent makes a patient do something"
In an uneven or haphazard manner.
A book containing a set of rules.
Any of various small regulatory proteins that regulate the cells of the immune system.
A thin-walled, cartilaginous tube connecting the larynx to the bronchi.
One of the cuticle-lined primary tubes in the respiratory system of an insect, which extend throughout its body.
e: From late Middle English, from Medieval Latin trāchēa (“the windpipe”) (also borrowed as Late Latin trāchīa), from Ancient Greek τρᾱχεῖᾰ ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (“windpipe, trachea”).

s: Marked by light that blazes out.
Adorned with prominent markings or ornamentation.
Prominent in people's thoughts, highly salient; unforgettable.
The action of a locomotive or train leaving the rails along which it runs.
An instance of diverting a conversation or debate from its original topic.
An instance of thwarting or frustrating something.
A pattern of discourse (in speech or writing) that is a sequence of unrelated or only remotely related ideas.
The chemical element (symbol F) with an atomic number of 9. It is the lightest of the halogens, a pale yellow-green, highly reactive gas that attacks all metals.
A forespin pitch thrown by rotating the index and middle fingers down and resulting in motion down "curve"
An unexpected turn of events initiated by an opponent or chance; an exception or outlier.
To restore to a previously operational state.
A session of being immersed in a tank.
An act of a deliberate loss in a game or match with the intent of gaining a perceived future competitive advantage.
Characterised by a twist or twists; twisting.
Something that is twisty, such as a road
A strand of hair twisted together in a braid-like fashion
A collapsible element having a marker such as a small triangle that rotates between horizontal and vertical positions to indicate whether the content is currently hidden or expanded.
A minimal unit of reading, such as a sentence or sentence fragment
e: From the French lexie, originating in the writings of Roland Barthes. Further from Ancient Greek λέξῐς (“a saying, a word”).

s: The act by which something is replayed.
A Latin-American musical genre, adapted from rumba, originating from Cuba in the 1940s, or a dance or rhythm of this genre.
e: From manbo (“voodoo priestess”) (ultimately from mambo (“to talk”)), in later senses via Cuban Spanish mambo (“dance”).

s: Of or relating to the wall of a body part, organ or cavity.
Of or relating to the parietal bones.
Of or relating to college living and, especially, its regulation.
Attached to the main wall of the ovary, and not to the axis; said of a placenta.
Either of the two parietal bones, on the top and side of the skull.
Any of the scales of a snake that are located on the head and connected to the frontals towards the posterior.
A flat Roman wall tile with roughened surface, used as a base for plasterwork.
Dormitory rules governing visits from members of the opposite sex.
often in reference to a word or phrase
used so many times that it is commonplace, or no longer interesting or effective; worn out, hackneyed.
So well established#Adjective as to be beyond debate: trite law.
A denomination of coinage in ancient Greece equivalent to one third of a stater.
In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, pitched lower than the paranete and higher than the paramese.
e: From Latin trītus (“worn out”), perfect passive participle of terō (“to wear away, wear out”).

s: To frighten greatly; to fill with terror.
e: From Middle French terrifier, from Latin terrificare.

s: An isomer of a benzene derivative having two substituents adjacent on the ring.
A certain type of flat eyepiece.
To indulge in fantasy; to imagine things only possible in fantasy.
To portray in the mind, using fantasy.
The act by which something is severed.
The surgical discipline focused on treating those central and peripheral nervous system diseases.
Any surgical procedure performed on the nervous system, especially the brain.
Of a person, having eyes filled with tears; inclined to cry.
So as to stun or amaze.
Grey trousers and/or jackets worn by prisoners on relatively formal occasions.
Under the control of a mentor
Gerund of shriek: an act of uttering a loud, sharp, or shrill cry or sound; also, a sound that shrieks.
That emits shrieks or high-pitched noises.
(Of a sound, voice, etc.) sharp, loud, and shrill.
The chemical element (symbol Be) with an atomic number of 4; a soft silvery-white low density alkaline earth metal with specialist industrial applications.
e: Borrowed from Latin bēryllium beryl + -ium, so called because the element is a key component of the mineral beryl.

s: Not tractable; not able to be managed, controlled, governed or directed.
Not able to be solved in polynomial time; too difficult to attempt to solve.
Difficult to deal with, solve, or manage. (of a problem)
Difficult to treat (of a medical condition).
To sink or fall to the bottom; to settle, as lees.
To fall downward; to become lower; to descend; to sink.
To fall into a state of calm; to be calm again; to settle down; to become tranquil.
Rendered free from microorganisms and spores.
Of, pertaining to, or near the femur or thigh.
e: Borrowed from Latin femorālis, from Latin root femor-, from femur (genitive femoris). Equivalent to femur + -al.

s: Someone who is unwilling to settle for anything that is not perfect or does not meet extremely high standards.
Someone who thinks that religious or moral perfection can be attained in this life.
One of the Bible Communists or Free-lovers, a small American sect founded by J. H. Noyes (1811-86), which settled at Oneida in 1848, holding that the gospel if accepted secures freedom from sin.
Demanding perfection; being a perfectionist; imposing overly high standards.

Either of the two main arteries that supply blood to the head of which the left in humans arises from the arch of the aorta and the right by bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery with each passing up the side of the neck and dividing opposite the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into an ext
Of or pertaining to the carotid artery.
e: Borrowed from French carotide or New Latin carōtides, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτῐ́δες (“carotid arteries”), from κᾰρόω (“to plunge into deep sleep or torpor”) + -τῐ́δες, from the fact that the carotid artery supplies blood to the brain, and interruption of this flow causes loss of consciousness.

s: A spasm of the diaphragm, or the resulting sound.
A case of the hiccups; the condition of having the spasms of hiccupping; singultus; diaphragmatic myoclonus.
To produce a hiccup; have the hiccups.
To produce an abortive sound like a hiccup.
e: From earlier hickop, alteration of earlier hicket, hyckock, from hic (Onomatopoeic) + -ock.

s: The chemical element (symbol B) with an atomic number of 5, which is a metalloid found in its pure form as a dark amorphous powder.
e: From the stem of borax (boro-) + -on. Coined by Q131761 as a modification of his earlier word boracium.

s: Of or relating to a ventricle or ventriculus.
e: From New Latin *ventricularis, from ventriculus (“belly, stomach, ventricle”), diminutive of venter (“belly, stomach, womb”). Equivalent to ventricle + -ar; See ventricle.

s: Of or relating to the pituitary gland.
The pituitary gland; sometimes including together with the pituitary stalk.
An extract from the pituitary gland.
e: Learned borrowing from Latin pītuītārius (“mucous”), from Latin pītuīta First attested as a noun by 1899. The term was adopted as the name for the gland, because it was believed that it channeled mucus to the nose.

s: A female reproductive organ, often paired, that produces ova in most animals, and in mammals, secretes the hormones estrogen and progesterone.
The lower part of a pistil or carpel that bears ovules and ripens into fruit.
e: From New Latin ovarium, from Medieval Latin ovaria (“bird ovary”), from Latin ovum (“egg”). Doublet of ovarium.

s: Showing willingness to take bold risks; recklessly daring.
e: From Latin audacia (“boldness”) + -ious, from audax (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

s: The act of one who hedges (in various senses).
Any plant used to form a hedge.
The use of intentionally ambiguous or noncommittal statements.
the practice of taking a position in one market to offset and balance against the risk adopted by assuming a position in a contrary or opposing market or investment
With insufficient light for easy discernment or comprehension.
In a manner which is not readily visible or noticeable; inconspicuously.
In a manner which retards or prevents discernment; clandestinely.
In a manner which is difficult to understand, or which retards or prevents understanding; incomprehensibly.
In a manner which tends to produce uncertainty or confusion; bewilderingly.
In a manner which produces an inward conviction of future misfortune; ominously.
In a morbid manner; morbidly, sinisterly.
e: From Middle English derkly, derkely, derkliche, derkeliche; equivalent to dark + -ly. Compare Old English deorclīċe, a parallel formation.

s: Tending, or causing, to recede from the center.
Expanding first at the summit, and later at the base, as a flower cluster.
Having the radicle turned toward the sides of the fruit, as some embryos.
A rotating machine used to separate massecuite into sugar crystals and molasses.
e: From New Latin centrifugālis, coined by Christiaan Huygens from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”) al.

s: To do without (something enjoyable); to relinquish.
To refrain from, to abstain from.
e: From Middle English forgon (“to go by, pass up”), from Old English forgān (“to go away, forgo”); equivalent to for- + go.

s: Pertaining to the adrenal glands (suprarenal glands), their secretions, or the function derived therefrom.
e: From ad- (“near”) + renal (“pertaining to the kidneys”), from Latin rēn (“kidney”).
From French métastatique, from méta- + statique, as an adjective corresponding to métastase (“metastasis”), perhaps after Koine Greek μεταστατικός. meta- + static.

s: The property, state, or condition of being sore; painfulness.
A lingering emotional pain resulting in bitterness or resentment.
e: From Middle English sornes, sornesse, sarnesse, from Old English sārnes (“bodily pain; mental pain, affliction, grief”), from Proto-West Germanic *sairanassī, equivalent to sore + -ness.

s: The period of time during which an animal or human offspring physically develops inside the mother's body until it is born.
The process of development of a plan or idea.
The state of enlightenment that finally ends the cycle of death and rebirth and leads to nirvana.
e: From Sanskrit बोधि. Doublet of synonymous Doublet of bodai, which came via Japanese.

s: Anxious behaviour in migratory animals, especially in birds, experienced at the beginning of the normal migration period.
e: Borrowed from German Zugunruhe, from Zug (“move, migration”) and Unruhe (“anxiety, restlessness”).

s: A traditional Mexican dish of fried tortilla chips topped with salsa.
To praise, celebrate or pay homage to (someone), especially in an eloquent formal eulogy.
Made of or covered with wax.
Having the pale smooth characteristics of wax, waxlike, waxy.
Easily molded, influenced, or bent; yielding, impressible.
Easily effaced, as if written in wax.
e: From Middle English waxen, from Old English weaxen, ġeweaxen, from Proto-Germanic *wahsanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *wahsijaną (“to wax, grow, increase”), equivalent to wax + -en.
From Middle English waxen (“made of wax”), from Old English weaxen (“waxen, made of wax”), equivalent to wax + -en (“made of”).

s: An exclamation of happiness, excitement or accomplishment.
e: Borrowed from Japanese やった (“hurrah!, I did it!”).

s: Thank you (used in the context of, or to evoke, Japanese culture).
A plant, Strychnos toxifera, formerly used in arrow poisons in South America due to its D-tubocurarine content.
Other South American plants with similar toxins that were also used in arrow poisons, mostly in the family Menispermaceae.
A substance containing the alkaloid D-tubocurarine, used historically as a muscle relaxant during surgery.
e: From a language; compare urari, urari, wïrari, urari, urari, urari, referring to various vines of genus Strychnos.

s: A type of amusement ride characterized by teacup-shaped spinning vehicles atop a turntable-like floor, which may also spin.
Impossible to dispute or rebut; irrefutable; conclusive.
A small motorized ferry or sampan that serves mostly remote islands.
Made of tweed, or having a similar rough texture.
The middle of a stream or river.
A torture technique in which the victim is immobilized, has towels or rags wrapped over their face, and has water poured onto them, causing them to experience the sensation of drowning.
A craftsperson or company who makes and/or maintains watches.
God in His role as the creator according to the watchmaker analogy.
The action by which someone is scalped.
A fraudulent form of market manipulation in which a person buys shares immediately before recommending the shares to others, thus driving the price up.
A legitimate method of arbitrage of small price gaps created by the bid-ask spread.
The quality or state of being selfless.
A decaffeinated coffee, tea, or soft drink.
An amount or power (especially electric), expressed in watts, kilowatts etc.
The power requirement of some electric appliance.
Excessively protective, wanting to give too much protection (especially to children).
One who is noted for being very fast.
A vehicle or other device used for racing.
Someone being interviewed, i.e. the person answering the questions.
Abhorrence, a sense of loathing, intense aversion, repugnance, repulsion, horror.
A sudden violent feeling of disgust.
The treatment of one diseased area by acting elsewhere; counterirritation.
A strong pulling or drawing back; withdrawal.
A sudden reaction; a sudden and complete change of the feelings.
e: Partly from Middle French révulsion and partly from Latin revulsiō.

s: A long, narrow fishing boat used in shallow waters.
A member of a violent, fashionably dressed youth gang of the 1960s and 1970s.
A Sharpie or other brand of felt-tipped marker pen.
Of an action performed, overly repetitive and unchallenging, not requiring any careful attention or providing any significant stimulation.
The act of one who delves.
A book or pad with blank pages for sketching; a sketch pad.
A printed book of literary sketches or skits.
Of, relating to, or using telepathy.

e: Regular addition of the past tense suffix -ed to saw.
Nonstandard addition of -ed to saw, which is already a strong past tense form of see.

s: Easily forgotten; not special or notable.
Fitted with a bench, or benches.
Having the paws and head (but not the tail) detached from the body.
Cut into pieces at the joints.
possibly not standard in any era
(Of food) intended to be eaten off the premises from which it was bought.
A stone that hits another stone, removing it from play, a takeout shot.
A double of an opponent's bid, intended to invite one's partner to compete in the auction, rather than to penalise one's opponents.
A designated point for canoes, rafts, etc. to be removed from the water after use.
An open passage through a wood; a grassy open or cleared space in a forest.
An opening in the ice on a river or lake.
A bright surface of ice or snow.
A bright patch of sky; the bright space between clouds.
e: From Middle English glade, glode, glede (“a gleam of light, bright space, an open space; an open or cleared space in a forest; a bright patch of sky; a bright surface of snow or ice”), of Uncertain origin, perhaps from Old English *glǣd, *glād, related to Old English glæd (“shining, bright”), (compare Old Norse glaðr (“bright”)).

s: Small humanoid creatures, such as gnomes and halflings.
To disapprove of or dislike (someone or something); to have an aversion to.
Aversion or distaste for something; dislike; an instance of this.
Lack of comfort; discomfort; also, difficulty; trouble; or sadness; unhappiness.
The characteristic or state of incapacity, physical distress, or weakness due to poor health; sickliness; an instance of this.
Discontent, unrest; an instance of this.
Not like or similar; different, unlike.
One who slays his or her own kin; a parricide.
The state or quality of being impetuous; making arbitrary decisions.
The result of being impetuous; arbitrary decisions.
The final stage of pregnancy; confinement.
The bed upon which a baby is born.
e: From Middle English child bed; equivalent to child + bed.

s: In a heedless manner: with unawareness; without noticing; carelessly, inattentively.
To say something in contradiction to.
e: From Middle English gainsayen, ȝeinseggen (“to say against, say in opposition to”), equivalent to gain- + say. Compare Old Danish gensige (“to speak against; gainsay”), Swedish gensaga (“a speaking against; protest”).

s: Obstinate and stubborn to the point of stupidity.
e: From Middle English pyge heddyde, equivalent to pig + headed.

s: Without or deprived of a rider.
Given, received, or done grudgingly; resented.
Not the subject of any remark
like or as an imbecile; so senseless as to be laughable; absurd, foolish, stupid, idiotic.
To exclude from inheritance; to disown.
A foothold small enough to support just the toe.
Any small advantage which allows one to make significant progress; a slight footing or foothold.
A hold in which the aggressor bends back the opponent's foot.
One born illegitimately (i.e., out of wedlock); a bastard.
A person born into infelicitous circumstances.
A person who designs, builds and repairs ships, especially wooden ones.
e: From Middle English shipwright, shippwright, schipwricht, ship-wriȝth, from Old English sċipwyrhta, equivalent to ship + wright (“builder”).

s: Obscure; taking place unseen, as if in the dark.
A child of darkness; someone dark by nature or who has grown dark in character.
A creature that lives in the dark.
e: Coined by Mary Tighe, likely as an extension of the adverbial sense, and popularized by John Keats.
From darkle + -ing, darkle itself a backformation from Tighe's adjectival sense.

s: A feudal lord with a fortified manor.
The governor or caretaker entrusted to oversee a castle or keep for its lord.
e: From Middle English castelain, from Old French castelain (compare modern châtelain), from Latin castellanus (“pertaining to a castle, an occupant of a castle, or a governor of a castle”), from castellum castle, citadel, diminutive of castrum fortified place. See castle. fro:castel + -an and castle + -an.

s: Demonstration of an obedient attitude, especially by bowing deeply; a deep bow which demonstrates such an attitude.
e: From Middle English obeisaunce (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French obeïssance, derived from obeïssant (“obedient”), participle of obeïr (“to obey”), from Latin oboediō, obēdiō; ob- (“to, for”) + audiō (“to hear”). Cognate with Doublet of obedience.

s: To attack with harsh words or violent force.
To overcome or successfully argue against; defeat.
e: From Middle English assailen, from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assault.

s: A familiar name for a person or thing; a nickname (sometimes assumed by the person, but often given by others) that is descriptive.
e: Borrowed from French sobriquet (“nickname”), from Middle French soubriquet (“a chuck under the chin”).

s: Engaged in or associated with the act of carousing.
The state of being deprived of or lacking an attribute formerly or properly possessed; the loss or absence of such an attribute.
The state of being very poor, and lacking the basic necessities of life.
The act of depriving someone of such basic necessities; deprivation.
Degradation or suspension from an office.
e: Inherited from Middle English privacioun, from Middle French privation, privacion, from Old French privacion, from Latin prīvātiō; compare French privation. See private.

s: The state or quality of being small.
The result or product of being small.
Unwilling to compromise or moderate a position; unreasonable; stubborn.
e: Borrowed from French intransigeant, from Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- (“un-, not”) + trānsigēns, present participle of trānsigō (“to come to an understanding”), from trāns (“across”) + agō (“to do”).

s: To predict; to tell (the future) before it occurs; to prophesy.
To tell (a person) of the future.
e: First use appears before 1400, from Middle English foretellen, equivalent to fore- + tell.

s: Transported on the sea or ocean, especially by floating on the sea.
The action of forbearing; an instance of this.
The action of refraining from enforcing something which is due (such as a debt or obligation) or a right which one has; an instance of this.
Restraint and tolerance under provocation; patient self-control; indulgence, lenity.
The state of being glad; joy.
Excessive or inordinate desire of gain; greed for wealth
Inordinate desire for some supposed good.
e: From Middle English avarice, from Old French, from Latin avāritia, from avārus (“greedy”).

s: The act by which something is tempered.
A non-plastic material, such as sand, added to clay to prevent shrinkage and cracking during drying or firing; temper.
To lose strength and become weak; to be in a state of weakness or sickness.
To pine away in longing for something; to have low spirits, especially from lovesickness.
To live in miserable or disheartening conditions.
To be neglected; to make little progress, be unsuccessful.
To make weak; to weaken, devastate.
To affect a languid air, especially disingenuously.
e: From Middle English languysshen, from the present participle stem of Anglo-Norman and Middle French languir, from Late Latin languīre, alteration of Latin languēre (“to be faint, unwell”).

s: Ragged clothing or fabric, paper, etc.
Without a known author or inventor.
e: From Middle English faderles, federles, from Old English fæderlēas, from Proto-Germanic *fadērlausaz, equivalent to father + -less. Cognate with German vaterlos.

s: Someone who aspires (for high office, etc.)
Beheading; the act of beheading or decapitating.
The ousting or destruction of the ruling body of a government or other organization.
The unseating of a senior politician.
Not giving in; not bending; stubborn.
The act of one who trifles; frivolous behaviour.
The act of making a petition or appeal.
Fatally; in such a way as to cause death.
A muse, a personified source of inspiration, especially one that also causes anguish.
An idea depicted as an entity.
A process (a running program) that does not have a controlling terminal.
e: + (classical mythology) A borrowing of Latin daemōn (“tutelary deity”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (“dispenser, tutelary deity”).
+ (computing) A reference to Maxwell's demon. The putative derivation from "disk and execution monitor" is generally considered a backronym.

s: rapidity of movement or activity; agility or dexterity
To run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.
of interests, opinions, or anything else
To become different; to run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.
To separate, to tend into a different direction (from another line or path).
of an interest, opinion, or anything else
To become different, to separate (from another line or path).
of a sequence, series, or function
Not to converge: to have no limit, or no finite limit.
A point where a lane branches off from the main flow.
e: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

s: A stigma attaching to a person's character that disqualifies them from being a witness.
e: From late Middle English infamie, from Old French infamie, from Latin īnfāmia (“infamy”), from īnfāmis (“infamous”), from in- (“not”) + fāma (“fame, renown”). Displaced native Old English unhlīsa.

s: The meat of a deer, especially one that was hunted in its own natural habitat.
The meat of any wild animal that has been hunted rather than raised domestically.
e: From Middle English venisoun, venesoun, from Anglo-Norman veneisun, venesoun, venesun (“meat of large game, particularly deer or boar; hunt”), from Latin vēnātiō, vēnātiōnem (“hunt; meat from a hunt”), formed on vēnātus, perfect participle of vēnor (“to hunt”). Doublet of venatio and venation.

s: Angry or resentful due to unjust treatment.
Having one's rights denied or curtailed.
A large highly decorative German/Dutch-style piece of furniture, which combines aspects of a clothing wardrobe, curio, and cabinet.
The grantee of a fief, a subordinate granted use of a superior's land and its income in exchange for vows of fidelity and homage and (typically) military service.
Any direct subordinate bound by such vows to a superior.
Any subordinate bound by similar close ties.
To treat as a vassal or to reduce to the position of a vassal; to subject to control; to enslave.
To subordinate to someone or something.
e: From Middle English vassal, from Old French vassal, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).

s: A military action consisting of armed forces of one geopolitical entity entering territory controlled by another such entity, generally with the objective of destruction, plunder, or bodily harm rather than an intent to conquer territory or alter the established government; contrast invasion
An aggressive movement into somewhere; an invasion in the general sense.
A function hosted within an educational institution, especially by or for students, for recreation, research, education or a display of works.
e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French, from Latin incursiō.

s: Having had all desires, wishes, and whims granted; having been brought up lavishly, wanting for nothing.
Offspring or descendants considered as a group.
A result of a creative effort.
e: From Middle English progenie, from Old French progenie, from Latin prōgeniēs, from prōgignō (“beget”).

s: Attending movies, especially habitually or regularly.
Unable to be bridged or crossed; impossible to span.
An emotional state of mind, a tendency to regard things in an emotional manner; emotional behaviour or characteristics.
imprudent or excessive expenditure or the waste of resources
A person who studies or teaches logic.
e: From Middle English logicien, logissian, from Old French logicien. Equivalent to logic + -ian.

s: The seam of a trouser up the inside of the leg.
To impress or mark with a seam or cicatrix.
In a terrific or extreme way.
To reduce the velocity of something.
To reduce the rate of advancement of something, such as a disease.
The act by which one cradles a child etc.
The act of using a cradle (the tool).
The cutting of a cask into two pieces lengthwise, to enable it to pass a narrow place, the two parts being afterwards united and rehooped.
The framework in arched or coved ceilings to which the laths are nailed.
The theory that reason is a source of knowledge independent of and superior to sense perception.
The theory that knowledge may be derived by deductions from a priori concepts (such as axioms, postulates or earlier deductions).
A view that the fundamental method for problem solving is through reason and experience rather than faith, inspiration, revelation, intuition or authority.
Elaboration of theories by use of reason alone without appeal to experience, such as in mathematical systems.
The rationalist community or its ideology.
The act of slipping, especially from a secure location.
The amount by which something has slipped.
A lessening of performance or achievement.
A decrease in motion, or in the power of a mechanical system, due to slipping.
The difference between estimated and actual transaction costs.
Movement of earth on a slope, a landslip.
Specialized knowledge that is mysterious to the uninitiated.
e: From Latin arcānus (“hidden, secret”), from arcēre (“to withhold”), arca (“a chest”).
Back-formation from glitzy, in turn from German glitzern (“glint”). Cognate with Old Norse glitra, glita (“glitter”) and Gothic 𐌲𐌻𐌹𐍄𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌾𐌰𐌽 (“glisten”).

s: The process or result of rationalizing, or expressing in rational terms.
A statement of one's motives, or of the causes of some event.
The reorganization of a company or organization in order to improve its efficiency through the reallocation of resources and changes in its workforce.
The concealment of true motivation in some non-threatening way.
The simplification of an expression without changing its value.
Instructive or intended to teach or demonstrate, especially with regard to morality.
Teaching from textbooks rather than laboratory demonstration and clinical application.
A treatise on teaching or education.
e: From French didactique, from Ancient Greek διδακτικός (“skilled in teaching”), from διδακτός (“taught, learnt”), from διδάσκω (“to teach, educate”). didact + -ic.

s: Having a red colour around the edge, especially said of eyes after crying.
That has become or been made sour.
A person (usually a man) involved in putting on shows (of various types); especially, one who plays a central role in doing so.
One who produces or presents shows as a profession, especially the proprietor, manager, or MC of a circus or variety show.
One skilled in dramatic or entertaining presentation, performance, or publicity.
The act by which something is perceived.
Being or making a clunk sound.
and having no uncertainty or ambiguity.
Accompanied by tears; crying, or about to cry.
Away (from the home or starting point, physical or conceptual). (Often preceded by far, farther, or further.)
e: From Middle English afeld, a-felde, o felde, on felde, from Old English on felde (“afield”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + field.

s: Any substance, produced by a mold or fungus, that is injurious to vertebrates upon ingestion, inhalation or skin contact.
The practice of entering many competitions in order to win as many prizes as possible.
To attack someone (especially verbally) unfairly in a deceitful, underhand, or treacherous manner, especially when they're not present in the place or situation that it happens.
or a similar dish replacing beef with some other ingredient.
In a style typical of Burgundy (whether the administrative region, the earlier duchy, or both).
The act of giving a headbutt.
overemotional behaviour, especially when calculated to elicit a response; melodramatics.
A newly hatched bird, reptile or other animal that has emerged from an egg.
A person who has (especially recently) realized that they are transgender.
e: From hatch + -ling. in reference to the term crack one's egg (“realize one is transgender”).

s: An enclosed, roofed structure, often an outbuilding, used primarily to store firewood.
A place where punishments or reprimands are administered.
To practice or rehearse using a musical instrument.
To practice or rehearse a script.
To self-isolate in order to work on one's artistic development or to produce work without interruptions.
A human, a specimen of Homo sapiens.
e: The word is a singular form, derived by back-formation and shortening of Homo sapiens by interpreting the latter as an English plural form. However, in Latin the word sapiens is strictly singular, its plural form being sapientes (and the Latin plural of homo sapiens is homines sapientes).

s: A light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn cart used in harness racing.
Any carriage seating only the driver.
e: See sulk. The vehicle is so called as it obliges the rider to be alone, as though sulking.

s: extended or expanded beyond a safe limit
To surrender on stipulated terms, end all resistance, give up, go along with or comply.
To draw up in chapters, heads or articles; to enumerate, specify.
To draw up articles of agreement with; to propose terms, treat, bargain, parley.
To make conditions, stipulate, agree, formulate, conclude (upon something).
Capitulated: agreed upon, convened, settled on, stipulated.
Reduced to heads, laid down under a certain number of heads or items.
The act by which something is reprogrammed.
The process of changing the programming of a system or device
The erasure and reestablishment of DNA methylation during mammalian development
A child-like character with exaggerated features, particularly in anime.
A style of cartooning in which the characters are drawn to be very small and cute.
e: Borrowed from Japanese ちび (“something small; runt, dwarf; pipsqueak”)

s: A person who trades in ice; a person employed to deliver block ice to those lacking electric refrigeration.
A man who is skilled in travelling upon ice, as among glaciers.
A human figure carved out of ice.
An ancient human male mummified in ice.
One who is cool under pressure.
A man in attendance at a frozen pond where skating etc. is going on.
A sideways shuffling or sliding motion.
To walk or travel fast; to go quickly.
To move with the forelegs while sitting, so that the floor rubs against its rear end.
To move sideways (especially along a seat for multiple people), usually to make room for someone else (to sit, stand, etc.).
To dispatch someone or something at speed; Synonym of shoo.
A sudden flow of water; a squirt.
e: Of Uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse skjóta (“to shoot”), or perhaps related to Middle English scottlynge (“moving one's feet quickly, scampering”), see scuddle, scuttle.

s: The world, considered as lacking in purpose, design, or predictability.
The hypothetical group of all the possible universes in existence.
The different canons, continuities or timelines of a fictional property, considered as a whole.
An act in which something is conjured.
Equipped with armoured motor vehicles; compare motorized (“equipped with unarmoured vehicles”).
Having a damaged appearance or form; defaced or deformed.
A member of this species; a human being.
e: From Latin sapiēns, present active participle of sapiō (“discern, be capable of discerning”).

s: The drift of a ship or aeroplane in a leeward direction.
A varying degree or amount of freedom or flexibility.
An adverse discrepancy or variation in a cumulative process, usually in the phrase make up leeway.

e: Borrowed from Korean 라면, from Japanese ラーメン, from Mandarin 拉麵 (“pulled noodles”). Doublet of laghman, lamian, ramen.

s: An unspecified large number (of); a gazillion.
A racquet sport resembling tennis, played with solid paddles and a perforated ball, which combines elements of badminton, table tennis and wiffleball.
The ball used in the sport of pickleball.
e: From pickle boat and ball. Coined by the sport inventor's wife who was reminded "of the pickle boat in rowing where oarsmen were chosen from the leftovers of other boats." Similarly, the game initially used left-over equipment from badminton, table tennis, and wiffleball.

s: A sturdy bench or table at which manual work is done by a carpenter, machinist, etc.
A horizontal padded surface, usually adjustable in height and inclination and often with attached weight rack, used for proper posture during exercise.
Marked with rings, circles, or loops.
Wearing a wedding ring; hence, lawfully wedded.
The preserving of a dead body, by making it into a mummy.
The practice of wrapping a person's arms, torso, and legs in order to restrict their movement.
A small increase or upward change in something that has been steady or declining.
A stock market transaction or quote at a price above a preceding one.
A pair of eyebrows which meet in the middle.
The voluntary control of urination and defecation.
Moderation or self-restraint, especially in sexual activity; abstinence.
e: Dated from the 14th century as Middle English contynence, from Old French continence, from Latin continentia (“a repression”). See also Doublet of countenance.

s: To depose; to forcibly relieve a monarch of the monarchy.
To remove any governing authority from power.
To remove from any position of high status or power.
To remove (something) from a position of power or paramount importance.
To clean one's mouth by holding water or some other liquid in the back of the mouth and blowing air out from the lungs so as to make the liquid bubble.
To make a sound like the one made while gargling.
To clean a specific part of the body by gargling (almost always throat or mouth).
To use (a liquid) for purposes of cleaning one's mouth or throat by gargling.
To perform oral sex on (a person or genitals).
The sound or act of gargling.
e: From French gargouiller (“to gargle”), from Old French gargouille, gargole (“gutter, throat”). Compare Doublet of gargoyle and Spanish garganta. Displaced non-native Middle English gargargisen (“to gargle”) from Latin, and native Old English swillan (“to gargle”) (ancestor of English swill).

s: A cryptid supposedly found in Washington State, the Columbia River sand squink, which has a body like a fox, the head and ears of a jackrabbit, and a bushy tail like a squirrel.
To scrunch up, squinch (one's face, nose, etc).
A person who cringes or shies away.
To apprehend in thought so as to fix and hold in the mind; to memorize.
The actual existence supposed to correspond with an idea; the correlate in real existence to the idea as a thought or existence.
Imagery of one or more muscular, well-built men.
Such a male, especially as seen as physically desirable.
e: From beef + cake. In sense 1, by analogy with cheesecake (“an image of a sexy young woman”).

s: The act of one who manhandles; rough physical treatment.
A thick Italian pasta sauce, made with guanciale, grated cheese, beaten egg yolks and pepper.
A spaghetti dish made using such a sauce.
A spaghetti dish made using a similar sauce made from a different type of cured pork than guanciale (such as bacon, pancetta, lardons, gammon or ham).
e: From the Italian carbonara, shortening of alla carbonara, ultimately from carbone (“coal”).

s: One who finds a way: either a physical route or a means to achieve something.
The ability of a person or animal to orientate itself and to navigate; the process used by a person or animal for orienting and navigating.
A variety of pumpkin, a cultivar of Cucurbita moschata.
The subjects of reading, writing, and arithmetic.
A person or creature capable of changing their appearance or form at will.
A person who is inconsistent and elusive.
The protection of the interior walls of a fortification from enfilading fire, as by covering them, or by a high parapet on the exposed side.
To replace or restore the weapons or arms of a previously defeated or disarmed army, country, person or other body.
To arm, or prepare for use, again.
The act by which something is trashed.
A tradition of throwing food, confetti, etc. over students after their final examinations.
A lack of law; a lack of law and order; anarchy.
Defiance of the law; outlawry, exorbitant levels of crime.
To correct insignificant mistakes or find fault in unimportant details.
To pick nits (lice eggs) from someone’s hair.
A quibble about a minor mistake or fault.
e: From nit + pick, originally referring to literally removing tiny louse eggs by hand.

s: A spasmodic, nervous system disease brought on by the tetanus bacteria, causing muscles to seize up and may cause death by suffocation.
Dijon mustard, a prepared mustard containing white wine in place of vinegar.
The act or process of dividing a complex task or structure into smaller, often more manageable pieces.
A defense mechanism in which thoughts and feelings that seem to conflict are kept separated or isolated from each other in the mind.
The act of dividing complex code into libraries with common functionality to help make the process of programming more manageable and reusable.

The dissemination of information and knowledge between different people or organisations on a need-to-know basis, so as to reduce the risk of espionage should one person or organisation be compromised externally.
To cause to feel extreme apprehension or unease; to cause to experience horror.
e: From horror + -ify, or Borrowed from Latin horrificare (cf. French horrifier). 1791, in form horrifying.

s: The act by which something is downplayed, or made to seem less important.
Any of a long series of boards laid from side to side as a path across wet or muddy ground.
Wooden, low walkway or short part of a path with one or more planks, logs, or boards laid after each other lengthwise, often two planks wide.
A panel of wooden slats typically laid on a concrete floor in a workshop, to reduce fatigue for a person operating a machine tool or working at a bench.
e: Possibly a metaphorical use of a name for a board connecting a duck hutch to a yard.

s: Devilish action or conduct; wickedness; troublemaking behaviour; mischief; an instance of this.
A devilish, mischievous, or reckless nature; mischievousness.
Something cruel or evil; also, something which causes distress or suffering.
A dish which is devilled; a devil; also, the elements of the dish which make it spicy, or the piquancy or spiciness of the dish.
A traditional Jewish marriage contract that outlines the rights and responsibilities of the groom in relation to the bride.
Associated with or filled with pike (fish).
An itinerant person, especially one of Romani or Irish Traveller heritage.
A working-class (often underclass) person with negative qualities stereotypically ascribed to itinerant people, including rowdiness, theft and poor hygiene.
e: Possibly from obsolete pike (“depart or travel”), or possibly from turnpike. The verb is derived from the stereotype that the Romani people or other travellers are thieves.

s: To surgically remove the foreskin (prepuce) from the penis of.
To surgically remove the clitoris (clitoridectomy), clitoral hood, or labia.

e: Derived from Latin salāx, salācis (“provocative, lustful”) -ious, ultimately from saliō -acious.

A hallucinogenic alkaloid, C12H15N2O·H2PO3, present in several species of Central American mushroom and producing effects similar to LSD. The prodrug of psilocin.
e: Borrowed from German Psilocybin (coined by Albert Hofmann), from Psilocybe (“genus of mushroom”) + -in.

A diploma, especially the one representing a university or college degree.
A representation of an erect penis, especially symbolising fertility or potency.
The signifier of the desire of the Other, and the signifier of jouissance.
e: Borrowed from Latin phallus (“membrum virile, phallus, or a figure thereof”), from Ancient Greek φαλλός.

s: Fitted with a pivot or pivots.

Any aircraft capable of taking off from, and alighting on the surface of water.
e: From sea + plane. Supposedly coined by Winston Churchill.

To play a sequence of records with no talk between them.
An instance of segueing, a transition.
e: Borrowed from Italian segue (“it follows”), from seguire (“to follow”), from Latin sequor; originally a term used in a musical score to indicate that the next movement or passage is to follow without a break. Cognate with Spanish seguir. Doublet of sue. Related to suit and sequence.

s: That attenuates or lessens the seriousness of something, e.g. by providing a mitigating excuse for it.
e: From Latin ex (“to delete, to cross out”) and tenuatus, past participle of tenuare (“to make thin”) + Middle English -ing. ex- + tenuate + -ing.

The computation of a hash value.

Evil or malignant in disposition, nature, intent or influence.

To treat with malice; to show hatred toward; to abuse; to wrong.
e: From Middle English maligne, from Old French maligne, from Latin malignus, from malus (“bad”) + genus (“sort, kind”). Compare benign.

s: The act of making an activity or substance no longer criminalized (no longer a crime, subject to criminal penalties, to perform or possess). (Compare legalization, which often implies regulation.)

The act of ceasing to treat a person as a criminal, by making their activities legal or no longer subjecting them to the criminal justice system (but instead possibly the mental healthcare system, etc).
A leader of a group of people, especially an unofficial group.
A person who starts and leads a disturbance (such as a riot), a conspiracy, or a criminal gang.
One who agitates; one who stirs up or excites others, for example political reformers.
An implement for shaking or mixing.
One of a body of men appointed by the army, in Oliver Cromwell's time, to look after their interests.
Magic mushrooms, which produce drug-like hallucinations.

To give (something) in return; to pay back; to pay, as something earned or deserved.
e: From Middle English recompense, borrowed from Old French recompense or Medieval Latin recompensa.
From Middle English recompensen, borrowed from Old French recompenser, from Late Latin recompensare, from Latin re- (“again”) + compensare (“to balance out”).

s: A woman who performs massage; a female masseur.

A payment of time, effort or money to compensate for past transgression(s).
The act of renewing, restoring, etc., or the state of being renewed or repaired.
Not valued or appreciated as highly as one should be.
A decorative covering or ornament worn on the head.
a defense to the validity of a contract because it was in violation of the law
A female prostitute, especially one with high-status or wealthy clients.
The mistress of a royal or noble.
A woman of a royal or noble court.
A fairy chess piece that can move to any adjacent square, that, when captured, the capturing piece is also eliminated.
e: Borrowed from Middle French courtisane, from Italian cortigiana, feminine of cortigiano (“courtier”), from corte (“court”), itself from Latin cohors.

s: Not similar or congruent; not matching or fitting in.
Of two numbers, with respect to a third, such that their difference can not be divided by it without a remainder.
Not having been initiated; not having the special knowledge of a particular group.
People who have not been initiated and thus do not have the special knowledge of a particular group.
The sound of the ticking of an analog clock.
Time is running out; a deadline is approaching.
Expresses warning of some fateful, impending event.

When marching, to swing arms and legs on the same side at the same time.

A step-by-step account of an event or timeline.
Hunger, especially a craving for food as a result of alcohol or cannabis consumption.
That provides a view from or to the rear.
A weight that is put in opposition to an equal weight so it keeps that in balance.
A force or influence that balances, checks or limits an opposite one.
To apply weight in order to balance an opposing weight.
To match or equal in effect when applying opposing force.
A tall, square, tapered, stone monolith topped with a pyramidal point, frequently used as a monument.

A symbol resembling a horizontal line (–), sometimes together with one or two dots (for example, ⨪ or ÷), which was used in ancient manuscripts and texts to mark a word or passage as doubtful or spurious, or redundant.

A dagger symbol (†), which is used in printed matter as a reference mark to refer the reader to a footnote, marginal note, etc.; beside a person's name to indicate that the person is deceased; or beside a date to indicate that it is a person's death date.
An RNA structure similar to a viroid, with a rod-like secondary structure, which comprises its own phylogenetic group.
To adopt the obelisk posture; to point the tip of the abdomen towards the sun.
e: From Middle French obelisque, from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος, diminutive of ὀβελός (“needle”). Compare obelus.

s: Beside the ring, especially a boxing ring.
Peers as a group; the titled nobility or aristocracy.
The rank or title of a peer or peeress.
A book listing such people and their families.
e: Inherited from Middle English perage, from Old French parage. peer + -age. Doublet of parage.

s: Having caused to suffer a blight.
Cannabis sativa, a widely consumed form of cannabis.
A person who guards or monitors passage through a gate.
A person or group who controls access to something or somebody.
A common orange and brown butterfly with eyespots, Pyronia tithonus, of the family Nymphalidae.
In dissociative identity disorder, an aspect of the personality that controls access to the various identities.
A provider of core platform services with specific characteristics (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council)
A pebble, stone chip or piece of gravel.
An Irish Republican, especially one who has supported the armed struggle.
e: From Irish tiocfaidh, from the Republican slogan tiocfaidh ár lá (“our day will come”), perhaps punning on etymologies 1 and/or 2.

s: A person who breeds or trains hawks or other birds of prey.
One who follows the sport of fowling with hawks.
e: From Middle English fauconer, from Old French falconer, fauconer, from faucon (“falcon”).

s: Snide and sarcastic; usually out of irritation.
e: From snark + -y; 1906, as “irritable”, from snark (“to snort”), by onomatopoeia (1866). Compare Low German snarken (“to snore”), snarke, Swedish snarka. In the sense “sarcastic” popularized in the late 1990s.

s: A subgenre of electronic music employing unstable rhythms, complex time signatures, and mid-range synths.
Technically worded, in the style of jargon.
Technical in nature, difficult for non-specialists to understand.
Alternative spelling of forgo; to abandon, to relinquish.
e: From Middle English forgan, from Old English foregān, equivalent to fore- + go.

s: In the form of a dome.
A battle (or a duel) using small arms.
To engage in battle using small arms.
Similar or comparable to a prince.
In the manner of a royal prince's conduct.
e: From Middle English princely,pryncely, equivalent to prince + -ly. Compare Dutch prinselijk.

s: Already in existence before something else.
In a free way: without charge.
Sloping; having a rake or incline.
The act or process of using a rake; the going over a space with a rake.
A space gone over with a rake; also, the work done, or the quantity of hay, grain, etc., collected, by going once over a space with a rake.
a bass guitar playing technique in which multiple notes are played rapidly from one string to another.
The reduction of loan principal over a series of payments.
The distribution of the cost of an intangible asset, such as an intellectual property right, over the projected useful life of the asset.
e: From Middle English amortisen (“to kill, alienate in mortmain”), from Anglo-Norman amorteser, alteration of Old French amortir, from Vulgar Latin *admortire (“to kill”), from Latin ad- and mors, mortem (“death”).

s: The weight or significance given to something, sometimes by means of a statistical multiplier.
Moving from the sea towards the land.
Positioned on or near the shore.
From the sea towards the land.
To relocate production, services or jobs to lower-cost locations in the same country.

s: A large, palatial urban building in Italy.
e: Borrowed from Italian palazzo, from Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome, where aristocrats built large homes. Doublet of palace, Pfalz.

s: Lasting for a short period of time.
Existing for only one day, as with some flowers, insects, and diseases.
Usually dry, but filling with water for brief periods during and after precipitation.
Something which lasts for a short period of time.
e: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος, the more common form of ἐφημέριος (“of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (“on”) + ἡμέρα (“day”).

s: Being overly concerned with material possessions and wealth.
Synonym of materialist, of or concerning materialism.
A theological lecturer attached to a cathedral church.
A person who has a personal knowledge of God through prayer, asceticism, and mystical experience.
To determine a person's speech by watching the movement of their lips.
Any of several species of perennial herbs of the genus Symphytum, often specifically common comfrey (Symphytum officinale).
e: From Middle English cumfiria, from Latin (herba) cōnfirma in Pseudo-Apuleius, also called cōnsolida, cōnserva, cōnferva, from conferveo (“to boil together”); from the use of the plant in tea to aid in healing bones.

s: A maid that waits at hand; a female servant or attendant.
A moth of the species Dysauxes ancilla.
e: Inherited from Middle English handemayde, hand-maide, handmaide, handmayd, hand mayde, hand-mayde, haundmaid, hondemayde, hondmaide, hond-mayde. en + hand + maid, the first component in the sense of "ready at hand".

s: Happening by fortune or chance; accidental, coincidental.
Happening by good fortune or success; fortunate, lucky.
Happening independently of human control; uncontrollable.
e: From *fortu- (“chance, fortune, luck”) + -ītus. *Fortu- is thought to be from *fortus, from fors (“chance, luck”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -tus. Doublet of fortuity.

s: Without any delay; in an instantaneous manner.
The motion of one who limps.
The act of restoring something to its previous state.
Someone whose beliefs are contrary to the fundamental tenets of a religion they claim to belong to.
Someone who does not conform to generally accepted beliefs or practices.
Heretical; of or pertaining to heresy or heretics.
e: From Middle English heretyk, heretike, from Old French eretique, from Medieval Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (“able to choose, factious”), itself from Ancient Greek αἱρέω (“to choose”).
From Middle English flaun, flaon, flawn, from Old French flaon, from Late Latin fladonem, accusative of flado, from Frankish *flaþō. Doublet of flan, flathe, flathon.

s: Vicarious joy associated with seeing one's partner have a joyful romantic or sexual relationship with another person.
The feeling of joy one has experiencing another's joy, such as in witnessing a toddler's joy and feeling joy in response.
e: In the early 1990s by a group of members of the Kerista Commune, a polyamorous group based in San Francisco, California, U.S.A., in existence between 1956 and 1991, apparently randomly using an alphabet board (similar to a Ouija board), with -ion.

e: From peri- (“near”) + menopause. The term has been in use since at least 1931, when it was used in Joseph Bolivar De Lee and Jacob Pearl Greenhill's book, Obstetrics: Gynecology.

A type of tropical savanna biome found in much of central Brazil and parts of Paraguay.
Someone who studies, or is an expert in, sex and sexuality.
Resembling or characteristic of an animal.
pertaining to the nervous system and endocrine system together
In an immaculate manner; in a manner free of stain or blemish; without being defiled.

A device for checking electrical equipment for short circuits etc.

The act of anal penetration of a man by someone, usually a woman, wearing a strap-on dildo.

The organization and structure of the church, as distinct from sodality or parachurch organizations.

The way in which infrastructure and knowledge of how to use it give rise to a meaningful pattern of interaction (a concept in Anthony Giddens's structuration theory).
The quality of being limited by a condition.
That whether a zodiac sign is cardinal, fixed or mutable
Of a person, chatting a lot or fond of chatting.
Of a text or speech, expressed in a conversational style.
Supplying more information than necessary; verbose.
Infested with lice; or, dirty, worn or of poor quality; lousy.
A greyhound racing event; the sport of greyhound racing.
A rifle with a short barrel.
The erection of hairs or papillae.
The presence of larval cysts of Taenia solium, the pork tapeworm, in the parenchyma of the brain, often associated with seizures and sometimes fatal.
Any of several muscles of the lateral side of the leg, which arise from the fibula and act to move the foot.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin peroneus, clipping of mūsculus peroneus.

s: Any substance that can be crystallized from solution; a water-soluble crystalline substance that can diffuse through a semipermeable membrane, as opposed to a colloid which cannot.
One of the microscopic particles resembling crystals, consisting of protein matter, which occur in certain plant cells.
Crystal-like; transparent like crystal, or shaped like a crystal.
Of or pertaining to the supraclavicle in fishes.
Relating to or involving the sternum, the clavicle and the mastoid process of the temporal bone.
Of or pertaining to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
e: Borrowed from New Latin sternocleidomastoīdēs, from sternum (“the breastbone”) + κλείς (“the collarbone”) + mastoīdēs (“like a breast”), equivalent to sterno- + cleido- + mastoid.

s: Of, resembling, or capable of forming a thread; filamentous.
e: From Middle English *thredi, *thredy (suggested by derivative Middle English thredines, þredinez (“fibrousness, stringiness”)), equivalent to thread + -y.

A wire used to restrict and control the movement of other equipment, such as a catheter being inserted into the body.
To defraud (someone) by giving them less change than they should be given after a transaction.
To deprive (someone or something) of something due; to treat unfairly; to cheat, deceive; to half-ass.
The official yell of the US Army.

e: From tropomyosin. Coined by the Japanese researcher Setsuro Ebashi in 1963.[http://jb.oxfordjournals.org/content/vol59/issue4/index.dtl].

e: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrictus (“compressed, contracted”), past participle of cōnstringō (“to draw or bind together; to compress”). Doublet of constrain.

A habit-forming compound that is derived from codeine and is administered in the form of its bitartrate C18H21NO3·C4H6O6 usually in combination with other drugs (as acetaminophen) as an analgesic or antitussive.
of a group or body etc.
Having components that act independently of each other.
The collarbone; the prominent bone at the top of the chest between the shoulder and the neck connecting the shoulder and the breastbone.
The upper part of a spiral shell.
e: Borrowed from Middle French clavicule, from Latin clāvicula (“a small key”), diminutive of clāvis (“a key”).

s: A rapid resting heart rate, especially one above 100 beats per minute; palpitations.
e: New Latin tachycardia, from Ancient Greek ταχύς (“swift”) + καρδία (“heart”). tachy- + -cardia. Compare French tachycardie.

The act of perfusing, the passage of fluid through the circulatory system.
The introduction of a drug or nutrients through the bloodstream in order to reach an internal organ or tissues.

In whist, to throw away a high card so as not to interrupt one's partner's long suit.
To enable communication again, via telephone, instant messaging, etc., with (somebody previously blocked).
The removal of a block or blockage.

A slender tube inserted into a blood vessel, a ureter or the oesophagus in order to provide support and to prevent disease-induced closure.

To keep within limits; to restrain; to cause to stop, or cease; to stint.
To stint; to stop; to cease.
