s: The person whose aim is to kill the bull in a bullfight.
A certain game of dominoes in which four dominoes (the 4-3, 5-2, 6-1, and double blank), called matadors, may be played at any time in any way.
The jack of clubs, or any other trump held in sequence with it, in the game of skat.
One of the three chief cards in ombre and quadrille.
e: Borrowed from Spanish matador (“killer”). Used in the English language as title for a bullfighter, however referred to as a torero in Spain.
Borrowed from French luzerne, from Occitan luzerno, of uncertain origin.

s: The quality of being adaptable; a quality that renders adaptable.

Variability in respect to, or under the influence of, external conditions; susceptibility of an organism to that variation whereby it becomes suited to or fitted for its conditions of environment; the capacity of an organism to be modified by circumstances.
Causing a person to lose heart; making despondent or gloomy.
Below the level of conscious awareness.
Planned, considered or estimated in advance; deliberate.

e: Middle English werkedei, from Old Norse virkr dagr (“working day”). Cognate to later workday; see work and day. Used in adjective sense from 16th century. work + -a- + day..

s: A chronic disease of the lungs, caused by inhalation of beryllium compounds.
The state or condition of being sucky; inferiority or badness.
inflammation of multiple blood vessels or lymph vessels
To perform an action at the wrong time; especially to misjudge the timing of coordinated events.
A poisonous plant of the species Datura stramonium, part of the nightshade (Solanaceae) family, occasionally ingested as a hallucinogen.
Any poisonous plant of the genus Datura.
A carpet woven on a wide loom.
Woven on a wide loom, and so needing fewer seams.
One who controls the action of a slave owned by others.
A spicy Senegalese dish of marinated meat poultry, fish, or lamb with onions, lemon or mustard.
Motion of a celestial object from one place to another; local motion.
To treat in an intellectual manner; to discuss or express intellectually.
To endow with intellect; to bestow intellectual qualities upon; to cause to become intellectual.
To find a seemingly rational explanation for.
To use (excessive) reasoning and rationalization to block out emotional stress and anxiety associated with painful or traumatic experiences.
The act of moving material using a ladle.
An enhanced state of sensory sensitivity accompanied by an exaggerated intensity of behaviors whose purpose is to detect threats.
A parasympathomimetic, a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor alkaloid of the Calabar bean, used to treat certain medical conditions.
The use of a computerized calendar to schedule events or appointments.
Any disease or condition accompanied by multiple granulomas.
Parts of the mind one is subconsciously aware of.
A person who diagnoses, especially a medical doctor.
A small elevator used to move food etc. from one floor of a building to another.
A table or set of trays on rollers used for serving food.
e: From dumb (“unable to speak”) + waiter, originally separate words and describing the portable table's inability to relate gossip after the meal. By the use of the term to describe small service elevators in American homes in the 1840s, it simply meant dumb as “mechanical”, “unable to speak at all”.

s: Of or pertaining to an oxymoron.
Of or relating to an embolus or an embolism.
The eight trigrams used in Daoist cosmology.
The act of casting off the skin or shell; ecdysis.
Being the process of the temporal bone behind the ear.
Being any of several bony elements that occupy a similar position in the skull of lower vertebrates.
Of or relating to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.
e: Borrowed from New Latin mastoīdēs, from Ancient Greek μᾰστοειδής (“like a breast”), from μᾰστός (“a woman's breast”) + -ειδής (“-like, -oid”).

s: Having the psychological condition of egomania.
The state or characteristic of being shameless.
An utterance or action which is shameless.
Having the character of folk music
The striped bass, Morone saxatilis, a popular sport fish native to North America.
A person who is authorized to wear a certain number of stripes on his or her uniform.
Of or pertaining to neurochemistry, the study of the chemical basis of nerve and brain activity
A chemical substance that is involved in neural activity, such as a neurotransmitter
Of, pertaining to, or caused by thrombosis
The act or operation of neutering an animal; normally used in reference to performing the operation on a female.
A semisynthetic macrolide antibiotic C38H72N2O12 (trademarks Zithromax, Z-PAK) that is derived from erythromycin and is used especially as an antibacterial agent.
In a fiendish manner; evilly, wickedly.
Extremely, very in harsh or negative contexts.

An antihistamine and anticholinergic drug that blocks the effect of histamine at H1 receptor sites, relieving allergy symptoms. It also reduces smooth muscle contraction, increases heart rate, and sedates the user by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs).
Any of various diseases of humans caused by parasitic blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma.
e: From schistosome + -iasis. From scientific name Schistosoma + Ancient Greek -σις.

s: Afflicted, or looking as if afflicted, with mange.
Worn and squalid-looking; bedraggled or decrepit.
The formation of a polydentate chelate compound from a metal salt.
The use of this process to remove metal ions from solution, especially to counter poisoning by heavy metals.
A chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterized by hardening the skin or other organs through excessive deposits of collagen.
e: From New Latin sclēroderma, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (“hard”) + δέρμα (“skin, hide”). sclero- + -derma.

s: Having a negative view of mankind. This may express itself as, e.g., distrust, dislike, hate, or contempt.
The remains of something; a wreck.
Vengeance; revenge; persecution; punishment; consequence; trouble.
Remnant from a shipwreck as washed ashore; flotsam or jetsam.
The right to claim such items.
Any marine vegetation cast up on shore, especially seaweed of the family Fucaceae.
Weeds, vegetation, or rubbish floating on a river or pond.
A high, flying cloud; a rack.
e: From Middle English wrake, wrache, wreche, from a merger of Old English wracu, wræc (“misery, suffering”) and Old English wrǣċ (“vengeance, revenge”). See also wrake.

Late Middle English, from Middle Dutch wrak, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *wrekaną (“to drive out”), the source of wreak and wreck. Doublet of vraic. Cognate with German Wrack, Old Norse rek, Danish vrag, Swedish vrak, Old English wræc); also compare Gothic 𐍅𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽, 𐍅𐍂𐌰𐌺𐌾𐌰𐌽 (“persecute”), Old Norse reka (“drive”).

s: Affected with disease of the shank or footstalk
The action of one who philanders.

A glycopeptide antibiotic C66H75Cl2N9O24 produced by the actinomycete Amycolaptosis orientalis, used in the form of its hydrochloride C66H75Cl2N9O24·HCl against Gram-positive bacteria, especially staphylococci resistant to meticillin and enterococci.
e: From vanquish + -o- + -mycin (“antibiotic produced by a Streptomyces strain”)

s: The doctrine that all events are subject to fate or inevitable necessity, or determined in advance in such a way that human beings cannot alter them.
One who is very strong and courageous.
Of or pertaining to the hypothalamus.
Overly filled with fluid; used especially of blood vessels.
To make something form into crystals.
To give a definite or precise form to (something).
To coat something with crystals, especially with sugar.
e: From crystal + -ize. The double l reflects the classical stem found in its etyma, Latin crystallus and Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος, rather than the simplified spelling of the English base noun. Compare Hellenistic Greek κρυσταλλίζειν (“to shine like crystal”), post‐classical Latin crystallizare (“to change into crystal”), and French cristalliser.

s: An item, material or feature that makes something stiffer.
The act of checking again; reverification.
The branch of medicine concerned with the study of kidney function and the diagnosis and treatment of kidney diseases.
To relegate (something, especially a topic or a group of people) to the margins or to a lower limit; to exclude socially or otherwise.
To find a marginal distribution of a joint probability distribution.
A powerful portable audio system for listening collectively to recorded or broadcast sound.
Treatment by a doctor; the practice of treating the sick; practising medicine.
The treating of a person or people, especially older people, differently from others based on assumptions, prejudices or/and stereotypes relating to their age.
Any minor ailment causing a runny nose; the symptom of a runny nose itself.
An abnormal developmental feature of offspring.
To helicopter: to transport by helicopter.
To helicopter: to travel by helicopter.
Any American marsupial of the family Didelphidae in the order Didelphimorphia.
e: From aposoum (“white animal”), from *wa·p-aʔθemwa (“white dog”); compare Ojibwe waabasim (“white dog”).

s: An antimetabolite and antifolate drug used in treatment of cancer, autoimmune diseases and ectopic pregnancies.
Done by moving the hand (and arm) from below.

A personality disorder characterized by impaired empathy and remorse, and bold, disinhibited, and egocentric traits masked by superficial charm and the outward presence of apparent normality. Violent and criminal offenses may be indicative of this disorder.
A cabin, for the use of the captain, in the after part of a sailing ship under the poop deck.
A donkey, especially one driven by a huckster or greengrocer.
A pony that works in a mine.
A lever mounted on a tripod for lifting stones, leveling up railroad ties, etc.
e: Uncertain. Perhaps a contraction from Dutch kajuit (“cabin”).
From Scots cuddie; compare Gaelic cudaig, cudainn, or English cuttlefish, or cod.
From, with the initial "B" replaced with "C" in Crip slang.

s: Of, related to, or suffering from paraplegia. Paralyzed from the lower half of the body down.
A person who suffers from paraplegia.
Containing oxygen, or oxygen-containing radicals, as substituents
The ceremonial meal held on the first night or first two nights of Passover.
(usually as part of the phrase "Tu BiShvat seder") A ceremonial meal held on Tu BiShvat, consisting of several types of fruits and nuts.
One of the 6 parts into which the Mishnah is divided.
A motion that veers; a sudden swerve.
mentally mixed-up or confused due to the usage of mind-bending drugs.
Of, or in the manner of a brute.
Extreme sensitivity to a substance such as a foreign protein or drug.
A severe and rapid systemic allergic reaction to an allergen, causing a constriction of the trachea, preventing breathing; anaphylactic shock.
e: Borrowed from French anaphylaxie, Coined by Q214851 and Coined by Q3372029 from the Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νᾰ- (“(intensifier) thoroughly”) from ᾰ̓νᾰ́ (“to, again, upon”) and φύλαξις (“protection, watching, guarding”).

s: The organic chemical compound propene. An alkene which is a colorless gaseous (at room temperature and pressure) hydrocarbon with the chemical formula C3H6.
Of, relating to, or designating a disease or condition having no known cause.
e: From idio- + -pathic. First appears c. 1669, in the publications of William Simpson.

s: A person who feels compelled to work excessively, including while at home.
In the nature or manner of a workaholic.
In a courageous manner; bravely; boldly.
A medical instrument used for listening to sounds produced within the body.
To auscultate, or examine, with a stethoscope.
e: Borrowed from French stéthoscope, a word coined by its inventor, physician René Laennec, equivalent to stetho + scope.

s: The rounded portion of a ship's hull, forming a transition between the bottom and the sides.
The lowest inner part of a ship's hull, where water accumulates.
The water accumulated in the bilge; bilge water.
The bulging part of a barrel or cask.
To spring a leak in the bilge.
To break open the bilge(s) of.
e: Likely derived from bulge. Compare Middle English bulgen (“to ground or scuttle a ship”).

s: A medical doctor specializing in the eye: deficiencies of vision requiring correction, and diseases.
A sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a species of bacteria (the gonococcus) that affects the mucous membrane of the genital and urinary tracts.
e: From New Latin, from Late Latin gonorrhoea, from Ancient Greek γονόρροια, from γόνος (“sperm, seed, offspring”) + ῥοία (“flow”) (ca. 1526). gono- + -rrhea.

s: A chronic eating disorder characterized by a binge-and-purge cycle: extreme overeating followed by self-induced vomiting.
e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek βουλῑμῐ́ᾱ (“ravenous hunger”)

s: Pertaining to a systole or heart contraction
Relating to the mathematical concept of a systole
the univalent anion HCO3-; any salt of carbonic acid in which only one of the hydrogen atoms has been replaced.
Clipping of sodium bicarbonate, especially that used as a mild antacid.
Closely following a formula or predictable pattern, as
Aged between thirteen and nineteen inclusive; teenage.
To have sex (with someone) without using a condom.
A bird, raised for meat, that lacks feathers, seen as an undesirable trait.
The doctrine that all actions are determined by the current state and immutable laws of the universe, with no possibility of choice.
The property of having behavior determined only by initial state and input.
The state or quality of being irritable; quick excitability.
A natural susceptibility, characteristic of all living organisms, tissues, and cells, to the influence of certain stimuli, response being manifested in a variety of ways.
A condition of morbid excitability of an organ or part of the body; undue susceptibility to the influence of stimuli.
The clogging or hardening of arteries or blood vessels caused by plaques (accumulations of fatty deposits, usually cholesterol).
Causative of or relating to an act or policy of genocide.
Able to be transmitted between people or animals.
A long, narrow crack or opening made by breaking or splitting, especially in rock or earth.
A groove, deep furrow, elongated cleft or tear between body parts or in the substance of an organ.
A break or slit in tissue usually at the junction of skin and mucous membrane.
A state of incompatibility or disagreement.
e: From Middle English fissure, from Old French fissure, from Latin fissūra (“a cleft, chink”), from findō (“to cleave, split, divide”) + -tūra.

s: A hormone that stimulates contractions during labor, and then the production of milk; also plays a role in social bonding.
A person who decodes secret messages
A device that decodes a scrambled electronic signal e.g. of a satellite television signal
Able to be treated; not incurable.
e: From Middle English tretable, from treten (“treat”) and Old French traitable, Anglo-Norman tretable; equivalent to treat + -able.

s: Agent noun of manipulate; one who manipulates.
A device which can be used to move, arrange or operate something.
A puppeteer, especially one controlling marionettes.
A thick, colourless liquid, C2H4(OH)2, of a sweetish taste, produced artificially from certain ethylene compounds and used as an antifreeze; ethylene glycol.
Opposing the theory that diseases are caused by bacteria.
A drug having the effect of killing or inhibiting bacteria.
Produced by or exhibiting imprinting; showing distinction by its origin from the paternal or maternal genome.
The ritual act of driving out evil spirits from persons, places or things that are possessed by them.
e: From Old French exorciser, from Late Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (“to ward off, to charge under oath, adjure”), from ἐξ + ὅρκος.

s: One who professes misogyny; a person who hates or is prejudiced against women.
e: From Ancient Greek μῑσογύνης, from μῑσέω (“I hate”) + γυνή (“woman”), equivalent to misogyny + -ist.

s: The transparent layer making up the outermost front part of the eye, covering the iris, pupil, and anterior chamber.

An acute febrile disease of the (sub)tropics caused by the Dengue virus, a flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, and characterized by high fever, rash, headache, and severe muscle and joint pain.
e: From West Indian Spanish dengue in 1828, from the Kiswahili term dinga (in full kidingapopo or kidinga pepo, "a kind of sudden cramp-like seizure caused by an evil spirit", dinga itself meaning sudden cramp-like seizure).

s: Of, or relating to the eye, or the sense of sight
Seen by, or seeing with, the eye; visual.
The eyepiece of a microscope or other optical instrument, i.e., the optical element closest to the eye.
Any of the scales forming the margin of a reptile's eye.
e: Derived from the Latin oculāris (“of the eye”), from oculus (“eye”).

s: In a diagonal manner, not square to any direction.
e: From Middle English diagonaly, modeled on Medieval Latin diagōnāliter; equivalent to diagonal + -ly.

s: Any of various techniques for the qualitative or quantitative separation of the components of mixtures of compounds; all characterized by the use of a mobile phase (gas or liquid) moving relative to a stationary phase (liquid or solid) – the differences between the rates of migration of the compound
e: Back-formation from chromatographic, Borrowed from German chromatographisch (see there for more); chromato- + -graphy. The technique is so named because it was developed primarily for the separation of the plant pigments, which would separate in bands of different "colors" (chromato-).

s: A sword having a blade made of a powerful beam of light or energy.
A real-world toy, prop, or device fashioned after the fictional lightsaber.
e: From light + saber; for the Star Wars film franchise. First mentioned in the film Star Wars (later retitled Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope) which was released on May 25, 1977.

s: Pertaining to or composed of nitre; having the properties of nitre, bitter.
Of, relating to, or derived from nitrogen, especially in which the valence of the nitrogen is lower than that of a corresponding nitric species.
Of or relating to nitrous acid or its derivatives.
Having a sharp odor like ammonia or nitric acid.
The system in some racing vehicles which pumps nitrous oxide into the engine to improve performance.
e: From Middle French nitreux, and its source, Latin nitrōsus (“nitrose”). Doublet of nitroso. nitro- + -ous.

s: The backwards flow of any fluid.
A technique, using a reflux condenser, allowing one to boil the contents of a vessel over an extended period.
The leaking of stomach acid up into the oesophagus.
To boil a liquid in a vessel having a reflux condenser.
The state or condition of being joyless; lack of joy.
To act (perform in a play etc.).

e: From Middle English bordel, from Old French bordel (“brothel”). Doublet of bordello. la:borda + -el (“diminutive”).

s: A movie that is one projector reel in length.
The private parts of the body, particularly the sex organs.
A mosquito that has not had a blood meal.

e: From Middle English wayferande, weyverinde, wayverinde, from Old English weġfarende, weġfērende (“wayfaring”), equivalent to way + faring. Cognate with Icelandic vegfarandi. More at wayfare.

s: In a preternatural manner; beyond what could possibly be natural.
a draft garment made of inexpensive cloth for the purposes of fitting and design evaluation
Excessively or falsely sentimental; showing a sickly excess of sentiment.
Sickening or insipid in taste or smell.
Lacking taste or flavor; without seasoning, spice, or discernible qualities of taste.
A heavy hammer or beetle, often made of wood or lead.
A colourless, soluble protein found in blood plasma, egg white, etc.; albumin; chiefly preceded by a descriptive word: one form of such a protein.
The endosperm of seeds of most flowering plants, especially when found in mature seeds.
e: Late Latin albūmen (“egg white, albumen; type of eye disease”) (whence Late Middle English albuminium (“clear fluid in the eyeball between the cornea and lens, aqueous humour”)), from Latin albus (“white”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”)) + -men, modelled after ferrūmen (“cement; glue”). The form albumina is a Late Latin albūmina.

s: Gerund of intermingle: the act by which things intermingle.
A flat, rectangular piece of rock or stone used for paving or roofing.
One of several types of rock easily split and suitable for making flagstones.
A teacher or lecturer at some universities (in central Europe, etc.)
A tour guide at a museum, art gallery, historical site, etc.
e: From Latin docēns, present participle of doceō (“to teach”). In the meaning of a university grade, as used in some Central European countries, it is clipped version of private docent, privat-docent, from German Privatdozent, from German Dozent.

s: Having the traits of a vampire.
Pertaining to, derived from, or containing iron.
Of compounds of iron in which it has a valence or oxidation number of +3.
A claim or aspiration to a particular status or quality.
To apply tension to an object before some other event or process.
To apply tension to reinforcing strands before concrete is poured in.
e: From Middle English pretencioun, pretensioun, from Medieval Latin prētēnsiō.

s: The apparent elegance and precision exhibited by a confident, accomplished dancer.
In an imperfect manner or degree; not fully or completely.
The chance or random quality of an event or circumstance.
A chance or random event or circumstance.
The connection of an electrical component in parallel with another, the current being divided between them.
The manipulation of railway rolling stock into different combinations or onto different tracks.
Arbitrage conducted between certain local markets without the necessity of the exchange involved in foreign arbitrage.
The activity of keeping a diary, or journal.
The change log of the file system or database.
Causing, or relating to, redemption or saving; redeeming.

e: From Middle English torterous, from Anglo-Norman torturous, from Old French tortureus, from Latin tortūra. torture + -ous.

s: The act of one who prowls.
The lower edge of the side of the face (below the cheek), defined by the jawbone.
An act or ability to simulate or effect the appearance, characteristics, or behavior of someone or something else.
A coarse mat at the entrance to a house, upon which one wipes one's shoes.
Someone who habitually yields to others' demands or mistreatment, failing to assert their own rights or interests.
Seeking favor by way of flattery; flattering, servile.
To make a hole in (something); to hollow.
To remove part of (something) by scooping or digging it out.
Any member of a major grouping of unicellular eukaryotes, of the clade Excavata.
e: From Latin excavātus (“hollowed out”), perfect passive participle of excavō (“to hollow out”) (see -ate and -ate), from ex (“out”) + cavō (“to hollow out, pierce”), from cavus (“cave, hole”) + -ō. Participial usage up until Early Modern English.
From a substantivization of Latin excavātus through the associated taxon's name (Excavata), see -ate and Etymology 1 for more.

s: (northern England) an area of land which has been cleared of trees, an assart
e: From Middle English riddyng, reddyng, ryddyng, rudyng, from Old English hryding (“a clearing, a patch of cleared land”), equivalent to rid + -ing.

s: In the manner of a ritual.
Of or relating to habitual behavior.
Describing something in a technicolor model, a model that is similar to the Standard Model but lacks a scalar Higgs field.
A process of colour cinematography using synchronised monochrome films, each of a different colour, to produce a colour print.
A collection of theories based on quantum chromodynamics
Having only one color, represented by differing hues and tints. For example shades in a black and white television.
Perceptive of only one color; unable to distinguish colors; total color blindness.
e: From mono- + chromatic, mono- from Ancient Greek μόνος (“alone, only, sole, single”), chromatic from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (“color”).

s: Pruriently detailed and sensationalistic about something shocking or horrifying, especially with regard to violence or sex.
Being of a light yellow hue.
Having a brown colour tinged with red.
A narrow street formed by the proximity of adjacent buildings.
A passage between two rows of cabins in a ship.
Equipped with a bridge (in many contexts).
The inability to decide on a course of action, especially if two or more possibilities exist.
An extra card or set of cards that is allowed to play at the end of various card games.
e: Borrowed from French merci (“thank you”). Doublet of mercy.

s: An act of driving or urging onward; propulsion.
Asphyxia—a condition in which an extreme decrease in the concentration of oxygen in the body accompanied by an increase in the concentration of carbon dioxide leads to loss of consciousness or death.
A particular act of death or killing by means of asphyxia.
e: Inherited from Middle English suffocation, suffocacioun, from Middle French suffocation, from Latin suffocatio.

s: Liveliness, or active mind and spirit.
e: Borrowed from French esprit (“spirit”). Doublet of spirit, spiritus, spirytus, sprite, spright, possibly also spree.

s: The act of dispensing or dealing out; distribution
The distribution of good and evil by God to man.
That which is dispensed, dealt out, or given; that which is bestowed on someone
A system of principles, promises, and rules ordained and administered; scheme; economy
The relaxation of a law in a particular case; permission to do something forbidden, or to omit doing something enjoined; exemption.
In the Roman Catholic Church, an exemption from some ecclesiastical law, or from an obligation to God which a person has incurred of his own free will (oaths, vows, etc.).
e: From Middle English dispensacioun, from Old French despensacion, from Latin dispensātiō. en + dispense + ation.

s: Encircled by, or as if by, a girdle; drawn up or wrapped tightly.
Of clothes: not loose; close-fitting, tight-fitting.
Compressed into a small area; compact.
Of an action, etc.: lasting a short time; brief, curt.
Of speech or writing: brief and to the point; concise.
The land immediately next to, and inland from, a coast.
The rural territory surrounding an urban area, especially a port.
That which is unknown or unexplored about someone.
An area of land far from the sea.
Anything vague or ill-defined, especially something that is ill understood.
An individual's depth and breadth of knowledge, especially a politician's in areas outside politics, such as of academic, artistic, cultural, literary and scientific pursuits.
e: Borrowed from German Hinterland, from hinter (“behind”) + Land (“land”), cognate to English hinder (“back, rear”) + land. First used in English in 1888 by George Chisholm in his work Handbook of Commercial Geography originally as hinderland, but the current spelling (following German) became more popular.

s: A person or a thing that crawls or creeps.
Any creeping animal (such as a serpent), reptile.
A one-piece garment for infants designed to facilitate access to the wearer's diaper.
A device which allows a small child to safely roam around a room from a seated or standing position.
A metal plate with spikes, designed to be worn with shoes to prevent slipping.
A spur-like device strapped to the boot to facilitate climbing.
A small low iron, or dog, between the andirons.
An instrument with iron hooks or claws for dredging up items from a well or other water.
Any device for causing material to move steadily from one part of a machine to another, such as an apron in a carding machine, or an inner spiral in a grain screen.
Any plant (as ivy or periwinkle) that grows by creeping, especially a climbing plant of the genus Parthenocissus.
Strophitus undulatus, a freshwater mussel of the eastern United States.
A small four-hooked grapnel used to recover objects dropped onto the sea bed.
The lowest gear of some tractors or trucks: one with so low a gear ratio that the vehicle creeps along at the speed of a human's slow walk.

A low-profile wheeled platform whereupon one may lie on one's back and gain better access to the roof of a space with very low height (such as the underbody of a vehicle), or a low stool similarly wheeled.
A person who creeps people out; a creepy person.
e: From Middle English crepere, from Old English crēopere, equivalent to creep + -er. Slang usage derived from phrase give the creeps or creep out (distinct from merely one who creeps).

s: Displaying bravery and daring in attempting some task.
Very able and ingenious in business dealings or social advancement.
The undertaking of an enterprise; purposeful activity; doings.
Cooked or prepared in a traditional manner as would be done at home.
Of a camp or event in which participants sleep away from home.
Ellipsis of sleepaway camp; a camp or event in which participants sleep away from home.
Careful with small amounts of money or over small matters.
A piece of excrement. A turd.
A functional group with two sulfur atoms bonded to one another, described by the following formula: R–S–S–R'.
A binary compound of sulfur and another element in the ratio 2:1 (formula XS2).
Of or relating to antisepsis or the use of antiseptics.
Free of unpleasantness; prim, sanitized or bowdlerized.

Any substance that inhibits the growth and reproduction of microorganisms. Generally includes only those that are used on living objects (as opposed to disinfectants) and aren't transported by the lymphatic system to destroy bacteria in the body (as opposed to antibiotics).
The act by which something is fractured.
A sexual encounter during lunch hour, especially one which is illicit.
Synonym of smithsonite, a pink form of zinc oxide (mainly zinc carbonate ZnCO3) formed as a byproduct of zinc sublimation, now used in skin lotions.
Synonym of hemimorphite, an orthorhombic-pyramidal mineral containing zinc.
To coat or treat with calamine.
e: From French calamine, from Medieval Latin calamīna, from Latin cadmīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κᾰδμείᾱ, from Κάδμος (“Cadmus”) + -εια (“-ia: forming related substances”). Doublet of cadmia, calaminaris, lapis calaminaris.

s: A polymer, polyethylene terephthalate PET, as used for making thread and cloth.
e: Originated in 1951 (as Dacron) as a trademark, modern coinage by E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. on the model of nylon.

s: The shiny finish on shoes that have been polished.
A person who writes advertising copy (the text used in advertisements).
Expanded polystyrene foam, such as is used in cups and packaging.
Having teeth of a specified colour.
A highly flammable, viscous substance, designed to stick to the body while burning, used in warfare as an incendiary especially in wooded areas.
To spray or attack with napalm.
e: Formed from na(phthenic) palm(itic) acid, the two original components of the substance.

s: A flowering plant of species Anacyclus pyrethrum.
e: From German Bertram (according to Kluge appearing first in English in 1578), well-known, from Middle High German bërtram, bërhtram, from Old High German bërhtram, from Latin pyrethrum, from Ancient Greek πύρεθρον.
From quite + -ly. Probably unconnected with Middle English quitly.

s: Unwanted paper that has been discarded.
The act or process of a person being chaperoned.
The act of playing as a quarterback
The action of making criticisms after the event

A small assemblage of cut and folded paperboard comprising a folded sheet (the matchcover) and some rows of matches (paperboard strips with the ends dipped to produce the matchheads), generally with a striker on the outside.
A book in which data from sports matches is recorded.
e: From match + book, since the 1890s. Paper matches were developed in the 1880s; folded books containing them, and the strike-on-cover concept, were developed in the 1890s; more in Wikipedia at matchbook.
From match + book, since the mid-19th century or earlier.

s: The act of one who smites.
e: From Middle English smytinge, smitende, smytende, smitand, from Old English smītende, from Proto-Germanic *smītandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *smītaną (“to throw, hurl, bespatter”), equivalent to smite + -ing.

s: Of, pertaining to, capable of, or aiding digestion.
e: From Latin pepticus, from Ancient Greek πέψις (“digestion”), a form of πέσσω.

s: A roofed structure for automobile storage, usually attached to a house and not fully enclosed like a garage but with at least one side open to the outdoors.
e: From car + port, Coined by Frank Lloyd Wright and modeled on the French porte cochère.

s: The ordinal form of the number one billion.
The person or thing in the billionth position.
One of a billion equal parts of a whole.
A small cloth used to wash the face and body.
A fast boat, usually small (for 1-8 people).
A boat designed and built for racing.

A machine, used for the purpose of giving cloth, paper etc., a smooth, even, and glossy or glazed surface, by cold or hot pressure, or for watering them and giving them a wavy appearance; it consists of two or more cylinders revolving nearly in contact, with the necessary apparatus for moving and re
One who pursues the business of calendering.
To press between rollers for the purpose of making smooth and glossy, or wavy, as woolen and silk stuffs, linens, paper etc., as in a calender.
e: From Middle English calendren, from Middle French calandrer.
From قلندر (“wandering dervish”), from Arabic قَلَنْدَار (“wandering dervish”), itself from Early کلندر (“uncouth man”), from کلند (“rough, unshaven”). qalandar.

s: A tightly-compressed bandage used to stop bleeding by stopping the flow of blood through a large artery in a limb.
Any of several similar methods of clamping components into position.
Of, relating to, or derived from instinct.
Suggesting or reflecting the efforts of an amateur; not seeming professional or polished.
The making of mistakes or blunders.
One who knowingly allows themselves to be used for another's profit; a dupe.
A magician's assistant who pretends to be a member of the audience.
A confederate; a person who is secretly working for the researcher, unknown to the study participant.
To act as a straight man.
e: Perhaps an abbreviation of Russian студе́нт [stʊˈdʲent]; the original meaning was “stage assistant, actor who assists a comedian”. It may have been a Yiddish vaudeville term.

s: A book containing stories, especially children's stories.
As in a story for children; pleasant and idealized, or having a happy conclusion.
Action by law enforcement personnel to lead an otherwise innocent person to commit a crime, in order to arrest and prosecute that person for the crime.
A method of isolating specific cells or molecules from a mixture, especially by immobilization on a gel.
An injury suffered as a result of freezing of some part of the body, typically fingers, toes or the nose.
To expose to the effect of frost, or a frosty air; to blight or nip with frost.
An area allocated for someone to work in, especially in an office.
A file (or system of files) in which related software and data can be manipulated or developed in isolation from others.
An empty portion of the screen or window that serves as a container for other windows or objects.
Any of the screens that can be switched between in a virtual desktop.
The set of points that can be reached by the end-effector of a robotic manipulator.
The act by which things are spliced.
The point at which two things are spliced.
A sheltered place where bees, usually honey bees (genus Apis), live.
Such a home prepared by the bees themselves, in which some species of honey bees live and raise their young.
A man-made structure in which honey bees are kept so that humans can harvest their honey.
Any place full of activity, or in which people are very busy.
A women's hairstyle, popular in the 1960s, in which long hair is styled into a hive-shaped form on top of the head and usually held in place with lacquer.
A type of anti-personnel ammunition round containing flechettes, and characterised by the buzzing sound made as they fly through the air.
In Conway's Game of Life, a particular still life pattern with a rounded appearance.
A diagram showing where balls have passed the batter, used in analysis.
To fill (a place) with busy activity.
To style the hair in a hive-shaped or bouffant form.
In a sensible manner; in a way that shows good sense.
In a way that can be sensed or noticed; perceptibly.
Either of two New World vultures, Vultur gryphus of the Andes or Gymnogyps californianus, a nearly extinct vulture of the mountains of California.
A gold coin of some South American countries bearing the figure of one of these vultures.
An Argentinian short range ballistic missile.
The completion of a hole four strokes under par (a quadruple birdie, triple eagle, or double albatross).
A combination of four options of the same type at four strike prices, giving limited profit and limited risk.
e: From Spanish cóndor, from kuntur. The change /t/ to /d/ was characteristic of the "coastal" variety of the language.

s: Any of several North American subspecies Rangifer tarandus of the reindeer.
e: Borrowed from Canadian French caribou, from qalipu (“caribou”; compare qalipi, “to shovel snow”), from *maka·lipowa (“caribou”).

s: Small, inconsequential, or not worth spending time on.
A Jewish prayer of praise to God recited during services, and specifically when mourning the death of a close relative.
e: Borrowed from Hebrew קַדִּישׁ (“kaddish”), from Aramaic קַדִּישׁ (“holy; holy person”). Doublet of kiddush. The plural form kaddishim is borrowed from Hebrew קַדִּישׁים.

s: A loudspeaker that produces low-frequency sound.
To perform as a human blockhead.
To behave in a stupid manner.
Fitted to trench or cut; gutting; sharp.
Keen; biting; vigorously articulate and effective; severe.
e: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French trenchant, the present participle of trenchier (“to cut”).

s: Lacking substance; not real or strong.
e: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. in- + substantial.

s: Having been cleaned with a vacuum cleaner.
Given to taking by force or plundering; aggressively greedy.
of an animal, usually a bird
e: Perhaps from rapacity ous, in any case ultimately from Latin rapāx (“grasping, greedy”) -acious.

s: A ride in a vehicle taken solely for pleasure or enjoyment, especially a vehicle ride taken with no particular goal or purpose and just for the pleasure or enjoyment of a vehicle ride.
An instance of driving a motor vehicle in a carefree or reckless manner, especially a vehicle which has been taken without the permission of the owner.
One who kids, or teases light-heartedly.
A term of endearment/address for a child or young adult, usually male.
A small explosive device, typically containing a small amount of gunpowder in a tightly-wound roll of paper, primarily designed to produce a large bang.
A peanut butter cracker baked with marijuana, similar in concept to an Alice B. Toklas brownie.
Someone or something that is exciting, energetic, or unpredictable.
A type of Eurasian plant widely cultivated for its flowers.
other members of genus Dianthus and hybrids
The type of flower they bear, originally flesh-coloured, but since hybridizing found in a variety of colours.
The pinkish colors used in art to render human face and flesh.
Of a rosy pink or red colour.
e: From Middle French carnation (“flesh color, complexion”), either via Italian carnagione (“flesh color”) or directly from Late Latin carnātiō (“fleshiness”), from Latin carō (“flesh, meat”) + ātiō (“-ation”).

s: An electronic speaker designed to produce high-frequency sound.
One who or that which makes a tweeting noise.
One who posts messages ("tweets") on the social networking site Twitter.
A poster on a microblogging social networking service.
The sloping side of a mountain.
A stroboscopic lamp: a device used to produce regular flashes of light.
A pulse of light, such as from a flashing or rotating light source.
An electronic signal in hardware indicating that a value is ready to be read.
To flash like a stroboscopic lamp.
To practice the makeup technique of strobing.
A network of anastomosing or interwoven nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic vessels.
An interwoven combination of parts or elements in a structure or system.
The system of equations required for the complete expression of the relations which exist between a set of quantities.
e: Borrowed from Latin plexus (“a twining, plaiting, braid”)

s: Human nature or the human body as representative of the wider universe; man considered as a miniature counterpart of divine or universal nature.
A smaller system which is seen as representative of a larger one.
A small natural ecosystem; an artificial ecosystem set up as an experimental model.
e: From French microcosme, from Latin microcosmus, from Ancient Greek μικρός (“small”) + κόσμος (“universe, order”), equivalent to micro- + -cosm.

s: A place where many varieties of tree are grown for research, educational, and ornamental purposes.
e: Borrowed from Latin arborētum (“place with trees growing, plantation of trees”), from arbor (“tree”).

s: To make longer, to extend the length of.
Superlative of inner; the very deepest within; farthest from the surface or external part.
That which is innermost; the core.
e: From Middle English innermost, innermest, in-nermast, alteration (due to Middle English inner, innere (“inner”)) of Old English innemest (“innermost”), equivalent to inner + -most.

s: Of, relating to, or containing allegory.
Not bound by chains or shackles.
Awaiting the effects of nature, with little active treatment.
A triage classification for a patient in a mass casualty event with injuries so severe they are unlikely to survive even with maximum medical care.
A person who expects or awaits something.
A device that projects a flame for starting fires, and sometimes also additional fuel to help ignition. Used either as a weapon or a tool.
Someone who is extremely good at throwing or shooting balls.
A dish made by fermenting finely chopped cabbage.
e: Borrowed into English around 1600 from German Sauerkraut, from sauer (“sour, acidic, spoiled”) + Kraut (“herb; cabbage”). Doublet of choucroute.

s: A compensation gift given to a woman when divorced or repudiated by her husband.
e: Borrowed from Arabic مُتْعَة. Doublet of mut'ah. Arabic م ت ع.

s: In Central and Eastern Europe, boiled fruits (typically fresh or dried) served either as a drink or a dessert depending on the region.
A crude Polish preparation of heroin made from poppy straw.
A guitar-like musical instrument of Romania, having originally two strings and now four or five.
Alternative form of of sum, particularly in relation to Buryatia, Russia.
e: From Russian сомон, from сомон, from Mongolian ᠰᠤᠮᠤ. Ultimately from *sumun (“arrow”).
From Sanskrit दूर्वा. Doublet of doob as in doob grass.

s: Someone who plays a tenor saxophone.
Obsolete form of little, not much.
Obsolete form of little, not much.
Obsolete form of little, not much.
Obsolete form of little, a small amount, a small person, a small thing.
A male priest, shaman or religious or spiritual leader of traditional Meitei religion.
Of or pertaining to an elm tree.
e: From Middle English elmen, elmyn, equivalent to elm + -en (“made or consisting of”).
From Middle English tenden, from Old English tendan (“to kindle”). See tinder.

s: a cyclic sulfonamide in which the S-N bond is part of the ring
The Barbary macaque (Macaca sylvanus) native to the Atlas Mountains of Algeria and Morocco along with a small population of uncertain origin in Gibraltar.
A seated oriental figurine, usually of porcelain or ivory, of a grotesque form
A piece of ribbon worn as a streamer.
e: Perhaps an alteration of falbala (“furbelow”), from French.

s: A tree, Canarium luzonicum, native to the Philippines.
A resin harvested from the tree.
The passage or space between the outer and inner door of a cottage; the partition between the passage and the room.

e: From Middle English lymail, from Anglo-Norman limaille, from Latin limare, a form of limo; see further there.

s: living quarters occupied by elite women of the of Moscow.
A weight placed on an anchor to stop it dragging.
A permission or privilege granted by the church authority that excepts an individual from what is otherwise a norm of church law, such as a release from monastic vows.
The official or principal currency of São Tomé and Príncipe, divided into 100 cêntimos.
An outlaw, highwayman or freedom fighter in the Balkans.
A mercenary foot soldier in Hungary.
A halberdier of a Hungarian noble.
An attendant in German or Hungarian courts.
e: Borrowed from Hungarian hajdúk, plural of hajdú (“foot-soldier”). The Hungarian word may derive from hajtó which meant “(cattle) drover”. In 16th century Hungary, cattle driving was an important and dangerous occupation and drovers traveled armed. Some of them ended up as bandits or retainers in the service of local landowners and many may have become soldiers.

s: A confection usually made from crushed sesame seeds and honey. It is a traditional dessert in South Asia, the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
e: From Yiddish חלווה, from Romanian halva, from Ottoman Turkish حلوا, from Persian حلوا, from Arabic حَلْوَى. Cognate with Halwai.
From Malay bene, or possibly from or.

s: A kind of wine of a deep red color, chiefly from Galicia or Malaga in Spain.
Tinta barroca; a grape variety used in the production of Portuguese port wine.
Tinta miúda; a lesser-known grape variety that is used in blends of some Portuguese wines.
The basic unit of currency of Hungary; formerly subdivided into 100 fillér.
e: From Hungarian forint, from Italian fiorino (“florin, the former currency of Tuscany”). Doublet of florin.

s: Heated oil or ghee in which spices and onion, etc. are well-stirred and browned.
A traditional article of clothing worn in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka, consisting of a loose, collarless, long-sleeved, knee-length shirt worn by both men and women.
Almsgiving, usually in the form of an annual tax on certain types of property which is then used for charitable purposes; the third of the five pillars of Islam.
e: Borrowed from: all from Arabic زَكَاة (“almsgiving, zakat; purification”), from زَكَوٰة (archaic), from Aramaic זכותא/ܙܟܘܬܐ (“goodness, probity, uprightness; merit; victory”), from זכי (“to gain; to overcome, triumph over”).

s: Lying or remaining in a place; hence, resident.
An ambassador or minister resident at a court or seat of government.
Anything that lies in a place; that which, or one who, remains in a place.
e: Borrowed from Middle French legier, from Old French legier, apparently from Late Latin *leviārium, from levis (“light in weight”). See levity.

s: A long and complicated formal procedure.
e: From ragman roll (“long list; catalogue”). Recorded since c1736.

s: Tending to grab, especially rudely or greedily.
Humanlike hand of some animals, mainly rodents and primates.
Any member of the species Pan paniscus of great apes, from Africa south of the Congo river.
e: From Bolobo, a village on the Congo River where Europeans first made contact with the species. Bolobo is possibly imitative of the bubbling of the rapids at that section of the Congo.
From Middle English frendles, from Old English frēondlēas. en + friend + less.

s: The act of appearing again following absence.
To obscure something by casting a shadow.
To dominate something and make it seem insignificant.
e: From Middle English overschadwen, overschadewe, from Old English ofersċeadwian (“to overshadow”), equivalent to over- + shadow.

s: Of, relating to, or characteristic of vampires.
Having a memory (of a given kind).

e: Onomatopoeic, from the ejection of a liquid. Compare with spooge, spoo, spooch. The term is first attested isolatedly in ("ejection", "ejaculation"), referring to a dripping mop, in a 1919 St.

s: A man who has charge of dogs, such as a dog breeder or dog trainer; specifically, a man who trains dogs for the bloodsport of dogfighting.
An alleged cryptid or mythological creature that is part dog and part man; also a deity who is part dog and part man.
A man who sells dog meat.
An assistant to a crane operator, responsible for securing the crane's load and directing the operator.
e: From dog (“the domesticated mammal Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris”) + -man or man (senses 2 and 3).
From dog (“part of a crane that holds the items to be lifted”) + -man, from the fact that such a person would often ride on the load lifted by the crane when carrying out their duty.

s: In an abominable manner; very odiously; detestably.
The act of one who relents.
Someone or something that makes a loud, harsh, grinding or rasping noise, like that of a circular saw.
One who attacks violently and/or mindlessly.
To cut with a circular saw.
To spin rapidly like the blades of a circular saw.
To produce a loud, harsh noise like that of a circular saw.
To free (someone) of a misconception or misapprehension; to unveil a falsehood held by (someone).
Alternative form of sea bass, used especially in compound terms.

e: Borrowed from French beaucoup, early 20th century. Popularized by American GIs during the Vietnam War. The pronunciation /ˈbuːkuː/ was influenced by boucoup, a variant.

s: Any of the genus †Pterodactylus of pterosaurs.
e: From French ptérodactyle, a term coined by Cuvier from Ancient Greek πτερόν (“wing”) + δάκτυλος (“finger”). en + ptero + dactyl.

s: A bank or financial institution that processes credit card or debit card payments on behalf of a merchant.
A gripping listlessness or melancholia caused by boredom; depression.
To make bored or listless; to weary.
e: French ennui, from Old French enui (“annoyance”), from enuier (modern French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiō, from Latin in odiō (“hated”). Doublet of annoy.

s: Someone who enjoys pain or humiliation, or who derives pleasure from harming oneself or being harmed by others.
Someone who puts up with teasing.
e: Leopold von Sacher-Masoch ist. and popularized by Freud in relation to sadomasochism.

s: Of or pertaining to slaves or slavery.
Not belonging to the original root.
Not sounded, but serving to lengthen the preceding vowel, like the e in tune.
An element which forms no part of the original root.
e: From Middle English servyle, from Old French servil, servile, from Latin servīlis, from servus (“slave”). serve + -ile.

s: A political orator or leader, especially in a democratic system, who gains favor by pandering to or exciting the passions and prejudices of the audience rather than by using rational argument.
To speak or act in the manner of a demagogue; to speak about (an issue) in the manner of a demagogue.
e: From Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (“popular leader, mob leader”), from δῆμος (“people”) + ἀγωγός (“guide”). demo- + -agogue.

s: To remove tangles or knots from.
To remove confusion or mystery from.
Showing or characterized by a contemptible lack of moral standards.
Any member of the family Squalidae of dogfish sharks.
e: Latin squālidus, from squālēre (“to be rough or dirty”).

s: Of, pertaining to, or advocating anarcho-capitalism.
e: From anarcho- + capitalist. Its possible earliest appearance is in the 1971 article “Know Your Rights” by Murray Rothbard, who is credited with coining it and its cognate anarcho-capitalism; though the latter's earliest extant attestation is in Karl Hess's 1969 article “The Death of Politics”.

s: A type of bread dough leavened with yeast and lactobacilli that produce acids giving a sour taste.
A permanent resident of the territory. Someone who has lived in the Yukon during all four seasons.
A 49er, a California Gold Rush miner.
Leaven; an agent that makes dough rise.
e: From Middle English sour dogh, equivalent to sour + dough. Compare Suurdee (“sourdough”), Dutch zuurdeeg (“sourdough”), Low German Suurdeeg (“sourdough”), German Sauerteig (“sourdough”), Danish surdej (“sourdough”), Swedish surdeg (“sourdough”), Icelandic súrdeig (“sourdough”).

s: A shooting from a concealed place.
A miserly person; a person with an excessive dislike of spending money or other resources.
A grinch; one who dislikes the Christmas holidays.
To behave in a greedy or miserly way.
To crush or press; to squeeze (past, into, together, etc.).
e: From the character Ebenezer Scrooge in the Charles Dickens' novel A Christmas Carol.

s: A male vassal (subject of a sovereign or lord).
e: From Middle English lege man; equivalent to liege + -man.

s: The stagnant water that collects in a ditch.
e: From Middle English dich water,dyche water, equivalent to ditch + water.
From Latin reprehendō (“I hold back, check, blame”), from re- (“back”) + prehendō (“I hold, seize”). Compare French reprendre (“to reprove”).

s: A bag used for carrying post (mail).
To reduce (an adult) to the state or status of an infant.
To treat (an adult) like a child.

e: From Middle English drerinesse, drerynesse, from Old English drēoriġnys (“dreariness, sadness”), equivalent to dreary + -ness.

From Latin incūriōsus (“careless”), from in- (“un-”) and cūriōsus (“careful”). Attested since the 1560s, originally meaning ‘heedless and negligent.’ The sense of ‘uninquisitive’ dates from the 1610s, and the sense of ‘unworthy of attention’ from 1747.

s: In a way that cripples, or is crippling.
Not given the appropriate tools to deal with a situation.
Of or pertaining to the reign of a monarch (or pope).
Describing the year of a monarch's reign starting from the date of accession.
Pertaining to a taxon at the rank of regnum (or kingdom).
An officer responsible for the care and supervision of the horses of a person of rank.
A personal attendant to a head of state, a member of a royal family, or a national representative.
e: From an alteration of earlier esquiry (through the influence of the unrelated Latin equus), from Middle French escuirie, escuerie, derivative of escuyer (“squire”), or alternatively from Medieval Latin scuria (“stable”), from Old High German scura (“barn”). Compare esquire.
From the Latin superannuatus (“more than one year old”), from super (“over”) (English super-) + annus (“year”) (English annual).

s: Addicted to censure and scolding; apt to blame or condemn; severe in making remarks on others, or on their writings or manners.
Tending to engage in or support censorship.
e: From Latin cēnsōrius (“of or pertaining to a censor; severe”). In ("tending to engage in or support censorship"), reanalyzed as censor + -ious.

s: In an unprecedented manner; without precedent.
Like a statesman, demonstrating the skills and qualities of a respected leader.
An unhappy state of mental or physical suffering.
A state of prolonged misfortune, privation or anguish.
A traitor who collaborates with the enemy.
e: From Quislinus, Latinization of Quislin, based on the Danish place name Kvislemark. This term first appeared in 1940. The surname is seemingly supposed to mean "one who is from Kvislemark", and is equivalent to Kvislemark + -ing.

s: In a manner exhibiting skill at handling situations, particularly difficult situations.
The condition of being vindictive; a malevolent desire for revenge.
Without asking questions or having doubts. With complete obedience and without making any opposition.

e: From Middle English inconstant, inconstante, inconstaunte, from Middle French inconstant and its etymon, Latin incōnstāns.

s: A region ruled by a duke or duchess.
The rank or title of a duke.
e: From late Middle English dukdom, dukedom; equivalent to duke + -dom.

s: A thick, juicy cut from the center of a beef tenderloin.
e: Borrowed from French chateaubriand, Named after François-René de Chateaubriand, who is said to have enjoyed this type of steak.

s: Unbearded (not having a beard or other facial hair).
Unmasked (not wearing a mask) or not wearing a face covering.
Not wearing makeup on the face.
e: Perhaps an alteration of barefast (compare shamefast); or from bare + faced. Compare typologically cheeky; Italian sfacciato (ex- + faciēs); French effronté, Italian sfrontato (ex- + frōns), Polish czelny (czoło).

s: Uneasy with desire; itching; especially, having a lascivious anxiety or propensity; lustful.
Arousing or appealing to sexual desire.
The quality of being magnanimous; kindness of nature; generosity.
e: From Middle French magnanimité, from Old French, from Latin magnanimitās.

s: Not having been coated with varnish.
Made for, fit for sailing on, or used on the high seas.
Difficult, undesirable, or unpleasant; not to be envied.
Lack of permanence or continued duration.
The quality or state of being impermanent.
Anicca, the doctrine which asserts that all of conditioned existence is transient.
A gradual healing after illness or injury.
The period of time spent healing.
e: Borrowed from Middle French convalescence, from Late Latin convalēscentia (“regaining of health”), from Latin convalēscēn(t-)s, present participle of convalēscere (“to become strong or well”); see convalesce.

s: Characteristic of or relating to a narrow-minded concern with the morals of others; self-righteous
The act by which somebody or something is cherished.
A supporter of, or believer in, monarchy.
Beyond alteration, criticism, or interference, especially due to religious sanction; inviolable.
Without the use of matches for ignition.
e: From match + -less, modelled after or partly continuing Middle English makeless (“having no peer or equal, matchless”), equivalent to make + -less. Compare Swedish makalös (“incomparable, matchless”), Danish mageløs (“matchless”).

s: To give or leave by will; to give by testament.
To give; to offer; to commit.
e: From Middle English biquethen, from Old English becweþan (“to say, to speak, to address, exhort, admonish, blame, bequeath, leave by will”). Cognate with Old Frisian biquetha.

s: The act of investing, as with possession or power; formal bestowal or presentation of a possessory or prescriptive right.
The formal installation or, generally, the appointment of a bishop, or bishops in general.
That which invests or clothes; covering; vestment.
The parliamentary vote required to inaugurate the Prime Minister of Spain.
e: From Middle French investiture, from Medieval Latin investītūra, from investīre (“to clothe”).

s: A piece of currency made of paper or polymer.
A promissory note issued by a bank, payable at a given time to a specific beneficiary.
To agree or assent; to give way.
To come to an office, state or dignity; to attain, assume (a position).
To become a party to an agreement or a treaty.
To approach; to arrive, to come forward.
To give one's adhesion; to join up with (a group, etc.); to become part of.
e: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English acceden, from Latin accēdō (“approach, accede”), formed from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”) (English cede). Compare French accéder. Unrelated to ascend, aside from the common ad prefix.

s: An act of supplicating; a humble request.
du'a', minor or private prayer performed individually.
A prayer or entreaty to a god.
In Ancient Rome, a solemn service or day decreed for giving formal thanks to the gods for victory, etc.
The process by which a doctorate at Oxford university is officially requested after a thesis has been approved.
e: From Middle English supplicacioun, supplication, from Old French supplication, from Latin supplicatio, supplicationem, from supplicare (“to supplicate”). supplicate + -ion.

s: Beyond compare, far surpassing any other, unparalleled, without rival.
Not deemed to have any value, valueless, worthless, not appreciated.
In a manner that is incapable of being disputed or argued against.
Not in keeping with the expected standards of one's position.
The process by which something unbecomes.
e: From un- + becoming. Compare Middle English unbicomelich (“unbecoming”). Equal to unbecome + -ing.

s: The act of contravening (a rule, regulation, law, or order) or of not fulfilling (an obligation, promise, or agreement).
More interested in individual people than in society as a whole.
Interested in oneself rather than others; egocentric.
The dignity, rank or office of a king; the state of being a king.
The territory or dominion of a king; a kingdom.
The quality or state of being incompatible; inconsistency; irreconcilability.
Weakened or worn out from age or wear.
e: From Middle English decrepyt (ante 1439), from Middle French décrépit, from Latin dēcrepitus (“very old”), from crepō (“to creak”).

s: The quality of being exuberant; cheerful or vigorous enthusiasm; liveliness.
Of or related to royalists or some royalist faction.
A monarchist (supporter of monarchy) or supporter of a particular royal régime.

A legitimist, a supporter of a particular royal line, especially one in danger of being dispossessed of a throne or actually dispossessed of such, and claiming to have the better claim to the throne on the basis of line of descent; especially
a Cavalier, a supporter of King Charles I of England during the English Civil War.
a supporter of the House of Bourbon, in France since the 18th century and especially during the French Revolution.
a supporter of Ferdinand VII of Spain in Spanish South America during the South American Wars of Independence of the 1810s and 1820s.
Causing a deprivation of courage, strength, confidence, etc.
Lacking experience due to lack of challenges; untested.
A person employed in one of several aviation-adjacent professions other than flight crew, such as a mechanic or air traffic controller.
A member of an air force.
A person of a rank in the U.S. Air Force above airman basic and below airman first class.
A naval seaman, especially one in the U.S. Navy, who works on and/or handles aircraft.
Easily approached; easy to talk to.
The act of something that sags.
A manner of wearing pants or shorts below the waist, revealing some or all of the underwear.
Worn low on the waist, or wearing pants or shorts low on the waist.
In full through line of action: a theme that runs through the plot of a book, film, or other narrative work, or a series of such related works.
A railway route that passengers can take without needing to change trains.
e: From through (“passing from one side of something to the other”) + line. Compare Middle English thurghline (“a brail or buntline”).

s: An arrangement of strands or plies.
Utterly consuming one's time and attention.
The act of one who engrosses, or buys up wholesale.
Emitted outwards from a centre like rays.
Having been exposed to radiation (as for example by imaging, food-safety sterilization, or a nuclear blast).
A slightly ovoid, orange-coloured citrus fruit with a rough peel and a sour-sweet taste which is larger than a clementine and sometimes classed as a variety of mandarin orange.
A deep yellowish-orange colour, like that of a tangerine fruit.
Of, pertaining to, or employing chemiluminescence
A political theory based on the idea of a social contract between a ruler and their subjects.
The characteristic of being dope (great, extraordinary).
Agent noun of hump: one who humps.
An exclusive focus on a particular area, group, sect, etc.
The principle that only certain people are chosen by God for salvation.
The principle that individual states, races of a federation, etc., may act independently of a central authority.
The normative ethical theory that the morality of an action is based on whether the action follows certain obligations or rules, rather than on its inherent goodness, consequences, etc.
To dissociate atoms or molecules into electrically charged species; to be thus dissociated.
Possessing excessive vanity or unwarranted pride.
e: From Middle English veinglorious, from Old French vain glorios, from Latin vānus (“empty”) + glōriōsus.
Back-formation from triceps. In Latin, triceps is both singular and plural.

s: To play guitar (especially the electric guitar) quickly.
One who destroys religious images or icons, especially an opponent of the Orthodox Church in the 8th and 9th centuries, or a Puritan during the European Reformation.
One who opposes orthodoxy and religion; one who adheres to the doctrine of iconoclasm.
One who attacks cherished beliefs; a maverick.
e: Borrowed from French iconoclaste and its etymon Medieval Latin īconoclastēs, from Byzantine Greek εἰκονοκλάστης. icono- + -clast.

s: One who is not a friend; an enemy.
To defriend; to remove from one's friends list (e.g. on a social networking website).
e: From Middle English unfreend, onfrend, equivalent to un- + friend. Cognate with Scots unfrend (“unfriend”). Compare Old English unfriþmann, unwine.
From un- + friend. Compare Dutch ontvrienden (“to unfriend”), German entfreunden (“to unfriend”).

s: A small agile dinosaur, of the genus Velociraptor, having sickle-shaped claws. It is also thought to have had a feathered coat. Fossils have been found in Late Cretaceous deposits in Mongolia and China (around 75-71 mya).
e: From Velociraptor genus name, from vēlōx (“swift”) + raptor (“thief”). The application to Deinonychus came about because Gregory S. Paul proposed that Velociraptor and Deinonychus were the same genus and this idea was taken up in the book leading to the Jurassic Park film series.

In Scots, dookie, doukit, and douker (terms related to the British English duck, equivalent to the American English dunk) have all been used to refer to Baptists. Hence a dookie in Scots is, jocularly, someone who ducks or dunks people in water when baptising them.
Probably clipping of doo-doo -kie, later repopularized by the 1989 film No Holds Barred and later still the 1994 Green Day album Dookie.

s: Doctrine of preordination; doctrine of absolute decrees; doctrine that God acts in an absolute manner.
The principles or practice of absolute or arbitrary government; Synonym of despotism.
Belief in a metaphysical absolute; belief in Absolute.
Positiveness; the state of being absolute.
The characteristic of being absolute in nature or scope; absoluteness.
e: First attested in 1753 (in the theological sense); attested in 1830 in the political sense. From absolute + -ism, based after French absolutisme.

s: A device or person that applies caps, as to bullets or bottles.
A person that makes or sells caps.
A finale; something that is conclusively better, or "caps it all off".
A by-bidder; a decoy for gamblers.
A person who records a television broadcast or video stream to their computer.
A person who caps i.e. is inclined to untruth, a fibber.
Used three times in a row, or in combination with other words, to indicate part of a sentence which would be annoying to include, or which is incomprehensible, or which is just unimportant.
One of a set of items which do not need to be specified; often used in conjunction with the catch phrase yadda yadda yadda.
The sport of gliding with a paraglider.
The use of a paraglider in other settings, such as surveillance or military applications.
A concise expression of a principle in an area of knowledge; an axiom, a precept.
A concise or pithy, and memorable, expression of a general truth; a maxim, a saying.
The essence or heart of something.
To speak or write one or more aphorisms.
A system of ethics based on the premise that something's value may be measured by its usefulness.
The theory that action should be directed toward achieving the "greatest happiness for the greatest number of people" (hedonistic universalism), or one of various related theories.
Practicality, functionality, as opposed to e.g. aesthetics.
Not human; not of the human race.
A creature or thing that is not human.
In a concise manner, briefly, without excessive length.
Of or relating to the characteristics of an encyclopedia; concerning all subjects, having comprehensive information or knowledge.

Relating to or containing descriptive information rather than only linguistic or lexical information; about facts and concepts, and not only a word or term; including proper names, biographical and geographical information and illustrations.
The remote-control device used to change settings on a television set, VCR, or other electronic equipment.
An electronic device used by individual students in the classroom to respond to multiple-choice questions, etc.
A person who cuts out the uppers of shoes from pieces of leather using a flexible knife that clicks as it changes direction.
A machine that cuts materials using a steel rule die. The name comes from the sound (click) when the material is cut. May be hand, pneumatic, or hydraulic powered.
A signalling device used by military forces. Pressed between thumb and fingers, it makes a small but distinctive click understood by other members of a unit.
A small mechanical device that produces a clicking sound, used in dog training.
Someone who clicks, for example using a computer mouse.
Someone who stands by a shop door to invite people to buy; a tout.
One who has charge of the work of a companionship.
An employee who locks the type in the form to make it ready for printing.
Drugs of the alkyl nitrate class used recreationally as a sexual stimulant, especially among gay men.
e: Amyl nitrites were originally sold in small glass ampoules wrapped in cloth. Recreational users would crush or "pop" these vials between their fingers to release their vapours, which is thought to be the origin of the slang term.

s: The condition of being hot, heat.
e: From Middle English hotnes, from Old English hātnes (“hotness, heat”), equivalent to hot + -ness.

s: Having the characteristics of a god.
A plant in the genus Salvia, such as sage.
Salvia divinorum, a plant used for its hallucinogenic properties; diviner's sage.
e: Borrowed from Salvia, in turn from Latin salvia (“sage”). Doublet of sage.

s: The bone of the lower jaw; the mandible.
Any of the bones in the lower or upper jaw.
A shaken musical instrument (an idiophone) made from the jawbone of an animal and shaken such that the teeth vibrate in their sockets to produce sound.
To talk persistently in an attempt to persuade somebody to cooperate.
To try to persuade (someone) through implied threats of punitive action, such as tighter regulatory control.
e: From Middle English jawe bone, a partial calque of earlier Middle English chawlbone, chawylbon, chavylbone, chawle boon, chavyl bon (“jaw bone”), see chavel-bone; equivalent to jaw + bone.
From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).

s: Dead branches or wood on a tree, or coarse woody debris.
People or things judged to be superfluous to an organization or project.
Money not realized by exiting a winning pump trade too early.
Pins that have fallen and have not been cleared from the alley.
Vertical planks between the keel and the sternpost that act as reinforcement.
Structural material on a load-carrying vehicle that reduces the available cargo space.
Cards in a hand that do not contribute to sets and which are usually counted as points against the player holding the hand.
The breastbone, consisting of the manubrium, gladiolus, and xiphoid process.
The sclerotized ventral plate of spiders, between the coxae, marking the floor of the cephalothorax.
e: Learned borrowing from New Latin sternum Cognate with Old English steorn (“forehead”).

s: That cannot be admitted as evidence at a trial.
of an assertion, point, fact, etc
Who cannot be allowed to enter a place or event.
A person who is not to be admitted (to a country, a group, etc).
e: Borrowed from French inadmissible, from Middle French inadmissible, from in-, admissible.

s: Conflict or hostility or an instance of such that stands in contrast to expected friendliness or interest.
Indifference or an instance of indifference; lack of friendliness or interest not necessarily rising to hostility.
Social advantage or enviability, typically due to traits like popularity, confidence, skill, or fashion.
e: From Middle English colnes, colnesse, from Old English cōlnes, cœ̄lnes, cēlnes (“coolness; cool air, breeze”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlinassī, equivalent to cool + -ness. Cognate with Middle High German kuolnisse, küelnisse (“cooling, coolness”).

s: In a ruthless manner; with cruelty; without pity or compassion.
Done after the fact; applying to events that have previously transpired.
Very cheery and peppy; extremely cheerful, energetic and enthusiastic.
Unusually proliferative, widespread or extreme, particularly in relation to a disease, immune reaction, or tissue
e: From Middle French exubérant, from Latin exūberāns, the present active participle of exūberō (“be abundant”). Put together from ex (“out”), and uber (“udder”), and originally would have referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

s: The characteristic or property of being imperishable.
The chief advisor of the oyabun in the yakuza.
e: From the Japanese yakuza hierarchy. Borrowed from Japanese 最古顧問, literally “senior advisor”.

s: A renewal of a commitment, or an act of recommitting
One hundredth of the former German mark (Deutsche Mark).
A hollow six-pointed star formed by overlapping two equilateral triangles.
Any of the 64 sets of solid and broken lines, formed by pairs of trigrams, used for divination in the I Ching.
A large silvern coin minted during the Byzantine Empire.
Superlative of inner; the very deepest within; farthest from the surface or external part.
That which is inmost; the core.
e: From Middle English inmost, from Old English innemest, a double superlative form from inne (“within”), from in (“in”). The modern form is due to confusion with most.

s: A poisonous alkaloid C17H21NO4 similar to atropine that is found in various solanaceous plants and is used for its anticholinergic effects (such as preventing nausea in motion sickness and inducing mydriasis).
e: Borrowed from German Skopolamin, from Scopolia (“genus of plants”) + Amin (“amine”).

s: The act of aggrandizing, or the state of being aggrandized or exalted in power, rank, honor, or wealth; exaltation; enlargement.
The state or quality of being decisive.

A traditional Japanese confection; most have an outside made from flour, rice powder, kudzu, and buckwheat, and a filling of red bean paste, usually made from boiled azuki beans and sugar; in Hawaii, Okinawan ones are made with a filling of purple sweet potato, butter, milk, sugar, and salt, but the
e: From Japanese 饅頭, from Chinese 饅頭. Doublet of mandu, manti, mantou.

s: The act of educating again or anew so as to rehabilitate or adapt to new situations.
from the perspective of a japanese person
e: Borrowed from Japanese 外人 (“foreigner”), from 外人. Compare Mandarin 外人, from 外人 (“foreigner, outsider” 外 (“outside, outer”) + 人 (“person”).

s: The act by which something is flouted.
Plural of counterattack; Alternative spelling of counter-attacks.
Infl of counterattack; Alternative spelling of counter-attacks.
A form of ritual suicide by disembowelment using a blade, practiced by Japanese samurai, especially to rid oneself of shame, as a means of protest, or, formerly, as a method of capital punishment.
e: Borrowed from Japanese 切腹, from 切 (“to cut”) + 腹 (“belly”). Compare Cantonese 切腹 and Mandarin 切腹.

s: and disappointed, especially by the loss of a beloved person or thing, such as the end of a romantic relationship.
A cry or cheer of enthusiasm, or to celebrate victory.
A cry or cheer of "banzai", to express enthusiasm or celebrate victory.
To carry out a banzai charge (against).
e: From Japanese, from 萬歲, from 萬歲 (“10,000 years [of life]”, i.e. “immortality”), from 萬 (“10,000”) 歲 (“year (of age)”). Compare Mandarin.

s: Historical quality or authenticity based on fact.
The characteristic of having appeared or developed in history, as opposed to being natural or universal.
e: Probably from French historicité, or from historicus + -ity. Equivalent to historic + -ity.

s: A short film containing news or current affairs; especially one of several shown in sequence.
A fast military offensive, typically involving a large and highly mobile tank force with air support.
Made into, or to serve as, a weapon.
Separated from others of the same kind.
Separate from a mass and collected together along lines of fraction.
In particular, to separate and organize by characteristics.
To separate (races, sexes, or other groups, especially black and white people), especially by social policies that directly or indirectly keep them apart.
An entity that is separated in some way from a reference group or entity.
e: From Latin sēgregātus, perfect passive participle of sēgregō (“to separate”), from sē- (“apart”) + gregō (“to flock or group”), from grex (“flock”). Compare gregarious, aggregate.

s: Something fit to be imitated; an ideal, a worthy model or role model: a desirable example.
Something typical or representative; an example that typifies its class.
A pattern after which others should be made; an archetype.
A well-known use of a scientific theory.
A manuscript used by a scribe to make a handwritten copy; the original document to be reproduced in a copy machine.
A copy of a book or piece of writing.
e: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplair, and its source, Latin exemplar, from Latin exemplum (“example”).
From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplaire, and its source, Latin exemplāris. example + -ar. Doublet of exemplary.

s: Having a mutual or reciprocal relation or parallelism; correlative.
A continuous roll of film containing photographs of documents at a greatly reduced size.
Without peer or equal; unparalleled, nonpareil. Of the highest quality, best.

The science of objects that predominantly fly under the effects of gravity, momentum and atmospheric drag, and dealing with details of their behaviour at the origin and destination of their flight, as of bullets or missiles or rockets.
e: From la-new:ballistica + -s, use as noun of feminine of ballisticus (“ballistic”). Compare later ballistic and French balistique. ballista + -ics or ballistic + -s.
From effect + -ing. The adjective likely follows from the verb, perhaps with influence from effective, affecting, or both.

s: The study of good citizenship and proper membership in a community.
e: From Latin civicus (“having to do with citizens or a town or city”).

s: Verbal noun of rename: An act in which something is renamed.
A hundred-millionth (10) of a bitcoin; the same as 10 nanocoins (nBTC) or 10 BTC.
e: Named after Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous designer of Bitcoin, from Japanese さとし, nominalization of the classical adjective 聡し, modern 聡い (“clever, smart, sharp”).

s: The act or an instance of eliminating contamination: a purification, a cleansing, particularly
The cleansing of a device by flushing it with water, steam, or some other liquid or gas.
The removal of waste from the human body, particularly
The removal of excess humors through bloodletting, induced vomiting, etc.
The removal of digested waste: defecation; defecation induced by laxatives.
That which is purged: contamination, a contaminant; refuse; sin; etc.
Synonym of purgation: the act or an instance of removing guilt or suspicion of a misdeed.
The process in which acne temporarily worsened due to the introduction of skincare products that increase cell turnover, bringing underlying acne to the surface more quickly.

A social philosophy or practice which advocates the improvement of human hereditary qualities through selective breeding, either by encouraging people with superior genetic qualities to reproduce (positive eugenics), or discouraging people with inferior genetic qualities from reproducing (negative e
