A circular platform allowing a board game to be rotated to face each player.
To play (a record) using a turntable.
To rotate or turn around using, or as if using, a turntable.
To manipulate sound using turntables; to perform turntablism; to scratch
An inn or hotel in a Spanish-speaking country.
e: From Spanish fonda, from Arabic فُنْدُق (“inn, hotel; manor”), from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον, from πᾰν- (“all, every”) + the combining form of δέχεσθαι (“to receive”) + -εῖον (“-ium: forming building names”). Doublet of fonduk, fondaco.

s: A drink made of wine, often port, mixed with hot water, oranges or lemons, spices and sugar.
A ruler of Abyssinia (Ethiopia), or of a province of Ethiopia; specifically, the king of Ethiopia before 1974.
e: Named after Colonel Francis Negus, its creator.
Fitst use appears c. the 1590s, borrowed from ንጉሥ (“king, ruler”), itself a loan from ንጉሥ (“king, ruler”), from the verb ነግሠ (“rule”).

s: A striped variety of hornfels, resembling wood in appearance.
A small-diameter tree branch or limb that extends out of the water in flooded or submerged timber, as in a lake or river.
A wing collar with white bow tie, worn with school dress by distinguished senior boys at Eton College.
A smooth-textured Italian pork sausage with lumps of fat, flavoured with spices; eaten cold.
e: From Italian mortadella, from diminutive of Latin murtatum (“sausage seasoned with myrtle berries”), from myrtatum, from myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος.

s: Someone who purports to rid a place of ghosts.
e: From ghost + buster, popularized by the 1984 film Ghostbusters.

s: Engaging in economic production or distribution in an illegal way.
The activity of making, transporting and/or selling illegal alcoholic liquor.
The activity of making, transporting and/or selling an illegal version or copy of a copyrighted product.
The activity of operating a mine illicitly.
To design and record the choreography for a dramatic work such as a ballet.
To direct the development of a project; to orchestrate.
The act of making somebody a scapegoat.
Used as a call for coordinated physical effort, as in hoisting.
Used as a cheer indicating exaltation, enjoyment, or approval.
A cheer often associated with sailors, shouted by a group in praise of a thing or event.
To cheer (someone or something) with a huzzah sound.
e: Likely originally a hoisting cry, possibly related to hoise. Compare possibly to the cognate Swedish hissa (“to hoist; huzzah”), Spanish izar (“to hoist”) and French Ho, hisse! (“Hey, hoist!”)..

s: To resume something that has been convened and then paused.
Held in place by strips of lead.
Containing or treated with the element lead.
Infl of lead (to add lead to)
Infl of lead (to guide, plus similar meanings)
A vehicle, often on tracks, used to dig ditches etc.
A curette used to scrape out pathological material.
Characterized by spots (used especially of animals and plants); dappled.
A mischievous elf supposed sometimes to take the form of a hedgehog.
A street urchin, a child who lives, or spends most of their time, in the streets.
One of a pair in a series of small card cylinders arranged around a carding drum; so called from its fancied resemblance to the hedgehog.
A neutron-generating device that triggered the nuclear detonation of the earliest plutonium atomic bombs.
e: From Middle English yrchoun, irchoun (“hedgehog; sea urchin”), from irechon, from Vulgar Latin *ērīciōnem, from Latin ērīcius. Compare modern French hérisson, whence the English doublet Doublet of herisson.

s: Powdered spice made from dried and ground fruits of sweet pepper (bell pepper) or chili pepper (cultivars of Capsicum annuum), or mixtures of these (used especially in Hungarian cooking).
A dried but not yet ground fruit of sweet pepper (bell pepper) or chili pepper sold for use as a spice.
A bright reddish orange colour resembling that of the ground spice.
Of a bright reddish orange colour, like that of the dried paprika.
e: Borrowed from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian pàprika, from pȁpar, from *pьpьrь, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (“pepper”), from; compare Sanskrit पिप्पली (“long pepper”). Akin to paprikash.

s: A system of national government in which power is divided between a central authority and a number of regions with delimited self-governing authority.
The belief that such a system is superior to other forms of government.
One who removes dirt or debris off of the front end of an aircraft, car, or other vehicle (referred to as the nose).
An act of handing out something.
An act of dealing playing cards; a deal.
A printed sheet such as a leaflet or pamphlet, or a worksheet, that is given out free of charge (usually by hand) for a certain use, for example as an advertisement or for information.
A gift of money or material assistance to the needy or poor.
Something obtained without effort; a gift, a present.
Of a thing: given out free of charge, usually by hand.
Of or pertaining to the giving of handouts (gifts of money or material assistance, printed sheets, etc.).
Any of several massive, herbivorous sauropod dinosaurs, of the genus Brachiosaurus, from the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.
A large toothless pterosaur of the genus Quetzalcoatlus.
Any of the extinct clade †Sauropoda of long-necked dinosaurs which walked on four thick, pillar-like legs.
A sedimentary deposit, especially in urine.
The essential person, specifically the single person of Christ (as distinguished from his ‘nature(s)’, human and divine), or of the three ‘persons’ of the Trinity (sharing a single ‘essence’).
The underlying reality or substance of something.
A relationship between a name and a known quantity, as a cultural personification (i.e. objectification with personality) of an entity or quality.

Referring to the hypostatic model of personality; i.e., asserting that humans present themselves in many different aspects or hypostases, depending on the internal and external realities they relate to, including different approaches to the study of personality.
The effect of one gene preventing another from expressing.
e: From Ecclesiastical Latin hypostasis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόστασις (“sediment, foundation; substance, existence, essence”), from ὑπό (“under”) + στάσις (“standing”). Morphologically hypo + stasis.

s: Any flying reptile, of the extinct order †Pterosauria, including the pterodactyls.
e: From ptero- + -saur, from Ancient Greek πτερόν (“feather, wing”) and σαῦρος (“lizard, reptile”).

s: A large, extinct, carnivorous dinosaur of genus †Spinosaurus, with a long snout like that of a crocodile and with a sail on its back. It is considered to be the largest theropod dinosaur.
Any interaction between two species that benefits both; typically involves the exchange of substances or services.

An economic theory and anarchist school of thought that advocates a society where each person might possess a means of production, either individually or collectively, with trade representing equivalent amounts of labor in the free market.
The psychometric theory that general intelligence emerges from the interaction between specific cognitive abilities.
e: From mutual + -ism. Compare French mutualisme and Italian, Portuguese and Spanish mutualismo.

s: In a state of fossilization; preserved in rock.
Old-fashioned, outmoded, or rigidly fixed in a way that is resistant to change.
Having become a fossil; no longer productive.
A relationship of mutual benefit, especially among different species.
The close and long-term relationship or interaction between two or more different species.
The close and long-term relationship or interaction between two or more different species in which all organisms benefit; mutualism.
The state of people of different types, races, cultures, communities, etc., living together.
The occurrence of two different or opposing things in the same time and place.
Having wanes, i.e. rounded corners caused by lack of wood, often showing bark.

The iron-containing substance in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body; it consists of a protein (globulin), and haem (a porphyrin ring with an atom of iron at its centre).
e: Originally hematinoglobulin, from hematin (from Ancient Greek αἷμα (“blood”) + -in) + -o- + globulin (from Latin globus (“ball, sphere”) + -in).

s: A black (African or African-American or an Aboriginal Australian) person.
e: From spear + chucker, in the offensive sense, alluding to a stereotype of Africans as primitive savages who use spears in hunting and war.

s: The state or quality of being snotty.
The condition of being excessively acidic
A specially shaped nut used to hold the wheels on an automobile.
A person who has a fondness or appreciation for wine.
Any cod, pollock, haddock, or other whitefish.
e: One theory derives it from scrawed, past participle of Cornwall dialect scraw (“to split and dry fish”), but the further origin of this word seems not to have been traced.

s: A spread that goes on a bagel.
A batch of things that go together.
To spread something, often a bagel spread.
e: Borrowed from Yiddish שמיר (“smear, spread”); compare German schmieren. Doublet of smear, smearcase. schm- + smear. The sense is from Yiddish שמירן, senses found also in German schmieren. The implication is that a bribe helps “lubricate” an interaction.

s: Like a pig, resembling a swine; gluttonous, coarse, debased.
A container for storing bread and other baked goods to keep them fresh.
Having no sensation or consciousness; unconscious; inanimate.
Not responsive to sensory stimuli; unfeeling.
To render insensate; to deprive of sensation or consciousness.
e: From the substantivation of the above adjective. See -ate.

s: The state or quality of being angry and obstinate.
The state or quality of being poorly-ventilated and close.
The result or product of being stuffy.
The amount that fills a bag.
e: From Middle English bage-ful, bage full, baggeful, bagg-ful; equivalent to bag + -ful.

s: Mixed with water so that a true chemical combination has taken place.
Underwear, especially men's underwear and especially men's underpants.
To laugh or giggle in a somewhat subdued or restrained way, as from nervousness or poorly-suppressed amusement.
A nervous or somewhat repressed giggle.
e: First attested in the 1610s. Probably from Middle English *titeren, *titren (attested in Middle English titering (“hesitation, vacillation”)), probably a frequentative of Middle English titten (“to waver”), ultimately of Onomatopoeic origin. Related to Old Norse titra (“to shake, shiver, quiver”) (if not borrowed from it), dialectal Swedish tittra (“to snicker”).

s: Active at or around dusk, dawn or twilight.
A recording of electrical brain activity (brain waves) made by an electroencephalograph.
Frivolous and silly; featherbrained or scatterbrained; stupid.
One who tattles (reports others' wrongdoings), often a child seeking attention.
One who gossips, often for the sake of attention.
To act as a tattletale; to tell on; to give away, reveal, or expose.
The act or process of vomiting.
e: From Ancient Greek ἔμεσις, from ἐμέω (“vomit”). Compare ἔμετος (“vomit”)., suffixed with -esis.

s: Of or pertaining to hermaphrodism; being a hermaphrodite.
Possessing the reproductive organs of both sexes.
Relating to the metaphysical integration of two complementary principles, often framed as masculine and feminine, active and receptive, solar and lunar, force and form, etc.
Of, related to, or having both male and female connectability for fastening.

e: From Yiddish דרעק (“dirt, crap”), from Middle High German drek, from Old High German *threc (in mūsthrec), from Proto-West Germanic *þraki, from Proto-Germanic *þrakjaz. Compare drèkh (“excrement, manure”), Dutch drek (“dung; semi-liquid filth; mud”), German Dreck (“dirt; filth”), Latin stercus (“dung, manure”).

s: The relative likelihood of something or someone to grant permission or allow something to happen.
Originally, a cask with a hole cut into its top, used to provide drinking water on board a ship; now, a drinking fountain on a modern ship.
To spread (information) by way of gossip or rumour.
To chat idly or gossip; also, to spread rumours.
e: The noun is derived from scuttle#Etymology_2 (“to cut a hole through (something)”) + butt#Etymology_3 (“wooden cask”). (“gossip, idle chatter; rumour”) refers to the fact that sailors would gather around the scuttlebutt to drink and exchange gossip; compare furphy and water cooler. The verb is derived from the noun.

s: To make a line of holes in (a thin material) to allow separation at the line.
e: The adjective is, in Middle English, the verb in 1538; from Middle English perforat(e) (“perforated, pierced”), borrowed from Latin perforātus, the perfect passive participle of perforō (“to bore or pierce through, to perforate”) (see -ate and -ate), from per- (“through, thorough”) + forō (“to bore, pierce”).

s: The state or characteristic of drunkenness.
A magnetic tape that stores analog sound for later playback on a tape player.
Any of a cassette tape, 8-track tape, reel-to-reel tape, DAT, etc.
The surgical removal of the tonsils, especially the palatine tonsils. Frequently accompanied by an adenoidectomy.
Having characteristics of a human, usually in terms of shape or appearance.
Of the pelvis, having an anteroposterior diameter equal or exceeding the transverse diameter.
Having a tendency to argue or fight; aggressive, combative.
A recreational ride in a vehicle full of hay.
A jot or tittle; the smallest amount.
A strong, pressurized, heated vessel, as for laboratory experiments, sterilization, cooking or mineral processing.
To sterilize laboratory equipment in an autoclave.
e: Borrowed from French autoclave, formed with prefix auto- + Latin clavis (“key”).

s: An enlisted person in the U.S. Army who works as a field medic.
The quality of being callous; emotional hardheartedness or indifference.
Pursuing pleasure, especially in reference to food or comfort.
One who is devoted to pleasure.
A river steamboat having a resident theatre.
A person, often an athlete or performer, who behaves in an ostentatious, flashy manner to attract attention or admiration; a showoff.
The act by which something is thumbed.
A person who suffers from amnesia.
To lay (the mizzen) aback by bringing the sheet to the mizzen rigging.
To masturbate a person's penis in one's armpit.
Any tree or shrub of the dogwood subgenera, Cornus subg. Arctocrania (syn. Cornus subg. Chamaepericlymenum) or Cornus subg. Cornus, especially Cornus mas, the European cornel.
The cherry-like fruit of such plants, certain of which are edible.
e: From Middle English corneille, borrowed from Middle French corneille, from Vulgar Latin *cornicula, from Latin cornus (“the European cornel”).

s: An excessive or unwarranted degree of confidence.
A defect in which a testpiece is deformed into a barrel-like shape.
Made thrice as much; threefold; tripled.
The making of three identical copies of something.
Each of a set of three identical objects or copies.
To make three identical copies of something.
e: Early 15th century. From Latin triplicātus, perfect passive participle of triplicō (“to triple”) (see -ate), from tri- (“three”) + plicō (“to fold”). tri- (“three”) + plicate, analogous with duplicate.

s: Charming, engaging, winning; inspiring approval and trust, especially if in an innocent manner.
e: Inherited from Middle English wynsom, winsom, winsome, winsum, wunsum (“beautiful; agreeable, gracious, pleasant; generous; of situations: favourable, propitious”), from Old English wynsum (“joyful, merry, pleasant; winsome”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunnjusam (“joyful”). winne (“delight, joy, pleasure”) + -some.

s: That is pleasing to the sense of taste; appetizing.
Of, relating to, affecting or within the colon.
Syn of colon cleansing (the removal of nonspecific toxins from the colon and intestinal tract considered pseudomedicine)
A feeling of long-lasting ire for another, sometimes to the point of hatred, over a perceived wrongdoing; bitterness.
e: First attested in the 13th century as Middle English rancour, from Old French rancor, from Latin rancor (“rancidity, grudge, rancor”), from ranceō (“to be rotten or putrid”), from which also English rancid.

s: Treating serious issues with (often deliberately) inappropriate humour; flippant.
(Of an idea or statement) humorously silly or counterproductive for the purpose of sarcastically advocating the opposite.
e: From French facétieux, from Latin facētia (“jest, wit, humor”), from facētus (“witty, jocose, facetious”).

s: Taking care when choosing that what is chosen best suits one's tastes, desires or requirements.
A portable, bidirectional radio transceiver, usually one of a pair.
reaching from the top of the head down the side of the face to the side of the chin.
e: Reformed from burnside, Named after Ambrose Burnside, noted for his unusual facial hair.

s: or lacking in social graces; bumbling; apt to make gaffes.
e: Borrowed from French gauche (“left, awkward”), from gauchir (“to veer, turn”), from Old French gaucher (“to trample, walk clumsily”), from Frankish *walkan (“to full, trample”), from Proto-Germanic *walkaną (“to full, roll up”).

s: spanked with a paddle, e.g. in corporal punishment.
A young female cow, (particularly) one over one year old but which has not calved.
e: Inherited from Middle English heyfre, hayfre, heyfer, from Old English hēahfore, hēahfru, of disputed origin; see the Old English entry for more discussion.

s: The motion of something that wiggles.
A primitive trombone having wide tubes.
A shoulder-held rocket launcher used as an antitank weapon, developed by America during World War II and so-called from its resemblance to the bazooka musical instrument.
A woman's breast, especially a large one.
A large rescue or stimulus package.
e: From an extension of the word bazoo (“mouth, boastful talk”), which ultimately probably stems from Dutch bazuin (“trumpet”). In the finance sense first used by policymakers during the European debt crisis (2010).
Alteration of Spanish bazuco, basuco, derived from base. Doublet of basuco.

s: The state or quality of being solid.
The solid contents of a body; volume; amount of enclosed space.
e: From solid + -ity, from Middle French solidité, from Latin soliditās.

s: of decency; the property or degree of being indecent.
Something showing lack of decency; something (such as a word) that is indecent.
A conditional provision to an agreement.
e: Borrowed from Latin proviso (“it being provided”), ablative singular neuter of provisus, past participle of providere (“to provide”); see provide.

s: Severe pains that grip the abdomen or the disease that causes such pains (due to intestinal or bowel-related problems).
Severe fussiness and crying, especially of infants with certain medical conditions.
A medicinal plant used to relieve such symptoms.
e: Borrowed from French colique. Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek κωλικός (“suffering in the colon”).

s: Any of a variety of thermoplastics created from nitrocellulose and camphor, once used as photographic film.
An item, such as a jacket, made from celluloid.
e: Former trademark of Celluloid Manufacturing Company; from cellulose + -oid.

s: Supported on both sides by other charges.
Beyond imitation, surpassing all others; matchless.
e: Borrowed from Middle French inimitable, from Latin inimitabilis, corresponding to in- + imitable.
From Middle English *dountroden, past participle of Middle English dountreden (“to tread down, trample”), equivalent to down- + trodden.

s: Not subject to being alienated, that is, surrendered, taken away or transferred to another.

Of or pertaining to a noun belonging to a special class in which the possessive construction differs from the norm, especially for particular familial relationships and body parts, regarding permanence.
e: Borrowed around 1645 from French inaliénable, from in- + aliénable (“alienable”), equivalent to in- + alienable.
From Middle English homward, from Old English hāmweard, from Proto-Germanic *haimawarda, equivalent to home + -ward. Cognate with Dutch heimwaarts, German heimwärts (“homeward”).
From Middle English homward, from the adverb (see above).

s: A maker of wooden furniture or fittings.
A woodworking machine used to prepare edges of wooden elements to join to other wood pieces.
A thing that joins two separate items, e.g. software to connect video or music clips.
A person who joins societies or organizations.
e: From Middle English joynour (“maker of furniture, small boxes, etc.”), from Old French joigneor (“joiner, carpenter”), agent noun from joindre (“to join”), equivalent to join + -er.

s: Deviation from what is right; gross injustice, sin, wickedness.
An act of great injustice or unfairness; a sinful or wicked act; an unconscionable deed.

e: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).

s: A device that captures sound waves onto an engraved archive; a lathe.
A device that records or plays sound from cylinder records.
A character or symbol used to represent a sound, especially one used in phonography.
To record for playback by phonograph.

e: From Old French affluence, from Latin affluentia. Only relation to antonym indigence is common Latinate suffix; affluence only acquired sense of wealth in 16th century English and French, while indigentia meant “poverty” or “lack” in Latin.

s: Any of the subtribe Tamiina of small, striped rodents, mostly found in North America, with the exception of the Siberian chipmunk which is found primarily in Asia.
To speed up (an audio recording, especially a song), to make the voices high-pitched.
To fill (one's mouth or cheeks) with food.
To stuff (food) into one's mouth or cheeks, sometimes as part of competitive eating.
e: 1832; alteration (influenced by chipping squirrel) of earlier chitmunk, from older Ojibwe ačitamo˙nˀ (“squirrels”) (modern ajidamoo), literally ‘those who descend headlong’, from ačit- (“headfirst, face-down”) (compare modern ajijibizo (“he falls headfirst”), ajidagoojin (“he hangs upside down”)).

s: A female spirit, usually taking the form of a woman whose mournful wailing warns of an impending death.
e: Borrowed from Irish bean sí, from Old Irish ben síde. The term banshee entered English in 1771.

s: A (commercial) facility where eggs, especially those of fish or poultry, are hatched under artificial conditions.
A place where something is fostered or nurtured; a nursery.
A movie with sound, as opposed to a silent film.
A song in which the lyrics are spoken rather than sung.
e: Clipping of talking picture, via ie, and thus morphologically parallel with movie.

s: To make something dangerous or toxic by introducing impurities or foreign matter.
To soil, stain, corrupt, or infect by contact or association.
To make unfit for use by the introduction of unwholesome or undesirable elements.
To infect, usually of a deadly virus.
e: In Middle English; from Middle English contaminaten (“to defile; to infect with desease”), from contaminat (“sullied, defiled; infected with desease”) + -en, from Latin contāminātus, the perfect passive participle of contāminō (“to touch together, blend, mingle, corrupt, defile”) (see -ate), which see for further informations. More at taste, tax, and taxi.
In Middle English; from Middle English contaminat(e) (“sullied, defiled; infected with desease”), see -ate and Etymology 1 for more. Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

s: The process which causes an infarct.
In an astonishing manner; so as to surprise or astonish.
Causing much harm in a subtle way.
Insidiously villainous: intending to cause harm, especially in a subtle way.
e: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).

s: A person who lives in, or comes from, a village.
One who demonstrates anything, or proves beyond doubt.
One who takes part in a demonstration; a protester.
One who demonstrates products in a retail environment; a merchandiser.
An item, particularly a vehicle, used in demonstrations to a customer or user.
One who teaches anatomy from the dissected parts.
Equivalent in meaning or effect; amounting to the same thing in practical terms, even if being technically distinct.
To amount to as much; to be equivalent.
Something which has the same value or amount (as something else). (attributive use passing into adjective, below)
e: First attested in English in 1628. Either inherited from an unattested Middle English borrowing from Anglo-Norman tant amount, from amunter, from tant (“as much”) amonter (“to amount to”) or borrowed in the early 17th century from Italian tanto montare.

s: Relating to the myocardium, the thick muscular wall of the heart.
One who traps animals; one who makes a business of trapping animals, for their pelts, meat, etc.
A worker (usually a child) who opens and shuts a door in a gallery or level of a mine, to manage ventilation and access.
An ornamental covering for a horse. See trapping and caparison.
low body temperature; specifically, below 35 degrees Celsius for humans.
e: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (“under”) + θέρμη (“heat”) + -ία (“feminine suffix”). hypo- + therm- + -ia.

s: A decorative knot of hair on the crown of the head, sometimes having ribbons or feathers.
A crest of feathers upon the head of a bird.
A crested pigeon, or, a topknot pigeon.
The wool shorn from the crown of a sheep.
Any fish in one of several genera
The New Zealand topknot, Notoclinus fenestratus
Several species in the genus Zeugopterus
A small European flounder (Phrynorhombus regius, syn. Rhombus punctatus).
A Chinese unit of land area equivalent to 15 mu or about one hectare.
The act of one who peeks.
Nonce variation of the word slap, usually used to indicate a series of small slapping actions.
Capable of being grounded (supplied with a rational basis).
Capable of being grounded (forbidden from going out).
a person who uses psychic powers.
An authority (the power to enforce rules or give orders).
e: An alteration of authority. Originated from the catchphrase, "Respect my authoritah!" by Eric Cartman in the American animated sitcom South Park. First used in the episode "Chickenlover" (S2E4), which aired on May 27, 1998.

s: Of a person, or movement: not handy; inept; clumsy; not dexterous.
A Japanese amulet in the form of a red doll without a face, traditionally made for grandchildren or as a charm to ensure a good marriage.
e: From Japanese さるぼぼ, literally "baby monkey".
Unknown, perhaps from snatch. Popularized by and often attributed to the US animated series South Park (the 2007 episode "The Snuke").

s: One who griefs: a player who plays a game primarily to reduce other players’ enjoyment of it.
A penis, especially one that is short and thick.
A loser or undesirable person; an insulting name.
A panel of buttons to which users can assign frequently used commands.
A strip on a TAB (tape automated bonding) chip where components are attached by using a reflow head to hold them down while applying pressure and pulse heat to form a bond.
A jazz musician who plays the tenor saxophone.
An act of putting a person in a headlock and rubbing one's knuckles on the other person's head, often a playful gesture of affection when done lightly.
e: Unknown, possibly from Yiddish נודזשען (“to badger”), or possibly from Hebrew נוגות (“afflict”) (see Eicha/Lamentations 1:3) or possibly via an alteration of nudge, matching the alteration of wedge to wedgie.

s: One who can go out in the sunlight, distinguished from vampires, etc., who cannot.
Female genitalia; the vulva or vagina.
A woman, especially when discussed from a heavily sexualized, sexist and misogynist perspective.
e: Origin Uncertain. Likely from French putain (“prostitute”). Compare punani (“female genitalia”); also Tagalog putang ina (“contemptible person”) from Spanish puta (“prostitute”).

s: An irregular-shaped splash, smear, or patch.
To make a splodge; to render as a splodge.
The sound or release of trapped air from the vagina, often during or after sexual intercourse or exercise.
An oxidation product of adrenaline or epinephrine; its semicarbazone is used as a drug to reduce bleeding.
A fictional drug obtained from human adrenal glands.
To flop and droop, as a sign of aging or poor physical condition.
Vaccinium erythrocarpum, the southern mountain cranberry.
Dried fecal matter adhering to anal hair.
The sexual act of rimming; anilingus.
The act or process by which something shrivels.
A factor or agent resident in a country for traffic.
The book in which a corporation or other body registers its particular acts.
e: From Middle English coucher, from Anglo-Norman; equivalent to couch + -er.

s: In the manner of a rascal.
A regional English measure of capacity of a heavy cart (a butt), containing 6 seams, or 48 bushels, equivalent to 384 gallons.
A large amount carried in a butt.
e: From butt + load. Butt in this context may be possibly one or both of: Alternatively, the term may either be a corruption of English boatload or have been influenced by that term (except for the specific, West Country dialect sense). All senses above also synchronically reanalyzed as buttocksful.

s: The recreational activity of travelling on ziplines.
An act or instance of cutting (removing) with or as if with scissors, especially an act of cutting and censoring a film.
A clipping; something cut out (e.g. of a newspaper) with scissors.
A sex act in which two women intertwine their legs and rub their vulvas against each other.
A group of men assembled for some common purpose; a club, or cabal.
e: Erroneous adaptation of junta, by assimilation with Spanish nouns in -o.

s: Eye dialect of oh my God.
To endure, to put up with, to tolerate.
A pin in the side of a boat which acts as a fulcrum for the oars.
A pin, or handle, of the snath (shaft) of a scythe.
A cupola, a dome, a rotunda; a tholus.
e: From Middle English thōle, from tholen, tholien, from Old English þolian, from Proto-West Germanic *þolēn, from Proto-Germanic *þulāną (“to suffer”), from Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“to bear, suffer; to support”), compare Norwegian tåle.

the building up of muscles with exercise
walking along contour lines, usually to save energy or simplify navigation
Small and cute; pretty in a delicate way; dainty.
A cute or pretty person; a dandy; a pretty child.
One of the court favourites of Henry III of France.
e: From French mignon, from Middle French mignon (“lover, darling, favourite”), from Old French mignon (“dainty, pleasing, gentle, kind”), from Frankish *minnju (“love, friendship, affection, memory”), from Proto-Germanic *minjō (“affectionate thought, care”), from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think”).

s: The line formed by the edge of an article of clothing that surrounds the neck, especially as seen at the front.
a strap or straps; usually describing women's clothing without shoulder straps.
The penis of a trans woman.
e: From strap + -less. The noun sense is by analogy of strap-on.

s: A flat-bottomed boat or other floating structure used as a buoyant support for a temporary bridge, dock or landing stage.
A box used to raise a sunken vessel.
A lighter or barge used for loading or unloading ships.
A card game in which the object is to obtain cards whose value adds up to, or nearly to, 21 but not exceed it.
A two-card hand totalling 21 in this game.
e: Borrowed from Middle French ponton, from Old French ponton, from Latin pontō, pontōnem (“ferryboat”), from pōns (“bridge”).
Probably from vingt-un, an obsolete variant of vingt-et-un (“twenty-one”), from French.

s: Covered with iron, steel or any other tough metal; armor-plated.
or certain; not able to be disputed or questioned; irrefutable.
A ship, vessel, or vehicle with a covering of iron, steel or any other tough metal.
An armor-plated warship, (especially) one preceding the invention of harveyized steel.
A wooden warehouse with an outer skin of corrugated metal.
Having an increased state of activity
having attention deficit disorder (no longer used by the scientific community)
Any of various kinds of pain, especially pain that is suffocative, spasmodic, and/or acute and severe (fulminant).
An inflammatory infection of the throat, especially quinsy; any sore throat, with or without tooth and gum involvement.
e: From Latin angina (“quinsy; strangling, choking”), from angō (“to press together, to choke, to hurt (cause pain)”).

s: A turret or other raised structure offering a pleasant view of the surrounding area.
A shotgun with a barrel and sometimes buttstock which have been shortened by sawing them off; a sawed-off shotgun.
The winner of a fixed race, a fixed race.
A candidate or contestant generally agreed upon as the presumptive winner; a favorite, somebody who is well-liked or widely agreed upon.
e: From a sense of the verb shoo, where racehorses would fall back and allow a chosen rider to win a fixed race. See 1910 quotation.

s: Someone or something that saves lives.
Any lifesaving tool or item of supplies.
Someone or something that is very useful or helpful.
A person who uses diet and exercise to build an aesthetically muscular physique, in order to compete in bodybuilding.
clothing that is comfortable to wear when exercising or partaking in sport; activewear.
A figure that brings sleep and dreams by sprinkling magical sand into people's eyes.
Used as a symbol of the passage of time toward death.
e: From sand + -man. The mythological sense may be from Calque of German Sandmann, Sandmännchen, as it is apparently first attested in English in the context of E.T.A. Hoffmann’s novella The Sandman (1816). The German is attested in the relevant sense since at least the mid-18th century.

s: Any of the grasshoppers, often polyphenic and usually swarming, in the family Acrididae that are very destructive to crops and other vegetation, especially migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria).
A fruit or pod of a carob tree (Ceratonia siliqua).
Any of various often leguminous trees and shrubs, especially of the genera Robinia and Gleditsia; locust tree.
Anything or anyone considered a nuisance or plague.
e: Inherited from Middle English locuste, locust, from Anglo-Norman locuste, Middle French locuste, and their source, Latin locusta (“locust, crustacean, lobster”).

s: In an affected manner; hypocritically; with more show than reality.
Not giving reflection or thought to one's actions, words, conclusions, etc.; (of an action, statement, conclusion, etc.) done without reflection or thought. (of a person)
That does not reflect light or sound.
Any member of the genus Convallaria; a lily of the valley.
A smaller, common Eurasian sturgeon, of the species Acipenser ruthenus.
A bag containing tools or material used for work, especially needlework.
In an amiable, cheerful, or pleasant manner.
Resembling or characteristic of a schoolgirl.
In a constrained manner; subject to constraint.
An open horse-drawn carriage, especially in Russia.
e: Borrowed from Russian дро́жки, plural diminutive of дро́ги (“wagon, hearse”), plural of дрога́ (“centre pole of a carriage”).

s: In an irresolute or wavering manner.
A business where alcoholic beverages and often food are served: a bar, a public house, a saloon, a tavern.
The state or quality of being transitory.
The state of being partially clothed.
A garment worn when one is in a state of undress; a négligée.
e: Borrowed from French déshabillé (“undressed”), the past participle of déshabiller (“to undress”).

s: Having the manner of a thief; furtive; stealthy.
e: From Middle English thevysch, equivalent to thief + -ish. Cognate with däifsk (“thievish”), Dutch diefs (“thievish”), Low German deevsk (“thievish”), German diebisch (“thievish”).

s: Lack of resolution; lack of decision or purpose; vacillation.
e: Probably from Middle French irresolution (modern French irrésolution), from ir- + resolution (“resolution”); compare Italian irresoluzione. ir- + resolution.

s: One whose life is devoted to sensual appetites; a pleasure-seeker, a sensualist.
Of or relating to the seeking of sensual pleasure.
A fur-lined robe or cloak, especially as part of a uniform.
A long cloak formerly worn by women, with a shoulder cape or hood, often lined or trimmed with fur.
An overgarment worn by children when outside.
e: Borrowed from French pelisse, from Late Latin pellicia, from Latin pellis (“skin”). Doublet of pilch.

s: Plural of flunkey (Alternative spelling of flunkies).
The state or quality of being sly.
The result or product of being sly.
A small tray containing pens and an inkwell; a pot for holding ink, inkpot, inkwell.
In a diffident manner; without confidence in oneself.
Having or showing a strong aversion or repugnance.
Opposed in nature or character; antagonistic.
Causing a feeling of antipathy; repugnant.
In a manner suitable for some particular purpose.
In a manner convenient or advantageous at some particular time.
The driver of a hackney cab.
The quality of being obsequious; servile compliance.
The act of gesticulating, or making gestures to aid expression of thoughts, sentiments or passion.
A gesture; a motion of the body or limbs when speaking, or in representing action or passion, and enforcing arguments and sentiments.
The state of extreme shock or astonishment.
e: From Middle French stupéfaction, from Latin stupefaciō (“strike dumb, stun with amazement, stupefy”), from stupeō (“to be stunned, speechless”) (English stupid, stupor) + faciō (“to do, make”).

s: To make a series of chirps, clicks or clucks.
To quicken or animate by chirping.
A series of chirps, clicks or clucks.
e: Expanded variant of earlier chirp, with addition of extra syllable to imitate multisyllabic bird vocalisations.

s: An often wooden structure that projects from a coastline or riverbank to prevent erosion, longshore drift etc.; a breakwater.
e: From Middle English groyn (“snout”), from Old French groign, from Late Latin grunium, grunia, from Latin grunnire (“grunt like a pig”).

s: The quality or state of being plump.
The property or characteristic of possessing angles.
A stiff, cranky, crotchety manner or behaviour.

e: Inherited from Middle English foully, from Old English fūllīċe; foul + ly.

s: To conciliate, appease, or make peace with someone, particularly a god or spirit.
e: From Latin propitiāt-, the past participial stem of propitiāre (“make favourable”), from propitius (“favourable, gracious”).
From Middle English drerily, from Old English drēoriġlīċe; equivalent to dreary + -ly.

s: Having an ample bosom, having large breasts.
Calmly, without excessive emotion or force; in a composed manner.
Having no covering on the head.
With no covering on the head.
To make gestures or motions, as in speaking.
To say or express through gestures.
e: Borrowed from Latin gesticulātus, perfect active participle of gesticulor (“to gesticulate”) (see -ate), from gesticulus (“a mimic gesture”), diminutive of gestus (“gesture”), from gerō (“to bear, carry, perform”).

s: An open declaration of affirmation or admission of knowledge.
The blending together of property so as to achieve equal division, especially in the case of divorce or intestacy.
A kind of mutton broth with green peas instead of barley or rice.
e: From Middle English hochepoche, a variation of hochepot, from Old French hochepot, from hocher (“to shake”) + pot (“pot”), of Dutch or German origin. Equivalent to hotch + pot. Compare Dutch hutspot and Low German Hüttspott (“hodgepodge”).

s: Of a person: deeply affected or overwhelmed by suffering or trouble, and so filled with woe#Noun; forlorn, sad, unhappy.
Of a person or thing: having a distressed, miserable, or sad appearance.
Of a thing: in a deplorable state.
A person who is deeply affected or overwhelmed by suffering or trouble, and so filled with woe.
The quality or degree of being sensitive.
The ability to be aware of (and, usually, react with regard to) the feelings of others.
An ill-defined medical condition characterized by lassitude, fatigue, headache, and irritability, associated chiefly with emotional disturbance.
In a quiet manner, without any noise.
To bring forward or offer, as an argument, passage, or consideration which bears on a statement or case.
e: From Middle English adducen, from Latin addūcere, adductum (“to lead or bring to”), from ad- + dūcere (“to lead”). See duke, and compare adduct.

s: In a sorrowful manner; with sorrow and regret.
Tools and hardware that can be bought in an ironmonger's shop.
The various metal items used by mountaineers.
The state of being abrupt or broken
a witty remark; a bon mot; an epigram; a zinger.
e: From witty + -icism; coined in the 1670s by John Dryden, by analogy to criticism.

s: The property or degree of being distinct.
Of the feet: bent backward and apparently unfit for walking.
The act of speaking with a drawl.
A child whose baptism is sponsored by a godparent. In some cases the relationship is maintained indefinitely, with the godchild being treated much like a niece or nephew.
An abnormal beating of the heart that may be perceived by the patient, a result of excitement, exertion, or illness.
The state of being diffident, timid or shy; reticence or self-effacement.
Mistrust, distrust, lack of confidence in someone or something.
e: From Latin diffīdentiam (“distrust”), from diffīdere (“to mistrust”), from dis- and fīdere (“to trust”). Attested since ∼1400. The original sense was antonymous with confidence, and the modern sense of ‘distrusting oneself’ dates from the 1650s.

s: A traditional Polish folk dance in triple time, usually moderately fast, containing a heavy accent on the third beat and occasionally the second beat.
A classical musical composition inspired by the folk dance and conforming in some respects to its form, particularly as popularized by Chopin.
A figure skating move that combines elements of the toe loop and bunny-hop.
e: Via German Mazurka and Russian мазу́рка, from Polish mazurek (“dance of the Masurian”), the Masurians being the inhabitants of Mazowsze (compare Medieval Latin Mazovia), an ancient cultural region in east-central Poland.

s: A metal urn with a spigot, for boiling water for making tea. Traditionally, the water is heated by hot coals or charcoal in a chimney-like tube which runs through the center of the urn. Today, it is more likely that the water is heated by an electric coil.
Not feminine; not characteristic of, typical of, or appropriate for a woman.
The sound made by bells as they peal.
The quality of being acute or pointed.
Of the senses or feelings: the faculty of precise discernment or perception; sensitiveness.
Violence of a disease, which brings it speedily to a crisis.
Covered with scales or scabs; hence, very coarse or rough.
Salacious, scandalous; concerning oneself with lurid or lascivious substance.
Of music, writing, etc.: lacking refinement; unmelodious, unmusical.
Covered with a crust of dirt or grime.
e: Borrowed from Latin scaber (“scabrous, rough; scabby, mangy, itchy”) (from scabō (“to scratch, scrape, abrade”), from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”)) + English -ous; compare French scabreux, Late Latin scabrōsus.

s: A state of the body or mind caused by exhaustion or disease and characterized by a languid or weary feeling; lassitude; an instance of this.
Melancholy caused by lovesickness, sadness, etc.; an instance of this.
Dullness, sluggishness; lack of vigour; stagnation.
Listless indolence or inactivity, especially if enjoyable or relaxing; dreaminess; an instance of this.
Heavy humidity and stillness of the air.
Sorrow; suffering; also, enfeebling disease or illness; an instance of this.
The state of being out of proportion; an abnormal or improper ratio; an imbalance.
Lack of suitableness, adequacy, or due proportion to an end or use; unsuitableness.
To make unsuitable in quantity, form, or fitness; to violate symmetry in; to mismatch.
of, relating to or containing carbolic acid
e: Derived from German Carbolsäure (modern German Karbolsäure), which was coined in 1834 by its discoverer Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge. carb- + -ol + -ic.

s: Made of or resembling flax fibers.
A pale yellow brown as of dried flax; blonde.
e: From Middle English flaxen, flexon, flexin, from Old English fleaxen (“of flax; flaxen”), equivalent to flax + -en (“made of”). Compare Dutch vlassen.

s: Any of the Biblical blessings given by Jesus in Matthew 5:3–12. E.g.: "Blessed are the meek for they shall inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5).
e: From Middle English beatitude, beatytude, from Middle French béatitude, from Latin beātitūdō (“happiness, blessedness”), from beātus (“happy, blessed”).

s: The quality or state of being sublime.
e: From Middle English sublimite, sublimitee, from Middle French sublimité and/or Latin sublīmitās. sublime + -ity.

s: The action of vexing, annoying, or irritating someone or something; an instance of this.
The action of physically annoying or irritating a person or an animal; an instance of this; also, a physical discomfort or disorder.
The action of vexing or annoying someone by bringing unjustified legal proceedings against them; an instance of this.
The state of being vexed, annoyed, or irritated; annoyance, irritation; also, disappointment, discontentment, unhappiness; an instance of this.
The state of being mentally distressed or troubled.
The state of being physically annoyed or irritated.
A source of mental distress or trouble; an affliction, a woe; also, a source of annoyance or irritation; an annoyance, an irritant.
The action of using force or violence on someone or something; an instance of this.
The act by which something crumples.
Having or displaying no guile, cunning, or deceit.
Lacking art, knowledge, or skill; uncultured and ignorant.
Of, being, or characteristic of a young, flirtatious girl.

e: From Middle English pleuresi, pleresye, that borrowed from Old French pleuresie (French pleurésie), from Late Latin pleurisis, alteration of Latin pleuritis. pleur- + -isy.

s: Any mild disorder of digestion characterised by stomach pain, discomfort, heartburn, and nausea, often following a meal.

e: A borrowing of Italian violoncello (“little violone”), from violone (“an early form of the double bass”) + -cello (“-elle”), violone itself being derived from viola + -one (“-oon”).

s: The pelt of a bear, especially when used as a rug.
A tall ceremonial hat worn by members of some British regiments for ceremonial occasions; a busby.
A coarse, shaggy, woollen cloth for overcoats.
Calm, not ruffled, serene, at peace, unbothered.
Not having been asked; unspoken, as a question.
Not asked or invited to an event.
e: From Middle English un asked,unaskyd,uneasket; equivalent to un- + asked.

s: A negative view or hatred of the human race.
e: From Ancient Greek μισανθρωπία, from μισάνθρωπος, from μῖσος (“hatred”) + ἄνθρωπος (“human”). The word is analysable as miso- + -anthropy.

s: Of a glance or look: with disapproval, skepticism, or suspicion.
Turned to the side, especially of the eyes.
To look at (someone or something) with a sideways glance.
To turn (one's eye or gaze) to the side.
e: Unknown. Possibly from Middle English askances (“as if”), or from Old French a escone (“hidden”) or Italian a scancio (“obliquely”). Compare asquint, Middle English askoyn (“at a slant, askance”), Dutch schuin, schuins (“sideways”), schuiven (“to shove”), schuinte (“slope”).
From Latin diffīdentem, present participle of diffīdere (“to mistrust”). Doublet of defiant.

s: In an agreeable or pleasing manner.
Wearing nothing on the feet; barefoot.
Wearing nothing on the feet; barefoot.
Of stocks or bonds: whose holders agree to deposit them by way of assent to an agreement altering their status, as in a readjustment.
A sleeveless garment generally worn over other clothes as a protective apron or as a decorative garment.
e: . The pinafore was originally pinned to the front of a dress, as it had no buttons.

s: Not elegant; not exhibiting neatness, refinement, or precision.
e: From Middle French inélégant, from Latin inēlegāns; equivalent to in- + elegant.

s: The clothes and linen, etc., that a bride collects or that is given to her for her wedding and married life, especially a traditional or formal set of these.
An idle, trifling talker; a gossip.
A psychopathological condition characterized by delusional fantasies of wealth, power, or omnipotence.
An obsession with grandiose or extravagant things or actions.
Excessively eager and attentive to please or to obey instructions; fawning, subservient, servile.
Obedient; compliant with someone else's orders or wishes.
Of or pertaining to obsequies, funereal.
e: From Middle English obsequyous, from Latin obsequiōsus (“complaisant, obsequious”), from obsequium (“compliance”), from obsequor (“comply with, yield to”), from ob (“in the direction of, towards”) + sequor (“follow”) (cf. sequel).

s: The state or quality of being perplexed.
A measure of the accuracy with which a probability distribution or model predicts a sample.
e: From Middle English perplexite, borrowed from Middle French perplexité or post-classical Latin perplexitās, from perplexus (“entangled”). en + perplex + ity.

s: Having a disposition or mood of a specified kind.
Partaking in idolatry; worshipping idols or false gods.
Engaging in excessive attachment or reverence; inordinately or profanely devoted.
Used in or designed for idolatry; devoted to idols or idol-worship.
Unnatural paleness, especially as a sign of sickness or distress.
e: From Middle English pallour, from Old French palor (“paleness, pallor”), from Latin pallor, from palleō (“to look pale, blanch”).

s: The act by which something is foreseen; a prophetic vision.
The sound of something that lows.
A loose shirtlike undergarment, especially for women.
A short nightdress, or similar piece of lingerie.
A woman's dress that fits loosely; a chemise dress.
A wall that lines the face of a bank or earthwork.
e: From French chemise, from Old French chemise, from Late Latin camisa, camisia ("shirt, undergarment, nightgown"; whence Old English cemes (“shirt”)), from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”) (whence Old English hemeþe, Old High German hemidi, modern German Hemd (“shirt”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱam- (“cover, clothes”).

s: The sound of something that croaks.
Straightness; the state or quality of having a constant direction and not being crooked or bent.
The fact or quality of being right or correct; correctness of opinion or judgement.
Conformity to the rules prescribed for moral conduct; (moral) uprightness, virtue.
e: From Middle English rectitude, from Middle French rectitude, from Late Latin rectitūdō (“straightness, uprightness”), from Latin rectus (“straight”), perfect passive participle of regō (“regulate, guide”).

s: Wearing too many clothes for the weather or the occasion.
Wearing clothes too formal or too elaborate for the occasion.
Of or pertaining to a serf, peasant, or rustic.
Difficult to till, lacking pliancy; unmanageable.
e: From Middle English cherlisch, cherlissh, from late Old English ċeorlisċ, ċierlisċ (“of or pertaining to churls”), equivalent to churl + -ish..

s: The state of being profound; magnitude, gravity, or intensity.
A great depth; a deep place.
Depth; the state of possessing great downwards extent.
e: Inherited from Middle English profundite, from Middle French profondite or its etymon Latin profunditās; profound + ity. Compare profoundness.

s: The act by which something is snipped or cut.
Removal of the irrelevant parts of quotations in the reply message.
A piece cut off; a clipping.
Without energy, gusto or drive, enervated, without the will to accomplish, disheartened.
Argumentative; fond of or prone to quarreling.

e: From glyco- + -ine, from French glycérine, from Ancient Greek γλυκερός (“sweet”) (compare γλυκύς (“sweet”)).

s: The state of being near; closeness; intimacy.
e: From Middle English nernes, equivalent to near + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian nearens (“nearness”).
From Middle English arbere, arber, an alteration of herber, erber (“pleasure garden; herb garden”) influenced by Latin arbor (“tree”).

s: The act by which something is clasped.
Sweetened, with, or as if with, honey.
A factory where perfume is made.
A lack or absence of gratitude; thanklessness.
e: From in- + gratitude, from Old French ingratitude, from Late Latin ingrātitūdō. in- + la:grātus + -itude.

s: The characteristic or state of being immense.
A sensation of extreme shame or embarrassment.
The death of part of the body.
A bringing under of the passions and appetites by a severe or strict manner of living.
A bequest to a charitable institution.
e: From Middle English mortificacioun,mortification, from Middle French mortification and its etymon Latin mortificātiō. mortify + -ication.

s: The act of running away from home with a paramour.
The act of running away secretly for the purpose of getting married.
The act of running away from home (for any reason).
The act of a person with dementia or other mental illness wandering away from the area where they are safe.
Extreme; used of environmental or bodily conditions.
The act of something that perishes; decay or destruction.
The state, quality, or condition of being fat.
e: From Middle English fatnesse, fattenesse, from Old English fǣtnes (“fatness, the richest part of anything”), equivalent to fat + -ness.

s: The act by which somebody is swindled.
Having, or showing, no pity; merciless, ruthless.
Senses relating to asking or pleading.
To ask earnestly or beg for (something, such as a benefit or favour).
To earnestly ask or beg (someone); to beseech, to implore.
To try to influence or persuade (someone); to induce, to prevail upon.
Often followed by for: to ask earnestly or to beg for a benefit, favour, etc.; to appeal, to plead.
To make a petition or request on behalf of someone; to intercede, to plead.
Senses relating to dealing with or negotiating.
To act towards or deal with (someone or something) in a specified manner; to handle, to treat.
To discuss or negotiate (something); also, to discuss or negotiate with (someone).
Sometimes followed by of or upon: to give an account or description of a matter; to deal with.
Often followed by about, for, or of: to discuss or negotiate, especially in order to reach a settlement.
Synonym of entreaty; an appeal, a plea.
An important or influential person, or one of high rank or position.
Something that is false; an untrue assertion.
e: Corresponding to false + -ity. From Middle French fausseté, Old French falseté, from Late Latin falsitas, from Latin falsus.

s: A totally ignorant person—unknowledgeable, uneducated, or uninformed; a fool.
A grand jury's ruling on an indictment when the evidence is determined to be insufficient to send the case to trial.
To make such a ruling against (an indictment).
e: After the ignorant lawyer Ignoramus, the titular character in the 1615 play Ignoramus by the English playwright George Ruggle; from Latin ignōrāmus (“we do not know, we are unacquainted with, we are ignorant of”), the first-person plural present active indicative of ignōrō (“to not know, to be unacquainted with, to be ignorant of”).
Directly from Latin ignōrāmus (“we do not know”).

s: In a manner intended to convince or persuade.
Preference, bias in favor of, tendency.
The quality of being partial or incomplete.
e: From Middle English parcialite,parcialtee,parcyalte,partialte,percialite, from Middle French partialité and its etymon Medieval Latin partiālitās. Doublet of partialitas.

s: The horny, translucent, mottled covering of the carapace of the hawksbill turtle, used as a veneer etc.
A domestic cat (or a rabbit, guinea-pig, etc.) whose fur has black, brown and yellow markings.
Any of several butterflies, mostly of the genera Nymphalis and Aglais that have similar markings.
Made of the covering of carapace of hawksbill turtle.
Having markings resembling covering of carapace of hawksbill turtle.
The production of a trill sound.
A compound crystal consisting of three individuals.
One of three offspring born at the same birth; a triplet.
A traveller, especially one on foot.
Sharp and harsh, or bitter and not to the taste.
e: From Latin ācer (“sharp”), genitive ācris; probably reshaped on the model of acid and other adjectives like rancid and fetid. Doublet of eager.

s: speed, swiftness; the condition of being rapid
A measure of velocity relative to the speed of light; defined as artanh(v), where artanh is the hyperbolic arctangent, and v = speed (with c = speed of light = 1).
A measure of the velocity of a particle in a beam relative to the beam's axis
The act of inflicting or something inflicted; an imposition.
e: From Latin īnflīctiō (“imposition”), from Latin īnflīctus, from in- + flīctus, past participle of īnflīgō (“to knock or strike against”), from in- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence in-). inflict + -ion.

s: Not polished; not brought to a polish.
Not refined in manners or style
The tendency to think selfishly with exclusive self-interest in mind.
The belief that moral behavior should be directed toward one's self-interest only.
by confusion of the similar words
Egotism (tendency to talk excessively about oneself).
e: From French égoïsme, from New Latin egoismus, from Latin ego. ego + -ism.

s: A person, especially one who is famous or important.
A character (in a film, book, play, etc).
The creation of corporate persons named after living people.
e: From Middle French personnage, from Old French personage; person + -age (compare French suffix -age).

s: The land or abode of fairies.
Any place of great natural beauty, or having a magical atmosphere.
Having qualities ascribed to fairies and their realm; fanciful, delicate, surreal, or diminutive.
Favouring peace rather than conflict; not aggressive, tending to avoid violence (of people, actions etc.).
e: From Anglo-Norman pesible, peisible, Middle French paisible, from pais (“peace”) + -ible; later remodelled after peace + -able.

s: Lacking critique or critical examination; undiscriminating.
Having a disregard for critical standards or procedures.
Having cheeks (skin on side of the face) of a healthy, ruddy complexion.
Of the eyes, a facial expression, etc.: looking downwards, usually as a sign of discouragement, sadness, etc., or sometimes modesty.
Of a person or thing: cast or thrown to the ground.
Of a person: feeling despondent or discouraged.
Of a person or thing: defeated, overthrown; also, destroyed, ruined.
An act of looking downwards, usually as a sign of discouragement, sadness, etc., or sometimes modesty; hence, dejection, melancholy.
An act, or the situation, of being cast or thrown to the ground.
A defeat, an overthrow; also, an act of destruction or ruin.
A cast from supertype to subtype.
A ventilating shaft down which air passes in circulating through a mine.
To turn (the eyes) downwards, usually as a sign of discouragement, sadness, etc., or sometimes modesty.
To cast or throw (something) downwards; also, to drop or lower (something).
To demolish or tear down (a building, etc.).
To make (someone) feel despondent or discouraged; to discourage, to sadden.
To cast (a data type) from supertype to subtype.
e: From Middle English downcast (“misfortune”), adoun-cast (“destruction, overthrow”), from adoun (“downward”) + cast (“a throw, a cast”) (from Old Norse kast (“a throw”), from kasten (“to cast, throw”)), from Middle English casten adoun: see etymology 1. The English word is analysable as down- + cast (“act of throwing”).

From Middle English doun-casten, *adoun-casten (“to cast or throw (something) downwards; to break down (something); to overcome (someone); to overturn (something)”), from down (“in a downward direction; (figurative) to destruction”), adoun (“downward”) + casten (“to throw (something), fling, hurl; to overcome (someone), defeat, overpower; [etc.]”): see etymology 1.

s: The transport of goods by cart.
The transport of someone in a cart through the streets as part of a public punishment or humiliation.
To completely renounce claims to; to deny ownership of or responsibility for
To relinquish or deny having a claim; to disavow another's claim; to decline accepting, as an estate, interest, or office.
To make a caveat or admission.
e: From Middle English disclaimen, from Anglo-Norman disclaimer, from Old French desclamer (French déclamer), des- + clamer.

s: A member of the plebs, the common citizens of ancient Rome.
A commoner, particularly a low, vulgar person.
Of or concerning the plebs, the common citizens of ancient Rome.
Of or concerning the common people.
Common, particularly vulgar, crude, coarse, uncultured.
e: From Latin plēbēius (“a commoner; common”) + -an, from Latin plēbēs + -ius, possibly under the influence of Middle French plebeyen, plebein, plebien (“a commoner”) and plebeien (“concerning the common people”). Cf. Medieval Latin plēbēiānus (“a commoner”), from plēbēius + -ānus.
From Middle English pleintif, plentyff, from Old French pleintif (“aggrieved, lamenting”) (whence modern French plaintif), from plainte (“lament, complaint”); see plaint. Doublet of plaintiff.
From Middle English perdicioun, from Old French perdiciun, from Late Latin perditio, from Latin perdo (“to destroy, to lose”).

s: In a noisy manner; in such a way as to create a great deal of noise or sound.
Of, relating to, or producing soot.
To blacken or make dirty with soot.
e: From Middle English sooty, soty, equivalent to soot + -y. Probably influenced by similar Middle English suti (“dirty, filthy”), derived from the same root as Old English besūtian (“to befoul”).

s: The state of being uneasy, nervous or restless.
An anxious state of mind; anxiety.
Without any grounds to support it; baseless.
Bottomless; having no bottom or floor.
e: From Middle English groundles (“bottomless”), from Old English grundlēas, from Proto-Germanic *grundulausaz, equivalent to ground + -less. Cognate with Dutch grondeloos, Low German grundlos, German grundlos, Danish grundløs, Swedish grundlös.

s: The act of one who implores; imploration.
A receptacle for decanted liquor, especially a crystal bottle with a stopper.
A man who drives a horse-drawn coach: a male coach driver.
A fish in the genus Heniochus, especially Heniochus acuminatus or Heniochus diphreutes.
An experience or expression of celebratory feeling, merriment, gaiety.
e: Inherited from Middle English festivite, from Middle French festivité, from Latin festīvitas, equivalent to festive + -ity.

s: In an initial stage; beginning, starting, coming into existence.
A verb tense of the Hebrew language.
e: Borrowed from Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō (“begin”).
From Middle French, from Latin indēfatīgābilis (“untiring”), from in- (“not”) + dēfatīgō (“to tire out”).
From obsolete French précipiteux, from Vulgar Latin *praecipitōsus, from praeceps + -ōsus, from prae- (“before”) + caput (“head”). Equivalent to precipice (“steep cliff, brink”) + -ous.

s: The art of applying gold leaf to a surface.
A coating of gold or gold-colored paint, etc.
In a clumsy manner or way; without care or finesse, often hurriedly or awkwardly.
Characteristic of what is considered the ideal behaviour pertaining to fatherhood.
Befitting of a father; protective, paternal.
In a way pertaining to, befitting, or of a father.
e: From Middle English faderly, from Old English fæderlīċ (“fatherly, paternal”), from Proto-West Germanic *faderlīk, from Proto-Germanic *fadurlīkaz (“fatherly, paternal”), equivalent to father + -ly.
From Middle English faderly, fadirly, from Old English fæderlīċe (“in a fatherly way, as a father”), equivalent to father + -ly.

s: The act of repelling or the condition of being repelled.
An extreme dislike of something, or hostility to something.
The repulsive force acting between bodies of the same electric charge or magnetic polarity.
e: Borrowed from Middle French répulsion, from Late Latin repulsio, repulsionem, from Latin repulsus.

s: Not able to be placated or appeased.
Impossible to prevent or stop; inexorable, unrelenting, unstoppable.
The state of being degenerate (in all senses).
The ability of one part of the brain to take over another's function without being overexerted.
A limiting case of a class of objects which appears to be qualitatively different from (and usually simpler than) the rest of the class.
Crocks or earthenware vessels, especially domestic utensils, collectively.
Dishes, plates, and similar tableware collectively, usually made of some ceramic material, used for serving food on and eating from.
A vicious female monster from Greek mythology with sharp fangs and hair of living, venomous snakes. One of the three sisters: Medusa, Stheno and Euryale
An intimidating, ugly, or disgusting woman; anything hideous or horrid.
Like a gorgon; very ugly or terrifying.
e: From Middle English gorgon, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ, from γοργός (“terrible”). Possibly from the same root as the Sanskrit word "garğ" (गर्जन), which is defined as a guttural sound, similar to the growling of a beast, thus possibly originating as an onomatopoeia.

s: Having a strong association with gender; gendered.
A bridge over a road, railway, river, etc for pedestrians.
Such a wave or similar action.
A clause, phrase, or word which is inserted into a grammatically complete passage of text for explanation or as an aside, and usually marked off with brackets, commas, or dashes.
An aside serving as an explanation; also, an afterthought.
The making of asides or explanations in grammatically complete passages of text.
Either of a pair of brackets, chiefly the round brackets "(" and ")" but occasionally also the square brackets "[" and "]", which are used together to enclose parenthetical material in a text.
Either of a pair of curved lines or shapes resembling a round bracket.
Either of a pair of brackets used to clarify an expression by grouping terms affected by a common operator, or to enclose the components of a vector or the elements of a matrix.
An intervening event; an interlude, an interruption.
A departing or straying from the main activity or subject; deviation, digression; an instance of this; an irrelevant interruption.
Doomed to destruction or misery; cursed; anathematized.
e: From Middle English acursed, from acursen (“to curse”), from Old English ācursian, from ā- + cursian, from curs (“curse”)..

s: A very short, unspecified length of time.
A unit of time defined by the frequency of its basic timer – historically, and by convention, 0.01 of a second, but some computer operating systems use other values.
The length of an alternating current power cycle (1/60 or 1/50 of a second).
The time taken for light to travel a specified distance in a vacuum, usually one centimetre (approximately 33.3564 picoseconds), but sometimes one foot or the width of a nucleon.
Ellipsis of jiffy bag, a padded envelope.
e: Origin Unknown; said to have been thieves’ cant for “lightning”. Also formerly written "giffy", to which a connection with gliff has been proposed. As a kind of envelope, a genericization of Jiffy bag.

s: Having been cooked by slowly boiling or simmering (see stew).
Of tea: bitter from having been steeped too long.
A serious infectious disease leading to inflammation of mucous membranes of the upper respiratory tract, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
e: From French diphtérie (later for a while also spelled diphthérie) in 1857, which was coined in 1855 with the suffix -ie to replace -ite in the previous term diphtérite for the disease because it affects more than one part of the body.

s: Under the influence of a magical spell; enchanted, bewitched, or supernaturally constrained.
Fascinated by something; entranced as if by a spell; captivated.
unable to be accounted for or explained.
Not responsible; free from accountability or control.
A small, one-wheeled (or rarely, two-wheeled) cart with handles at one end for transporting small loads.
To cause the weight of an aeroplane to become concentrated around the nosewheel.
A loud, hard sound of metal hitting metal.
To cause to sound with a clank.
An emotional and physical intimate relationship which includes a common living place and which exists without legal or religious sanction.
A place where two or more individuals reside together.
The act of two species living together in the same habitat.
Cooperation between politicians of opposing political parties; especially, in France, between a President and Prime Minister.
e: From Middle English cohabitacioun, from Old French cohabitacion and Late Latin cohabitātiō. co- + habitation.

s: In low spirits from loss of hope or courage.
e: From Latin dēspondēns, from the verb despondere (“to give up, to abandon”).

s: exhibiting sorrow; dejected; distraught; sad. (of a person)
e: From Middle English sorweful, from Old English sorhful, sorgful (“full of care; anxious; sorrowful”), from Proto-Germanic *surgafullaz (“full of care; anxious”), equivalent to sorrow + -ful. Cognate with Old High German sorgfol (“careful; anxious”), Norwegian sorgfull (“sorrowful”), Icelandic sorgfullur (“lamentable”).

s: A binary compound of bromine and some other element or radical.
The anionic form of a bromine atom.
A dull person with conventional thoughts.
A dose of bromide taken as a sedative, or to reduce sexual appetite.
A print made on bromide paper.
e: From brom + ide. First used in the sense “dull person” by Coined by Q15998059. Figurative sense ("platitude") by extending the medicating sense through the metaphor of pacifying or placating.

s: A person of learning, especially one who is versed in literature or science.
A person who is considered eminent because of their achievements.
A person with or without significant mental disabilities who is very gifted in one area of activity, such as playing the piano or mental arithmetic.
e: Borrowed from French savant, from Latin sapiō. Doublet of sapient. Sense 3 is a clipping of idiot savant, literally ‘wise idiot’.
From Middle English piramidal,piramydale, from Medieval Latin pȳramidālis. pyramid + -al.

s: An addendum to a letter, added after the author's signature.
An addition to a story, play, etc. after its completion.
To extend (a letter or another document) with additional remarks.
e: From New Latin postscriptum, from Latin, neuter of postscriptus, past participle of postscrībō (“write after”), from post (“after”) + scrībō (“write”). post- + script.

s: In a blissful, happy or joyful manner.
The state of being tranquil; peacefulness, the absence of disturbance or stress; serenity; calm.
e: From tranquil + -ity, from Middle English tranquillite, from Old French tranquillite, tranquilité, from Latin tranquillitas.

s: Any of assorted small seashells with a pink or partially pink color, usually of the family Muricidae.
the indentation of a surface caused by an incorrect hammer strike (missing the nail)
A woman's nipples, namely when erect.
The act, art, or process of inserting grafts.
The act or method of weaving a cover for a ring, rope end, etc.
The transplanting of a portion of flesh, hair or skin to a denuded surface; autoplasty.
A scarfing or endwise attachment of one timber to another.
A carved figure on the prow of a sailing ship.
Someone in a nominal position of leadership who has little to no actual power.
To lead (something) nominally and with little to no actual power.
A pipe with a long flexible tube that draws the smoke through water, traditionally used for smoking tobacco, which is often flavored.
A tankless surface air compressor pump and umbilical piping system that supplies air to a diving mask.
e: Borrowed from حقہ / हुक़्क़ा and, in turn, derived from Arabic حُقَّة (“pot, jar”), from حُقّ (“cavity, hollow”).

s: Having a sturdy construction or constitution.
Having a dull, blunt wit or mind; unintelligent.
The quality of artistry and persuasiveness in speech or writing.
e: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquency, directly from.

s: Of or relating to work normally performed by a servant.
Of or relating to unskilled work.
A servant, especially a domestic servant.
A person who has a subservient nature.
e: From Middle English meyneal, from Anglo-Norman mesnal, from maisnee (“household”), from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, from Latin mānsiō (“house”).

s: A boundary or border, especially of the Roman Empire.
Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable.
e: From Middle English abhomynable, from Old French abominable, from Late Latin abōminābilis (“deserving abhorrence”), from abōminor (“abhor, deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ōminor (“forebode, predict, presage”), from ōmen (“sign, token, omen”).

s: To interfere in or with; to concern oneself with unduly.
To interest or engage oneself; to have to do (with), in a good sense.
To mix (something) with some other substance; to commingle, combine, blend.
e: From Middle English medlen, from Anglo-Norman medler, from misculāre, derived from Latin misceō (“to mix”).

s: Characteristic of a burden; arduous or demanding.
In a usual or expected way; in characteristic manner.
Having a replacement crankshaft with a longer stroke than normal
An edible fish, of species Argyrosomus regius, of the family Sciaenidae, found from the Black Sea to the eastern Atlantic.
Deficient or inferior in amount, quality or extent
Of a set: such that, considered as a subset of a (usually larger) topological space, it is in a precise sense small or negligible.
Dry and harsh to the touch (e.g., as chalk).
e: From Middle English megre, borrowed from Anglo-Norman megre, Old French maigre, from Latin macer, macrum, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Cognate with Old English mæġer (“meagre, lean”), Dutch mager (“lean”), German mager (“lean”), Icelandic magur (“lean”).

s: To subject to bitter verbal abuse.
To dip in dilute sulfuric acid; to pickle.
e: From Middle English vitriol, from Old French vitriol, from Medieval Latin vitriolum (“sulfuric acid”), from vitrum (“glass”).

s: that produces or is accompanied with a hiss
The act by which something is unpacked.
The separation of the features of a segment, such as a nasal vowel or palatal consonant, into distinct segments.
A material with binder and aggregate that is used to coat interior walls or to make interior mouldings.
A material with binder and aggregate that is used to coat exterior walls or to make exterior mouldings.
A work made of stucco; stuccowork.
To coat or decorate with stucco.
e: Borrowed from Italian stucco (“coating made of pulverised gypsum, plaster, stucco”) from stucco, from stucki, *stucchi (“crust, fragment, piece”) from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją (“stump, piece”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to shock, butt, impact”). Akin to German Stück (“piece”), Old Saxon stukki (“piece, fragment”) and Old English stycce.

s: A bag or case with one or two shoulder straps, especially used to carry books etc.
e: First recorded circa 1340 as Middle English sachel, from Old French sachel, from Late Latin saccellum (“money bag, purse”), a diminutive of Latin sacculus, itself a diminutive of saccus (“bag”). See sack.

s: An expert in virtù or art objects and antiquities; a connoisseur.
Someone with special skill or knowledge; an expert.
Specifically, a musician (or other performer) with masterly ability, technique, or personal style.
Exhibiting the ability of a virtuoso.
e: Borrowed from Italian virtuoso, from Late Latin virtuōsus (“virtuous”), from Latin virtus (“excellence”). Doublet of virtuous.

s: monotonous; lacking significant or noteworthy events
Of a bristle, having split, bushy ends.
Of a swab, having dense fibers with a desirable nap to optimize collection and elution of specimens.
Of a Christmas tree, covered with artificial snow.
e: From flock (“tufts of wool, lock of hair”).

s: Having no interest or stake in the outcome, and no conflicts of interest; free of bias, impartial.
e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- From disinterest (“to cause to be impartial”) + -ed, or from dis- + interested (“having a stake in; showing interest”).

s: A small long, narrow boat with a high prow and stern, propelled with a single oar, especially in Venice.
A hanging platform or car for transporting people or cargo.
An enclosed car attached to a cable mechanically lifted up the side of a mountain; an enclosed ski lift; a cable car.
The car or basket of a hot-air balloon, airship, zeppelin, etc.
The hanging cart in which a glass-cleaning worker stands to clean exterior glass on tall buildings.
That part of a transporter bridge that carries passengers, vehicles, along the length of the bridge span.
A type of open railway car with low sides, used to carry heavy freight such as crushed rock or steel.
A free-standing display unit in a supermarket or other retail store, where goods are shelved or hung on pegs or hooks for sale; An end bay; A parasite display.
e: Borrowed from Italian gondola, from Venetian góndoƚa. Possibly from Byzantine Greek κοντοῦρα (“cutter, kind of ship”).
Borrowed from Middle French cursoire (“rapid”), from Latin cursorius (“hasty, of a race or running”).

s: The act of one who vies; rivalry.
the violin section of an orchestra
With a fine or fashionable appearance.
The state of being wicked; evil disposition; immorality.
A wicked or sinful thing or act; morally bad or objectionable behaviour.
e: Inherited from Middle English wikkednesse, wikkednes, equivalent to wicked + -ness.

s: To use up or waste; squander.
To cause energy to be lost through its conversion to heat.
e: The verb is, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765; from Middle English dissipaten, from Latin dissipātus, perfect passive participle of dissipō (see -ate and -ate), also written dissupō (“to scatter, disperse, demolish, destroy, squander, dissipate”), from dis- (“apart”) + supō (“to throw”). Doublet of dissipe, now obsolete.

s: The quality or state of being plastic.
The property of a solid body whereby it undergoes a permanent change in shape or size when subjected to a stress exceeding a particular value (the yield value).
Speaking openly and honestly, neglecting privacy and consequences.
the relative whiteness or transparency of a colour
The state of having little (or less) weight, or little force.
e: From Middle English lightnes, lightnesse, from Old English līhtnes, lȳhtnys (“enlightening, illumination”), from Proto-West Germanic *liuhtinassī; equivalent to light (“to make bright, illuminate”) + -ness. Cognate with Old High German liuhtnissi (“illumination, enlightening”).

From Middle English lightnes, lightnesse, from Old English *lēohtnes (“lightness”) (compare Old English lēohtmōdnes (“lightness”), līhtingnes (“lightness, alleviation”)); equivalent to light (“not heavy”) + -ness. Cognate with Middle Low German luchtnisse, lüchtnisse (“lightness, frivolity, joyfulness”).

s: That overpowers; so strong as to be overwhelming.
The process of something being overpowered.
The act by which something is combed.
Individual hairs that drop out when the hair is combed.
A creature with the head of a person and the body of an animal, commonly a lion.
A person who keeps their thoughts and intentions secret; an enigmatic or impassive person.
A mandrill (Mandrillus sphinx), formerly classified as a baboon, and called sphinx baboon.
To adopt the posture of the Sphinx.
To be inscrutable, often through silence.
To behave in a manner characteristic of the Sphinx.
e: From Sphinx, from Middle English Spynx, from Latin Sphinx, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ, perhaps either from σφίγγω (“to squeeze, to strangle”) (whence also sphincter), of origin, or from Egyptian šzp-ꜥnḫ (“divine image”).
