In Dutch, the word is instanced in a description of golf in an early seventeenth-century edition of Pieter van Afferden's Tyrocinium linguae latinae. All derive from Proto-Germanic *putōną.
Probable variant of pot or butt.

s: Someone who or something that gives up: Synonym of quitter.
To avoid (something) by moving suddenly out of the way.
To go, or cause to go, hither and thither.
To make an area of an image lighter (when processing photographs in a darkroom, this is accomplished by decreasing the exposure of that area to light).
To follow by dodging, or suddenly shifting from place to place.
A trick, evasion or wile. (Now mainly in the expression tax dodge.)
e: Likely from dialectal dodge, dod, dodd (“to jog, trudge along, totter", also "to jerk, jig”), of Uncertain origin.

s: to oppress, suppress, exploit, persecute, step down on; put down; denigrate, subjugate
A Boer who surrendered and joined the British during the Boer Wars.
e: From Afrikaans hensop or hendsop, a phonetic rendering of English hands up, + -er.

s: A bet; a stake; a pledge.
A contract by which two parties or more agree that a certain sum of money, or other thing, shall be paid or delivered to one of them, on the happening or not happening of an uncertain event.
To bet something; to put it up as collateral.
Agent noun of wage; one who wages.
e: From Middle English wajour, wageour, wager, from wageure, from wagier (“to pledge”) (compare Old French guagier, whence modern French gager and contemporary Walloon wadjî), ultimately from Frankish *waddjōn (“to pledge”), from Frankish *wadi ~ *waddī (“pledge”). See also wage.

s: To refuse; to offer sudden or harsh resistance; to turn down or shut out.
e: From obsolete French rebuffer, from Middle French rebuffer (compare French rebiffer (“to rise up, revolt”)), from Italian ribuffare.

s: Pertaining to utility or general purpose.
A small, blocky, military-style vehicle with four-wheel drive, suited to rough terrain.
A light utility truck from WWII used by the U.S. Army, and subsequently turned into the trademark Jeep when civilianized by originating manufacturer Willys-Overland.
A sport utility vehicle or similar four-wheel-drive vehicle.
A device for detecting discontinuity in a protective coating, also called a "holiday detector"
A covered shopping cart, also called a "shopping stroller".
A trans woman who is sexually attracted to women and transitioned due to autogynephilia.
e: Derived from GP, initialism of general-purpose. Noun from General Purpose Vehicle (military light utility truck).
Disputed. Possibly from Eugene the Jeep, a character in Popeye cartoons.
An ironic pronunciation of AGP, the initialism of autogynephilia in Blanchard's transsexualism typology.

s: A metric unit of mass equal to exactly 200 mg, chiefly used for measuring precious stones and pearls.
Any of several small units of mass used for measuring precious stones and pearls, equivalent to 189–212 mg.
A 24-point scale used to measure the purity of gold.
e: From Middle French carat, from Italian carato, from Arabic قِيرَاط (“carat, similarly small units such as inches”), from Ancient Greek κεράτιον (“hornlet, carob seed”), from κέρας (“horn”) + -ιον. Doublet of quilate, keratin.

s: Someone who binds books; a bookbinder.
A cover or holder for unbound papers, pages etc.
Something that is used to bind things together, often referring to the mechanism that accomplishes this for a book.
A software mechanism that performs binding.
A program or routine that attaches malware to an existing harmless file on the target system.
A machine used in harvesting which cuts the stalks of a crop and then ties them into a bundle or sheaf.
A chemical or other substance that causes two other substances to form into one.
A down payment on a piece of real property that secures the payor the right to purchase the property from the payee upon an agreement of terms.
Material or clothing used in binding or flattening the breasts.
The player who squats behind home plate and receives the pitches from the pitcher.
The bottom partner in a homosexual relationship or sexual encounter between two men.
The webbed glove that the goaltender wears on the hand opposite the hand that holds the stick.
A device that opens something; specifically a tin-opener/can-opener, or a bottle opener.
The player who starts the betting.
Cards of sufficient value to enable a player to open the betting.
A person employed to separate sheets of hot metal that become stuck together.
The first act in a variety show or concert.
A batsman or bowler who normally plays in the first two positions of an innings.
The first in a series of events, items etc.; the first remark or sentence of a conversation.
The first game played in a competition.
A period of time when it is legal to commercially fish.
A pitcher who specializes in getting the first outs of a game before being replaced, either by a long reliever or a pitcher who would normally start.
e: From Middle English oppinnare,opynnare, from Old English openere, equivalent to open + -er.

s: To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked.
A ball of fire, especially one associated with an explosion, or thrown as a weapon.
A bright glow caused by a spacecraft re-entering an atmosphere.
A meteor bright enough to cast shadows; a bolide.
A class of sailing dinghy with a single trapeze and a symmetrical spinnaker, sailed by a crew of two.
A bag or ball filled with combustible material which is thrown as a weapon or to set something alight.
A charge depicting a disc-shaped bombshell with flames emitted from the top, or sometimes from the top, bottom, and on either side.
An emanation of St. Elmo's fire; also, of ball lightning.
A ball of heat-resistant material placed in a fire to slow down the burning of the fuel.
A statement intended to cause dissension or as a provocation.
To attack (someone or something) with balls of fire.
To explode in a ball of fire or flame.
e: The noun is derived from fire + ball. The adjective and verb are derived from the noun.

s: One who imitates or plagiarizes the work of others.
A criminal who imitates the crimes of another; specifically, a criminal who commits the same crime, especially a highly-publicized one, that has recently been committed by someone else.
To act as a copycat; to copy in a shameless or derivative way.
Syn of rohypnol: flunitrazepam, a hypnotic drug (sleeping pill), sometimes used as a date rape drug.
To put roofies in; to spike with roofies.
To cause someone to (usually unknowingly) ingest roofies.
A person who is psychotic, psychopathic, or (broadly) otherwise insane.
A person who acts in a bizarre or dangerous manner.
A class, at a college or university, in which psychology is taught.
Someone who succumbs to authority, someone who excessively flatters or submits to authority figures in order to gain favor or secure a reward.
e: Said because the ass is considered vulgar and being willing to kiss another's is considered a sign of submission and patronage.

s: A ball or wad of semen or vaginal fluid.
Playing around; frolicking; originally, running about the rigging of a vessel for fun; horseplay.
A small piece of enclosed ground.
To eat with a feeble appetite.
To struggle; to work with great effort.
to bother or create work for.
An onerous and difficult task; a hardship.
A small pot with a lid.
To make a light, ringing, percussive sound.
A rectangular piece of processed fish coated in breadcrumbs that is cooked by frying or grilling.
A distich of Sanskrit verse, in which each line contains sixteen syllables.
A salutation, especially a drinking toast.
e: From chin-chin, a of 請 (“please”). Sometimes, especially in Italianate spellings, reborrowed from Italian cincin.
Duplication of chin in its various senses. Compare chinwag.

s: A member of a fraternity in a college or university.
To supply with more funds than necessary or appropriate
to; indicating opinion, advice, or instruction, about what is required or desirable.
Used to issue an instruction (traditionally seen as carrying less force of authority than alternatives such as 'shall' or 'must').
Used to give advice or opinion that an action is, or would have been, beneficial or desirable.
With verbs such as 'see' or 'hear', usually in the second person, used to point out something remarkable in either a good or bad way.
In questions, asks what is correct, proper, desirable, etc.
Indicates that something is expected to have happened or to be the case now.
Will be likely to (become or do something); indicates a degree of possibility or probability that the stated thing will happen or be true in the future.
Used to form a variant of the present subjunctive, expressing a state or action that is hypothetical, potential, mandated, etc.
An alternative to would with first person subjects.
Used to express a conditional outcome.
outside certain combinations such as with 'imagine' or 'think'
Used to impart a tentative, conjectural or polite nuance.
Used to express what the speaker would do in another person's situation, as a means of giving a suggestion or recommendation.
To suggest (that someone ought to do something, or that something ought to be the case) by, or as if by, using the word should.
Something that ought to be the case as opposed to already being the case.
e: From Middle English scholde, from Old English sċolde, first and third person preterite form of sċulan (“should,” “have to,” “to owe”), the ancestor of English shall. shall + -ed. Cognate with German sollen, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐌻𐌰𐌽, Swedish skulle. Related to Middle English shild and shildy.

s: Usually solid excretory product evacuated from the bowels; feces.
(the shit) The best of its kind.
A nasty, despicable person, used particularly of men.
The smallest amount of concern or consideration.
Any recreational drug (e.g. cannabis, heroin, etc.).
e: From Middle English schit, schyt, from Old English *sċite (“dung”) and sċitte (“diarrhoea”), from Proto-West Germanic *skiti and *skittjā, from Proto-Germanic *skitiz, from Proto-Indo-European *skeyd- (“to split, divide, separate”).
Cognate with West Frisian skite, Low German schieten, Dutch schijten, German scheißen, Danish skide.

s: A flat tortilla that has been fried or toasted, or a dish based on this, usually associated with the cuisine of Latin America.
A bowl-shaped tortilla that has been fried and filled with various ingredients.
A piece of Latin American toast (toasted bread).
The act by which an employee is hired.
A fair or market where servants were engaged.
The E string of a violin.
In piquet, a sequence of five playing cards of the same suit; equivalent to a straight flush in poker.
A vehicle used by firefighters that combines the capabilities of a fire engine and a fire truck, having the ability to provide vertical access as well as pump water to fight a fire.
quinte; the fifth fencer in parrying or attacking position.
—an expression of acknowledgment or affirmation, now sometimes used in an ironic or condescending sense.
e: Nasalized variant of okay. Perhaps popularized by Mr. Mackey's catchphrase in South Park. Earlier use is apparently chiefly in linguistic transcriptions of speech.

s: To inflect (a verb) for each person, in order, for one or more tenses; to list or recite its principal parts.
To multiply on the left by one element and on the right by its inverse.
To join together, to unite; to juxtapose.
To temporarily fuse, exchanging or transferring DNA.
Any entity formed by joining two or more smaller entities together.
More generally, any of a set of irrational or complex numbers that are zeros of the same polynomial with integral coefficients.
of an element of an extension field
Given a field extension L / K and an element α ∈ L, any other element β ∈ L that is another root of the minimal polynomial of α over K.
A word agreeing in derivation with another word, and therefore generally resembling it in meaning.
A weak and a strong antigen covalently linked together
United in pairs; yoked together; coupled.
Containing two or more radicals supposed to act the part of a single one.
Agreeing in derivation and radical signification; said of words.
e: The adjective (as “combined, united”) and noun are, in Middle English, the verb in 1530; partly from Middle English conjugat(e) (“combined, united”), partly directly Borrowed from New Latin coniugātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin coniugō (“to yoke together, combine; (New Latin) to conjugate, decline, inflect”) (see -ate), from con- (“with”) + iugō (“to join”).

s: A part of any of several scientific or measuring instruments that moves back and forth to indicate a position.
A moving icon or other representation of the position of the pointing device.
An indicator, often a blinking line or bar, indicating where the next insertion or other edit will take place.
A reference to a row of data in a table, which moves from row to row as data is retrieved by way of it.
A design pattern in object oriented methodology in which a collection is iterated uniformly.
To navigate by means of the cursor keys.
e: Borrowed from Latin cursor (“runner”), from currō (“run”) + -or. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European.

s: Any small-scale verbal or physical interaction between those of different races, cultures, beliefs, or genders that may have no malicious intent, but that can be interpreted as an aggression.
e: From micro- + aggression, Coined by Chester M. Pierce.

s: A species of penguin, Pygoscelis antarcticus, with a distinctive black strip under the head.
A group of five, particularly a tuplet of five notes to be played in the time for four.
One of a group of five, particularly babies born from the same mother during the same birth.
A cycle adapted for five riders, all of whom can assist in the propulsion.
A lump of something, especially earth or clay.
The ground; the earth; a spot of earth or turf.
A stupid person, a dolt, a clodpate, a clodhopper.
Part of a shoulder of beef, or of the neck piece near the shoulder.
To collect into clods, or into a thick mass; to coagulate; to clot.
e: From Middle English clod, a late by-form of clot, from Old English clot, from Proto-West Germanic *klott (“mass, ball, clump”). Compare clot and cloud; cognate to kloot (“clod”).

s: An expression used to show displeasure. A less emphatic, less profane version of dammit.
A secondary mineral deposit of calcium carbonate or other mineral, in shapes similar to icicles, that lies on the ground of a cave.
e: From New Latin stalagmītēs, from Ancient Greek στάλαγμα (“drop”) or σταλαγμός (“dripping”).

s: To pinch and pull with a sudden jerk and twist; to twitch.
To tease, to annoy; to get under the skin of (someone, typically so as to irritate them, or by extension to enamor, frighten, etc).
To abuse methamphetamines, especially crystal meth.
To exhibit extreme nervousness, evasiveness when confronted by authorities, compulsiveness, erratic motion, excitability, etc, due to or mimicking the symptoms of methamphetamine abuse.
To be extremely confused; to have no clue what is happening.
From a catapult, to strike a target with a missile.
A sharp pinch or jerk; a twist or twitch.
An additional input to a block cipher, used in conjunction with the key to select the permutation computed by the cipher.
e: From Middle English twikken, from Old English twiccian (“to pluck”), from Proto-West Germanic *twekkōn (“to fasten; clamp; pinch”). Related to twitch. The drug-related sense may be a blend of twitch and freak.

s: To admonish in blame; to reproach angrily.
To utter words of disapprobation and displeasure; to find fault; to contend angrily.
To make a clamorous noise; to chafe.
e: From Middle English chiden (“to chide, rebuke, disapprove, criticize; complain, grumble, dispute; argue, debate, dispute, quarrel”), from Old English ċīdan (“to chide, reprove, rebuke; blame, contend, strive, quarrel, complain”). Cognate with German kiden (“to sound”); Old High German kīdal (“wedge”).

s: To blather; to talk foolishly or incoherently.
To blab; to reveal a secret.
A person who blabs; a tattler; a telltale.
The number or expression written below the line in a fraction (such as 2 in ½).
One who gives a name to something.
e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēnōminātor (“that which names”)

s: Mutually dependent (especially of an unhealthy psychological relationship in which one person perpetuates another's addiction or harmful behaviour).
A person in such a relationship.
A person or thing that foreshadows or foretells the coming of someone or something.
One who provides lodgings; especially, the officer of the English royal household who formerly preceded the court when travelling, to provide and prepare lodgings.
To announce or precede; to be a harbinger of.
e: Originally, a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings. From Middle English herberjour, herbergeour, from Old French herbergeor (French hébergeur), from herbergier (“to set up camp; to shelter; to take shelter”) + -or, from Old High German heribergan, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu (“army camp, shelter”).

s: A doll made from cloth and stuffed with rags.
In reference to where a baby is carried, the abdomen, or specifically the womb, especially of a woman, but also of animals in general (usually mammals).
e: Imitating a child's attempt to say stomach, via archaic colloquialism stummy. Compare twee and pasghetti for similar phonetic reductions.

s: In a manner such that the face, front, or surface which is normally directed forward for viewing is positioned downward.
Having the face, front or surface positioned downward.
Any of several African mammals of the family Bovidae distinguished by hollow horns, which, unlike deer, they do not shed.
A fierce legendary creature said to live on the banks of the Euphrates, having long serrated horns and being hard to catch.
e: From Middle English antelope, from Old French antelop, from Medieval Latin antilops, from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ, which is of obscure origin.

s: A gymnastic and recreational device consisting of a piece of taut, strong fabric or rubber stretched over a (usually steel) frame using many coiled springs as anchors.
A competitive sport in which athletes are judged on routines of tricks performed on a trampoline.
Any of a variety of looping or jumping instructions in specific programming languages.
Any of a variety of indirection techniques in specific programming languages.
To jump (as if) on a trampoline.
To rewrite (computer code) to use trampoline instructions.
e: From Spanish trampolín and/or Italian trampolino; in English, a based on the Spanish word trademarked in 1936, but attested since 1798.

s: A rotund, overweight, or obese person.
A jibe used on someone disliked, frequently someone regarded as lazy.
One of the two tonsils that can be seen on the left and right sides at the back of the throat.
To be dismayed or worried about (someone), particularly because of their situation or what has happened to them.
e: From Middle English bemenen, bimenen, from Old English bemǣnan (“to bemoan, bewail, lament”); equivalent to be- (“about, concerning”) + moan. Alteration of vowel from Middle to Modern English due to analogy with moan.

s: False, especially of money; intended to deceive or carry appearance of being genuine.
Assuming the appearance of something; deceitful; hypocritical.
That which resembles another thing; a likeness; a portrait; a counterpart.
To falsely produce what appears to be official or valid; to produce a forged copy of.
To produce a faithful copy of.
Of a turn or river card, to invalidate a player's hand by making a better hand on the board.
e: From Middle English counterfeit, countrefet, from Anglo-Norman countrefait, from Old French contrefait, from Latin contra- (“against”) + Latin facere (“to make”)..

s: A ring or hoop suspended by a rope or strap from the saddle, for a horseman's foot while mounting or riding.
Any piece shaped like the stirrup of a saddle, used as a support, clamp, etc.
A portable, flexible ladder-like device used in climbing.
A rope secured to a yard, with a thimble in its lower end for supporting a footrope.
A bent rebar wrapped around the main rebars to reinforce against shear stress.
Referring to women's pants/trousers: being of a form, commonly worn by women, that includes a strap beneath the arch of the foot.
e: From Middle English stirop, stirope, from Old English stiġrāp (“stirrup”), a compound of stiġe ("ascent, descent, a going up or down"; related to stīġan (“to climb”)) and rāp (“rope”), equivalent to sty + rope.

s: The pungent aromatic rhizome of a tropical Asian herb, Zingiber officinale, used as a spice and as a stimulant and acarminative.
The plant that produces this rhizome.
Other species belonging to the same family, Zingiberaceae, especially those of the genus Zingiber.
A person with reddish hair; a redhead.
or can or bottle of such (especially if dry).
Any fizzy soft drink, or can or bottle of such; pop; soda.
Having hair or fur of this color.
To apply ginger to the anus of a horse to encourage it to carry its tail high and move in a lively fashion.
To inspire (someone); to give a little boost to.
Very careful or cautious; also, delicate, sensitive.
In a very careful or cautious manner; also, delicately, sensitively.
Slightly sexually suggestive; bordering on indelicate.
The probability of a negative outcome to a decision or event.
The magnitude of possible loss consequent to a decision or event.
The potential negative effect of an event, determined by multiplying the likelihood of the event occurring with its magnitude should it occur.
A possible adverse event or outcome.
A type of adverse event covered under an insurance policy.
A thing (from the perspective of how likely or unlikely it is to cause an adverse effect).
A borrower (such as a mortgage-holder or person with a credit card).
An entity insured by an insurer.
To incur risk of (an unwanted or negative outcome).
To incur risk of harming or jeopardizing.
To incur risk as a result of (doing something).
e: From earlier risque, from Middle French risque, from risco (“risk”) (modern Italian rischio) and rischiare (“to run into danger”). Displaced native Old English pleoh (“risk”) and plēon (“to risk”).

s: To cover (someone or something) with small marks or spots; to dapple, to freckle, to speckle.
Not showing proper respect; impertinent, impudent.
Physically active and healthy; robust, vigorous.
Often followed by for or to: eager to do something; also, quick to act when an opportunity arises; prompt.
e: From Middle English frecch, frecche (“bold, brave; fierce; greedy, voracious”), frek (“bold, brave; fierce; eager, zealous; fast, quick; greedy (?)”), from Old English frec, fræc (“audacious, bold; greedy”) from Proto-West Germanic *frek (“greedy”), from Proto-Germanic *frekaz (“greedy”), from Proto-Indo-European *preg- (“to covet; to yearn”).

s: To do with a place or places.
A road, a direction, a (physical or conceptual) path from one place to another.
A means to enter or leave a place.
A method or manner of doing something; a mannerism.
A set of values and customs associated with and seen as central to the identity of a group of people.
Possibility (usually in the phrases 'any way' and 'no way').
Determined course; resolved mode of action or conduct.
A tradition within the modern pagan faith of Heathenry, dedication to a specific deity or craft, Way of wyrd, Way of runes, Way of Thor etc.
A degree, an amount, a sense.
as the head of an interjectory clause, followed by an infinitive starting with "to"
Acknowledges that a task has been done well, chiefly in expressions of sarcastic congratulation.
The timbers of shipyard stocks that slope into the water and along which a ship or large boat is launched.
e: From Middle English way, wey, from Old English weġ, from Proto-West Germanic *weg, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Doublet of voe and possibly Doublet of via.
From the sound it represents, by analogy with other (velar) letters such as kay and gay#Etymology_2.

s: Formed with deliberation; carefully considered; not sudden or rash.
Of a person, weighing facts and arguments with a view to a choice or decision; carefully considering the probable consequences of a step; slow in determining.
To consider carefully; to weigh well in the mind.
To consider the reasons for and against anything; to reflect.
e: Inherited from Middle English deliberat, Borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate and -ate), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see librate. Doublet of deliber.

s: To break something down into its component parts.
To analyse in terms of deconstruction (a philosophical theory of textual criticism).
To question and reexamine the beliefs taught in one's religious upbringing.
To prepare (a dish) in an experimental way that presents the core ingredients separately.
The action of stopping operations; a closing, of a computer, business, event, etc.
A statement, insult, etc. that prevents the opponent from replying further.
An autistic response to stress or sensory overload, in which the individual freezes up and becomes silent, motionless, and unresponsive.
A defensive ploy that prevents the opposing players from attacking.
A big success; a hyped atmosphere.
Part of a website or other network where visitors can converse in typed messages.
To reduce in size or number.
To make into a mummy, by preserving a dead body.
The purchase of one company by another; a merger without the formation of a new company, especially where some stakeholders in the purchased company oppose the purchase.
The acquisition of a public company whose shares are listed on a stock exchange, in contrast to the acquisition of a private company.
A time or event in which control or authority, especially over a facility is passed from one party to the next.
An event at which teens gather in public and act out; a street takeover.
A systematic method of obtaining obedience.
A state of order based on submission to authority.
A set of rules regulating behaviour.
A punishment to train or maintain control.
A specific branch of knowledge, learning, or practice.
A category in which a certain art, sport or other activity belongs.
To train someone by instruction and practice.
To teach someone to obey authority.
To punish someone in order to (re)gain control.
e: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French descipline, from Latin disciplina (“instruction”), from discipulus (“pupil”), influenced by disco (“to learn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dek- (“(cause to) accept”).

s: To repair by stitching with thread or yarn, particularly by using a needle to construct a weave across a damaged area of fabric.
e: From Middle English dernen (“to keep secret, hide, conceal (a hole)”), from Old English diernan (“to hide, conceal”), from Proto-West Germanic *darnijan, from Proto-West Germanic *darnī (“hidden, secret”). Related to Old English dyrne, dierne (“secret”).

s: A tractor with caterpillar tracks and an attached blade for pushing earth and building debris for coarse preliminary surface grading, demolishing building structures, etc.

A member of a self-identified group of white US Southerners who colluded to influence outcomes of post-Reconstruction elections by intimidating, coercing and bullying black voters and legislators, including burning down houses and churches, flogging and murdering opponents.
e: Originally bull-dozer (1875, Louisiana, US), in the bullier and terrorizer sense; bulldoze + -er. The name for the earthmoving machine came later, figuratively, from that sense.

s: A simple, collapsible trap consisting of a circular net stretched across metal or plastic hoops, used for catching crabs.
An act or instance of lending, an act or instance of granting something for temporary use.
A sum of money or other property that a natural or legal person borrows from another with the condition that it be returned or repaid over time or at a later date (sometimes with interest).
The contract and array of legal or ethical obligations surrounding a loan.
The permission to borrow any item.
An area of uncultivated ground near a village or farmhouse.
e: From Middle English lone, lane, from Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave (over)”).
From Scottish Gaelic lòn (“marshy meadow”) (compare lèana (“wet meadow, marsh, meadow”)).

s: A motion of the limbs or body, especially one made to emphasize speech.
An act or a remark that serves as a formality or as a sign of attitude.
A motion made with a pointing device, or on a touchscreen, that is recognised by the system as a command.
The manner of carrying the body; position of the body or limbs; posture.
To make a gesture or gestures.
To express (something) by a gesture or gestures.
To accompany or illustrate with gesture or action.
To express or signal (to someone) by a gesture or gestures (to do something, go somewhere, etc).
e: From Medieval Latin gestūra (“a mode of action”), from Latin gerō (“to bear; (reflexive) bear oneself, behave, act”), past participle gestus. la:gestus + -ure.

s: To set back to the initial state.
To adjust; to set or position differently.
The act of resetting to the initial state.
The act of setting to zero.
A device, such as a button or switch, for resetting something.
That which is reset; printed matter set up again.
The cleaning and tidying of one's home. [https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy69x9wl2no]
The crime of knowingly and dishonestly receiving stolen goods, or harbouring an outlaw.
To receive and hide (stolen goods, or a criminal, etc.)
e: Borrowed from resett, from reset, from Anglo-Norman recet, recetter, from Latin receptus, receptāre. Compare receipt.

s: Any vegetable of certain species in the onion family.
e: Borrowed from French échalote, from Middle French eschalote, alteration of Old French eschaloigne, from Medieval Latin escalonia, from Latin ascalonia (cēpa) (“onion of Ashkelon”). Doublet of scallion.

s: A solemn promise to perform some act, or behave in a specified manner, especially a promise to live and act in accordance with the rules of a religious order.
To make a vow; to promise.
To declare publicly that one has made a vow, usually to show one's determination or to announce an act of retaliation.
e: Inherited from Middle English vowe, voue, that from Old French vut, in turn from Latin vōtum (“a promise, dedication, vow”), from vovēre (“to promise, vow”). Not related to avow. Doublet of vote.

s: Of or pertaining to a difference.
Dependent on, or making a difference; distinctive.
Having differences in speed or direction of motion.
Of or pertaining to differentiation or the differential calculus.
The differential gear in an automobile, etc.
A qualitative or quantitative difference between similar or comparable things.
One of two coils of conducting wire so related to one another or to a magnet or armature common to both, that one coil produces polar action contrary to that of the other.
A form of conductor used for dividing and distributing the current to a series of electric lamps so as to maintain equal action in all.

A quantity representing an infinitesimal change in a variable, now only used as a heuristic aid except in nonstandard analysis but considered rigorous until the 20th century; a fluxion in Newtonian calculus, now usually written in Leibniz's notation as \operatorname{d}\!x.

A function giving the change in the linear approximation of f at a point x over a small interval \Delta x or \operatorname{d}\!x, the function being called the differential of f and denoted \operatorname{d}\!f(x,\Delta x), \operatorname{d}\!f(x), or simply \operatorname{d}\!f.
Any of several generalizations of this concept to functions of several variables or to higher orders: the partial differential, total differential, Gateaux differential, etc.
The Jacobian matrix of a function of several variables.
of a smooth map <math>\phi</math> between smooth manifolds

The pushforward or total derivative of \phi: a linear map from the tangent space at a point x in \phi's domain to the tangent space at \phi(x) which is, in a technical sense, the best linear approximation of \phi at x; denoted \operatorname{d}\!\phi_x.
Any of several generalizations of the concept(s) above: e.g. the Kähler differential in the setting of schemes, the quadratic differential in the theory of Riemann surfaces, etc.
A musical instrument producing a sound when struck, similar to a bell (e.g. a tubular metal bar) or actually a bell. Often used in the plural to refer to the set: the chimes.
An individual ringing component of such a set.
A small bell or other ringing or tone-making device as a component of some other device.
The sound of such an instrument or device.
A small hammer or other device used to strike a bell.
To make the sound of a chime.
To cause to sound in harmony; to play a tune, as upon a set of bells; to move or strike in harmony.
To utter harmoniously; to recite rhythmically.
To make a rude correspondence of sounds; to jingle, as in rhyming.
e: From Middle English chymbe, chyme, probably from chimbe (“cymbal”), a back-formation from chimble, cimble, from Latin cymbalum; perhaps reinforced by a misinterpretation of a Middle English (from Old English ċimbala, ċimbal (“cymbal”)) as chymbe belle.

s: A medieval hammerlike weapon used in close combat.
To make something flat or flatter.
To press one's body tightly against a surface, such as a wall or floor, especially in order to avoid being seen or harmed.
To knock down or lay low.
To become flat or flatter; to plateau.
To be knocked down or laid low.
To make vapid or insipid; to render stale.
To reduce (a data structure) to one that has fewer dimensions, e.g. a 2×2 array into a list of four elements.
To combine (separate layers) into a single image.
A punk-derived subculture of people who predominantly dress in black and usually old fashioned clothing, associated with mournful and macabre music and attitudes.
A style of punk rock influenced by glam rock; gothic rock.
A person who is part of the goth subculture.
A member of any alternative subculture based around rock music.
Relating to goth music or people.
A piece, pattern, or sample, generally of cloth or a similar material.
A selection of such samples bound together.
A clump or portion of something.
A demonstration, an example, a proof.
A tag or other small object attached to another item as a means of identifying its owner; a tally; specifically the counterfoil of a tally.
To create a swatch, especially a sample of knitted fabric.
A channel or passage of water between sandbanks, or between a sandbank and a seashore.
e: From earlier Northern England dialectal swache (“the counterfoil or counterstock of a tally”) (1512); further etymology unknown. Cognate with Scots swach, swatch. Compare English swath, swathe. Compare also Old English swæcc (“taste; flavour; odour; fragrance”).
Unknown; originally used chiefly in the East of England.

s: Tending to create things, or having the ability to create; often, excellently, in a novel fashion, or any or all of these.
A type of set of natural numbers, related to mathematical logic.
Designed or executed to deceive or mislead.
A person directly involved in a creative process; a creator of creative content.
Artistic material used in advertising, e.g. photographs, drawings, or videos.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin creātīvus, from Latin creō. Equivalent to create + -ive. Displaced native Old English orþanclīċ.

s: To take hold (of), particularly with the hand.
To figuratively take hold of or grasp.
Of an emotion or situation: to have a strong effect upon.
To firmly hold the attention of.
A hold or way of holding, particularly with the hand.
Ability to resist slippage when pressed in contact with another object or surface.
A place to grip; a handle; the portion of a handle that the hand occupies.
A device, or a portion of one, that grasps or holds fast to something.
An apparatus attached to a car (e.g., cable car, funicular car, mine car) for clutching a traction cable.
Control, power or mastery over someone or something; a tenacious grasp; a holding fast.
A medium-sized bag or holdall for one's belongings, made of soft leather, canvas etc., and carried in the hand by two handles, one either side of the opening.
A visual component on a window etc. enabling it to be resized and/or moved by dragging with a mouse or finger.
(film or television production) A person responsible for handling equipment on the set.
As much as one can hold in a hand; a handful.
e: Verb from Middle English grippen, from Old English grippan, from a Proto-Germanic *gripjaną (compare Old High German gripfen); compare the related Old English grīpan, whence English gripe. See also grope, and the related Proto-Germanic *grīpaną.

From Middle English grip, grippe, gryppe (“a ditch, drain”), from Old English grēp (“a furrow, burrow”) and grēpe (“a furrow, ditch, drain”), from Proto-Germanic *grōpiz (“a furrow, groove”). Cognate with Middle Dutch grippe, gruppe (“ditch, drain”), greppe, Low German Gruppe (“ditch, drain”).

s: A vulture, Gyps fulvus; the griffin.
e: From Middle English gripe, from Old French gripe, from Latin gryps, grȳphus, from Ancient Greek γρῡ́ψ.

s: An organism which eats others of its own species or kind, especially a human who consumes human flesh.
e: Borrowed from Spanish caníbal, from caniba, the Taíno form recorded by Christopher Columbus for the Caribs, who were greatly feared. From an language, probably, and ultimately from *karipona (“person”). Doublet of Carib, caribe, Garifuna, Carijona, Kari'na, Caribbean.

s: An unborn or unhatched vertebrate showing signs of the mature animal.
A human embryo after the eighth week of gestation.
A line that is tangent to the velocity of flow of a fluid; equivalent to the path of a specific particle in that flow.
On a weather chart, a line that is tangent to the flow of the wind.
To design and construct the contours of a vehicle etc. so as to offer the least resistance to its flow through a fluid.
To simplify or organize a process in order to increase its efficiency.
A flattened portion of ground meat or a vegetarian equivalent, usually round but sometimes square in shape.
A pastry with various fillings and spices baked inside a flaky shell, often tinted golden yellow with an egg yolk mixture or turmeric.
e: From earlier meaning "small pie" from pattipan (“something baked in a small pan”), from French pâté (“liver paste, pâté”), from pâte (“pastry, dough, paste, batter”) + -é. Doublet of pastie//pasty, pâté and related to pasta and paste.

s: A person or thing that shakes, or by means of which something is shaken.
A container from which granular condiments are shaken so as to be sprinkled onto food.
One who holds railroad spikes while they are hammered.
A musical percussion instrument filled with granular solids which produce a rhythmic sound when shaken.
A kind of straight-sided, stackable glass for beer, soda, etc.
A foodstuff made by baking dough made from cereals.
Food; sustenance; support of life, in general.
A piece of embroidery; a braid.
e: From Middle English bred, breed, from Old English brēad (“fragment, bit, morsel, crumb", also "bread”), from Proto-West Germanic *braud, from Proto-Germanic *braudą (“bread”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; to brew”), from *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”).

From Middle English brede (“breadth, width, extent”), from Old English brǣdu (“breadth, width, extent”), from Proto-Germanic *braidį̄ (“breadth”). Cognate with Scots brede, breid (“breadth”), Dutch breedte (“breadth”), German Breite (“breadth”), Swedish bredd (“breadth”), Icelandic breidd (“breadth”).
Variant of braid, from Middle English breden, from Old English brēdan, breġdan (“to braid”).

s: A man set to watch: a man who keeps guard, especially one who guards a building, or the streets of a city, by night; any such person of any sex or gender.
A tree that bears wild apples.
To make (something old or outdated) up to date, or modern in style or function by adding or changing equipment, designs, etc.
To become modern in appearance, or adopt modern ways
Used to show encouragement or approval to a girl, woman or female animal.
A cry of encouragement; an accolade.
e: A variant pronunciation of That's the girl!, a cry of encouragement, especially to children and pet dogs.

s: A biological structure found in many animals that is used for locomotion and that is frequently a separate organ at the terminal part of the leg.
Specifically, a human foot, which is found below the ankle and is used for standing and walking.
The base or bottom of anything.
The part of a flat surface on which the feet customarily rest.
The end of a rectangular table opposite the head.
A short foot-like projection on the bottom of an object to support it.
A unit of measure equal to twelve inches or one third of a yard, equal to exactly 30.48 centimetres.
A unit of measure for organ pipes equal to the wavelength of two octaves above middle C, approximately 328 mm.
The end of a cigar which is lit, and usually cut before lighting.
The part of a sewing machine which presses downward on the fabric, and may also serve to move it forward.
The bottommost part of a typed or printed page.
The base of a piece of type, forming the sides of the groove.
e: From Middle English fot, fote, foot, from Old English fōt, from Proto-West Germanic *fōt, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. The plural feet is the result of i-umlaut in Proto-West Germanic *fōt, see more at Old English fōt. Doublet of pes, pie, pous.

s: A bog or fen; a peatland which is actively forming peat, such as an active bog or fen.
To cause or permit to become stuck in mud; to plunge or fix in mud.
To soil with mud or foul matter.
e: From Middle English mire, a borrowing from Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzijō, whence also Swedish myr, Norwegian myr, Icelandic mýri, Dutch (in placenames, for example Mierlo). Related to Proto-Germanic *meusą, whence Old English mēos, and Proto-Germanic *musą, whence Old English mos (English moss). Doublet of mizzy.
From Middle English mire, myre, from Old English *mīere, from Proto-West Germanic *miurijā, from Proto-Germanic *miurijǭ (“ant”), from Proto-Indo-European *morwís (“ant”).

s: To be very happy, be delighted, exult; to feel joy.
To have (someone) as a lover or spouse; to enjoy sexually.
e: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Doublet of rejoy. Compare French réjouir; Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire.

s: An institution where one can place and borrow money and take care of financial affairs.
A branch office of such an institution.
An underwriter or controller of a card game.
A fund from deposits or contributions, to be used in transacting business; a joint stock or capital.
The sum of money etc. which the dealer or banker has as a fund from which to draw stakes and pay losses.
In certain games, such as dominos, a fund of pieces from which the players are allowed to draw.
A safe and guaranteed place of storage for and retrieval of important items or goods.
A device used to store coins or currency.
A collection of instrument data on a digital synthesizer.
To deal with a bank or financial institution, or for an institution to provide financial services to a client.
To put into a bank (financial institution).
To conceal in the rectum for use in prison.
An edge of river, lake, or other watercourse.
e: Inherited from Middle English banke, from Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's bench or table”), from bank (“bench, counter”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to turn, curve, bend, bow”). Doublet of bench, banc, banco.

From Middle English bank, banke, from Old English *banca (“bench”) (attested in Old English hōbanca (“couch”) and Old English banc (“bank, hillock, embankment”), from Proto-West Germanic *bankō, from Proto-Germanic *bankô. Akin to Old Norse bakki (“elevation, hill”), Norwegian bakke (“slope, hill”).
From Middle English bank, banke, from Old French banc (“bench”), from Frankish *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). Akin to Old English benċ (“bench”).
Probably from French banc. Of origin, and akin to English bench.

s: Relating to the form or structure of something.
Proper, according to strict etiquette; not casual.
In accordance with a methodological framework with well-defined rules or laws; rigorous.
Relating to mere manipulation and construction of strings of symbols, without regard to their meaning.
An event with a formal dress code.
e: From Middle English formel, borrowed from Old French formel, from Latin fōrmālis, from fōrma (“form”); equivalent to form + -al.

s: An unsophisticated person from a working class background.
An Anglo-Celtic member of a lower socioeconomic group, stereotypically classified as wearing black jumpers or black concert T-shirts.
Any narrow water or creek, particularly a tranquil backwater.
e: Unknown. First appeared in Australia in the 1980s. Possibly in reference to supposedly unsophisticated people from remote outback places such as the Bogan River or Bogan Gate (cf. dubbo from Dubbo).
Uncertain. Perhaps a contraction of pokelogan influenced by bog (or bogue), or a logan + bog.

s: Any of the Papally-endorsed military expeditions undertaken by the Christians of Latin Europe in the 11th to 13th centuries to reconquer the Levant from the Muslims, as well as expeditions along the Baltic Sea and against the Cathars.
Any war instigated and blessed by the Church for alleged religious ends, papal-sanctioned military campaigns against infidels or heretics.
A grand, concerted effort towards some purportedly worthy cause.
A mass gathering in a political campaign or during a religious revival effort.
To go on a military crusade.
To make a grand concerted effort toward some purportedly worthy cause.
e: From French croisade, introduced into English (in the French spelling) by 1575. The modern spelling emerges,.

s: altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of humankind.
e: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία. phil- + -anthropy.

s: Not having the power of speech; dumb.
Not uttered; unpronounced; silent; also, produced by complete closure of the mouth organs which interrupt the passage of breath; said of certain letters.
Not giving a ringing sound when struck; said of a metal.
An actor who does not speak; a mime performer.
A person who does not have the power of speech.
A hired mourner at a funeral; an undertaker's assistant.
An object for dulling the sound of an instrument, especially a brass instrument, or damper for pianoforte; a sordine.
An electronic switch or control that mutes the sound.
An action of muting, especially in a discussion forum as a penalty for breaking rules.
To turn off the sound of.
To cause the content or messages of (a social media account, a website, etc.) to no longer appear on one's feed, trigger notifications, or similar, especially without fully blocking.
e: From Middle English muet, from Anglo-Norman muet, moet, Middle French muet, from mu (“dumb, mute”) + -et, remodelled after Latin mūtus.
From Middle French muetir, probably a shortened form of esmeutir, ultimately from Proto-Germanic.

s: To imagine or conceive something in a new way
A one-on-one competition in rapping or breakdance.
A general action, fight, or encounter, in which all the divisions of an army are or may be engaged; a combat, an engagement.
A division of an army; a battalion.
The main body of an army, as distinct from the vanguard and rear; the battalia.
To join in battle; to contend in fight
To fight or struggle; to enter into a battle with.
Of grass or pasture: nutritious to cattle or sheep; fattening, nourishing.
Of land (originally pastureland) or soil: fertile, fruitful.
To feed or nourish (someone or something).
To render (land, soil, etc.) fertile or fruitful.
e: From Middle English batel, batell, batelle, batayle, bataylle, borrowed from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (“fighting and fencing exercises”) from Latin battuō (“to strike, hit, beat, fight”), of Uncertain origin.
From batell, probably from Middle English *batel (“flourishing”), from Old English *batol (“improving, tending to be good”), from batian (“to improve, to get better”) + -ol (le).

s: To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.
To keep erect; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling.
To support by approval or encouragement; to vindicate; to confirm (something which has been questioned).
e: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold. Compare Dutch ophouden (“to stop, cease, hold up”), German aufhalten (“to stop, halt, detain”). Compare also Middle Low German upholt, Old Norse upphald (“uphold, support”).

s: A concrete margin along the edge of a road; a kerb (UK, Australia, New Zealand).
A raised margin along the edge of something, such as a well or the eye of a dome, as a strengthening.
Something that checks or restrains; a restraint.

A riding or driving bit for a horse that has rein action which amplifies the pressure in the mouth by leverage advantage placing pressure on the poll by means of the crown piece of the bridle and chin groove by means of a curb chain.
A sidewalk, covered or partially enclosed, bordering the airport terminal road system with adjacent paved areas to permit vehicles to off-load or load passengers.
A swelling on the back part of the hind leg of a horse, just behind the lowest part of the hock joint, generally causing lameness.
To furnish (a well etc.) with a curb; to restrain (a bank of earth, etc.) by a curb.
To bring to a stop beside a curb.
To damage vehicle wheels or tires by running into or over a pavement curb.
e: From Middle French courbe (“curve, curved object”), from Latin curvus (“bent, crooked, curved”). Doublet of curve.

s: A person who behaves in a conflicting or contradictory manner.
in teleosemantics, being a representation with both indicative and imperative content.
e: From Pushmi-pullyu, the name of a fictional animal with two heads at opposing ends of its body, along with very sharp horns on each side of the head, in Hugh Lofting's The Story of Doctor Dolittle.

s: An opening, usually covered by one or more panes of clear glass, to allow light and air from outside to enter a building or vehicle.
An opening, usually covered by glass, in a shop which allows people to view the shop and its products from outside; a shop window.
The shutter, casement, sash with its fittings, or other framework, which closes a window opening.
A period of time when something is available or possible; a limited opportunity.
Something that allows one to see through or into something.
A rectangular area on a computer terminal or screen containing some kind of user interface, displaying output and allowing input, often for a single task in a multitasking system.
A figure formed of lines crossing each other.
The time between first infection and detectability.
A function multiplied with a signal to reduce spectral leakage when performing a Fourier transform.
A fenster: a geologic or tectonic window.
To place at or in a window.
To apply a window function to (a signal).
A musical instrument, endemic to the Top End of Australia, consisting of a long hollowed-out log which, when blown into, produces a low, deep mesmerising drone with sweeping rhythms.
e: Likely in reference to the sound made by the instrument, or the words spoken into the instrument to play it. The earliest known description of the instrument was in 1829 by Captain Collet Barker, in which it was described as making the sound didoggerry whoan.

s: To dismiss (someone, especially military personnel) from service.
One who works at a till or receives payments.
Person in charge of the cash of a business or bank.
To work as a cashier (at a till or receiving payment).
e: From Dutch casseren, kasseren, from Old French casser (“to break (up)”). During a ceremonial cashiering of a ranking military officer, the breakup was often symbolized dramatically by literally breaking the officer’s sword.
Borrowed from Dutch cassier or French caissier, from French caisse.

s: A storm characterized by lots of large hail.
To break a promise or commitment; to go back on one's word.
To break one's commitment to follow suit when capable.
e: Borrowed from Latin renegō, from negō (“to deny”). Possibly influenced by renegotiate. Doublet of renay. See also renegade.

s: An area where gold ore is found
that is suitable for farming and agricultural production.
Covered with fur, or with something resembling fur.
Of or related to the furry fandom, a subculture defined by an interest in anthropomorphic animal characters.
Someone who identifies with or as an animal character with human-like characteristics (an anthropomorphic animal character).
An anthropomorphic animal character of this kind.
Any member of the furry fandom or subculture (including those without fursonas).

e: Late 15th century, from fore- + beer (“one who is or exists”).

s: Everyone who comes to a given event.
Of, or relating to the fusion of atomic nuclei at high temperatures.
Of, or relating to the use of atomic weapons based on such fusion, especially as distinguished from those based on fission.
A foolish, incompetent, awkward, or contemptible person.
A dense, baked or fried flatbread made of cornmeal.
Something used to moisten, especially a cosmetic.
Characterized by the presence of moisture; not dry; slightly wet; damp.
Of eyes: wet with tears; tearful; also, watery due to some illness or to old age.
Of a climate, the weather, etc.: damp, humid, rainy.
Of the vagina: sexually lubricated due to sexual arousal; of a woman: sexually aroused, turned on.
Characterized by the presence of some fluid such as mucus, pus, etc.

a clear broth made from reduced meat or vegetable stock, served either hot as a soup or chilled as a jelly

e: From Cantonese 金橘 or 金桔. Related to loquat – same second character.

s: A coop where hens are kept.

The open counter (negative space) formed by two downward strokes that meet at an internal acute angle, potentially above a vertex, as in the letters "V" and "Y".

To shoplift or smuggle by hiding between one's thighs or in one's underwear.

A combination of outcomes (not a permutation) that a gambler bets on in the football pools.

Having less than an expected standard of familiarity with language and literature, or having little formal education.

Ignorant in a specified way or about a specified subject.

e: In Middle English; from Middle English illiterat(e) (“uneducated, ignorant of Latin”), borrowed from Latin illīterātus, illitterātus (“unlearned, ignorant”), itself from in- (“un-”) + līterātus, litterātus (“furnished with letters”) (see -ate), from lītera, littera (“letter, character”).

s: Situated or occurring on the summit of a mountain.

Any semi-aquatic, carnivorous mammal in the Mustelinae subfamily, similar to weasels, with dark fur, native to Europe and America, of which two species in different genera are extant: the American mink (Neogale vison) and the European mink (Mustela lutreola).
The fur or pelt of a mink, used to make apparel.
An article of clothing made of mink.
A person with poor personal hygiene; a smelly person.
e: From Late Middle English mynk (“fur of the European mink”), apparently from Swedish mink, mänk, menk (“stinking animal in Finland, mink”). Compare Danish mink (“mink”), Icelandic minkur (“mink”).

s: A short rope used for fastening rigging, as a handle, etc.
A cord worn around the neck, shoulder, or wrist which is attached to a small object to be carried such as an identity card or security pass, key, knife, or whistle.
A craft activity done by intricately braiding thin colored plastic lines to make patterns, or the product of such a craft.
A cord with a hook which is secured to an artillery piece, and pulled to fire the weapon.
A civil servant or mid-level bureaucrat, viewed as officious and overly concerned with social justice.
e: Old Dutch gmw-pro From late Middle English lainer, lainere, lanyer (“strap or thong used to fasten armour”) (with the ending modified in the 17th century under the influence of yard), from Old French laniere, lasniere (“thong, lash”) (see modern French lanière (“lanyard, strap”)).

s: A confusion, mistake, muddle or misunderstanding.
An occasion on which something stirs or is stirred
A baked dish made from beaten egg whites and various other ingredients, usually prepared and served in a small earthenware bowl (ramekin).
Decorated with very small drops or sprinkles of colour, as if blown from a bellows.
To treat analogously to the way one prepares a soufflé.
To whirl around or beat violently.
To give a light, airy, and/or fluffy texture to, especially if done by whipping or blowing.

A person qualified to make or repair boilers.
A whiskey with a beer chaser.
A tube of fried pastry filled with ricotta.
A very small thing; something tiny or insignificant.
A variant of oom-pah played in triple time.
Extremely precise or specific, especially regarding location.
To identify or locate (someone or something) precisely or with great accuracy.
One of a set of small cylindrical tubes used to curl hair.
A pass or a shot of the ball which swerves.
A wave which breaks with a barrel
A drink made from alcoholic liquor (usually whisky) mixed with sugar, spice and hot water.

e: From Middle English jutten (“to project, jut out”), an alteration of jetten (“to strut, be showy”). More at English jet.

s: An outline, boundary or border, usually of curved shape.
A line on a map or chart delineating those points which have the same altitude or other plotted quantity: a contour line or isopleth; (metonymically) the landform or its surface.
A speech sound that functions as a single segment while exhibiting an internal transition between distinct phonetic qualities, places of articulation, or manners of articulation.
A general description giving the most important points.
To form a more or less curved boundary or border upon.
To practise the makeup technique of contouring.
To shape conditions regarding salient points.
e: Borrowed from French contour, from contourner, equivalent to con- + tour.

s: To paint anew or again, especially if recently painted.
To draw or render again on the display.
The act or process of painting something again, especially if recently painted.
The act of drawing or rendering again on the display.

e: From Old Norse fylja (whence Danish føl), related to Doublet of foal. Cognate with Dutch veulen, German Fohlen.

s: To go aboard a craft or vessel for transportation.
To cause to go on board a vessel or boat; to put on shipboard.
To engage, enlist, or invest (as persons, money, etc.) in any affair.
To cover or enclose with bark.
e: Borrowed from Middle French embarquer, from em- + barque (“small ship”). Compare with Portuguese embarcar, Spanish abarcar.

s: To distribute or arrange methodically; to work over and classify; to reduce to portions for ready use or application.

To separate (the food) in its passage through the alimentary canal into the nutritive and nonnutritive elements; to prepare, by the action of the digestive juices, for conversion into blood; to convert into chyme.
To think over and arrange methodically in the mind; to reduce to a plan or method; to receive in the mind and consider carefully; to get an understanding of; to comprehend.
To bear comfortably or patiently; to be reconciled to; to brook.
To expose to a gentle heat in a boiler or matrass, as a preparation for chemical operations.
To cut with one or more restriction endonucleases.
To suppurate; to generate pus, as an ulcer.
To cause to suppurate, or generate pus, as an ulcer or wound.
To quieten or reduce (a negative feeling, such as anger or grief).
That which is digested; especially, that which is worked over, classified, and arranged under proper heads or titles.
A compilation of statutes or decisions analytically arranged; a summary of laws.
Any collection of articles, as an Internet mailing list including a week's postings, or a magazine arranging a collection of writings.
The result of applying a hash function to a message.
e: From Middle English digesten, from Latin dīgestus, past participle of dīgerō (“carry apart”), from dī- (for dis- (“apart”)) + gerō (“to carry”), influenced by Middle French digestion. Partly displaced native Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both “to melt, to digest,” whence Modern English melt.
From Latin dīgesta, neuter plural of dīgestus, past participle of dīgerō (“separate”).

s: Intermittent crushing chest pain caused by reversible myocardial ischemia.
Of a person or animal, or their behaviour: calm and composed (often in a dignified manner), and avoiding or unaffected by activity or excitement.
Of an object, particularly a building: not overly ornate or showy; not having a strong colour or design.
Of writing: not emotional; calm, composed.
To give (a person) a sedative to calm them or put them to sleep; to tranquilize.
To make (someone or something) calm or tranquil; to assuage, to calm, to soothe.
e: The is derived from Late Middle English sedate (“not painful or sore”), and directly from its Latin sēdātus (“calm, quiet, composed”), participial adjective from sēdō (“to allay, appease, calm, settle; to end, stop”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”). Compare English -ate.

s: To shake with small, rapid movements to and fro.
To brandish; to swing to and fro.
To mark or measure by moving to and fro.
To affect with vibratory motion; to set in vibration.
To pleasure someone using a vibrator.
The setting, on a portable electronic device, that causes it to vibrate rather than sound any (or most) needed alarms.
e: The adjective (then also used as a participle) is, in Middle English, the verb in 1620; partly from Middle English vibrat(e) (“reverberant”), partly directly Borrowed from Latin vibrātus, perfect passive participle of vibrō (“to agitate, set in tremulous motion”) (see -ate), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyp- (“to oscillate, swing”) or *weyb-.

s: Something that is beneficial to the body.
A person who is a member of a panel.

e: From the Termes, from Late Latin termes, late variant of Classical Latin tarmes (“woodworm”).

The snap of the ball to start a play.
A sharp upward tug to raise something.
To take a long walk (on something) for pleasure or exercise.
To unfairly or suddenly raise a price.
To snap the ball to start a play.
To lean out to the windward side of a sailboat in order to counterbalance the effects of the wind on the sails.
To pull up or tug upwards sharply.
Let's go; get moving. A command to a dog sled team, given by a musher.
e: From English dialectal hyke (“to walk vigorously”), probably a Northern form of hitch, from Middle English hytchen, hichen, icchen (“to move, jerk, stir”). Cognate with Scots hyke (“to move with a jerk”), dialectal German hicken (“to hobble, walk with a limp”), Danish hinke (“to hop”).

s: To labour about; labour over; to work hard upon; to ply diligently.
To discuss or explain (something) excessively or repeatedly; to harp on or overelaborate.
The sound of the call of one of these birds.
e: Onomatopoeic; for the pronunciation /ˈpjuːɪt/ and corresponding form pewit, compare leeward, Seward, steward.

s: A latticework used to shape or train the branches of a tree or shrub into a two-dimensional ornamental or useful design, as along a wall or fence.
A plant that has been shaped in this manner.
A row of plants that have been shaped in this manner.
To train a plant in this manner.
e: Borrowed from French espalier, from Italian spalliera, from spalla (“shoulder”).

s: Of an aircraft or ship: having large operational range.
A traditional Russian pastry made from a yeast dough and shaped into a twisted or braided ring.
Roe of the sturgeon or of certain other large fish, considered a delicacy.
A food preparation made through the spherification of a flavorful liquid, resulting in small roe-like balls similar in texture and appearance to caviar.
Something whose flavor is too fine for the vulgar taste.
e: Borrowed from Middle French caviar, from Venetian caviaro (earlier found as Italian caviale), probably by way of Ottoman Turkish خاویار, from خَاوْیَار. Doublet of ajvar.

Of or pertaining to neurasthenia; that is, tendencies of a person who has suffered a nervous breakdown.

A repetitive ping, knock, or similar sound coming from an engine in which there are repeated uncontrolled explosions in the combustion chamber.
A woman holding a baronial title in her own right; a female ruler of a barony.
To undo the result of brushing.
To obtain something by wit or guile; to convince people to do something they might not normally do.
A circular frame on which cadgers carry hawks for sale.
To carry hawks and other birds of prey.
To hawk or peddle, as fish, poultry, etc.
e: From Middle English caggen (“to tie, fasten, bind”), probably from Old Norse. Compare Old Norse kǫgurr (“quilt”), kǫgurbarn (“swaddled child”).

To turn (meat) into a rissole or rissoles.
To reject or eject; to get rid of.

e: From Middle English lustre, from Latin lustrum, from Old Latin *loustrom, of Uncertain origin. More at lustrum.
From Latin lustra (“wilds, woods”), thought to derive from unattested *dustrum, from unattested Ancient Greek *δύστρον (“place animals wallow”), from δύω (“to plunge, to wallow”).

Anything, such as a burgee, of a similar forked shape.
A type of tailcoat with two long tapering tails.
Any of various butterflies of the family Papilionidae, many of which have a long extension to each hindwing.
Fastidious and fussy, especially when eating.
A fancy cookie, pastry, or square, frequently homemade, served at a social event.
e: From Middle English deynte (as noun), from Old French deintié, from Latin dignitātem. Doublet of dignity.

A win by a previous loser.
To take revenge for (a particular harmful action) or on behalf of (its victim); to avenge.

To take vengeance; to revenge itself.
e: From Middle French revenge, a derivation from revenger, from Old French revengier (possibly influenced by Old Occitan revènge (“revenge, comeback”), from Old Occitan revenir (“to come back”)), a variant of Middle French revancher (whence deverbal French revanche), from Old French revenchier.
From Middle English revengen, from Old French revengier, revenger.

s: The power to attract, entice; the quality causing attraction.
The walkway along the top of a castle wall, sometimes entirely covered and normally behind a parapet; the wall walk.
e: From Middle English aluren, from Old French aleurer, alurer, from a (“to, towards”) (Latin ad) + leurre (“lure”). al-#Etymology_2 + lure.
From Middle English alure, alour, from Old French alure, aleure (“walk, gait”), from aler (“to go”) + -ure.

by confusion of the similar words

A newly sprouted leaf or blossom that has not yet unfolded.

Potent cannabis taken from the flowering part of the plant (the "bud"), or marijuana generally.
Cannabis that has been taken from the flowering part of the plant intended to be smoked.
A weaned calf in its first year, so called because the horns are then beginning to bud.
To reproduce by splitting off buds.
To begin to grow, or to issue from a stock in the manner of a bud, as a horn.
To be like a bud in respect to youth and freshness, or growth and promise.
To put forth as a bud.
To graft by inserting a bud under the bark of another tree.
Synonym of guy, term of address for a man or person.
e: From Middle English budde, bodde (“bud, seed pod”), from Old English *budde, from Proto-West Germanic *buʀdā, from Proto-Germanic *buzdǭ (compare archaic German Butte (“rosehip”), Swedish dialect bodd (“head”)), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bu- (“to swell”).

s: To graciously give, to condescendingly grant a right, benefit, outcome, etc.; to deign to acknowledge.
To receive or accept in condescension.
e: From vouch + safe, written as two words in Middle English and early Modern English.

e: From Middle English hochepoche, a variation of hochepot, from Old French hochepot, from hocher (“to shake”) + pot (“pot”), of Dutch or German origin. Equivalent to hotch + pot. Compare Dutch hutspot and Low German Hüttspott (“hodgepodge”).

s: A crystalline alkaloid (4,5-epoxy-17-methyl-7,8-didehydromorphinan-3,6-diol), extracted from opium, the salts of which are soluble in water and are used as analgesics, anaesthetics and sedatives; it is one of a group of morphine alkaloids.
e: Borrowed from French morphine or German Morphin, from Ancient Greek Μορφεύς (“the god and personification of dreams”).

s: Any of various small terrestrial isopod crustaceans of suborder Oniscidea, having a rigid segmented exoskeleton, usually feeding on dead plant matter and living in damp, dark places, such as under stones or bark. Several common species roll into a ball when disturbed, hence names such as pill bug an

e: From Middle English beseken, equivalent to be- + seek. Cognate with Scots beseik (“to beseek”). be- + seek. Doublet of beseech.

The action of saying something to persuade, encourage, or remind someone to do or say something.
The action of inputting prompts to an artificial intelligence system.
To make (something) diverse or varied in form or quality; to give variety to (something) to distinguish by numerous aspects or differences.
To make the scope of (business, investments, etc.) diverse, especially so as to balance and mitigate risks.
e: Borrowed from Middle French diversifier, equivalent to diverse + -ify.

s: Given as an honor, with no duties attached, and without payment.

A person who holds an honorary appointment.
A kind of secret society that operates in name only, with membership given to honor some achievement.
An honorarium; a fee for services of no fixed value.
e: From honor + -ary, modelled after French honoraire, from Latin honōrārius.

To shackle or bind up with fetters.
To restrain or impede; to hamper.
e: From Middle English feter, from Old English feter, Proto-West Germanic *fetur, from Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”). Related to foot.

A small intricate piece of metalwork.
e: Borrowed from bijou, ultimately from Occitan pichon (“small, little”), influenced by English bijou (“jewel”).

e: From Middle English cipres, from Old French cipres (French cyprès), from Late Latin cypressus; compare Hebrew גֹּפֶר, the name of the tree whose wood was used to make the ark (Genesis. vi:14), also κύπρος (relating to aromatic pitch).

A small unit of cavalry or armour commanded by a captain, corresponding to a platoon or company of infantry.

A particular roll of the drum; a quick march.
To move in numbers; to come or gather in crowds or troops.
To march on; to go forward in haste.
To move or march as if in a crowd.
e: Attested in English since 1545, from French troupe, from Back-formation from troupeau, from Middle French trope, troupe, from Old French trope, trupe, of unknown origin. Compare troppus. Doublet of troupe, and possibly also of Doublet of thorp, dorp, trip. Cognate with German Dorf (“village”).

s: A man very concerned about his physical appearance, refined language, and leisurely hobbies, pursued with the appearance of nonchalance in a cult of self.
A yawl, or a small after-sail on a yawl.
A horse-drawn railway carriage used on some branch lines.
Very good; better than expected but not as good as could be.
A Shaiva mendicant who carries a small rod.
An open sedan chair formed by suspending a rudimentary frame or strong cloth from a pole or set of poles.
e: Borrowed from Scots dandy (“a fop; one who is well-dressed”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Dandy, a diminutive of Andrew, yet the Scots word is used also in reference to women. Alternatively, possibly a back-formation of Scots dandilly, dandillie (“one who is spoiled or pampered; a "pet"”). Compare English dandle and dander.
From Hindi डंडी (“rod, pole”), from 𑀟𑀁𑀟𑀺𑀕𑀸, from Sanskrit दण्डिका, from दण्ड + -इका.

s: Alternative form of dandy, a kind of litter or sedan chair.
A bowed bass instrument held between the knees.
e: Clipping of violoncello, the original name, from Italian violoncello (“little violone”), from violone (“an early form of the double bass”) + -cello (“-elle”), violone (“big viola”) itself being derived from viola + -one (“-oon”).

s: To undo the asking of (a question).
A legal instrument that conveys real estate to an heir under the terms of a will.
e: From Middle English assent and assenten, from Old French assent and assentir, from Latin assentiō (whence as-#Etymology_2).

s: A smooth, chewy, sticky confection made by heating sugar and other ingredients until the sugars polymerize and become sticky.
A (sometimes hardened) piece of this confection.
A yellow-brown color, like that of caramel.
e: Borrowed from French caramel, from Spanish caramelo, from Portuguese caramelo, dissimilated from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”) (and a Doublet of chalumeau, shawm). Alternatively from Medieval Latin cannamellis, which is a compound of canna + mellis.

s: The act of anticipating, taking up, placing, or considering something beforehand, or before the proper time in natural order.
The eagerness associated with waiting for something to occur.
Prepayment of a debt, generally in order to pay less interest.
A non-harmonic tone that is lower or higher than a note in the previous chord and a unison to a note in the next chord.
e: From Middle English anticipacioun, from Middle French anticipation and its etymon Latin anticipātiō, anticipātiōnem. anticipate + -ion.

s: Any of various deciduous trees of the genus Populus.
e: From Middle English popler, from Anglo-Norman popler and Old French poplier (compare French peuplier), from Latin pōpulus, with a suffix later added.

A small group of individuals in very close proximity to one another.
A session in which a group of journalists assemble in an informal, dense cluster to question a person of interest.
A brief meeting of all the players from one team that are on the field with the purpose of planning the following play.
A hesitation during play to think about one's next move.
To curl one's legs up to the chest and keep one's arms close to the torso; to crouch; to assume a position similar to that of an embryo in the womb.
To get together and discuss a topic.
To crowd (things) together; to mingle confusedly; to assemble without order or system.
To do, make, or put, in haste or roughly; hence, to do imperfectly; usually with a following preposition or adverb (huddle on, huddle up, huddle together).
To hesitate during play while thinking about one's next move.

The act of carrying, conveying, transporting or sweeping along by force of movement; the force of such movement; the fact of being carried along by such movement.
A spasm; a fit; a syncope; delirium.

To experience great happiness or excitement.

To take part in the Rapture; to leave Earth and go to Heaven as part of the Rapture.
To state (something, transitive) or talk (intransitive) rapturously.
e: Borrowed from Middle French rapture, from Latin raptūra, future active participle of rapiō (“snatch, carry off”).

Pertaining to (or, especially of a language: spoken in) in an area which is at a lesser elevation, closer to sea level (especially near the sea), than other regions.
Of less than normal height or upward extent or growth, or of greater than normal depth or recession; below the average or normal level from which elevation is measured.
Not high in status, esteem or rank, dignity, or quality. (Compare vulgar.)
Lacking health or vitality, strength or vivacity; feeble; weak.
