e: From Middle English doucet, from Old French doucet, from dulz, dulce (“sweet, pleasant”) + diminutive -et, from Latin dulcis (“sweet, pleasant”). Cognate with Spanish dulce, French doux, Italian dolce, Portuguese doce, and Romanian dulce. Doublet of dolcetto, doucet.

s: A valve or movable plate in the flue or other part of a stove, furnace, etc., used to check or regulate the draught of air.
A contrivance (sordine), as in a pianoforte, to deaden vibrations; or, as in other pieces of mechanism, to check some action at a particular time.
A device that decreases the oscillations of a system.
Bread made from a basic recipe of flour, water, milk and salt, but without yeast.
e: From damp + -er. The name of the type of bread is, and originally likely refers to damping the appetite.

s: Speaking or spoken with a drawl.
In an educated and knowledgeable manner.
The act of causing fertilised eggs to lose viability, by killing the developing embryo within through shaking, piercing, freezing or oiling, without breaking the shell or other outer layer.
Failure to notice; failure to be aware of; lack of apprehension.
the state or the quality of being radical.
Resembling or characteristic of a pug dog.
A revolver with a barrel length of 3 inches (76.2 mm) or less.
To remove the string or strings from.
To shake the nerves of; to cause anxiety or panic in.
To remove from a string; to release something that has been strung up or strung together.
To split (a text string) into smaller strings by separating on a delimiter.
Any of a series of oxides of a particular metal that has the fewest atoms of oxygen per molecule
A type of wall plaster that is a byproduct of the manufacture of asbestos from serpentine.
An act of doing more than is required.
An action that is neither morally forbidden nor required, but has moral value.
e: From Late Latin superērogātiō (“payment in addition”), from superērogāre (“to pay in addition”), from super (“in addition to”) + ērogāre (“to pay, pay out, expend, disburse”), equivalent to supererogate + -ion.

s: Having to do with the psyche.
The state or fact of being nothing; nothingness, nullity; nonexistence.
To undo or remove the incorporation of.
The state or quality of being stertorous.
The state of being guiltless; innocence.
The state or quality of being cadaverous.
Trembling caused by fear or nervous agitation.
Incapable of being reclaimed; not reclaimable.
Spurious; substituted for the genuine, counterfeit; fake.
The state of being wan; pallor.
The state or quality of being collected.
Not awed; not afraid, impressed or in awe.
In a cadaverous manner; like a cadaver.
The degree or property of being extreme.
The act of thinking, thinking about, considering, reflecting, or remembering.
e: From Middle English bythenkynge, from Old English *beþenċende (compare Old English þenċende, ymbþenċende), equivalent to bethink + -ing.

s: A machine for drilling or tunneling underground.
Situated in or moving towards the west.
The property or state of being tremulous.

e: From Middle English by-sprenkled, be-spryngeld, besprengild, equivalent to be- (“on, about, around, upon, all over”) + sprinkled.

s: The state or quality of being definitive.
A metaphysical approach to a subject.
The state or quality of being alimentive.
The instinct or faculty of appetite for food.
e: 1828, George Combe, from a German term coined by Johann Spurzheim.

s: The state or quality of being amative; propensity to love or sexual feelings.
Covered with verdure; green and lush; verdant.
The motion of something that welters; a billowing.
Dressed or ornamented in a gaudy, showy, or tasteless manner; ostentatious.
A leaf, often of tissue paper or other thin paper, inserted between the pages of a book to protect illustrations.
A sheet of paper or cardboard, placed between layers on a pallet to create a cohesive structure.
scored for too many instruments (or types of instrument)
A decorator; one who provides decor.
The state or condition of being interminable.
The quality or state of being wearisome; tiresomeness; tediousness.
The act of removing the contents of something; the state of being empty.
A state of advanced lack of adequate nutrition, food, or water or a physiological inability to utilize them, with resulting weakness.
A spiritual emptiness or lack of purpose or will to live, akin to nausea in existentialist philosophy.
e: From Middle English inanicioun, borrowed from Old French inanition, itself borrowed from Late Latin inānītio, from inānīre (“to make empty”), from inānis (“empty, vain”); see inane.

s: In an unresisting manner; without objection or opposition.
Not having been shaped or molded.
An earnest affirmation; a declaration of support.
Utter darkness, without any ray of light.
In the native state, before being worked on; especially used of bars of bullion and other metal
e: From Middle English unwrought, unwroght, unwrouȝt, equivalent to un- + wrought. Doublet of unworked.

s: Occurring before or in preparation for a concert
Something concerted or arranged beforehand; a previous agreement.
To concert or arrange beforehand; to settle by previous agreement.
In a sagacious manner, in a way that is clever, shrewd, observant, keen of intellect or discernment, cunning or with ability and aptitude; sagely.
Involving the danger of death; fatal, deadly.
Resembling or pertaining to death; deathly.
The state or quality of being unpicturesque.
Having an ermine tincture in a colour other than black and white.

e: Equivalent to blossom + -y; possibly from Middle English blosmy (from Old English blōstmig).

s: Any member of the genus Bignonia of flowering plants in the catalpa family.
A type of cotton cloth, especially as dyed and waterproofed.
e: From Hindi जगन्नाथ / Urdu جگنّاتھ, former name of Puri in India, where the material came from. Compare juggernaut.

s: In a clerical manner; as a cleric.
The state or quality of being affectionate.
Relating to the fauces, or opening of the throat; faucial.
A sound produced in the fauces.
The quality of being profuse; profusion
A behaviour or manner that is characteristic of a coxcomb; a foppish behaviour.
Behaviour or airs characteristic of a coxcomb; foppishness.
In a stubbornly resolute manner; tenaciously holding one's course of action or opinion.
e: From pertinacious + -ly, from Latin pertināx, from per- (“very”) + tenāx (“tenacious”), from teneō (“to hold”).

s: In a supine way, with the head facing up.
In an unresisting way; without resistance.
The dimensions of the timbers of a ship
The state or condition of being unlovely; ugliness.
Of or pertaining to the cryptogams.
To direct the course of (a flow, journey etc.); to lead in a particular direction.
To infer or deduce (a result, theory etc.) from existing data or premises.
To draw out or bring forth from some basic or potential state; to elicit, to develop.
To isolate (a substance) from a compound; to extract.
To cause or generate; to bring about.
e: Borrowed from Latin ēdūcere (“lead out, raise up”); from ex- (“out, up”) + dūcō (“lead, pull”).

s: Pertaining to, characteristic of, or produced by a demon or evil spirit; devilish, demonic, fiendish.
The state or quality of being spare.
The result or product of being spare.
Adorned with one or more gauntlets
Having a gauntlet (overlapping parallel rail tracks).
The condition of being putrid; decay
To holler, shout loudly at someone
The act of sepulchring, committing the remains of a deceased person to the grave or sepulchre.
e: From Middle English sepulture, sepultur, from Old French sepulture, from Latin sepultura.

s: The motion or pattern of something that wreaths.
A writing desk with a hinged door that provides the writing surface.
e: From French escritoire, from escrire (“to write”) (obsolete forms of écritoire and écrire, respectively) + -oire (“a tool or object”). Doublet of scriptorium.

s: The division of a word into syllables.
e: First attested in 1764; a regular Anglicisation (see -fication) of a hypothetical etymon of the form *syllabificātiō, *syllabificātiōn-, formed regularly on the base of the Latin syllabificō, itself from syllaba (“syllable”).
From grave + en- -en; Alteration of engrave, influenced by verbs formed with the circumfix en- -en.

s: A long unpadded strap to pass over and keep in place a blanket, pack or saddle on an animal.
A piece of tack wrapped around the belly of a horse, to use when longeing.
A girdle to fasten a garment, especially a cassock.
e: From Old French surcengle, formed with sur (“over”) and cengle (“girdle”).

s: Coloured or stained with a dye or pigment; coloured, dyed, stained, tinged.
A state of disquiet, uneasiness, or anxiety.
A fear or an instance of uneasiness.
Shaped like a strap or long tongue
The range of a melody, especially those of ecclesiastical chants.
The exterior edge or border of a thing, such as a leaf or shell.
The state or characteristic of being pertinacious.
e: From Middle French pertinacité, from Old French pertinace (“obstinate, stubborn”).

s: Affected wit; a witty turn of phrase; a conceit.
e: Borrowed from Italian concetto, from Latin conceptus. See Doublet of conceit, concept, which are doublets.

s: A small, strong triangular sail sometimes set in place of the mainsail in heavy weather.

e: As decipher, but retaining the y from the Old French etyma of cipher (cyfre, cyffre); the i spelling tends to be preferred etymologically, being consistent with its cognates, the French déchiffrer and the Italian decifrare, and with their common ancestor, the Medieval Latin cifra, cifera, ciphra. de- + cypher.

s: The state of carousing; (drunken) revelry; an instance of this; a noisy social gathering, often with much alcohol consumption.
e: Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- From carouse (“to engage in a noisy or drunken social gathering”) + -al, possibly also influenced by an erroneous understanding of the meaning of carousel (“merry-go-round”).

s: Having admitted defeat and surrendered; defeated.
Unfaithful to someone, or to one's duties or honour; disloyal, false.
Somebody who is recreant, who yields in combat; a coward or traitor.
e: From Middle English recreaunt, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French recreant (“defeated”), from recroire (“to yield in a trial by combat, surrender allegiance”). Compare miscreant.

s: In a persevering manner; with perseverance.

e: Borrowed from French azote, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (“without”) + ζωή (“life”) + -τικός (“adjective suffix”). Named by French chemist and biologist Antoine Lavoisier, who saw it as the part of air which cannot sustain life.

s: The condition of being a woman; femininity.
Situated beneath the moon; specifically, between the moon and the earth.
In or of this world (as opposed to heaven, etc.); earthly, terrestrial.
Of or relating to the material world (as opposed to clerical, sacred, or spiritual); ephemeral, temporal, worldly.
A person or thing which is of the (material) world.
A less important person; an inferior, a subordinate.
e: The adjective is a Late Latin sublūnāris (“sublunar, sublunary”) + English -ary. Sublūnāris is derived from Latin sub- + lūnāris (“of or pertaining to the moon, lunar”) (from lūna (“moon”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”)) + -āris). sub- + lunary. The noun is derived from the adjective.

s: Alternative form of mores, a set of moral norms or customs derived from generally accepted practices.
e: From the French mœurs (“ways, character, morals”), from Latin mōrēs (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of mōs. Doublet of mores.

s: Something written (or engraved) on the surface, outside, or above something else; specifically, an address on a letter, envelope, etc.
An editorial addition at the beginning, often indicating the authorship of a piece.
e: From Middle French superscription, or its source, Late Latin superscriptio, from superscribere.

s: In the interior part; internally; inwardly.
A ruler-shaped instrument, generally used to slap naughty children on the hand.
e: From Middle French ferule (modern French férule), from Latin ferula (“giant fennel”). Doublet of ferula.

s: The motion or position of things that recross; an interweaving.
In a manner unbecoming a woman.
A first name or given name; particularly the first of the tria nomina (three nouns) borne by free male Roman citizens.
The throne name of a pharaoh, the fourth of the five names of the royal titulary, traditionally encircled by a cartouche and preceded by the title nswt-bjtj.
The genus name in a binomial scientific name.
e: From Latin praenōmen, from prae- (“pre-: before”) + nōmen (“name, family name”).

s: A person who is obsessed with a single thing, to the exclusion of other concerns.
Focused on one thing above all others.
The basic form of an organism; the seed or germ.
Affected with or suffering from distemper.
Pertaining to, or affected by, catalepsy.
Long-windedness, tiresome length, an excess of words.
Synonym of grotesquerie, the quality of being grotesque.
To beat strongly or rapidly; said especially of the heart.
To cause to beat strongly or rapidly.
In a tardy fashion; belatedly; late.
To inspire fright in; to frighten, to terrify.
e: From Middle English afrighten, from Old English āfyrhtan, equivalent to a- + fright.
From Middle English afright, from Old English āfyrht (“terrified; afraid”), past participle of āfyrhtan (“to terrify; make afraid”).

s: Not leased to or occupied by a tenant; unoccupied.
The downward slope of a curve.
A downward bend in a path.
An inward curve of the exoskeleton of an insect, such as between body segments; a segment of an insect's body where the exoskeleton curves inward.
e: 1610s, from French déclivité, from Latin declivitatem, dēclīvitās, from dēclivis (“a sloping downward”), from de (“down”) + clīvus (“a slope”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱleywo-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”) (English lean).

s: (of the hull of a wooden ship) sheathed below the waterline with thin sheets of copper to prevent the attack of teredo shipworms and limit the buildup of weed
The state or sensation of being chilly; a disagreeable sensation of coldness.
Reasoning, conscious deliberate inference; the activity or process of reasoning.
Thought or reasoning that is exact, valid and rational.
A proposition arrived at by such thought.
e: Borrowed from French ratiocination, from Latin ratiōcinātiō (“argumentation, reasoning, ratiocination; a syllogism”), from ratiōcinātus (“reckoned”) + -tiō.

s: The quality of being perverse; doggedness, obstinacy.
To follow (something) closely, either as a consequence or in contrast.
To be dependent on an earlier event.
To be dependent on something else for existence, truth or instantiation.
To occur as an interruption or change to an existing situation.
e: From Latin supervenīre (“come over or upon, overtake”), from super (“above”) + veniō (“come”).

s: Having no obvious cause; fortuitous or inexplicable.
Having, or formed as, a trellis.
The state or quality of being icy or very cold; frigidity.
Linked together; forming a chain or interrelated sequence.
Not free; bound by chains or as if by chains; in bondage.
An instance of grotesqueness, a grotesque thing.
the quality of being grotesque or macabre.
A genre of horror literature that was popular in the early 20th century, and practiced by writers such as Ambrose Bierce and Fritz Leiber.
e: From French grotesquerie, from grotesque (“farcical, grotesque”) + -erie (“-ery”), from Italian grottesco, from grotta (“cave, grotto”) +‎ -esco (“-esque, -ish”). Equivalent to grotesque + -erie.

s: To take out of the grave or tomb.
To bring out, as from a grave or hiding place; to bring from obscurity into view.
To kindle; to arouse or evoke.
The state or property of being luxurious, of being expensive or indulgently pleasant.
The quality of being sweet or pleasing to the mind; agreeableness; pleasantness
Sweetness or agreeableness to the senses, especially of taste and odour.
e: From Middle English suavite,suavitee,suavyte, from Middle French suavité and its etymon Latin suāvitās.

s: Food or fodder, particularly that taken in by plants or animals.
Bland intellectual fare; an undemanding diet of words.
e: Borrowed from Latin pābulum (“food, nourishment; fodder or pasture for animals; nourishment for the mind, food for thought”), from pāscō (“to nourish”) + -bulum, or directly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-dʰlom (*peh₂- (“to protect, shepherd”) + *-dʰlom, variant of *-trom).
From Middle English trompery, from Middle French tromperie (“deceit”).

s: The action of expectorating, of ejecting phlegm or mucus from the throat or lungs by coughing, hawking, or spitting.
That which is expectorated, as phlegm or mucus.
At or on a slant; in a slanting or sloping direction.
Across or over in a slanting or diagonal direction.
One who romances another; one who attempt to win another's affections via romance.
A person who writes romance or adventure stories, especially stories relating to chivalry, knights, heroes, quests, etc.
A romantic film or television show.
A liquor made from mead by jacking (freeze concentration) rather than distillation; jacked mead.
Having abundant bushes, shrubs or trees.
The condition of being insipid; insipidness.
Something that is insipid; an insipid utterance, sight, object, etc.
A person who dons a disguising costume, as for a parade or a festival.
An actor in a pantomime; one who communicates entirely through gesture and facial expression.
e: From Middle English mummer, mommer, equivalent to mum + -er, perhaps conflating with Old French momeor (“jester, entertainer”), from mommer (“to wear a mask”), from momon (“mask”).

s: To physically make (letters and words) on a writing surface; to inscribe.
To write (something, especially a literary or artistic work); to compose.
To indict (someone); to accuse; to censure.
An extremely rare indium-iron sulfide mineral.
e: Originally a variant of indict; from Middle English enditen, endyten, from Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from in- + dictare (“to declare”). Doublet of indict.

s: A lustration: a ceremonial purification of the people of Rome performed every five years after the census.
A low plinth or pedestal used to display a statue or other artwork.
A plain face or plinth at the foot of a wall.
The sum of the minimal normal submodules of a given R-module of a given ring R.
The subgroup generated by the minimal normal subgroups of a given group.
e: From French socle, from Italian zoccolo (“wooden shoe”), from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock”). Doublet of zoccolo.

s: A central carpal bone or tarsal bone.
A medium, or form of media, that conceptually lies between others.
The property of being little, smallness.
e: From Middle English litelnes, litelnesse, from Old English lytelnysse, lȳtelnes, equivalent to little + -ness.

s: In a luxuriant manner; with luxuriance.
To express in a denomination (i.e., a monetary unit).
Having a specific name or denomination; specified in the concrete as opposed to abstract; thus, 7 feet is a denominate quantity, while 7 is mere abstract quantity or number.
A noun derived from some other noun, a denominative.
e: Inherited from Middle English denominat(e) (“named, called”), borrowed from Latin dēnōminātus, perfect passive participle of dēnōminō, see -ate. de- + nominate.

s: followed by ''with'' or ''for'', and formerly ''of'' before the object
To charge with something wrong or disgraceful; to reproach
To object or urge as a matter of reproach
The act of reproaching; scorn; disdain.
e: From Middle English upbreiden, from Old English upbreġdan, equivalent to up- + braid. Compare English umbraid (“to upbraid”), Icelandic bregða (“to draw, brandish, braid, deviate from, change, break off, upbraid”). See up, and braid (transitive).

s: The removal of something from a sheath.
To fold or coil into numerous overlapping layers.
To confuse, mix up (something) with something else.
Coiled such that one edge is inside, and one outside the coil, giving a spiral effect in cross section.
e: Borrowed from Latin convolūtum, past participle of convolvere (“to roll together”).

s: A person engaged in various literary works: literary critic, essayist, writer.
e: From the French littérateur, from the Latin litterātor (“critic”). Doublet of literator.
From here + upon. Spelled as two words before the 16th century.

s: A widget allowing multiple users to paste and share text or other items.
One who attends revels; a partygoer.
A prayer for the peaceful repose of the soul of a dead person
e: First word of the Latin phrase requiēscat in pāce (“may he/she rest in peace”). The Latin word requiēscat means "may he/she rest" and is a form of the Latin verb requiēscō (“to rest, repose”).

s: A state of being bright and radiant, splendor, brilliance.
e: From Latin ex- (“out of, from”) and fulgere (“to shine”). ef- + la:fulgere + -ence.

s: Characterized by or pertaining to rapid changes in light intensity and colour.
Characterized by or pertaining to a dreamlike blurring of real and imaginary elements.
The act of profaning; desecration, blasphemous behaviour, defilement.
e: From Middle French prophanation, profanation, and its source, Late Latin profanatio, from the participle stem of Latin profānō. profane + -ation.

s: A phrase or expression peculiar to or characteristic of a given person or group of people.
The use of a word or phrase in an unusual or specialized way.
Style of discourse or usage, or any particular utterance in such style.
A supernatural revelation where a religious figure, statue or icon speaks, usually to a saint.
e: Borrowed from Latin locūtiō, locūtiōnem (“speech”), from loquor (“speak”). Compare the French cognate locution.

s: To spread over or across (something); cover over; be scattered over; permeate, overrun.
To be spread or scattered about.
e: From Middle English overspreden, from Old English ofersprǣdan; equivalent to over- + spread. Cognate with Dutch overspreiden (“to overspread”), German überspreiten (“to overspread”).

s: An act or expression of condemnation or disapproval, especially on moral grounds.

Originally, a kind of coarse fabric made from cotton and flax; now, a kind of coarse twilled cotton, or cotton and linen, stuff with a short pile and often dyed a dull colour, which is chiefly prepared for menswear.
A class of fabric including corduroy and velveteen.
Inflated, pompous, or pretentious speech or writing; bombast; also, incoherent or unintelligible speech or writing; gibberish, nonsense.
Chiefly in rum fustian: a hot drink made of a mixture of alcoholic beverages (as beer, gin, and sherry or white wine) with egg yolk, lemon, and spices.
Of a person, or their speech or writing: using inflated, pompous, or pretentious language; bombastic; grandiloquent; also using incoherent or unintelligible language.
e: The noun is derived from Middle English fustian (“type of fabric, probably made from cotton, flax, or wool; piece of fustian spread over a bed or mattress”), from Old French fustaine, fustaigne (modern French futaine), from Medieval Latin fūstāneum, from (pannus) fūstāneus or (tela) fūstānea, of disputed origin.

s: In a veritable manner; in a way that truly and accurately describes something.
The lowest (and usually the largest) square sail hung on the foremast
A square fore-and-aft sail set on the foremast, but behind it, on a schooner or other similar vessel.
A triangular sail set forward of the foremast: forestaysail.
e: From fore- + sail. Compare Dutch voorzeil, German Vorsegel, Danish forsejl, Swedish försegel.

s: An atrophy of the body or part of the body, especially pulmonary tuberculosis.
e: Borrowed from Latin phthisis, from Ancient Greek φθίσις (“consumption, decline, wasting away”), from φθίω (“to waste away”).

s: The act of impelling or driving onward, or the state of being impelled; the sudden or momentary agency of a body in motion on another body; also, the impelling force, or impulse.
Influence acting unexpectedly or temporarily on the mind; sudden motive or influence; impulse.
e: From Middle English impulsioun, from Old French impulsion, from Latin impulsio, impulsionem.

s: From then on; from that time on.
Coquettish behaviour; actions designed to excite erotic attention, without intending to reciprocate such feelings (chiefly of women towards men); flirtatious teasing.
An act constituting such behaviour; an affectation of amorous interest or enticement, especially of a woman directed towards a man.
The act of one who trepans.
A severe bodily condition, described in psychiatric pathology, marked by sudden rigidity, fixation of posture, and loss of contact with environmental conditions.
e: From Ancient Greek κατάληψις (“act of seizing”), from καταλαμβάνω (“to seize”), from κατά (“against”) + λαμβάνω (“to take”)..

s: To bring (oneself) back to a state of calm.
e: From re + compose; semantically partly Borrowed from Latin recompōnō.

s: Able to be endured; tolerable; bearable.
Capable of enduring; likely to endure; durable.
Humbled; lowered, especially in rank, position, or prestige.
In an inconsiderate manner; without consideration for others.
The state or quality of being infinite or having no limit.
e: From Old French infinité, from Latin infinitas (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + finis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tas.

s: A thin silk or woollen material for women's dresses.
e: From the town of Hernani in Spain.
From Old French insensibilité, from Late Latin insensibilitas.
From Middle English cirurgical, from Middle French cirurgical, from Medieval Latin chirurgicālis.

s: The act of one who hearkens or listens.
In a cheerless, dreary manner; in a manner which suggests that one is beyond consolation.
The act of burying vessels in warm earth in order to expose their contents to a steady moderate heat; the state of being thus exposed.
Turning to stone: the process of replacement of the organic residues of plants (and animals) with insoluble salts, with the original shape and topography being retained.
Incapable of being touched or felt; incorporeal, intangible.
Not able to be perceived, or able to be perceived only with difficulty; insubstantial, thin.
e: From Middle French impalpable, from Medieval Latin impalpabilis. See in- + palpable.

s: Of or relating to necromancy: the resurrection of or communication with the dead, especially through the use of black magic.
Having more than one shape or appearance.
An organism, folktale, etc. that appears in more than one form.
Pertaining to, or resembling, a monk or monasticism.
Persistent or pressing, often annoyingly so.
Given to importunate demands, greedily or thoughtlessly demanding.
To importune, or to obtain by importunity.
e: In Middle english; from importūnus + -ate, modelled on Middle French importuné. importune + -ate (compare inopportune). The noun was substantivized from the adjective, see -ate.

s: The state of being voracious; rapacity or extreme gluttony.
e: From Middle French voracité, from Latin vorācitās (whence -acity), from vorāx.

s: The meaning (sense) in which a word or expression is understood, or generally received#Adjective.
Acceptance; reception; favorable reception or regard; the state of being acceptable.
The active divine decision to approve an act or circumstance, held by Scotists to be necessary to render it meritorious.
e: From Middle English acceptacioun, acceptation, from Middle French acceptacion and Late Latin acceptātiō. accept + -ation.

s: A covering of, or like, clothing.
e: From Middle English vesture and vesturen, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French vesteüre, from Vulgar Latin vestītūra (“clothing”), from Latin vestītus, perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to clothe”), from vestis (“garment”).

s: A roundabout or indirect way of speaking; thus

Unnecessary use of extra words to express an idea, such as a pleonastic phrase (sometimes driven by an attempt at emphatic clarity) or a wordy substitution (the latter driven by euphemistic intent, pedagogic intent, or sometimes loquaciousness alone).
Necessary use of a phrase to circumvent either a vocabulary fault (of speaker or listener) or a lexical gap, either monolingually or in translation.
An instance of such usage; a roundabout expression, whether an inadvisable one or a necessary one.
e: From Latin circumlocūtiō (“the act of speaking around; circumlocution, periphrasis”). circum- (“around”) + locution (“talk”), thus "getting around (a problem) in speaking or writing". Probably a calque of Ancient Greek περίφρασις (“periphrasis”).

s: Excessive interest or concentration on a singular object or subject.
A pathological obsession with one person, thing or idea.
The act of making very lean.
The state of being emaciated or reduced to excessive leanness; an excessively lean condition.
The quality or state of being ideal.
The capacity to form ideals of beauty or perfection.
e: From Medieval Latin ideālitās (“ideality”), from Late Latin ideālis (“ideal”). ideal + -ity.

s: Lacking a house, or, by extension, a residence or place of refuge in general; thus, having no home.
Lacking a permanent place of residence but not a ‘home’ in the broader sense, for example in the form of a community.
Containing no house or place of refuge; wild or inhospitable.
e: From Middle English housles, from Old English *hūslēas, from Proto-West Germanic *hūslaus, from Proto-Germanic *hūsalausaz, equivalent to house + -less.

s: The quality of making rash or arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive or forceful manner.
The condition or quality of being impetuous, impatient; fury; violence.
e: From English impetuous + -ity, from Middle French impétuosité, from Old French.

s: The degree to which something is piquant, stimulating or exciting.
Somebody having a particular way of thinking.
Not strung; having had the strings undone or removed.
Emotionally upset; not able to keep it together.
A piece of work produced using a chisel.
The top edge of the hull of a nautical vessel, at or above where the hull meets the deck.
e: From Middle English gonnewalle, itself from gonne (“gun”) + wale, as it used to support the ship's guns; equivalent to gun + wale.

s: The state or act of being a connoisseur.
Tediously lengthy; dwelling on trivial details.
e: From Old French prolixe, from Latin prōlixus (“stretched out; courteous, favorable”). The verb is derived from the adjective.

s: From side to side, often in an oblique manner; across or over.
Across the path of something, so as to impede progress.
Against the anticipated or appropriate course of something; improperly, perversely, wrongly.
From one side to the other side of; across.
Across the course or path of, so as to meet; hence, to the attention of.
Across the course or path of, so as to oppose.
Across the line of a ship's course, or across its deck.
An extreme abundance; abundance to a vast degree that seems almost excessive.
A musical note one beat long in 4/4 time.
A sharp curve or crook; a shape resembling a hook
A hook-shaped instrument, especially as used in obstetric surgery.
An indentation in the glacis of the covered way, at a point where a traverse is placed.
The arrangement of a body of troops, either forward or rearward, so as to form a line nearly perpendicular to the general line of battle.
to play music in measured time
e: From Middle English crochet, from Old French crochet (“small hook”), from croc + -et, from Old Norse krókr (“hook”). The musical note was named so because of a small hook on its stem in black notation (in modern notation this hook is on the quaver/eighth note). Doublet of crochet, crocket, croquet.

s: Corpselike; hinting of death; imitating a cadaver.
e: From Latin cadāverōsus; compare Middle English cadaverous (“gangrenous, mortified”).

s: An advocate or follower of romanticism.
The act of one who hushes, or calls for silence.
The use of a heavy discharge of water to uncover a mineral vein or wash ore.
One bound by a common oath with others.
The quality or state of being prone, or of bending downward.
The state of lying with the face down.
Inclination of mind, heart, or temper; propension; disposition.
A soft white mineral, chiefly used for smoking-pipes and cigar holders.
e: Borrowed from German Meerschaum; its low relative density and high porosity means pieces may float on water, and visually appear similar to sea-foam.

s: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, equivalent to about 50 mg.
e: From Spanish grano (“grain, 1/9216 Spanish pound”), from Latin grānus (“grain”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Doublet of grain.

s: Someone refusing to attend Church of England services, between the 16th and early 19th centuries, whether a Protestant dissident or a Roman Catholic.
Anyone refusing to submit to authority or regulation.
Pertaining to a recusant or to recusancy.
e: Borrowed from Latin recūsans, recūsāntis, from recūsō (“to refuse, decline; to object to; to protest”). See recuse.
From Middle English me thoght, from Old English mē þūhte; equivalent to me + thought.

s: Distinction by contrast; the provision of one example against which another example may be defined.
The palace of the Grand Seignior in Constantinople.
A profligate or decadent residence of a rich person.
The sequestered living quarters used by wives and concubines (odalisques) in a Turkish Muslim household.
A brothel or place of debauchery.
An interior cage or enclosed courtyard for keeping wild beasts.
e: From Italian serraglio, from Vulgar Latin *serrāculum, from a late form of Latin serāre (“lock up, close”), from sera (“lock, bolt”). The Italian word was used (because of phonetic similarity) to translate Phono-semantic matching of Turkish saray (“palace”). Compare serai, serail.

s: The act or conduct of an impostor; deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
e: From Middle French imposture, from Late Latin impostura, Latin impostus.

s: Untrained, not taught or educated in a field of knowledge.
busyness; making oneself busy with something
Infl of glue; Alternative spelling of gluing.
To have an upward direction or inclination.
To rebel or revolt; to take part in an uprising.
The act of rising; appearance above the horizon; rising.
e: From Middle English uprisen, from Old English ūprīsan (“to rise up”), equivalent to up- + rise. Cognate with Icelandic upprisa (“resurrection”), Middle Low German oprīsinge (“uprising”). Compare also Icelandic uppreisn (“an uprising, revolt”).
From Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (“penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Doublet of pain.

s: An instance or act of undulating.
A wavy appearance or outline; waviness.
A tremulous tone produced by a peculiar pressure of the finger on a string.
A wavelike curve; a smooth and regular rise and fall.
A wavelike motion of the air; electromagnetic radiation.
A feeling as if of an undulatory motion about the heart.
The distinctive motion of the matter within an abscess on being pressed when it is ripe for opening.
e: From undulate + -ion, or borrowed from Medieval Latin undulātiō; compare French ondulation.

s: One who participates, attends, or works remotely; a remote worker; a teleworker.
An inferior racing boat, or one who rows in such a boat.

e: From Spanish platina (“little silver”) del Pinto ("of the Pinto"). It was called "little" (or "lesser") silver because the metal was found as an impurity in gold, and del Pinto for the Pinto River in Grand Columbia where Europeans discovered it being mined by Native Americans. Doublet of platinum.

s: Capable of being presumed, or being presumed as such.
Very liberal in giving or bestowing.
Not redeemed; not granted redemption or salvation; unsaved.
not used in a purchase, and thus still usable.
something that is surrounded by a structure
Syn of morning: the part of the day between sunrise and noon.
In an imperious manner; in the style of an emperor.
In a way that brooks no refusal; commandingly.
A form of media censorship where discussions are limited in topics on the basis of broadcast time allotments.
A cutting off; a division; a schism or faction.
penile mutilation, emasculation (used as a polemical term in Paul's epistles)
The fortified tower and main residence of a motte or early castle; a keep.
e: A variant of dungeon remodelled on its etymon, Old French donjon.

s: A spectacular and beautiful game of chess, generally featuring sacrificial attacks and unexpected moves.
e: From brilliant + -ancy; attested earlier than brilliance. Compare French brillance.

s: The measure of the synergism of the strength of individual interactions between proteins.
e: From Middle English avidite, from Old French avidite (modern French avidité), from Latin aviditās (“avidity, covetousness”), equivalent to avid + -ity.
1520s, from Middle English sidlyng (early 14th century), from side + -lyng (“(frequentative)”) (modern English -le (“(frequentative)”)). Reanalyzed as side + long.

s: A cartilaginous marine fish in the subclass Holocephali and especially the order Chimaeriformes, with a blunt snout, long tail, and a spine before the first dorsal fin
e: A variant of chimera under influence from Latin Chimaera.

s: Castle-like: built or shaped like a castle; usually, specifically, having castellations (crenellations).
Having grooves or recesses on an upper face.
Castled: having or furnished with castles.
Housed or kept in a castle.
Syn of enclosed, when used for fountains, cisterns, &c.
e: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified, castellate”) + -ed. Equivalent to the past participle of castellate but attested earlier than other uses of the verb.

s: From now on; from this time on.
e: From Middle English hennes forward, equivalent to hence + forward. Compare Middle English hens-forthward, hennes forthward (“henceforward”).

s: Indicating contempt, disgust, irritation, impatience or disbelief.
To express disgust or contempt by saying.
e: A natural expressive noise of rejection..

s: In a manner which is incapable of being heard or not loud enough to be heard.
A Japanese fashion style of the late 20th century, characterized by bold, bright colours and numerous accessories such as hair clips and bows.
e: Borrowed from Japanese デコラ, a clipping of デコレーション.

s: Thin or watery discharge of mucus or serum, especially from the eyes or nose, formerly thought to cause disease.
or disease thought to be caused by such secretions; a catarrh, a cold; rheumatism.
e: From Middle English reume, rewme, from Anglo-Norman reume, from Late Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (“stream, humour”). Doublet of stream.

s: Having or showing keen discernment, sound judgment, and farsightedness; mentally shrewd.
e: Coined between 1600 and 1610. Borrowed from Latin sagāx, -acious.

s: Moving in a circle, or spirally; revolving; whirling around.
A large traffic roundabout with non-standard lane markings or priorities, or with buildings on the central island.
A Eurasian rose (Rosa rubiginosa, syn. Rosa eglanteria), having prickly stems, fragrant leaves, pink flowers and red hips.
e: From French églantine, Middle English eglentyn, from Old French aiglantin (adj.), from Old French aiglent (“sweetbrier”), from Latin aculentus (with the ending of spinulentus (“thorny, prickly”)), from aculeus (“prickle”), from acus (“needle”).

s: Similarity or resemblance to something else.
A way in which two people or things share similitude.
Someone or something that closely resembles another; a duplicate or twin.
A similarity: a transformation of Euclidean space that preserves angles and the ratios of distances.
To dye with a fast or lasting colour.
To make (something) deeply part of something else.
Dyed before manufacture; said of the material of a textile fabric.
Thoroughly inwrought; forming an essential part of the substance.
An ingrain fabric, such as a carpet.
e: Inherited from Middle English engreynen, from the French phrase en grain; reinforced by the phrase (dyed) in grain. See grain.

s: The fleshy, often edible, parts of plants.
The natural pasture of a land, considered as distinct from the land itself; hence, right of pasture (on another man's land).
e: From Middle English herbage, from Old French erbage, from herbāticum, from Latin herba (“grass”). herb + -age.

s: A friendly, good-natured, pleasant manner; an affable and approachable disposition; friendliness.
An atmosphere of friendliness and good cheer.
e: Borrowed from French bonhomie, bonhommie (“good-heartedness; extreme credulity”), from bonhomme (“chap, fellow; courageous man; peasant; unwise man who allows himself to be deceived and dominated”) (from bon (“good”) + homme (“man”)) + -ie.

s: The state of being dilapidated, reduced to decay, partially ruined.
The act of dilapidating, damaging a building or structure through neglect or intentionally.
Ecclesiastical waste: impairing of church property by an incumbent, through neglect or intentionally.
Money paid at the end of an incumbency by the incumbent or his heirs for the purpose of putting the parsonage etc. in good repair for the succeeding incumbent.
Acquiescence or tacit compliance with some circumstance, behavior, or instruction.
A permission granted by the customs authorities for the shipment of goods.
Endurance, especially patiently, of pain or adversity.
e: From Middle English sufferaunce, from Anglo-Norman suffraunce, from Late Latin sufferentia. suffer + -ance.

s: To perform a reconnaissance (of an area; an enemy position); to scout with the aim of gaining information.
An act or instance of reconnoitring.
e: From French reconnoître (obsolete spelling of reconnaître), from Latin recognoscere (“to recognise”). There is also an obsolete 19th-century British English spelling reconnaitre, influenced by the modern French form.

s: A flowerbed, particularly an elevated one.
A garden with paths between such flowerbeds.
A part of the section of theater seats located on the ground floor, on the same level as the orchestra.
The part of the ground-floor section nearest the orchestra and the stage; the stalls.
The part of the ground-floor section behind the stalls and underneath the galleries; the pit.
That part of a theater audience seated in the parterre, sometimes regarded as belonging to a lower social class.
e: Borrowed from French parterre (“on the ground”), from par (“on”) + terre (“ground”).

s: The method or power of gaining control over someone's personality or actions.
The theory and practice of Mesmer himself or his disciples, which involved hypnosis and a superstructure of theory that included animal magnetism.
The state induced by hypnotic methods (especially those of Mesmer himself).
e: From French mesmérisme, analysable as Mesmer + -ism; so called after Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), a German physician who developed the animal magnetism theory.

s: The act of those who throng or form a crowd.
The tallest mast of a sailing ship that has more than one mast; particularly a full-rigged ship.
The second-foremost mast of a non-sailing ship with more than one mast.
The left side of a ship, looking from the stern forward to the bow; port side.
e: From Middle English ladde-bord, latebord, most likely referring to the side of the ship on which cargo was loaded. Changed to larboard in the 1500s by association with starboard. (Texts from the 1500s have spellings like lerbord, leereboord, larboord, corresponding to how they spell sterbord, steereboord, starboord.)

s: The act of entombing or the state of being entombed
The decommissioning of a radioactive site by encasing it in concrete
To deliberately ignore something; to pretend not to notice.
To falsely hide one's opinions or feelings.
e: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; Inherited from Middle English dissemblen, dissimblen, dissemelen, borrowed from Old French dessambler, dissembler, disembler, itself borrowed from Latin dissimulō and modified after sembler, semblance, etc. Doublet of dissimulate, dissimilate, dissimule.

s: Without shifting one's gaze; intently, steadily.
e: From fixed (“not changing; not able to be changed, staying the same”) + -ly.

s: Of, pertaining to, or resembling pitch.
In a dull manner; without liveliness; without lustre.
In an inconceivable manner, in a way not believable or understandable.

e: Borrowed from Middle French quiétude, from Late Latin quiētūdō, from Latin quiētus, perfect passive participle of quiēscō (“rest”).

s: A finely ground relatively pure form of silicas used as a paint filler etc.
Of, relating to, or made of bone; bony.
Not able to be explained logically. Without being accountable, or reasonable.
The sound or action of something that thrums.
The state of being physically clean and free of contamination or dirt; cleanliness.
e: From Middle English clennesse, from Old English clǣnnes, corresponding to clean + -ness.

s: Any tree of the genus Catalpa, in the family Bignoniaceae. The two North American species, the southern catalpa, Catalpa bignonioides, and the northern catalpa, Catalpa speciosa — along with the yellow catalpa, Catalpa ovata, from China — are often planted as ornamentals because of their showy flowe
The emission of light without any perceptible heat; the quality of being phosphorescent.

e: A variant of Doublet of errant, from Middle English erraunt, from Anglo-Norman erraunt, from Old French errant, the present participle of errer (“to walk (to); to wander (to); (figuratively) to travel, voyage”), and then: The original sense was sense 3.

s: A cask of a certain size; its volume used as a measure of capacity for liquids, containing 63 wine gallons, or about imperial gallons (a half pipe).
A large barrel or cask of indefinite contents, especially one containing from 100 to 140 gallons.
Highly injurious or destructive to life: deadly.
Harmful to morals or public order.
e: Middle English, from Latin pestilens, from Latin pestis.

s: In an unsteady manner, so as to shake or falter.
In an uncertain manner; with hesitation or timidity.
The state or quality of being definite.
Any of several alloys of precious metals and base metals that are used (where legal) to make coins, medals etc.
e: Borrowed from French billon, from Old French bille (“stick of wood”).

s: A bulge, knob, swelling, spine or anything that protrudes.
e: From French protubérance, from Latin prōtubērantia (“bulge; protuberance”), from prō + tūber (“swelling; protuberance”) + -antia (“-ance”).

s: A church court held by certain Reformed denominations.
A discussion during a trial in which a judge ensures that the defendant understands what is taking place in the trial and what his or her rights are.
A collection of scripted dialogues written as a textbook, or a set of exercises, to help students to practice and improve their Latin or Ancient Greek. See: Colloquy
e: From Middle English colloquies, from Latin colloquium (“conversation”), from com- (“together, with”) (English com-) + form of loquor (“speak”) (from which English locution and other words). Doublet of colloquium.

s: The state of being quiescent; dormancy.
The state of being at rest, quiet, still, inactive or motionless.
The action of bringing something to rest or making it quiescent; the action of coming to rest or to a quiescent state.
The period when a cell is in a term of no growth and no division.
In insects, a temporary slowing down of metabolism and development in response to adverse environmental conditions, which, unlike diapause, does not involve physiological changes.
In computer chess algorithms, the property of a position that is relatively stable and not liable to be disrupted by a winning tactical move.
e: From quiescent + -ence, or borrowed from Latin quiescentia, from quiescens, present participle of quiesco, from quies.

s: A discrete organ in the center of a flower capable of receiving pollen and producing a fruit, it is divided into an ovary, style and stigma.
The metaphysical idea that the universe contains everything that is possible.
e: From Middle English plenitude, that borrowed from Anglo-Norman plenitude, Middle French plenitude, and their source, Latin plēnitūdō.

s: In an insulting manner; to a degree that causes insult.
The tonnage of a ship based on the number of tuns of wine that it could carry in its holds.
Rarely used musical tempo, meaning slow and ponderous (e.g., moving under a burden); similar to largo.
A section of music with the tempo mark burthen.
e: Old form of burden. Compare similar development in murder.

s: Existing in multitudes or great numbers; very numerous; innumerable.
Comprising a large number of features or parts; manifold, multiple, myriad; also, having a large number of forms.
Of a sound: made by many people.
Of a body of water, the sea, etc.: huge, vast; also, having innumerable ripples.
Followed by with: crowded with many people or things.
Of or relating to the multitude.
e: Latin multitūdin- (the of multitūdō (“great number (of people), multitude”)) + English -ous. Multitūdō is derived from multus (“many; much”) + -tūdō. multitude + -in- + -ous.

s: A traditional short Portuguese unit of length usually about equal to 0.2 mm.
In a sluggish manner; responding or moving slowly.
Made from the wood of the oak tree. Also in metaphorical uses, suggesting robustness.
e: Inherited from Middle English oken (also eken), from Old English ācen, ǣċen (“of oak”), from Proto-Germanic *aikīnaz, equivalent to oak + -en. Cognate with Dutch eiken (“oaken”), German eichen (“oaken”), Icelandic eikinn (“oaken”).

s: That causes sniffing and nasal irritation due to dust.
In a conjoint manner; jointly or together.
A pale, dry sherry from Montilla.

e: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.

s: Relating to a grave or to death; funereal.
Suggestive of a grave or of death; gloomy; solemn.
Having a hollow and deep sound.
The string of an archer's bow.
The string of an archer's bow, as used by the Turks for strangling offenders.
Characterized by accumulation; serving to collect or amass
Having a propensity to amass; acquisitive.
In a fitful manner; irregularly or unsteadily.
An invisible being of the air.
The elemental being of air, usually female.
A slender woman or girl, usually graceful and sometimes with the implication of sublime station over everyday people.
Any of the mainly dark green and blue hummingbirds (genus Aglaiocercus), the male of which has a long forked tail.
e: First attested in 1657. From New Latin sylphes, coined by Paracelsus in the 16th century. The coinage may derive from Latin sylvestris (“of the woods”) and nympha (“nymph”). Ultimately from the root silva (“woods, forest”). Related to sylvan. More at Wikipedia.

s: The act or process by which something lapses.
A name acquired from one's father.

A name acquired from the first name of one's father, grandfather or earlier (male) ancestor. Some cultures use a patronymic where other cultures use a surname or family name; other cultures (like Russia) use both a patronymic and a surname.
e: From French patronymique and its etymon Late Latin patrōnymicum, from patrōnymicus, from Ancient Greek πατρωνυμικός (“derived from or like a father’s name”), from πατρώνυμος (“named from the father”) + -ικός (“of or pertaining to”). patr- + -onymic.

s: The act of something that recoils.
In a witty manner; using wit.
Impressed or convinced by someone to an unreasonable degree, sometimes with an implication of gullibility.
A balm or something that soothes.
A quality in language, address or delivery which expresses sober and fervent emotion.
Unctuousness: A smug, exaggerated use of language; smarminess.
Being a bad idea; poorly thought out.
Unable to be expressed; not able to be put into words.
The grouping or juxtaposition of things, especially words or sounds.

A sequence of words or terms that co-occur more often than would be expected by chance (i.e., the statistically significant placement of particular words in a language), often representing an established name for, or idiomatic way of conveying, a particular semantic concept.

A method of finding an approximate solution of an ordinary differential equation L[y]=0 by determining coefficients in an expansion y(x) = y_{0}(x) + \sum_{l=0}^{q}\alpha_{l} y_{l}(x) so as to make L[y] vanish at prescribed points; the expansion with the coefficients thus found is the sought approxi

A service allowing multiple customers to locate network, server, and storage gear and connect them to a variety of telecommunications and network service providers, at a minimum of cost and complexity.
e: col- (“together”) + location. The technical sense in linguistics was established in 1951, although it may actually be earlier..

s: The act of, or an instance of, reduplicating.
The folding or doubling of a part or organ.
Alternative case form of Sophist, certain teachers in Ancient Greece, particularly skilled orators.
A teacher who uses plausible but fallacious reasoning.
One who is captious, fallacious, or deceptive in argument.
e: Latin sophista and sophistes, borrowed from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (“wise one”), from σοφίζομαι (“to become wise”).

s: Of or pertaining to an inquisition, specifically the Inquisition.
In a manner of inquisition or inquisitors.
Describing a trial system in which the prosecutor also acts as judge.
The act of extinguishing, putting out, or quenching, or the state of being extinguished.
The annihilation or extinction of a right or obligation.

e: Either Inherited from Middle English modinesse (“pride”), from Old English mōdiġnes, or formed anew from moody + -ness.

s: Not having a definite form; shapeless; amorphous.
Decomposed, or resolved into parts; having the form destroyed.
Unable to move due to lack of wind.
By constraint of circumstances; of necessity; as a matter of course.
e: From Middle English par force, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French par force (“by force”).

s: The movement of a fluid through a porous or permeable solid.
The spreading of something (especially something malignant) through the body via blood vessels etc.

Referring to a biphasic clinical course of poliomyelitis, typically occurring in children, characterized by a minor illness, followed by an asymptomatic period of several days before the onset of a major illness involving the central nervous system.
e: From Middle English dromedari, dromedarie (“dromedary; any camel”), from Old French dromedaire, from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Latin *dromadārius, from dromas, dromadis (“dromedary”) + -ārius.

s: Soft, fibrous cotton or wool used to make a wad, or as a packaging material.
Dangling, drooping, hanging down or suspended.

Either hanging in some sense, or constructed of multiple elements such as the voussoirs of an arch or the pendentives of a dome, none of which can stand on its own, but which in combination are stable.
Hanging or pointed downward; with its horns pointing downward.
Incomplete in some sense, such as lacking a finite verb.
e: From Middle English pendaunt, Anglo-Norman pendaunt, pendant, respelled to reflect Latin pendēns, pendentis, present participle of pendere (“to hang, to be suspended”). Compare pendant, which retained the spelling.
From Middle French pétulance, and its source, Latin petulantia.

s: A member of the genus Acanthus of herbaceous prickly plants with toothed leaves, (family Acanthaceae, order Lamiales (formerly Scrophulariales)) found in the south of Europe, Asia Minor, and India.
An ornament resembling the foliage or leaves of Acanthus spinosus, used in the capitals of the Corinthian and composite orders.
Belonging or pertaining to, or existing in, the time prior to the great flood described in Genesis, or to a great or destructive flood or deluge described in other mythologies.
Of animals and plants: long extinct; prehistoric.
Of a person or thing: very old; ancient.
Of attitudes, ideas, etc.: extremely old-fashioned, especially to a laughable extent; antiquated.
A person who lived in the time prior to the great flood described in Genesis, especially one of the biblical patriarchs.
A person with extremely old-fashioned attitudes, ideas, etc., especially to a laughable extent; a fogey or old fogey.
Inherent baseness, depravity or wickedness; corruptness and evilness.
An act evident of such depravity.
e: Borrowed from Middle French turpitude, from Latin turpitūdō (“baseness, infamy”), from turpis (“foul, base”).

s: Offensively intrusive or interfering in offering advice and services.
e: 15th century, from Middle English offycyous, from Latin officiōsus (“kindly”), from officium (“service”).

s: The normal process by which bone is formed.
The calcification of tissue into a bonelike mass; the mass so formed.
The process of becoming set in one's ways or beliefs; rigid conventionality.
The occurrence of something being discontinued; a cessation; an incomplete ending.
The act by which something is beheld; regard; contemplation.
Unable to be perceived by the senses.
Incapable or deprived of physical sensation.
Incapable of emotional feeling; callous; apathetic.
e: From Middle English insensible, from Old French insensible, from Late Latin īnsēnsibilis.

s: Beyond or not conforming to what is natural or according to the regular course of things; strange.
Having an existence outside the natural world.
e: From preter- + natural, after Latin prēternātūrālis/praeternātūrālis, from praeter nātūram, from praeter (“beyond”) + nātūra (“nature”); compare supernatural.

s: Jumping, or passing, from one thing or subject to another, without order, planning, or rational connection; lacking logical sequence.
Out of course; by the way; not connected with the subject.
Leaping, skipping or flitting about, generally in a random or unsteady manner.
e: From Latin dēsultōrius (“hasty, casual, superficial”), from dēsultor (“a circus rider who jumped from one galloping horse to another”), from dēsiliō (“jump down”), from dē (“down”) + saliō (“jump, leap”).
From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).

s: The act of enunciating, announcing, proclaiming, or making known; open attestation; declaration.
The mode of utterance or pronunciation, especially with regards to the fullness and distinctness of articulation.
That which is enunciated or announced; words in which a proposition is expressed; formal declaration
Of or relating to a funeral.
Similar to or befitting the mood or elements of a funeral: slow; black colors; formal; dignified or solemn.
impossible to pardon; impossible to excuse or justify
Of or relating to mesmerism or mesmerization.
Having undergone the process of ossification (transformation into bone or a bone-like mass).
A storyteller, especially a person noted for telling stories with skill and wit.
To make witty remarks or stories.
To publish once again; to print and distribute copies of a work that has previously been printed and distributed.
Difficult to comprehend or understand; obscure.
e: Latin abstrūsus (“concealed, hidden; having been concealed”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of abstrūdō (“to conceal, hide; to push or thrust away”), from abs- (from ab-) + trūdō (“to push, shove; to thrust”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push; to thrust”)).

s: The merging of two segments into one.
e: From Middle French coalescence and its etymon Latin coalēscentia. Doublet of coalescency. coalesce + -ence.

s: The act by which something is dislodged.
Of an oscillating electric or magnetic field: not propagating as an electromagnetic wave but having its energy spatially concentrated in the vicinity of its source.
Of a number or value: diminishing to the point of reaching zero as a limit; infinitesimal.
Of plant parts: shed after a period.
e: Borrowed from French évanescent (“evanescent”), from Latin ēvānēscēns (“disappearing, vanishing”), present participle of ēvānēscō (“to disappear, vanish; to die out, fade away; to lapse”), from ē- (variant of ex-) + vānēscō (“to vanish”) (from vānus (“empty, vacant, void”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to abandon, leave”)) + -ēscō).

s: The time of noon; the time of day when the sun is highest in the sky, especially on a hot day.
In a casual or informal manner, as with a close acquaintance; especially when such behavior may be considered inappropriate.
Colloquially; of common or vernacular speech, as opposed to scholarly language.
In a manner prompting recognition or recollection.
In a manner expressing comprehensive or intimate knowledge.
The movement of one who totters.
Of, or relating to heraldry, or to heraldic arms.
A book etc concerning heraldry, especially a collection of coats of arms.
Together with the rest; besides; in addition.
at the end of a clause or sentence
e: The adverb is derived from Middle English withal, with-al, withalle (“against, in opposition to; in association with, together with; by means of”), from with (“against; close to, near; directly opposite to; in the company of, together with; on, upon; within; etc.”) + al (“total number in a group, all, everyone, everything”). The word displaced Old English mid ealle.

s: To unite in a body or mass.
The quality or degree of being round.
The degree of accuracy to which a manufactured object intended to be round fulfills that requirement; it is measured by parameters such as TIR (total indicator reading).
Located, facing or moving in the direction of the land, as opposed to the sea.
Of the country as opposed to the city, rural; agricultural.
A dwelling within, especially lodgement or habitation in the mind or soul.
existing as an inner principle; inherent
The pseudoscience which studies the relationships between a person's character and the morphology (structure) of the skull.
The act of flowing or proceeding (of something, quality, or feeling) from a source or origin.
That which issues, flows, or proceeds from any object as a source; efflux; an effluence.
The generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit, as distinct from the origination of created beings.
One who bases all decisions on perceived morals, especially one who enforces them with censorship.
A teacher of morals; a person who studies morality; a moral philosopher.
The quality of lacking worth, of being valueless, useless or devoid of benefit.

e: Inherited from Middle English digne, from Old French digne, from Latin dignus.

s: Extreme aversion or detestation; the feeling of utter dislike or loathing; a visceral revulsion toward something repugnant.
An expression of abhorrence, in particular any of the parliamentary addresses dictated towards Charles II.
A person or thing that is loathsome; a detested thing.
Marked by or having the nature of convulsions.
To enclose (a sacred relic etc.) in a shrine or chest.
To preserve or cherish (something) as though in a shrine; to preserve or contain, especially with some reverence.
To protect (an idea, ideal, or philosophy) within an official law or treaty.
A small screw-tipped tool for boring holes.
A cocktail, usually made with gin and lime juice.
To pierce or bore holes (as if using a gimlet).
To turn round (an anchor) as if turning a gimlet.
e: From Middle English gimlet etc., from Old French guinbelet, guimbelet, guibelet, probably a diminutive of the Anglo-Norman wimble, a variation of guimble (“drill”), from the Middle Low German wiemel; continued in Modern French as gibelet.

s: Indulging any appetite or passion to excess, especially the drinking of alcohol.
The state or quality of being strict.
The result or product of being strict.

e: From profligate + -acy (with -acy a suffixal construction from -ate + -cy), from Latin prōflīgātus, past participle of Latin prōflīgō, from prō- (“forward”) + flīgō (“to strike, dash”) (whence pro-).

s: To tangle up; to twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated.
To involve in such complications as to render extrication difficult.
To involve in difficulties or embarrassments; to embarrass, puzzle, or distract by adverse or perplexing circumstances, interests, demands, etc.; to hamper; to bewilder.
e: From Middle English entanglen (“to involve [someone] in difficulty”, “to embarrass”). Equivalent to en- + tangle.

s: Not applicable; that does not apply or cannot be applied; unsuitable or irrelevant.
Divination involving the dead or death.
Loosely, any sorcery or witchcraft, especially involving death or the dead, particularly sorcery involving raising or reanimating the dead.
e: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία, νεκρός (“dead”) + μαντεία (“divination”). Medieval Latin spelling, incorporating niger (“black”), influenced by the notion of black art.

s: Of or relating to the stars.
Relating to a measurement of time relative to the position of the stars.
Relating to a measurement of time relative to the point of the vernal equinox.
e: From Latin sīdereus -al (cf. Latin sīderālis), from sīdus (“star, constellation”), of Unknown ultimate origin, likely a language such as.

s: The action of the verb to divine in any sense.
That or who divines (in any sense of the verb).
Characterized by sudden bursts of activity with periods of inactivity in between; intermittent, irregular, unsteady.
e: From fit (“convulsion, seizure; sudden burst of activity”) + -ful.

s: The motion or position of things that interweave; an elaborate tangle.
A search for something; a pursuit or quest.
A completion or putting into effect of something already begun; a prosecution.
The state of being pursuant; consequence.
Study of set or fixed expressions.
The style in which words and phrases are used in writing or speech.
A group of specialized words and expressions used by a particular group.
A collection of phrases; a phrasebook.
To make or become grave (serious or sombre)
e: From Middle English graven, igraven, from Old English grafen, ġegrafen, from Proto-Germanic *grabanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *grabaną (“to dig, trench”).

s: The regular throbbing of the heart, an artery etc. in a living body; the pulse.
The rhythmic increase and decrease of size in naked zoospores and plasmodia.
A single beat, throb or vibration.
Any similar beings of other mythologies.
People possessing extraordinary intelligence or skill.
The condition or quality of being instrumental; being useful; serving a purpose.
Something that is instrumental; an instrument.
A governmental organ with a specific purpose.
The property of being in the instrumental case.
Of a brilliant dark blue or slightly purplish color like that of the pigment (noun sense 1).
In full ultramarine blue: a brilliant blue pigment traditionally made from ground-up lapis lazuli, and now usually either extracted from mineral deposits or made synthetically.
A brilliant dark blue or slightly purplish colour like that of the pigment.
e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ultrāmarīnus, from Latin ultrā (“beyond”) + marīnus (“of or relating to the sea, marine”). ultra + marine. Noun sense 1 (“pigment”) refers to the fact that lapis lazuli was obtained from foreign countries and hence “beyond the sea”.

s: An emblem, badge or device, used as a distinguishing mark by the body of retainers of a royal or noble house.
e: From Middle English conysaunce, from Old French conysance (“recognition," later, "knowledge”), from Old French conoissance (“acquaintance, recognition; knowledge, wisdom”), from conoistre (“to know”), from Latin cognōscō (“know”), from con- (“with”) + gnōscō (“know”). en + cognize + ance.

s: Able to be factored into polynomials of lower degree, as x^2-1.
Able to be factored into smaller integers; composite.
Containing a sphere of codimension 1 that is not the boundary of a ball.
The act of making pregnant; fertilization.
The fact or process of imbuing or saturating with something; diffusion of some element, idea etc. through a medium or substance.
That with which anything is impregnated.
An ore deposit, with indefinite boundaries, consisting of rock impregnated with ore.
e: From Middle English impregnacioun, from Old French impregnacion, in turn from Late Latin impregnatio.

s: Not governable; unable to be governed.
Unable to be managed or controlled.
A measure of how easy something is to excite
An encampment for the night, usually without tents or covering.
A temporary shelter constructed generally for a few nights.
The watch of a whole army by night, when in danger of surprise or attack.
A structure formed by migratory ants out of their own bodies to protect the queen and larvae.
To watch at night or be on guard, as a whole army.
To encamp for the night without tents or covering.
e: French bivouac (earlier biouac, bivac), from Biiwacht (“reinforcements of guard or town watch”), from bii- + Wacht (“watch, guard”).

s: The quality of being congenial; the state of being agreeable or of having similar tastes.
In an abstract way or manner
The state or quality of being irreverent; want of proper reverence; disregard of the authority and character of a superior.
e: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia. ir- + reverence.
Latin bibliothēca, borrowed from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (“library”). Equivalent to biblio- + -theca. Doublet of bibliotheque.

s: The quality or state of being vivacious.
Marked by fondness; filled with delight
An act of pondering over, meditation, or reflection.
To make known or make public.
To put into effect as a regulation.
To advocate on behalf of (something or someone, especially of an idea); to spread knowledge of and make more widely known.
e: Inherited from Middle English promulgaten, from Latin prōmulgātus, of prōmulgō (“to make known, publish”), either from provulgō (“to make known, publish”), from pro (“forth”) + vulgō (“to publish”), or from mulgeō (“to bring forth”); see -ate and -ate. Doublet of promulge.

s: Abundant or generous to the point of excess; copious; volubly expressed.
To pour out; to give or spend liberally; to lavish; to squander.
A cheap showy ornament or piece of jewellery; a gewgaw.
A small shiny spherical decoration, commonly put on Christmas trees.
A club or sceptre carried by a jester.
e: From Middle English bable, babel, babull, babulle, from Old French babel, baubel (“trinket, child's toy”), most likely a reduplication of bel, ultimately from Latin bellus (“pretty”).

s: Not in accordance with the season.
The quality or degree of being fine.
The ratio, in a precious metal, of the primary metal to any additives or impurities.
The ratio of length to width of a ship, aircraft or rocket
The state of being cheerful; joy.
Related to, or affected by hypochondria.
Related to, or located in the hypochondrium.
e: From French hypocondriaque, from Ancient Greek ὑποχονδριακός (“of the region between the ribs and navel”), from ὑποχόνδριος (“the space between the ribs and the navel”), from ὑπό (“below”) + χόνδρος (“cartilage”). See also hypochondrium, hypochondria, and Wikipedia at hypochondriasis § Etymology.

s: The act of speeding up; a growing faster.
to make (someone’s) wounds go away, to heal
e: From un- + wound (“to hurt”). Possibly backformed from the more common unwounded.

s: Comprising soft cartilage rather than bone.
Having a tough or fibrous texture, usually in reference to a mushroom stipe.
e: Borrowed from Latin cartilāginōsus (“full of cartilage, very gristly”), from cartilāgō (“cartilage, gristle”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”); compare French cartilagineux. Equivalent to cartilage + -ous, with modifications made to its morphology.

s: A sheet of paper 7 to 10 inches (= 17.78 to 25.4 cm) high and 4.5 to 6 inches (= 11.43 to 15.24 cm) wide, the size varying with the large original sheet used to create it. It is made by folding the original sheet three times to produce eight leaves.
A cisgender woman who supports transgender rights.
e: From Middle English hande mayden, handmaiden, hand mayden, hand-mayden, handmayden, hondemaiden, hond maydyn, hoondmaydyn. hand + maiden. is an allusion to Canadian writer Margaret Atwood's novel The Handmaid's Tale (1985), in which "handmaids" are women who serve the male commanders in a patriarchal dystopia.

s: The act of one who errs; sin.
or an act of hesitancy or hedging, especially as expressed in speech through the interjection er.
A thin rhombus, having two acute and two obtuse angles.
A small tablet (originally diamond-shaped) or medicated sweet used to ease a sore throat.
To form into the shape of a lozenge.
To mark or emblazon with a lozenge.
e: Vulgar Latin cel-gau From Middle English losenge, from Old French losenge (“rhombus”), of uncertain origin.

s: The practice of fraudulent medicine, usually in order to make money or for ego gratification and power; health fraud.
An instance of practicing fraudulent medicine.
Extended or expanded, as from internal pressure; swollen.
Something seen but having no physical reality; a phantom or apparition.
An impression as received by the senses, especially an image, often prior to any interpretation by the intellect.
e: A learned variant of phantom; from Middle English fantosme, from Old French fantosme, fantasme, from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα. Doublet of phantom.

s: The quality of not making logical sense or of not being logically connected.
The quality of not holding together physically.
Something incoherent; something that does not make logical sense or is not logically connected.
Thinking or speech that is so disorganized that it is essentially inapprehensible to others.
e: From in- + coherence, formed on model of Italian incoerenza.

s: An elaborate design of intertwined floral figures or complex geometrical patterns, mainly used in Islamic art and architecture.
An ornate composition, especially for the piano.
A dance position in which the dancer stands on one leg, with the other raised backwards, and the arms outstretched.
Elaborate or ornate creations in general.
To move in an arabesque motion.
To decorate with an arabesque pattern.
e: Borrowed from French arabesque, from Italian arabesco, from arabo (“Arab”). Arab + -esque.

s: That causes one to become extremely wet.
The act by which something is drenched; a soaking.
The administering of a medicinal draught to an animal.
e: From Middle English drenchyng, drenchynge, drenchende, from Old English drenċende, from Proto-Germanic *drankijandz, present participle of *drankijaną (“to drench”), equivalent to drench + -ing.

s: A tree of species Sassafras albidum of the eastern United States and Asia having mitten-shaped leaves and red, aromatic heartwood.
A tree of any species in the genus Sassafras.
The bark of the root of this plant, used for medicinal and (mostly historically) culinary purposes and formerly a main ingredient in root beer.
Any of various trees of the family Atherospermataceae, having aromatic bark.
e: From Spanish sasafrás, possibly from Latin saxifragus (“stone-breaking”) from the habit of certain plants growing in cracks in boulders. If this etymology is correct, it is a Doublet of saxifrage.

s: An immoral person devoted to sensual pleasures.
In a manner that can be laughed at, humorous, in a laughable manner.
In a secret or covert manner.
In an illicit way, i.e. not permitted by the law or regulations.
Producing the intended result; entirely adequate.
e: From Middle English effectual, effectuel, from Old French effectuel, from Late Latin effectualis.

s: The party who initiates a lawsuit; a plaintiff.
A thing that is the most perfect example of its type; the most perfect embodiment of something; epitome, prototype.
The essence of a thing in its purest and most concentrated form.
The fifth alchemical element, or essence, after earth, air, fire, and water that fills the universe beyond the terrestrial sphere.
A hypothetical form of dark energy postulated to explain observations of an accelerating universe.
To reduce to its purest and most concentrated essence.
e: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French, from Medieval Latin quinta essentia (“fifth essence, aether”), equivalent to quint- + essence. "Essence" in this context is a synonym for "element".

s: Not redeemable; not able to be restored, recovered, revoked, or escaped.
Not able to be cancelled by a payment or converted to another form of currency or financial instrument, especially one considered more secure or reliable.
A financial instrument that cannot be freely redeemed.
A tract of soft, wet ground; a marsh; a fen.
Anything that entraps or makes progress difficult.
e: From Dutch moeras (“marsh, swamp”), an alteration (with influence from Dutch moer (“moor”)) of a direct descendant of Middle Dutch marasch (“marsh”). The Middle Dutch word is a borrowing from Old French mareis, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk. Doublet of marish, marsh, and linked in part to moor. Compare quagmire.

s: Having two or more equally applicable meanings; capable of double or multiple interpretation.
Capable of being ascribed to different motives, or of signifying opposite feelings, purposes, or characters; deserving to be suspected.
Uncertain, as an indication or sign.
A word or expression capable of different meanings; an ambiguous term.
Of or pertaining to galvanism; electric.
Of a current that is not alternating, as opposed to faradic.
e: From French galvanique, Named after Luigi Aloisio Galvani + -ique.

s: To make holy; to consecrate; to set aside for sacred or ceremonial use.
To free from sin; to purify.
To make acceptable or useful under religious law or practice.
e: From Anglo-Norman seintefier, from Old French saintefier, from Late Latin sānctificō, from Latin sānctus (“holy”) + faciō (“do, make”). Form altered to conform with Latin.

s: Impatient under delay, duress, or control.
Refusing to move, especially in a forward direction.
e: Modification of earlier restiff, from Middle English restyf, from Old French restif, from rester (“to stay, remain”), from Latin restō.

s: The act of something being subdued.
A dominating shadow or malign influence.
Any plant of the genus Clematis, vigorous climbing lianas found throughout the temperate zones.
e: Borrowed from Clematis, from Latin clēmatis, from Ancient Greek κληματίς, from κλῆμα (“vine, branch with vines”).

s: Turned out of its straight course.
Bent back at an acute angle.
Of or pertaining to a duke, a duchess, or the duchy or dukedom they hold.
e: From Middle French ducal, from Latin ducālis. Doublet of dogal.
From Middle English swiftnesse, swyftnesse, from Old English swiftnes (“swiftness”), equivalent to swift + -ness.

s: The empty shell of a marine mollusk.
The animal living inside a seashell.
A very light pink colour, like that of some seashells.
Of a very light pink colour, like that of some seashells.
Profound knowledge acquired from learning and scholarship.
The refinement, polish and knowledge that education confers.
e: . From Middle French érudition, from Latin eruditio (“an instructing, learning, erudition”), from erudire (“to instruct, educate, cultivate”), from e (“out”) + rudis (“rude”). erudite + -ion.

s: One who is an inspiration to others; one who has achieved success in one's chosen field; a leading light.
A body that gives light; especially, one of the heavenly bodies.
The act or process of exhaling; breathing out
That which is exhaled, or which rises in the form of vapor, fume, or steam
e: From Latin exhālātiō, from exhālō (“to breathe out, to exhale”), from hālō (“to breathe”). Equivalent to exhale + -ation.

s: capable of being maintained or justified; well-founded
Capable of being defended against assault or attack; defensible
Fit for habitation, similar, or related use.
e: From the French tenable, from tenir (“to hold”); compare tenible.

s: Having the shape of a column.
Of or pertaining to an epithelium with has cells taller than they are wide (column-shaped).
The act or process of making diminutive.
